en: Homage to that Blessed One, the Worthy One, the Perfectly Self-Awakened One.
The Commentary on the Birth Stories (Jātaka-aṭṭhakathā) in the Minor Collection (Khuddakanikāya).
The Fourth Part, 10.
The Chapter of Tens [439] 1.
The Commentary on the Catudvāra Jātaka (The Four-Door Birth Story)
"This city has four gates"—this was spoken by the Teacher while dwelling at Jetavana concerning a certain monk who was difficult to speak with.
The present-day account has already been explained in detail in the first Jātaka of the Navaka-nipāta.
Here, however, the Teacher asked that monk, "Is it true, monk, that you are difficult to speak with? and he replied, "It is true, Bhante."
Having said, "Monk, even in the past, because of your obstinacy you failed to act on the words of the wise and brought a razor-wheel upon yourself," he related a story of the past.
In the past, in the time of the Blessed One Kassapa, there was a son of a merchant in Bārāṇasī who possessed a fortune of eight hundred million, named Mittavindaka.
His parents were stream-enterers, but he himself was immoral and lacked faith.
Later, after his father had passed away, his mother, while managing the household, said to him: "Dear son, you have obtained this human state which is so difficult to find;
give gifts, guard your virtue, observe the Uposatha rites, and listen to the Dhamma.
"Mother," he replied, "I have no need for giving and the like; do not say anything more to me, for I shall go according to my own karma."
Even as he was speaking thus, one day on the full-moon Uposatha day, his mother said to him: "Dear son, today is the distinguished Great Uposatha day;
having observed the Uposatha today, go to the monastery, listen to the Dhamma throughout the entire night, and then return.
I will give you a thousand [pieces of gold]. Saying "Very well," out of greed for wealth, he observed the Uposatha.
Having eaten his morning meal and gone to the monastery, he spent the day there;
then, at night, he lay down in a certain place and fell asleep in such a way that not even a single verse of the Dhammapada reached his ear.
On the following day, having washed his face at dawn and returned home, he sat down.

His mother, thinking, "Today my son will return early in the morning after hearing the Dhamma, bringing with him the Elder who preaches the Dhamma," prepared rice gruel, hard food, and soft food, and having arranged a seat, waited for his arrival.
Seeing that he had come alone, she said, "Dear son, why has the preacher of the Dhamma not been brought? He replied, "I have no need for a preacher of the Dhamma."
When he said, "I have need," she replied, "In that case, drink some gruel.

He said, "You promised me a thousand pieces; give that to me first, and afterwards I will drink. "Drink first, dear one, and we shall give it to you later. "I will drink only after I have received it.
Then his mother placed a bundle of a thousand pieces before him. After he had drunk the gruel, [she gave] the bundle of a thousand pieces.
Engaging in trade, he soon amassed two million [pieces of money]. Then it occurred to him:
"I shall engage in trade by means of a ship. Having procured a ship, he said, "Mother, I am going to engage in trade by sea.
Then his mother said to him, "My dear son, you are my only child; there is wealth in this house..."
"The sea is vast and full of many dangers; do not go! he said, trying to dissuade him. He replied, "I shall certainly go; you cannot stop me.

When his mother took his hand, saying, "I will hold you back, dear son," he released her hand, struck her down, and having placed a barrier between them, he went and boarded a ship to set out across the ocean.
On the seventh day, the ship came to rest motionless upon the surface of the ocean, having depended upon Mittavindaka.
When the lots for ill fortune were drawn, they fell three times into the hand of Mittavindaka himself.
Then, giving him a raft, they cast him onto the surface of the ocean, thinking, "Let not many perish because of this one man. At that very moment, the ship [proceeded] with speed.
He leaped into the great ocean. He too, having lain down upon a raft, reached a certain island.
There he saw four celestial nymphs (*vemānikapetī*) in a crystal mansion. For seven days they experienced suffering, and for seven days they experienced happiness.
Together with them, he enjoyed divine splendor for seven days. Then, for the sake of experiencing suffering, they...
As they were departing, they said, "Master, we shall return on the seventh day; until we come back, please remain right here without longing," and then they went away.
Subject to craving, he lay down upon that very plank and, traveling again across the surface of the ocean, reached another island where there were eight Vemānika petīs in a silver mansion.
Having seen this, by that very same means he saw sixteen Vemānika petīs in a jeweled mansion on another island, and thirty-two in a golden mansion on yet another island;
after experiencing celestial prosperity together with them, when the time came for him to experience their suffering as well,
he was traveling again across the surface of the ocean and [saw] a city enclosed by a wall and possessing four gates.
He saw a city. This was indeed the Ussada Hell, the place where many hell-beings undergo the results of their karma;
it appeared to Mittavindaka like a city fully adorned and prepared for him.
Thinking, "Having entered this city, I shall become king," he raised a razor-wheel toward his head.
He saw a being in hell being roasted. Then, that razor-wheel appeared to him like a lotus upon his head;
the fivefold bond upon his chest appeared as an ornament of breast-plates;
the blood streaming from his head appeared like an ointment of red sandalwood; and the sound of his lamentation was like the sweet melody of a song.
Having offered it, he waited upon him. He went to that person and said, "O man, you have held this lotus for a long time;
give it to me. "Friend, this is not a lotus; this is a razor-wheel. "You say this only because you do not wish to give it to me.
The hell-being thought, "My karma must be exhausted; even by this [I am released]."
"He must have come after striking his mother as if she were a doll; I shall give him the razor-wheel.
Then, saying to him, "Come here, sir, take this," he hurled the razor-wheel at his head.
As it was grinding against the top of his skull, Mittavindaka realized at that moment that it was indeed a razor-wheel and cried out, "Your razor-wheel..."
"Take it! Take your wheel of blades! he lamented, overcome by pain, as the other vanished.
At that time, the Bodhisatta, having become a tree deity, arrived at that place while wandering on his usual rounds with a great retinue.
Mittavindaka looked at him and said, "Master, King of Devas, this wheel of mine is like sesame seeds for the purpose of grinding them fine."
Descending while being crushed, he asked, "What evil deed have I committed? and spoke these two verses:
"This city has four gates and iron walls that are firm;
I am besieged and confined within—what evil deed have I committed?"
“All the doors are closed, and I am trapped like a bird;
for what reason, O Yakkha, have I been struck by your wheel?
In this context, *daḷhapākāraṃ* means a firm wall. There is also a reading, *daḷhatoraṇaṃ*, which means a firm gate.
"Surrounded and besieged" means being enclosed on all sides by a wall, having been hemmed in within; no place for escape is discerned. "What evil have I committed? means:
what indeed is the wicked deed done by me? "Shut in" means confined.
"Like a bird" means like a bird cast into a cage. "On account of what? means for what reason. "Struck down by a wheel" means struck by a chariot wheel.
Then the King of the Devas spoke six verses to explain the reason:
“Having received more than two hundred thousand [pieces of gold] from your compassionate kinsmen,
you did not, my dear, act upon their word.”
“Leaping over the ocean, he crossed the sea that yields few successes;
from four he reached eight, and from eight, sixteen.
From sixteen he reached thirty-two; the wheel-attainer went beyond.”
For a person overcome by desire, a wheel spins upon the head.
"Vast above, difficult to fill, desire spreads far and wide;
those who greedily pursue it become bearers of that wheel."
“Having abandoned much property, without examining the path,
those for whom this has not been prepared become the bearers of the wheel.
One should examine one’s work and vast wealth, and one should not pursue a desire that is connected with harm.”
"One should heed the words of those who are compassionate; one should not overstep such a person’s wheel.

In this context, "having obtained one hundred and twenty thousand" means that after you had observed the Uposatha and taken a thousand from your mother, you engaged in trade and obtained one hundred and twenty thousand.
It shows that being dissatisfied with that wealth, he did not act accordingly; and while entering the ocean by ship,
even though his mother spoke of the dangers of the sea and tried to restrain him, he did not heed the words of his compassionate kinsmen, but having struck his mother— a stream-enterer—
and created a separation between them, he indeed departed.
"Laṅghi" means a boat capable of leaping over [the waves]. "Pakkhandī" means you have jumped [into it]. "Appasiddhikaṃ" means one of little success, characterized by much destruction.

"Catubbhi aṭṭha" means: even though you were cast into the ocean after being given a plank from a ship that was staying supported by that [boat], by the influence of the Uposatha observance performed for a single day in reliance upon your mother, [you now dwell] in a crystal celestial mansion.
"Having obtained four women, you then attained eight in a silver mansion, sixteen in a jewel mansion, and thirty-two in a golden mansion.
Regarding the phrase "you grasped for too much" (*aticcham cakamāsa*):

being dissatisfied with what you had already obtained, you thought, "I shall obtain something superior here," and thus, through *aticchā*—which is defined as greed for surpassing whatever has been gained—[you fell].

"Because he was possessed of excessive greed (*aticcha*), that wicked person, having exhausted the merit of his observance of the Uposatha, passed beyond thirty-two women and came to this city of ghosts (*petanagara*).
Due to the outflow of that unwholesome act of striking his mother, you have arrived here with this wheel of razors (*khuracakkam*).
There is also a reading, "atriccha," which means "one who desires here and there. There is also the reading, "atricchā."

"Reading" (*pāṭho*) means "lack of desire" (*atricchā*). "It whirls" (*bhamati*): for that person whose desires have been struck down, this wheel now whirls upon his head like a potter’s wheel; such is the meaning.
And those who hanker after it: this thing called craving (*taṇhā*), as it goes on, becomes wider and wider, like the ocean.
And it is difficult to fill; it spreads out through the desire for this or that among forms and so forth.
Those who are greedy and obsessed, who become infatuated and cling to such craving again and again—they are "wheel-bearers," for they thus carry a razor-edged wheel upon their backs.
"Much property" refers to the great wealth belonging to one's mother and father.
"Having abandoned"— that is, having set out upon a path to be traveled that yields little success, without reflecting upon the sea route; just as you have practiced,
so too others for whom this was unexamined and uninvestigated, being likewise enslaved by craving,
abandoned their wealth and set out upon the road of departure without regard [for it], bearing wheels.
[They] exist. Therefore, a wise person examines his own action, reflecting and reviewing it thus: "Is this deed tainted with hatred, or is it without hatred?
He should also examine his own vast accumulation of wealth acquired through righteous means.
[The Buddha says: "He should not overstep"—this wheel should not overstep or extend beyond such a person.
“*Nātivatteti*” is also a reading, meaning “he does not disregard.

Having heard this, Mittavindaka thought: “This son of a god knows my deed exactly as it was done; he will know even the measure of my counter-attack. I shall question him. Having reflected thus, he spoke the ninth verse:
“How long, O Yakkha, will the wheel remain upon my head? ... [the rest of the verse] ...”
“How many thousands of years [did he live]? Tell me that when you are asked.
Then, as he spoke to him, the Great Being recited the tenth verse:
“Listen to me, Mittavindaka, regarding Atisara and Paccasara;”
“The wheel shall not be driven over your head; you shall not escape with your life.
In this context, *atisara* means both that which has already transgressed and that which will transgress. *Paccasara* is a synonym for the same.
This is what is meant: “Friend Mittavindaka, listen to my words, for you have indeed [transgressed against] one who is exceedingly cruel...”
"Because of the deed committed, there is a 'transgression' (*atisara*); however, it is not possible to specify its result by counting years.
You will experience and undergo immeasurable and exceedingly great suffering as a result—this is what is meant by 'transgression.
Therefore, I am unable to say to you, 'It shall last for this many thousands of years. As for this wheel that has been fixed upon your head, like a potter's wheel..."
"It revolves. You shall not escape from that life" means: as long as the ripening of your karma is not exhausted, you shall not escape while living;
but when the ripening of karma is exhausted, having abandoned this wheel, you will go according to your karma.
Having said this, the son of the gods departed for his own celestial abode, and the other also underwent great suffering.
Having delivered this Dhamma teaching, the Teacher identified the Jātaka: "At that time, Mittavindaka was this monk of harsh speech, while the king of the gods was none other than myself.
This concludes the first commentary, the Kaṇhajātakavaṇṇanā.
[440] 2. Commentary on the Kaṇhajātakavaṇṇanā.
"This man is indeed dark-skinned"—this was said by the Teacher while residing at the Nigrodha Monastery near Kapilavatthu, concerning the manifestation of a smile.

At that time, it is said, in the evening, while the Teacher was walking for exercise surrounded by the community of monks in the Nigrodha Monastery, he manifested a smile at a certain spot. The Elder Ānanda [asked], "Who..."
“What now is the cause, what is the condition for the Blessed One’s manifestation of a smile? Tathāgatas do not manifest a smile without a cause. I shall ask him.
Having thus spoken, he extended his joined palms and asked the reason for the smile.
Then the Teacher said to him: “Ānanda, in the past there was a seer named Kaṇha; he dwelt in this very spot of ground, meditating and delighting in jhāna. Of him—”
Having stated the reason for his smile— “The palace of Sakka trembled by the power of his virtue”— the Elder, because that matter was not yet manifest,
brought forth the past when requested. In the past,
while Brahmadatta was reigning in Benares, there lived in Benares a man with a fortune of eight hundred million.
A childless brahmin, having undertaken the precepts and longing for a son, was blessed with a son who was conceived in the womb of his wife.
Because of his dark complexion, they gave him the name "Kaṇhakumāra" on the day of his naming ceremony.
When he reached the age of sixteen, having attained a beauty like that of a jeweled statue, he was sent by his father to learn a craft.
Having been sent to Takkasilā, he returned after mastering all the arts. Then his father united him with a suitable wife.
Later, upon the passing away of his parents, he took over the entire sovereignty.
Then one day, having inspected the treasuries and seated himself upon an excellent couch, he had a golden plate brought and said: "This much..."
Seeing the letters inscribed on golden plates by his former kinsmen, which read, "This wealth was produced by so-and-so;
this much was produced by so-and-so," he thought: "Those by whom this wealth was produced are no longer seen, yet the wealth alone remains visible.
Not a single person has gone away taking this wealth with them; indeed, it is not possible to tie up a bundle of wealth and carry it off."
In order to go to the next world: for the essence of wealth—which is otherwise essenceless—is its distribution through the commonality of the five dangers;
the essence of the body—which is otherwise essenceless—is the performance of acts such as salutation toward those possessed of virtue through the commonality of many diseases;
and the essence of life—which is otherwise essenceless due to being overwhelmed by impermanence—is the application to insight meditation regarding impermanence and so forth. Therefore:
“I shall give gifts for the sake of grasping the essence from these insubstantial enjoyments.
Rising from his seat, he went into the presence of the king; having taken leave of the king, he set forth a great almsgiving.
Seeing that his wealth was not being exhausted even until the seventh day, he thought: “What use have I for wealth? As long as old age does not overcome me...”
Thinking, "I shall go forth this very moment, and having attained the higher knowledges (*abhiññā*) and the meditative absorptions (*samāpatti*),
I will make the Brahma-world my final destination," he opened all the doors of his house and, loathing sensual pleasures like impurity, saying, "What has been given to me,
let them take it," he departed from the city while the great multitude wept and lamented, and went to the region of the Himalayas.
Having entered [the city] and gone forth into the ascetic life of an *isi*, he surveyed a delightful region for his own dwelling;
upon reaching this spot, thinking, "I shall dwell here," he resolved that a certain *indavāruṇī* tree would be his village for alms and dwelt at the foot of that very tree.
Abandoning a monastery within the vicinity of a village, he became a forest-dweller and constructed a leaf-hut.
Without constructing a dwelling, he became a tree-root dweller, an open-air dweller, and a perpetual sitter.
If he wished to lie down, he would lie down only upon the ground; having become one who uses his teeth as a pestle, he ate only what was not cooked over fire.
He did not eat anything surrounded by husks; he ate only once a day, and he was a single-session eater. He was like the earth, water, fire, and wind in his patience.
Having made this offering, he lived having undertaken these various ascetic virtues (*dhutaṅga*). It is said that in this Jātaka, the Bodhisatta was one who possessed supreme fewness of wishes.
Before long, having realized the higher knowledges (*abhiññā*) and the meditative attainments (*samāpatti*), he dwelt right there, sporting in the play of jhāna.
He did not go elsewhere even for the sake of fruit; he ate fruit only when it was available on the tree at its time of ripening.
When it was in flower, he ate the flowers; when it had leaves, he ate the leaves; and when it was leafless, he ate the bark.
Thus, being supremely contented, he lived in this place for a long time.
One day, in the morning, he gathered ripe fruits from that tree; while gathering them, however—
Rising up with a conduct free from greed, he does not go to another place to take [fruit];
rather, while remaining exactly where he is seated, he stretches out his hand and gathers the fruits situated within the reach of his extended arm.

Even among those, he does not discriminate between what is pleasant and unpleasant, but takes whatever is encountered. Thus, through the power of the virtue of that one who is supremely content, Sakka’s Pandukambala stone seat—

He manifested a sign of heat. It is said that this heat arises either from the exhaustion of Sakka’s lifespan, or from the exhaustion of his merit, or when another being of great power aspires to that station, or through the power of the virtue of righteous ascetics and brahmins possessing great psychic might.
Sakka, reflecting, "Who indeed wishes to displace me from my position? [perceived] in this...
Seeing the seer Kaṇha dwelling in that region picking the fruits of the tree, he thought: "This seer is one of fierce asceticism and has his senses perfectly conquered.

Having caused him to roar the lion’s roar of a Dhamma discourse, and having satisfied him with a boon after hearing the excellent reason [for it], I shall return and make this tree one that bears fruit perpetually. With great majesty, he descended swiftly.
Standing behind him at the foot of that tree, and wishing to test whether he would indeed become angry when his own dispraise was spoken, he recited the first verse:
“Black indeed is this man; he eats black food;”
“In the region of Kaṇha, it is not dear to my mind.
Therein, *kaṇha* means black-colored. *Bhojana* means food consisting of the fruits of trees.

Having heard Sakka’s words, the seer Kaṇha thought, “Who is this speaking with me? Examining with his divine eye, he recognized it was Sakka; then, without turning back and without even looking back, he spoke the second verse:
“One is not black by reason of the skin; for a brahmin has inner substance.
He in whom evil deeds reside, he indeed is black, O Sujampati.

In this context, “by reason of the skin” means that one is not called black on account of the skin. “Has inner substance” means [one who possesses] within the core of virtue, concentration, wisdom, liberation, and the knowledge and vision of liberation.
One who is thus endowed is indeed called a *brāhmaṇa* because he has cast out evil. But he knows:
"Wherever there are evil deeds, one is black regardless of the family into which one is born or whatever the color of one's body may be.
Having said this, [he explains] the evil deeds that cause these beings to become black, according to their divisions into single types and so forth.
Having explained this in detail, censured all those [wrong views], and praised virtues such as moral discipline (*sīla*), he taught the Dhamma to Sakka as if raising the moon in the sky.
Having heard his discourse on the Dhamma, Sakka was delighted and filled with joy;
inviting the Great Being to choose a boon, he spoke the third verse:
“Since you have spoken so well, with such fitting and beautiful words, O brahmin, I grant you a boon—whatever you desire in your mind.
In this context, “since you have spoken so well” refers to that very eloquent speech of yours, which was like that of an omniscient Buddha. It belongs to you alone.
"Because it is appropriate and well-spoken, whatever you desire in your mind—every boon that you have wished for or prayed for—I give that to you"; this is the meaning.
Having heard that, the Great Being thought: "Will he now become angry because his own faults were spoken of? Or not?"
While examining me, he criticized my complexion, my food, and my dwelling place;
but now, having understood my state of being free from anger, he gives a boon with a confident heart.

However, he might think that "he practices the holy life for the sake of Sakyan sovereignty and Brahminical sovereignty. Therefore, in order to remove his doubt in this regard, [I shall speak] to others concerning myself...
“May neither anger nor hatred arise; may neither greed for the prosperity of others nor affection for others arise;
may I remain equanimous. Thinking, “It is fitting that I take these four boons,” he spoke the fourth verse while taking the boons in order to ensure his state of freedom from doubt:
“If you would grant me a boon, O Sakka, Lord of all beings:
freedom from anger, freedom from hatred, freedom from greed, and a livelihood sufficient for my needs—I long for freedom from passion;
these are the four boons I seek.”
In that context, "If you would grant me a boon, O Sakka," means if you were to give me a boon.

"Free from anger" (*sunikkodha*) means perfectly free from anger by way of not being provoked to wrath. "Free from hatred" (*suniddosa*) means perfectly free from hatred by way of not being malicious. "Free from greed" (*nillobha*) means free from longing for the prosperity of others.

"Such as my own livelihood" (*vuttimattano*) refers to such a mode of existence for oneself. "Free from affection" (*nisneha*) refers to [affection] toward children, daughters, and so forth, or toward sentient beings.
"Free from attachment" means being without affection and devoid of greed even toward one's own possessions, such as wealth and grain, which are inanimate.
"I desire" means: "I desire for myself a livelihood endowed with these four factors.
"'These four boons for me' means: 'Grant me these four boons, beginning with freedom from anger.'"
But did he not know that it was impossible to eliminate anger and the like by receiving a boon from Sakka?

He did indeed know this; however, since it would have been improper to say "I will not accept a boon" when Sakka was offering one, he accepted it in order to demonstrate his state of being free from doubt.
Then Sakka thought: "The wise Kaṇha, while accepting the boon..."
“He chose the most blameless and excellent [qualities]. Among these excellences, I shall ask him precisely about their virtues and faults.
Then, questioning him, he spoke the fifth verse:
“O Brahmin, regarding anger or hatred, greed or affection—”
“You see danger in these; tell me that when you are asked. The meaning of this is:
“O Brahmin, do you indeed see danger in anger, hatred, greed, and affection? Tell me that when you are asked; for we do not know the danger in these matters.
Then the Great Being said to him, “In that case, listen,” and spoke these four verses:
“Having been few, one becomes many; he increases through the lack of forbearance.
Clinging and full of distress, therefore one should not take pleasure in anger.
For the harsh speech of the corrupted person is immediately followed by transgression.”
From that comes the hand, from that the staff; the sword is the ultimate resort.
Hatred arises from anger; therefore, one should not take pleasure in hatred.
"Taking food by force, violence, fraud, and deception;"
“States of greed are seen; therefore, one should not delight in greed.
‘The knots, bound together by affection, are manifold and mind-made;
they cause intense torment; therefore, one should not delight in affection.’”
In this context, "the fire of intolerance" refers to the anger born from the intolerance of one who is by nature unable to endure;
having first been slight, it later becomes great and increases further and further.
The manner of its increase should be illustrated by the *Khantivādī Jātaka* and the *Cūḷadhammapāla Jātaka*. Furthermore, in this regard, the wife of the minister Tissa should be cited as an example.
Having done all this and having caused his entire family to be killed, he should afterwards relate the story of how he himself was killed.
"Āsaṅgī" means that which causes attachment (*āsaṅgakaraṇo*). That which arises [in the mind] makes one attached and clinging;
it does not allow one to leave that object and go away, but causes one to turn back and engage in reviling and so forth. "Bahupāyāso" means by way of much suffering, both physical and mental.

He is possessed of distress and exhaustion. For, by relying on anger and through the influence of anger, those who commit transgressions against the Noble Ones and others experience many sufferings—both in this very life and in future lives—including execution, imprisonment, remorse, and the like, as well as the five kinds of bondage, forced labor, and so forth;
thus, anger is said to be "full of distress. Therefore, because it possesses such manifold disadvantages...
Therefore, I do not approve of anger.

Regarding "of one who is corrupt": having first become angry by means of anger characterized by the act of being angry, one subsequently becomes corrupt by means of hatred characterized by the act of hating;
first, harsh speech such as "Hey, slave! Wretched man! issues forth, and immediately following that speech—
The grasping of the hand occurs by way of pulling toward oneself and pulling away; immediately after that, the hand proceeds by way of an undertaking;

then comes the staff; and having exceeded the striking with the staff, the ultimate limit is the sword—whether single-edged or double-edged—the completion of which constitutes the culmination of all [the stages].
For when one has deprived another of life with a sword...
When one subsequently deprives oneself of life by that very same weapon, then the fault has reached its culmination.

Regarding the statement "hatred is originated from anger": just as sour buttermilk or sour gruel, having transformed through the process of ripening, becomes sour—though being of the same nature, it is spoken of differently as "sour" or "not sour"—so too, at an earlier time...
Anger, having undergone transformation, later becomes hatred (*dosa*). Although they are of the same nature in being a root of unwholesomeness, anger is spoken of separately as "hatred.
Just as sourness arises from what was not sour, so too does this [hatred] arise from anger; thus it is said to be "originating from anger" (*kodhasamuṭṭhāna*).
Therefore, because hatred possesses such manifold disadvantages, I do not approve of hatred either.

"Acts of violence" refers to plundering and looting villages by attacking them even during the day, as well as acts of audacity such as carrying weapons on one's person and saying, "Give me this or that.
"Deceit and trickery" means taking another's property by showing a counterfeit;
deceit (*nikati*) is the act of taking from another by displaying something resembling it, such as giving counterfeit coins while calling them "gold coins" when they are not gold.

These cases should be understood as involving the taking of what belongs to another. However, through the power of ingenuity and skillful means (*upāyakosalla*), the taking of another's property may indeed be called "deception. Its occurrence should be seen as follows:
it is said that a certain honest villager, having brought a hare from the forest and placed it on the riverbank, descended into the water to bathe. Then a rogue, placing that hare upon his head...
The first one had gone down to bathe. The other, having come out, not seeing the hare, looked here and there.

The rogue said to him, "My friend, why are you looking about? When he replied, "I placed a hare in this spot, but I do not see it," the rogue said, "You blind fool, you do not know; hares placed on a riverbank flee away. Look! I..."
“I will bathe only after placing my own hare upon my head,” he said. Because of his inability to respond, the other departed, thinking, “So be it.
Herein, the story should be told of how a young deer was taken for one kahāpaṇa, and after giving that back, a deer worth two kahāpaṇas was taken.
Sakka, these morsels and so forth are seen among the phenomena of greed.
Evil qualities are seen in beings who are of a greedy nature and who are overcome by greed;
for those who are not greedy do not perform such deeds. Thus, greed has many disadvantages; therefore, I do not approve of greed either.
"The knots are bound together by affection" means they are bound together by affection—which has the characteristic of clinging to objects—again and again.
The bodily fetters of covetousness (*abhijjhākāyagantha*) are so called because they are joined by way of arising, bound like flowers with a string, and proceed toward various kinds of objects.
"They lie manifold, mind-made" means that these bodily fetters of covetousness are "mind-made" (*manomaya*) because they are produced by the mind,
just as ornaments made of gold and so forth are produced from gold and other materials when they arise in relation to various objects.

They lie and lie latent within those objects. They cause intense torment; thus, having become latent in this way, they produce a powerful heat and cause intense torment—that is, they cause extreme exhaustion.
Regarding their intense torment, there is the basis for the verse: "As if pierced by an arrow, one is afflicted," and:
"For, householder, grief, lamentation, pain, dejection, and despair are born of what is dear."
Furthermore, such suttas as "Sorrow originates from what is dear" and "From the beloved arises grief" should be cited.
Moreover, when the Bodhisatta Maṅgala gave his children away, his heart burst from intense sorrow; and for the Bodhisatta Vessantara, great dejection arose.
Thus, even in Great Beings who have fulfilled the perfections, affection indeed causes torment. This is with regard to affection (*sneha*).
“There is danger; therefore, I do not approve even of affection.

Having heard the answer to his question, Sakka said, “O wise Kaṇha, you have explained these questions with the grace of a Buddha and with great skill; I am exceedingly pleased with you. Choose another boon as well,” and he spoke this tenth verse:
“In this which you have so well spoken, so fittingly and beautifully uttered;”
“I grant you a boon, O Brahmin, whatever you desire in your mind.
Thereupon the Bodhisatta spoke the following verse:
“If you would grant me a boon, Sakka, Lord of all beings—”
"While I dwell in the forest, always living alone,
may no afflictions arise that would cause great obstacles.
In this context, "great obstacles" means those things that would create obstacles for this practice of asceticism of mine.
Having heard this, Sakka thought, “The wise Kaṇha, when choosing a boon, does not choose one dependent on material gain; he chooses only that which is dependent on the practice of austerity.
Becoming even more deeply inspired with faith, he gave another boon, speaking this further verse:
“In this well-spoken [speech] of yours, fitting and beautifully uttered;”
“I grant you a boon, O Brahmin, whatever you desire in your mind.
And the Bodhisatta, using the pretext of accepting the boon to teach him the Dhamma, spoke this concluding verse:
“If you would grant me a boon, Sakka, Lord of all beings:”
"Neither the mind nor the body, O Sakka, belongs to anyone;
may they never be harmed—this, Sakka, is the boon I choose.
In this passage, "the mind" means the mind-door (*manodvāra*); "the body" means the body-door (*kāyadvāra*), and by the inclusion of these two, the door of speech (*vacīdvāra*) is also understood.
It should be understood that this has already been grasped. "On my account" means for my sake. "Should be harmed" means it would incur injury or become impure.
This is what is meant: O Sakka, King of the Gods, on my account, by reason of me, and out of a desire for my harm, may no being at any time cause harm to these three doors of action.
"May it be entirely pure, liberated from the ten unwholesome courses of action, beginning with the destruction of life.
Thus, while choosing a boon in all six places, the Great Being chose only that which was based on renunciation; for he knew:
"The body is subject to disease; it is not possible, even by Sakka, to make it free from disease. Indeed, for beings...

Although his state of complete purity regarding the three doors was already evident through his lack of egoism (*asakkāyatā*), he nevertheless accepted these boons for the sake of teaching the Dhamma.

Sakka, having ensured that the tree would bear fruit perpetually, paid homage to the Great Being, placed his joined palms to his head, and said, "May you dwell here in health," before returning to his own abode. The Bodhisatta, too—
Without falling away from his meditative absorption, he was reborn in the Brahma-world.

Having delivered this Dhamma teaching, the Teacher said, "Ānanda, this is the very spot where I dwelt in former times," and he identified the Jātaka: "At that time Sakka was Anuruddha, but the wise Kaṇha was none other than myself.
This is the second commentary on the Kaṇha Jātaka.
[441] 3. Commentary on the Catuposathika Jātaka (The Four Uposatha Days).
24–38. "He who is prone to anger"—this Catuposathika Jātaka will be revealed in the Puṇṇaka Jātaka.
This concludes the third commentary, the Catuposathika Jātaka.
[442] 4. The Commentary on the Saṅkha Jātaka.
"One who is well-versed in the scriptures"—this was spoken by the Teacher while dwelling in Jetavana, concerning the gift of all requisites.
It is said that in Sāvatthī, a certain lay follower, having heard the Tathāgata’s teaching of the Dhamma, with a mind full of faith, [invited him] for the following day.
Having invited him, he had a pavilion constructed and decorated at the door of his own house, and on the following day, he announced the time for the Tathāgata’s arrival.
The Teacher, accompanied by a retinue of five hundred bhikkhus, went there and sat upon the prepared seats.
The lay follower, together with his sons, wife, and kinsmen, offered a great alms-giving to the Saṅgha of bhikkhus headed by the Buddha.
Again, saying "I come for my own sake," he invited them for seven days; having thus offered a great almsgiving, on the seventh day he gave all his requisites.
While giving those, however, he made sandals the most abundant offering. The set of sandals given to the One of Ten Powers was worth a thousand pieces of gold;
those for the two Chief Disciples were worth five hundred each; and for the rest of the five...

It was worth one hundred pieces of gold for each of the hundreds of bhikkhus. Having thus given the gift of all his requisites, he sat down in the presence of the Blessed One together with his own retinue.
Then the Teacher, offering words of thanksgiving in a sweet voice, said: "Lay follower, this gift of all your requisites is sublime;
be joyful! Formerly, when no Buddhas had arisen, [it was given] to a Paccekabuddha..."

“Having given a single pair of sandals, even when their boat was wrecked in the middle of the great ocean where there is no foothold, they obtained a foothold through the result of that gift of sandals.
Since you, however, gave all requisites to the Saṅgha of monks headed by the Buddha, why would you not obtain a foothold as the fruit of that gift of sandals? Having said this, he...
Being requested, he brought forth a story of the past:
"In the past, this city of Bārāṇasī was named Moḷinī.

While Brahmadatta was reigning in the city of Moḷinī, there was a brahmin named Saṅkha, who was wealthy, possessing great riches and vast enjoyments, with abundant property and equipment, and an abundance of wealth, grain, gold, and silver."

Having caused six alms-halls to be built at six locations—namely, at the four city gates, in the center of the city, and at the door of his residence—he established a great distribution of alms for the poor and the destitute, spending six hundred thousand [pieces of gold] every day.
One day he thought: "When the wealth in my house is exhausted, I will not be able to give; therefore, while it is still unexhausted..."
“Having gone to Suvaṇṇabhūmi by ship, I shall bring back wealth. Having had a ship moored and filled with goods,
he addressed his wife and children, saying, “Until I return, you must continue giving alms without interruption,” and then,
surrounded by his slaves and laborers, taking his sunshade and mounting his sandals, he set out at midday.

He set out toward the town and village. At that moment, a certain Paccekabuddha on Mount Gandhamādana, having directed his attention and seeing him departing for the purpose of bringing back wealth, reflected: "This Great Being is going to fetch wealth;
will there be an obstacle for him at sea, or not? Having directed his attention and knowing, "There will be," he thought, "If he sees me..."
“By giving me a parasol and sandals, he will find a firm footing when his ship is wrecked at sea through the power of that gift of sandals;

I shall show him favor,” he thought. Then, arriving through the air and alighting not far from him, he came toward him, treading upon the hot sand—which, under the fierce wind and heat, was like a bed of glowing coals.
Upon seeing him, he thought, "A field of merit has come to me; today it is fitting for me to plant the seed of generosity here.
With a joyful heart, he quickly approached him, paid homage, and said, "Venerable sir, out of favor toward me, please step aside from the path a little and approach the foot of this tree.
As the Elder was approaching the foot of the tree, [the man continued].
Having strewn sand at the foot of a tree, having spread out his upper robe, and having seated the Paccekabuddha, she paid homage to him.
Having washed his feet with scented, strained water and anointed them with fragrant oil, she took off her own sandals, shook them out,
anointed them with fragrant oil, and fastened them onto his feet, saying, "Venerable sir, these sandals..."
"Mount it, hold the parasol over your head, and go," he said, and gave him the parasol and sandals.
Taking them for the sake of favoring the horse, and in order to increase his faith, he leapt up right before the horse's very eyes and went straight to Mount Gandhamādana.
The Bodhisatta, seeing this, was filled with exceeding faith; he went to the port, boarded a ship, and then— [the text continues].
On the seventh day, as they were proceeding across the great ocean, the ship took on water, and they were unable to bailing it out.
The great multitude, terrified by the fear of death, paid homage to their respective deities and raised a great cry of lamentation.
The Great Being, taking one attendant with him, smeared his entire body with oil and [mixed] sugar-dust with ghee.
Having eaten as much as he desired and having had the other eat as well, he climbed with him onto the rim of the well.

Having determined the direction, saying, "In this direction lies our city," and freeing himself from the obstruction of fish and turtles, he fell along with the other after they had traveled about the distance of a bull.
The great multitude met their destruction. The Great Being—
However, he began to cross the ocean together with his attendant. As he was crossing, the seventh day arrived.
Even at that time, having rinsed his mouth with salt water, he remained strictly observant of the Uposatha vow.
At that moment, the divine maiden named Maṇimekhalā, [seeing] that the ship had been wrecked in the ocean by the four World Guardians...
"Whether they have gone for refuge to the Triple Gem, are endowed with virtue, or are supporters of their parents—if such people fall into distress, you should protect them.

Thus she was appointed to guard the ocean. Having enjoyed her own sovereignty for seven days and become negligent, on the seventh day, while looking out over the ocean, she saw the Brahmin Saṅkha, who was devoted to virtue and right conduct.
“It is now seven days since he fell into the ocean; if he dies, I shall be greatly censured.

With her heart thus filled with agitation, she filled a golden bowl with various kinds of exquisite food and, traveling there by the force of the wind, stood in the air before him and said: “Brahmin, you have been without food for seven days; here is divine food.”
"Eat," he said. He looked at him and replied, "Take away your food; I am observing the Uposatha.
Then his attendant, who had followed behind, not seeing the deity but hearing only the voice, thought: "This brahmin is naturally delicate;
having gone without food for seven days, he is suffering and seems to be lamenting out of fear of death. I shall comfort him. Having thought this, he...
He spoke the first verse:
“O Saṅkha, you are one who has heard much and knows the Dhamma; you have seen recluses and brahmins.
Yet at this very moment you utter lamentation; who else indeed could be your counselor besides me?”
In this context, "the Dhamma has been heard by you" means that the Dhamma has indeed been heard by you in the presence of righteous recluses and brahmins.
"They have been seen by you" means that righteous recluses and brahmins have been seen by you while giving them requisites and performing services for them;
for one who does not do so, even though they look, they truly do not see them. "Then, at an opportune time" (athakkhaṇe) means then, at an opportune moment.
Because there was no one else to converse with him, there was no occasion for speech. "He showed his lamentation" means that by saying, "I am observing the Uposatha," he displayed his wailing.
"Who is your interlocutor? means: who else besides me is your interlocutor, the one who gives you a reply;
for what reason do you thus prattle on?
Having heard his words, he thought, "I suppose no deity appears to him," and said, "Friend, I do not fear death, but I have another counselor. Having spoken thus, he recited the second verse:
"Subhū, with beautiful conch-shell ornaments well-fastened, holding [the bowl] in a golden vessel, says to me, 'Eat your meal. O you who possess faith, I say to him: 'No.'"
In this context: *subhūti* means having a beautiful face. *Subhā* means lovely, possessing a supreme form.
*Suppaṭimukkakaṃbū* means one who has put on golden ornaments. *Paggayha* means having taken up and lifted food from a golden platter.
*Saddhāvittā* means both faithful and joyful-minded. There is also a reading, *saddhaṃ cittaṃ*; its meaning is: "faithful" means one who has faith.
"Citta" means a joyful mind. "I do not [approve] of that" means that, because I am observing the Uposatha, I am rejecting that deity;
I say "no," I do not speak incoherently, but correctly.
Then he spoke this third verse to him:
“Having seen such a yakkha, O brahmin, a person desiring his own happiness should question him:
‘Arise and ask him with palms joined: Are you a goddess, or are you perhaps a human woman?
In this context, “desiring his own happiness” means that upon seeing such a yakkha, a wise person wishing for his own well-being [should act].
“Will there be happiness for us, or will there not?”—thus he would ask. “Arise! means: showing the manner of rising from the water, “arise.
“Ask with palms joined” means: having placed your hands in the añjali gesture, ask. “Is she human? means:
“Or rather, is she a human being possessed of great psychic power?”
Thinking, "He has spoken appropriately," the Bodhisatta questioned him with the fourth verse:
"You who look upon me with such pleasure, and say to me, 'Eat your meal';
I ask you, O woman of great majesty, are you a queen or are you perhaps a human woman?"
In that regard, "since you" (*yaṃ tvaṃ*) means because you look upon me with pleasure, regarding me with eyes of affection. "Therefore I ask you" (*pucchāmi taṃ*) means for that reason I ask you.
Then the goddess spoke two verses:
"I am a goddess of great power, O Saṅkha, who has come here into the midst of the waters of the ocean."
“Compassionate toward us and not of evil mind, I have come here for your very sake.
Here, food and drink, bedding and seats, and various kinds of vehicles in abundance—
I shall provide all of these for you, whatever you desire in your mind.”
In this context, "here" means in this great ocean. "Various and manifold" means there are many and of diverse kinds, such as elephant-vehicles, horse-vehicles, and so forth.
"I shall make you the master of all that" means having made you the owner of all that—food, drink, and the rest—I shall provide and give it to you.
"Whatever else" means whatever else is desired by the mind, all of that I give to you.
Having heard this, the Great Being thought, "This daughter of the gods speaks on the surface of the ocean, saying, 'I give this and that.
Is she wishing to give because of some meritorious deed performed by me, or is it through her own power?
I shall ask her first. Having reflected thus, he spoke the seventh verse while questioning her:
“Whatever has been offered and sacrificed by me, you are the mistress of it all, O fair-limbed one!
O lady with beautiful hips, lovely eyebrows, and a well-tapering waist—of what karma is this the result for me?
In this context, *yiṭṭha* means that which is sacrificed by way of giving; *huta* means that which is given by way of oblations and offerings. Of all this...

“*Issarā tvan*ti means ‘you are the mistress of our meritorious deeds’; the sense is that you are capable of explaining, ‘This is the result of this [deed], and that is the result of that. *Sussoṇī* means one who possesses the auspicious marks of beautiful thighs. *Subbhamū* means one with beautiful eyebrows.
*Suvilaggamajjhā* means one whose slender waist is well-proportioned. *Kissa me* means ‘of which deed among those performed by me’.”
“This is the ripening [of my merit], by which I obtain a foothold in the shoreless ocean.
Having heard this, the goddess thought, “This brahmin asks as if he does not know that this wholesome deed was performed by him; I shall explain it to him. As she spoke, she uttered the eighth verse:
“O Brahmin, on a hot road, you saw a single mendicant with blistered feet, thirsty and exhausted;”
“He provided him with a conch-shell and sandals; that gift of yours was like a cow that milks all desires.
Therein, “one bhikkhunī” refers to one Paccekabuddha.

“With feet bruised” means with feet struck by hot sand. “Thirsty” means parched with thirst. “Provided” (paṭipādayī) means he gave; the sense is that he offered them. “Milking all desires” means granting every wish.
Hearing this, the Great Being, his heart filled with joy, thought: "Even in such a supportless great ocean, the gift of sandals I gave has become a granter of all my desires;
oh, well-given was the gift I made to the Paccekabuddha! He then spoke the ninth verse:
"May that ship, equipped with planks, free from leaks, and driven by the wind of *eraka* grass, [bring us safely home]."
“There is no ground here for another vehicle; lead me away today with my hair still matted.
The meaning of this is: “O deity, that being so, fashion a boat for me; indeed, fashion a small boat of a single *doṇa* capacity.
Whatever boat you shall fashion, let that boat be constructed from many well-fastened planks.”
"Because there is no entry of water, she is not drenched; she is joined with the wind as it moves along, properly grasped by Eraka.
There is no ground here for any vehicle other than a divine ship; therefore, by means of that divine ship, cause me to reach the city of Moḷini this very day."
Having heard his words, Devadhītā, with a joyful heart, had a ship constructed out of the seven precious gems.
It was eight usabhas in length, four usabhas in width, and twenty cubits in depth.
Its three masts were made of sapphire, its ropes of gold, its buckets of silver, and its sails of gold.
The deities filled that ship with the seven kinds of jewels, embraced the brahmin, and placed him on the adorned ship;
however, they did not look upon his attendant. The brahmin gave the merit of his own good deed to him, and he expressed his appreciation.
Then the deity embraced him as well and established him on the ship. Then that ship—
Having led her to the city of Moḷini and established wealth in the house of the brahmin, she returned once more to her own dwelling place.
After the Teacher had attained full enlightenment, he said:
“Rich there, joyful and delighted, she fashioned a beautifully decorated boat by supernormal power;”
"Taking the conch shell together with the man, he brought him to the city, which was most delightful"—
thus he spoke this concluding verse.
Therein, "Sāti," monks, refers to that deity who, having heard his words there in the midst of the ocean, [was filled] with what is called joy...

Because she was endowed with joy (*pīti*), she was "elated" (*vitta*). Being "well-minded" (*sumanā*)—that is, having a mind delighted by gladness (*pāmojja*)—she fashioned a variegated ship and, taking the brahmin along with his attendant, led him to that most delightful and exceedingly beautiful city.

The brahmin, too, dwelling in a house of immeasurable wealth for as long as he lived, gave gifts and guarded his virtue; at the end of his life, he filled the city of the gods together with his retinue.
Having delivered this Dhamma teaching and proclaimed the Truths, the Teacher identified the Jātaka. At the conclusion of the Truths, the lay follower was established in the fruit of Stream-entry.
At that time, the celestial maiden was Uppalavaṇṇā, the attendant man was Ānanda, and as for the Brahmin Saṅkha, he was none other than myself.
This is the fourth commentary on the Saṅkha Jātaka.
[443] 5. The Commentary on the Cūḷabodhijātaka:
"He who [gave] this to you, O large-eyed one... The Teacher, while residing at Jetavana, spoke this concerning a certain angry bhikkhu.
It is said that although that bhikkhu had gone forth in the Buddha’s liberating dispensation, he was unable to subdue his anger.
He was prone to anger and full of distress; even when spoken to only slightly, he became resentful, grew angry, became malevolent, and remained stubborn.
When the Teacher heard of his irascible nature, he summoned him and asked, "Is it true that you are indeed prone to anger?
When he replied, "It is true, Venerable Sir," the Teacher said, "Monk, anger must be restrained. For such as this, both in this world and in the world beyond—"
"And you, having gone forth in the teaching of the Buddha who is free from anger, why do you become angry?
Even the ancient wise men, though they had gone forth in non-Buddhist teachings, did not give way to anger. Having said this, he related a story of the past.
In the past, while Brahmadatta was reigning in Benares, there lived a certain brahmin in a market town of Kāsi.
He was wealthy, possessing great riches and vast enjoyments, yet he was childless; his Brahmin wife longed for a son.
At that time, the Bodhisatta, descending from the Brahma world, was conceived in her womb.
On the day of his naming ceremony, they gave him the name "Bodhi Kumāra. When he reached maturity, he went to Takkaśilā, mastered all the arts, and returned home.
Although they did not desire it, their parents brought them a maiden from a family of the same caste.
She too, having passed away from the Brahma-world, possessed supreme beauty and resembled a celestial nymph. Even though neither of them consented, they performed the marriage ceremony between them.
Yet, for both of them, the manifestation of defilements had never occurred before, nor had there ever been any mutual passion toward one another.
There was no looking [at others], nor had sexual intercourse ever been seen even in a dream; thus they were of perfectly pure virtue.
Later on, when the Great Being’s parents had passed away, he performed their funeral rites, summoned her, and said:
“Bhadde, take this wealth of eight hundred million and live happily. She asked: “What will you do?”
“But what about you, noble sons? “I have no need for wealth;

having entered the Himalayan region and gone forth into the ascetic life of an *isi*, I shall establish my own foundation. “But noble son, is that which is called ‘going forth’ appropriate only for men?
“It is appropriate for women as well, dear lady. “In that case, I [shall go] with you...”
“I will not take spit that has been spat out; I have no need for wealth either, for I too shall go forth.
“Very well, lady,” he replied. Both of them, having given a great alms-offering and departed, established a hermitage on a delightful piece of ground.
Having gone forth and subsisting there on fruits and roots gathered by gleaning, they lived there for about ten years.
They lived there, yet meditative absorption (jhāna) had not yet arisen for them.

Having stayed there for ten years in the happiness of the renunciant life, they went wandering through the countryside to seek salt and sour food; eventually reaching Bārāṇasī, they dwelt in the royal park.
Then one day, the king saw the park keeper returning with a gift and said, "We shall go to play in the park."
Having said, "Cleanse the park," he went with a great retinue to the park that had been cleansed and prepared by him.
At that moment, both those people were sitting on one side of the park, spending their time in the happiness of the renunciant life.
Then, as the king was wandering through the park, he saw those two sitting there—extremely serene and possessing the most excellent form.
As he gazed at the female wanderer, his mind became bound to her. Trembling under the influence of defilement, he thought, "I shall ask her first:
what is this female wanderer to him? Approaching the Bodhisatta, he asked, "Renunciant, what is this female wanderer to you?
"Great King, she is nothing at all; it is simply because we have both gone forth together."

"He has gone forth; however, she was my wife during my time as a householder. Upon hearing this, the king thought: "It seems he has nothing at all; yet it is said she was his wife during his time as a householder.
If I were to take her by force through my power and go, what indeed could he do? I shall seize her."
Thinking, "I will not let him go," he approached and spoke this first verse:
"O Brahmin, if someone were to take by force this woman of yours, who has large eyes and speaks so affectionately, what indeed would you do?"

In that context, "speaking with smiles" means speaking with a gentle smile. "He might go by force" means he might take her away by means of physical compulsion. "What indeed would you do? means, "O Brahmin, what would you do to him?
Then, having heard his words, the Great Being spoke the second verse:
"He might arise against me, yet he shall not escape; he shall not escape while I am alive."
“O King, like a vast rain, one should quickly restrain it.
The meaning of this is: O Great King, if anger should arise within me toward anyone who takes this and goes away, let it not be released once it has arisen within;
as long as I live, let it not be released. Let it not remain within...

"I shall give [the opportunity] for it to settle by means of dense dwelling; rather, just as a vast rain from a cloud quickly suppresses dust as soon as it arises, so too shall I quickly restrain and ward it off through the cultivation of loving-kindness (*maitrī-bhāvanā*).
Thus did the Great Being let out a lion’s roar. But even after hearing his words, the king remained bound by his blind folly.
Unable to restrain his own mind, he commanded a certain minister, "Take this female wanderer to the royal palace.
Having agreed, saying "Very well," the minister took her away while she was still lamenting, crying out, "Unrighteousness prevails in the world! This is improper!
and so forth. The Bodhisatta, hearing the sound of her lamentation, looked back once; then again—
She did not look back. As she was weeping and lamenting, they led her right back to the royal palace.
The King of Bārāṇasī also, without making any delay in the garden, went even more quickly, had that female wanderer summoned, and invited her with great honor.
She spoke of the disadvantages of honor and the advantages of the religious life. By some means, the king—
Not obtaining her consent, he had her confined in a single room and thought: "This female wanderer does not desire such fame;
even that ascetic, having taken such a woman, did not show anger when she departed, nor did he so much as look at her.
Furthermore, those who have gone forth are full of guile; she might employ some stratagem and bring about my ruin."
"I shall go now and find out what he is doing while sitting there. Unable to remain still, he went to the park.
The Bodhisatta sat sewing his robe. The king, with only a small retinue and making no sound of footsteps, approached slowly.
Without looking at the king, the Bodhisatta continued sewing the robe alone. The king thought, "This man is angry..."
Thinking, "He does not converse with me," and perceiving, "This false ascetic first thundered, saying, 'I shall not allow anger to arise,
and even if it does, I will quickly suppress it,' but now, having become stiff with anger,
he does not converse with me," he spoke the third verse.
“Formerly you used to boast, relying as if upon strength;
yet now, having become silent, you wish to sew your outer robe.
In this context, *balamhiva apassito* means being like one who relies on strength. *Tuṇhikato* means not saying anything at all. *Sibbamacchasī* means you remain while sewing.

Having heard this, the Great Being thought, "This king thinks, 'He does not address me out of anger,' so I shall tell him that he has indeed fallen under the power of the anger that arose. Having reflected thus, he spoke the fourth verse:
"It arose within me, yet it was not released; it was not released while I lived.
Like a vast rain of dust, I quickly suppressed it."
The meaning of this is: "O Great King, it arose for me; it did not fail to arise.
Yet it was not released from me, nor did it allow itself to enter and remain in my heart. Thus, while I was alive, it was never released;
I quickly warded it off, as one would ward off a vast rain of dust."

Having heard this, the king thought, "Does he speak with reference only to anger, or does he speak referring to some other craft? I shall question him first. Thinking thus, he spoke the fifth verse while questioning him:
"What arose for you but was not released? What was not released while you were living?
Like a vast rain of dust, what was it that held it back?"
In that context, "What arose for you but was not released? means: what arose for you and yet was not released.

Having heard this, the Bodhisatta, explaining the danger of anger—saying, "Great King, thus anger has many disadvantages and brings about great ruin; it arose within me, but once arisen, I warded it off through the cultivation of loving-kindness"—declared:
"When he is born, one does not see; when he is unborn, one sees well."
Thus arose in me, it did not cease: anger, the domain of the foolish.
"He by whose birth enemies who seek suffering rejoice— that anger, the domain of the foolish, arose in me, it did not cease."
“When anger arises in one who does not understand his own true welfare, it has arisen for me but has not been released; it is the domain of the foolish.
Overcome by it, one abandons what is wholesome and even neglects great benefit.”
That Bhimasena is powerful and crushing; O Great King, anger did not release me.
"When wood is being rubbed together, that which is called fire is born;
it burns that very wood from which the flame was produced."
“Thus for a dull-witted person, a fool who does not understand,
anger arises from provocation, and he is consumed by that very same anger.
Like a fire in grass and wood, so is it for one in whom anger increases.”
“His fame diminishes, like the moon in the dark fortnight.
But for one whose anger is stilled, like a smokeless fire, his fame increases,
like the moon in the bright fortnight.”— with these verses he spoke.
In this context, "he does not see" means he does not see even his own welfare, let alone the welfare of others.
"He sees well" means he sees well his own welfare, the welfare of others, and the welfare of both. "The domain of the dull-witted" means a domain that serves as a support for those lacking wisdom.
"Seeking suffering" means desiring suffering. "His own welfare" refers to that which constitutes one's own benefit, both in terms of worldly purpose (*attha*) and spiritual truth (*dhamma*).
And he increases it. He exerts himself; even when a great benefit has arisen from another, he causes it to be removed, saying, "Take this away, I have no need of it.
He is "Bhīmasena": that anger is possessed of a great army of defilements (*kilesa-senā*) that is terrifying (*bhīmā*), meaning it produces fear.
It is "crushing" (*pamaddī*): by virtue of its own power, it brings even exalted beings under its control.

“Capable of crushing”: it does not escape from me; that is, it does not obtain release from my presence, or alternatively, the meaning is that it did not settle in my heart for even a moment, like milk turning into curd.
“While rubbing the wood”: while being rubbed with the fire-drill (araṇī); there is also a reading, “while crushing.”

"From whatever [material] fire is produced, it burns that very same material. "Fire" (*ginī*) means flame. "Of the ignorant fool who does not understand": of the foolish person who lacks understanding.

"Arising from provocation" (*sārambhā*): for one who engages in pulling and dragging, saying "I" and "you," fire—meaning anger—arises from provocation characterized by the desire for superiority, just as fire arises from the friction of rubbing fire-sticks together. "He too, by that very same [anger]" means that the fool, by that very same anger...
"He is consumed like wood by fire. "Like a smoke-bannered fire without fuel" means like a fire that has no fuel.
"Of him"—of that person endowed with patience through acceptance—"the fame he has gained fills out further and further, like the moon in the bright fortnight.
Having heard the Great Being’s discourse on the Dhamma, the king was delighted; he gave an order to a minister and had the female wanderer brought before him.
“Venerable one, O undisturbed ascetic, may both of you dwell right here in this park, spending your time in the happiness of the renunciant life;
I shall provide you with righteous protection, defense, and security,” he said. Having thus asked for forgiveness, paid homage, and departed, they both remained right there.
Later on, the female wanderer passed away. Upon her death, the Bodhisatta...

Having entered the Himālaya mountains, he developed the higher knowledges (*abhiññā*) and the meditative attainments (*samāpatti*), cultivated the four divine abodes (*brahmavihāra*), and became destined for the Brahma-world.

The Teacher, having delivered this Dhamma teaching and proclaimed the Truths (*sacca*), identified the Jātaka. At the conclusion of the Truths, the monk Kodhana was established in the fruit of Non-returning (*anāgāmiphala*).
At that time, the female wanderer was Rāhulamātā, King Ānanda was the king, and I myself was the male wanderer.
This concludes the fifth narrative, the Cūḷabodhi Jātaka.
6. The Narrative of the Kaṇhadīpāyana Jātaka.
"Only for seven days," the Teacher said, while dwelling at Jetavana, concerning a certain monk who was disenchanted with the religious life.
The story will be revealed in the *Kusa Jātaka*. The Teacher asked that monk, "Is it true, monk, that you are disenchanted?
When he replied, "It is true, Venerable Sir," the Teacher said, "Monk, in ancient times, when no Buddha had appeared, the wise men of old went forth as outsiders..."
Having gone forth, for more than fifty years they lived the holy life without joy;
out of fear of the destruction of their sense of shame and dread of blame, they did not tell anyone of their state of dissatisfaction.
Why, having gone forth in such a liberating teaching, do you reveal your state of dissatisfaction while standing in the presence of me, your venerable Teacher, in the midst of the fourfold assembly?
"You are doing this; for what purpose do you not guard your own sense of shame and moral dread? Having said this, he related a story of the past.
In the past, in the kingdom of Vaṃsa, in the city named Kosambī, a king named Kosambaka reigned.
At that time, in a certain market town, there were two brahmins with a wealth of eighty crores who were dear friends to one another in matters of sensual pleasure.
Having seen the fault [in sensual pleasures] and having bestowed great alms, both of them renounced sense-desires and departed while the great multitude wept and lamented.
Having established a hermitage in a region of the Himalayas and gone forth into homelessness, they lived for fifty years subsisting on gleanings and forest roots and fruits;
yet, they were unable to produce meditative absorption (*jhāna*). At the conclusion of those fifty years, they...
While wandering through the countryside for the sake of obtaining salt and sour gruel, they arrived at the kingdom of Kāsi.
There, in a certain market town, there was a man named Maṇḍavya who was a lay friend of the ascetic Dīpāyana; both of them went into his presence.
Upon seeing them, he was delighted and, having had a leaf-hut constructed, he attended upon both of them with the four requisites.
Having lived there for three or four years, they took leave of him and, wandering on as pilgrims, reached Bārāṇasī and stayed in the Atimuttaka cemetery.
There, Dīpāyana dwelt for as long as he desired and then returned once more to the presence of that very companion.
The ascetic Maṇḍabya remained right there.
Now one day, a certain thief, having committed a robbery within the city and taken his precious wealth,
was recognized as a "thief" by the householders and the guards who had woken up; pursued by them, he escaped through a drain,
entered the charnel ground with great speed, and hid his bundle at the door of an ascetic’s leaf-hut.
He fled. When people saw the bundle, they rebuked him, saying, "Hey, you wicked ascetic! You commit theft at night and wander about by day in the guise of a recluse!
Having threatened and beaten him, they seized him, led him away, and presented him to the king.
Without even investigating, the king said, "Go, impale him on a stake! They led him to the cemetery and fixed him upon a stake of acacia wood.
The spear did not enter the ascetic’s body. Then they brought a neem-wood spear, but that too did not enter.
They brought an iron spear, but that also did not enter. The ascetic reflected, "What indeed was my past karma?
and then the knowledge of recollecting former births arose within him. Having examined his past karma by means of that, he saw it. But what was his past karma?

The piercing of flies with a *koviḷāra* thorn. It is said that in a previous existence, having been the son of a carpenter, he went to his father’s place of tree-hewing, caught a fly, and pierced it as if with a thorn on a *koviḷāra* splinter.
Having reached this state, that evil deed seized him. Realizing, "It is not possible for me to be released from this evil," he [addressed] the king’s men:
He said, "If you wish to impale me on a stake, bring a *koviḷāra* stake.
They did so, impaled him on the stake, and having provided a guard, they departed.
The guards remained hidden and watched as people approached him. Then Dīpāyana thought, "It has been a long time since I have seen..."

Thinking, "He is my companion," he was coming toward Maṇḍabya when he heard on that very day, while still on the road, that Maṇḍabya had been impaled on a stake.
