The king, having paid homage to the ascetics and asked for their forgiveness, settled both of them in the pleasure grove and looked after them.
From that time on, Maṇḍabya became known as Āṇimaṇḍabya. He lived right there, depending upon the king, while Dīpāyana—
Having healed his wound, he went back to his own house-friend Maṇḍavya.
Seeing him entering that leaf-hut, a certain man informed his friend. Upon hearing this, he was filled with joy;
taking his wife and children, and carrying many perfumes, garlands, oils, molasses, and other provisions, he went to that leaf-hut and [approached] Dīpāyana.
Having paid homage, washed his feet, anointed them with oil, and given him a drink, he sat down to hear news of Āḷavaka.
Then his son, Prince Yaññadatta by name, was playing with a ball at the edge of the walking path, where a venomous snake lived in a termite mound.
The ball, struck by the prince, went toward the opening of the termite mound.
It fell upon the head of a venomous snake. Unaware of this, he thrust his hand into the hole.
Then the enraged snake bit him on the hand. Overcome by the force of the poison, he fell down right there.

When his parents learned that he had been bitten by the snake, they lifted the boy up, brought him into the presence of the ascetic, made him lie down at the teacher’s feet, and said, "Venerable sir,..."
"Those who have gone forth know medicinal herbs or protective charms; please make our child healthy," they said.
"I do not know medicinal herbs, nor will I perform the work of a physician," he replied.
When they said, "In that case, venerable sir, out of loving-kindness for this boy, please perform an act of truth (*saccakiriya*)," the ascetic said, "Very well, I shall perform an act of truth."
Having spoken thus, he placed his hand upon Yaññadatta’s head and recited the first verse:
“For seven days only, with a confident heart and seeking merit, did I practice the holy life (brahmacariya).
But as for this other conduct of mine that has followed since then, it has been for fifty years and more.”
"Even though I wander against my will, by this truth may there be well-being;
let the poison be destroyed and Yajñadatta live!
In that context, "furthermore, that which I have practiced" refers to the holy life (*brahmacariya*) I have lived for more than seven days. "Even though [I wander] against my will" means...
"Even though I did not desire the going forth. By this truth, may there be well-being!

If it is true that while I lived for more than fifty-five years in a state of dissatisfaction, I never told anyone [of my intention], by this truth may the young Yaññadatta be safe; may he regain his life!"
Then, simultaneously with his declaration of truth, the poison rose up from Yaññadatta’s breast and entered the earth.
The prince opened his eyes, looked at his parents, and saying, “Mother, Father,” he turned over and lay down.
Then Kaṇhadīpāyana said to his father: “I have indeed exercised my power; you too—”
“Make your own strength manifest! He, thinking, “I too shall perform an act of truth,” placed his hand upon his son’s chest and spoke this second verse:
“Since I never took delight in giving alms when I saw a guest at the time for lodging;”
"Nor did the learned recluses and brahmins know of my displeasure;
even though I was unwilling, I gave it away. By this truth, may there be well-being!
May the poison be destroyed and Yaññadatta live!"
"In that place, at the time of dwelling" means at the time when [the guests] have come to the house for the purpose of staying.
"And they did not know my lack of affection" means that even the learned ascetics and brahmins did not perceive this state of mine—that I neither delight in giving nor [delight] in them.
He explains: "For I look upon them only with eyes of affection. "By this truth" means if I [have indeed] given...
The meaning is: "While giving, I gave without faith in the karmic result and against my own will;
yet others did not know my state of unwillingness. By this truth, may there be well-being!
Thus, by means of his act of truth (*saccakiriyā*), the poison rose up from his waist and entered the earth. The prince—
He rose up and sat down, but he was unable to stand. Then his father said to his mother, "My dear lady, I have performed my own act of truth;
now you, having performed an act of truth, must cause our son to rise and walk.
She replied, "Husband, I have one truth, but I am not able to speak it in your presence. He said, "My dear lady..."
"In whatever way possible, dear son, make my child free from disease. Having agreed, saying "Very well," she spoke the third verse, making it true:
"Dear son, there was a venomous snake of great power who bit you after emerging from its hole;
because of my lack of affection for him today, there is no difference for me between him and your father."
"By this truth, may there be well-being; let the poison be destroyed and Yajñadatta live!

In this passage, "dear one" (tāta) is an address to the son. "Abundant in power" (pahūtatejo) means potent poison. "Holes" (bilarā) refers to openings, or this is simply another reading for the same word.
"Having risen up" (udiccā) means having emerged; the meaning is "having risen from the opening of an anthill. And "your father" (pitarañca te) refers to the father.
And so it was. However, in the *Aṭṭhakathā* (the Commentary), this very reading is found. This is what is meant:
“Dear Yaññadatta, there is no distinction for me between that venomous snake and your father in terms of my lack of affection for them.
Yet, apart from that lack of affection, there has never been anyone whom I have previously made known [as such] today; if this is true, by this truth—”
"May you have well-being!
With that act of truth, all the poison was consumed and entered the earth.
Yaññadatta rose up with his body free from poison and began to play. When his sons had thus risen, Maṇḍabya [reported] Dīpāyana’s intention...
Questioning him, he spoke the fourth verse:
“Only those who are peaceful and self-controlled go forth into homelessness; there are none other than the dark ones who are free from desire.
Dīpāyana, out of what disgust do you lead the holy life against your will?”

The meaning of this is as follows: whatever kṣatriyas and others there may be who, having abandoned sensual pleasures, go forth in this world, there are none among them—setting aside the venerable Kaṇha—who are not unwilling [to abandon desire].

They are all peaceful because they have stilled the defilements through the cultivation of meditative absorption (jhāna), and because they have subdued their sense-faculties, such as the eye and so forth, so that those doors become free from worldly activity.
"Having become [wise] like the teeth, they practice the holy life with delight;
but you, venerable Dīpāyana, for what reason do you practice the holy life loathing austerity and being unwilling? Why, moreover, do you not dwell in a household?
Then, explaining the reason to him, he spoke the fifth verse:
“Having set out with faith, he has now turned back; indeed, this fool is like a deaf-mute.
Disgusted by this doctrine, I lead the holy life against my will;
yet I shall thus become a doer of merit, a state praised by the wise and esteemed by the virtuous.”
The meaning of this is as follows: Having placed faith in both dark karma and its fruit, he abandoned such vast wealth and went forth from the home;
yet, having renounced it, he returned for that very same purpose. Thinking, "This man is a fool, like that village boy who was deaf and mute," he felt loathing for such talk.
Thus, out of fear of the destruction of his own sense of shame (*hiri*) and dread of wrongdoing (*ottappa*), even though he did not desire it, [he remained].

"I am practicing the holy life (*brahmacariya*). Furthermore, this merit of going forth (*pabbajjāpuñña*) is praised by the wise, such as the Buddha and others, and it is the very dwelling place for them.
Thus, for this reason as well, I am a doer of merit;
even though I weep with tears falling from my face, I am indeed practicing the holy life."
Having thus expressed his own intention, he spoke the sixth verse, questioning Maṇḍabya again:
“You satisfy recluses, brahmins, and travelers with food and drink as they seek alms;
this home of yours is like a public well, fully provided with food and drink.”
“Then, loathing what kind of doctrine do you give this gift against your will?
In that regard, “to those who beg” means to those wandering for alms; he gives after having prepared the alms-food. “Like a well” means like a common lotus pond dug at a crossroads.
Then Maṇḍabya, speaking of his own intention, spoke the seventh verse:
“My fathers and grandfathers were faithful, masters of generosity, and charitable.
Following that family tradition, may I not be the one who brings disgrace to my lineage.
Feeling a sense of revulsion toward this talk, I give this gift even though I am unwilling.”
In this context, the word "āsu" (they were) is connected with the word "saddhā" (faithful); thus the meaning is: "They became faithful.
Being faithful, they subsequently became preeminent in giving and understood the meaning of the words spoken [by others], such as "Give!
and "Do it! "Taṃ kullavattaṃ" means that family custom; however, in the Aṭṭhakathā, this very reading [is used]. "Māhaṃ... [I might...]
Thinking, “May I not be the last of my lineage and a ruin to my family,” one who is the final descendant of the clan,
loathing the reputation of being “the last of the clan and a ruin to the clan,” proclaims, “I am giving this gift,” even though he does not wish to give it.
Having spoken thus, Maṇḍabya, questioning his own wife, spoke this eighth verse: “O fair-limbed one,
though I brought you from your kinsmen while you were still a young girl and lacking in wisdom,
you did not let me know your lack of affection for me, except when you were sporting with others out of lust.”
"Then for what reason, O lady, did such a state of cohabitation come to pass between us?
In this context, "one of unequal wisdom" means one whose wisdom was incapable of managing a household, being still very young.
"Whom I brought here" means that while I was still a youth, I brought her from her kinsmen's family; thus it is said.
"Except for lust, they attended upon me"—meaning that during all this time, even while attending upon me without lust or desire, they did not let me know their lack of affection;
rather, they attended upon me as if full of love. "For what reason? means for what cause.
"Madam," he addresses her. "Of such a kind" means [she was] with me in a state of loathsomeness equal to that of a venomous snake.
"How has your way of living together become such that it seems like a pleasant companionship?
Then, as she spoke to him, she recited the ninth verse:
"Near and far do not exist here at any time; there is only a succession [of generations] within this family."
"Following that minor service, may I not be the last ill-smelling woman in my family;
loathing this talk, I am following you as your foot-follower against my will.
In this passage, *ārā* and *dūra* are synonyms for one another. Or, showing [the distance] as being "exceedingly far," she spoke thus. *Idha* is merely a particle.
The meaning is "never. "Succession" (*paramparā*) refers to a lineage of men (*purisaparamparā*). This is what is meant:
"Sir, in this family of ours, from afar back as far as the seventh generation of ancestors, there has never been a succession of men;
that is to say, not even a single woman has ever previously abandoned her husband to take another man."
"Thinking, 'I too, following that family custom and family tradition, must ensure that I do not become the last woman in my family,
reduced to mere chaff,' and loathing the reputation of being the final member of the lineage or a defiler of the family name,
I have become your companion, your servant, and your foot-attendant, even though it was against my own will."
Having spoken thus, she thought, "I have spoken a secret that was never spoken before in the presence of my husband; he might even be angry with me.
I shall ask for forgiveness right here in the presence of our family’s attendant ascetic. Thinking this, as she asked for forgiveness, she spoke the tenth verse:
"O Maṇḍabya, I have spoken what should not have been spoken; may you forgive me today for the sake of your son."
“There is no love for a son here or in the next world; this Yaññadatta of ours is alive.
In that regard, “may he forgive that” means: may he forgive that. “Because of his son, may he forgive me today” means: may he forgive my speech today on account of this son.
“This one of ours” refers to the son for whose sake I have spoken these words.
“Therefore, my son does not live; because of this gain of life for him, forgive me, Master. From this day forward, I shall be subject to your will.
Then Maṇḍabya said to her, “Rise up, blessed lady; I forgive you, but from now on, do not harbor a harsh heart.”
“Since he was displeasing to me, I too shall not do anything displeasing to you,” he said.
The Bodhisatta said to Maṇḍabya, “Friend, by amassing wealth that is difficult to accumulate and giving gifts while lacking faith in both action and its fruit, you have done what is improper;
from now on, give gifts with faith. He accepted this, saying, “Very well.”
They said to the Bodhisatta: “Venerable sir, while standing in the position of one worthy of our offerings, you have done what is improper by practicing the holy life without joy.
From this day forward, please practice the holy life with a pure mind and full delight, so that the service rendered to you may bear great fruit. Thus they addressed the Great Being.
Having paid homage, they rose and departed. From that time forth, the wife became affectionate toward her husband, and Maṇḍabya, with a serene mind, gave gifts out of faith.
The Bodhisatta, having dispelled his discontent and attained the jhānas and super-knowledges (abhiññā), was destined for the Brahma-world.
Having delivered this Dhamma teaching, the Teacher proclaimed the Truths and identified the Jātaka; at the conclusion of the Truths—
The weary bhikkhu was established in the fruit of stream-entry.
At that time, Maṇḍabya was Ānanda, his wife was Visākhā, their son was Rāhula, Āṇimaṇḍabya was Sāriputta, and I myself was Kaṇhadīpāyana.
This concludes the sixth commentary, the Kaṇhadīpāyana Jātaka.

"I do not know this," the Teacher said, while residing at Veḷuvana, concerning Devadatta.
For one day, the monks said to him: "Friend Devadatta, the Teacher has been very helpful to you; for you [have served] the Teacher..."

When the bhikkhus said, "Relying on him, he received the going-forth and received full ordination; he mastered the word of the Buddha consisting of the Three Piṭakas; he attained meditative absorption (jhāna);

even his gains and honors belong to the One Possessed of Ten Powers," [the King] threw down a blade of grass and said in the Dhamma Hall, "I do not see even this much of a virtue performed for me by the ascetic Gotama."
How did they originate [this discussion]? The Teacher came and asked, "Monks, with what discussion are you gathered here now?
When they replied, "With this one," he said, "Monks, it is not only now; in the past as well, Devadatta was ungrateful and treacherous toward his friends.
Being requested by them, he related the past.
In the past, in Rājagaha, a great king named Magadha reigned. At that time, the merchant of Rājagaha brought home a daughter from a merchant of the countryside for his own son;
she was barren. Consequently, her honor declined later on. [People said:
"How will our son’s family lineage increase while a barren woman dwells in his house? Just as...

She heard that they were instigating such talk in this manner. Having heard it, she thought, "Very well, I shall deceive them by feigning pregnancy," and said to her nurse, who was her attendant: "Mother, what various things do those who are pregnant do?
Having thus inquired about the requirements for a pregnant woman, she concealed herself during the time of her menses and developed a craving for sour things and so forth.
When her hands and feet began to swell, she had them rubbed and made them thick;
day after day, she increased the enlargement of her belly by wrapping it in rags.
She made the nipples of her breasts black, and even when performing bodily functions, she did not do so in the presence of anyone other than that nurse.
Her husband provided her with the necessary care for her pregnancy. Having thus dwelt there for nine months, she thought, "Now I shall go to my father’s house in the countryside to give birth.
She asked her father-in-law for permission, mounted a chariot, and set out from Rājagaha with a great retinue, taking the road.
Ahead of her, however, a caravan was traveling. After staying with the caravan—
This place she had reached was now within reach at the time for the morning meal.
Then one day, a certain poor woman in that caravan gave birth to a son at the foot of a banyan tree during the night;
when the caravan set out in the morning, she thought, "I will not be able to go without the caravan, yet it is possible..."

Thinking, "I must obtain a son while I am still alive," she spread out a water-pot and her own womb-filth upon a thicket at the foot of a *nigrodha* tree, and having covered the child with it, she departed.
Deities took charge of the protection of the boy; for he was no ordinary person, but the Bodhisatta himself.
At that time, he had taken such a rebirth. Later, at the time of the morning meal, the other woman—
Having reached that place, thinking, "I shall perform the funeral rites for the body," she went with that nurse to the foot of a banyan tree.
Seeing a golden-colored boy, she said, "Mother, our task is accomplished!
She removed her rags, smeared the region of her lap with blood and the impurities of childbirth, and announced her own delivery from the womb. At that very moment, [she placed] him...
Having surrounded it with a fence, she, joyful and elated along with her attendants, sent a letter to Rājagaha.
Then her mother-in-law and father-in-law, from the time she gave birth, sent word saying, "What will she do at her father’s house? Let her come right here.
She turned back and entered Rājagaha itself. There, having received her, they were giving a name to the child.
Because he was born at the foot of a banyan tree (*nigrodha*), they gave him the name "Nigrodhakumāra.

On that very same day, the daughter-in-law of the chief merchant (*seṭṭhi*), while traveling to her parents' home to give birth, gave birth to a son beneath the branch of a certain tree along the way;
they gave him the name "Sākhakumāra. On that very same day, [the son] of one who was living dependent upon the merchant...

Having grown up together and reached maturity, they went to Takkasilā and mastered their crafts.
Both merchant’s sons gave two thousand pieces of money to their teacher.
Nigrodha Kumāra established his craft under Pottika. When they had completed their training, they took leave of their teacher and set out, thinking, "We shall travel through the countryside.
Eventually reaching Bārāṇasī, they lay down at the foot of a tree. At that time, the King of Bārāṇasī...
"It is now the seventh day since Kālaka died; 'Tomorrow we shall harness the Phussa chariot,' they announced by beating the drum throughout the city.
While those companions lay sleeping at the foot of a tree, Pottika rose at dawn and sat down massaging Prince Nigrodha’s feet.
When the cocks dwelling in that tree had finished crowing, the cock above [called out] to the cock below."
He dropped excrement upon his body. Then he asked him, "By whom was this dropped? He replied, "Good sir, do not be angry;
it was dropped by me unknowingly. He said, "Hey! Do you consider my body to be your own place for excrement?
Do you not know my size? Then the other said to him, "Hey! Even when I say, 'I did this unknowingly,'..."
"You are angry indeed; but what is your reason for it? he asked. "He who kills me and eats my flesh receives a thousand pieces of gold every morning;
therefore, I am arrogant. Then the other said to him, "Are you so arrogant over such a trifle?
But he who kills me and eats my thick flesh becomes king every morning; and he who eats my medium-sized flesh..."
"He who eats what depends on bones becomes a commander; he who eats what depends on bones becomes a treasurer," he said.
Having heard their conversation, Pottika thought, "What use have we for a thousand pieces? Kingship alone is better.
He slowly climbed the tree, seized the cock that was sleeping above, killed it, roasted it over coals, and [offered] the choice meat to Nigrodha.
He gave the flesh of the trunk to the branch, while he himself ate the flesh of the heart.
Having eaten, he said, "Friend Nigrodha, you shall be king today; friend Sākha, you shall be the commander-in-chief;
as for me, I shall be the treasurer. When asked, "How do you know this?", he related the entire occurrence.

Then those three men, having entered Bārāṇasī at the time of the morning meal, ate milk-rice mixed with ghee and sugar in the house of a certain brahmin. Having departed from the city, they entered a park.
Prince Nigrodha lay down upon a stone slab, while the other two lay down outside. At that moment, the five royal insignia were inside...
They dismissed the Phussa-chariot. A detailed account of this matter will be revealed in the Mahājanaka Jātaka.
Having gone to the park, the Phussa-chariot returned and stood ready for mounting.
The chaplain, thinking, "There must be a meritorious being in the park," entered the park; seeing the prince, he [removed] the cloth from his feet.
Having removed [the cloth] and examined the marks on his feet, [the soothsayers] said, "Let alone the kingdom of Bārāṇasī;
he is worthy to become the sovereign king of the entire Jambudīpa," and they had all the musicians play.
Prince Nigrodha woke up, removed the cloth from his face, looked at the great crowd, and after turning over and lying down for a short while, he remained there.
He sat cross-legged upon a stone slab. Then the chaplain, supporting him with his knee, said, "O King, the kingdom has come to you.
When [the prince] replied, "Very well," the chaplain placed him right there upon the heap of jewels and consecrated him.
Having attained the kingship, he gave the position of commander-in-chief to Sākha and entered the city with great honor; Pottika also—
He went along with them. From that time forth, the Great Being ruled the kingdom in Bārāṇasī according to the Dhamma.
One day, remembering his parents, he said to Sākha: "Friend, it is not possible to live without one's mother and father;
go with a great retinue and bring our parents here. Sākha replied, "I have no business to go there."
He refused, saying, "There is [no need]. Then he gave orders for Pottika.
He said, "Very well," went there, and told Nigrodha’s parents, "Your son has been established in the kingdom; come, let us go. They refused, saying, "We still have sufficient wealth;
there is no need to go there. He spoke likewise to Sākha’s parents, but they too did not wish to go.
He said to his own parents, "Father, we shall live by the work of tailoring," but they refused him.
Failing to gain their consent, he returned to Bārāṇasī itself;
thinking, "After dispelling the fatigue of the journey at the general's house, I will see my friend Nigrodha," he went to the door of that man's residence.
“Go and inform the commander that a companion of yours named Pottika has arrived,” he said to the doorkeeper, and the latter did as he was told.
However, Sākha harbored a grudge against him, thinking, “He gave the kingdom not to me, but to my companion Niṅgrodha.
Upon hearing those words, he became enraged and came forward, saying, “Who is this madman, the son of a slave-girl, who is his companion?”
Saying, "Seize him! he had [the man] beaten with his hands, feet, knees, and elbows; then, having him seized by the neck, he had him led away. The man thought:
"Sākha, having obtained the position of commander-in-chief from me, is ungrateful and treacherous to friends;
he had me beaten and had me led away. But Nigrodha is wise, grateful, and a true friend; I shall go to him."
“I shall go. Having gone to the royal gate, he announced to the king: “Your Majesty, it is said that your friend named Pottika is standing at the gate.
The king had him summoned; seeing him approaching, the king rose from his seat, went out to meet him, and exchanged greetings with him.
He then had him have his beard and hair groomed and so forth, and provided him with all kinds of ornaments and various exquisite foods to eat.
Sitting comfortably with him, he inquired after his parents' welfare and heard that they had not yet arrived.
Sākha, thinking, "Pottika might slander me in the presence of the king; but once I have gone there, he will not be able to say anything," remained right where he was.
Pottika, having summoned the king to his very presence, said, "Your Majesty, I am weary from the road."
“‘I thought, “Having gone to Sākha’s house and rested there, I will come back here,” and so I went.
Then Sākha said to me, “I do not know you,” and after having me beaten and seized by the neck, he had me driven out. Would you believe this?
Having said this, Tissa recited three verses: [The verses follow.]
“I do not know this at all—‘Who is he? or ‘To whom does he belong?’—just as Sākhā spoke, so too, Nigrodha, what do you think?
Then, with a halter around my neck, men led me away.
Having delivered blows to his face, they acted upon Sākha’s words:
“O lord of people, such ignoble acts were committed by your friend Sākha—
acts done by one who is evil-minded, ungrateful, and treacherous.”
In that context, "What do you think? means: "Just as Sākho behaved toward me, do you also think in exactly the same way, or do you think otherwise?
Do you believe that Sākho would speak thus to me, or do you not believe it? This is the intended meaning.
"By the neck" means by seizing the throat. "A betrayer" means one who betrays friends.
Having heard that, Nigrodha spoke these four verses:
“I do not know this myself, nor has anyone told it to me;
that which you have told me, friend, is that the branch was made into a fire-stirring stick.”
“You are the one who provides sustenance for my friends, and you are both the life-sustainer and the nourisher for me.
You are the giver of sovereignty to us, and of greatness among human beings;
that these powers have been obtained by me through you—in this, there is no doubt for me.”
“Just as a seed that is burned in fire does not sprout,
so what is done for a person of bad character perishes and does not sprout.
But for a person who is grateful, virtuous, and noble in conduct...”
"Like seeds in a fertile field, what is done there does not perish.

In this context, *saṃsati* means "he explains. *Kāraṇaṃ kataṃ* means "the process has been performed"; the meaning is that the process consisting of pulling, dragging, pounding, and threshing has been carried out.
"O Pottika, you make a good living for your friends; you are one who provides a good livelihood for your companions."
"One who produces a livelihood. "Both for me and for Sākha" means "friends of both myself and Sākha.
"You are our lord" means "you are the giver of sovereignty to us; these successes were obtained by us from you. "Greatness" means the state of being great.
Having spoken thus, while Nigrodha was still speaking these words, the branch remained fixed right there.
Then the king asked it, "Do you recognize this Pottika? It remained silent. Thereupon, the king, ordering its punishment, spoke the eighth verse:
“Let them strike this base, deceitful man who thinks like an ignoble person with spears; I do not wish for his life.
In that passage, *jamma* means contemptible, and *nekatika* means a deceiver.
Having heard this, Pottika thought, "May this fool not perish because of me," and spoke the ninth verse:
"Let him have forgiveness, O Great King; living beings are not to be retaliated against.
O Lord, forgive this base man; I do not desire his death."
In this context, "of one who forgives" means "may he forgive"; the sense is: "forgive this wicked man. "Not to bring back the life" means that once dead, his life cannot be brought back.
Having heard Sākha’s words, the king forgave him; he even wished to grant Pottika the position of commander-in-chief, but Pottika did not desire it.
Instead, [the king] gave him the post of treasurer, which is worthy of overseeing all the armies.
He gave it that name. It is said that previously this office did not exist, but it originated from that time onward.
Later on, as Pottika the treasurer grew old with sons and daughters, he spoke the final verse by way of exhorting his own children:
“One should attend only upon the *nigrodha* tree; one should not dwell near the *sākhā* tree.”
"In the Banyan tree life is better than in the Sākhā tree.
Having delivered this Dhamma teaching, the Teacher said, "Thus, monks, even in the past Devadatta was ungrateful," and he identified the Jātaka:
"At that time Sākhā was Devadatta, Pottika was Ānanda, and Nigrodha was [the Buddha]."
"But it was indeed I who was he.
This concludes the seventh commentary, the Nigrodha Jātaka.
[446] 8. The Commentary on the Takkala Jātaka.
"There are no plantains, nor are there any bananas"—this was said by the Teacher while dwelling at Jetavana, concerning a lay follower who supported his father.

It is said that he was born into a poor family; when his mother passed away, he would rise early in the morning and, performing tasks such as providing tooth-sticks and water for rinsing the mouth, or working at wages or farming, he would prepare rice gruel, meals, and other provisions according to the means he had acquired.
He supported his father. Then his father said to him: “Dear son, you alone perform all that must be done both inside and outside the house;
I will bring you a maiden from a family of good standing, and she will do the work in your home.
“Father, women who have come into the house will bring neither mental happiness to me nor to you; do not think such a thing.”
“I shall support you for as long as I live, and after your passing, I will look after [your son].
Then his father brought him a young woman against his will. She was helpful to both her mother-in-law and her husband and behaved with humility.
Her husband, pleased that she was helpful to his father, would bring whatever pleasing things he obtained and give them to her; she, in turn, [gave them to him].
She presented it to her father-in-law. Later on, she thought:
"My husband gives whatever he receives only to me, without giving anything to his father; surely he has become devoid of affection for him.
By some means, I shall make this old man repulsive to my husband and have him driven out of the house."
From that time on, she would provoke his anger by making the water too cold or too hot, the food too salty or unsalted, or the rice too hard or too soggy;
and when he became angry, she would increase the quarrel by speaking harshly, saying, "Who could possibly attend upon this old man? In that regard:
There, even after throwing away lumps of spittle and other refuse, she complained to her husband: "Look at your father's work!
He gets angry when told, 'Do not do this or that. Either let your father live in this house, or let me. Then he said to her:
"My dear, you are young and can live anywhere; my father is old."

“You cannot endure him; leave this house,” he said. Terrified, she fell at her father-in-law’s feet, asked for his forgiveness, saying, “From now on I will not do such a thing,” and began to attend to him according to her usual custom.
Then that lay follower, having been vexed by her on previous days, did not go to the presence of the Teacher to hear the Dhamma, but [remained] with her.
When he had returned to his natural state, he went away. Then the Teacher asked him, "Why, lay follower, have you not come for seven or eight days to hear the Dhamma?
He explained the reason. The Teacher said, "At present, you did not have your father removed without first taking her word;
but in the past, you took her word and [removed] your father."
"Having been led to the raw charnel ground, a pit was dug and I was cast therein;
at the time of my death, when I was seven years old, I spoke of the virtues of my parents and dissuaded them from the act of patricide.
At that time, having heard my words, you attended to your father for as long as he lived and became destined for heaven—this was the exhortation given by me."
"Even when she has passed into another existence, she does not abandon [this nature]; for this reason, why did you not take her word and rescue your father now?
Having said this, being requested by him, he related a story of the past:
"In the past, while Brahmadatta was reigning in Benares, in a certain village of Kāsi belonging to a certain family..."
In his house there was an only son named Saviṭṭhaka. While he was looking after his parents, later on, when his mother had passed away, he supported his father;
the entire story should be told according to the pattern of the present narrative.
However, this is the distinction here: at that time, the woman said, "Look at your father’s work! Even when told, 'Do not do this or that,' [he did it]."
Having said, "He is angry," she replied, "Master, your father is fierce and harsh, constantly quarreling;
he is aged and afflicted by disease, and will die before long. I am unable to live in the same house with him, for even he himself will surely die within a few days.
You should take him to the raw charnel ground, dig a pit there, and place him in it."
“Having thrown him inside, cut off his head with a spade, bring him to the end of his life, cover him over with earth on top, and then come back,” she said.
Being told this by her again and again, he replied, “My dear lady, killing a human being is a grave matter;
how shall I kill him? “I will tell you a means,” she said. “Tell me then,” he said. “My lord, [she continued:]”
At dawn, you went to the place where your father was sitting and, making a great noise so that everyone could hear, said:
“Father, in such-and-such a village there is someone who owes you money; he will not pay while I am away, nor will he pay after your passing.
Tomorrow morning we shall set out early, seated in a carriage. Then, at the very time he had specified, [you departed].
“Rise up, harness the carriage, have him sit therein, and lead him to the raw charnel ground.
Having dug a pit there, kill him by making the sound of robbers being plundered; throw him into the pit, cut off his head, bathe, and then return.
Savitthaka, thinking “this is a good plan,” accepted her words and made the carriage ready for departure.
Now he had a seven-year-old son who was wise and clever. Having heard his mother’s words, [the boy thought], "My mother is of evil character;
she is making my father commit the crime of patricide. I will not allow him to commit this act of patricide.
So, moving slowly, he lay down with his grandfather. Meanwhile, Saviṭṭhaka, at the time appointed by the other woman—
Having yoked the carriage, he said, "Come, father, let us clear the debt," and had his father sit in the carriage.
The prince also mounted the carriage first. Unable to stop him, Saviṭṭhaka went with him to the charnel ground;
having set his father aside with the boy in a secluded spot, he himself alighted.
Taking a spade and a basket, he began to dig a square trench in a secluded spot.
The boy descended, went up to him, and as if not knowing what was happening, started a conversation and spoke the first verse:
“There are no *takkaḷa* plants here, nor *āluva* roots, nor *biḷāli* creepers, nor *kaḷamba* stalks, father.”
“O father, what is your purpose, and for whom do you dig in the midst of the charnel ground in the forest?
In that place, “there are no *takkaḷa* roots” means there are no *piṇḍāluka* tubers. “*Āluvāni*” means *āluva* tubers. “*Biḷāliyo*” means *biḷārī* creeper tubers. “*Kaḷambāni*” means *tāla* tubers.
Then his father spoke this second verse:
“Father, your grandfather is very weak, afflicted with suffering by many diseases;
I shall bury him in a pit, for I do not approve of his life.
In this context, “by many diseases” means afflicted by the suffering arisen from numerous ailments. “For I do not approve of his” means...
"I do not desire such a miserable life for your grandfather;
thinking, 'For one such as this, death is better than life,' I shall bury him in a pit.
Upon hearing this, the prince spoke the following half-verse:
“Having conceived this evil intention, you perform a deed that is harmful, O hunter.

The meaning of this is: “Dear one, having conceived this evil intention—thinking ‘I will release my father from suffering’ while instead joining him to the suffering of death—and because you have acted beyond what is beneficial by virtue of that intention, it is a harmful deed (accāhitaṃ).”
“You are doing cruel work.
Having said this, the prince took a spade from his father’s hand and began to dig a certain pit not far away.
Then his father approached him and asked, “Why, dear son, are you digging a pit?”
Thus, as he spoke, he uttered the third verse:
“Father, you too shall receive such a fate as this when brought low by old age;
following that same conduct, I too shall bury you in a pit.”
The meaning of this is: "Dear son, I too shall bury you in this pit when you have grown old;

thus, dear son, when you have reached old age and are brought to this very pit by me—having performed such an action as this family duty which was established by you—you, while following that tradition, will experience it yourself when you have reached maturity and are living with a wife."
“I too shall bury you in a pit.
Then his father spoke this fourth verse:
“O youth, speaking harsh words, you assail me as you speak.”
“Though you are my own legitimate son, O son, you are one who shows no compassion for me.
In this context, *pakubbamāno* means overcoming; *āsajja* means having struck.
When this was said, the wise boy spoke three verses: one verse by way of reply and two verses as an inspired utterance (*udāna*).
“O dear one, I am not one who feels compassion for your harm; rather, O dear one, I am one who feels compassion for your welfare.
Since you are performing that evil deed, I ought to restrain you from it.
For that person of evil nature who, having found fault, harms his mother or father when they are innocent—”
“Upon the breakup of the body, after death, he will undoubtedly go to hell. But he who,
having sought his mother or father, serves them with food and drink—
upon the breakup of the body, after death, he will undoubtedly go to a happy destination.”
Having heard this discourse on the Dhamma from his son, the father spoke the eighth verse:
“O son, you are not one who seeks my harm; you are one who seeks my welfare, O son.
And yet, though I am being spoken to by my mother, I perform such a cruel deed.”
In that context, *ahañca taṃ mātarā* means "I and your mother," or rather, this is the reading: *ahañca te mātarā*.
Having heard that, the prince spoke the ninth verse: "Father, women indeed, when a fault has arisen, do not restrain themselves and commit evil again and again;
it is fitting to dismiss my mother so that she may not do such a thing again."
“That wife of yours who was so ignoble—she is my own mother, my Sakyan birth-giver.
Drive her out from your home yourself; she would bring you further suffering.
Having heard the words of the Wise Son, Savitthaka became joyful and said, “Let us go, dear ones,” and together with him...
Seated in a carriage with her son and her father, she set out. That woman of ill-conduct, thinking, "The ill-omened one has left our house," was delighted and joyful;

she smeared the house with fresh cow dung, cooked milk-rice, and while watching the road for their return, she saw them coming and became angry, thinking, "The ill-omened one has come back after having left!"
“You are a relative, yet you have come back bringing with you that ill-omened Kāḷakaṇṇī! he rebuked him.
Saviṭṭhaka said nothing; he unyoked the cart, struck the man—who was already well-beaten—once more, saying, “What do you say about improper conduct?
and grabbing him by the feet, he dragged him out, saying, “From now on, do not enter this house. Then [he spoke to] both father and son...
Having bathed her, they themselves also bathed, and all three of them partook of the milk-rice.
That woman of evil character stayed for several days in another house. At that time, the son said to his father: "Father, my mother does not understand by this much;
in order to cause shame to my mother, you should say, 'In such-and-such a village there is the daughter of my maternal uncle.'"
"She will look after my father, my son, and me; we shall bring her back," he said.
Taking flowers, perfumes, and other such items, he departed by carriage, wandered through the fields, and returned in the evening, saying, "I have been there.
The women in the neighboring households said, "It seems your husband has gone to such-and-such a village to bring another wife."
They informed her of this. Thinking, "Now I am lost; there is no further hope for me," she became terrified and anxious.
"I shall beg only for my son," she thought, and went to the presence of the wise man's son.
Falling at his feet, she said, "Dear one, apart from you, I have no other refuge. From now on, [protect] both your father and grandfather..."
“I shall tend to it as if it were a decorated shrine; please enter this house of mine once again,” she said.
He replied, “Very well, mother; if you do not act in such a way again, I will come. Be careful!
Having spoken thus, when her father returned, he recited the tenth verse:
“She who was your wife of ignoble character, she is now my mother, my own Sakyan kin.
Tamed like a female elephant brought under control, may that woman of evil nature never return.

In this context, “like a female elephant” means, dear son, she has now become free from wickedness, like a female elephant who performs the act of immovability (*āneñja*) and is brought under control, being tamed. “May she never return” means may she never come back to this house again.
Having thus preached the Dhamma to his father, he went and brought back his mother. She asked forgiveness from both her husband and her father-in-law;
from that time forth, being endowed with self-restraint and righteousness, she looked after her husband, her father-in-law, and her son.
Both of them, abiding by their son’s advice and performing meritorious deeds such as giving alms, became destined for heaven.
Having delivered this Dhamma teaching and proclaimed the Truths, the Teacher identified the Jātaka.

At the conclusion of the Truths, the son who supported his father was established in the fruit of stream-entry. At that time, the father, the son, and the daughter-in-law were those very same individuals;
as for the wise youth, he was none other than myself.
The eighth: The Commentary on the Takkalājātaka.
[447] 9. The Commentary on the Mahādhammapālajātaka.
"What is this garment of yours?"—this was spoken by the Teacher while staying in the Nigrodha Park after having gone to Kapilavatthu on his first visit.

He spoke concerning the lack of faith in his father, the king. At that time, after the Great King Suddhodana had given rice gruel and solid food to the Blessed One—who was accompanied by a retinue of twenty thousand bhikkhus—in his own residence, and while they were engaged in pleasant conversation during the interval between meals, [the King said]:
"Venerable Sir, at the time of your striving, deities came and stood in the sky and said: 'Your son, Prince Siddhattha..."

“...and they reported to me, ‘He died from eating too little food,’” he said. When the Teacher replied, “I believe it, Great King,” he said, “I did not believe it, Bhante, even when the deities standing in the sky spoke;
I rejected it, saying, ‘There is no such thing as my son’s final passing away (parinibbāna) until he has attained Buddhahood at the foot of the Bodhi tree. “Great King, formerly too...”
“Even when you were a great protector of the Dhamma, you did not believe the world-renowned teacher who came to show you, saying, ‘Your son is dead;
here are his bones,’ for you said, ‘In our family, there is no such thing as death while one is still young.
Why then do you believe now? Having said this, at his request, he related a story of the past.
In the past, while Brahmadatta was reigning in Benares, there was a village in the kingdom of Kāsi named Dhammapāla.

It received this name because it was inhabited by a family of Dhammapālas. There lived a brahmin well-known as "Dhammapāla" because he protected the ten paths of wholesome action; in his family, even down to the slaves and laborers, [all were likewise so].
They gave gifts, observed moral discipline, and performed the Uposatha rites. At that time, the Bodhisatta was reborn into that family, and they gave him the name "Prince Dhammapāla.
When he reached maturity, his father provided him with a thousand pieces of gold and sent him to Takkasilā to study the arts. Having gone there, he [approached] a world-renowned teacher...
He learned his craft in the presence [of the teacher] and became the senior pupil among five hundred young brahmins.

At that time, the teacher’s eldest son passed away. Surrounded by his young brahmin pupils and weeping and wailing together with the circle of kinsmen, the teacher had the funeral rites for the body performed at the charnel ground.
There, both the teacher and the group of his kinsmen, along with his pupils—
They wept and lamented, yet Dhammapāla alone neither wept nor lamented.
Furthermore, while those five hundred young brahmins, having come from the cemetery and sat down near their teacher, were saying, "Alas!
Such a youth, so perfected in conduct, has been separated from his parents at such a tender age and has met with death," [Dhammapāla remained silent].
“Sir, you say they are ‘young,’ but then why do they die at the very time they are young?
Is it not improper to die while still young? he asked.
Then they said to him, “But sir, do you not know that these beings are subject to death?”

“I know that people do not die in their youth, but only die when they have reached old age. “But are not all conditioned phenomena (*saṅkhārā*) impermanent, having come to be and then ceased? “It is true they are impermanent;
however, beings do not die in their childhood, but die in their old age, reaching the state of impermanence. “Friend Dhammapāla, is it that no one at all dies in your house?”
"But they do not die in their childhood; they die only when they are old. "Is this, then, your family tradition?
"Yes, it is our family tradition. The young men reported those words of his to the teacher. Then, having summoned him, the teacher asked:
"Is it true, my dear Dhammapāla, that in your family no one dies in childhood? "It is true."
“Teacher. Having heard his words, he thought: “This man speaks of something truly extraordinary.
I shall go to his father, ask him about it, and if it is true, I too will fulfill that very same Dhamma.
After performing the duties required of a son toward his father, and after the lapse of seven or eight days, he summoned Dhammapāla.
“Father, I shall return quickly; until my arrival, please teach these young men their craft,” he said.
Then, taking the bones of a goat, washing them, and putting them into a small bag, he took one junior attendant and departed from Takkasilā.
Traveling by stages, he reached that village and asked, “Which is the house of Mahādhammapāla?”
Having asked for permission and gone there, he stood at the door.
Among the brahmin’s servants, whichever one saw him first took the parasol from the teacher’s hand, took his sandals, and took the bag from the attendant’s hand.
[He said: "The teacher of your son, Prince Dhammapāla, is standing at the door. Regarding the prince—
When they were told, "Go and inform your father," they replied, "Very well," and went to inform him.
He hurried to the gateway, saying, "Come this way," and led him into the house. Having seated him on a couch, he performed all the necessary duties, beginning with washing his feet.
When the teacher had finished his meal and was sitting in pleasant conversation, [the son said]: "Brahmin, your son, Prince Dhammapāla..."
“He was wise and had attained mastery in the three Vedas and the eighteen arts;
yet, due to a single ailment, he met his end. All conditioned phenomena are impermanent; do not grieve,” he said.
The brahmin clapped his hands and laughed a great laugh. When asked, “Brahmin, why do you laugh? he replied, “My son...”
“He does not die; someone else must have died,” he said. “Brahmin, it is your own son who has died;
have faith only after seeing your son’s bones. Having extracted the bones, he said, “These are the bones of your son.
[The Brahmin thought: “These must belong to a sheep or a dog, for my son does not die. For us...”
"In your family, even through seven generations of ancestors, there has never been anyone who died in their youth; you speak falsely.
At that moment, they all clapped their hands and laughed a great laugh.
Seeing this marvel, the teacher was filled with joy and said, "Brāhmaṇa, because of the immortality of the young in your family lineage..."
“It is not possible to exist without a cause; for what reason do the young among you not die? Asking this, he spoke the first verse: “What is your vow?
What indeed is your holy life (*brahmacariya*)? Of what well-practiced deed is this the result? Explain this matter to me, O Brahmin: why is it that the young among you do not die?”

In this context, *vata* refers to the undertaking of a vow. *Brahmacariya* means the supreme conduct. When he asked, "Of what well-practiced [deed]? he was asking: "What is the ripening of which good deed that results in the non-death of the young ones in your family?
Having heard that, the brahmin, describing those qualities by whose power the young ones in his family do not die, said:
"We practice the Dhamma, we do not speak falsehoods, and we avoid evil deeds."
"We avoid everything that is un-Ariyan; therefore, our children do not die.
We listen to the Dhamma of both the non-virtuous and the virtuous, yet we do not take pleasure in the Dhamma of the non-virtuous.
Having abandoned the non-virtuous, we do not forsake the virtuous; therefore, our children do not die."
“Before giving, we are joyful; while giving, indeed, we are delighted;
even after having given, we do not regret it afterwards. Therefore, our children do not die young.
Toward recluses, brahmins, travelers, mendicants, beggars, and the poor...”
“We satisfy them with food and drink; therefore, our young do not die.
We do not transgress against our wives, nor do our wives transgress against us;
we lead the holy life with none other than them; therefore, our young do not die.”
“Let us all abstain from taking life, and let us avoid what is not given in this world;
let us drink no intoxicants and speak no falsehoods—therefore, among us, the young do not die.
Indeed, those who are born into these families, which are like fine threads, become wise and possessed of abundant wisdom.”
“They are learned and possessors of true knowledge; therefore, we children do not die.
Our mother and father, our sisters and brothers, our sons and wives, and we ourselves—all of us practice the Dhamma for the sake of the next world; therefore, we children do not die.”
“Both male and female slaves, dependents, attendants, and all laborers—everyone practices the Dhamma for the sake of the next world; therefore, indeed, our young do not die.
Thus he spoke these verses.
In this context, "let us practice the Dhamma" means we practice the Dhamma of the ten courses of wholesome action (*dasakusalakammapatha*).
This should be expanded in full: "We do not deprive even a tiny ant of life for the sake of our own livelihood; we do not look upon another's property with a covetous mind," and so forth.
Furthermore, regarding false speech, it is stated here in an emphatic sense that there is no evil greater than the non-doing of false speech by one who speaks falsely.
He spoke again. It is said that they do not speak falsehood even with the intention of joking.
"Evil deeds" refers to all actions leading to rebirth in hell. "Noble" means we avoid all ignoble, unwholesome, and impure actions censured by the noble ones (*ariya*).
Therefore, in the phrase "for this reason, among us," the particle *hi* is merely an expletive; for that reason, our children do not die prematurely.
The meaning is: "There is no such thing as untimely death for us. There is also a reading: "Therefore, we...

As for "we hear," it means that we hear the Dhamma—both that which reveals the wholesome of virtuous persons who maintain the doctrine of action, and that which reveals the unwholesome of non-virtuous persons;
yet that remains to us merely as something heard, and we do not find it pleasing. Furthermore, with them there is neither dispute nor contention.
"May it not be so!"—thus we shall listen to the Dhamma; having heard it, we shall abandon the non-existent and abide in the existent; we shall not forsake the existent for even a single moment;
and having abandoned evil friends, we shall indeed become those who associate with virtuous friends.
"We are recluses, we are brahmins"—we [refer to ourselves] as those who have stilled evil and driven away evil, even in the case of the Pacceka-buddhas, the recluses, and the brahmins.
The meaning is: "We shall satisfy with food and drink the remaining monks and brahmins who follow the Dhamma, as well as travelers, beggars, and other people.
However, in the Pāḷi, this verse follows after the verse beginning with "pubbeva dānā" (before giving). "Nātikkamāma" means:
we do not commit adultery outside [the home] by transgressing against our own wives. "Aññatra tāhi" means: except for those [wives].
"Except for our own wives, we practice celibacy toward all other women; likewise, our wives behave in the same manner toward other men.
*Jāyare* means "they are born. *Suttamāsū* means "among women of excellent character, among superior women. This is what is meant:
those sons who are born to us from these women of perfected virtue and superior character—they are wise.
They are of such a nature; how could there be an untimely death for them? Therefore, no children die young in our family.
"Let us practice the Dhamma" means: let us practice the Dhamma of the threefold good conduct for the sake of the world beyond. "Dāsīyo" means female slaves. At the end—
“Dhamma indeed protects the one who lives by Dhamma; Dhamma well-practiced brings happiness.
This is the benefit when Dhamma is well-practiced: the one who lives by Dhamma does not go to a state of misery.
Dhamma indeed protects the one who lives by Dhamma, like a great umbrella in the rainy season.”
"Protected by the Dhamma, my Dhamma-protector, the prince lives happily, his bones [unharmed] by another.
With these two verses, he spoke of the virtue of those who live according to the Dhamma.
In this context, "it protects" means that this thing called the Dhamma, when protected, protects what is protected by oneself. It "brings happiness."

It brings about both the happiness of gods and humans as well as the bliss of Nibbāna. "Not an unhappy destination" means that one does not go to an unhappy destination such as the various hells and so forth.
Thus, O Brahmin, he shows: "We protect the Dhamma, and the Dhamma also protects us.
"Guarded by the Dhamma" means protected by the Dhamma which one has guarded oneself, like a great umbrella. "The bones of another" means...
"The bones brought by her must be the bones of some other sheep or dog; throw them away!
My son is a happy youth.
Hearing this, the teacher thought, "My coming has been a good coming; it is fruitful, not fruitless," and he was filled with joy.
Having asked Dhammapāla’s father for forgiveness, he wrote on a leaf: "These sheep bones were brought by me while coming here for the purpose of testing you;
your son is indeed healthy. Grant me also the protective charm (rakkhitadhamma) that you possess.
Having stayed there for a few days, he went to Takkasilā and [taught] all the crafts to Dhammapāla.
Having instructed him, he sent him forth with a great retinue.
The Teacher, having delivered this Dhamma instruction to King Suddhodana and proclaimed the Truths, identified the Jātaka.
At the conclusion of the Truths, the king was established in the fruit of Non-returning (Anāgāmiphala). At that time, the parents were members of a great royal family.
The teacher was Sāriputta, the assembly was the Buddha’s assembly, and as for the youth Dhammapāla, it was I myself who was he.
This concludes the ninth commentary, the Mahādhammapāla Jātaka.
[448] 10. The Commentary on the Kukkuṭa Jātaka.
“We do not fear those who have committed evil”— this was spoken by the Teacher while dwelling in Veḷuvana concerning Devadatta’s attempt to kill him.
For in the Hall of Truth, the monks had raised a discussion regarding Devadatta’s lack of virtue,
saying, “Friends, Devadatta is devising means for the very purpose of killing the One of Ten Powers by employing archers and other such methods.”
The Teacher arrived and asked, "Monks, with what discussion are you sitting together here now?
When they replied, "With this one," he said, "Monks, it is not only now; in the past as well, he plotted against my life. Having said this, he related a story of the past.
In the past, in Kosambī, a king named Kosambaka reigned. At that time, the Bodhisatta was in a certain bamboo grove.
Having been reborn in the womb of a hen, he lived in the forest with a retinue of many hundreds of hens; not far from him lived a hawk.
By means of a stratagem, the hawk seized and ate each hen one by one until, having devoured all the rest, only the Bodhisatta remained alone.
Remaining vigilant, he went out for his meal at the proper time and entered the Bamboo Grove.
He lived there. Being unable to seize that cock, the hawk thought, "I will catch him by winning his confidence through some stratagem.
He then hid himself in a branch not far from him and said, "Friend King Cock, why are you afraid of me?
I wish to establish a bond of friendship with you. In such-and-such a place there is excellent foraging; there—"
"Both of us, having taken up our respective ranges, shall dwell together in mutual affection," he said.
Then the Bodhisatta replied to him, "Friend, I have no confidence in you; go away.
"Friend, you do not believe me because of the evil I committed in the past; from now on, I will never do such a thing again. "No..."

“I have no need for such a companion; you go away. Having thus rejected him up to three times, he declared, “It is not proper to place one’s trust in a person endowed with these characteristics,” while raising his voice like a forest elephant, as the deities gave their applause and he launched into a discourse on the Dhamma:
We do not trust one who has committed evil; we do not trust a speaker of falsehood;
we do not trust one whose wisdom seeks only his own ends; nor do we trust even one who speaks excessively.
There are some men who are like cattle longing for water.
"Friends, it seems, devour one another with speech but not with action.
Like a hollow hand clapped empty, or like a mere covering of words, a person who lacks gratitude is like rotten wood among men; such a one should not be approached."
“Indeed, we do not desire even such association with women or men whose minds are variously directed,
on account of their diverse dispositions. This is an ignoble deed that has been undertaken, which brings about the destruction of all.”
We do not trust even one who is like a sharp sword hidden under a sheath.
We do not trust even one who, in the guise of a friend,
acts with insincere kindness through various means.
“Whether it be food or wealth, wherever such a one sees it, the foolish person acts with treachery and, having destroyed that very thing, departs”—these verses he spoke.
Therein, *nāsmase* means “one should not trust. Or rather, this is the reading: *na vissase*, which means “one should not place confidence. *Katapāpamhi* means...
First, one should not trust a person who has committed evil deeds. Nor should one trust a speaker of falsehood (*alīkavādin*);

for there is no evil that such a person will not do. One should not place confidence even in one whose wisdom is directed solely toward their own self-interest—meaning, one whose wisdom does not associate with others out of affection, but associates only for the sake of wealth; one should not trust such a person of self-interested wisdom (*attatthapañña*). Furthermore, one should not trust an over-familiar person (*atisanta*).

And by perceiving tranquility externally even when internal tranquility is non-existent, [one encounters] deceitful persons who, like a venomous snake hidden in its burrow, appear as if perfectly calm while their actions are concealed.
"Born of the nature of thirsty cattle" means they are like cattle that are thirsty;
it is said they are similar to thirsty cows. Just as thirsty cows, having descended to a watering place, [drink] mouthfuls...
They drink water, yet they do not perform what is appropriate to be done for water;
in the same way, some "lick the honey" of friendship with sweet words, thinking, "We shall do this and that," but they do not act in a manner befitting those affectionate words.
He illustrates that placing trust in such people leads to great harm.
"With empty hands raised in salutation" means having raised empty palms. "Enveloped by words" means concealing [one's lack] with such speech as, "We shall give this," or "We shall do that.
"The pithless among men" means such insubstantial people are called the "pithless among men.
"One should not sit down" means one should not approach or associate with such persons. "In whom there is nothing" refers to that in whom...
There is no gratitude toward a person; the meaning is that one should not even dwell with such a person. "Of those with various minds" means of those possessed of different minds;
the meaning is "of those with fickle minds. This explains that one should not place trust in such women or men.
"Having discerned through various diversions" refers to those obstacles which cannot be prevented without approaching them.
Having manifested association through various means for the purpose of creating an obstacle, he makes it firm and subsequently creates that obstacle;
this indicates that one should not honor nor trust such a person.
"Engaged in ignoble deeds" means having descended into and remained within the conduct of the ignoble and immoral. "Then this" means unstable.
"Without a foundation" means having no support. "Destroying all" means that, having found an opportunity, it causes harm to everyone.
"Like a sharp sword concealed" means like a sharpened sword hidden by a sheath or a rag.
"Even such as this" means one should not place trust even in such a friend who merely resembles a friend. "With kindness" means with smooth speech. "By those without conscience" means...
"Without thought" (*acittakena*): for their speech alone is polished, but their mind is stubborn and harsh.
"By various means" (*vividhehi*): they approach seeking an opportunity through various stratagems. "Even one such as that" (*tādisampi*):

the meaning is that one should not place trust even in someone who is similar to these friends in appearance, though they are actually enemies. "Food" (*āmisaṃ*): edible and consumable items. "Wealth" (*dhanaṃ*): beds and bedsteads.
Starting from the beginning, the remainder is as follows: "Where he sees" means in his friend's house, at whatever place he sees [the treasure].
"He acts treacherously" means he conceives a treacherous thought and carries off that wealth. "And having slain him" means he departs after having also killed that friend.
Thus these seven verses were spoken by the cock-king.
“Many beings, disguised in the form of friends, serve one while hiding their true intent;
one should abandon such base men, just as Senaka did the cock.
And he who does not quickly perceive a matter that has arisen—
One is pursued by enemies and later regrets it.
But he who quickly understands a matter that has arisen is released from the oppression of his foes,
like a cock from the claws of a hawk.
“A wise man should avoid from afar such a person— who is like a snare set in the forest, unrighteous, and constantly causing destruction— just as a pheasant avoids a hawk in a bamboo grove.
These four verses were spoken by the Dhamma-King after his full enlightenment.
"In this regard, O monks, one should abandon these base men"—here, the word *ha* is merely an expletive.
"And later he regrets it" means that later on he experiences remorse.
"Like a snare set in the forest" means like a trap laid in the woods for the purpose of capturing deer. "Constantly causing destruction" means always bringing about ruin.
"Vaṃsakānana" means: just as a cock in a bamboo grove avoids a hawk, so should a wise person avoid evil friends.
Having spoken those verses, Sena addressed the hawk and threatened him, saying, "If you stay in this place, I shall know what must be done to you. Sena then fled from there and went elsewhere.
The Teacher, having brought forth this Dhamma instruction, said: "Thus, monks, even in the past Devadatta sought my death..."
Having said, "I shall strive," he concluded the Jātaka by identifying the births: "At that time, the hawk was Devadatta, but the cock was none other than myself.
The commentary on the Kukkuṭa Jātaka, the tenth, is finished.
11. The commentary on the Maṭṭhakuṇḍalī Jātaka.
"Adorned and wearing polished earrings"—this was spoken by the Teacher while residing at Jetavana concerning a certain householder whose son had died.
It is said that in Sāvatthī, a dear son of a certain householder who supported the Buddha passed away.
Overcome with grief for his son, he would neither bathe nor eat, nor attend to his business, nor go to wait upon the Buddha.
He departed, merely lamenting in delusion, saying such things as, "O dear son, you have left me and gone on ahead.

At dawn, the Teacher surveyed the world and, seeing the necessary conditions for that man to attain the fruit of stream-entry, he went the following day to Sāvatthī for alms accompanied by the Saṅgha of bhikkhus. Having finished his meal and dismissed the bhikkhus, he—
With the Elder Ānanda as his attendant monk, he went to the householder’s door. They informed the householder that the Teacher had arrived.
Then the members of his household prepared a seat and, having seated the Teacher, escorted the householder into the presence of the Teacher after first taking hold of him.
After the householder had paid homage and was seated to one side, the Teacher addressed him with words cooled by compassion.
Having addressed him, he asked, "Lay follower, why do you grieve for your son?

When he replied, "Yes, venerable sir," the Buddha said, "Lay follower, in the past, even when wise men wandered about overwhelmed by grief for their deceased sons, they heard the words of the wise, understood according to reality that 'this is a state that cannot be obtained,' and did not indulge in even the slightest grief. Having said this, [he spoke] to him...
Being requested, he brought forth a story of the past.

In the past, while Brahmadatta was reigning in Bārāṇasī, the son of a certain very wealthy brahmin, having been afflicted by a certain disease at the age of fifteen or sixteen, passed away and was reborn in the world of the gods. The brahmin...
From the time of his death, [the man] went to the cemetery and, while stirring up the heap of ashes, lamented;
having abandoned all his work, he wandered about overwhelmed by grief. Then a son of the gods, wandering about, saw him and thought, "I shall remove his grief by making a simile.
He went to that very cemetery at the time of his lamentation, assuming the form of his son.
Having offered the sacrifice and adorned himself with all his ornaments, he stood in one place, placed both hands upon his head, and lamented with a loud cry.

Hearing the sound, the brahmin looked at him; regaining his affection for his son, he stood beside him and, asking, "Dear young man, why do you lament here in the midst of this charnel ground? spoke the first verse:
“Adorned, wearing polished earrings, bearing a garland, and anointed with yellow sandalwood—why do you weep, stretching out your arms, distressed in the midst of the forest?
In this context, “adorned” means decorated with various ornaments. “Wearing polished earrings” refers to those earrings that have been perfected by the process of polishing.
“Adorned with earrings” means possessed of earrings. “Wearing a garland” means wearing a garland of various flowers. “Smeared with yellow sandalwood” means anointed with golden-colored sandalwood.
“In the middle of the forest” means in the midst of a cemetery. “Why are you suffering? means: for what reason are you suffering? Tell me;
I shall give you whatever you desire—thus he spoke.
As he was speaking, the young man recited this second verse:
“A golden, radiant chariot-fender has appeared for me;
yet I cannot find a pair of wheels for it, and because of that suffering, I am losing my life.”
The Brahmin, accepting [the offer], spoke this third verse:
“Whether it be made of gold, of jewels, of iron, or of silver—proclaim what kind of chariot I shall make for you;
I will provide you with the wheels and the yoke.”
In that context, "speak" means: "Speak whatever you require, whatever you prefer; I shall make a chariot for you. "I provide it" means: I cause you to obtain wheels and a yoke suitable for that cage.
Having heard that, the Teacher, having attained full enlightenment, spoke the first line of the verse uttered by the young brahmin;
the rest was spoken by the young brahmin: "That young brahmin spoke to him: 'The moon and the sun, both brothers here;'"
“My chariot is made of gold; it shines with its wheels and yoke.
Immediately after that, the brahmin said:
“You are a fool, young man, you who desire what should not be desired.”
“I think you will die, for you shall not see the moon and the sun.
Regarding this verse spoken by the brahmin, “apatthiyaṃ” means that which should not be wished for.
Then the young man said:
“Going and coming are seen, and the element of beauty is in both paths;
yet the deceased is not seen at all—who indeed is more foolish than those who weep?
In the verse spoken by the young brahmin, “going and coming” refers to rising and setting. “Beauty” itself is the “element of beauty.”
"Both paths are seen here": in this sky, both the ground for going and coming are discerned, such that one can say, "This is the path of the moon; this is the path of the sun.
"But the deceased," however, the being who has gone to the other world, is not seen at all.
"Who then, indeed?"—this being so, between the two of us who are weeping, who indeed is the more foolish?
While the young man was speaking thus, the brahmin, having observed him, spoke this verse:
“Truly you speak the truth, young man; I alone am the more foolish among those who weep.
Like a child crying for the moon, I long for a deceased one who has passed away.”

In this context, "like a child crying for the moon" means that just as a young village boy might cry out, "Give me the moon! for the sake of the moon, so too does he say, "I also long for this one who has passed away.
Thus, having become free from grief through the young brahmin's words, the brahmin spoke the remaining verses in praise of him:
"Just as a fire fed with ghee, While I am burning, alas!— ... [the rest of the verse follows]"
"Sprinkling him as with water, he extinguished all my pain.
'Truly, you have extracted the arrow that was lodged in my heart;
for you have dispelled the grief for my son from me who was overcome by sorrow.'"
“I have pulled out the arrow, I am free from sorrow and undisturbed;
I do not grieve nor do I weep, having heard you, young man.
Then the young man said to him, “Brahmin, for whose sake you weep—I am your son; I [am in] the world of the gods...”
Having been reborn, he instructed him, saying, “From now on, do not grieve for me; give gifts, guard your virtue, and observe the Uposatha,” and then he departed for his own abode.
The brahmin, abiding by that instruction, performed meritorious deeds such as giving alms and, when he passed away, was reborn in the world of the devas.

The Teacher, having delivered this Dhamma teaching and proclaimed the Truths, identified the Jātaka. At the conclusion of the Truths, the householder was established in the fruit of Stream-entry. "At that time, I myself was the deity who preached the Dhamma.
This concludes the eleventh narrative, the Maṭṭhakuṇḍalī Jātaka. [450] 12.
The Narrative of the Cat and the Quail (Bilārakosiya Jātaka)
"Even those who do not give," this was said by the Teacher while dwelling at Jetavana concerning a certain monk who was devoted to giving.
It is said that after hearing the Blessed One’s teaching of the Dhamma, he went forth into the Dispensation;
from the time of his going forth, he was devoted to giving and inclined toward generosity. He would not eat even the almsfood contained in his own bowl without first giving some to another.
Even when he obtained water, he would not drink it without first giving some to another; thus he was devoted to generosity.

Then, while the monks were discussing his virtues in the Dhamma Hall, the Teacher arrived and asked, "Monks, about what discussion are you gathered here now? When they replied, "About this very matter," he summoned that monk.
Having asked, "Is it true, monk, that you are devoted to giving and have a disposition toward generosity?

and being told, "It is true, venerable sir," [the Buddha said], "Monks, this man was formerly faithless and lacked confidence; he did not give even a drop of oil extracted by the tip of a blade of grass to anyone.
Then, having tamed him and made him free from wickedness, I made known to him the fruit of giving. Regarding that very same person...
"A mind inclined toward giving does not abandon its inclination even in another existence," he said, and being requested by the bhikkhus, he related a story of the past.
In the past, while Brahmadatta was ruling in Benares, the Bodhisatta was reborn into a family of wealthy merchants.
Upon reaching maturity, he established a household, and after his father passed away, he attained the position of chief merchant. One day, he conducted an inventory of his wealth.
Having reflected, "Wealth is seen, but those who produced it are not seen;
it is fitting to give a great gift by distributing this wealth," he had an alms-hall constructed and performed great giving for as long as he lived.
At the end of his life, having given his son the instruction, "Do not let this practice of giving be interrupted," he was reborn in the Tāvatiṃsa heaven as Sakka.
Putta also gave alms in the same manner and, having exhorted his son, was reborn at the end of his life as the deity Canda;
his son was reborn as Sūriya; his son was reborn as Mātali the charioteer;
and his son was reborn as Pañcasikha the Gandhabba deity. As for the sixth...
He was faithless, stubborn-minded, unaffectionate, and miserly;
having demolished and burned the hall for almsgiving, he had supplicants beaten and driven away, not giving even a drop of oil to anyone, nor allowing even a blade of grass to be taken.
At that time, Sakka, the king of the gods, reflected upon his own past karma, wondering, "Does my lineage of generosity continue, or does it not?"
Reflecting on this, he saw: "My son, having performed acts of giving, was reborn as Canda; his son was Suriya;
his son was Matali; his son was reborn as Pañcasikha, a son of the Gandhabba deities;
but the sixth one has brought that lineage to an end."
Then it occurred to him: "I shall go after I have subdued this man of evil character and made him recognize the fruit of giving.

He summoned Canda, Sūriya, Mātali, and Pañcasikha, and said: "Sirs, the sixth in our lineage has cut off the family tradition, burnt down the hall of giving, and driven away the supplicants; he gives nothing to anyone. Come now!"
Thinking, "We shall subdue him," he went to Bārāṇasī together with them.
At that moment, the merchant, having returned from his attendance upon the king, was walking back and forth along the side street while looking out from the seventh gate-tower.
Sakka said, "When I have entered, you must follow one after another behind me," and having spoken, he went into the presence of the merchant.
Standing there, he said, "O great merchant, give me food. "Brāhmaṇa, there is no rice for you here;
go elsewhere," [the merchant replied]. "O great merchant, it is not permitted to refuse food when it is requested by brāhmaṇas.
"Brāhmaṇa, in my house there is neither cooked nor even uncooked rice to be prepared; go elsewhere," [he said]. "Great merchant..."
“I shall recite a single verse for you; listen to it. “I have no need for your verse;
do not stand here,” he replied. Sakka, as if not hearing his words, spoke two stanzas:
“Even those who do not cook desire [to give], when the virtuous obtain food;”
“What is the point of you cooking that which you would neither give away nor consume yourself?
Out of stinginess and negligence, one does not give such a gift.
One who desires merit and possesses discernment should give.”

The meaning of these verses is as follows: Great merchants, even though they do not cook for themselves, being true persons (*sappurisa*), desire to give away even the food obtained through alms-round;
they do not consume it alone. How much more so you, who are cooking—should you not give, that would not be right;
it is neither fitting nor appropriate for you. For giving is [the opposite] of stinginess and negligence.
"Thus, because of these two faults, it is not given; rather, a wise person who understands and desires merit must certainly give.
Having heard his words, he said, "In that case, enter the house and sit down; you shall receive a little.
Sakka entered and sat there reciting those verses. Then Canda came and asked for food. "There is none," [he replied].
When he was told, "Eat your meal and go," he replied, "Great merchant, there is a brahmin sitting inside;
I suppose there will be a recitation for the brahmins, so I too shall stay.
Even when told, "There is no recitation for the brahmins, get out," he said, "Great merchant, please listen to these verses," and recited two stanzas:
“Whatever fear the miser fears because of which he does not give, that very same fear comes to him who does not give.
Hunger and thirst— those very things of which the miser is afraid—
touch that fool in this world and in the next.”
“Therefore, having overcome stinginess, one who has conquered impurity should give gifts;
for merits are the support for living beings in the world beyond.
In this context, “of whom one is afraid” means: “I shall become hungry and thirsty myself after giving to others.”
"That very thing" means that very fear consisting of hunger and thirst;
this fear touches and afflicts the fool in every place of rebirth, both in this world and in the next, and he reaches a state of absolute poverty.
