"Overcoming the stain" means overcoming the stain of stinginess.

Having heard his words as well, he said, "In that case, enter; you shall receive a small portion. He too entered and sat down in the presence of Sakka. Then, after some time had passed, the Sun arrived and, requesting food, spoke these two verses:
"For those who give what is hard to give, And perform what is difficult to do, The wicked do not follow their example;
The way of the virtuous is hard to emulate."
“Therefore, for the virtuous and the unvirtuous, the destination after death is different:
the unvirtuous go to hell, while the virtuous have heaven as their ultimate goal.
In this context, “difficult to give” means that what is called giving is difficult to give because it must be given by overcoming stinginess; [it refers to] those who give such gifts.
"Difficult to do" means that very act of giving is difficult to perform, like a battle;
they "do not follow after" means that ignoble persons, being ignorant of the fruit of giving, do not follow the path taken by those [givers].

"The Dhamma of the good" means the Dhamma of the noble ones, the Bodhisattvas, which is difficult for others to follow. "Being non-existent" means that through stinginess, ignoble persons fail to give gifts and go to hell.
Seeing no one to take what was to be taken, the treasurer said, "In that case, enter and sit down near the brahmins;
you will receive a little. After some time had passed, Mātali arrived, requested food, and at the very moment the words "there is none" were spoken, he recited the seventh verse:
“Some give even from little; some do not wish to give from much.
A gift given from little is measured as equal to a thousand.
In this regard, “some give even from little” means that certain wise men, such as the great merchant, [give] even when the object to be given is small.
They desire to give; the meaning is that they simply give. Some beings, even though endowed with abundant things worthy of being given (*deyyadhamma*), do not wish to give nor do they give.
"Sacrificial gift" (*dakkhiṇā*) refers to a gift given with faith in both the action and its fruit.
"Equal to a thousand" means that even a sacrificial gift consisting of merely a spoonful of rice, when given in this manner, is equal to a gift of a thousand.
The meaning is that because it yields great fruit, it is indeed equivalent to the gift of a thousand.
He said to him, "In that case, enter and sit down. Then, after some time had passed, Pañcasikha came and asked for food;
when told, "There is none, go," he replied, "I have never been here before. In this house, there is a brahmin recitation..."
Thinking, "He will surely become one," he began a discourse on the Dhamma and spoke this eighth verse:
"Whether one practices the Dhamma or lives as a scavenger, supporting a wife and children while giving away only a trifle—
such a person is not worth even a fraction of one who gives hundreds of thousands of sacrifices."
In this context, "dhamma" refers to the dhamma of the three kinds of good conduct (*sucarita*).

"Gathering gleanings" (*samuñchaka*) means that whoever should practice the gathering of gleanings—whether by wandering for alms of raw or cooked food in the village, or by collecting fruits and nuts in the forest—that person too practices only the dhamma.
"And supporting his wife" means supporting one's own wife and children. "Giving even when there is little" means giving even when the object to be given is small.
The meaning is that one who gives to righteous recluses and brahmins practices the Dhamma.

"Even a hundred thousand of those who perform the thousandfold sacrifice"—referring to lords who perform sacrifices by striking and harassing others with a thousand [animals]—even a hundred thousand of such thousand-sacrificers do not equal even a fraction of one such as he. "Of those" refers to those counted as a hundred thousand thousand-sacrificers.
"Compared to one who, having acquired wealth through righteous and equitable means, gives it as a gift to such a person, the offerings of a man in distress are not worth even a sixteenth part.
Having heard Pañcasikha’s words, the merchant reflected upon them. Then, asking for the reason why they were priceless, he spoke the ninth verse:
“How does a sacrifice that is vast and of great value not equal the worth of what is given with equanimity?
How is it that even a hundred thousand sacrifices performed by those who offer a thousandfold do not merit even a fraction of such a person as you?

In this context, “sacrifice” (yañña) refers to a gift-offering (dānayāga); it is “vast” (vipula) by virtue of the relinquishment of a hundred thousand [pieces of gold], and it is “of great value” (mahagghato) precisely because of its vastness.
"Of that which is given righteously": for what reason does it not equal the value?

"How, O Brahmin, [are] hundreds of thousands?"—how is it that the lords numbering hundreds of thousands belonging to many thousands of men who perform the *sahassayāga* sacrifice do not equal even a fraction of a single poor man who, having produced such wealth righteously, gives it away?
As he was speaking, Pañcasikha recited this concluding verse:
"Some give while established in injustice—having cut, having slain, and having caused grief.
That gift, with tears on the face and accompanied by punishment, is not worth even a fraction of what is given with equanimity."
"Even a hundred thousand such as these, who perform a thousand sacrifices, are not worth even a fraction of one such as you.

In this context, "in the uneven" means settled upon uneven bodily actions and so forth. "Having cut" means having caused distress. "Having struck" means having killed. "Having made to grieve" means having caused them to be full of sorrow.
Having heard the Dhamma talk from Pañcasikha, he said: "In that case, go, enter your home, and sit down for a short while..."
“Will you accept? he said. He too went and sat down in their presence.
Then the merchant Bilārakosiya called a female slave and said, “Give each of these brahmins a nāḷi of husked rice.
She took the rice, approached the brahmins, and said, “Take this, have it cooked wherever you like, and eat it.”
He said, "We have no need for rice; we do not touch raw rice. "Noble sir, they say these people do not touch rice?
"In that case, give them the husked grain. She took the husked grain and went there, saying, "Brāhmaṇas, take the husked grain!
"We do not accept what is raw," they replied. "Noble sir, they say you do not accept what is raw? "In that case—"
"Fill their bowls and give them cow-food," she said. She filled their bowls for them, brought cooked rice fit for large oxen, and gave it to them.
All five men, having stuffed their mouths with mouthfuls, allowed the food to hang in their throats;
their eyes rolled back, and they lay down as if dead, their consciousness lost. When the slave girl saw them, she...
Thinking, “They will be dead,” she went in fear and informed the merchant: “Sir, those brahmins, unable to swallow the cow-food, are dead. He thought:
“Now this man of evil character has had the cow-food for these delicate brahmins served;
they will blame me, saying that they died because they were unable to swallow it. Then he said to his slave girl: “Go quickly and [place it] in their bowls...”
“Take the rice and increase the meal with various choice flavors, such as rice from the *sāli* field. She did exactly so.
The merchant summoned the people who had entered through the inner gate and said, “I had this food for these brahmins prepared according to my own standard of eating;
yet, because they were greedy, they made large mouthfuls and ate them, causing the food to get stuck in their throats and die. My innocence—”
Having said, "Do you know?", he caused the assembly to gather. When the great multitude had assembled, the brahmins rose, looked at the crowd, and said:

"Behold this merchant's falsehood! He says, 'He had our own food for our consumption provided,' yet having first given us the cow-food while we lay down as if dead, he now provides this food [for himself]."
Having said, "We have caused [the meal] to increase," they threw down upon the ground the food they had taken from their own mouths and showed it to him.
The great multitude reviled the merchant: "O blind fool! You have destroyed your own family lineage; you burned the hall of giving;
you had supplicants led away by the neck; and now, while giving food to these delicate brahmins, you cause them to be given cow-feed!"
“As you depart for the next world, I think you will go having bound your wealth in this house around your neck.
At that moment, Sakka asked the great multitude, “Do you know whose wealth belongs to this house?
“We do not know,” they replied. [Sakka continued,] “At such-and-such a time in this city, in Bārāṇasī, a great merchant named Mahāseṭṭhi built a hall for almsgiving...”
“Have you ever heard before that he bestowed a great gift? “Yes, we have heard it. “I am that very merchant;
having given the gift, I was reborn as Sakka, the king of the gods. My son also did not let that lineage perish, but having given a gift, was reborn as the divine son Canda.
His son was Suriya; his son was Mātali; his son was Pañcasikha, the Gandhabba-deva-son.”

"Having made offerings, they were reborn there. Among them are this moon, this sun, this Mātali the charioteer, and this Pañcasikha, the son of a Gandhabba deity and the father of this man of evil character. Thus, giving is indeed a gift of many virtues;
the wise must certainly perform wholesome deeds. Speaking thus, in order to cut through the doubts of the great multitude, he leaped into the air with great majesty.
With a great retinue, they stood there with their bodies ablaze, and the entire city seemed as if it were on fire.

Sakka addressed the great multitude: "We have come here abandoning our own celestial splendor because of this wicked cat Kosiya, who is destroying our family lineage. This wicked one, having destroyed his own family line..."
"Having burned down the hall of almsgiving and having had beggars led away by the neck, he has utterly destroyed our lineage.
We have come out of compassion for him, thinking, 'May this man, having become one who lacks the habit of giving, not be reborn in hell.
Having said this, he taught the Dhamma to the great multitude, proclaiming the virtue of generosity. Then Bilārakosiya placed his joined palms to his head."
“Your Majesty, from this day forward, I shall practice giving without regard for my own ancient family lineage;
starting from today, I will not consume even water or tooth-wood without first giving a portion of whatever food I have obtained to another.
Having thus given his promise to Sakka, Sakka tamed him, made him free from wickedness, and established him in the five precepts.
Taking four sons of the gods, he returned to his own place. That merchant, too, having given alms for as long as he lived, was reborn in the Tāvatiṃsa heaven.
Having delivered this teaching on the Dhamma, the Teacher said: "Thus, monks, this monk was formerly faithless and gave nothing to anyone;
however, I tamed him and made him understand the fruit of giving. That very same mind—"
"Even when one has passed into another existence, one does not abandon [this quality]," he said, and then identified the Jātaka: "At that time, this present donor was the merchant;
Canda was Sāriputta; Suriya was Moggallāna; Mātali was Kassapa; Pañcasikha was Ānanda;
and Sakka was indeed I myself."
The twelfth: The Commentary on the Bilārakosiya Jātaka.
[451] 13. The Commentary on the Cakkavāka Jātaka:
"You are handsome and beautiful"—this was told by the Teacher while dwelling at Jetavana, concerning a certain greedy bhikkhu.
It is said that, dissatisfied with robes and other requisites, he wandered about searching, "Where is there a meal for the Saṅgha?
Where is there an invitation? and took delight only in talk concerning material things. Then, out of compassion for him, some other well-behaved bhikkhus informed the Teacher.
The Teacher had him summoned and asked, "Is it true, bhikkhu, that you are greedy? He replied, "It is true, Bhante."
Having said, "Bhikkhu, why have you become so fickle after going forth in such a liberating dispensation?
Fickleness is indeed an evil thing; formerly too, on account of fickleness, you entered the great forest in Benares unsatiated by the elephant carcasses and other things," he related the past.

In the past, while Brahmadatta was reigning in Bārāṇasī, a certain greedy crow, unsatisfied with the elephant carcasses and other scraps in Bārāṇasī, thought, "What must the forest be like? and went into the forest.
There too, dissatisfied with the fruits and berries, he went to the bank of the Ganges and, while wandering about, saw a pair of cakravāka birds and thought, "These birds are exceedingly beautiful."
"These [birds] on this bank of the Ganges, I think, eat much fish-flesh;
it would be right for me too, after questioning them, to eat their food as their range of sustenance and thus become beautiful.
Having sat down not far from them, he addressed the ruddy goose with two verses:
“You are handsome and beautiful, thick-fleshed and covered in fine hair;
you are as well-formed as a ruddy sheldrake, with serene facial features and faculties.
[I offer] the *pāṭhīna*, the *pāvusa* fish, the *balaja*, and the *muñjarohita*.”
"Sitting on the bank of the Ganges, you eat food in this manner.
In that context, *ghana* means having a solid body. *Sañjātarohita* means having the color of well-formed red flesh, like refined gold.
*Pāṭhīna* refers to a stone-fish named *pāṭhīna*. *Pāvusa* refers to a large-mouthed fish; it is also called *pāhusa*.
*Pāṭho*: "Balajanti" refers to the *balaja* fish. "Muñjarohitaṃ" refers to the *muñja* fish and the *rohitaka* fish.
"Evaṃ bhuñjasī" means "I suppose you eat such food as this"—thus he asks.
The cakravāka bird, rejecting his words, spoke the third verse:
“I do not eat this, whether it be from the land or from the water, except for algae and moss; this, my friend, is my food.

The meaning of this is: “My friend, apart from algae and moss, I do not take and eat any other meat, whether from the land or from the water; but as for this algae and moss, that, my friend, is my food.”
Then the crow spoke these two verses:
“I do not believe this, that the cakravāka bird eats [only] food;
I too, my friend, eat salted oil-cakes in the village.”
“Among humans, food is prepared—pure, with meat as its sauce;
yet my complexion is not like yours, O ruddy goose.

In this regard, “as yours” means: just as your bodily complexion has attained such excellence, such a complexion does not exist for me. For this reason, I do not believe your words when you say, “My food is water-moss and duckweed.”
Then the Cakkavāka crane, having explained the cause of his disfigurement, spoke the remaining verses while teaching the Dhamma:
“Seeing enmity within yourself, you devour the human race, harming them;
you eat in terror and fear, and for that reason your complexion is such as this.”
“You are at odds with the whole world, O vulture, because of your evil deeds;
even the alms you have obtained do not satisfy you, and for that reason your complexion is such as this.
I too, my friend, eat while practicing non-violence toward all living beings.”
Free from anxiety, free from fear, sorrowless, and without dread from any quarter:
exert your power, transcend the ways of the world, and live in this world with harmlessness; you will become dear to me, just like I am.
“He who neither kills nor causes to kill, neither conquers nor causes to conquer, whose heart is full of loving-kindness toward all beings—for him there is no enmity with anyone.
In this regard, O crow, you should clearly perceive: while perceiving the hostile mind that has arisen in others, reflect upon it as being within yourself.
"By harming and harassing the human race," [he means] by terrifying and frightening them. "You devour" means you consume.
"Because of that, such a hideous appearance has been produced for you. "O vulture!"—this is how he addresses the crow. "Morsel" refers to food.
"Without harming any living beings"—by this he says, "I, however, eat while not harming any sentient beings. "May you also exercise your power"—this [means] you too...
Exert effort; transcend your own state of immorality, which is known as "bad character.
"In harmlessness": being endowed with harmlessness, move through the world. "You will be dear to me": this being so, you will be as dear to the world as you are to me.

"He does not conquer": he does not suffer the loss of wealth. "Nor does he cause others to conquer": he does not cause others to suffer such loss either. "One who possesses loving-kindness" (mettaṃso).
“With a portion of loving-kindness, with a mind of loving-kindness. ‘With no one at all’ means that he has no enmity whatsoever even toward a single sentient being.
Therefore, if you wish to be dear to the world, abstain from all enmities. Thus did the ruddy goose teach the Dhamma to the crow.
The crow, crying out, “You do not tell me of your own domain; who are you?”—[continued:]
Having flown up, he alighted right there on a dung-heap in Bārāṇasī.
Having delivered this Dhamma teaching and proclaimed the Truths, the Teacher identified the Jātaka:
at the conclusion of the Truths, the greedy bhikkhu was established in the fruit of Non-returning. At that time, the crow was the greedy bhikkhu, and the ruddy goose was Rāhula’s mother.
"But as for the ruddy goose, it was I myself.
The Thirteenth Story: The Commentary on the Cakkavāka Jātaka.
[452] 14. The Commentary on the Bhūripañña Jātaka.
145–154. "Saccaṃ kira" (Is it true?)—this *Bhūripañña-jātaka* will be revealed in the *Mahāmaṅgala-jātaka*.
The commentary on the *Bhūripañña-jātaka* is the fourteenth.
[453] 15. Commentary on the *Mahāmaṅgala-jātaka*.
"What is a man?"—this was spoken by the Teacher while dwelling in Jeta’s Grove concerning the Mahāmaṅgala Sutta.
For in the city of Rājagaha, in the midst of a great crowd assembled in the assembly hall for some business, a certain man rose and departed, saying, "Today I have auspicious rites to perform.
Another, hearing his words, thought, "This man speaks of 'auspiciousness' (maṅgala)."
Having said this, he departed, asking: "What is this that is called 'auspicious'? Another replied: "The sight of forms that are highly auspicious is what is called 'auspicious.

For someone, having risen early in the morning, might see a bull entirely white, or a pregnant woman, or a rohita fish, or a full water-pot, or fresh butter, or cow's ghee, or unwashed cloth, or milk-rice."
"Or sees; beyond this, there is no such thing as an auspicious sign," he said. Some who were told this rejoiced, saying, "Well said!
Another said, "This is not an auspicious sign; what is called an auspicious sign is 'hearing.
For one person hears those saying 'Full! and likewise hears those saying 'Increasing! or 'Growing! and hears those saying 'Eat! or 'Consume!'"
"Beyond this, there is no such thing as an auspicious sign," he said. Some who heard what he had said praised it, saying, "Well said!
But another said, "This is not an auspicious sign; rather, the sense-object of touch (*muta*) is the auspicious sign.
For someone, having risen early, touches the earth, green grass, fresh cow dung, a clean cloth, a red fish, or vessels of gold and silver."
"He touches it; beyond this, there is no such thing as a 'blessing,'" he said. Some who heard what he said rejoiced, saying, "Well spoken!
Thus, although there were three assemblies—the Diṭṭhamangalika, the Sutamangalika, and the Mutamangalika—they were unable to convince one another.
Starting from the earth deities up to the Brahma-world, [they all agreed]: "This..."
They did not know what "auspiciousness" truly is.
Sakka thought: "In this world with its devas, there is no one other than the Blessed One capable of explaining this question on auspiciousness;
I shall approach the Blessed One and ask him this question. During the night, he...
Having approached the Teacher, paid homage, and raised his hands in reverential salutation, he asked the question: "Many are the gods and humans.
Then the Teacher explained the thirty-six great blessings (*maṅgala*) to him in twelve verses.
Even as the *Maṅgala Sutta* was being concluded, approximately one hundred thousand crores of deities attained *arahantship*, while others reached the stages of stream-entry and beyond.
There is no way to calculate it. Having heard the *maṅgala*, Sakka returned to his own place.
When the Teacher had spoken the *maṅgala*, the world with its devas rejoiced, saying, "Well-spoken! Then, in the Dhamma Hall, they initiated a discussion on the virtues of the Tathāgata:
"Friends, the Teacher has [spoken] the question of the *maṅgala*, which is beyond the scope of others, to the mind of the world with its devas..."
"Having grasped the matter and severed his anxiety, he spoke as if raising the moon in the vault of the sky;
such is the great wisdom of the Tathāgata, friends. The Teacher approached and asked, "Monks, about what conversation are you gathered here now?
When they replied, "About this very one," he said, "Monks, it is not surprising that even now, for one who has just attained full enlightenment..."
"Regarding my discourse on the question of auspiciousness: even while practicing the conduct of a Bodhisatta, I resolved the doubts of gods and humans and spoke upon the question of auspiciousness.
Having said this, he related a story of the past.
In the past, when Brahmadatta was reigning in Benares, the Bodhisatta was born in a certain village into a family endowed with great wealth.
He was reborn in a brahmin family, and they gave him the name Rakkhitakumāra.

When he reached maturity, having mastered the arts at Takkasilā and taken a wife, he passed away from his parents. After performing the examination of the jewels (*ratnavilokana*), his mind was filled with spiritual urgency;
he distributed a great almsgiving, renounced sensual pleasures, went forth in a region of the Himalayas, and attained the meditative absorptions (*jhāna*) and direct knowledges (*abhiññā*).
Subsisting on forest roots and fruits, he made his dwelling in a certain place. Gradually his retinue became large;
there were five hundred pupils. Then one day, those ascetics approached the Bodhisatta, paid homage to him, and said:
"Teacher, during the rainy season we descended from the Himālaya to travel through the countryside for the sake of consuming salt and sour gruel."
“Let us go,” they said, “so that our bodies will remain firm and we shall have performed the practice of walking.

When he replied, “In that case, you may go; I shall remain right here,” they paid him homage, descended from the Himalayas, and while wandering on tour, reached Bārāṇasī and stayed in the royal park. There, they received great honor and hospitality.
It came to pass. Then one day, when a great multitude had assembled in the assembly hall at Bārāṇasī, a question concerning auspicious signs arose.
Everything is to be understood according to the method of the present narrative;
however, at that time, [the King], seeing no one capable of resolving the people's doubts and explaining the question of auspicious signs, [sent for the Bodhisatta].
The great multitude went to the park and asked the company of seers about the question of auspiciousness. The seers addressed the king, saying:
"Great King, we shall not be able to explain this. However, our teacher, the ascetic named Rakkhita, who dwells in the Himālayas, possesses great wisdom;
having grasped the minds of the world including the devas, he [can answer] this question of auspiciousness."
They said, "He will tell us. The king replied, "Venerable sirs, the Himavat is far away and difficult of access;
we shall not be able to go there. It would be well if you yourselves were to go to the teacher, ask him, learn it, and then return and tell it to us.
They accepted, saying, "Very well," and went into the presence of the teacher.
Having gone there and paid homage, they exchanged greetings with the teacher.

When the teacher asked about the king’s righteousness and the conduct of the people, they explained from the beginning how the auspicious sights and other such things had arisen. Then, at the king’s request and for the purpose of hearing the answer to their own question, they declared:
“It would be well, venerable sir, if you would make the discourse on auspicious signs clear to us.”
“Having done so, please speak,” they requested. Then the senior pupil, questioning the teacher, spoke the first verse:
“What indeed should a man constantly recite at the proper time? What knowledge or what among the heard teachings [should he study]?
How should that mortal act in this world and the world beyond to be protected by safety?”
In this context, "at the time" means at the time of praying for auspiciousness (*maṅgala*). "Vijjanti" refers to the Veda.
"Of what has been heard" refers to the scriptures (*pariyatti*) suitable for study. "And in this" (*asmiñca*): here, *ca* is merely a particle.

"By means of safety" means by means of an auspiciousness that brings about well-being. This is what is meant: "Teacher, when a person desiring auspiciousness recites what at the time of auspiciousness?"
Among the three Vedas, having studied which Veda or which portion of the scriptures (*suta-pariyatti*) among the various recensions,
how does that mortal act in this world and the world beyond? By performing what among these [rites] such as *jappa* (recitation) and so forth,
and by what method, is he protected and guarded by a state of safety— a blessing free from transgression— having grasped that which is beneficial for both worlds?

“Tell us the blessing that brings stability,” thus was the Great Being questioned regarding the question on blessings by his senior pupil. Cutting through the doubts of gods and humans, he spoke with the grace of a Buddha, declaring what constitutes a blessing:
“That for whom the gods, the ancestors, all reptiles, and all beings alike—”
"They are always honored through loving-kindness; indeed, they say that among beings this is safety.
In this context, "of whom" means of whichever person. "Gods" refers to all gods of the sense-sphere (kāmāvacara), beginning with the earth-bound gods (bhummadeva).
"And fathers" refers to the Brahmās of the form-sphere (rūpāvacara) who are beyond those. "Reptiles" refers to the long-bodied species. And "all beings" as well—

"And all beings remaining unmentioned" means that all these beings are constantly honored by the development of loving-kindness (*mettā*) that has reached absorption (*appanā*), which proceeds by pervading the ten directions.
"Or among beings" refers to that person’s constant, faultless blessing for the welfare of all beings.
They said: "For a person who dwells in loving-kindness is dear to all and cannot be shaken by the aggression of others.
Thus, he is protected and guarded by this auspicious sign.
Having thus spoken the first auspicious sign, the Great Being spoke the second and the others:
“He who behaves with humility toward the whole world— toward women, men, and even children—
who patiently endures harsh words and speaks without offense, that they call ‘endurance,’ which is security.
He who does not despise his mere companions on account of craft, lineage, wealth, or birth;”
One who possesses wisdom and insight during times of need, they say, finds safety among friends.
"He who has virtuous friends, who is trustworthy and does not deceive them;
who does not betray his friends and shares his wealth with them—it is in such friends that one finds safety," so they say.
“Whose wife is of equal age, harmonious, obedient, devoted to the Dhamma,
well-born, virtuous, faithful, and a source of security for her husband— of him, they say, there is safety in his home. Whose king,
the illustrious lord of beings, recognizes his purity and his prowess— ”
"Absence of duplicity and a kind heart—this, they say, is safety among kings.
"The faithful one gives food and drink, garlands, perfumes, and ointments;
with a clear mind and feeling gratitude, this, they say, is safety in the heavens."
“The elders purify themselves by means of noble qualities;
the virtuous ones, being honored for their even conduct, are wise seers of great learning and possessed of virtue. Among the Arahants, they say that there is safety.”—He spoke these verses.
In this context, "living in humility" means that through a gentle mind, one conducts oneself with lowliness toward the whole world.
"Patient with harsh words" means one endures the abusive speech uttered by others.
"One who speaks without hostility" means that, without harboring resentment such as "He abused me, he struck me," one speaks only what is agreeable. "Endurance" refers to this very endurance.
The wise say that his safety is a blessing free from blame.
Regarding the phrase "companions and mere companions": therein, those who played in the dust together are called "companions" (*sahāya*);
those who have lived together for ten or twelve years are called "mere companions" (*sahāyamatta*). All of them [think], "I am skilled in a craft; these others are unskilled."

Thus, he does not despise others on account of their craft, thinking, "I am well-born, these are not well-born," nor on account of the noble lineage known as *kulyā*, thinking, "I am wealthy, these are poor," nor on account of wealth, thinking, "I am of noble birth, these are ill-born," nor on account of caste (*jāti*).
"One of pleasing wisdom" (*rucipañño*) means one of excellent wisdom, one of beautiful wisdom. "At the proper time" (*atthakāle*) refers to [the time] for anyone at all.
"At the time when the matter or purpose has arisen": having become wise (*matimā*) through the capacity to discern and investigate each respective matter, he does not despise those companions.
Regarding "among companions," the ancient wise ones said that this non-despising of him is called "safety" among companions.
Therefore, by means of that auspicious state free from fault, he [finds security] both in this world and in the world beyond.
And he is guarded. In this regard, the state of safety by relying on wise companions should be explained by means of the Kuśanāḷi-jātaka.

"Peaceful" (santa) refers to those who have wise and virtuous persons as their friends. "Confidently entrusting" (saṃvissatthā) means having gained confidence by entering the house and taking whatever they desire.
"Of one who does not deceive" (avisaṃvādakassa) means of one whose character is non-deceptive.
"Not treacherous toward friends" means one who does not betray a friend. "Sharing with wealth" means one makes a distribution of one's own wealth among friends.
"Among friends" refers to that security which is obtainable by depending on friends;
for indeed, protected by such friends, he reaches safety. In this regard, depending on friends...
The state of well-being is to be explained by means of the Mahāukkusajātaka and others.
*Tulyavayā* means of equal age. *Samaggā* means living in harmony. *Anubbatā* means submissive. *Dhammakāmā* means they delight in the Dhamma of the threefold good conduct (*sucarita*).
*Pajātā* means having given birth, not barren. Regarding the word *dāresu*, [they are so called] because of these qualities of virtue (*sīla-guṇa*).
The wise say that when a woman endowed with these qualities lives in the home, there is safety for her husband.
In this regard, the state of safety by relying on a virtuous woman should be explained by means of the Maṇicora-jātaka, the Sambūla-jātaka, and the Khaṇḍahāla-jātaka.
"Purity" (soceyya) means the state of being clean. "Sincerity" (advejjhatā): by way of sincerity, he does not split from me and become twofold.
"One will be" refers to that which one knows with such a state of non-doubt. "He is a friend to me" and "he is a well-wisher to me" refer to that which one knows.
Regarding the phrase "or among kings," the wise say that this is what is called the security of servants among kings.
"The faithful one gives" means that having faith in both the action and its fruit, he gives. Regarding the phrase "or in the heavens," it refers thus to the heavenly world of the devas.
The wise declare that safety is a blessing free from offense; this should be explained in detail by means of the *Petavatthu* and *Vimānavatthu*.
"They purify" (*punanti*) means they increase; they increase a person through wisdom and purify them with the noble Dhamma. "By even conduct" (*samacariyāya*) means by right practice.
"The learned" (*bahussutā*) refers to those who are deeply learned in penetration (*paṭivedha*). "Sages" (*isayo*) are those who have sought out virtues. "Virtuous" (*sīlavanto*)...
Endowed with noble virtue. Regarding "in the midst of Arahants": the wise declare that the safety to be obtained in the midst of Arahants is a secure refuge.

For the Arahants, by explaining the path they themselves have realized and instructing others in its practice, purify the person who strives through the Noble Path; such a person also becomes an Arahant indeed.

Thus the Great Being, grasping the pinnacle of the teaching through his attainment of Arahatship, spoke eight stanzas on the eight great blessings (*mahāmaṅgala*). Then, offering praise for those very blessings, he uttered the concluding stanza:
“These indeed are the states of safety in the world, praised by the wise and resulting in happiness.
A man of wisdom should cultivate them here; for there is nothing else in blessings that is truly real.”

In that regard, concerning the phrase "for there is no blessing," among those blessings classified as seen, heard, and sensed, there is not even a single blessing that can be called true; rather, Nibbāna alone is the one supreme-truth.
Having heard those blessings, after seven or eight days had passed, the seers took leave of their teacher and returned to that very place.
The king went into their presence and questioned them. They [answered] his question on blessings according to the method explained by their teacher.
Having spoken thus, they returned to the Himālayas. From that time forth, auspiciousness became manifest in the world.

By practicing these auspicious rites, those who died filled the path to heaven. The Bodhisatta, having cultivated the four divine abodes (brahmavihāras), took the company of seers with him and was reborn in the Brahma-world.
Having delivered this Dhamma teaching, the Teacher said, "Monks, it is not only now;
in the past as well, I spoke on the question of blessings," and he concluded the Jātaka thus: "At that time, the company of seers was the assembly of the Buddha;
the senior pupil who asked the question on blessings was Sāriputta; and the teacher was none other than myself."
The Fifteenth: The Commentary on the Mahāmaṅgala Jātaka.
[454] 16. The Commentary on the Ghaṭapaṇḍita Jātaka.
"Arise, O Kaṇha!"—this was spoken by the Teacher while dwelling at Jetavana, concerning a householder whose son had died.
The background story is exactly like that of Maṭṭhakuṇḍalī. However, here the Teacher said to that lay follower, "Lay follower, why do you grieve?
When he replied, "Yes, venerable sir," the Teacher said, "Lay follower, in the past, wise men, having heard the words of the wise, did not grieve for their dead sons.
At his request, the Teacher then related a story of the past.
In the past, in the northern region of Kaṃsabhoga, in the city of Asitañjana, a king named Mahākaṃsa reigned.
He had two sons, Kaṃsa and Upakaṃsa, and one daughter named Devagabbhā.
On the day she was born, the Brahmin soothsayers declared: "The sons born from her womb will [overthrow] the Kaṃsa clan and the Kaṃsa lineage."
“They will destroy her,” they declared. Out of intense affection, the king was unable to destroy his daughter;
thinking, “Her brothers will find out,” he lived out his full lifespan and passed away. When he had died, Kaṃsa became king and Upakaṃsa became viceroy.
They thought, “If we were to destroy our sister, we would become objects of reproach; this [must be kept secret] from anyone.”
“Without giving it away, we shall make it ownerless and look after it. Having had a palace built with a single pillar, they settled her there.
A maidservant named Nandigopā was her attendant, and a slave named Andhakaveṇḍa acted as her husband and provided protection.
At that time, a king named Mahāsāgara reigned in Uttaramadhurā. He had two sons, Sāgara and Upasāgara.
Thus there were two sons. After their father’s passing, Sāgara became king and Upasāgara was the viceroy.
This [Upasāgara] was a companion of Upakaṃsa, having learned his craft together with him in the same teacher’s school.
Having become disaffected toward his brother’s inner apartments and fearing [punishment], he fled and went to Upakaṃsa in the territory of Kaṃsa. Upakaṃsa received him...
He showed it to the king, and the king bestowed great honor upon him.
As he was going to attend upon the king, he saw a palace with a single pillar that served as Devagabbhā’s residence; asking, "Whose residence is this?
and hearing the reason, his heart became bound to Devagabbhā. One day, Devagabbhā [also saw] him together with Upaka...
Seeing him coming to attend upon the king, she asked, "Who is this?
Having heard from Nandigopā that he was the son of Mahāsāgara named Upasāgara, her heart became bound to him.
Upasāgara gave a bribe to Nandigopā and said, "Sister, will you be able to show me the divine womb? She replied, "This is not possible, my lord."
Having said, "It is weighty," he explained the reason to Devagabbhā.

She, whose heart was already naturally bound to him, upon hearing those words, accepted them, saying, "Very well. Then Nandigopā gave notice to Upasāgara and, during the night, led him up to the palace.
He entered into a union with Devagabbhā. Then, as they did so again and again—
Through living together, Devagabbhā conceived a child.
Later, her pregnancy became manifest. Her brothers questioned Nandigopā;
she, having requested immunity from fear, explained the matter to them. Having heard this, they said, "It is not possible to destroy our sister; if [she gives birth to] a daughter..."
Thinking, "She will give birth; we shall not destroy her even then, but if it be a son, we will destroy him," they gave her to Upasagara as a divine wife.
When her pregnancy was full, she gave birth to a daughter.
Upon hearing this, the brothers were delighted and joyful, and they gave her the name Añjanadevī. They had a village of wealth called Bhogavaḍḍhamāna.
They gave [it]. Upasāgara, having taken Devagabbhā as his wife, lived in the village of Bhogavaḍḍhana.
Devagabbhā again conceived a child, and on that very same day, Nandigopā also became pregnant.
When their pregnancies were full term, on one and the same day, Devagabbhā gave birth to a son, and Nandigopā gave birth to a daughter. Of the son, Devagabbhā...
Out of fear of being destroyed, he secretly sent his son to Nandigopa and had her daughter brought back.
When they informed her brothers that she had given birth, they asked, "Did she give birth to a son or a daughter?
When it was said, "A daughter," they replied, "In that case, raise her. By this means, Devagabbhā gave birth to ten sons, and [Nandigopa’s wife] to ten daughters.
Nandigopā gave birth to daughters. Ten sons grew up in the care of Nandigopā, while the daughters were raised by Devagabbhā.
During that interval, no one knew [of their existence]. The eldest son of Devagabbhā was named Vāsudeva;
the second was Baladeva; the third was Candadeva; the fourth was Sūriyadeva; the fifth was Aggideva; and the sixth was Varuṇadeva.
The seventh was Ajjuṇa, the eighth Pajjuṇa, the ninth Ghaṭapaṇḍita, and the tenth was named Aṅkura.
These ten brothers, the sons of Andhakaveṇḍa the slave, became famous as the "Ten Servants.
Later, as they grew up, they became endowed with great strength and power, and having become harsh and cruel, they began to commit plunder.

They roamed about, plundering even the royal tribute as it was being carried. People gathered together and shouted in the king’s courtyard, “The ten Andhakaveṇḍa brothers, sons of a slave-woman, are plundering the kingdom!
The king summoned Andhakaveṇḍa and rebuked him, saying, “Why have you caused your sons to commit this plunder? Thus it happened a second and a third time when people raised the outcry.
When he had finished speaking, the king rebuked him. Terrified by the fear of death, he begged the king for safety and disclosed the truth, saying, "Your Majesty, these are not my sons;
they are the sons of Upasāgara. The king, being afraid, asked his ministers, "By what means can we seize them?
Having been told, "Your Majesty, these men are skilled in wrestling; you should have a fight staged in the city," [he acted accordingly].
When it was said, "We shall have them seized and killed once they have entered the arena for the wrestling match," he had two Mallas named Cāru and Muṭṭhika trained.
Then, having caused a drum to be beaten throughout the city to announce,
"The match will take place on the seventh day from now," he had the wrestling arena prepared in the royal courtyard, the pits dug, and the arena decorated.
He caused a banner to be fastened. The entire city was thrown into commotion.
Having set up wheel-over-wheel and platform-over-platform, beautiful wrestlers came to the arena, moving about, roaring, and slapping their arms.
The ten brothers also arrived, plundered the laundry street, put on dyed garments, and took perfumes from the perfume shops.

Having plundered garlands from the florists' shops, with their bodies anointed and wearing garlands, with earrings dangling, shouting, roaring, and clapping their hands, they entered the arena of battle.
At that moment, Cāruro was wandering about clapping his hands. Seeing him, Baladeva thought, "I will not touch him with my hand."
Having brought a large elephant-rope from the elephant stable, the wrestler Vaggu trumpeted and roared;

he cast the rope, wound it beautifully around Cāru’s belly, joined the two ends together, twisted them, lifted him up, whirled him over his head, dashed him against the ground, and threw him outside into the drain.
When Cāru was dead, the king ordered the wrestler Muṭṭhika to take charge.
So, having risen up, he roared and thundered and slapped his arms. Baladeva struck him down, crushed his bones, and while he was still crying out, "I am no wrestler!

I am no wrestler!", said, "I do not know whether you are a wrestler or not a wrestler," seized him by the hand, dashed him against the ground, brought about his death, and threw him outside the arena. Muṭṭhika—
As he was dying, he made a resolution, thinking, "May I become a *yakkha* and be allowed to devour him.
He was reborn as a *yakkha* named Kālamattika in the forest of Aṭavī. The king rose up, saying, "Seize the ten brothers and the servant!
At that moment, Vāsudeva hurled his discus. It struck off the heads of both brothers. The great multitude was terrified and trembling.
Saying, “Be our refuge,” he fell at their feet and lay down.
Having killed both uncles and seized the kingdom in the city of Asitañjana, he established his parents there and set out, thinking, “We shall seize the sovereignty over the whole of Jambudīpa.
Traveling by stages, he reached the city of Ayujjhā, the residence of King Kālayona, and stood encircling it.
Having destroyed the thickets of trees surrounding the moat and breached the rampart, they captured the king, brought that kingdom into their own hands, and reached Dvāravatī.
On one side of that city was the ocean and on the other side was a mountain;
it was said, moreover, that the city was guarded by non-human beings.
A yakṣa who had taken charge of its protection, seeing the enemies, brayed with the cry of a donkey in the form of a donkey.
At that moment, through the power of the yakṣa, the entire city leaped up and came to rest upon an island in the great ocean.
When the enemies had departed, it returned again and settled back in its own place. Even then...
When that donkey perceived the arrival of those ten brothers, he brayed with a donkey’s cry.
Having flown up from the city and alighted upon an island, and finding them not in the city as they were returning, he came back again and settled in his own place.
They turned back once more; again the donkey acted in the same way. This happened while they were at the city of Dvāravatī.

Being unable to seize the kingdom, they went into the presence of the seer Kaṇhadīpāyana, paid homage to him, and asked, "Venerable sir, we are unable to take the kingdom at Dvāravatī; please provide us with a means.
He replied, "At such-and-such a place along the edge of the moat, a single donkey grazes. For when he sees enemies, he brays loudly."
"At that moment, it will fly up and depart from the city; you must seize its feet. This is the means for your success," he said.

Having paid homage to the ascetic and departed, they seized the donkey by its feet, prostrated themselves, and entreated him, saying, "Master, there is no other refuge for us but you; do not bray when we are taking our city."
The donkey said, "It is not possible for me not to cry out;
however, you four should come first, take large iron ploughs, and drive large iron stakes into the ground at the four city gates.
When the city is about to fly up, you must take the ploughs and bind the iron chain attached to the ploughs to those iron stakes."
“The city will not be able to fly up,” he said.
They replied, “Very well,” and while the donkey was still braying, they took their ploughs, drove stakes into the ground at the four city gates, and stood there.
At that moment, the donkey brayed again, and the city began to fly up.
Standing at the four gates, they seized ten iron chains bound to ploughs with four yokes and fastened them to stakes;
thus, the city was unable to rise up. Then the ten brothers entered the city, killed the king, and took possession of the kingdom.
In this way, they [subjugated] all the kings throughout the sixty-three thousand cities of the entire Jambudīpa.
Having brought about the end of their lives by means of the wheel, while residing in Dvāravatī, they divided the kingdom into ten portions;
however, they did not remember their sister, Añjanadevī. Then, when it was said again, "Let us make eleven portions," Aṅkura said, "Give my portion to her;
I shall live by engaging in trade, while you yourselves [take the rest]."

“Relinquish my toll in the kingdom,” he said. They agreed, saying, “Very well,” and having given their share to his sister, the nine kings lived together with her in Dvāravatī. Aṅkura, however, engaged in trade.
Thus, as they increased through sons and daughters from one generation to the next, and much time had passed, their parents died.
At that time, it is said, the human lifespan was twenty thousand years.
At that time, a son of the great king Vāsudeva passed away. Overcome with grief, the king abandoned all his duties and lay down, clutching the footboard of his bed, lamenting.
At that moment, the wise Ghaṭa thought: "Except for me, no one else [can console him]."
“There is no one capable of removing Bhaṭu’s grief; however, by means of a stratagem, we shall remove his grief.
Taking on the guise of a madman, he wandered through the entire city looking up at the sky and crying out, “Give me a hare! Give me a hare!
The whole city was thrown into commotion, saying, “The wise Ghaṭa has gone mad. At that time, there was one named Rohiṇeyya...
The minister, having gone into the presence of King Vāsudeva and engaging him in conversation, spoke the first verse:
“Arise, Kaṇha! Why do you lie there? What is the use of your sleeping?
Even he who is your own brother—your very heart and your right eye—”
“His winds grow violent, and his head throbs, O Keshava.
In this passage, “Kaṇha” is addressed by way of his clan; it is said that he belongs to the Kaṇhāyana clan. “What is the benefit? means: what kind of prosperity indeed?
“The heart and the right eye” means: he is equal [to me] both in heart and in the right eye. Of him—
"The winds grow stronger" means that the epilepsy-winds overwhelm his heart. "He raves" means he prattles incoherently, saying, "Give me my calf.
"O Keśava": it is said that he was known as "Keśava" because of the beauty of his hair;
therefore, he addresses him by that name.
When the minister had spoken thus, the Teacher, having become fully enlightened, recognized the man’s state of madness and uttered the second verse:
“Having heard those words of Rohiṇeyya,
Kesava, Agitated by grief for his brother, rose up in great haste.”
The king rose quickly, descended from the palace, and went to the presence of Ghaṭapaṇḍita. Taking him firmly by both hands and conversing with him, he spoke this third verse:
"Why indeed do you act like one mad, crying out 'hare, hare' throughout this entire city? Who has brought a hare for you?"
Therein, why do you act like a madman, wandering through this entire city of Dvāravatī and crying out, “A hare! A hare!”? “Who took your hare? By whom was your hare seized? he asks.
Although the king spoke thus to him, he repeated those same words over and over again. The king then spoke two verses:
“Whether it be made of gold, or made of jewels, or made of iron, or even made of silver;”
“I shall have a hare made for you out of crystal, silver, and coral.
There are other hares as well, roaming in the forest wilds;
I will bring those for you too—what kind of hare do you desire?”
In this regard, the summary of the meaning is as follows: "Regarding those made of gold and so forth, tell me which you desire;
I shall have one made and give it to you. Or, if that does not please you, there are other hares who roam the forest in the wilderness; I will bring them to you as well.
Speak, good sir—what kind of hare do you desire?"
Having heard the king’s words, Ghaṭapaṇḍita spoke the sixth verse:
“I do not desire these hares that dwell upon the earth;
I desire a hare from the moon—bring that down for me, O Keśava.”
In this context, "oharā" means "bring down.
Having heard his words, the king, overcome with dejection, thinking, "Without a doubt my brother has truly gone mad," spoke the seventh verse:
"Surely you will now abandon your sweet life, O kinsman!"
“He who desires what should not be desired, seeks a hare from the moon.

Therein, “kinsman” was said by addressing his younger brother. This is what was meant: “Dear one, you who are my beloved kinsman will surely give up your own very sweet life, you who desire that which should not be desired.
Having heard the king’s words, the wise Ghaṭa stood motionless and said: “Brother, for one who desires a hare from the moon...”
“Since you know that he has met his end and could not be recovered, for what reason do you grieve for your dead son?
Having said this, he spoke the eighth verse:
“If it is thus, O Kaṇha, that you understand, when you instruct another;”
"Why do you still grieve today for a son who died long ago?
In this context, "if" (*evaṃ*) means: if you know that this is indeed an unattainable state and thus should not be craved;

and "if you advise another" (*yad aññaṃ anusāsasi*) means: if, while knowing this very thing, you advise another. "Long ago" (*pure*) means: then why [do you grieve] now, when it has been four months since?
"Do you still grieve for your mother and son? he said.

Standing right there in the middle of the street, he continued, "Brother, I at least long for what is still known to exist, but you grieve for that which no longer exists. Speaking thus, as he taught him the Dhamma, he further uttered two verses:
"What cannot be obtained by a human being, nor again by a non-human being..."
“My son was born, may he not die! But how can that which is unobtainable be obtained?
‘Neither by mantras nor by root-medicines, nor by herbs, nor by wealth, O Kaṇha, can he be brought back—him for whom you grieve as a peta.’”
In this context, "That" means: "Brother, that which you—thinking 'my son born thus must not die'—desire, whether from a human or a deva, is impossible and cannot be obtained.
From where could that be obtained, and for what reason would it be possible to obtain it?
It is not possible," thus he demonstrates. Why? Because it is unobtainable; for it is a state that cannot be attained.
“Nāmena” means by name. “Mantā” means by the application of spells. “Mūlabhesajjā” means by means of root-medicines. “Osadhehi” means by various kinds of herbs.
“Dhanena vā” means even by wealth numbering hundreds of millions. This is what is meant:
“That which you grieve for as a departed one cannot be brought back by these means, such as the application of spells and so forth.”

Having heard this, the king said, “It is fitting, dear one; I have observed it well that you have done this for the sake of removing my grief,” and praising Ghaṭa the wise, he spoke these four verses:
“Whose ministers would be such wise men, Just as today Ghaṭa, the wise man, has consoled me.”
“Indeed, while I was burning like a fire drenched with clarified butter,
you have quenched all my distress as if sprinkling it with water.
Truly, you have extracted the arrow that was lodged in my heart.”
“He who dispelled the grief for my son while I was overcome by sorrow—by hearing your words, young man, I have had the arrow pulled out;
I am free from grief and undisturbed. I do not grieve, nor do I weep.”

Therein, the summary meaning of the first verse is as follows: Just as, for whatever reason, today this wise man Ghaṭa has caused me—who am overwhelmed by grief for my son—to reflect, that is, to have me enlightened;
for one who possesses such wise ministers as these, from where could there be any sorrow? The remaining verses have already had their meaning explained.
At the conclusion:
“Thus do the wise act, those who are compassionate;
they turn one back from sorrow, just as the pot turned back his elder brother.”
This verse on the Perfectly Enlightened One is of plain meaning.
Thus, when Ghaṭakumāra had removed the sorrow and Vāsudeva was ruling the kingdom, after the lapse of a long period of time, the ten brothers, the princes, thought:
“They say Kaṇhadīpāyana possesses the divine eye; we shall test him.”
“Not yet. They then adorned a young boy, made him appear as if pregnant by binding a cushion to his belly, and led him before the ascetic, asking, “Venerable sir, what will this girl give birth to?
The ascetic thought, “The time for the destruction of the ten royal brothers has arrived; what, then, is the state of my own life-span?”
Looking [into the future], he knew, "Death will occur this very day," and said, "What use have you for this boy?
When they insisted, saying, "Tell us, venerable sir," he replied, "On the seventh day from now, she will give birth to a Khadiraghaṭikā;
by her, the lineage of Vāsudeva will perish. Nevertheless, you should take that Khadiraghaṭikā and burn her."

"Throw the ashes into the river," he said. Then they replied to him, "Kūṭajaṭila, there is no such thing as a man who gives birth," and having subjected him to the torture known as the "rope of the loom," they caused him to meet his death right there.
The kings summoned the princes and asked, "For what reason did you kill the ascetic?"

Having heard everything, they became afraid; they provided him with protection, and on the seventh day, after burning the acacia wood splinter that had emerged from his belly, they threw the ashes into the river.
As it was being carried away by the current, it stuck on one side at the mouth of the river, and from that, the Eraka tree grew.
Then one day, those kings, thinking, "We shall enjoy a sea-sport," went to the seashore and had a great pavilion constructed.
While eating and drinking in that decorated pavilion, they engaged in playful touching of hands and feet;
however, they split into two factions and broke into a great quarrel. Then, one of them, finding no other club, [seized one] from a thicket of *eraka* grass.
He took a single blade of *eraka* grass. As soon as it was taken, it became an acacia pestle. With that, he beat the great multitude.
Then, for all the others, whatever they each took became an acacia pestle. Striking one another, they met with great destruction.
While they were being destroyed in that great slaughter, Vāsudeva, Baladeva, and their sister—
Añjanadevī and the chaplain—these four people—mounted the chariot and fled;
all the others were destroyed. As those four were fleeing by chariot, they reached the Kāḷamattikā forest.
For that wrestler Muṭṭhika, having made a vow, was reborn there as a *yakkha*; knowing that Baladeva had arrived there, he...
Having built a village and assumed the guise of a Malla, he wandered about roaring, bellowing, and slapping his arms, crying out, "Who wishes to fight?

Upon seeing him, Baladeva said, "Brother, I shall fight with him," and even as Vāsudeva tried to restrain him, he descended from his chariot, went before him, and began roaring, bellowing, and slapping his arms. Then—
He took it with his outstretched hand and ate it like a root-tuber.
Vāsudeva, learning that he had died, traveled all night with his sister and the chaplain;
at sunrise, having reached a frontier village, he sent his sister and the chaplain into the village with the command, "Cook food and bring it back," while he himself remained in one place.
He lay down concealed within the thicket.
Then a certain hunter named Jarā, seeing the thicket moving, thought, "There must be a boar here," and threw a spear, piercing his foot.
When [the Bodhisatta] asked, "Who has pierced me?", [the hunter] realized that it was a human being who had been struck.
Realizing this, he became afraid and began to flee. The king, restoring his mindfulness, stood up and called out, "Uncle, do not be afraid;
come here! When the man had approached, the king asked, "Who are you? He replied, "Sir, I am called Old Age.
The king thought, "The ancients have indeed prophesied that I would die when pierced by Old Age; undoubtedly, I must die today."
Having understood this, he said, "Uncle, do not fear; come, let me bind the wound for you. After having him bind the opening of the wound, he sent him away.
Intense pains arose, and he was unable to consume the food brought by the others.
Then, addressing them, he said, "Today I shall die; however, you are delicate, so you must live by performing other work."
“You will not be able [to do so]; learn this spell. Having taught them one spell and sent them away, he met his death right there.
Thus, with the exception of Añjanadevī, they all met their destruction.
Having delivered this Dhamma teaching, the Teacher said, “Lay follower, in this way the ancient wise ones [acted] upon the word of the wise...”
"Having heard this, they removed the grief for their own sons; do not worry," he said, and having proclaimed the Truths, he identified the Jātaka.
At the conclusion of the Truths, the lay follower was established in the fruit of stream-entry.
At that time, Rohiṇeyya was Ānanda, Vāsudeva was Sāriputta, the rest were the Buddha’s retinue, and Ghaṭapaṇḍita was none other than myself.
The sixteenth: The Commentary on the Ghaṭapaṇḍita Jātaka.
Thus ends the commentary on the meaning of the Jātakas of the Ten-Fold Collection (Dasakanipāta), adorned with sixteen birth stories.
The Summary of Birth Stories (Jātakuddāna): Catudvāra, Kaṇhuposa, Saṅkha, Bodhi, Dīpāyana;
Nigrodha, Takkala, Dhammapāla, Kukkuṭa, Kuṇḍalī.
The Cat’s Wheel, the Abundant, the Auspicious Jar, and the Sixteen.
The commentary on the Ten-Verse Chapter is finished.
11. The Eleven-Verse Chapter.
[455] 1. The Commentary on the Mātuposaka Jātaka.
“Because of that nāga’s absence”—this was spoken by the Teacher while dwelling at Jetavana concerning the monk Mātuposaka.
The story of the present is exactly like the story of the Sāma Jātaka. However, the Teacher addressed the monks:

“Monks, do not find fault with this monk. In the past, even wise beings born in the animal realm—who, separated from their mother, were wasting away for seven days without food—upon receiving food fit for a king, thought, ‘We will not eat without our mother,’ and only after seeing their mother did they take their meal.
Having said this, at their request, he related a story of the past.
In the past, when Brahmadatta was reigning in Bārāṇasī, the Bodhisatta was reborn in the region of the Himālaya in the womb of an elephant.
He was entirely white, handsome, beautiful to behold, pleasing, endowed with auspicious marks, and accompanied by a retinue of eighty thousand elephants.
He supported his aged mother, for she was blind. He [offered her] fruits and foods that were most delicious.
Having given [the elephants] to his mother, he sent them to her side. But the elephants, instead of giving them to her, ate them themselves.
Observing this, he learned of the situation and thought, "I shall abandon the herd and support my mother alone.
Then, during the night while the other elephants were unaware, he took his mother and went to the foot of Mount Caṇḍoraṇa, where he settled near a certain lotus pond.
Having placed his mother in a mountain cave, he supported her while remaining there.
Then a forest-dweller from Bārāṇasī, who was lost on the road and unable to determine his direction, lamented with a great cry. Hearing his voice, the Bodhisatta thought:
"This man is helpless; it would not be fitting for me, while standing here, to let him perish."
Having gone into his presence and seeing him fleeing out of fear, he asked, "O man, there is no danger for you because of me;
do not flee! Why are you wandering about lamenting? When he replied, "Sir, I am lost;
today is my seventh day," he said, "O man, do not be afraid; I shall place you on the path of men."
Having seated him upon his own back, he led him out from the forest and turned back.
That wicked man, thinking, "I will go to the city and inform the king," departed, creating the illusion of trees and mountains as he went, and arrived at Bārāṇasī.
At that time, the king’s auspicious elephant had passed away. The king said, "If anyone anywhere [should find] a riding-elephant..."
“A suitable elephant has been seen; let him describe it,” he proclaimed by beating the drum.
That man approached the king and said, “Your Majesty, I have seen a pure white, virtuous king of elephants fit to be your mount;
I shall show you the way. Send an elephant trainer along with me to [capture] him.”

“Have him captured,” he said. The king replied, “Very well,” and dispatched the elephant trainer with a large retinue along with that guide, commanding them: “Go into the forest, take this guide as your guide, and bring back the noble elephant described by him.
He went with him and saw the Bodhisatta having entered a lotus pond to feed. The Bodhisatta, too—
Seeing the elephant trainer, [he thought]: "This danger has not arisen from elsewhere; it must have arisen from that man.

Now, I am indeed possessed of great strength and capable of destroying even a thousand elephants; were I to become angry, I could annihilate the entire army and its mounts along with their territories.
However, if I should become angry, my virtue (sīla) would be broken. Therefore—"
Having resolved, "Even if I am struck with weapons today, I shall not become angry," he lowered his head and stood perfectly motionless.
The elephant trainer descended into the lotus pond, and seeing the perfection of his auspicious marks, cried out, "Come, my son!
He seized him with his trunk, which resembled a silver wreath, and reached Bārāṇasī on the seventh day. Meanwhile, the mother of the Bodhisattva, as her sons did not return, [became anxious].
“‘My son must have been taken away by kings, royal ministers, and others;
now, because of his absence, this forest grove will grow,’ she lamented and spoke these two verses:
‘In the absence of that Naga, the sallakī and kuṭaja trees have grown tall;’”
“Kuruvindas, karavīras, abhisas, and sāmās, and kaṇikāra trees blooming in a windless place.
‘Perhaps some gold-armored men will support the Naga King with their alms-food,
so that the king or a prince may put on his armor there undaunted.’”
In this context, "grown" means increased; he speaks thus by way of being beyond doubt, as there is no uncertainty here.
"Sallakī and kuṭaja" refers to *indasāla* trees and *kuṭaja* trees.
"Kuruvinda, karavīra, bhisā, and sāmā" means *kuruvinda* trees, the great grasses called *karavīra*, water-lily roots (*bhisā*), and *sāmā* grasses.
And she laments, "All these will now flourish. "In a windless place" means at the foot of a mountain.
"In bloom" means that even the *kaṇikāra* trees, which would not have bloomed had my son not broken off their branches and eaten them, will now be in flower—this is what is meant.
"Somewhere or other" means in some village or city. "Wearing golden armlets" refers to kings and great ministers adorned with golden ornaments.

“They nourish with a morsel” means that they sustain today the Nāga king who supports his mother with a well-prepared morsel of food fit for a king. “Where” means in which Nāga king the king sits down.
“He shall strike armor” means that having entered battle, he will strike and break the armor of his enemies. This is what is meant: “Where...”
“My son, seated there, whether he be a king or a prince, will fearlessly strike down the armor of his enemies;
today, those golden ornaments shall provide food for my son, that Nāga-king.
Even while on the way, the elephant trainer sent a message to the king. Upon hearing this, the king had the city decorated.
The elephant trainer led the Bodhisatta—whose body had been anointed with perfumes and who was fully adorned and prepared—to the elephant stable.
Having enclosed him with a variegated curtain, he informed the king. The king took various kinds of choice food and went there to offer it to the Bodhisatta;
however, he did not accept the morsel, saying, "I will not take fodder without my mother."
Then the King, entreating him, spoke this third verse:
“Take a morsel, O Naga; do not become emaciated, O Naga.
There are many royal duties that you, O Naga, must perform.”
Having heard that, the Bodhisatta spoke the fourth verse:
“She must surely be a wretched woman, blind and without a guide;
she strikes a stump with her foot while seeking a fierce, roaring mountain.”
In this regard, "Surely it is she," O Great King, means "it is surely she. "The wretched woman" means she is miserable due to the separation from her son.
"A stump" refers to a fallen tree trunk lying here and there.

"She strikes" means that, while lamenting, she surely beats it with her foot, striking it here and there with her foot. "She falls toward the mountain Caṇḍoraṇa" means she is heading toward the mountain Caṇḍoraṇa; [she falls] at the foot of the mountain.
The meaning is "struggling.
Then, questioning him, the king spoke the fifth verse:
"Who was that woman of yours, O Great Naga—blind and without a guide?"
“He stirs up a stump with his foot and falls upon a mountain of fierce lions.
The Bodhisatta spoke this sixth verse:
“She was my mother, O Great King, blind and without a guide.”
“He strikes a stump with his foot and leaps over a mountain like a fierce bull.
Having heard the meaning of this sixth verse, the king spoke the seventh verse while granting him his release:
“Release this great nāga, who supports his mother!”
"Let the Naga come together with his mother and all his kinsmen.
In this context, he who says "I support" is this Naga: "Great King, I support my blind mother;
without me, my mother will meet her end. Without her, I have no need for sovereignty."
"Today is the seventh day that my mother has not found food," he says.
Therefore, release this Great Naga quickly—he who supports his mother! Let him be reunited and come together with all his kinsmen, including his mother.
The eighth and ninth verses concern the Fully Enlightened One:
“The elephant, freed from his bonds, the great tusker having cast off his fetters,
rested for a moment and then went toward the mountain.
Then he went to the cool lotus pond frequented by elephants.”
“Having drawn water from the trunk of the elephant, sprinkle it upon your mother.
It is said that the nāga, having been released from his bonds, rested for a short while and taught the Dhamma to the king by means of the verses on the ten royal duties (*dasarājadhamma*).
Then, after giving the exhortation, “Be heedful, O Great King,” he was honored with perfumes, garlands, and other offerings by the great multitude.
Having departed from the city, he reached that lotus pond on that very day.

Thinking, "I will let my mother gather food first, and then I myself shall take some," he took a great quantity of lotus roots and stalks, filled his trunk with water, and emerged from his cave-dwelling.
He went into the presence of his mother, who was seated at the entrance of the cave, and because she had been without food for seven days, [he saw] his mother...
The Teacher spoke two verses to reveal that matter: he sprinkled water over [the body] from above for the sake of restoring sensation to the corpse.
The Bodhisatta’s mother also, perceiving that "the god is raining," spoke the tenth verse while reviling him:
"Who is this ignoble god who rains even out of season?"
“My own son has gone away, he who was my attendant.
Therein, “own-born” (atrāja) means born from oneself.
Then, comforting him, the Bodhisatta spoke the eleventh verse:
“Arise, mother! Why do you lie there? I, your own brother, have come.
I have been released by the illustrious King of Kāsi, the Prince of Videha.
In this passage, “I have come to you” means *āgato te ahaṃ*. “By the Prince of Videha” means by one endowed with wisdom (*ñāṇasampanna*). “Illustrious” means having a great retinue (*mahāparivāra*).
"Although I was seized by that king for the sake of being his auspicious state elephant, I have been released; now I have come into your presence—arise and take your fodder.
With a joyful heart, she offered her thanks to the king and spoke this concluding verse:
"May that king live long, the increaser of the kingdom of Kāsi!"
“He who has liberated my son is ever devoted to honoring his elders.

Then the king, having gained confidence in the Bodhisatta’s virtues, established a village not far from Naḷinī and instituted a regular provision for both the Bodhisatta and his mother. Later, when the Bodhisatta’s mother had passed away...
Having performed the funeral rites for her body, he went to the place called Kāraṇḍaka Assamapada.
In that location, five hundred seers who had descended from the Himālayas were dwelling; he provided them with their requisites.
The king had a stone statue made in the likeness of the Bodhisattva and established a great festival of honor for it. All the inhabitants of Jambudīpa [gathered] every year...
Having assembled, they made him the elephant-king named Hatthimaṅga.
Having delivered this Dhamma teaching and proclaimed the Truths, the Teacher identified the Jātaka.
At the conclusion of the Truths, the bhikkhu who supported his mother was established in the fruit of stream-entry. At that time, the king was Ānanda, and the wicked man was Devadatta.
Sāriputta was the elephant trainer; Mahāmāyā was the mother-elephant; and as for the Mātuposaka Nāga, he was none other than myself.
Thus ends the first commentary, the Mātuposaka Jātaka.
[456] 2. The Commentary on the Juṇha Jātaka.
"Listen to my words, O lord of men"—this was spoken by the Teacher while residing at Jetavana concerning the boon obtained by the Elder Ānanda.
For during the first twenty years after his enlightenment, the Blessed One had attendants who were not permanently assigned to him:
sometimes it was the Elder Nāgasamāla, sometimes Nāgita, sometimes Upavāṇa, sometimes Sunakkhatta, and sometimes Cunda.
At one time Nanda attended upon the Blessed One, at another time Sāgata, and at another time Meghiya. Then one day the Blessed One addressed the bhikkhus:
"Bhikkhus, I am now old; some bhikkhus, when told 'Go by this path,' go by another, and some place my bowl and robe on the ground. [Therefore, appoint] a regular attendant..."
“Know me as one monk,” he said. “Venerable Sir, I shall attend upon you; I shall attend upon you!
they replied, raising their joined palms to their heads. But the Elder Sāriputta and the others refused, saying, “Your aspiration has reached its fulfillment;
enough. Then the monks said to the Elder Ānanda, “Friend, you should request the position of attendant.”
They said: "Venerable sir, if the Blessed One does not give me the robe he has obtained for himself,
does not give me almsfood, does not allow me to dwell in the same fragrant chamber, and does not go with me to the invitation,
yet if the Blessed One goes to the invitation accepted by me, and if I [am able to come] from across kingdoms and across districts..."
"I shall be able to see the assembly that has come to see the Blessed One at the very moment they arrive;
whenever a doubt arises in me, I shall be able to approach the Blessed One at that very moment;
and if the Blessed One speaks the Dhamma in my absence, he will speak it to me upon my arrival"—thus [I shall serve] the Blessed One.
“I shall attend upon you. Thus he requested these eight boons—four refusals and four entreaties—and the Blessed One granted them to him.

From then on, for twenty-five years, he was a constant attendant. Having attained placement among the foremost in five respects—perfection in the Agamas, perfection in realization, perfection in past causes, perfection in inquiry regarding his own welfare, and [perfection in inquiry regarding the welfare of others]—he...

Endowed with these seven perfections—perfection of dwelling at a sacred site, perfection of wise attention, and perfection of the Buddha’s supportive condition—he received the eightfold gift of boons from the presence of the Buddha.
Consequently, he became renowned in the Buddha’s dispensation and as prominent as the moon in the midst of the sky. Then, one day, the monks began a discussion in the Hall of Truth...
They raised the discussion, saying, "Friends, the Tathāgata has gratified the Elder Ānanda with a boon.
The Teacher, having arrived, asked, "Monks, for what discussion are you gathered here now?
When they replied, "For this very one," he said, "Monks, it is not only now that I have gratified Ānanda with a boon; in the past as well, I gratified him with whatever [he desired]."
"Whenever he asked for this or that, I gave it to him," she said, and related a story of the past.
In the past, when Brahmadatta was reigning in Benares, the Bodhisatta was his son, named Prince Juṇha.
Having mastered his arts at Takkasilā and having given the teacher his fee, one night during the darkness...
Having departed from his teacher’s house, he was hurrying toward his own dwelling when he saw a certain brahmin returning to his residence after wandering for alms;
not seeing him, the prince struck him with his arm and broke his bowl of food.
The brahmin fell down and cried out. Out of compassion, the prince turned back and took him by the hand.
Having taken it, he made him stand up. The brahmin said, "My dear son, you have broken my alms-bowl;
give me the price for the meal. The prince replied, "Brahmin, I am not able to give you the price for the meal now;
however, I am Prince Juṇha, the son of King Kāsika. When I am established in the kingdom, come and [take] wealth from me."
Having said, "You should ask," the youth, having completed his training, paid homage to his teacher and went to Bārāṇasī, where he displayed his craft to his father.
His father thought, "I have seen my son alive; I shall see him even when he has become king," and so he consecrated him in the kingdom.
He became known as King Juṇha and ruled the kingdom with righteousness. When the brahmin heard this news, [he thought], "Now..."
Thinking, “I shall fetch my master’s meal,” he went to Bārāṇasī.
Seeing the king making a circumambulation of the decorated city, he stood on a high spot, extended his hand, and offered a blessing of victory.
But the king passed by without even looking at him. Realizing that he had not been seen by him, the brahmin began to speak:
He spoke the first verse:
“Listen to my words, O Lord of Men; I have arrived here for a purpose.
It is said, O Best of Bipeds, that one should not pass by a brahmin who is standing on the road.”
In this context, "when you are weary," O Great King, he indicates: "When you are weary, I have come here for one specific purpose;
I have not come here without a reason. Regarding "the traveler": it means one who has arrived on a journey. "It should be gone" means that the wise do not say, nor do they speak thus:
"One should go without even looking back at the requesting brahmin who has arrived on his journey."
Having heard his words, the king restrained the elephant with a goad tipped with adamant and spoke this second verse:
“I hear you, stay and speak, O Brahmā! Tell me for what purpose you have come here.
What goal do you desire from me, that you have come here, O Brahmā? Pray, tell me that.”
In this context, *iṅgha* is a particle used in the sense of an exhortation.
Following that, the remaining verses were spoken by way of the brahmin’s speech and the king’s reply:
“Give me five excellent villages, seven hundred female slaves, and seven hundred oxen;”
“Give me a thousand gold coins and two wives who are my equals.
“Is it through ascetic power, brahmin, that you are so formidable? Or is it through mantras, brahmin, that you are so versatile?
Do you have some yakṣas under your command, or do you understand my purpose and what must be done?”
“I have no ascetic power, nor do I possess spells; there are no *yakkhas* whatsoever who are obedient to me.
I do not even know your purpose, O Kappa, though we were once merely acquaintances in the past.
This is my first time seeing you; I did not know you existed before this.”
"Tell me this matter when asked: when and where did our meeting take place?
"In the delightful city of the King of Gandhāra, O Lord, we dwelt in Takkasilā;
there, in the darkness of the night, shoulder to shoulder, we brushed against one another."
“Having stood there together, O Lord of Men, we exchanged friendly greetings on that occasion.
That alone was our meeting; after that, there was neither more nor less.
Whenever, O Brahmā, a meeting with a true person occurs among human beings...”
The wise do not destroy their friendships or associations, nor even what was done in the past.
It is only fools who destroy their friendships and associations, as well as what was done in the past.
Even much that is done for fools perishes, for fools are indeed ungrateful by nature.
“The wise do not destroy their associations or intimacies, nor do they forget what was done in the past.
Even a small favor done for the wise is not lost, for the wise are truly grateful for what has been well-done.
‘I give you five excellent villages, seven hundred female slaves, and seven hundred oxen.’”
“I give you a thousand gold coins and two wives equal to yourself.
“Thus it is for those who meet, O King, like the moon, the king of stars, among the constellations.
Just as a garment of Kāsī cloth fills [its wearer], so too have I obtained union with you today.”
In this context, "one like me" (*sādisī*) means: "Give me a wife who is my equal, one and the same as myself in terms of physical beauty, birth, lineage, and status—a wife of great renown.
