"Of terrifying appearance" (*bhiṃsarūpo*): he asks, "O Brahmin, do you possess the ascetic practice (*tapokamma*) known as strength of form, virtue, conduct, and qualities?
"Do you have spells" (*mantā nu te*): or rather, "Do you have various kinds of spells that accomplish all goals?"
"They exist. "Obedient ones" means those who carry out one's word, some *yakkhas* who grant whatever is desired;
he asks, "Do you know of any purpose of mine that was accomplished by them?
"Merely a meeting" means he says, "There was previously a mere encounter with you. "Of me who knows" means of me who is aware.
"This was the first time I saw you. "I do not recall that" means I do not remember it.
"In the thick darkness" means on a night of dense gloom. "Standing there" means we stood in that place where shoulder met shoulder and exchanged greetings;
"we exchanged greetings there" means we conversed in that very spot about matters worthy of recollection. I...
“I said to you, ‘My alms-bowl was broken by you;
give me the cost of the meal,’ and you replied, ‘I cannot give you the cost of the meal now; however, I am Prince Juṇha, the son of King Kāsika.
When I have been established in kingship, come and ask me for wealth. Thus we engaged in this conversation that brings one back to mind.”
He said: "O King, she was merely our acquaintance; that is, she was merely an acquaintance of ours to one another, meaning she was a friend for only a single moment.
'From then on' means that after that momentary state of friendship, neither before nor after, at any time, has there ever been such a thing as an acquaintance between us."

“O Brahmin, those called ‘wise’ do not lose their sense of gratitude for whatever service was previously rendered to them, whether it be a brief acquaintance or a long-standing friendship. ‘Even much’ means even a great deal. ‘Those whose nature is ungrateful’:
because fools are by nature ungrateful, therefore even what has been done for them in abundance is lost among them—this is the meaning. ‘Those whose nature is grateful’ means well...”
They are by nature grateful. Here too, as there, the word *hi* (for) has the sense of a reason.
"I give to you"—saying this, the king spoke while giving whatever was requested by the brahmin. "Thus it is for the virtuous"—the brahmin said this while offering words of thanksgiving to the king;
such is the nature of the meeting and association of even a single instance with the virtuous, the good people. "Like the king of the stars" (the moon).
Here, the letter *ra* is merely a grammatical particle (*nipātamatta*). "Among the stars" means in the midst of the host of stars. "Lord of Kāsi" is an address to the king.

This is what is meant: "O King, just as the moon, the sovereign of the kingdom of Kāsi, stands among the stars surrounded by the host of stars and waxes full from the first day of the lunar fortnight until the full moon, so too do I today [wax] through the excellent villages and other gifts bestowed upon me by you."
"I am fulfilling [my desire]," he said. By her saying "Yes," he meant that although their union had been obtained by him previously, it was as if it had not been obtained;
however, because his heart's wish has now been fulfilled, their union with her is truly "obtained.
Thus he said, "The fruit of my friendship with you has been realized. The Bodhisatta bestowed great honor upon him.
Having delivered this Dhamma teaching, the Teacher said, “Monks, it is not only now that I have satisfied Ānanda with a boon;
I did so in the past as well,” and he then identified the Jātaka: “At that time, the brahmin was Ānanda, and I myself was the king.”
The second *Juṇhājātaka* commentary.
[457] 3. The *Dhammadevaputtajātaka* commentary:
"I am a bringer of fame, a doer of merit"—this was spoken by the Teacher while dwelling at Jetavana, concerning Devadatta’s sinking into the earth.
He spoke concerning this. For at that time, the monks had raised a discussion in the Hall of Truth, saying, "Friends, Devadatta, having come into conflict with the Tathāgata, has entered the earth.
When the Teacher arrived and asked, "Monks, about what discussion are you gathered here now? and they replied, "About this very matter," he said, "It is not only now that he [did so]."
“Monks, having struck my Wheel of the Victor, he has entered the earth;
even in the past, having struck the Wheel of Dhamma, he entered the earth and was destined for the Avīci hell,” he said, and then related a story of the past.
In the past, while Brahmadatta was reigning in Benares, the Bodhisatta was the Dhamma [Deva] in the world of the Kāmāvacara gods.
Devadatta was reborn as a son of the gods named Adhamma. Among them, Dhamma—
adorned with celestial ornaments and mounted upon a magnificent divine chariot, surrounded by a host of nymphs— would eat his evening meal among humans on the full-moon uposatha day in villages,
market towns, districts, and royal capitals, while people sat at their respective doorways engaged in pleasant conversation.
Standing in the sky, he circumambulated Jambudīpa, exhorting the people to the ten courses of wholesome action, saying:

“Refrain from the ten unwholesome courses of action, such as the taking of life, and fulfill the duty of honoring your mother, the duty of honoring your father, and the dharma of the three types of good conduct; thus, being destined for heaven, you shall enjoy great glory.”
Dhamma, however, causes Jambudīpa to turn to the right by exhorting [beings] to the ten courses of wholesome action in the manner beginning with, "Kill living beings.

But the deity Adhamma causes it to turn to the left by exhorting them to the ten courses of unwholesome action in the manner beginning with, "Kill living beings. Then their chariots came face to face in the sky.
Thereupon, their retinues asked, "Whose are you? Whose are you? and replied, "We are Dhamma's; we are Adhamma's."
Having spoken thus, they departed from the path and split into two. Then Dhamma addressed Adhamma, saying: "Friend, you are Adhamma and I am Dhamma;
the path is suitable for me. Make way for my chariot and give me the path.
Thus he spoke the first verse:
“I am the maker of fame, I am the maker of merit; I am always praised by recluses and brahmins.
I am the Dhamma worthy of the path, honored by gods and men; give me the path, not the non-Dhamma.
In this context, “maker of fame” means I am the giver of glory to gods and men. The same applies to the second phrase. “Always praised” means constantly lauded and eternally extolled. Following that—
“Having mounted the firm vehicle of the Dhamma, I am powerful and not one who is weak.
For what reason would I give you today the path of Dhamma that has never been given before?
Indeed, in the past the Dhamma appeared, and afterwards unrighteousness (adhamma) arose in the world.”
“O eldest, best, and eternal one, step aside from the path for the sake of the youngest.
“It is not by begging, nor because you are worthy, nor because of your fitness that I would give you the path.
Let there be a battle between us both today; he who is victorious in the battle shall have the path.”
“I have pervaded every direction; I am of great power, immeasurable fame, and incomparable.
Endowed with all virtues, how will you, who are unrighteousness (adhamma), overcome me, who am the Dhamma?
Indeed, iron is struck down by gold, but gold does not strike down iron.”
“If unrighteousness is struck down today by righteousness, it will be as beautiful to behold as gold.
‘If you, though powerful in battle, have abandoned unrighteousness, then your elders and teachers are not in vain.
I grant you the path through what is dear and what is not dear, and I forgive even the harsh words you have spoken to me.’”
These six verses were spoken by way of question and answer between them.
Therein, [the question is]: "For what reason today do you give? I am indeed Adhamma; having mounted the chariot of the vehicle of Adhamma, I am fearless and powerful.
[The answer is]: "For what reason, O Dhamma, do you give today? I give to you the path that has never before been given to anyone."
"Formerly" means that in the time of the first aeon (*paṭhamakappa*), in this world, the dharma of the ten paths of wholesome action appeared first, and unrighteousness (*adhamma*) appeared later.
"And I am the elder" means: because I was born earlier, I am the elder, the best, and the ancient one;
you, however, are the younger. Therefore he says, "Depart from my path. "Nor am I suitable for you" means: for I am not... [to you].
"I would give the way to one who asks with fitting words and by taking the right path.
"Anuvisaṭo" means that I am spread out, renowned, and well-known throughout all directions—the four cardinal and the four intermediate points—by virtue of my own qualities.
"Lohena" means with an iron club. "Hañchatī" means he will strike. "Tvaṃ yuddhabalo adhammā" means if you are one who relies on the strength of battle, you are unrighteous.
"Adhamma. As for "elders and venerables," if you do not have [the thought], "These are elders;
these are venerable, wise ones," then the meaning of "whether by the dear or the undear" is that even when giving to one who is dear or one who is undear, you give the path as if to a beloved person.
However, at the very moment this verse was spoken by the Bodhisatta, Adhamma, unable to remain upon the chariot, [vanished].
Falling head-first upon the earth, when a fissure opened in the ground, he went and was reborn right in the Avīci hell.
Having understood this matter, the Blessed One, having attained full enlightenment, spoke the remaining verses:
“Having heard these words, Adhamma fell head-first with his feet upwards;”
“If I, seeking battle, do not find a fight, to that extent unrighteousness is defeated.
Having conquered the power of battle with the strength of patience, having struck down and destroyed unrighteousness upon the earth,
he— joyful, exceedingly powerful, and firm in his commitment to truth— ascended his chariot and set forth by the very path.
“Those by whom their mother, father, and ascetics and brahmins have not been honored in their own home—
they cast off this physical body right here, and with the breakup of the body, they go to hell,
like one fallen through unrighteousness with head downward.”
“Those by whom mother, father, and ascetics and brahmins are well-honored in their own home—
they cast off the physical body right here, and with the breakup of the body, they go to a happy destination,
just as one who has mounted a chariot driven by Dhamma.”
In that regard, "seeking battle" was his lamentation; it is said that while he was thus lamenting, he fell and entered the earth.
"To this extent," monks, as far as he had entered the earth, to that extent unrighteousness (*adhamma*) is said to have been destroyed.
"The power of patience," monks, refers to how unrighteousness, having thus entered the earth, was overcome by the power of endurance and patience.

Having conquered that army of battle, having slain it, having struck it down and cast it upon the ground, he—being "vitta" (wealthy) by virtue of his wealth of merit (*vittajātatā*)—mounted his own chariot and departed by way of the path;
thus was Saccanikkama, possessed of such exertion (*parakkama*), the son of Dhammadeva. "Asammānitā" means unhonored.
"Sarīradehaṃ" means having cast off the body known as the physical frame (*sarīra*) in this very world. "Nirayaṃ"—into hell.

"They go" means that those wicked persons in whose house these individuals worthy of honor are not honored—just as unrighteousness falls headlong, so too do they go headlong to hell; this is the meaning.

"They go to a happy destination" means that those in whose [house] these are honored, such wise ones, just as one who has mounted a chariot according to the Dhamma has gone to the world of the gods, so too do they go to a happy destination.
Having thus taught the Dhamma, the Teacher said, "Monks, it is not only now;
in the past as well, Devadatta, having opposed me, was swallowed up by the earth," and he then identified the Jātaka:
"At that time, the god Adhamma was Devadatta, and his retinue was Devadatta's retinue; but Dhamma was I myself, and his retinue was none other than the Buddha's retinue."
The third explanation: the Dhammadevaputtajātakavaṇṇanā.
[458] 4. The Explanation of the Udayajātakavaṇṇanā:
"Sitting alone..."—this was spoken by the Teacher while dwelling at Jetavana, concerning a certain monk who was disenchanted with the religious life.
The background story will be made clear in the Kusajātakaya. However, the Teacher asked that bhikkhu, "Is it true, bhikkhu, that you are disenchanted?
When he replied, "It is true, Bhante," the Teacher said, "Bhikkhu, why have you become disenchanted after going forth in such a liberating teaching under the influence of the defilements?
In the past, wise men [lived] in the prosperous city of Surundhana, twelve yojanas in extent..."

"Even while exercising sovereignty and dwelling for seven hundred years in a single chamber with a woman resembling a celestial nymph, he did not break his sense-faculties or look upon her out of greed," he said, and then related a story of the past.
In the past, in the city of Surundhana in the kingdom of Kāsi, a king of Kāsi reigned; he had neither son nor daughter.
He said to his queens, "Pray for sons. The chief queen, having accepted the king's word, did so accordingly.
At that time, the Bodhisatta, descending from the Brahma-world, was conceived in the womb of that very king’s chief queen.
Because he caused the hearts of the great multitude to swell with joy at the moment of his birth, he was given the name Udayabhadda.

They gave him that name. At the time when the prince began to walk on foot, another being, having passed away from the Brahma-world, was reborn in the womb of one of the king’s queens as a girl; they gave her the name Udayabhaddā.
When the prince reached maturity, he attained perfection in all the arts, yet he remained a celibate from birth.
Even in his dreams he did not know the act of sexual intercourse, nor did his mind cling to the defilements.
The king, desiring to anoint his son in the kingdom, sent a message saying, "It is now time for the prince to enjoy the pleasures of sovereignty;
I shall provide him with female dancers as well. The Bodhisatta replied, "I have no need for kingship; my mind does not cling to the defilements."

Having been refused again and again despite being urged repeatedly, he had a golden image of a woman made out of red Jambunada gold and sent it to his parents with the message: "If I can obtain such a woman, I shall accept the kingdom.
They had that golden figure paraded throughout the whole of Jambudīpa; finding no woman of such appearance, they adorned Udayabhaddā and sent her.
They placed it before him. It stood there, outshining that golden image.
Then, even though they were unwilling, they made the half-sister Princess Udayabhaddā the chief queen and consecrated the Bodhisatta in the kingdom.
Yet both of them lived only the life of celibacy.
In a later period, following the passing of his parents, the Bodhisatta reigned as king.
Although the two had dwelt together in the same womb, they did not look upon one another, having restrained their faculties out of fear of greed; rather, they made this agreement:
"Whichever of us dies first shall come from the place where he has been reborn and say, 'I have been reborn in such-and-such a place.'"
"Let him announce it," they made this agreement. Then the Bodhisatta passed away seven hundred years after his consecration.
There was no other king; Udayabhaddā alone exercised authority, while the ministers governed the kingdom.
At the very moment of his passing, the Bodhisatta attained the status of Sakka in the Tāvatiṃsa heaven, and due to the greatness of his glory, he was able to recollect [the past] for seven days.
He was unable [to see her]. Thus, after seven hundred human years had passed, he reflected and thought:
"I shall test Udayabhaddā, the king’s daughter, with wealth, cause her to let out a lion’s roar, teach her the Dhamma, release my promise, and then return.
At that time, it is said, the lifespan of humans was ten thousand years. On that very day, the king’s daughter also...

During the night, when the doors were closed and guards stationed, she sat alone and motionless on the upper floor of the excellent seven-storied palace, in her decorated bedchamber, reflecting upon her own virtue.
Then Sakka, taking a golden bowl filled with gold coins, arrived and appeared right there in the bedchamber; standing to one side, he [conversed] with her.
Conversing with him, he spoke this first verse:
“Seated alone, pure and with limbs well-restrained, having ascended the palace, you of blameless form;
I entreat you, O one with eyes like those of a kinnara, let us both dwell together for this single night.”
In this context, "pure" (*sucī*) means she was dressed in pure garments. "With well-restrained limbs" (*saññatūrū*) means her thighs were properly set;

what is meant is that, having composed her posture, she sat all alone while dressed in pure garments. "With blameless limbs" (*aninditaṅgī*) means from the tips of her feet up to the crown of her hair, her body was irreproachable, having attained the highest degree of beauty.
"With eyes like those of a *kinnara*" (*kinnaranettacakkhū*) [refers to] the three circles and the five...
Because they were adorned with serene confidence, they were endowed with eyes resembling those of *kinnaras*.
"For this one night" means: "May we dwell together for this single night today in this bedchamber decorated with ornaments"—thus she requested.
Thereupon, the princess spoke two verses:
“This city has its inner moats strewn [with corpses], its towers and ramparts are firm, and it is guarded by those with swords in hand;
it is difficult to enter. There is no entry for anyone, whether young or old.”
“Now, for what reason do you desire union with me?

In this context, “with its moats strewn within” means that this city of Surundhana, twelve yojanas in extent, has its inner moats—whether water moats, mud moats, or dry moats—strewn [with corpses], and is thus called “with its moats strewn within. “With strong watchtowers and battlements” means...
It was equipped with very firm watchtowers and gatehouses.
"Guarded by ten thousand warriors with weapons in hand" means it was protected by ten thousand soldiers bearing arms.
"This city is difficult to enter" means that neither this entire city built within its walls nor my own residence-city could be entered by anyone. And as for the arrival...

"In this place, at this time, there is no arrival of anyone—young, or having reached the prime of youth, or a warrior endowed with strength, or anyone else—even if they were coming with a great gift. You meet [with me] here;
for what reason, then, do you desire a meeting with me at this very hour?"
Then Sakka spoke the fourth stanza:
“I am a yakkha, O beautiful lady, and I have come into your presence;
gladden me, O blessed one, and I shall give you a full bronze bowl.”

The meaning of this is: "O beautiful one, I am a single son of the gods who has come here through divine power; please delight me today by satisfying me, and I shall give you this golden bowl filled with gold coins.
Having heard that, the princess spoke the fifth verse:
"I do not desire another, even if he were a god, a yakkha, or a human, surpassing Udaya."
“Go then, O powerful Yakkha; having gone, do not return again.
The meaning of this is: “O King of Devas, I desire nothing other than you, whether you be a Deva or a Yakkha, beyond this rising [of your presence].
Therefore, go indeed; do not remain here. I have no need for the gift brought by you; go!”
"And do not return to this place again.
Having heard her lion’s roar, he remained there as if having vanished, appearing as though he had already departed.
On the following day, at that very same time, taking a silver bowl filled with gold coins, he conversed with her.
He spoke the sixth verse:
“That which is the supreme delight of those who enjoy sensual pleasures, on account of which beings behave recklessly—do not let that delight overcome you, O Sucimhitā;
I give you a bowl of silver full to the brim.”

The meaning of this is as follows: "O Bhaddā, Princess, do not lose that supreme delight called the pleasure of sexual union among beings who enjoy sensual pleasures—that delight for the sake of which beings practice the irregularities of bodily misconduct and so forth.
O Bhaddā, you of pure smiles and charming laughter, I too have not come here with empty hands."
"Yesterday I brought a golden bowl filled with gold coins; today I bring a silver bowl.
Here, I give you this silver bowl filled with gold.
The princess thought, "If he continues to engage in such conversation, he will come back again and again; I shall not speak with him now. She said nothing at all.
Sakka, knowing that she had not told him, vanished right there.
On the following day, at that same hour, he took a copper bowl filled with kahāpaṇa coins and said, "Bhadde, satisfy me with sensual pleasure;
I will give you this copper bowl full of kahāpaṇa coins. Upon seeing him, the princess spoke the seventh verse:
“A man, by means of wealth, entices a woman where he sets his desire;
yet your divine nature is contrary to this, for you seek even a small thing that is directly before you.
The meaning of this is: O man, you are dull-witted. For a man indeed, when enticing a woman with wealth for the sake of sensual pleasure—
Persuading her, he extolled and praised whatever would arouse desire in the woman, tempting her with even greater wealth, saying: "But this divine nature of yours is perverse;
for you, whom I witnessed in person, accepted less from me—on the first day, having brought a golden bowl full of gold, on the second day, a golden bowl full of..."
"Three days ago you brought a silver bowl, and today you bring a copper bowl full of kahāpaṇas.
Hearing this, Sakka said, "O noble princess, I am a clever merchant; I do not pursue profit without purpose.
If you were to increase in either lifespan or beauty, I would bring back your gift after having increased it."
"But you yourself are declining; therefore, I too am losing my wealth," he said, and then recited these three verses:
"O fair-limbed one, both life-span and beauty in the world of men are waning for mortals;
because of that very fading of beauty, your wealth also wanes, for today you are more aged."
“As I behold you thus, O illustrious princess,
your beauty wanes as the days and nights pass by.
Even at this very age, O wise princess— ”
"You should lead the holy life; thus you will become even more beautiful.
In this context, "wastes away" means that one diminishes like water poured into a strainer.
For in the human world, beings indeed waste away day by day in terms of their lifespan, their complexion, and their visual acuity and other faculties. "One who is older than I"—this refers to me.
For the life that was proceeding on the day you first arrived did not reach the day before yesterday;
it ceased right there, as if cut by an axe. That which was proceeding the day before yesterday did not reach today;
it ceased even then, as if cut by an axe. Therefore, you have become older today. "So it is for me"—let alone the day before yesterday or the day before that.
"And yet, even as I watch you right now, your complexion is fading away.
'With the passing of days and nights' means that from this point forward, as the nights and days elapse, with the passing of those days and nights, you will go to a state of non-existence;
this is what he shows. 'By this very process,' [he says]: therefore, O lady, if you, by this very process, [should lose] this golden-colored body..."
"Even while remaining unshaven by the king, you should practice the noble conduct; having gone forth, you should perform the duty of a recluse.
'Bhiyyo vaṇṇavatī siyā' means you would become even more beautiful.
Then the princess spoke the other verse:
“Gods do not age like humans, and there are no wrinkles on their limbs;
I ask you, O powerful yakkha, how is the bodily form of the gods?
In this context, “bodily form” (*sarīradeho*) means the body designated as a physical frame; he says, “I ask you this: how is it that the bodies of the gods do not age?”
Then, as he was speaking to her, Sakka recited the following verse:
“The gods do not age as humans do, nor are there wrinkles upon their limbs;
day by day their divine radiance increases, as do their vast enjoyments.”
In this context, "just as humans" means that humans age through their physical form, complexion, wealth, and the clarity of their eyes and other faculties;
gods do not age in such a way. For on their limbs there are no wrinkles, and their bodies are like polished golden plates.
"Day by day" means every single day. "Even more" means even more than those [humans], their divine...

There is beauty and abundant wealth; among humans, the decline of physical form is a witness to the state of being long-born, whereas among the devas there is an excellence of surpassing beauty and an excellence of surpassing retinues.
Thus, this world of the devas is by nature free from decline.
Therefore, you should go forth into homelessness before reaching old age; for [this world] is of a nature subject to decline.
"Having passed away from the human world, you will go to such a celestial realm, a state from which there is no falling back.
Having heard this praise of the celestial realm, she asked about the path leading there, reciting the next verse:
"Why is it that these many people here are afraid, and why is the path said to have so many different stations?"
“I ask you, O powerful Yakkha: standing where does one not fear the world beyond?
Therein, “What is it that they fear here, O King of Gods?”—he asks this: what is it that these various people, divided into kṣatriyas and so forth, fear;
by fear of what do they, being of a nature prone to decline, fail to go from the human world to the world of the gods? “The path”—this is the path leading to the world of the gods.
Here, however, having brought forward the word "what," the question "which" (*ko*) should be asked. This is the meaning here:

"Which one, of the many paths to the world of the gods proclaimed by the wise, is it?"—that is to say, which one has been spoken of? "Established where? means: established upon which path while going to the next world does one not fear?
Then, as he was speaking to her, Sakka recited this other verse:
“Having rightly directed speech and mind, and committing no evil deeds with the body;
dwelling in a house with abundant food and drink, being faithful, gentle, sharing, and generous;”
“Being inclusive, gentle, and soft-spoken—one established in this does not fear the next world.

Its meaning is as follows: O Bhaddā, one who has properly settled speech and mind, who does no evil with the body, and who lives in a house abundant with food, drink, and many things worthy of being given, having undertaken these ten courses of wholesome action—
Possessing faith that "there is a result of giving," with a gentle mind, he is one who shares through the practice of giving and distribution.
When those who have gone forth go wandering for alms and say [the traditional words], he is "one who knows that speech" by providing them with the necessary requisites.
He is "one who gathers" through the four bases of sympathy; he is "gentle" through pleasant speech and "smooth-tongued" through his polished manner of speaking.
“Being gentle in speech and established here in such a mass of virtues, one does not fear when going to the next world.
Then, having heard those words of his, the princess offered praise and spoke this other verse:
“You instruct me, O Yakkha, just as a mother or a father would.”
“Of noble appearance, I ask you: who indeed are you, O fair youth?

The meaning of this is: “Just as parents instruct their children, so do you instruct me. Of noble appearance, having attained such beauty, who indeed are you, young man, with a body so exceedingly tall?
Thereupon, the Bodhisatta spoke the following verse:
“I am Udaya, O beautiful one; having been bound by a promise, I have come here.
I bid you farewell and depart; I am released from your bond.
The meaning of this is: in a previous existence, in the realm of the Thirty-three, I was your husband named Udaya, O lady of lovely appearance.
"Having been reborn as Sakka, I have not come here under the influence of defilements;
rather, thinking 'I shall test him and then release my promise,' I have come out of regard for that promise because it was made previously. Now, having addressed him, I depart;
I am released from your promise."

The princess, having taken heart, said, "My lord, you are King Udayabhadda," and as she shed a stream of tears, she spoke this second verse: "I cannot live without you; instruct me so that I may dwell in your presence."
“If you are indeed Udaya, come here out of love for our agreement;
instruct me, O prince, so that there may be a reunion once again.
Then, instructing him, the Great Being spoke these four verses:
“Time passes away, and likewise the opportune moment; there is no certainty, for beings surely fall away.
The body decays and is impermanent; do not be negligent regarding the arising of the Dhamma.
Even if the entire earth were filled with wealth, belonging to one person alone and not shared by another...”
Even one who is not yet free from passion abandons that [body]; therefore, do not be negligent when the time has come, but practice the Dhamma.
“Mother and father, brothers, and even a wife purchased with wealth—even they abandon one another;
therefore, do not be negligent when the time has come, but practice the Dhamma.”
“Knowing the body to be food for others, both the happy and miserable states in *saṃsāra*;
knowing it to be but a temporary dwelling—do not be negligent regarding the arising [of suffering]; practice the Dhamma.
In this context, *atipatati* means it falls away excessively; it passes by swiftly. *Vaya* refers to all three stages, beginning with the first stage of life.
“Time; likewise the moment”: even the moments of arising, presence, and dissolution pass away in that very same way.
By both [phrases], he shows that the life-process (*āyusaṅkhāra*) of these beings—broken apart by both—is like a river with a swift current, passing quickly without turning back.
“There is no standing place”: even with the aspiration, “May the arisen formations remain after having reached their peak,” there is no such thing for them.
"There is no certainty; it is certain and absolute that all beings, beginning with the Buddha, the Blessed One, pass away.
Thus, develop mindfulness of death, thinking: 'Death is certain, life is uncertain. By this he shows:
"It wastes away" means that even this body, though golden-hued, surely decays; know it thus. Therefore, "do not be negligent."
"O Udayabhaddā, do not fall into negligence; being diligent, practice the Dhamma of the ten courses of wholesome action.
"Kasiṇā" means "entire. "If it belongs to one alone" means that if it belongs to a single king, then in that very person alone it would not be dependent on another.
"And he abandons even that, being one who is not free from passion" means that a person ruled by craving is unsatisfied even with such glory and, at the time of death—
One who has not yet abandoned passion likewise leaves them behind. Thus, he illustrates that one should understand the insatiable nature of craving.
And as for those others—mother leaving son, son leaving mother; father leaving son, son leaving father; brother leaving sister, sister leaving brother;
wife leaving husband, husband leaving wife—these leave one another and become separate. Such is the case for beings.
It illuminates the meaning: "Know the separation from various states of existence.
"The food of others" means the food of other beings, such as crows and the like.

"A temporary dwelling" refers to both this human state within this saṃsāra, which is a happy destination, and the animal state, which is a miserable destination; both of these are called a "temporary dwelling."
"Knowing this, do not be negligent; practice the Dhamma.
For these beings, the meeting together in one place after coming from various places is limited; these beings dwell together for only a short time. Therefore, be heedful.
Thus the Great Being gave her this exhortation. She too, having gained confidence through his discourse on the Dhamma, spoke this concluding verse in praise of him:
“Excellent is what you have said, O Yakkha: short is the life of mortals;
it is meager and trifling, and it is joined with suffering.
Therefore, I shall go forth alone, abandoning Kasi, the source of my delight.”
In this context, when he says, "Excellent! Short is the life of mortals," this king of the gods speaks excellently. For what reason?
Because this [life] is both meager and painful, devoid of satisfaction; it is limited and not extensive, being of short duration.
For if it were to persist for a long time even while being meager, or if it were to be pleasant even while being limited, then this—
"But [this life] is indeed miserable and limited, yet it is joined with and encompassed by the entire suffering of the cycle of existence (*saṃsāra*). "Sāham" means "I.
"Surundhana": she said, "Having abandoned both the city of Surundhana and the kingdom of Kāsi, I shall go forth alone.
After the Bodhisatta had given her this exhortation, he returned to his own place. On the following day, she [entrusted] the kingdom to the ministers...
Having concealed [her identity], she went forth as an *isi* in a delightful park right within the city;
having practiced the Dhamma, at the end of her lifespan, she was reborn in the Tāvatiṃsa heaven as a female attendant to the Bodhisatta.
Having delivered this teaching on the Dhamma, the Teacher proclaimed the Truths and identified the Jātaka. At the conclusion of the Truths—
The monk who was distressed established himself in the fruit of stream-entry. At that time, the king’s daughter was Rāhula’s mother, and Sakka was none other than myself.
This concludes the commentary on the Udaya Jātaka, the fourth.
[459] 5. The Commentary on the Pānīya Jātaka.
"A friend for a friend..."—this was spoken by the Teacher while dwelling at Jetavana concerning the subduing of the defilements.
For on one occasion, five hundred lay companions residing in Sāvatthī, having heard the Tathāgata’s teaching of the Dhamma, went forth into homelessness.
The fully ordained nuns, while staying on a mat with its fringes turned inward, indulged in thoughts of sensual desire at the time of midnight.

Everything should be understood according to the method already explained above. However, by the Blessed One’s command, when the Venerable Ānanda had assembled the community of bhikkhus, the Teacher sat down on the prepared seat and, addressing them without naming anyone specifically, said: "They indulged in thoughts of sensual desire."
Without omitting anything, but by way of a comprehensive summary, he said: "Monks, there is no such thing as a 'minor' defilement;

rather, whatever defilements arise, they must be restrained by a monk. In ancient times, even before the Buddha appeared, the wise of old restrained their defilements and attained the knowledge of Pacceka-Buddhahood.
Having said this, he related a story of the past.

In the past, while Brahmadatta was reigning in Benares, two friends from a certain village in the kingdom of Kāsi took their water-pots and went to a field. Setting them aside at one side, they plowed the field;
then, when they were thirsty, they would come back and drink the water. One of them, having come for water, while guarding his own supply, [did not give any] to the other.
Having drunk from the gourd, he emerged from the forest in the evening; after bathing, while standing there reflecting, "Have I committed any evil today through the door of the body or other doors?
he perceived that he had stolen and drunk the water. Overcome with a sense of spiritual urgency (*saṃvega*), he thought:
"This craving, if it increases, will cast me into the states of misery; I shall subdue this defilement."
Making the act of stealing and drinking water his object of meditation, he developed insight, realized the knowledge of *paccekabodhi*, and stood there reflecting upon the qualities he had attained.
Then, the other man, having bathed and emerged from the water, said, "Come, friend, let us go home.
[The first replied,] "Go yourself; I have no business with your house, for I am a *paccekabuddha*."
“Are they called ‘Paccekabuddhas’? “Those like you are not called Paccekabuddhas. “Then what are Paccekabuddhas like?
“They have hair two fingers long, wear saffron-colored robes, and dwell in the Nandamūlaka cave in the northern Himalayas.
He touched his head, and at that very moment his layman’s marks disappeared; he was already clothed in a well-dyed double-layered robe.
His waistband was fastened like a flash of lightning;
his upper robe (uttarāsaṅga) was of a saffron-pale red color and draped over one shoulder; his rag-robe (paṃsukūla), the color of a cloud, was placed upon the right shoulder;
and his alms-bowl, the color of a bee, was suspended from the left shoulder. Standing in the air, he taught the Dhamma and then flew up.
He descended right into the Nandamūlaka cave.
Furthermore, another householder sitting in a shop in the Kāsi village saw a man passing by with his own wife;
having looked at that woman of supreme beauty with his senses overcome, he thought again: "This..."

Thinking, "Greed, if it increases, will hurl me into the states of misery," he became deeply stirred in mind. Increasing his insight (*vipassanā*), he realized the knowledge of *paccekabodhi* (solitary enlightenment).
Standing in the air, he taught the Dhamma and returned to the Nandamūlaka mountain cave.
Furthermore, two other father and son who lived in a village of Kāsī set out together on the road. However, at the entrance of the forest...
The thieves rose up. Having captured both father and son, they took the son and released the father, saying, "Bring wealth and we will release your son.
Having captured two brothers, they took the younger and released the elder.
Having captured teacher and pupil, they took the teacher and released the pupil; for the pupil was [held] out of greed for his craft.
Having brought the wealth and taken his teacher, he departed.

Then those father and son, having learned of the presence of the robbers there, made an agreement, saying, "Do not call me 'father,' and I shall not call you 'son,'" so that when they were seized by the robbers and asked, "What are you to one another? they spoke a conscious lie, saying, "We are nothing to each other."

They did so. When they had emerged from the forest and stood there having bathed in the evening, the son—purifying his own virtue and seeing that falsehood—thought, "If this evil increases, it will hurl me into the states of misery; I shall suppress this defilement.
Developing insight (*vipassanā*) and realizing the knowledge of *paccekabodhi* (solitary enlightenment), he stood in the air before his father.
Having taught the Dhamma, he went back to the Nandamūlaka cave.
Now, in the village of Kāsī, there was another village headman who had a sacrificial slaughter performed.
Then, at the time of the offering, the great multitude gathered and said to him, "Master, we have killed deer, pigs, and other animals to perform an offering to the *yakkhas*. [What will you do?]"
“We shall do so; this is the time for the offering. “Perform it according to the procedure you previously used,” [he said].

Thus, people committed much killing of living beings. Seeing that great quantity of fish and meat, he felt remorse, thinking, “While these people were killing so many creatures, they did so solely at my word.
Standing right there by the window, he applied himself to insight (vipassanā).
Having increased his practice and realized the knowledge of *paccekabodhi*, he stood in the air, taught the Dhamma to the great multitude, and returned to the Nandamūlaka cave.
Furthermore, in the kingdom of Kāsī, there was a village headman who prohibited the sale of spirits.
When the people asked him, "Master, at this time of year there used to be a festival for spirits; what shall we do? he replied, "By your own ancient custom..."
"Make it so," he said. The people, having celebrated the festival and drunk liquor, began to quarrel;
they broke hands and feet, split heads, and cut off ears, and were bound with heavy fetters.
When the village headman saw them, he thought, "If I do not give my permission, these men will not experience such suffering. Having felt remorse over this much, he—

Relying on the window-lattice, he stood right there and, having increased his insight (vipassanā) and realized the knowledge of Pacceka-bodhi, he remained suspended in the air and taught the Dhamma, saying, "Be heedful! Then he departed for the Nandamūlaka Cave.
Later, those five Pacceka-buddhas descended at the gate of Bārāṇasī for the purpose of alms-round, well-robed and...
Well-veiled and inspiring with their graceful deportment, such as their dignified approach, they entered the royal gate while wandering for alms.

Upon seeing them, the king, with a mind full of faith, led them into the royal residence; having had their feet washed and anointed with fragrant oil, he served them with excellent solid and soft foods.
Then, sitting to one side, he said: "Venerable sirs, in your first stage of life..."
“Going forth is beautiful. Those who go forth at this age—how did you see the danger in sensual pleasures?
What was your object of focus? When they were explaining it to him, [they said]:
“I, as a friend, consumed water that had not been given by my friend.”
Because of that, I later felt revulsion for the evil deed I had committed;
lest I commit evil again, I have therefore gone forth.
Having seen another’s wife, desire arose within me.
Because of that, I later felt revulsion for the evil deed I had committed;
"May I never again commit evil"—for this reason I have gone forth.
"O Great King, thieves seized my father in the forest."
When questioned by them, though knowing the answer, I explained it otherwise.
Because of that, I later felt remorse for the evil deed I had committed.
"May I never again commit such evil"—for this reason, I have gone forth into homelessness.
“When the Soma sacrifice was set forth, they committed the taking of life;
I gave my consent to them.
Because of that, I later felt remorse for that evil deed committed by me.”
“May I never again commit evil; therefore have I gone forth.
Those people who were the first among us to consume fermented liquor and spirits for intoxication—that drinking of intoxicants brought about the ruin of many.”
I gave my consent to them:
"Because of that, I later felt revulsion; that evil was committed by me.
May I not commit evil again; therefore have I gone forth."
They recited these five verses in succession. Having heard the explanation of each one, the king offered praise, saying: "Venerable sirs, this renunciation is truly worthy of you.
In that regard, [the first verse says]: "A friend for a friend," O Great King; having become a friend to one person, I consumed the water belonging to that friend in this very manner.
"Therefore" means: because ordinary worldlings (*puthujjana*) indeed commit evil deeds.
"Therefore, I shall not commit evil again; having made that evil my object of contemplation, I have gone forth into homelessness.
'Lust,' O Great King—by this very process, upon seeing another's wife, lust for sensual pleasures arose in me. 'They took it' means they took it.
'They know' means that when asked by those thieves, 'What is this to you?', even though knowing, [he replied] 'It is nothing at all.'"
I answered otherwise. Regarding "the Soma sacrifice": when the new moon had arisen, they performed what is called a Soma sacrifice, a sacrificial offering to the *yakkhas*, as it appeared.
"I gave my consent" means I was in agreement. Regarding "those who [drank] fermented liquor, spirits, and honey":
thinking that fermented liquor such as *piṭṭhasurā* and spirits such as *pupphāsava* were as sweet as fresh honey, those people were the first to do so.
"Those people in our village who were previously of such a nature— 'of many' means that when a festival occurred on a single day,
they prepared intoxicating drinks for the harm of many.
Having heard their account, the king, with a mind full of faith, gave them robes, garments, and medicines, and [honored] the Paccekabuddhas."
He dismissed them. They too, having offered him their thanks, departed right there.

From that time forth, the king, dispassionate and indifferent toward sensual pleasures, ate various foods of exquisite flavor, yet without speaking to or looking at the women, his mind detached, he would rise and enter the inner chamber to sit and perform the preliminary exercises for the *kasiṇa* upon the white wall.
Having attained meditative absorption (jhāna), he produced it. Having reached that state of absorption, censuring sensual pleasures, he uttered this verse:
"Fie on these abundant sensual pleasures, foul-smelling and full of thorns!
For while indulging in them, I did not obtain such bliss as this."

In that context, "full of many thorns" means full of many enemies. "Ye ahan" means "I, who"; or rather, this is the reading: "yo ahaṃ. "Such as that" refers to this kind of meditative bliss (jhānasukha) free from defilements (kilesa).
Then his chief queen thought: "Having heard the Dhamma talk from the Paccekabuddhas, this king has become disenchanted;
he entered the inner chamber without even speaking with us. I shall first examine him."
Having reflected thus, she stood at the door of the bedchamber and, hearing the king’s utterance as he was censuring sensual pleasures, she spoke the following verse in praise of sensual pleasures:
“Sensual pleasures are highly gratifying and pleasant; there is no happiness higher than sensual pleasure.”
“Those who indulge in sensual pleasures are reborn in heaven.

In this context, “of great enjoyment” means, O Great King, that these so-called sensual pleasures possess great enjoyment; there is no other happiness superior to this. For those who indulge in sensual pleasures do not fall into the states of misery, but are instead reborn in heaven—this is the meaning.

Having heard that, the Bodhisatta rebuked her, saying, “Begone, you low-born woman! What are you saying? Where is there any happiness in sensual pleasures? These are suffering due to their changeability,” and he spoke the remaining verses:
“Sensual pleasures offer little gratification and are suffering; there is no suffering greater than sensual pleasures.
Those who indulge in sensual pleasures are reborn in hell.
Like a well-sharpened sword or a well-tempered spear, [they cut through one’s welfare].”
“Even a spear thrust into the chest— sensuous pleasures are more painful than that.
Like a blazing pit of glowing coals, or a plowshare heated all day long,
sensuous pleasures are more painful than that.”
“Just as the Halāhala poison, just as boiling oil, or like molten copper and iron—sensuous desires are more painful than those.
In this context, *nettimsa* means merciless; this too is a name for a certain type of sword. *Dukkhatarā* means [more painful] than such a pit of glowing embers.
The meaning is that whatever suffering arises in dependence upon the heat of the day or the heat of the ploughshare, even from that, sensual pleasures (*kāma*) are more painful.
In the following verse, just as these poisons and so forth are "sufferings" because they bring about suffering, so too are sensual pleasures sufferings;
moreover, the meaning is that this suffering of sensual pleasures is more painful than the other types of suffering.
Thus the Great Being, having taught the Dhamma to the queen and summoned his ministers, said, "Worthy ministers, you take charge of the kingdom;

I shall go forth into homelessness. As the great multitude was weeping and lamenting, he rose up, stood in the air, and after giving them exhortation, departed by way of the sky for the northern Himalayas, reaching a delightful region.
Having established a hermitage and gone forth into the ascetic life of an *isi*, he reached the Brahma-world at the end of his lifespan.
Having delivered this Dhamma teaching, the Teacher said, "Monks, there is no such thing as a minor defilement;
even a slight one must be restrained by the wise," and after proclaiming the Truths, he identified the Jātaka. At the conclusion of the Truths—
Five hundred bhikkhus were established in Arahatship. At that time, the Paccekabuddhas attained Parinibbāna;
the queen was Rāhulamātā, and the king was none other than myself.
This is the fifth, the Pānīya Jātaka.
[460] 6. The Commentary on the Yudhañcayajātaka.
“Surrounded by friends and ministers”—this was spoken by the Teacher while dwelling at Jetavana, concerning the Great Renunciation.
For one day, the monks assembled in the Hall of Truth said, “Friends, if the One of Ten Powers had remained in the household...”
If he had remained at home, he would have become a universal monarch within the entire expanse of the world-system, endowed with the seven treasures, perfected in the four supernormal powers,
and surrounded by a retinue of more than a thousand sons; yet, having renounced such glorious wealth and seeing the fault in sensual pleasures,
he departed at the hour of midnight with only his charioteer as companion, mounted upon Kaṇṭaka, and went to the bank of the Anoma River.
“Having gone forth and performed austerities for six years, he attained supreme perfect enlightenment,” they said, recounting the virtues of the Teacher.
The Teacher approached and asked, “Monks, about what conversation are you gathered here now?
When they replied, “About this very one,” he said, “Monks, it is not only now that the Tathāgata has made the Great Renunciation.”
"Having gone forth, he has indeed gone forth even before, having renounced his kingdom in the city of Bārāṇasī, which was twelve yojanas in extent," he said, and then related a story of the past.
In the past, there was a king named Sabbadatta in the city of Ramma.
For this very Bārāṇasī was known as Surundhana in the *Udaya Jātaka*, as Sudassana in the *Cūḷasutasoma Jātaka*, and as Brahmavaḍḍhana in the *Soṇananda Jātaka*.
In the Khaṇḍahāla Jātaka she was named Puṣpavatī; in the Saṅkhabrāhmaṇa Jātaka she was named Moḷinī;
but in this Yudhañcaya Jātaka, she was named Rammanagara. Thus her name changes from time to time.
There, King Sabbadatta had a thousand sons. To his eldest son, named Yudhañcaya, he gave the rank of viceroy.
He gave. Day after day, he established a great distribution of alms.

As time passed in this way, one day the Bodhisatta, having mounted his excellent chariot early in the morning and proceeding to the pleasure garden with great splendor and majesty, saw festive droplets clinging like nets of pearls to the tips of trees, the tops of grasses, the ends of branches, and spiderwebs.
Having seen them, he asked, "Good charioteer, what is this?"
“Your Majesty, these are called the festival drops that fall during the winter season. Having heard this, he spent part of the day sporting in the park;
returning in the evening, not seeing them, he asked, “Good charioteer, where indeed are those festival drops?
I do not see them now. “Your Majesty, they all dissolved into the earth as the sun rose.”
Hearing the words, “...falling,” he was seized with a sense of spiritual urgency (*saṃvega*). Thinking, “The life-processes of these beings are like drops of dew on the tip of a blade of grass;

it is fitting that I go forth into homelessness after taking leave of my parents while they are still unafflicted by disease, old age, and death,” he took those very drops of dew as his mental object.
Viewing the three realms of existence as if they were ablaze, he did not return to his own home, but [went instead] to his mother, who was dressed in her finery and prepared for the occasion.
Having gone into the presence of his father while he was seated in the hall of justice, and having paid homage to his father, he stood to one side and, requesting the going-forth,
spoke the first verse: “I pay homage to you, O bull among charioteers, surrounded by friends and kinsmen.”
“I shall go forth, O King; may Your Majesty grant me permission.
In this context, “surrounded” means encircled. “May Your Majesty [grant] that” means may Your Majesty allow my going forth.
Then the King, seeking to dissuade him, spoke the second verse:
“If there is anything lacking for you in sensual pleasures, I shall provide it for you;
for I will surely restrain you from harm—do not go forth into homelessness, O crusher of foes.
Having heard this, the prince spoke the third verse:
“There is no lack of sensual pleasures for me, nor is there anyone found who harms me;
yet I wish to make an island that old age shall not overwhelm. In this context, “an island” means:
“Dear one, there is indeed no lack of sensual pleasures for me, nor is there anyone found who harms me.”
"But as for me," he said, "I wish to establish a firm footing for myself on the journey to the next world. Of what kind? I wish to achieve that which old age does not overwhelm nor destroy;
I shall seek the great Nibbāna of the Deathless. I have no need for sensual pleasures;
grant me leave, O Great King. Thus he spoke.
Thus the prince requested ordination again and again, and the king forbade him, saying, "Do not go forth. Revealing this matter, the Teacher spoke the half-stanza:
"The son may entreat the father, or the father his own legitimate son.
Here, the word *vā* has the sense of conjunction. This is what is meant: "In this way, monks, the son entreats the father, and the father entreats his own legitimate son."
The King spoke the remainder of the half-stanza:
“O dear one, let the guildsman entreat you; do not go forth, Yudhañjaya.
Its meaning is this: “O dear one, these great people dwelling in your town entreat you; let not even the city folk [be left behind] as you go forth.”
The prince spoke again this fifth verse:
“O King, do not restrain me as I go forth, O bull among charioteers;
let me not, being intoxicated by sensual pleasures, fall under the power of old age.”
"In that regard, 'I am subject to its power' means: 'May I not, being intoxicated and heedless by sensual pleasures, become one who falls under the sway of old age;

rather, having exhausted the suffering of the cycle of existence (*saṃsāra*), may you look upon me so that I may become a penetrator of omniscient knowledge (*sabbaññuta-ñāṇa*). This was his intention.
When this was said, the king remained speechless. But his mother [said]: 'O Queen, your son has asked his father for the going-forth (*pabbajjā*')."

Having heard, "She is asking for permission," he asked, "What are you saying? Then, sitting in a golden palanquin with a face devoid of breath, he went quickly to the place of judgment and, while being entreated, spoke the sixth verse:
"I entreat you, dear father; I beg you, my son, to desist."
“I wish to see you for a long time; do not go forth, Yudhañjaya.
Having heard this, the prince spoke the seventh verse:
“Like dew upon the tip of a blade of grass at the rising of the sun;”
"Such is the lifespan of human beings; do not stop me, mother.

The meaning of this is: Mother, just as a drop of dew on the tip of a blade of grass cannot remain once the sun rises but falls to the ground, even so the life of these beings is limited, temporary, and short-lived.
"In such a world as this, how can you look upon me for long? Do not hinder me.
Even when he had spoken thus, she continued to entreat him again and again. Then the Great Being, addressing his father, spoke the eighth verse:
"O Bull among Charioteers, quickly cause me to mount this vehicle!"
“May my mother not be an obstacle for me as I cross over.

The meaning of this is: “Dear father, O bull among charioteers, let a man place this mother of mine upon a golden palanquin; may my mother not be an obstacle for me as I cross over, as I pass beyond the wilderness of birth, aging, sickness, and death.
Having heard his son’s words, the king said: “Go, lady; having sat upon your palanquin, go to the Palace that Increases Delight.”
“Climb up,” he said. Having heard his words, she was unable to remain where she was;
surrounded by a host of women, she went and ascended the palace. Standing there, she looked toward the place of judgment, wondering, “What is the outcome for my son?
When her mother had departed, the Bodhisatta again made his request to his father. The king, being unable to refuse him, said: “In that case, dear son...”
"Direct your mind toward the highest goal; go forth into homelessness," he granted permission.
At the time the King had given his consent, the Bodhisatta’s younger brother, Prince Yudhiṭṭhila, paid homage to his father and requested permission, saying, "Father, grant me leave to go forth.
Both brothers, having paid homage to their father and renounced sensual pleasures, departed from the court of justice surrounded by a great multitude.
They departed. The queen, too, having looked upon the Great Being, lamented, thinking, "Now that my sons have gone forth, the city of Ramma will become empty," and spoke these two verses:
"Run forth, O blessed ones! Ramma will become empty; ... [the rest of the verse follows] ... "
“Battle has been permitted by King Sabbadatta.
He who is the best of a thousand, a youth resembling gold—
he is this powerful prince who has gone forth, clothed in saffron robes.”
In that context, "run there" means he commands all the women standing around him, "run with speed.
"Bhadante" means, having gone thus, say, "May it be well with you. "Rammaka" refers to the city of Ramma.
"He who was the best of a thousand" refers to the king’s son who was the most excellent among a thousand; he speaks thus concerning him as he is departing for the going-forth (pabbajjā).
The Bodhisatta, however, did not yet go forth. Having paid homage to his parents and taken his younger brother, Prince Yudhiṭṭhila, he departed from the city.
After turning back the great multitude, both brothers entered the Himālaya mountains.
There, having established a hermitage in a delightful place, they went forth into the ascetic life of an *isi*, and having attained the *jhānas* and direct knowledges (*abhiññā*), they dwelt there.

Having sustained themselves for as long as they lived on forest roots, fruits, and the like, they became destined for the Brahma-world. At the conclusion, he illuminates this matter with a verse of perfect enlightenment:
“Both princes, Yudhañcaya and Yudhiṭṭhila, having gone forth, left behind their mother and father, cutting off the bond of death.”

In this context, "from Death" means from Māra. This is what is meant: "Monks, both those princes, Yudhañjaya and Yudhiṭṭhila, having abandoned their parents and severed the attachment of lust, hatred, and delusion belonging to Māra, went forth into homelessness.
Having delivered this Dhamma teaching and proclaimed the Truths, the Teacher said, "Monks, it is not only now;
in the past as well, the Tathāgata abandoned his kingdom and went forth," and he identified the Jātaka: "At that time, the parents..."
“Those who were the royal families became the Great Kings; Prince Yudhiṭṭhila was Ānanda, while I myself was Yudhañcaya.
This concludes the sixth narrative, the Commentary on the Yudhañcaya Jātaka.
[461] 7. The Commentary on the Dasaratha Jātaka.
"Come, Lakkhaṇa, Sītā," the Teacher said—this was spoken while he was dwelling at Jetavana concerning a householder whose parents had died.
For when his father passed away, that man was overcome by grief; abandoning all his duties, he remained solely following after his sorrow.
At dawn, the Teacher surveyed the world and, seeing the potential for that man to attain the fruit of stream-entry (*sotāpatti-phala*), on the following day...
Having walked for alms in Sāvatthī, finished his meal, and dismissed the other monks, he took a single attendant monk and went to that man’s house.
After paying homage and sitting down, he addressed him with sweet words, saying, “Lay follower, why do you grieve?
When he replied, “Yes, venerable sir, grief for my father afflicts me,” [the Buddha said], “Lay follower, in the past, the ancient wise ones...”
"Knowing the eight worldly conditions as they truly are, they did not feel even the slightest grief when their father passed away," he said,
and being requested by him, he related a story of the past. In the past, in Bārāṇasī,
there was a great king named Dasaratha who, having abandoned going on wrong paths, ruled his kingdom according to the Dhamma.
Of those sixteen thousand women, the eldest, the chief queen, gave birth to two sons and one daughter.
The elder son was named Rāmapaṇḍita, the second was named Lakkhaṇakumāra, and the daughter was named Sītā Devī.
Later, the chief queen passed away. After her death, the king fell under the sway of grief for a long time, and [was eventually] by his ministers...
Having been thus informed, he provided her with the necessary care and appointed another woman to the position of chief queen.
She became dear and pleasing to the king. Later, she conceived and, having received the care appropriate for pregnancy, gave birth to a son;
they gave him the name Prince Bharata. Out of affection for his son, the king said, "My lady, I grant you a boon; choose it."

She said: "Having taken it as a favor and set it aside, when the prince was seven or eight years old, she approached the king and said, 'Sire, you granted a boon to my son; now grant him that boon. [The king replied,] 'Take it, blessed lady.
When she said, 'Sire, grant the kingdom to my son,' the king snapped his fingers and cried, 'Begone, you outcaste!'"
"Two sons of mine blaze like masses of fire; having caused them to be killed, you ask for the kingdom for your own son," he rebuked her.
Terrified, she entered the inner chamber and, on subsequent days as well, repeatedly asked the king for the kingdom alone.
Without granting her that boon, the king thought: "Women are indeed ungrateful and treacherous to their friends; this one of mine..."
“Having forged a document or a forged seal, he will have his sons killed. He summoned his sons, informed them of that matter, and said:
“Sons, while you are living here, there may be an obstacle for you. You should go to a neighboring kingdom or to the forest;
then, at the time of my death, you should come back and take possession of the hereditary kingdom. Having said this, he—
Again, having summoned the Brahmins who were skilled in omens and asked them about the limit of his own lifespan, he heard that twelve more years would remain.
Upon hearing this, he said, "Sirs, after twelve years have passed from now, come back and raise the royal parasol.
They replied, "Very well," and after paying homage to their father, they descended from the palace weeping. Queen Sītā [thought], "I too..."
“I shall go with my brothers,” she said; and having paid homage to her father, she departed weeping.
The three of them, accompanied by a great retinue, set out, turned back the crowd of people, and gradually entered the Himalayas.
Having established a hermitage in a place well-supplied with water and abundant in fruits and roots, they dwelt there, subsisting on those fruits and roots.
Lakkhaṇapaṇḍita and Sītā requested Rāmapaṇḍita, saying, "Since you stand in the place of our father, please remain right here in the hermitage;

we shall bring fruits and roots and support you. Having obtained his promise, from that time forth Rāmapaṇḍita remained in that very place, while the other two brought fruits and roots and attended to him.
While they were living in this manner, subsisting on whatever fruits they could find, the great king Dasaratha passed away in the ninth year due to grief for his son.
After performing the funeral rites for him, the queen said, "Raise the royal parasol over my son, Prince Bharata.
However, the ministers did not grant it, saying, "The owners of the parasol are living in the forest. Then Prince Bharata...
Thinking, "I shall bring my brother, the scholar Rāma, from the forest and raise the royal parasol over him," he took the five insignia of royalty and,
with a fourfold army, reached the place where he was dwelling; having established his camp not far away and stayed there,
he went into the forest together with a few ministers to seek out Lakkhaṇa-paṇḍita and Sītā.
When the time had passed, he entered the hermitage and approached the wise Rāma, who was sitting comfortably and without fear like a golden statue placed at the entrance of the hermitage.
Having paid homage and stood to one side, he reported the news of the king and, together with his ministers, fell at Rāma’s feet and wept. Yet the wise Rāma neither grieved nor lamented.
Not even the slightest alteration of his faculties occurred. While Bharata sat weeping, at the time of evening, the other two arrived bringing fruits.
The wise Rāma thought: "These children do not possess the discerning wisdom for consideration that I have;
if told suddenly, 'Your father is dead,' they will be unable to sustain their grief."
"If they are unable [to endure it], even their hearts might burst; therefore, by some means I shall cause them to descend into the water and report this news.
Then, pointing out a body of water before them, he spoke half a verse: "You have arrived very late; let this be your punishment: descend into this water and stand there."
“Come, Lakkhaṇa, and Sītā too; both of you descend into the water.
The meaning of this is: “Come, Lakkhaṇa, and Sītā as well; both of you descend into the water.
Having descended with a single word, they stood there. Then, reporting the father’s condition to them, he spoke the remainder of the half-stanza:
“Thus spoke Bharata: ‘King Daśaratha has died.
Upon hearing the news of their father’s death, they lost consciousness. He told them again, and again they lost consciousness.
When they had thus fallen unconscious for a third time, the ministers lifted them up, carried them out from the water, and placed them on dry land.”
Having seated them, they all sat down after weeping and lamenting one another among those who had received the remainder of the food.

Then Prince Bharata thought: "When my brother Prince Lakṣmaṇa and my sister Queen Sītā heard the news of my father’s death, they were unable to sustain their grief; yet the wise Rāma does not grieve at all."
"He does not lament. What indeed could be the reason for his lack of sorrow? I shall ask him. Thus questioning him, he spoke this second verse:
"By what power of Rāma do you not grieve when there is cause for grief?
Having heard that your father has passed away, why does suffering not overcome you?"

In this context, "by its power" means by its majesty. "Suffering does not overcome him": for what reason does such suffering not oppress him? What is the cause of your not grieving? First, tell me that.
Then the sage Rāma, explaining the reason for his own lack of grief, said:
"That which cannot be guarded by a person, however much he may lament..."
Why would a wise and intelligent person cause himself such torment?
For both the young and the old, the foolish and the wise,
the wealthy and the poor— all have death as their final destination.
“Just as for ripe fruits there is constant fear of falling,
so for mortals who have been born there is constant fear of death.
Some people seen in the evening are not seen in the morning.”
Some who were not seen in the morning are seen in the evening as a great many people.
If lamenting could achieve any purpose, one would do it with clear vision;
for by grieving, one only harms oneself while being utterly deluded.
“Emaciated and discolored, he harms himself by his own hand;
the departed do not sustain themselves by that, for lamentation is useless.
Just as one would extinguish a burning house with water,”
In this way, the wise, learned, intelligent, and discerning person quickly disperses arisen sorrow, just as the wind blows away a tuft of cotton.
"A mortal passes away alone; alone he is born into a family."
The union with all living beings is indeed the supreme goal.
Therefore, for the wise one who is well-learned, who clearly perceives this world and the next,
and who has understood the Dhamma, as well as the heart and the mind, even great sorrows do not cause them to burn.
“I shall provide both sight and food, and I shall support my relatives;
I shall protect what remains—this is the duty of one who understands.
With these ten verses, he demonstrates impermanence.
In this context, "to guard" means to protect. "Of those who lament" refers to those who are lamenting. This is what is meant:

"Dear Bharata, that life of beings which cannot be protected from being cut off even by a single man, no matter how much he may lament—how could one such as I, who knows the eight worldly conditions as they truly are, being wise, intelligent, and learned..."
“Since all beings have lives that end in death, for what reason should one torment oneself? For what purpose should one burn oneself with grief and suffering that brings no benefit?
Thus he spoke the verse beginning with “And the young,” [meaning]: “O dear Bharata, this so-called Death does not spare even those who are young and resemble golden statues.”
This was spoken for the purpose of showing that [death] does not spare kshatriya princes and the like, nor great warriors who have reached maturity,
nor foolish ordinary beings (*puthujjana*), nor wise ones such as Buddhas, nor powerful lords such as universal monarchs (*cakravartin*),
nor even the destitute and poor; for all these beings have death as their final destination and inevitably become shattered and broken in the mouth of death.

"Constantly liable to fall": this is what is meant. Just as, my dear Bharata, for ripe fruits from the moment they have ripened, there is a constant, certain, and one-sided fear of falling—thinking, "Now they will break from the stalk and fall;
now they will fall"—so too, because they are subject to such apprehension, for mortals who have been born, [the fear of death] is likewise one-sided.
There is fear of death; there is no moment or instant when death might not be expected for them.
"They taste" means at the wrong time. By this, it is shown that those seen during the night are not seen during the day, and those seen during the day are not seen during the night.
"Something or other" refers to [expressions such as] "He is my father," "He is my son," and so forth.
"A person lamenting, bewildered and harming himself, might achieve even a trifling benefit while suffering.

"A wise man would do that"—if a discerning person were to lament in this way, it would be because he is unable to bring back the dead by lamenting or to effect any other growth for them; therefore, since lamentation is useless, [one should not do so].
The wise do not lament.
"Harming oneself by means of oneself" refers to one who harms one's own person with grief, lamentation, and suffering.

"They do not protect by that" means that beings who have gone to the next world are neither protected nor sustained by that lamentation. Therefore, for those deceased beings, this [lamentation] is useless.
Lamentation is useless. "Refuge" means a dwelling-house. This is what is meant:

just as a wise man, when his own house is on fire, does not allow even a moment's negligence but extinguishes it with water from a hundred or a thousand jars, so too should the steadfast one quickly extinguish arisen sorrow, like [blowing out] cotton wool.
And just as the wind cannot remain still, so too one should cause [the mind] to be scattered and destroyed; this is the meaning.
Regarding the phrase "The mortal goes alone," O dear Bharata, these beings are called "owners of their own karma";
for indeed, when a being goes from this world to the next world, he goes—that is, passes on—alone, even when being born into a family such as that of a Kshatriya, he is born alone.

Having gone [there], one is born. Yet, in each of those places, through association with kinsmen and friends—thinking, "This is my father," "This is my mother," "This is my friend"—the enjoyment of all living beings is characterized by attachment.
But in the ultimate sense, the meaning is that these beings in all three realms of existence have their own karma as their own property.
Therefore, because for these beings there is nothing beyond this—apart from the association with kinsmen and friends and the mere enjoyment of kinsmen and friends—that is why [it is said].
"Beholding" means seeing rightly both this world and the next as being characterized precisely by diversity and dissolution.
"Having understood the Dhamma" means having known the eight worldly conditions (*aṭṭhavidha-lokadhamma*). "The heart and the mind" means...
Both of these are merely names for the mind. This is what is meant:
“Gain and loss, fame and disrepute, blame and praise, pleasure and pain—these things among humans are impermanent. Do not grieve; why do you grieve, Poṭṭhapāda?”
If the mind of anyone is overwhelmed by any one of these eight worldly conditions, even great sorrows rooted in the death of a father, son,
or others do not burn the heart of that wise person who stands firm after knowing their impermanence. Or rather,
for one who stands firm having known these eightfold worldly conditions, even great [sorrows] do not afflict the physical heart-base and the mind.
"Sorrows do not burn me"—this is how the meaning should be understood here.
Regarding the verse "I shall both see and eat": "Dear Bharata, like those blind and foolish beings, weeping and lamenting is not fitting for me;
rather, upon my father’s passing, I shall stand in his place."
I shall give gifts to those worthy of giving, such as the poor; I shall grant positions to those worthy of positions; I shall bestow honor upon those worthy of honor;
I shall enjoy sovereignty in the manner my father enjoyed it; I shall support my kinsmen and protect the rest of my people, including the household staff;
and I shall provide righteous protection, defense, and security for righteous recluses and brahmins.
"I shall do so"—this is the meaning: for a wise man who knows this, it is an appropriate duty.
Having heard this Dhamma teaching by the wise Rāma, which elucidates impermanence, the assembly became free from sorrow.
Then Prince Bharata, having paid homage to the wise Rāma, said, "Please accept the sovereignty of Bārāṇasī. "Dear one..."
"Take Lakkhaṇa and Queen Sītā and go; rule the kingdom. "But what about you, sire?
"Dear father, my father said to me, 'When twelve years have passed, come back and rule the kingdom.
If I were to go right now, I would not be following his word; rather, let another three years pass."
“I shall return,” he said. “Who will rule the kingdom for all this time? “You yourselves shall rule,” they replied. “We will not rule,” he said.
“In that case, let these sandals rule until my return. Having spoken thus, he took off his own grass sandals and gave them to them.
Those three people, having taken the sandals and paid homage to the wise Rāma, were surrounded by a great multitude.
They went to Bārāṇasī. For three years they ruled the kingdom by means of sandals.
The ministers, having placed grass sandals upon the royal throne, would settle legal disputes. If a case was wrongly decided, the sandals would strike against one another.
By that sign, they would decide it again. When the decision was correctly made, the sandals would remain silent and still.
After three years had passed, the wise Rāma emerged from the forest and, having reached the city of Bārāṇasī, entered a royal garden.

Upon learning of his arrival, the princes, surrounded by a host of ministers, went to the garden and, making Sītā their chief queen, performed the consecration for both of them. Thus, the Great Being attained the status of king.
Having mounted his decorated chariot and entered the city with a great retinue, he performed a circumambulation and ascended the great terrace of the excellent Candaka Palace.
From that time forth, having ruled the kingdom righteously for sixteen thousand years, at the end of his lifespan, he filled the city of heaven.
“Ten thousand years and six hundred years;”
“Kambugīvo mahābāhu, Rāma ruled the kingdom”—this verse of the Perfectly Enlightened One illuminates that meaning.
In this context, *kambugīvo* means one whose neck resembles a golden conch shell (*suvaṇṇāḷiṅga*). For gold is called *kambu*.
Having delivered this Dhamma teaching and proclaimed the Truths, the Teacher identified the Jātaka.
At the conclusion of the Truths, the householder was established in the fruit of stream-entry. At that time, the Great King Dasaratha was the Great King Suddhodana;
Queen Mahāmāyā was his mother; Sītā was Rāhula’s mother; Bharata was Ānanda; Lakkhaṇa was Sāriputta; and the assembly was the assembly of the Buddha.
"But I myself was Rāmapaṇḍita.
This concludes the seventh narrative, the Commentary on the Dasaratha Jātaka.
[462] 8. The Commentary on the Saṃvara Jātaka.
"Knowing this, O Great King," the Teacher spoke these words while dwelling at Jetavana concerning a certain monk who had slackened his energy.
It is said that a noble youth from Sāvatthī, having heard the Teacher’s discourse on the Dhamma, went forth, received full ordination,
fulfilled his duties toward his preceptor and teacher, and made both versions of the Pātimokkha thoroughly familiar.

Having completed five years of seniority, he took up a meditation subject and, with the permission of his teachers and preceptors, thinking, "I shall dwell in the forest," went to a frontier village in the kingdom of Kosala.
There, people who were inspired by his deportment built him a leaf-hut and attended upon him;
having entered the rains retreat there, while applying himself, striving, and exerting himself, he did so with over-exerted energy.
Having cultivated the meditation subject for three months, being unable to produce even a mere radiance, he thought:
"Surely I am one of the four types of persons described by the Teacher who only reaches the words; what is the use of my dwelling in the forest?
I shall go to Jetavana and spend my time beholding the beauty of the Tathāgata’s form and listening to his sweet preaching of the Dhamma. Thus he...
Having abandoned his vigor, he departed from there and, traveling by stages, arrived at Jetavana.
When questioned by his teachers, preceptors, and his personal associates regarding the reason for his coming, he explained the matter.
They reproached him, saying, "Why did you do such a thing? and having led him into the presence of the Teacher, [the Buddha asked], "Monks, why have you brought a bhikkhu who was unwilling to come?"
When it was said, "Venerable sir, this man has come here having abandoned his energy," and it was reported, the Teacher asked, "Is it true?
When it was replied, "It is true, venerable sir," he said, "Why did the bhikkhu abandon his energy?
For in this teaching, there is no such thing as the supreme fruit of Arahantship for a person who is devoid of energy and lazy; those who have aroused their energy succeed in this Dhamma."
"Indeed, you were formerly energetic and capable of receiving instruction;
