for that very reason, although you were the youngest of a hundred sons to the King of Bārāṇasī, by abiding by the counsel of the wise, you attained the white parasol. Having said this, he related a story of the past:
"In the past, while Brahmadatta was reigning in Bārāṇasī, there was a youth named Saṃvara, the youngest of a hundred sons."
It came to pass that the king gave each of his sons to a respective minister, saying, "Teach them what is appropriate for their training.
The Bodhisatta was the wise and competent minister who served as the teacher for Prince Saṃvara, standing in the place of a father to the prince.
When the ministers presented the princes to the king once they had completed their training in the arts, the king granted them their respective provinces.
Having given [the kingdom], he sent him away. When Prince Saṃvara had attained mastery in all arts, he asked the Bodhisatta:
"Father, if my father sends me to the countryside, what shall I do? "My son, when the countryside is being bestowed, do not accept it.
Say: 'Your Majesty, I am the youngest of all; if I too were to go, your feet would be left empty.'"

“I shall dwell right at the soles of your feet,” you should say. Then one day, the king, having paid homage to Prince Saṃvara, asked him as he sat to one side, “My dear son, have you completed your training? “Yes, sire,” he replied.
“I give a province to you as well,” said the king. “Sire, your presence would be left empty; [I wish to remain] right at your feet.”
“I shall dwell [here]. The king, being pleased, accepted with the words, “Very well.
From that time forth, having remained at the very feet of the king, he asked the Bodhisatta once more, “Dear father, what else shall I do? “Dear father, ask the king for an old park,” he said.
He replied, “Very well,” and having requested the park, [he provided] the citizens of the city with flowers and fruits produced there.

Having gathered them together, he asked again, "What shall I do? [The ministers replied,] "Dear son, having obtained the king's permission, you yourself should distribute food and wages within the city.
He did accordingly; without depriving anyone within the city of anything, he distributed food and wages.
Then, having consulted the Bodhisatta and informed the king, he likewise provided for the male and female slaves and laborers in his own residence, as well as for the elephants.
Without neglecting the duties toward either the horses or the army, he personally performed all necessary tasks:
providing lodging and other facilities for messengers and others arriving from foreign lands, and collecting customs duties from merchants.
Thus, abiding by the Great Being’s counsel, he [attended to] all his own people, as well as outsiders, the city-dwellers, the country-folk, and visitors.
He bound them to himself through various means of conciliation and gathered them around him; thus, he became dear and pleasing to everyone.
Later, when the king lay upon his deathbed, the ministers asked him, "Sire, after your passing, to whom shall we give the white parasol?
"Dear ones, all my sons are indeed masters of the white parasol. Whoever—"
“However, you should grant the white parasol to whoever wins your favor.
When he had passed away, they performed his funeral rites, and on the seventh day they assembled and said, “The king declared,
‘You should raise the white parasol for whoever wins your favor,’ and this Saṃvarakumāra [wins ours].”
“Take charge of the kingdom! Surrounded by his kinsmen, they raised a golden-fringed white parasol over him.
King Saṃvara, abiding by the Bodhisattva’s counsel, ruled the kingdom with righteousness.
As for the other ninety-nine princes, they thought, “Our father has indeed passed away; they have raised the white parasol for Prince Saṃvara, yet he is the youngest of all.”
“The umbrella does not reach him; we shall raise the umbrella for the eldest of all.
Having come together from one side and sent a letter to King Saṃvara saying, “Give us either the umbrella or battle,” they besieged the city.
The king reported this situation to the Bodhisattva and asked, “Great King, what shall we do now? [The Bodhisattva replied: “Great King, your...”
"There is no need for you to fight with your brothers. Divide your father’s wealth into one hundred portions;
send ninety-nine portions to your brothers, and send this message: 'Take this portion belonging to your father;
I am not fighting with you. He did exactly so. Then his eldest brother—
The prince named Uposatha addressed the rest of them, saying: "Sirs, there is truly no one capable of overcoming a king.
Yet this younger brother of ours, though he has become our enemy, does not even stand his ground;
he has sent us the wealth belonging to our father with the message, 'I will not fight with you. However, none of us—"
"At this very moment we shall raise the parasol; we shall raise the parasol for one alone. Let this man himself be the king.
Come, having seen him and provided for the royal household, let us go back to our own country," he said.
Then all those princes, having caused the city gate to be opened and not acting as enemies, entered the city.
The king, having had his ministers take gifts for them, sent them back along the same road.
The princes, arriving on foot with a relatively small retinue, ascended the royal palace;
having shown their respectful homage to King Saṃvara, they sat down on low seats. King Saṃvara sat upon a lion-throne beneath a white parasol.
There was great fame and great splendor and glory; every place he looked upon trembled.
Prince Uposatha, having observed the majestic power of King Saṃvara, thought:
"I suppose our father, knowing that Prince Saṃvara would succeed him, gave the kingdom to him and did not give it to us in our own country. Having reflected thus, he [conversed] with him.
Conversing with him, he spoke these three verses:
“O Great King, the Lord of Men knows your virtue;
therefore, while honoring these princes, he does not think of you as being inferior to anyone.”
“Whether our great kings still stand, or whether the gods have passed away into heaven,
our kinsmen have given their consent, seeing it as for their own benefit.
By what practice of restraint do you remain steadfast once you have been born?”
"Why do the assembled circles of kinsmen not transgress against him?"—in this context, "jānanto nu" means "knowing indeed.
"Janādhipo" refers to our father, the lord of men. "Ime" refers to these one hundred and nine princes;
however, in the manuscript copies of the text, it is written as "aññe kumāre" (other princes). "Pūjento" means by means of various regions.

"Honoring him. "By no one at all" means he did not think that he should be honored by even any small district, thinking, "After my passing, this man will become king"; rather, perceiving this, he seems to have kept him right at his own feet.
"While he was still standing" means "while he was indeed still standing," "while he was indeed still living"—thus he asks. "Or perhaps, O King? means "or rather, [is it] for us?"

When his father had passed away, seeing his own welfare and prosperity, he was authorized by the royal officials, the merchants, and the people of the countryside, together with his kinsmen, saying, "Be king! By "conduct" (vatta) is meant moral behavior and custom.
"You stand surpassing those born [with you]" means that you stand having overcome your ninety-nine brothers who were of equal birth. "They do not overstep" means they do not overcome you.
Having heard that, King Saṃvara, speaking of his own virtues, uttered these six verses:
“I am not envious of the sons of kings, O Great Seer among ascetics;
I pay you due honor and I bow at the feet of you, the Tādin.”
“The ascetics, sages who delight in the qualities of the Dhamma, instruct me— who am devoted to those qualities of the Dhamma, desirous of hearing, and free from envy.
Having heard the words of those ascetics, the great seers, I— ”
“I do not despise anyone; my mind is devoted to the Dhamma.
As for the elephant-riders, the cavalrymen, the charioteers, and the infantry—of them I do not withhold their established food and wages.”
“I have great ministers, wise attendants,
who conduct business in Benares with abundant meat and fine rice. Furthermore,
there are prosperous merchants who have come from various countries.”
"In them I have established protection; know this, O Uposatha.
Therein, "I am not envious of the sons of kings" means that I, as a son of a king, do not feel envy toward any being, thinking, "May this prosperity not belong to him.

"Tādinam" refers to those great recluses endowed with the characteristics of a *tādi* (such as one who has stilled evil), by virtue of their having pacified wrongdoing through the aggregate of virtue (*sīlakkhandha*) and so forth.
Because they seek after virtues, I worship at the feet of those great seers—the righteous recluses and brahmins—with the fivefold prostration.

The meaning is: while giving them gifts and providing for their righteous protection, defense, and security, I pay them sincere homage and honor them with a mind full of affection. "Te maṃ" means those recluses [say] to me: "This [is] a portion of the Dhamma..."

"Applying himself appropriately, desiring to hear, and free from envy"—having known me to be thus, they instruct me who am devoted to the qualities of the Dhamma, desirous to hear, and free from envy;
the meaning is that they exhort me, saying, "Do this, do not do that. *Tesāhaṃ* means "of them, I.
*Hatthārohā* refers to warriors who fight having mounted elephants. *Anīkaṭṭhā* refers to those stationed in the elephant divisions and so forth. *Rathikā* refers to chariot-warriors.
“Pattikārakā” means the very same as “patti. “Niviṭṭhaṃ” means that whatever food and wages they have prepared, I do not withhold it;
the meaning is that I give it without omission.
“Mahāmattā” means, brother, my high ministers who possess great wisdom, who are skilled in counsel, both the chief ministers and the other advisors.
"And there are attendants. By this he shows: "You did not obtain wise teachers endowed with mantras;
however, our teachers were wise and skilled in means, and they provided us with the white parasol.
"Bārāṇasī, brother," [he said]. "From the time my parasol was raised, our king has been righteous, every half-month..."
"The god rains; because of that, the crops will flourish, and in Bārāṇasī there will be much fish and meat fit for eating, as well as sour gruel (suroda) fit for drinking.
Thus the inhabitants of the kingdom, having prepared much meat and sour gruel, trade with Bārāṇasī.
It is "prosperous" because it is free from calamity, having brought back the elephant-treasure, the horse-treasure, the jewel-treasure, and so forth.
"Carrying out their affairs, they are prosperous and flourishing. Know this, brother:
for all these reasons, although I am the youngest of all, I have surpassed my brother and obtained the white parasol; know it thus.
Then, having heard his virtue, Prince Uposatha spoke two verses:
“O Saṃvara, rule the kingdom over your kinsmen indeed according to the Dhamma;
for you are wise and learned, and moreover, a benefactor to your kin.
[Rule] that which is surrounded by your kinsmen and adorned with various jewels.”
"Enemies do not prevail over him, just as the lord of the asuras does not prevail over Indra.

Regarding this, "By righteousness, O Great King, you indeed overcome your kinsmen"—dear Saṃvara, by righteousness you indeed surpass the power of your ninety-nine kinsmen, your own elder brothers; from now on, you alone [shall rule] the kingdom.
"Make them; you alone are wise, learned, and a benefactor to your kinsmen"—this is the meaning. "That *tantrī* (lute)" refers to that very instrument endowed with such diverse qualities.

"Surrounded by kinsmen" means it was encircled by us, our ninety-nine kinsmen. "Adorned with various jewels" means it was embellished, accumulated, and possessed of a great collection of diverse gems.
"Like the Lord of the Asuras" means as he is surrounded by the Thirty-three gods (*Tāvatiṃsa*).

It illustrates that just as the Asura king does not overcome Indra, so too enemies cannot overcome him while he rules the kingdom of Bārāṇasī—twelve leagues in extent—within the Kāsi country of three hundred leagues, being surrounded by us who provide protection.
King Saṃvara bestowed great glory upon all his brothers. They remained in his presence for a month and a half-month.
Having stayed there, they said, "Great King, when bandits arise in the provinces, we shall deal with them;
you may enjoy the pleasures of sovereignty," and then each went to his own province. The king, abiding by the Bodhisatta’s counsel, at the end of his life departed filling the city of the gods.
Having delivered this Dhamma teaching, the Teacher said, "Monk, you were thus able to accept advice in the past; why do you not exert yourself now?
Having spoken thus, he proclaimed the Truths and identified the Jātaka.
At the conclusion of the Truths, that monk was established in the fruit of stream-entry (sotāpatti-phala).

At that time, this monk was King Saṃvara; Sāriputta was Prince Uposatha; the remaining brothers were the elder and younger elders; the assembly was the Buddha’s assembly; and as for the minister who gave the exhortation, it was I myself.
This concludes the eighth narrative, the Saṃvara Jātaka.
[463] 9. The Suppāraka Jātaka Narrative.
"Emerging and submerging"—this was spoken by the Teacher while dwelling at Jetavana, concerning the perfection of wisdom (paññāpāramī).
One day, in the evening, monks sitting in the Dhamma Hall, awaiting the Tathāgata’s departure to teach the Dhamma, said:
"Friends, oh, how the Teacher is of great wisdom, of vast wisdom, of smiling wisdom, and of swift wisdom!"

He possessed sharp wisdom, penetrative wisdom, and was endowed with skillful means (upāyapaññā) in various matters—wisdom that was vast like the earth, deep like the great ocean, and expansive like space.

Indeed, throughout the entire Jambudīpa, there was no one capable of surpassing the One of Ten Powers (dasabala) regarding questions posed to him. Just as waves arise in the great ocean, [so too did questions arise for him].
“They do not pass beyond their appointed time; rather, they break as soon as that time arrives. In the same way, no question ever passes beyond the One of Ten Powers;
having reached the Teacher’s feet, it surely breaks. Thus did they praise the Great Perfection of Wisdom of the One of Ten Powers.
The Teacher approached and asked, “Monks, about what discussion are you gathered here now? and they replied, “About this very one.”
When this was said, [the Blessed One] spoke thus: "Monks, it is not only now that the Tathāgata is wise; in the past, too, he was wise even while his knowledge was still unripened.
Even though he was blind, by means of the perception of water, he knew in this and that ocean: 'In this and that [ocean] there is such and such a jewel.
Having said this, he related a story of the past.
In the past, in the kingdom of Kuru, a king named Kururāja reigned, and there was a port town called Kurukaccha.
At that time, the Bodhisatta was reborn as the son of the chief navigator in Kurukaccha;
he was handsome and golden-hued, and they gave him the name Suppāraka Kumāra. As he grew up with a great retinue, at the age of sixteen...
Having attained mastery in the craft of a pilot, later on, after his father’s passing, he became the chief pilot and performed the duties of a pilot;
he was wise and endowed with insight. Consequently, there was no mishap whatsoever for the ship he boarded.
Later, however, both his eyes were destroyed by salt water. From that time forth, he served as the chief pilot.
Although he had performed the work of a pilot, he did not do so; instead, thinking, "I shall live by depending on the king," he approached the king.
Then the king appointed him to the office of appraiser. From that time forward, he appraised the king's treasures of elephants, horses, pearls, gems, and the like.
Then one day, [the king thought], "There shall be a state elephant for the king," and [he saw] a certain elephant with the color of a black stone peak.
They brought him. Upon seeing him, the king said, "Show him to the wise man. Then they led him into the presence of the wise man.
He stroked the elephant's body with his hand and said, "This one is not fit to be a state elephant;
he is physically stunted in his legs. For when his mother gave birth to him, she was unable to receive him in her lap."
"Therefore, having fallen to the ground, he became a dwarf with his hind legs," he said. When they returned having seized the elephant, they were questioned;
they replied, "The wise man speaks the truth. Having heard the reason for this, the king was pleased and had eight kahāpaṇas given to him.
On another day, they brought a horse, saying, "This shall be the king’s auspicious horse. The king sent that one as well to the presence of the wise man.
He too touched it with his hand and said, "This is not fit to be an auspicious horse;
for on the very day this one was born, its mother died. Therefore, not receiving her milk, it did not grow properly."
He said, "His story was indeed true. Having heard that as well, the king was pleased and caused eight kahāpaṇas to be given to him.
Then one day, thinking, "The king's auspicious chariot will be ready," they brought the chariot.
The king sent that too to him. He touched it with his hand and said, "This chariot was made from a hollow tree; therefore..."
"It is not suitable for the king," he said. That statement of his was indeed true. When the king heard this as well, he had eight more kahāpaṇas given.
Then they brought him a precious woolen blanket (*kambalaratana*). He sent that too to him.
Having touched it with his hand, he said, "There is one spot here where it has been gnawed by mice. While they were cleaning it...
Having seen him, they reported it to the king. Upon hearing it, the king was pleased and had eight kahāpaṇas given to him.
He thought: "Even after seeing such wonders as these, this king has only had eight kahāpaṇas given;
his park is the 'Barber's Park,' so he must be of barber stock. What use have I for such attendance upon a king? My own..."
“I shall go back to my own dwelling place. Thus he returned to the port of Kurukaccha.
While he was living there, the merchants prepared a ship and consulted among themselves, saying, “Whom shall we appoint as pilot?
[They decided: “A ship boarded by the wise Suppāraka does not meet with disaster; this man is wise and skilled in means. Even though he is blind, it is the wise Suppāraka alone [who can lead us].”
Approaching him and saying, "We have the best," they requested, "Please be our pilot. When he replied, "Sirs, I am blind;
how shall I perform the work of a pilot? they entreated him again and again, saying, "Master, though you are blind, you alone are our best. Being thus repeatedly requested, he said, "Very well, sirs;
by means of the signals you announce, I shall be the pilot," and [he boarded] their ship.
"Embark! They set out upon the great ocean by means of the ship. For seven days the ship proceeded without any misfortune, but then an unseasonable wind arose.
After wandering for four months upon the surface of the ordinary ocean, the ship reached the sea known as Khuramālī.
There, fish with bodies identical to those of humans and with noses like hoofs were leaping up and down in the water.
They were working there. Seeing the Great Being, those merchants asked him the name of that ocean and spoke this first verse:
“They emerge and they submerge, men with noses like hooves;
we ask you about Suppāraka—what ocean is this?”
Thus questioned by them, the Great Being, correlating their words with his own *niyāmaka-sutta*, spoke the second verse:
“For those merchants seeking wealth who have set out from Kurukaccha,
when their ship is lost at sea, it is called ‘Khuramālī’.”
"In that regard, 'those who have set out' means those departing from the port of Kurukaccha.
'Seeking wealth' means you merchants who are searching for riches. 'Having lost the ship' means:
'Dear ones, having crossed the ordinary ocean by means of this ship of yours which has ventured into foreign lands, you have reached this ocean called "Khuramālī" (the Razor-edged). "
"It is said that the wise speak thus.

However, in that ocean, diamonds were abundant. The Great Being thought, "If I tell them, 'This is a diamond ocean,' they will greedily take so many diamonds that they will sink the ship. Thus he spoke to them...
Without saying anything, he had the ship moored, and by a clever means, having taken hold of a single rope, he had a net cast down in the manner of catching fish.
Having extracted the diamond-hard [jewel], he placed it in the ship and caused other worthless goods to be discarded.
The ship, having crossed that ocean, proceeded further to a place named Aggimālinī. It was a mass of blazing fire.
He stood there emitting a radiance like that of the midday sun.
The merchants asked him with this verse: “Since the ocean appears like fire and like the sun, we ask you about Suppāraka: which ocean is this?”
The Mahāsatta also spoke to them with the following verse:
“For the merchants who set out from Kurukaccha seeking wealth,
whose ship was lost at sea, it is called Aggimālī.”
In that ocean, however, gold was abundant. In the same manner as before, the Great Being had them take gold from there as well and have it placed in the ship.
Having crossed that ocean too, the ship reached the ocean named Dadhimālī, which shone like milk and like curds. The merchants—
“As if curd or milk, the ocean appears reflected therein;
we ask about that Suppāraka—what ocean is this?
With this verse, they asked him for his name as well.
The Great Being explained it in the following verse:
“For the merchants who have set out from Kurukaccha seeking wealth,
and whose ship has gone astray, he is called Dadhimālī.”
In that ocean, however, silver was abundant. Having had it seized by means of a stratagem, he had it placed in the ship.
The ship, having crossed over that ocean as well, reached the ocean named Kusamāli, which was blue in color and shone like dark *kusatiṇa* grass or like a field of ripened grain. The merchants—
“Just as grain and crops are reflected in the ocean,
we ask about that Suppāraka: which ocean is this?”—
with this verse they asked even his name.
Thus it was declared in the following verse:
“For the merchants who set out from Kurukaccha seeking wealth,
when their ship was lost, she is called Kusamālī.”
In that ocean, however, blue gem-jewels were abundant. By means of a stratagem, he had them seized as well and caused them to be placed in the ship.
The ship, having crossed that ocean too, reached the ocean named Naḷamālin, which appeared like a forest of reeds or a forest of bamboos. The merchants—
"Just as a reed or a bamboo appears reflected in the ocean,
we ask about that Suppāraka: which ocean is this?"—
with this verse they asked even his name.
The Mahāsatta spoke in the following verse:
“Of the merchants set out from Kurukaccha seeking wealth,
whose ship had gone astray, he was called Naḷamāli.”
In that ocean, however, *masāragalla* and beryl were abundant. He had those also captured by means of a stratagem and had them placed in the ship.
According to another interpretation: "Reeds" (*naḷa*) refers both to scorpion-reeds and crab-reeds;
they are red in color. "Bamboos" (*veḷu*), moreover, is a name for coral; and that ocean was abundant with coral and possessed a reddish luster.
Therefore, they asked, "Is it as when one reed is pulled out from a thicket of reeds? The Great Being then had coral taken up.
Having passed beyond the Reed-Garland [ocean], the merchants saw the ocean called Balavāmukha (The Mouth of the Strong).
There, the water rises up from every side, having been drawn up again and again. When that water has risen up from every side, the water from every...
Divided by its sections, it appears like a great waterfall;
when a wave rises up, one side becomes like a precipice, and a terrifying sound arises that seems to pierce the ears and split the heart.
Seeing this, the merchants were struck with fear and trembling.
“A terrifying, great fear, an unhuman sound is heard;
it appears like a precipitous abyss, like the ocean itself.
We ask about Suppāraka: what ocean is this?”
They asked for his name by means of a verse.
Therein, "Suyyatimānuso" means "a superhuman sound is heard":
"For the merchants seeking wealth who have set out from Kurukaccha..."
“For a ship that has gone astray, it is called ‘the mouth of the strong one’.
Having thus declared its name in the following verse, the Bodhisatta said:

“Dear ones, once we have reached this ocean, the mouth of the strong one, there is no ship capable of turning back; this [ocean] will submerge any ship that reaches it and bring about its destruction.”
He said, "I will save them. Then seven hundred men boarded that boat.
All of them, terrified by the fear of death, let out a cry of extreme lamentation all at once, like beings being cooked in the Avīci hell.
The Great Being thought, "There is no one else capable of ensuring their safety except me; [I shall do so] by means of an Act of Truth."

Thinking, "I shall ensure their safety," he addressed them and said, "Sirs, quickly bathe me with scented water, clothe me in new garments, prepare a full bowl, and place it at the prow of the ship. They did so with haste.
The Great Being, taking the full bowl in both hands, stood at the prow of the ship.
Standing firm, performing an act of truth, he spoke this concluding verse:
“Since I can remember myself, since I have attained the state of discernment,
I do not recall intentionally having harmed even a single living being.”
“By this utterance of truth, may the ship turn back safely.
Therein, “since which time” means from the time I have remembered myself, from the time I attained the state of discernment (*viññutā*);
for the phrase “even a single living being was harmed” refers to the fact that during this interval, not even a single tiny insect such as a *kuntha* or a *kipillika* was intentionally harmed.

"I do not recall. This is merely a formal declaration; however, from the time he was a Bodhisatta, I have never before taken another's property even as much as a blade of grass, nor have I ever looked upon another's wife out of lust, nor have I spoken a lie, nor have I drunk intoxicants even with the tip of a blade of grass.
Having thus performed an act of truth (saccakiriya) by way of the five precepts, and having done so—
He poured water from a full bowl onto the prow of the ship.
After four months, the ship bound for a foreign land turned back and, by the power of his truth, reached the port of Kurukaccha in a single day as if he possessed supernormal powers.
Having arrived there, it leaped onto dry land, covering a distance of eight usabhas.
He stood right at the door of the boatman’s house. The Great Being divided the gold, silver, gems, coral, pearls, and diamonds among those merchants and gave them to them.
Giving them this advice, saying, “Enough with these many treasures;
do not enter the ocean again,” he performed meritorious deeds such as giving for as long as he lived, thereby filling the city of the gods.
Having delivered this Dhamma teaching, the Teacher said, “Thus, monks, even in the past the Tathāgata was possessed of great wisdom,” and he identified the Jātaka:
“At that time, the assembly was the Buddha’s assembly, and the wise man of Suppāraka was none other than myself.
This is the ninth commentary on the Suppāraka Jātaka.
The Summary of Birth Stories (Jātakuddāna):
Mātuposaka and Juṇha, Dhamma, Udaya, and Pānīya;
Yudhañcaya, Dasaratha, Saṃvara, and Suppāraka.
In the Eleventh Chapter, nine Jātakas have been chanted.
The commentary on the Eleventh Chapter is finished.
12. The Twelfth Chapter.
[464] 1. The Commentary on the Cūḷakuṇālajātaka.
Regarding the phrase "of the hunters with light minds," this Jātaka will be made clear in the Kuṇālajātaka.
This concludes the first commentary, the Cūḷakuṇālajātaka-vaṇṇanā.
[465] 2. The Commentary on the Bhaddasāla Jātaka:
"Who are you, dressed in pure garments?"—this was spoken by the Teacher while dwelling at Jetavana, concerning the conduct of one who acts for the benefit of those he knows.
For at the residence of Anāthapiṇḍika in Sāvatthī, there was a regular meal provided for five hundred bhikkhus.

It was likewise for Visākhā and the King of Kosala. In that regard, although various kinds of choice food were served there, the monks did not eat in the royal residence because they had no one there whom they could trust;
therefore, having taken their alms-food, they would go to the home of Anāthapiṇḍika, or Visākhā, or to other trusted people.
Having gone home, they ate. One day, the king sent messengers to the dining hall with a gift, saying, "Give this to the monks.
When it was reported that there were no monks in the dining hall, he asked, "Where have they gone?

Upon hearing that they had gone to sit and eat at the homes of those who were their personal acquaintances, the king went to the presence of the Teacher after his morning meal and said, "Venerable Sir, regarding food..."
“What is the highest [trust], sir? he asked. “Great King, trust is supreme;
even a mere measure of sour gruel becomes sweet when given by one who trusts. “Venerable sir, with whom do the bhikkhus have trust?
“With their kinsmen or with families of those in training (sekkha), Great King. Then the king thought: “I shall bring a daughter of the Sakyas here and make her my chief queen.”
"I shall do so; in this way, the monks will have confidence in me as if I were their own kinsman.
Rising from his seat and returning to his own residence, he dispatched a messenger to Kapilavatthu, saying: "Give me your daughter;
I desire kinship with you."
Having heard the messenger’s words, the Sākiyas gathered together and deliberated: “We live in a place where the commands of the King of Kosala prevail.
If we do not give the girl, there will be great enmity; if we do give her, our family lineage will be broken.
What indeed should be done? Then Mahānāma said to them: “Do not worry; my—
A daughter named Vāsabhakhattiyā was born from the womb of a slave-girl named Nāgamuṇḍā.

When she reached the age of sixteen, possessing supreme beauty and having attained the pinnacle of fortune, and being of the Khattiya caste by her father’s lineage, they thought, "We shall send her to him as a 'Khattiya maiden'.
The Sākiyas, saying "Very well," accepted this and summoned messengers, saying, "Excellent; we shall give the girl."
“Take her right now and go! they said. The messengers thought, “These Sakyans are indeed arrogant on account of their birth;
having said, ‘She must be our equal,’ they might give us someone who is not even like her.
We shall take her only while she is eating together with them. They spoke thus: “We will take her as we go, provided she eats together with you.”
“Having taken him, we shall go. The Sākiyas, having provided them with a place to stay, wondered, “What shall we do?
Mahānāma said, “Do not worry; I will devise a plan. At the time of my meal, you must bring Vāsabhakhattiyā adorned and present her to me.
As soon as I have taken a single mouthful, [you should say], ‘Your Majesty, such-and-such a king…’”
"Send a letter, saying: 'Please listen to this message first,' and then show them the letter.
They agreed, saying, "Very well," and while he was eating, they adorned the young woman.
Mahānāma said, "Bring my daughter; let her eat with me. Then, having adorned her...
Having made only a brief delay, they brought it. Thinking, "I shall eat together with my father," she dipped her hand into a single bowl.
Mahānāma also took a morsel from that same portion and placed it in his mouth.
When his hand was extended for a second morsel, [the messenger said], "Your Majesty, a letter has been sent by King Asuka; please listen first to this message," and he presented the letter.

They presented [the letter]. Mahānāma said, “Mother, you eat first,” and placing his right hand on the bowl, he took it with his left hand and looked at the letter. While he was reflecting upon that message, the other woman ate.
When she had finished eating, he washed his hands and rinsed his mouth. Seeing this, the messengers said, “She is certainly [in love] with him.”
They concluded, "She is a daughter," but they were unable to determine her lineage. Mahānāma sent his daughter with a large retinue.
The messengers, having brought her to Sāvatthī, declared, "This young woman is of noble birth; she is the daughter of Mahānāma.
The King was pleased and, having had the entire city decorated, placed her upon a heap of jewels.
He had her consecrated in the position of chief queen. She became dear and pleasing to the king.
Then, before long, she conceived. The king provided her with the necessary care for her pregnancy.
After ten months had passed, she gave birth to a son of golden complexion. Then, on the day of his naming ceremony, the king went into the presence of his own grandfather.
He sent [a messenger], saying, "The daughter of the Śākya king, Vāsabhakhattiyā, has given birth to a son; what name shall we give him?
Now, the minister who had gone to receive that message was somewhat deaf; having arrived, he announced it to the King, the Grandfather (Ayyaka).
Upon hearing this, the King said, "Even before Vāsabhakhattiyā gave birth to her son, he surpassed all people; now..."
"But she will become exceedingly dear to the king," he said. When the deaf minister heard the word "dear" (vallabhā), which he misheard, he perceived it as "Viṭaṭūbha.
Approaching the king, he said, "Your Majesty, you should give the prince the name 'Viṭaṭūbha'. The king replied, "This shall be our traditional family name."
Having reflected thus, he gave him the name "Viṭaṭūbha. From that time on, the prince grew up with the full care and privileges due to a prince.
When he was seven years old, seeing other princes receiving elephant figurines, horse figurines, and so forth being brought from their maternal grandfathers' families, he asked his mother:
"Mother, presents are being brought for others from their maternal grandfathers' families; will anyone bring anything for me?"

"Why have you sent nothing at all? Are you without a mother and without a father? Then she deceived him, saying, "Dear one, the Śākya kings are my maternal uncles, but they live far away; that is why they have sent nothing.
Later, when he was sixteen years old, he said, "Mother, I wish to see my maternal grandfather's family," to which she replied, "Enough, dear one, what..."
Although he was repeatedly dissuaded with the words, “Having gone there, you will do it,” he begged her again and again. Then his mother consented, saying, “In that case, go.
Having informed his father, he set out with a great retinue.
Vāsabhakhattiyā had previously sent a letter, saying, “I am living happily here; let no one reveal any secret to my husband. The Sākiyas—
Knowing that Viṭaṭūbha was approaching and that it would not be possible for him to pay his respects in person, they sent his youngest and youngest sons to the countryside.
When the princes arrived at Kapilavatthu, the Sakyans assembled in the assembly hall. The prince went to the assembly hall and stood there.
Then they said to him, "This, dear one, is your maternal grandfather; this is your maternal uncle," and he [recognized] them all.

He went about paying homage. Having prostrated himself as far as his back could bear, and seeing not even a single person paying homage to him, he asked, "Is it that there are no one to pay homage to me?
The Śākyas replied, "Dear brother, your younger brothers have gone to the countryside," and they rendered him great honor. After staying for a few days, with great...

He departed with his retinue. Then a certain maidservant, having reviled and abused the seat upon which he sat in the assembly hall, saying, "This is the seat where the son of Vāsabhakhattiyā’s slave sits," washed it with milk and water.
A certain man, having forgotten his weapon and returning to retrieve it, heard the sound of Vitatūbha Kumāra being reviled.
Having heard this and inquired into the matter, he learned that "Vāsabhakhattiyā was born from the womb of a slave-girl to Mahānāma the Sakyan.
Having gone there, he informed the army. A great clamor arose: "It seems Vāsabhakhattiyā is the daughter of a slave-girl!
When the prince heard this, he said, "Let them first wash my sitting-plank with milk-water; as for me, I shall [ascend] the throne."
He formed the intention: "When they are established [in their new homes], I shall take their throat-blood and wash my sitting-plank.
When he had gone to Sāvatthī, the ministers reported the entire occurrence to the king.
The king, becoming enraged with the Sākiyas for having given him all his slave-girls' daughters, [punished] Vāsabhakhattiyā and her son.
Without revoking the allowance previously granted, he ordered that she be given only the same allowance as was received by the male and female slaves.

Then, after a few days had passed, the Teacher came to the royal palace and sat down. The king paid homage to the Teacher and said, "Venerable sir, it is said that my kinsmen have given me a daughter of yours as a slave-girl;
therefore, I have revoked her allowance along with that of her son, and [ordered that she receive only what] the male and female slaves..."
"He gave her only the amount of exemptions she was entitled to," he said. The Teacher replied, "Great King, what the Sākiyas have done is improper;
when giving, one should give to those of the same caste. However, Great King, I say this:
Vāsabhakhattiyā was the daughter of a Kṣatriya king and received her consecration in the house of a Kṣatriya king; Viṭaṭūba, too, was a Kṣatriya king."
"Born from dependence [on others], what can the mother's lineage accomplish? Only the father's lineage is authoritative.
Thus did the ancient wise men grant the position of chief queen even to a poor woman who was a wood-gatherer;
and the son born from her womb, having ruled over Benares with its twelve leagues of territory, became known as King Kaṭṭhavāhana. This is the Kaṭṭhavāhana Jātaka.
The Teacher preached the Dhamma. Having heard the Teacher’s discourse on the Dhamma, and having heard that "the father's lineage alone is indeed the measure," the king was pleased;
he then provided for the mother and son their usual customary allowances.
Now, the king had a general named Bandhula, whose wife was named Mallikā, whom he considered barren, saying, "Go back to your own family home..."

"Go," he said, and sent her back to Kusinārā herself. She thought, "I will go only after I have seen the Teacher," and having entered Jetavana, she paid homage to the Tathāgata and stood to one side. When asked, "Where are you going?
she replied, "Venerable sir, my husband has sent me to our family home. When asked, "Why? she said, "Venerable sir, I am barren and childless. Then the Teacher—
When she was told, "If there is no purpose in going further, then turn back," she was delighted; she paid homage to the Teacher and returned once more to her own home.
When asked, "Why have you turned back? she replied, "I have been sent back by the One Possessed of Ten Powers.
The general said, "The Tathāgata must have seen some reason for this. Before long, she conceived a child.
Having conceived a pregnancy-longing, she announced, "A longing has arisen in me. "What is this longing?
"Lord, I wish to descend into the consecration-mangala lotus-pool of the Licchavi kings in the city of Vesālī, bathe there, and drink the water.
The general said, "Very well," and taking a bow with the strength of a thousand men, he placed her upon the chariot and departed from Sāvatthī.
Driving his chariot, he entered Vesālī.
At that time, near the city gate, there was a Licchavi named Mahāli, who had learned his craft in the same teacher’s school as the Kosalan King’s general Bandhula;
being blind, he was instructing the Licchavis in both their welfare and the Dhamma.
He was staying there. Hearing the sound of the chariot striking against the threshold, he said, "This is the sound of Bandhula Malla’s chariot overturning;

today fear will arise among the Licchavis. The protection both inside and outside the lotus pond was formidable, with an iron net spread overhead where even birds had no access. But as for the general, from his chariot—
Having descended and driven away the guards by striking them with his sword, he cut through the iron net, lowered his wife into the middle of the lotus pond, bathed her, and gave her water to drink.
Having himself bathed as well, he placed Mallikā upon the chariot, departed from the city, and set out back along the very path by which he had come.
The guards went and reported this to the Licchavis. The Licchavi kings—
Having become angry, they mounted five hundred chariots and set out, saying, "We shall seize Bandhula Malla.
They reported this occurrence to Mahāli. Mahāli said, "Do not go; for he will have you all killed.
They replied, "We shall certainly go. [Mahāli said: "In that case, as far as the hub of the wheel reaches the ground—"
"Upon seeing the place where he has entered, you should turn back; if you do not turn back from there, you will hear a sound like a thunderbolt ahead of you, so you should turn back from that place;
if you do not turn back from there, you will see a hole in the yokes of your chariots, so you should turn back from that place;
do not proceed further ahead. Despite his words, they did not turn back but continued to pursue him.
Seeing them, Mallikā said, "My lord, the chariots are visible. He replied, "In that case, inform me when they appear as if they were a single chariot.
When all of them appeared as one, she said, "My lord, only a single chariot-front is now visible.
Bandhula said, "In that case, take these reins," and having given her the reins, he [mounted] the chariot.
Standing still, he strung his bow; the wheel of his chariot sank into the earth up to its hub.
Even when the Licchavis saw that sight, they did not turn back. The other, having gone a short distance, twanged his bowstring, which sounded like a clap of thunder.
They did not turn back from there either, but continued on, pursuing him. Bandhula, while remaining standing in the chariot—
He discharged a single arrow. It pierced through the front of five hundred chariots, struck the five hundred kings at the place where their girdles were fastened, and entered the earth.
Not realizing they had been struck, they pursued him, crying out, "Stop! Stop! Bandhula halted his chariot and said, "You..."
“Dead men,” he said, “have no battle with those who are dead. They replied, “Those called ‘dead’ are certainly not like us.

He said, “In that case, untie the belongings of the very last one among you. They untied them. As soon as they were untied, he died and fell down. Then he said to them, “Are you all likewise such as this? To your own homes...”
"Having gone there, you must make preparations; having made the preparations and instructed your wife and children, you may then take off your armor," he said. Having done so, they all met their end.
Bandhula also brought Mallikā to Sāvatthī. She gave birth to twins sixteen times, and all of them—
They were heroic and endowed with great strength, and they attained mastery in every craft.
Each one was accompanied by a retinue of a thousand men. As they went to the royal palace together with their father, the royal courtyard was completely filled by them.
Then one day, when people who had been defeated in a fraudulent legal dispute saw Bandhula approaching, they raised a great outcry.
They reported the fraudulent nature of the lawsuit to the judges.
He too went to the court, investigated the case, and rendered the rightful owner as the rightful owner and the non-owner as the non-owner. The great multitude raised a loud shout of applause.
The king asked, "What is this? and having heard the matter, he was pleased and [honored] all those ministers.
Having taken [the case], he handed it over for Bandhula’s decision. From then on, he adjudicated correctly.
Consequently, the former judges, no longer receiving bribes and thus suffering a loss of income, slandered him at the royal court, saying, "Bandhula aspires to the kingship.
The king, having heard these words, was unable to restrain his mind; "In this..."

Thinking again, "If I am killed right here, blame will arise for me," he decided, "It would be better to have the border region attacked by hired men, drive them off, and then kill [Bandhula] along with his sons on the way back.
He summoned Bandhula and said, "The border region is reportedly in revolt; go with your sons and capture the bandits."
Having sent [this message], he said, "Right here, cut off his head along with his thirty-two sons and bring it back," and dispatched other powerful great warriors along with them.

Even as he was heading toward the border region, the bandits who had been mobilized fled upon hearing that the general was coming. Having established him in that district, he [settled] the countryside.
Having made his preparations, he turned back.
Then, at a place not far from the city, those warriors cut off the heads of him along with his sons.
On that day, Mallikā had invited the two chief disciples together with five hundred bhikkhus. Then, during the morning time—
They brought a letter and gave it to her, saying, “They have cut off your husband’s head along with those of your sons.
Having learned of this event, she said nothing to anyone; instead, placing the letter in her lap, she served the Saṅgha of bhikkhus alone.
Then, while her attendants were bringing oil-jars after giving food to the bhikkhus, they broke the jars in front of the elders.
The General of the Dhamma said, “Lay sister, when that which is subject to breaking has broken, it should not be grieved over.
She took a leaf out from her lap and said, “They brought this leaf to me saying, ‘Your father’s head has been cut off along with thirty-two sons.
Even having heard this, I do not grieve; what should I grieve for when a vessel of ghee has been broken, venerable sir? Thus spoke the General of the Dhamma.
Having spoken such words as “signless and unknown,” and having taught the Dhamma, he rose from his seat and went to the monastery.
She too, having summoned her thirty-two daughters-in-law, exhorted them: “Your husbands have received the fruit of their own past kamma;
do not grieve, do not lament, and do not harbor malice toward the king.”
Having heard those words, the King’s secret agents reported their innocence to the King.
Overcome with a sense of spiritual urgency (*saṃvega*), the King went to her residence, asked Mallikā and her daughters-in-law for forgiveness, and granted Mallikā a boon.
She said, "Let it be taken by me," and when he had departed, she gave a funeral feast, bathed, and approached the King.
Having paid homage, she said, “Your Majesty, you have granted me a boon; I have no other need.
Grant permission for my thirty-two daughters-in-law and myself to go to our own family homes. The king consented.
She sent her thirty-two daughters-in-law to their respective families, while she herself went to her own family home in the city of Kusinārā. The king—
The king appointed Dīghakārāyana, the nephew of the general Bandhula, to the position of general.
However, Dīghakārāyana thought, "My maternal uncle was killed by this man," and he wandered about seeking an opportunity to harm the king.
As for the king, from the time Bandhula—who was innocent—was put to death, he was filled with remorse and found no peace of mind; he could not enjoy the pleasures of sovereignty.
At that time, the Teacher was dwelling in dependence upon a market town of the Sakyans named Veḷu.
The king went there, and having encamped his army not far from the monastery, he thought, "I shall pay homage to the Teacher with a great retinue.
He then entered the monastery and, giving the five royal insignia to Dīghakārāyaṇa, proceeded alone to the fragrant chamber.
He entered. Everything is to be understood according to the procedure set forth in the *Dhammacetiya Sutta*.

When he had entered the fragrant chamber (*gandhakuṭi*), Dīghakārāyaṇa took those five royal insignia, installed Viṭaṭūbha as king, and having turned back the king’s horse and his female attendant, he went to Sāvatthī. The king [was reunited] with the Teacher.
Having engaged in pleasant conversation and departed, he did not see the army;
upon asking that woman and hearing the news, he thought, "I shall take my nephew Ajātasattu and come to capture Viṭaṭūbha.
While traveling toward the city of Rājagaha, the gates being closed at the wrong hour, he was unable to enter the city and lay down to rest in a certain hall.
Exhausted by the wind and heat, he passed away right there during the latter part of the night.
When the night had turned to dawn, they heard the sound of that woman lamenting, "O Lord, King of Kosala, you have now become protectorless," and they informed the king.
He performed the funeral rites for his maternal uncle with great honor.
Viṭaṭūbha, having obtained the kingdom, recalled that enmity and set out with a great army, thinking, "I shall kill all the Sākyans.
On that day, at the time of dawn, the Teacher surveyed the world and, seeing the destruction of his kinsmen's assembly, thought, "It is fitting to show compassion to my kin.
Having wandered for alms in the forenoon and returned from his almsround, he—
Having prepared his lion’s rest in the Fragrant Chamber, he traveled through the air in the evening and sat down at the foot of a tree with dense shade on the outskirts of Kapilavatthu.
Not far from there, within the royal domain of Viṭaṭūbha, stood a banyan tree with spreading shade;
seeing the Teacher, Viṭaṭūbha approached and paid homage to him.

“Venerable sir, for what reason do you sit at this time of heat under the shade of this tree with sparse foliage, instead of sitting, venerable sir, at the foot of this banyan tree which provides dense shade? When he was told, “Let it be so, Great King;
the shade of kinsmen is indeed cool,” [the king thought], “The Teacher must have come for the sake of protecting his kinsmen.”
Having reflected and paid homage to the Teacher, he returned to Sāvatthī. The Teacher, too, having risen up, went back to Jetavana.
The king, remembering the offense of the Sākiyas, set out a second time; seeing the Teacher there as before, he turned back again.
Setting out a third time, he saw the Teacher right there and turned back once more. On the fourth occasion—
But when he had departed, the Teacher, having examined the past karma of the Sākiyas and knowing that their evil deed of casting poison into the river was not yet exhausted,
did not go on the fourth occasion. King Viṭaṭūbha, having caused all the Sākiyas to be slain beginning with the infants who were still nursing,
returned after washing his sitting-plank with their blood from the necks.

On the third occasion of his departure, after the Teacher had returned from his journey, on the following day, having walked for alms and finished his meal, as he was entering the fragrant chamber, the monks who had assembled from all directions sat in the Dhamma Hall and said:
"Friends, the Teacher has shown himself, turned back the king, and liberated his kinsmen from the fear of death; thus it is with his kinsmen..."
They spoke of the Blessed One’s virtues, saying, “The Teacher acts for the welfare of others.

The Teacher approached and asked, “Monks, about what discussion are you gathered here now? When they replied, “About this very matter,” he said, “Monks, it is not only now that the Tathāgata acts for the welfare of his kinsmen;
he has done so in the past as well. Having said this, he related a story of the past.
In the past, in Bārāṇasī, a king named Brahmadatta, who ruled his kingdom righteously without violating the ten duties of a king, thought one day:
"On the surface of Jambudīpa, kings dwell in palaces with many pillars;
therefore, the construction of a palace with many pillars is nothing extraordinary. What if I were to build a palace with only a single pillar?"
“I shall have a palace built; thus I will become the preeminent king among all kings.
He summoned his carpenters and said, “Build for me a single-pillar palace of supreme beauty.
They agreed, saying, “Very well,” and entering the forest, they saw many straight and large trees suitable for a single-pillar palace, and [thought], “These trees...”
Thinking, "There are [steps], but the path is uneven and it is not possible to descend;
we shall inform the king," they did so. The king said, "By some means or other, descend slowly.
When it was replied, "Your Majesty, it is not possible by any means whatsoever," he said, "In that case, look for a tree in my pleasure garden. The carpenter—
Having gone to the garden, they saw a well-born, straight *sāla* tree that was honored by the village and the town, and from which offerings had been received even from the royal family;
seeing this auspicious tree, they went into the presence of the king and reported the matter to him.
The king said, "A tree in the garden is indeed dependent upon me; go, sirs, and cut it down. They accepted, saying, "Very well."

Carrying perfumes, garlands, and other offerings, they went to the park; having applied fragrant paste in five-finger marks upon the tree, encircled it with thread, tied a floral wreath around it, lit a lamp, and performed the ritual offering, they said: "On the seventh day from now, we shall come and cut down this tree;
the King is having it cut down. May the deity born within this tree go elsewhere."
“There is no fault on our part,” they reported.
Then the young deva reborn there, hearing those words, thought: “Without a doubt these carpenters will cut down this tree;
my celestial mansion (vimāna) will be destroyed. Indeed, my life itself extends only as far as this mansion.”
Furthermore, the many celestial mansions belonging to my kinsmen among the deities who have been reborn in the young *sāla* trees surrounding this protection will perish.
For the lives of my kinsmen among the deities extend only as far as their celestial mansions.
Indeed, my own destruction does not distress me as much as the destruction of my kinsmen; therefore, it is for the sake of their lives that I act.
Thinking, “It is right to give it,” at the hour of midnight, adorned with celestial ornaments, he entered the king’s bedchamber;
making the entire chamber one mass of light, he stood weeping by the side of the head of the bed.
Seeing him, the king was terrified and, conversing with him, spoke the first verse:
“Who are you, standing in the sky above us in pure garments?
By what means do these tears flow from you, and from where has this fear come upon you?
Therein, “Who are you? asks: “Among the nāgas, yakkhas, supaṇṇas, Sakkas, and so forth, who indeed are you? The word “in garments” is merely a statement.
But he said this with reference to all divine ornaments. *Agha* means in the unobstructed sky;
*vehāsa* is a synonym for that very same thing. "Why do tears flow from you? means: for what reason do tears flow from you?
"From where?"—he asks this by way of questioning what basis there is for that fear arising from such things as separation from kinsmen or the loss of wealth.
Then the king of the gods spoke these two verses:
“O Lord, in your own realm, I am known by the wise as Bhaddasāla;
for sixty thousand years I have remained here, being honored.”
“While Disampati was having cities built,
as well as houses and various palaces, they did not treat me with contempt;
just as they honored me, so too should you honor me.”

"Regarding 'he dwells there': this shows that while I was dwelling in this park—having been honored by the entire city of Bārāṇasī as well as by the villages and market towns, and receiving constant offerings and hospitality—so much time has passed.
"Cities" refers to the works of city maintenance. "Houses" refers to dwellings built on the ground. "Disampati" [is the name of the king].

"Lord of the quarters, Great King! 'They did not despise me'—those former kings who were restoring this city and performing such works did not disregard me, they did not overstep me, and they did not harm me;
they did not cut down the tree that was my dwelling and carry out their work [instead], but rather they paid me honor," he said. "Just as... [the rest of the verse follows].
"Therefore, just as those ancient kings honored me and not even one among them had this tree cut down, you too should honor me in the same way; do not have my tree cut down.
Then the king spoke these two verses:
“I do not see anyone like you, O tree, with such a thick trunk;
in height and circumference, you are beautiful by nature.
I shall have a delightful palace built for you, supported by a single pillar.”
"I shall lead you there; long will your life be, O Yakkha!"—therein, "by body" means by measure.

This is what is meant: I do not see another tree so thick and large as you in measure; rather, it is you alone who, in terms of height and girth, possess that which is called "well-born," characterized by symmetry, straightness, and beauty.
He was handsome by birth and possessed of great beauty, residing in a palace with a single pillar. "A palace," he thought, "therefore, having that [tree] cut down, I shall have a palace built.
Regarding the word "there": "But there, O friend King of Devas, I shall place you in that palace;
living together with me, receiving the finest perfumes, garlands, and so forth, you shall attain honor."
"You shall live happily; do not worry that you will perish for lack of a place to dwell—I shall provide one.
O Yakkha, your life shall be long.
Having heard this, the king of the gods spoke two verses:
“Such was the thought that arose: ‘There shall be separation from this body.
Having cut me apart in various ways, cut me into pieces.
Cut me at the top and in the middle, and afterwards cut me at the root.’”
"Even as I am being cut thus, may there be no suffering at death.
In this context, "thus a thought arose" means: if such a thought has arisen in you;
"separation from the body" means: if you have desired separation from my body, [which is] like a *bhaddasāla* tree; "many" (*puthuso*)...
"In many ways": having cut [me] up. "Into pieces": having made [me] into small fragments, cut me apart.
"And at the top": while cutting me apart, first cut at the top, then in the middle, and finally at the base.
"In this way, as I am being cut, may my death not be painful; would it not rather be pleasant?"—thus he requests.
Then the king spoke these two verses:
"Just as one might cut off the hands and feet, And the ears and nose while one is still alive,
And afterwards cut off the head— That would be the suffering of death."
“Is it pleasant for you, O Bhaddasāla forest tree, to be cut into pieces?
For what cause, by taking hold of what, do you wish to be cut into pieces?
In this context, “hands and feet” refers to both the hands and the feet. “That is painful” means for one who is being cut in such a sequence.
That death would be painful for the thief. "Is it not pleasant, Bhaddasāla? "Yes, sir.
"Thieves who have reached the point of execution, wishing to die in peace, beg for the cutting off of their heads, not for being cut into pieces;
yet you beg in this way. Therefore I ask you: 'Is it pleasant to be cut into pieces? Why so? [Because] that which is called being cut into pieces—
"It is not happiness, yet there must be some cause for it here," he said, asking this.
Then, explaining it to him, Bhaddasāla spoke these two verses:
"And whatever cause one takes up, a cause connected with the Dhamma;..."
“I wish for it to be cut into pieces; O Great King, listen to me.
My kinsmen were raised in comfort, living in my presence where there was no wind;
even they would be harmed by this, for they are unaccustomed to the suffering of others.”
In this context, "connected with the Dhamma as its cause" means, O Great King, that which is indeed endowed with the true nature of a cause, and not a mere semblance of a cause;
having taken up the cause and referring to it, I say: "I desire [it] cut into pieces"—listen to this with an attentive ear.
"My kinsmen" refers to those who were raised in comfort in the shade of my auspicious *sāla* tree, while I was among the young *sāla* trees.
The meaning is: "My kinsmen, who have been reborn as hosts of deities because they were protected from the wind by me, exist;
I might harm them by falling while cutting down the roots of this tree with its broad branches and twigs, or I might destroy them by causing their celestial mansions to collapse.
Regarding the phrase *paresam asukhocitaṃ*: even so, I would bring unhappiness (*asukha*) to those other kinsmen, the hosts of deities.
“Suffering has been accumulated and increased, yet I do not desire suffering for them; therefore, I shall have the Bhaddasāla tree cut into pieces, piece by piece”—this is the intended meaning here.

Hearing this, the king was pleased and thought, “This divine son is indeed righteous; even for the sake of his own destruction of his celestial mansion, he does not wish for the destruction of his kinsmen’s mansions. He practices benevolence toward his kin; I shall grant him safety. Having thus rejoiced, he spoke this concluding verse:
“You have thought what was worthy of thought, O Bhaddasāla forest tree;
you desire the welfare of your kinsmen, my dear friend, so I grant you freedom from fear.
In this context, “you have thought what was worthy of thought” means that because of your gentle heart toward your kinsmen, you have thought exactly what ought to be thought.
He thought. There is also a reading: *chedeyyarūpaṃ chedesīti*. Its meaning is: "Desiring it to be cut into pieces, you have cut that which was fit to be cut.
"O friend," he said, "having gained confidence in these qualities of yours, I grant you safety. I have no need for the palace; I will not have you executed.
Go, surrounded by your circle of kinsmen, honored and respected, and live in happiness. Thus he spoke.
The King of the Gods, having taught the Dhamma to the king, departed. The king, abiding by his advice, performed meritorious deeds such as giving and filled the city of heaven.
Having brought forth this Dhamma instruction, the Teacher said, "Thus, monks, even in the past the Tathāgata practiced for the welfare of those he knew," and he identified the Jātaka:
"At that time the king was Ānanda, and the deity reborn among the young *sāla* trees was [the Buddha]."
“The Buddha’s assembly was exactly as it is now, and the divine king Bhaddasāla was none other than myself.
This concludes the second commentary, the Bhaddasāla Jātaka.
[466] 3. The Commentary on the Samuddavāṇija Jātaka.
"Those who sow with patience..."—this was spoken by the Teacher while dwelling at Jetavana concerning Devadatta’s falling into hell after having gathered five hundred families.
For when the two chief disciples had departed taking their retinue with them, Devadatta was unable to sustain his grief;
hot blood issued from his mouth, and being oppressed by intense pain, he [approached] the Tathāgata.
Reflecting on his virtues, he thought: "I alone have harbored ill will toward the Tathāgata for nine months;
yet the Teacher has never had an evil thought toward me, nor have the eighty great elders ever felt resentment toward me.
By my own actions, I alone have now become destitute; I have been abandoned by the Teacher, by the great elders, and even by Rāhula, the foremost of kinsmen."
“I shall go to the Sakyan royal family and ask the Teacher for forgiveness,” he said, giving notice to his followers.
Having had himself escorted by five men, he traveled night after night until he reached the kingdom of Kosala.
The Elder Ānanda informed the Teacher, “Venerable Sir, it is said that Devadatta is coming to ask you for forgiveness. “Ānanda,…”
“Devadatta shall not obtain a sight of me.
Then, when he arrived at the gate of the city of Sāvatthī, the Elder spoke again, and the Blessed One likewise said the same.
When he reached the vicinity of the lotus pond in Jetavana, his evil reached its culmination, and a fever arose in his body.
When he was reborn there, having become desirous of drinking water upon realizing his state, he said, "Friends, lower me from the couch; I wish to drink some water.
As soon as they had lowered him and he had merely been placed upon the ground, before his mind could even find satisfaction, the great earth opened up.
At that very moment, flames of fire from the Avīci hell rose up, surrounded him, and seized him. He thought, "My evil karma has reached its culmination..."
"Taking [the bone-relics]," means having recollected the virtues of the Tathāgata:
"With these bones, I go for refuge with my very life to that Supreme Person, the God beyond gods,
the Charioteer who tames men, the All-Seeing One, marked with a hundred merits— the Buddha."
By means of this verse, he established himself in the refuges and became destined for the Avīci hell. He had five hundred families as his supporters;
they too, taking his side, reviled the One of Ten Powers and were reborn in Avīci itself.
Thus, having taken those five hundred families with him, he was established in Avīci.
Then one day, the bhikkhus raised a discussion in the Dhamma hall: "Friends, Devadatta was evil;

out of greed for gain and honor, he harbored anger toward the Perfectly Enlightened One at an improper time, and failing to consider the dangers of the future, he has gone to Avīci together with five hundred families.
The Teacher approached and asked, "Bhikkhus, what is it that you are discussing?"

Having asked, "For what discussion are you sitting together now? and being told, "For this very one," he said, "Monks, it is not only now that Devadatta, having become greedy for gain and honor, failed to look toward future danger;
in the past as well, failing to look toward future danger, he met with great ruin along with his assembly, being greedy for present happiness. Having said this, he related the past.
In the past, while Brahmadatta was reigning in Bārāṇasī, there was a large village of carpenters not far from Bārāṇasī where a thousand families resided.
There, the carpenters would say to people, "We will make you a bed, we will make you a chair,
we will build you a house," and having thus taken much debt from the hands of the people, they were unable to do anything for them.
People, whenever they saw them, would urge the carpenters on, saying, "They are being held back!
Oppressed by their creditors and unable to live in comfort, [the carpenters] thought, "Let us go abroad and live wherever we can.
They entered the forest, cut down trees, constructed a large boat, launched it into a river, and brought it back to a spot half a *yojana* from the village.
Having established him in his proper place, at the hour of midnight he returned to the village, took his wife and children, went to the landing-place for boats, and boarded one.
Gradually entering the great ocean, they were driven by the force of the wind until they reached an island in the midst of the sea.
On that island, there grew wild rice, sugarcane, plantains, mangoes, rose-apples, jackfruits, palmyra palms, coconut palms, and other such trees.
There were various fruits. A certain man whose ship had wrecked reached that island first;
eating rice-meat and chewing sugarcane and other foods, he lived on that island with a stout body, naked, and with his hair and beard grown long.
The carpenters thought, "If this island is possessed by a *rakkhasa*, then we too—"
"We shall meet with destruction; let us seize the island while we still can.
Then seven or eight men, brave and strong, equipped with their five weapons, descended and took possession of the island.
At that moment, the man who had eaten his breakfast and drunk sugarcane juice, having attained a state of well-being, was in a delightful place upon a sandy surface resembling a silver plate.

Lying on his back in the cool shade, he uttered this inspired utterance while singing: "The inhabitants of Jambudīpa, though they plow and sow, do not obtain such happiness; for me, this island is far superior to Jambudīpa.
Then the Teacher addressed the monks, pointing out: "Monks, that man uttered this inspired utterance."
He spoke the first verse:
“Those people, men who subsist on the fruit of their actions, plow and sow;
they do not share in this island. Jambudīpa alone is our choice.”
"There, they know" means those people dwelling in Jambudīpa. "Those who subsist on the fruits of karma" refers to beings who live upon the results of various karmic actions.
Then, those men who were surveying the island, hearing the sound of that singing, thought, "It sounds like the voice of a human;
we shall find out. Following the sound, they went and saw the man; thinking, "This must be a *yakkha*," they were terrified and trembling with fear.
They all put on their armor. He too, seeing them, out of fear of being killed, pleaded, "Sire, I am not a *yakkha*;
I am a human being; give me my life! When they replied, "Men such as you do not go about naked," he entreated them again and again until he made his human nature known.
They approached that man and engaged in friendly conversation.
Having heard this, they asked him about the manner of arriving there. He too told them everything, saying:
"You have come here through the excellence of your own merit; this is a supreme island. Here, people do not live by performing manual labor with their own hands;
since there is no rice that must be grown or sugarcane and such within this land, dwell here without longing for anything else."
"Furthermore, for us living here, there is no other obstacle; there is no other danger here.
However, this place is possessed by non-human beings (*amanussa*). Those non-human beings might become angry upon seeing your excrement and urine.
Therefore, when you do so, you should sweep away the sand and cover it with sand. This much is the danger here; there is no other."
"There is no [permanence]; you should remain constantly heedful. They took up residence there.
In that community of a thousand families, there were two master carpenters who were the elders of five hundred families each.
Of these two, one was foolish and greedy for flavors, while the other was wise and unattached to flavors.
In the course of time, while all of them were living there happily and had become stout of body, they thought, "We have drunk liquor for a long time;
let us now make wine from sugarcane juice and drink it. Having prepared and drunk the wine, they became intoxicated;
singing, dancing, and sporting about, they grew heedless and voided excrement and urine here and there without concealing it.

They made the island loathsome and repulsive. The deities, becoming angry because "these people are making our pleasure grove repulsive," consulted together, saying, "We shall cause them to be carried across the great ocean and wash away the island. Then they said, "This is the dark fortnight;
today our assembly has been broken. Now, on the fifteenth day from now, on the full-moon uposatha day..."
"Let us overturn the ocean at the time of the moon's rising and kill them all," they decided, and thus set a day.
Then, among them, a certain righteous son of the gods,

out of compassion so that "these men might not perish while I am looking on," appeared adorned with all his ornaments while they were sitting at their house doors enjoying pleasant conversation after having eaten their evening meal.
Having made the entire island a single mass of light and standing in the sky toward the northern direction, he said, “O carpenter, the deities are angry with you.
Do not dwell in this place; for after half a month has passed from now, the deities will cause the ocean to overflow its banks and will kill you all.
Depart from here and flee! Having spoken thus, he recited the second verse:
“When the moon has reached its fifth night, a great surge will arise in the ocean;
it will overflow this magnificent island. Do not let him destroy you; go to another refuge!
In this context, “it will overflow” means that the ocean, surging up and flooding over, will overwhelm this island. “Do not let him destroy you” means: may that surge of the ocean not kill you.
Having thus given them this advice, he returned to his own place.
When he had gone, another impetuous and cruel son of the gods thought, "If they take his word, they might flee;
I shall prevent their departure and bring all of them to total ruin. Thinking thus, adorned with celestial ornaments and illuminating the entire island with a single radiance, he approached.
Having arrived and stood in the sky over the southern direction, he asked, "Has a certain son of the gods come here?
When it was replied, "He has come," he said, "What did he say to you? When it was said, "He said this, sir," he remarked, "He does not wish for you to dwell here;
he speaks out of malice. Do not go elsewhere, but remain right here. Having said this, he recited two verses:
“Never indeed shall the surge of the ocean’s waters overflow this sublime island;
I have seen many omens to that effect. Do not be afraid, do not grieve, but rejoice!
This sublime dwelling has been reached, with abundant food and plenty of drink.”
“I see no fear whatsoever for you; rejoice, even with your sons’ sons.
In this context, *na jātuyaṃ* means “never indeed. *Mā bhettha* means “do not be afraid.
*Modathavho* means “rejoice,” being filled with joy and gladness. *Āputtaputtehi* means “rejoice even with the sons of your sons”; there is [no limit].
"You will have fear in this place.
Having thus comforted them with these two verses, he departed.

At the time of his departure, the foolish carpenter, disregarding the words of the divine son Dhammika, addressed the other carpenters, saying, "Listen to my words, sirs! and called out to the rest of the carpenters.
He spoke the fifth verse:
“This deity in the southern quarter who calls out ‘Safety!’—his word is true.
No one else knows what is beyond fear and fearlessness. Do not be afraid; why do you grieve? Rejoice!”
In that context, "dakkhiṇāyaṃ" means "in the south," or rather, this is the very reading used.

Having heard that, five hundred carpenters, greedy for the taste [of the reward], accepted the words of that fool. But the other, the wise carpenter, not accepting his words, addressed those carpenters and spoke these four verses:
"Just as these spirits speak at variance—one proclaiming danger, the other security;..."
Therefore, listen to my words: let us all quickly and swiftly act so that we do not all perish.
"Let us all come together and build a sturdy boat, equipped with all necessary provisions.
If this one on the right speaks the truth, then this one on the left speaks falsely."
"She will indeed be our refuge in times of distress, and we shall not abandon this island.
But if Uttara speaks the truth and the one from the South speaks falsely,
then by boarding that very boat, we shall all safely cross to the further shore."
“Indeed, one does not grasp the best by means of the first;
rather, having taken up that which has come into range as the youngest, he who here grasps it after having sifted through what is true, that man indeed reaches the supreme state.
In this context, *vippavadanti* means they speak in mutual contradiction. *Lahuṃ* is an illustration of the meaning of the preceding term.
"A *doṇī* is a deep, large boat. 'Equipped with all mechanisms' means equipped with all the mechanisms such as rudders and oars.
'And it will be for our benefit in times of distress' means that this boat will be of service to us even in future calamities, and we shall not abandon this island.
'We shall cross over' means we will cross over. Indeed, they do not easily grasp [the truth]."
It should certainly not be grasped easily. "Best" means supreme and true.
"Younger" means that, relative to the first statement, the subsequent statement is called younger. Here too, the phrase "it should certainly not be grasped easily" continues to apply.
This is what is meant: O carpenter, whatever first statement was uttered, [regarding it] "this alone is best..."
One should not accept even that which is said to be "this alone is the truth and reality" as being true;
and just as with that, one should not accept even the words spoken by a younger brother, thinking, "this alone is the truth and reality.

Rather, whatever comes within the range of the ear and enters the field of experience, a wise person here should take that which has entered the field of experience and carefully examine both the former statement and the latter statement.
Having examined, scrutinized, and investigated thoroughly, he grasps what is true;

that which is such, real, and of its own inherent nature—that alone he grasps by making it directly manifest before him. "That man indeed attains the highest state" means that he reaches, arrives at, finds, and obtains the supreme state.
Having spoken thus, he said: "O friend, we shall act upon the words of both deities;
let us first prepare the ship. If the word of the first deity proves true, we shall board that ship and flee;
but if the word of the other deity proves true, we shall leave the ship in a secluded spot right here."
"Let us dwell here. When this was said, Bālavaḍḍhakī replied: "O sir, you see a crocodile in the water-jar;
you see it as exceedingly long. The first son of the gods spoke to us out of malice, while the last spoke out of affection alone.
Having abandoned such a choice island as this, where shall we go? But if you wish to go, [take] your own retinue."

"Take the boat; we have no need for a boat," he said. The wise man took his own retinue, prepared the boat, loaded all the necessary equipment onto it, and stood upon the boat together with his followers.
Then, on the full moon day, at the time of the moon's rising, a wave rose from the ocean and reached the height of the knees.
Having washed the lamp, they departed. The wise man, knowing that the ocean was about to rise, set the ship adrift.
Five hundred families belonging to the foolish carpenter’s guild sat down, saying, "A wave from the ocean has come for the purpose of washing the lamp; it is only this much.
Then, in succession, [waves] reached the height of the waist, the height of a man, and the height of a palm tree.
A wave from the ocean, as high as seventy palm trees, came surging even over the island. Because of his skill in means, the wise man remained unattached to the savory flavor and escaped safely;
however, the foolish carpenter, greedy for the flavor and failing to look toward future danger, met his destruction along with five hundred families.
Following this, there are three verses of perfect enlightenment that illuminate that same meaning:
"Just as those merchants, in the midst of the ocean's waters, escaped in safety by means of their own karma;
so too, having penetrated the future state, he of vast wisdom did not neglect even the slightest matter."
“Fools, through delusion, are greedy for flavors and do not penetrate the welfare of the future;
they sink when the time for action arrives, just like those men in the midst of the ocean.
