One should prepare for the task that lies in the future, thinking: ‘May the task not distress me at the time when the task must be done.’”
"For one who has performed such duties, that duty does not fail at the time when it ought to be done.
In this context, "by their own karma" means by the karma they themselves had previously performed upon seeing the danger of the future.
"They went in safety" means they traveled in security. "Merchants" refers here to those who ply the ocean, meaning sailors. "Having penetrated" means...

Thus, monks, having penetrated the future benefit that ought to be done first, a clansman of broad wisdom does not neglect, does not overstep, and does not fail even his slightest own welfare—this is the meaning.
"Without having penetrated the benefit" means without having understood the benefit; it means without having done what ought to be done first.
Regarding "the present": when that future matter arises, they sink into it while it is still present;
once the matter has arisen, they find no footing for themselves and meet their destruction like those foolish masons in the ocean.
Regarding "the future," monks: a wise person [considers] first of all the future task pertaining to the life hereafter that ought to be done.
Or whatever must be done regarding matters pertaining to the present life, one should do it beforehand.

Why? Lest it should hinder me at the time when it ought to be done. For if that which is to be done beforehand is not done beforehand, then when it reaches the present moment—the time for its own performance—it hinders one through affliction of body and mind. Thinking, "Lest that should hinder me," one should perform it first.
A wise person should act in such a way—that is, like a wise man. "One who performs duties beforehand" means one who performs the duties that ought to be done in advance.

When that duty is being performed at its time—meaning a future duty being carried out later when it reaches the present state—it does not obstruct or hinder the previous [preparatory] stage at the time of its own performance, which is the time when body and mind are free from affliction. Why? Because it was already accomplished previously.

Having delivered this Dhamma teaching, the Teacher said, "Monks, it is not only now; in the past as well, Devadatta, being attached to present pleasure and failing to look toward future danger, met his destruction along with his followers. Having said this, he identified the Jātaka:
"At that time, the foolish carpenter was Devadatta, and the unrighteous son of a deity standing in the southern direction was Kokālika."
“Sāriputta was the son of a deva named Dhammika, stationed in the northern quarter; as for me, I myself was the wise carpenter.
This concludes the third commentary, the Samuddavāṇija Jātaka.
[467] 4. The Commentary on the Kāma Jātaka.
"Desiring sensual pleasure for one who desires it"—this the Teacher spoke while residing at Jetavana concerning a certain brahmin.
It is said that a certain brahmin living in Sāvatthī cleared a forest on the bank of the Aciravatī river for the purpose of cultivating a field.
The Teacher, seeing his underlying potential (*upanissaya*), stepped off the path as he was entering Sāvatthī for alms.

Having exchanged greetings with him, he asked, "What are you doing, brahmin? When he replied, "I am having a field site measured out, Master Gotama," he said, "Very well, brahmin, carry on with your work," and then departed.
By this same means, [the Buddha visited] when the felled trees were being removed, when the field was being cleared, when it was being ploughed, and when the seed was being sown.
Going again and again, he exchanged greetings with him.
On the day of the sowing, however, that brahmin said, "Today, Master Gotama, it is my auspicious day for sowing;
when this crop has ripened, I shall give a great alms-offering to the Saṅgha of bhikkhus headed by the Buddha. The Teacher, having consented by remaining silent, departed.
On another day, the brahmin stood watching his crops. The Teacher also went there and asked, "What are you doing, brahmin?
When he replied, "I am watching the crops, Master Gotama," the Teacher said, "Very well, brahmin," and departed.
Then the brahmin thought, "The ascetic Gotama comes here frequently; without a doubt, it must be for the sake of food."
"I am in need; I will give him a meal. Having thought thus, on the day he went home, the Teacher also arrived there.
Then the brahmin felt an exceeding sense of trust.

Later, when the crop had matured, the brahmin made a resolution, saying, "Tomorrow I shall harvest the field," and lay down to sleep. Not long after, during the entire night, over the Aciravatī River...
A rain of hailstones fell. A great flood came and, leaving not even a single stalk remaining, swept all the crops into the ocean.
When the flood had subsided, the brahmin looked upon the destruction of his crops;
unable to maintain his composure, overcome by intense grief, he struck his chest with his hand and lay down, lamenting and weeping.
The Teacher, seeing the brahmin overcome with grief at the time of dawn, thought, "I shall provide support for this brahmin.

On the following day, after walking for alms in Sāvatthī and returning from his almsround, he sent the monks back to the monastery and went to the door of the brahmin’s house accompanied by an attendant monk. When the brahmin heard that the Teacher had arrived, he...
Thinking, "A friend must have come for the sake of welcoming me," he took heart and prepared a seat.
The Teacher entered, sat down on the prepared seat, and asked: "Brāhmaṇa, why are you dejected? What is unwell with you?
"Master Gotama, from the time I began cutting down trees on the bank of the Aciravatī, the work I performed was for you."
"You know, I was wandering about thinking, 'When this crop is harvested, I will give you alms.
But now, a great flood has carried all that crop right into the ocean; nothing remains.
About a hundred cartloads of grain have been lost, and because of that, great sorrow has arisen within me. "But, Brahmin, does what is lost become restored simply by grieving?"
“...does it come back again? “Certainly not, Master Gotama. “That being so, why do you grieve?
For these beings, wealth and grain arise at the time of arising and perish at the time of perishing; there is nothing among conditioned things that is by nature imperishable.
Do not worry. Having thus comforted him, the Teacher [taught] the Dhamma suitable for him.
The Teacher preached the Kāmasutta. At the conclusion of the discourse, the grieving brahmin was established in the fruit of stream-entry (*sotāpatti-phala*).
Having freed him from sorrow, the Teacher rose from his seat and went to the monastery.
The entire city learned that the Teacher had freed a certain brahmin, who was pierced by the arrow of grief, from his sorrow and established him in the fruit of stream-entry.

In the Dhamma Hall, the bhikkhus started a conversation: "Friends, the One of Ten Powers, having formed a friendship with the brahmin and become his trusted confidant, taught him the Dhamma by means of a skillful method while he was pierced by the arrow of grief;
having freed him from sorrow, he established him in the fruit of stream-entry. The Teacher approached and asked, "Bhikkhus, what is it that you are discussing now?"
Having asked, "Sitting for what discussion? and being told, "For this very one," he said, "Monks, it is not only now;
in the past as well, I made him free from sorrow," and he related a story of the past.
In the past, in Bārāṇasī, King Brahmadatta had two sons. He [gave] the senior son the position of viceroy...
He gave the position of commander-in-chief to his younger brother. Later, when Brahmadatta had passed away, the ministers prepared for the consecration of the elder brother.
He said, "I have no need for kingship; give it to my younger brother," and though he was entreated again and again, he refused.
When the younger brother was consecrated, [the elder] said, "I have no need for sovereignty," and [declined] even the position of viceroy and so forth.
He did not consent. Even when they said, "In that case, please stay right here while enjoying delicious foods," he replied, "I have no business in this city.
Having departed from Bārāṇasī, he went to the borderlands and lived supported by a certain merchant family, performing manual labor with his own hands.
Later, those people, having learned of his status as a prince, [ceased] the work...
They did not make a formal claim, but instead avoided it by treating him with the same courtesy shown to a prince. Later on, royal officials came to that village to measure the extent of the fields.
The merchant approached the prince and said, "Sir, we support you; please send a letter to your younger brother and have him collect our tax.
Having agreed, saying "Very well," he [sent a message] to the family of such-and-such a merchant: [...the rest of the sentence continues...]
He sent a letter saying, "I dwell depending on you; therefore, grant me a tribute from these people.
The king said, "Very well," and acted accordingly.
Then, both the inhabitants of the entire village and those of the surrounding countryside approached him and said, "We [pay] tribute for you alone..."
"We will give it; please remit our tax as well," they said. He sent a letter on their behalf and had it remitted.

From then on, they paid tribute to him alone. Consequently, he received great gain and honor, and along with that, his craving also became great. Later, he even requested the entire country, and then half the kingdom.
He entreated him, and the younger brother indeed gave it to him. As his craving increased, he was not satisfied even with half the kingdom;
thinking, "I shall seize the kingdom," he went to that city surrounded by the people of the countryside.
Standing outside the city, he sent a letter to his younger brother, saying, "Either give me the kingdom or give me battle. The younger brother thought, "This fool, previously..."
Having rejected even the kingship and the status of viceroy, he now says, "I shall seize it by war. [The other thought:
"If I were to kill him in battle, I would incur reproach; what use have I for kingship? Then [the other] sent word to him:
"Enough with the war; let him take the kingdom. Having taken the kingdom, he gave the position of viceroy to his younger brother.
Having given [the kingdom], from that time forth while ruling the realm, he became subject to craving;
dissatisfied with one kingdom, he longed for two and three kingdoms, yet he saw no end to his craving.
Then Sakka, the king of the gods, thought: "Who in the world now attends upon their mothers and fathers? Who performs meritorious deeds such as giving?"
While observing, [the Buddha] perceived that he was dominated by craving, thinking, "This fool is not satisfied even with the sovereignty of Bārāṇasī;
I shall train him. Assuming the guise of a young brahmin, he stood at the king’s gate and had it announced, "A young brahmin skilled in means stands at the gate.
When told, "Let him enter," he entered, offered his congratulations to the king, and asked, "For what reason..."
When he was told, "You have arrived," he replied, "Great King, there is something you must say; I desire privacy.

By the power of Sakka, the people departed at that very moment. Then the young brahmin said to him, "Great King, I see three cities—prosperous, crowded with people, and endowed with armies and vehicles—and by my own power, I [shall give them] to you..."
"Having taken the kingdom from them, I shall give it to you; it is fitting that you go quickly without delay," he said.
The king, subject to craving, accepted with "So be it," and through his royal power did not ask, "Who are you? From where have you come?
What do you wish to obtain? Having said only this much, he too departed for the Tāvatiṃsa heaven itself.
The king summoned his ministers and said, “A certain young brahmin has said, ‘I will take back our three kingdoms and give them to you.
Summon him! Have the drum beaten throughout the city and assemble the army;
without delay, we shall take back the three kingdoms. Then he asked, “But what honor, Great King, did you show that young brahmin?”
When it was asked, "Did he do him honor, or did he ask where he lived?", he replied, "I neither paid him honor nor asked where he lived;
go and investigate him. While investigating, they reported, "Your Majesty, we do not see that young man anywhere in the entire city.
Upon hearing this, the king became despondent and said, "In three cities, my kingdom..."
"He has been lost; I have fallen away from great glory.
'He gave me no travel expenses, nor did he ask after my place of residence'—having become angry with me in this way, the young man will not return. Thus he thought again and again.
Then, as he was enslaved by craving, a burning fever arose in his body; as his body burned, it agitated his stomach, and dysentery broke out.
One vessel would enter [his body] and another would exit; physicians were unable to cure him, and the king grew weary.
Thus, his state of illness became known throughout the entire city.
At that time, the Bodhisatta, having mastered all the arts at Takkasilā, returned to the presence of his parents in the city of Bārāṇasī.
Having heard news of the king’s condition, he arrived at the palace gate saying, "I shall treat him," and had it announced:
"It is said that a young brahmin boy has come to treat you. The king thought, "Even the greatest physicians renowned throughout the world have been unable to treat me;
what can a young brahmin boy possibly do? Give him a travel allowance and send him away."
"No," he replied. Hearing this, the young man said, "I have no fee for my medical work;
I am merely curing you, so let them give me only the cost of the medicine. Hearing this, the king said, "Very well," and had him summoned.
The young man paid homage to the king and said, "Do not fear, Great King; I shall cure you. However, as for my illness—"
“Tell me its origin,” he said. The king, feeling ashamed, replied, “What is the use of its origin?

Just prepare the medicine. “Great King, physicians, having understood that ‘this disease has arisen on account of this,’ prescribe the appropriate medicine. The king said, “Very well, dear one,” and as he spoke of the origin, [he said]: “By one...”

Having related everything, beginning with, "A young brahmin will come and take the kingdoms in the three cities and give them to me," he said, "Thus, dear father, this illness has arisen because of my craving;
if you are able to cure it, please cure it. [The other replied: "But great king, can those cities be obtained through grieving? "They cannot be obtained, dear father."
“Since this is so, why do you grieve, Great King? For indeed, everything—whether animate or inanimate—is to be abandoned and departed from, beginning with one’s own body.
Even after taking up sovereignty over the four cities, you will not eat four bowls of food at once, nor will you lie upon four beds, nor will you wear four pairs of garments.”
"You will cover it over; it is not right to be one who is mastered by craving, for this thing called craving, as it increases, does not allow one to be freed from the four states of misery.
Having thus exhorted him, the Great Being, while teaching him the Dhamma, spoke these verses:
“If one who desires sensual pleasures succeeds in obtaining them,
that mortal surely becomes joyful, having gained what he wished for.
If one who desires sensual pleasures succeeds in obtaining them...”
Then he finds even greater craving for sensual pleasures, like thirst in the heat.
Just as the horn of a horned bull grows as the bull itself grows,
so it is with the dull-witted person, the fool who lacks understanding.
Furthermore, craving and thirst increase as one's possessions increase.
"Even if one were to give the rice and barley of the earth, along with cattle, horses, slaves, and servants, it would not be enough for even a single person.
Knowing this, one should live in equanimity.
“A king, having conquered the earth by force and dwelling over the great land as far as the ocean’s edge,
might still be unsatisfied with what is on this side of the sea and long for even the further shore.
As long as he recollects sensual pleasures, he does not find satisfaction even with his mind.”
Turning back from there, having seen them returning, he said: "Truly, those who are satisfied by wisdom are the ones who are satisfied.
One who is satisfied by wisdom is best; such a person is not tormented by sensual desires.
Craving does not bring a person satisfied by wisdom under its power."
“One who diminishes sensual desires, being of few wishes and not greedy—
like a man whose measure is the ocean— he is not satiated by sensual pleasures.
Like a leather-worker cutting out sandals from a hide,”
"Whatever one relinquishes of sensual pleasures, that very thing results in happiness; if one should desire all happiness, one should renounce all sensual pleasures.
In this context, "sensual pleasures" (*kāma*) refers to both objective sensual pleasures (*vatthukāma*) and defilements of sensual pleasure (*kilesakāma*).
"Of one who desires" (*kāmayamānassa*) means of one who yearns for them. Of him...
"If that succeeds" means: if that object desired by that person succeeds, that is, if it is accomplished.
"Then he desires another" (*tato naṃ aparaṃ kāmeti*): here, *naṃ* is a mere particle; *aparaṃ* indicates the subsequent portion;
*kāmeti* is the accusative plural form. This is what is meant: if, for one who is desiring a desire, that desired object...

When it succeeds, once that has succeeded, then that person, desiring further, just as one who is exhausted by the wind and heat during the hot summer season finds thirst and experiences a craving for water, even so he finds and experiences sensual pleasures known as the craving for sense-pleasures (*kāmatanha*);
and his craving for forms (*rūpatanha*) and so forth increases all the more. "Of cattle" (*gavaṃva*) means of a bovine animal.
"Like a horn": [this refers to] a horn that has arisen by splitting open the head. "Of the dull-witted" means of one with dull wisdom.
"Of the fool" means of one who is engaged in the qualities of a fool. This is what is meant:
just as when a calf grows, its horn grows along with its body, so too for a blind fool, both the craving for unobtained desires and the thirst for obtained desires [grow].
And it increases further and further.
"Rice and barley" refers to rice fields and barley fields. By this, he shows all grain such as rice and barley;
by the second phrase, he shows all bipeds and quadrupeds; or alternatively, by the first phrase, he shows all insentient things.
"By the other" means with consciousness. "Even having given" means even after giving. This is what is meant: let alone three kingdoms;

even if that youth were to go away after giving to someone else either another [kingdom] or even the entire earth filled with sentient and insentient jewels, this much of a thing would still belong to one person without limit. Thus, this craving is difficult to fill.

"By name. Thus, "knowing thus, one should live equanimously": a person who understands this should live fulfilling the bodily conduct and so forth, rather than being under the sway of craving (*taṇhā*).
"The near shore" (*ora*) refers to having reached the near side [of the ocean]; being dissatisfied with that, one would further aspire for the far shore of the ocean.
In this way, he shows that beings under the sway of craving are indeed difficult to satisfy. "As long as" (*yāva*) is an indefinite limit. "They recollect" (*anussaranti*).
"Recalling. "He does not find" means he does not obtain. This is what is meant: O Great King, even when a person mentally recalls sensual pleasures that are limitless, he finds no satisfaction;

he remains desirous of attaining them. Thus, for sentient beings, craving for sensual pleasures only increases. "Turning away from that": having turned the mind away from both objective sensual pleasures (*vatthukāma*) and defilements of sensual pleasure (*kilesakāma*).
Having retreated from the body and having seen the danger with wisdom, those who are satisfied and fulfilled by wisdom are called "satisfied.
This one is the most excellent among those satisfied by wisdom; this is the reading *paripuṇṇaseṭṭho*, or alternatively, the reading is *paññāya tittīnaṃ seṭṭho*.
Regarding the phrase "he is not tormented by sensual pleasures," there is also the reading *na hī*. Because a person satisfied by wisdom is not scorched by sensual pleasures.
The meaning is this: craving is not able to bring such a person under its control;
rather, having seen the danger in craving, like the young brahmin Sarabhaṅga and like the half-month king, he does not proceed under the sway of craving—this is the meaning.
"One should surely diminish it" means one should surely destroy it. "As vast as the ocean" refers to great wisdom.
Because he is endowed [with these qualities], he is equal in measure to the ocean. Like the ocean, he is neither satiated nor consumed by the defilements of sensual desire, even by a great fire.
"Rathakāra" means a leather-worker. "Parikantaṃ" means while cutting away. This is what is meant:
just as a leather-worker, while cutting away the leather for a sandal, sets aside whatever part of the hide is unfit for use and proceeds with the sandal.
Just as one who has made a sandal becomes happy upon obtaining its base,
even so, when a wise person, using wisdom similar to the leather-worker’s knife, cuts away whatever obstruction of sensual desires he abandons,
each of his bodily, verbal, and mental actions— being free from that respective obstruction of desire— proceeds happily and without distress; however, if...
One should desire all happiness of bodily action and so forth to be entirely free from feverish distress; having developed the kasiṇa and produced jhāna, one renounces all sensual pleasures.
However, as the Bodhisattva was reciting this verse, he took the King’s white parasol as his object and attained the white-kasiṇa jhāna.
[The medicine] arose, and the king also became free from illness. Delighted, he rose from his bed and, speaking with him, uttered the tenth verse:
“Indeed, so many physicians were unable to cure me; but the wise youth, by means of the medicine of his own knowledge, has made me free from disease.”
“Eight verses have been spoken by you, and all are worth a thousand.
Accept them, Great Brahmā; this speech of yours is excellent.

In this context, “eight” refers to the eight [verses] beginning with the second verse, which are connected to the danger of sensual desires. “Worth a thousand” means they are worthy of a thousand [pieces of gold]. “Accept them” means accept these eight thousand [verses]. “This speech of yours is excellent” means this statement of yours is good.
Having heard that, the Great Being spoke the eleventh verse:
“I have no need for thousands, nor for hundreds, nor for tens of thousands;
having spoken this final verse, my mind finds no delight in sensual pleasures.”

Therein, "the last" refers to the verse beginning, "Just as a leather-worker [deals with his hide]. While I was reciting this verse, "My mind does not delight in sensual pleasures," my mind took no pleasure in either objective sensual pleasures (*vatthukāma*) or defilement-sensual pleasures (*kilesakāma*).
Indeed, O Great King, while reciting this verse, I myself attained *jhāna* through that very teaching of the Dhamma.
The king, being even more highly pleased, praised the Great Being and spoke this concluding verse:
“Truly auspicious is this young man, a sage who knows all the world;
for he, the wise one, thoroughly understands this craving that gives rise to suffering.”

In this context, "the producer of suffering" means the producer of all the suffering within the cycle of existence (*saṃsāra*). "He fully understood" means he fully comprehended and cut it off; "having plucked it out, he removed it"—this was said while praising the Bodhisatta.
The Bodhisatta, having exhorted the king, saying, "Great King, being diligent, practice the Dhamma," went through the air to the Himālaya mountains.
Having gone forth as an ascetic, he remained for the duration of his lifespan, developed the divine abodes (*brahmavihāra*), and [passed away].
Having not fallen away from his meditative absorption, he went to the Brahma-world.
Having brought forth this Dhamma teaching, the Teacher said, "Thus, monks, even in the past I made this brahmin free from sorrow," and he identified the Jātaka:
"At that time, this brahmin was the king, and the wise youth was none other than myself."
The Fourth: The Commentary on the Kāmajātaka.
[468] 5. The Commentary on the Janasandhajātakaya.
"Indeed, ten..."—this was spoken by the Teacher while dwelling at Jetavana for the purpose of advising the King of Kosala. For once, in a certain...
At that time, the king, intoxicated by the pride of sovereignty and addicted to the pleasures of the defilements, did not even attend to judicial affairs and neglected his visits to the Buddha.
One day, however, recollecting the One of Ten Powers, he thought, "I shall pay homage to the Teacher.
Having eaten his morning meal, he mounted his excellent chariot, went to the monastery, paid homage to the Teacher, and sat down. Then the Teacher asked him, "What is it, Great King?"
Having said, "You have not been seen for a long time," and being told, "Venerable sir, because of our many duties, no opportunity has arisen to attend upon the Buddha," [the Teacher replied]:
"Great King, while an omniscient Buddha such as I, a giver of exhortation, is residing in your capital monastery, it is improper for you to be negligent.
A king must indeed be diligent in his royal duties; he should be like a mother and father to those who dwell within his realm."
It is fitting for you to rule the kingdom by abandoning wrong courses and by not violating the ten duties of a king;
for when a king is righteous, his assembly also becomes righteous. Indeed, it is no wonder that while I am instructing you, you should rule according to Dhamma;
even when the ancient wise teachers who instructed them were no longer present, the wise of old acted solely by their own intelligence.
"Having established themselves in the Dhamma of the threefold good conduct and taught the Dhamma to the great multitude, they departed filling the path to heaven," he said;
and being requested by him, he related a story of the past:
"In the past, while Brahmadatta was reigning in Benares, the Bodhisatta [was conceived] in the womb of his chief queen."
He was born, and they gave him the name Janasandha Kumāra.
When he had reached maturity and returned after having mastered all the arts at Takkasilā, the king had all the prisons cleared out and bestowed upon him the position of viceroy.
Later, when his father passed away, he was established in the kingdom; [he stationed guards] at the four city gates and in the middle of the city.
Having caused six alms-halls to be built at the royal gate, and giving away six hundred thousand [pieces of gold] day after day,
he agitated all of Jambudīpa by distributing a great gift; he caused the prisons to be kept perpetually open,
had the treasury of the Dhamma audited, and, winning over the world with the four means of attraction, [he ruled] for five...
Guarding his moral precepts and observing the Uposatha fasts, he ruled the kingdom in accordance with the Dhamma. From time to time, he summoned the inhabitants of the realm and exhorted them:
"Give alms, undertake moral conduct, cultivate meditation; engage in your work and business righteously;
learn your crafts while you are still young, and amass wealth. [Avoid] the treacherous practices of village headmen."
"Do not engage in divisive speech or harsh words; do not be fierce or cruel; fulfill your service to mother and father;
and be respectful toward those who are senior in the family. Having thus taught the Dhamma, he established the great multitude in the practice of virtuous conduct.
One day, on the Uposatha of the fifteenth day, having undertaken the Uposatha vows, he [thought], "For the greater benefit of the great multitude..."
Having thought, "I shall teach the Dhamma for the sake of their welfare and happiness, and for the sake of abiding in heedfulness," he had a drum beaten throughout the city;
then, having caused all the people of the city to assemble, beginning with his own harem, and having adorned the royal courtyard, he sat upon a well-prepared,
excellent throne in the center of a beautifully decorated pavilion made of precious gems, and said, "O inhabitants of the city!"

"I shall teach you the Dhamma that is to be practiced and the Dhamma that is not to be practiced; being heedful and lending an attentive ear, listen with respect," he said, and then he taught the Dhamma.
The Teacher, opening his mouth-jewel which was permeated by Truth, made that Dhamma-teaching known to the King of Kosala with a sweet voice:
“There are indeed these ten situations, which, having failed to perform them before,
one later regrets— so says the Lord of Men.
Not having acquired wealth, one suffers because it was not accumulated in the past.”
"I did not seek wealth before," he regrets later.
"Though I had the appearance of one capable, I did not train in a craft;
a life without a craft is difficult," he regrets later.
“In the past I was a deceitful speaker, a slanderer who bit at the backs of others;
I was fierce and harsh as well—thus one repents later.
In the past I was a taker of life, cruel and ignoble.”
"I shall not honor those who have been," thus one regrets later.
"Alas, while there were many women present, blameless and chaste,
I pursued another's wife," thus one regrets later.
“While there was much food and drink available, and it was set before me, I did not give gifts in the past; thus, later, I regret it.
My mother and my father too, when they were old and their youth had passed—”
“I will not support my master,” he regrets later.
“I have slighted my teacher and instructor, who brings me the essence of all desires;
I have slighted my father,” he regrets later.
“I did not previously attend upon ascetics and brahmins who were virtuous and learned”— thus one regrets it afterwards.
“Excellent is the practice of austerity, and excellent is the attendance upon the peaceful.”
And he does not later regret it, thinking, "I did not practice austerities before.
But he who practices these points with wise discernment, performing the duties of a man, does not regret it later. Thus he spoke these verses.
In this context, "grounds" (*ṭhānāni*) means causes (*kāraṇāni*). "Previously" (*pubbe*) means not having done [them] at the very beginning.
"He later regrets" (*sa pacchā anutappati*) means that the person who failed to do what ought to have been done first later suffers and is distressed both in this world and in the next world.
There is also the reading, "or he regrets later" (*pacchā vā anutappati*). "Thus it was said" (*iccevāha*): the word-division is *iti evaṃ āha*; thus, in this way.
King Janasandha said: "Iccassuhāti" is also a reading; in that case, *assu* is merely a particle, and the word-division is *iti assu āha*.
Now, in order to reveal those ten causes for remorse, there follows the Bodhisatta’s discourse on the Dhamma.
In this context, "previously" (*pubbe*) means at the very beginning, during youth, having failed to exert effort and thus not having acquired or accumulated [merit].
In old age, one suffers and grieves for not having acquired wealth;
seeing others living happily while one lives in misery oneself, one later regrets it, thinking, "I should have sought wealth before.
Therefore, he shows that those who desire to live happily in their old age should seek wealth by performing righteous work, such as farming, while they are still young.
"Pure santan" means that in my former youth, although I had the opportunity to do so by attending upon teachers, I did not train in any craft such as elephant-riding or other skills.
"Kicchā" means that in old age, one's livelihood is difficult because of the lack of a craft;
at that time, it is no longer possible to learn a craft. Therefore, those who desire to live happily in their old age [should acquire skills while young].
This shows that one should learn a craft while still young.

"Kuṭavedī" means one who knows how to cheat—a village cheat, or one who causes harm to the world, or one who practices cheating with scales and the like, or a maker of false dice; such is the meaning.
"Āsiṃ" means "I was such a person in the past. "Pisuṇo" means one who engages in backbiting. "Piṭṭhimaṃsiko" means one who, having taken a bribe, [speaks] against those who are not the owners.
"Devouring the back-flesh of others while acting as their master"—thus, later on, lying upon his deathbed, he regrets it;
therefore, he advises: "If you do not wish to dwell in hell, do not commit such evil deeds.
"Cruel" means harsh. "Un-Aryan" means one who is not noble, whose conduct is base. "They will not honor" means they will not show respect through patience, loving-kindness, and compassion.
I did not live a base life. The rest should be construed in the same manner as before.

"In those who are without a husband" (*anāpādāsu*): *āpāda* means taking hold of; the meaning is "possession. Those for whom there is no *āpāda* are "those without a husband"; the meaning is "those whose possession has not been made by others.

"When he was present" (*upaṭṭhite*) means when he was standing near. "Not before this" (*na pubbe*) means I did not give gifts prior to this. "Being able" (*pahu santo*) means even by the power of wealth.
Though he is capable and competent to support [them] even by means of his own physical strength;
"teacher" (*ācariya*) is intended here as the father, because he trains them in proper conduct (*ācāra*). "Instructor" (*anusatthāraṃ*) means one who gives guidance.

"One who brings all the flavors of sensual pleasure" means one who supports them by bringing all the flavors of sensual objects (*vatthukāma*). "They will despise him" means that, not accepting his advice, they will disregard and think ill of him.

"Na pubbe": previously, even toward righteous ascetics and brahmins, whether they were sick or healthy, I would not have waited upon them by giving robes and other requisites without attending to them.
"Tapo" means the austerity of good conduct. "Santo" means one who is peaceful through the three doors and is virtuous.
This is what is meant: such a person, who has practiced the austerity consisting of the threefold good conduct and is thus peaceful, has been waited upon.
"It is indeed good and beautiful. 'Not before' means: 'In my youth, I did not practice such asceticism';
thus, later on, when worn out by old age and terrified by the fear of death, one regrets and grieves. If you do not wish to grieve in this way, perform the work of asceticism—thus he says.
And as for 'one who [practices] these': however, one who applies these ten reasons through the proper method from the very beginning."

"Acting in accordance with what he has undertaken, performing the righteous duties that must be done by men, that person who dwells in heedfulness does not regret it later; he becomes possessed of joy.

Thus, in this manner, the Great Being taught the Dhamma to the great multitude every half-month. And the great multitude, abiding by his instruction and fulfilling those ten points, became destined for heaven.

Having delivered this Dhamma teaching, the Teacher said, “In this way, Great King, even though they were without a teacher, the ancient wise men of old taught the Dhamma by their own intelligence alone and established the great multitude on the path to heaven. Having said this, he identified the Jātaka:
“At that time, the assembly was the Buddha’s assembly, and Janasandha the king was none other than myself.”
The fifth: The Janasandha Jātaka Commentary.
[469] 6. The Mahākaṇha Jātaka Commentary:
"Kaṇho, Kaṇho!"—this the Teacher, while dwelling at Jetavana, spoke concerning his conduct for the welfare of the world.
One day, while the bhikkhus were seated in the Dhamma hall, they said: "Friends, to what an extent the Teacher has acted for the welfare of the many!
Having abandoned his own comfort, he works for the benefit of the world;
having attained supreme enlightenment, he himself took bowl and robe and traveled eighteen yojanas to reach the five bhikkhu elders."
Having set the Wheel of Dhamma in motion and preached the *Anattalakkhaṇa Sutta* on the fifth day of the fortnight, he bestowed Arahantship upon them all.
Having gone to Uruvelā and displayed three thousand five hundred miracles to the three brothers who were matted-hair ascetics, he ordained them;
and having preached the *Ādittapariyāya* at Gayāsīsa, he brought Arahantship to the thousand matted-hair ascetics.
Having gone out to meet Mahākassapa for three *gāvutas*, he gave him the full ordination through three exhortations.
After the meal, having traveled forty-five *yojanas* on the road, he established the noble youth Pukkusāti in the fruit of non-returning (*anāgāmiphala*).
Having gone out to meet Mahākappina for one hundred and twenty *yojanas*, he granted him the state of an arahant.
Having traveled thirty *yojanas* after his meal, he alone established the harsh and cruel Aṅgulimāla in Arahatship;
having traveled thirty *yojanas*, he established the Yakkha Āḷavaka in the fruit of Stream-entry and ensured the safety of the prince.
While dwelling for three months in the Tāvatiṃsa heaven, he brought about the realization of the Dhamma for eighty koṭis of deities.
Having gone to the Brahma-world, he shattered the view of the Brahmā Baka and bestowed Arahatship upon ten thousand Brahmās.
Traveling on tour through the three regions every year, he grants the Refuges, the precepts, and the paths and fruits to those humans who possess the necessary spiritual potential (*upanissaya*).
He likewise bestows various kinds [of benefits] upon the Nāgas, Supaṇṇas, and others.
“They practice for the welfare of the world,” they said, speaking of the quality of the Ten-Powered One’s conduct for the sake of the world.
The Teacher approached and asked, “Monks, for what discussion are you gathered here now?

When they replied, “For this very one,” he said, “It is not surprising, monks, that I should now, having attained full enlightenment, practice for the welfare of the world; even formerly, in the time when I was still subject to passion, [I did so].”
Having said, "He acted for the welfare of the world," he related a story of the past.
In the past, during the time of the Perfectly Enlightened One Kassapa, a king named Usīnara reigned in Bārāṇasī.

When the Perfectly Enlightened One Kassapa had liberated the great multitude from the bonds of the defilements through his teaching on the Four Noble Truths, and had filled the City of Nibbāna before attaining Parinibbāna—
After the passing of a long period of time, the teaching declined. The monks maintained their livelihood through twenty-one improper means;

they associated with householders and increased by having sons and daughters. The nuns also associated with householders and increased by having sons and daughters. The monks [neglected] the duty of a monk, and the nuns [neglected] the duty of a nun.
The laymen expounded the duty of laymen, the laywomen expounded the duty of laywomen, and the brahmins expounded the duty of brahmins.
For the most part, people lived having undertaken the ten courses of unwholesome action; as they died one after another, they filled the states of misery.
At that time, Sakka, the king of the gods, not seeing any new gods being born, looked toward the world of men and saw that men were [filling] the states of misery.
Having recognized that he had been reborn and seeing that the Teacher’s dispensation was declining, he thought, "What shall I do? He then resolved:
"There is a means. By terrifying the great multitude and perceiving their state of fear, I shall afterwards comfort them and teach the Dhamma;
thus I will cause the declining dispensation to be upheld once more and ensure it continues for another thousand years."
Having fashioned a great black dog of immense size and terrifying appearance— its fangs being as large as palm trees, its four fangs emitting rays of light that made it fearsome,
capable of causing miscarriages merely by being seen by pregnant women, and possessing the form of a fierce beast—
he bound it with fivefold fetters, draped a red garland around its neck, and commanded Mātali the son of the gods.
Taking a cord with a noose at its end, he himself put on two saffron robes, tied his hair in five knots at the back,
adorned himself with a red garland, and took up a great bow whose string was the color of coral. Twirling a diamond-tipped iron arrow with his fingernail,
he assumed the guise of a forest hunter and descended from the city to a place one *yojana* away.
Having cried out three times, “The world is perishing! The world is perishing! and having terrified the people, he reached the outskirts of the city and made the sound again.
When the people saw the dog, they were struck with fear; entering the city, they reported the matter to the king. The king—
He quickly had the city gates closed. Sakka, having leaped over the eighteen-cubit wall, landed inside the city together with the dog.
The people, terrified and trembling, fled and hid themselves within their houses.
Mahākaṇha too, running after every person he saw and frightening them, went to the royal palace. In the royal courtyard—
The people, fleeing in fear, entered the royal palace and closed the doors.
King Usīnara, taking his harem with him, ascended the palace. The dog Mahākāḷa raised his forepaws, stood at the window, and let out a great barking.
The sound of it reached from the Avīci hell below to the peak of existence above, throughout the entire Cakkavāḷa.
There was a single great roar. Indeed, these four sounds— the sound of King Puṇṇaka the Yakkha in the Vidhura Jātaka, the sound of King Kusa in the Kusa Jātaka,
the sound of King Sudassana the Nāga in the Bhūridatta Jātaka, and this sound in the present Mahākāṇha Jātaka—
were known as the "Great Sounds" of Jambudīpa.
The inhabitants of the city became so terrified and cowed that not even a single man was able to speak with Sakka.
Only the king, having regained his composure, leaned against the window and addressed Sakka, saying, "Ho, hunter! Why does your dog bark?
"Because of hunger, Great King," he replied. "In that case, I shall have food given to him."
He had all the cooked rice intended for his own household and himself served to the dog.
The dog swallowed it all as if it were a single mouthful and barked again.

Once more the king asked, and hearing, "Even now my dog is still hungry," he had all the cooked rice for the elephants, horses, and others brought and given to him. When that was consumed in a single moment—
When it was finished, he had cooked rice provided for the entire city. He ate that as well in the same manner and again made a sound.
The king, terrified and trembling, thought, "This is not a dog; without a doubt, this must be a *yakkha*.
I shall ask him the reason for his coming," and while asking, he spoke the first verse:
“Black, black indeed, and terrible, white-toothed and radiant;
bound with five ropes—why does your dog bark?
In this context, “black, black” is an emphatic repetition used out of fear or for the sake of intensity. “Terrible” means one who causes fear in those who see him.
"Pabhāsavā" means "radiant," due to the radiance of the fangs as they are bared. "Kiṃ ravī" means "why does he roar?
He spoke thus with the underlying intention: "What is this dog of yours doing? Why is he seizing deer, or perhaps your enemies?
What have you to do with him? Release him!"
Having heard that, Sakka spoke this second verse:
“This will not be for the sake of the deer, O Usīnara;
having brought misfortune upon men, then Kaṇha shall be released.”
The meaning of this is as follows: This one did not come here thinking, "I shall eat deer meat," and therefore there will be no harm to the deer;
rather, he came to eat human flesh. Therefore, by becoming the cause of great ruin for them, when he has brought humans to destruction, then this Kaṇha will be released.
“He will escape from my hand.
Then the king asked him, “Now, hunter, will this dog of yours eat the flesh of all people, or only of your enemies?
When he replied, “Only of your enemies, Your Majesty,” [the king said], “But who are they?”
Having asked, "Are these your enemies here? and being told, "They delight in unrighteousness and act with partiality, O Great King," he said, "Tell me about them first," and questioned him.
Then, as he was speaking, the King of the Gods recited ten verses:
"Shaveling ascetics with bowls in hand, shorn and clad in saṅghāṭī robes;..."
When they shall plough with ploughs, then Kaṇha will deliver us.
When women who have gone forth as ascetics, shaven-headed and clad in saṅghāṭī robes,
shall walk about in the world, then Kaṇha will deliver us.
“With long protruding lips, matted hair, and teeth like mud, with veins showing from dust, these brahmins go about demanding payment of debts; then Kaṇha will deliver them.
Having mastered the Vedas, the Sāvitrī, and the ritual system of sacrifice, the brahmins—”
When they offer sacrifices at the *bhaṭika* shrines, then Kaṇha will deliver them.
When people, though possessing ample means, do not support their mother and father who have grown old and lost their youth, then Kaṇha will deliver them.
“Even toward one’s mother and father, when they are aged and past their youth, fools will say, ‘You are old! Then Kaṇha will deliver them.
Toward the teacher’s wife, a female friend, a maternal aunt, or a paternal aunt...”
When people go about in the world, then Kaṇha will deliver them.
Taking up shields and swords, and grasping their blades, the brahmins will commit highway robbery; then Kaṇha will deliver them.
“Those with white skin, born of enmity, with thick arms and lacking in discernment, will cause a rift among friends; then Kaṇha will be liberated.
Deceitful, double-tongued, and thinking like unworthy persons...”
“When they exist in the world, then Kaṇha will be liberated.
In this context, he spoke thus using the contemptuous expression “samaṇakas” (mere ascetics) merely because of their profession, thinking, “We are ascetics. “They will plow”:
even then, they were indeed plowing; however, as if not knowing this, he spoke thus. For his intention was this: these...
"Such unvirtuous women are my enemies; when these have been killed by my dog and its flesh eaten, then this Kāḷa will be released from his fivefold rope-bonds.
By this method, the intended meaning (*adhippāya*) in all the verses is to be understood.

"Those who have gone forth" means those who have gone forth in the Buddha’s teaching. "They will go" means that while they were enjoying the five strands of sensual pleasure in the midst of the household life...
They will wander about. "With long protruding lips" means that their lips are long because their fangs have grown large.
"With mud-stained teeth" means that their teeth are possessed of the impurity of mud.

"Charging interest on loans" means that they earn their living by collecting wealth through wandering for alms, lending it out as interest-bearing loans, and charging interest on them; this is the meaning when they go about doing so.
"Having studied the *Sāvitti*" means having mastered the *Sāvitti* [hymn]. "And the ritual system of sacrifice" (*yaññatanta*) means the system that prescribes the performance of sacrifice;

the sense is: "having studied the sacrifice. "For the sake of wages" (*bhatikāya*) means when they will perform sacrifices for the purpose of earning a livelihood, approaching various kings and royal ministers and saying, "We shall perform your sacrifice;
give us wealth. "Being abundant" (*pahū santā*) means being sufficient to support and nourish [the family].
Being capable [of such acts]. "Fools you are" means: when they say, "You fools know nothing at all. "They will go" means:
they will go by way of indulging in worldly dharmas (*lokadhamma*). "Highway robbery" means: standing on the road, killing people, and seizing their goods. "Pale-skinned" means:
having the appearance of pale skin produced by rubbing with astringent powders and the like. "Widows" means: those whose husbands have died.
"Those without husbands" refers to widows; because they practice enmity [toward their former husbands], they are called "enmity-makers" (*vedhaverā*).

"Thūlabāhu" means those with large arms due to the development of muscle from massaging the feet and so forth. "Apātubhā" means "lacking manifestation," that is, devoid of the power to produce wealth. "Mittabheda" means the breaking of friendship;
this is indeed the reading. This is what is meant: when such women, who are harlots...
Thinking, "These [women] will not abandon us," widows accompanied by wealth will approach them, live together with them, consume their possessions, and then create a breach of friendship with them;
having destroyed their trust, they will go elsewhere with other wealthy men.
At that time, this [person] will escape after having consumed all those thieves. "Those who think like unworthy persons" means with the mentalities of unworthy persons.
"By nature intent on thinking of the suffering of others. "Then"—meaning at that time—"this Kāḷa will escape after having killed and eaten the flesh of all these.
Having spoken thus, [the dog] said, "These, O Great King, are my enemies," and leaping upon those various wrongdoers, he acted as if he wished to devour them.
Then, at a time when the great multitude was terrified, [he seized] the dog with a rope...
Having drawn himself up as if he were fixed in place, and having cast off his disguise as a hunter, he stood in the sky blazing with his own majesty and said:
"Great King, I am Sakka, the king of the gods. I have come because 'this world is perishing. For the masses are negligent;
having practiced unrighteousness, they now fill the states of misery one after another, and the heavenly realm is as if empty."
"Vita, from this day forward I shall know what must be done regarding those who act contrary to the Dhamma;

you, O Great King, must be diligent," he said, and having taught the Dhamma with the four *Satāraha* verses, established people in generosity and virtue, and ensured that the withdrawn teaching would be capable of prevailing for another thousand years, he took Mātali and returned to his own abode. The great multitude...
Having performed meritorious deeds such as giving and observing moral discipline, they were reborn in the world of the gods.

Having delivered this Dhamma teaching, the Teacher said, "Thus, monks, even in the past I acted solely for the welfare of the world," and he identified the Jātaka: "At that time Mātali was Ānanda, but Sakka was none other than myself.
This concludes the commentary on the Mahākaṇha Jātaka, the sixth.
[470] 7. The Commentary on the Kosiyajātakavaṇṇanā (73–93).
The Kosiyajātakam will be made clear in the Sudhābhojanajātakam.
This is the seventh commentary, the Kosiyajātakavaṇṇanā.
[471] 8. Commentary on the Meṇḍakapañha Jātaka (94–105).
The Meṇḍakapañha Jātaka will be revealed in the Umaṅga Jātaka.
This concludes the eighth commentary, the Meṇḍakapañha Jātaka.
[472] 9. The Commentary on the Mahāpaduma Jātaka.
"Do not look for faults in others"—this was spoken by the Teacher while residing at Jetavana, concerning the young woman Ciñcā Māṇavikā.

For during the first period of enlightenment, when the disciples of the One Possessing the Ten Powers had become numerous and immeasurable gods and humans had reached the plane of the Noble Ones (ariyabhūmi)...
As the multitude of his virtues spread abroad among those who had entered the fold, great gain and honor arose for him. The sectarians became like glow-worms at the rising of the sun;
deprived of gain and honor, they stood in the middle of the street and cried out:
"Is the ascetic Gotama alone the Buddha? We too are Buddhas! Is it only to him that what is given bears great fruit? To us as well, what is given..."
"It will indeed be of great fruit; give it to us as well and perform it for us!"—though they entreated the people in this way, they received no gain or honor.
Consequently, meeting in secret, they deliberated: "By what means might we create disrepute for the ascetic Gotama among the people and destroy his gain and honor?
At that time, in Sāvatthī, there was a young woman named Ciñcā Māṇavikā.
There was a certain female wanderer of supreme beauty, endowed with great fortune like a celestial nymph.
Radiance streamed forth from her body. Then a certain Kharamantin said:
"By inciting disparagement of the ascetic Gotama on account of the young woman Ciñcā Māṇavikā, we shall cause his gain and honor to perish. They agreed, saying, "This is a means."
Then she went to the monastery of the sectarians, paid her respects, and stood there; however, the sectarians did not speak with her. Thinking, "What fault could I have?
she said, "Venerable sirs, I pay my respects," up to three times. Then she asked, "Venerable sirs, what fault do I have?
Why do you not speak with me? They replied, "Sister, the ascetic Gotama is harassing us, depriving us of our gains and honor."
“Do you not know him as he wanders about? “I do not know him, noble ladies; what indeed could I do in this matter?
But if you, sister, desire our welfare, then by means of yourself, create dispraise for the ascetic Gotama and destroy his gain and honor.”
She said, “Very well, noble lady; this burden is mine alone, do not worry,” and having spoken, she departed.

Being skilled in feminine wiles, from that time forth, whenever the residents of Sāvatthī heard a Dhamma discourse and were about to leave the Jeta Grove, she would put on a robe the color of an *indagopaka* insect, carrying perfumes, garlands, and other offerings in her hands, and walking toward the Jeta Grove, she would say: “By this—”
When asked, "Where are you going at this hour? he replied, "What business of yours is it where I am going?

Then, having stayed overnight in a monastery of the non-Buddhist sects near the Jeta Grove, he would enter the city at dawn as if he had been staying in the Jeta Grove himself, while the lay followers were departing from the city thinking, "We shall pay our respects to the foremost [monks].
When asked, "Where did you stay? he replied, "What business of yours is it?"

Having said, "I have dwelt in my usual place," when questioned after the lapse of a month and a half, she replied, "I have been dwelling in a single fragrant chamber with the ascetic Gotama in Jeta’s Grove.
This gave rise to doubt among the worldlings as to whether this was true or not;
and after three or four months had passed, she wrapped her belly in rags and assumed the appearance of being pregnant.
Having displayed [her condition] and covered herself with a red cloth, she had a foolish woman seize her and declare, "I have conceived a child on account of the ascetic Gotama.

After the lapse of eight or nine months, she tied a wooden hoop around her belly, covered it with a red cloth, had her hands, feet, and back rubbed with a cow's horn, and displayed swellings; thus, with her faculties exhausted, she lay there.

Having made this offering, at the time of evening, when the Tathāgata was seated upon his adorned Dhamma-throne and teaching the Dhamma, she went to the Dhamma-hall, stood before the Tathāgata, and said: "Great Ascetic, you have indeed been teaching the Dhamma to the great multitude;
your voice is sweet and your lip-enclosure is well-formed. Yet, because of you, I have conceived a child and my pregnancy has reached full term."
“Once she was born, you knew nothing of my birth-chamber, nor of the ghee, oil, and other necessities.
While not doing it yourself, you did not even instruct any of your attendants, or the King of Kosala, or Anāthapiṇḍika, or the female lay follower Visākhā, saying:
‘Do what is appropriate for this young girl Ciñcā. You only knew how to take pleasure; you knew nothing of the care required for a pregnancy.”
Taking a lump of excrement, she reviled the Tathāgata in the midst of the assembly as if striving to defile the lunar disk.
Setting aside his discourse on the Dhamma, the Tathāgata roared like a lion and said, "Sister, both I and you alone shall know whether what you have spoken is true or not. "Yes, ascetic, by you and—"
"And this has arisen because of my state of being known [to her].
At that moment, Sakka’s palace manifested a state of heat.
Reflecting upon it, he realized, "The young woman Ciñcā is reviling the Tathāgata with untruth," and thinking, "I shall clear up this matter," he went together with four deva-sons.
Then the sons of the gods, having become young mice, simultaneously severed the binding ropes of the wooden wheel.
The wind blew up the cloth he was wearing, and as the wooden wheel fell, it landed upon the instep of her foot;
both of her toes were severed. People rose up and said, "You ill-omened woman, you revile the Perfectly Enlightened One!"
Spitting on her head, they drove her out from Jetavana with clods of earth, sticks, and other weapons in their hands.
Then, as she passed beyond the range of vision of the Tathāgata, the great earth split open and gave way; a mass of flames rose up from the Avīci hell.
She went along as if wrapping herself in a blanket given by a noble family and was reborn in Avīci. The gain and honor of the followers of other sects declined.
The Ten-Powered One’s growth increased even further. On the following day, they raised a discussion in the Hall of Truth:
"Friends, Ciñcā Māṇavikā, having slandered the Perfectly Enlightened One—the possessor of such exalted qualities and the supreme recipient of offerings—with what was untrue, has met with great ruin.
The Teacher, having arrived, asked: "Monks, for what discussion are you gathered here now?"
Having asked, "Is it indeed by her? and being told that it was, he said, "Monks, it is not only now;
in the past as well, she insulted me with untruths and met with great ruin. Having said this, he related the past:
In the past, while Brahmadatta was ruling in Bārāṇasī, the Bodhisatta was conceived in the womb of his chief queen.
Because his face was as beautiful as a full-blown lotus, they gave him the name "Padumakumāra" (Lotus Prince).
When he reached maturity, he went to Takkasilā, where he mastered all the arts and returned. Subsequently, his mother passed away.
The king appointed another woman as chief queen and bestowed the vice-regency upon his son. Later, the king [set out for] the border region...
In order to pacify the unrest, he said to the chief queen, “My dear lady, stay right here;
I am going to pacify the rebellion in the border regions. When she replied, “I will not stay here;
I too shall go,” he showed her the dangers of the battlefield and said, “Stay without longing until my return; meanwhile, [entrust] Prince Paduma...”
"Having given such orders that you will remain diligent in your duties, I shall depart," he said;
and having done so, he went away, drove off the enemies, satisfied the people of the countryside, and upon his return, encamped his army outside the city.
The Bodhisatta, learning of his father's arrival, had the city decorated and the royal palace prepared.
He went to her presence all alone.
Upon seeing his physical perfection, she became enamored with him. The Bodhisatta paid homage to her and asked, "Mother, what must we do?
Then, saying, "You call me 'mother'?", she rose up, took him by the hand, and—
"Ascend the bed," he said. "For what reason? "Until the king returns, let us both take delight in the pleasure of the defilements.

"Mother, you are my mother and have a husband; I have never, out of the influence of defilement, looked upon a woman who has a protector by breaking the sense-faculties. How could I commit such a defiled act with you?"
“I shall do so. After she had spoken thus two or three times, when he remained unwilling, she said, “You will not do as I say.
“Indeed, I will not,” he replied. “In that case, I shall have the king inform him and have your head cut off!
The Great Being, saying, “Do as you please,” made her feel ashamed and departed.
Terrified and trembling, she thought, "If he reports this to my father first, I shall have no life left; I myself will speak of it first.
Without eating her meal, she put on soiled hair and clothes, showed the nail-marks upon her body, and instructed her attendants:
"When the King asks, 'Where is the Queen?', you must say, 'She is ill.'"
Having given him a sign and made her bed as if she were ill, she lay down. The king, too, having circumambulated the city and ascended to his residence, not seeing her, asked, "Where is the queen?
Hearing that she was "ill," he entered the inner chamber and asked, "What is it, Queen, that makes you unwell?
As if not hearing his words, she [repeated] two or three times—
When questioned by Vāra, she said, "Great King, why do you speak? Be silent! Women like me do not belong to anyone.

When he replied, "By whom have you been harassed? Speak quickly to me, and I shall cut off his head," she said, "Who are you, Great King, that you have gone away after leaving [the city]? When he said, "Padumakumāra," she spoke.
“Thus, having come to my dwelling place, even though I was told, ‘Dear one, do not do this;
I am your mother,’ he said, ‘There is no other king but me; having taken you into my house, I shall enjoy you with sensual pleasure.
Seizing me by the hair, he tore at it back and forth, threw me down, beat me, and departed without doing as he was told,” she said.
Without even investigating, the king, enraged like a venomous snake, commanded his men: "Go, men, bind Prince Paduma and bring him here!
They went to his house as if overwhelming the city, bound him, struck him, and having bound his hands tightly behind his back, they fastened a garland of red *kaṇavera* flowers around his neck.
Having sentenced him to death, they brought him forward. Knowing, "This is the queen's doing," he came along lamenting, "O men, I have committed no offense against the king;

I am innocent! The entire city was thrown into turmoil, and having gathered together, they said, "It is said that the king, having taken the word of a woman, has caused Prince Mahāpaduma to be executed."
Falling at the prince’s feet, she lamented with a great cry, "My lord, this is unworthy of you!
Then, having led him away, they presented him to the king. As soon as the king saw him, he was unable to restrain his mind and said, "This man, though not a king, acts with the grace of a king;
being my own son, he offends against the chief queen. Go, throw him into the Corapapāta ravine."
"Having cast him down, bring about his destruction," he said. The Great Being pleaded with his father, "Father, I have committed no such offense;
do not destroy me by taking the word of a woman. But he did not heed his son's words.
Then the sixteen thousand women of the inner apartments cried out, "Dear Prince Mahāpaduma, this is unworthy of you..."
Having received [the command], they raised a great cry of lamentation. All the wealthy nobles and others, as well as the ministers and attendants, said:
"Your Majesty, the prince is endowed with virtue, conduct, and noble qualities; he is the protector of his lineage and the rightful heir to the kingdom.
Do not destroy him by taking the word of women and acting without due investigation. A king must indeed be one who acts with circumspection. Having spoken thus, they...
They recited these seven verses:
“One who does not perceive even the slightest fault in another, whether small or great,
in every respect— such a lord might impose punishment without having personally investigated the matter himself.”
“The kṣatriya who inflicts punishment without due investigation swallows a thorn,
like one born blind eating [food] with flies in it.
He punishes those who deserve no punishment, and fails to punish those who deserve punishment.”
A blind man does not know the uneven path, nor what is even and what is uneven.
But he who can thoroughly explain these points— both subtle and gross— in their entirety,
having clearly seen them, is indeed worthy to engage in discourse.
“It is not possible to establish oneself in greatness through being exclusively mild, nor by being exclusively harsh; therefore, one should practice both.
One who is disregarded becomes mild, while one who is excessively harsh incurs enmity.”
Having understood both of these, one should act with due reflection:
“Though one who is lustful might speak much, and one who is hateful speaks much as well,
O King, you ought not to slay your son on account of a woman.”
In this context, *nāddaṭṭhā* means "not having seen. *Parato* means "from another. *Sabbaso* means "all. *Aṇuṃthūlāni* refers to faults, both small and great.

*Sāmaṃ appaṭivekkhiyā* means that without having personally investigated by receiving the word of another, King Pathavissara should not inflict or impose punishment. For during the time of King Mahāsammata, [he was] always...
There is no punishment beyond this; there is nothing higher than beating, censuring, and banishment—namely, the cutting off of hands and feet or execution.
This arose only during the time of harsh kings; with reference to that, those ministers spoke thus, saying, "It is not proper to act without having personally seen the fault of another for certain."
"And he who, O Great King, without having investigated— meaning, without investigating whether a fault warrants the imposition of a penalty appropriate to that fault—
a king who, remaining on a wrong path, inflicts punishments such as the cutting off of hands upon one who has committed an offense,
is like one who swallows thorny food while creating his own cause of suffering, and is like one born blind."

"Eating with flies" means [eating while flies are present]. "One who punishes the unpunishable": he who punishes one who should not be punished and should not be subjected to punishment, yet fails to punish one who should be punished and should be subjected to punishment, acts solely according to his own whim;
like a blind man entering upon an uneven path, he does not know what is equal and what is unequal.
Consequently, stumbling over stones and the like, like that blind man, he will experience great suffering in the four states of misery (apāya).
The meaning is "he attains. Regarding the phrase "these grounds":

having clearly seen all these grounds for punishing and not punishing, as well as the minor and major [offenses] even among those grounds for punishing, he should instruct; the meaning is that he indeed deserves to conduct legal affairs and to instruct in the administration of the kingdom.
Regarding "having established himself on greatness": such a person, having generated wealth where it had not arisen and having made stable what has arisen, [should act].
The meaning is that he is unable to establish himself in great and sublime sovereignty. "Mudu" refers to King Mudu;
he was treated with contempt and looked down upon by the inhabitants of the kingdom, and thus he was unable to make his reign free from thieves.
"Veravā" means that all the inhabitants of the kingdom become his enemies because he is excessively harsh; therefore, he is called "Veravā. "Anumajjhaṃ" means experienced.
"One should practice moderation between the states of softness and sharpness; the meaning is that one should exercise sovereignty having become neither too mild nor too harsh.

"Not for the sake of a woman" means: O Great King, you ought not to commit a base and evil deed by relying on a woman to have your own son—who protects the lineage and is the heir to the royal parasol—put to death.
Although the ministers spoke in these various ways, they were unable to make him accept their advice.
The Bodhisatta, though entreating him, was likewise unable to make him accept his own counsel.
But the foolish king, commanding, “Go, throw him into the thieves’ precipice,” spoke the eighth verse:
“The whole world is on one side, and this woman alone is on the other;
therefore, I shall act accordingly. Go, and cast her into the path!
In that passage, “therefore I shall act” means: for the reason that the entire world stands as the faction of the prince alone, and this [woman]...
"A woman is alone; for that reason, I shall follow her word. Go, lead her up to the mountain and throw her over the precipice!
When this was said, not even one among the sixteen thousand royal women was able to maintain her composure, and all the inhabitants of the city...
Raising their arms and weeping, they lamented with disheveled hair. Thinking, "Let these people prevent him from being thrown over this precipice," the king went there with his retinue;
even as the great multitude was still wailing, he had the man seized and, placing him head-downwards with his feet upwards, threw him over the precipice.
Then, through the power of his loving-kindness (*mettā*), the deities dwelling upon the mountain—
“Do not fear, Mahāpaduma,” he said, comforting him; then, taking him with both hands and placing him against his own heart, he caused him to experience a divine touch.
Descending, he set him within the coils of the hood of the Nāga king who was stationed at the foot of the mountain.
The Nāga king led the Bodhisatta to his own abode and, displaying his own glory in the midst of the assembly, bestowed it upon him.
Having lived there for one year, he said, "I shall go to the path of men. When asked, "To what place?

he replied, "I will go to the Himavat mountains and go forth into the religious life. The Nāga king, saying "Very well," took him, established him on the path of men, gave him the requisites for going forth, and returned to his own abode. He too, having entered the Himavat, [proceeded].
Having gone forth into the ascetic life of a seer (isipabbajjā) and attained the meditative absorptions (jhāna) and higher knowledges (abhiññā), he dwelt there subsisting on forest roots and fruits.
Then, a certain forest-dweller from Bārāṇasī arrived at that place; recognizing him as the Great Being, he said, "Are you not, O Lord, Prince Mahāpaduma?
When [the Great Being] replied, "Yes, good man," he paid homage to him and stayed there for several days.

Having stayed there, he went to Bārāṇasī and informed the king: “Your Majesty, your son has gone forth as an ascetic in the Himalayan region and is living in a leaf-hut; I have come after staying in his presence.
“Was he seen by you with your own eyes? “Yes, Your Majesty,” he replied. The king, surrounded by a great army, went there to the edge of the forest.
Having established his camp and surrounded by a host of ministers, he went to the leaf-hut.
Seeing the Great Being seated at the entrance of the leaf-hut, resembling a golden image, he paid homage and sat down to one side. The ministers also paid homage, exchanged greetings, and sat down.
The Bodhisatta, in turn, questioned the king and returned his greetings. Then he [the king]—
The king, asking, “Dear son, you were thrown by me into a deep abyss; how did you survive? spoke the ninth verse:
“Having been cast into a many-storied hell, deep and very difficult to cross, in a mountain precipice—by what means did you not die there?”
In that context, "anekatāle" means at a distance of many palm trees. "Nāma" means not dead.
Following that:
"There, a powerful nāga with an expanded hood, born of a mountain peak,"
“He took me away with his wealth, and so I died there.
“Come, prince, I shall restore you to your own home;
rule the kingdom, O blessed one. What will you do in the forest?”
"Just as one might pull out a fishhook after swallowing it, bleeding,
and having pulled it out, one would be at ease— so do I see myself.
What indeed do you call 'the hook,' and what do you call 'with blood'?"
“What indeed do you call ‘uprooted’? Tell me that when asked.
“I call sensual pleasures ‘the hook,’ along with the elephant and the horse and the blood;
I have cast them off—I call this ‘uprooted. Know it thus, O Kṣatriya!”
Among these five, three verses in the alternate meter belong to the Bodhisattva and two to the King.

Therein, regarding the phrase "He accepted me": at the time of falling from the mountain, he accepted me—who had been protected by a deity, comforted by divine touch, and brought [to him]—and having taken me, he led me to the abode of the Nāgas. And there, a great...
Having given him honor, when told, "Lead me to the realm of men," he brought me to the realm of men.
Having come here, I went forth into the religious life; thus, by the power of that deity and the Naga king, I related everything, saying, "I am named So-and-so there.
Upon hearing his words, "Come! the King was filled with joy and said, "Dear son, through my foolishness, because of a woman—"
Having accepted his words, [the king] fell at his feet and said, "I have offended you, who are thus perfected in virtue and conduct;
forgive my fault. When [the other] replied, "Rise up, Great King! I forgive your fault;
from now on, do not again act so thoughtlessly," [the king said], "Dear one, you yourself, having raised the white parasol that belongs to your own lineage, [rule] the kingdom..."
"Even while instructing me, you say 'I forgive,'" he said.
"Having pulled it out" means: having pulled out his heart, lungs, and so forth, even before they had reached [the hook], may he be happy.
"In this way I see myself," O Great King, means: in this way I too see myself as a man who has attained safety after having swallowed a fishhook.
“I see myself. “What indeed?”—the King asks this in order to hear the matter in detail from him.
“The sensual pleasures,” he says, “are the five strands of sensual pleasure.
‘An elephant and horse with blood’—I call such wealth as elephants, horses, chariots, vehicles, the seven treasures, and so forth, ‘with blood. ‘I have abandoned’—I have abandoned all of that.”
"It has been abandoned, it has been relinquished; that gift, I call 'uplifted.
Thus, Great King, I have no need for the kingdom; however, you should rule the kingdom according to the Dhamma, without violating the ten duties of a king and abandoning the path of ruin.
Having thus given this advice to his father, the Great Being, that king—
Having wept and lamented, as he was going toward the city, he questioned his ministers along the way:
"Depending on whom have I come to such separation from a son endowed with such conduct and virtue? "It was the chief queen, Your Majesty," they replied.
The king had her seized by her feet and cast down into a thieves' precipice; then, entering the city, he ruled the kingdom according to Dhamma.
Having delivered this Dhamma teaching, the Teacher said, "Thus, monks, in the past these women reviled me and met with great ruin," and added:
"Ciñcā Māṇavikā was my mother, and Devadatta was my father;
Ānanda was the wise Nāga, and Sāriputta was a deity."
"I was a prince; remember this as the Jātaka.
With these words of the concluding verse, he identified the Jātaka.
This concludes the ninth commentary, the Mahāpaduma Jātaka.
[473] 10. The Commentary on the Mittāmitta Jātaka.
"What deeds?"—this was spoken by the Teacher while residing at Jetavana concerning a minister who served the King of Kosala.
It is said that he was of great benefit to the king; therefore, the king bestowed upon him exceptional honor. As for the rest...
Unable to tolerate this, they slandered him, saying, "Your Majesty, such-and-such a minister is working for your harm.
The king, investigating the matter, saw no fault whatsoever; thinking, "I do not see any fault in him.
How indeed can I know whether he is my friend or my enemy? he [spoke to] him...
Thinking, "No one else will be able to know this question once it has been posed to the Tathāgata; I shall go and ask him," he ate his morning meal, approached the Teacher, and asked:
"Venerable Sir, how indeed can a man know whether another is a friend or an enemy?
Then the Teacher said to him: "Great King, even in the past, the wise..."
"Having reflected on this question, having asked the wise, and having understood it according to what they said, they avoided enemies and cultivated friends.
Having said this, being requested by him, he related a story of the past:
"In the past, when Brahmadatta was reigning in Benares, the Bodhisatta was his advisor in matters of welfare and righteousness."
At that time, the other ministers slandered a certain minister who was a benefactor to the King of Bārāṇasī.
Since the king perceived no fault in him, he asked the Great Being, "How indeed can one distinguish between a friend and an enemy?
and spoke the first verse:
“What actions does one perform, and how should a wise person exert effort?
How should an intelligent man recognize an enemy after seeing or hearing of them?

The meaning of this is: what kind of actions does a wise and intelligent person perform such that, having seen with his own eyes or heard with his ears, he recognizes, “This person is my enemy”? And for the sake of recognizing him, how should a wise person exert effort?
Then, explaining the characteristics of a non-friend, he said:
“He does not smile upon seeing him, nor does he greet him;
he does not offer his eyes [to look at him], and he behaves in a contrary manner.”
“He associates with his enemies and does not serve his friends;
he restrains those who wish him well and praises those who revile him.
He does not disclose his secrets to him, nor does he keep his own secrets from him.”
He does not praise his own deeds, nor does he extol his wisdom.
He delights in non-existence and takes no delight in existence.
Even upon obtaining a rare meal, mindfulness does not arise within him.
Therefore, one does not feel compassion for him, thinking, "Oh, may he too obtain this!
Thus, these sixteen modes are established regarding an enemy;
by means of these, a wise person should recognize an enemy upon seeing or hearing them.
Having spoken these five verses, the Great Being further asked:
“What deeds should one perform? How should a wise person exert himself?
How does a discerning man recognize a friend—by seeing or by hearing?”
Having been asked about the characteristics of a friend by means of this verse, he spoke the remaining verses:
“He remembers one who has gone away, and rejoices when one has arrived;
thereafter, he cherishes that person and greets them with kind words.”
“He associates with friends and does not serve those who are not his friends;
he restrains those who revile him and praises those who desire his welfare.
He reveals his secrets to him and keeps his secrets hidden.”
He praises his own work and extols his own wisdom.
He delights in existence and does not delight in non-existence.
Upon obtaining unexpected food, mindfulness arises within him.
Then he feels compassion for him: "Oh, may he too obtain this!
Thus these sixteen modes are well-established regarding a friend;
by means of these, a wise person should recognize a friend through both seeing and hearing.
In that regard, "he does not smile upon seeing him" means that upon seeing that friend—who is merely a counterfeit friend—he does not smile nor show a joyful expression.
