"And he does not greet him back" means that when the other person initiates a conversation, he does not respond nor is he pleased.
"And he does not give him his eye" means that when the other looks at him, he does not look back. "And in the opposite manner... refers to his [behavior] toward him.
How does one oppose and act as an adversary? One "praises" when that person is speaking their own praise.
One "does not reveal" by not disclosing one's own secrets to them. "His work"—one does not commend the work performed by him.
"Of the wise"—one does not extol his wisdom; one does not praise his possession of knowledge. "In non-being"—in lack of prosperity. It does not arise for him.
“Mindful” means that mindfulness does not arise in that counterfeit friend with the thought, “I shall give this even to my friend.

“Does not feel compassion” means he does not reflect with a gentle heart. “He might obtain from me” means he might receive [something] from him. “Reasons” means causes. “One who has gone abroad” means one who has gone to a foreign land.
“One who cherishes” means he cherishes, treats as his own, longs for, envies, and desires; such is the meaning.
"By speech" means that by addressing him with sweet words, one greets him and is pleased. The remainder should be understood according to the method of the opposites as previously stated.
The king, being delighted by the Great Being’s discourse, bestowed great honor upon him.
Having delivered this Dhamma teaching, the Teacher said: "Thus, Great King, this very question arose in the past; it was only the wise who [resolved it]."
They said, "A friend or an enemy is to be known by these thirty-two signs. Having said this, he identified the Jātaka:
"At that time, Ānanda was the king, and I myself was the wise minister.
This concludes the commentary on the Mittāmitta Jātaka, the tenth.
The Summary of Birth Stories (Jātakuddāna): Kuṇāla, Bhaddasāla, Samuddavāṇija, Paṇḍita;
Janasandha, Mahākaṇha, Kosiya, and Sirimantaka.
The *Paduma*, the *Mitta*, and the *Amitta*— these ten Jātakas the Great Elders recited in the twelfth Nipāta.
The commentary on the Dvādasaka Nipāta is finished.
13. The Thirteen-Section Collection [474] 1.
The Commentary on the Mango Birth Story (Ambajātaka):
"In the past, he took my mango fruits"—this was spoken by the Teacher while residing at Jetavana concerning Devadatta.
For Devadatta, thinking, "I shall become a Buddha; for me, the ascetic Gotama is neither teacher nor preceptor," having thus rejected his teacher and fallen away from *jhāna*, he split the Saṅgha.
While traveling by stages toward Sāvatthī, when a fissure opened in the earth outside the Jeta Grove, he entered Avīci. At that time, the bhikkhus were discussing this matter in the Dhamma Hall.
They raised the cry: "Friends, Devadatta, having rejected his teacher, has met with great ruin and has been reborn in the Avīci Great Hell.
The Teacher, having arrived, asked, "Monks, about what conversation are you gathered here now?
When they replied, "About this very matter," he said, "Monks, it is not only now; in the past as well, Devadatta [rejected his teacher...]"
"Having rejected [the advice], he has met with great destruction," he said, and then related a story from the past.
In the past, while Brahmadatta was reigning in Bārāṇasī, his family of household priests was destroyed by a plague of snake-bite.
Only one son escaped by breaking through a wall. He went to Takkasilā and [approached] a world-renowned teacher...
Having mastered the three Vedas and the remaining crafts in the presence [of his teacher], he paid homage to his preceptor and departed, thinking, "I shall learn the customs of various lands.
As he traveled about, he reached a frontier city. Dependent upon that city was a large village of Caṇḍālas.
At that time, the Bodhisatta lived in that village; he was wise and skilled, possessing a mantra for causing fruit to ripen out of season.
He knows it. Rising early in the morning, he takes his staff, leaves that village, and approaches a mango tree in the forest.
Standing at a distance of seven steps, he recites that mantra and strikes the mango tree with a handful of water.
At that very moment, the old leaves fall from the tree, new ones emerge, and flowers appear.
Having blossomed, they fell; mango fruits rose up and, in a mere moment, having ripened, became sweet, full of essence, and like celestial nectar as they fell from the tree.
The Great Being gathered them, ate as much as he required, filled his basket, and went home. Having sold them, he supported his wife and children.
Thus, the brahmin youth, seeing the Great Being selling mangoes out of season after having brought them along, thought:
"Without a doubt, these must have been produced by the power of mantras; by relying on this man, I shall obtain this priceless mantra.
Having thus reflected, he observed the Great Being’s method of gathering the mangoes, understood it as it truly was, and [approached him] from the forest.
Before he had even arrived, [the Great Being] went to his house and, acting as if he did not know, asked his wife, "Where is the noble teacher, the master?
When she replied, "He has gone to the forest," he remained there waiting for him to return.
Seeing him approaching, he took the basket from his hand, brought it back, and placed it inside the house. The Great Being looked at it and said to his wife:
“Madam, this young man has come for the sake of the mantra, yet the mantra is being lost from his hands; he is no true man.
The young man, thinking, “I shall obtain this mantra by being helpful to my teacher,” began from that time on to perform all the duties in her house.
He brought firewood, pounded rice, and [prepared] the meal.
He cooked for him, provided tooth-sticks, water for rinsing the mouth, and so forth, and washed his feet.

One day, when the Great Being said, "Dear young man, give me a pillow for the legs of my bed," the youth, seeing nothing else available, sat there all night long with his thighs placed beneath them. Later, the Great Being’s wife [gave birth to] a son...

She gave birth. At the time of her delivery, she performed all the necessary services. One day, she said to the Great Being, "Master, this young man, being of noble birth, performs service for us for the sake of the spells;
whether or not the spell remains in his hands, please give him the spell. Having agreed, saying "Very well," he [gave it] to him.
Having given him the mantra, he spoke thus: "Dear son, this mantra is priceless;
by means of it, you will receive great gain and honor. When the king or a royal minister asks, 'Who is your teacher?', do not conceal me.
For if you feel ashamed, thinking, 'I received the mantra from a caṇḍāla,' you should say, 'A wealthy brahmin is my teacher.'"
“If you speak [of this], you will not obtain the fruit of this mantra. He replied, “For what reason would I conceal it?
When asked by anyone, I shall speak only to you. Having said this and paid homage to him, he departed from the Caṇḍāla village.
After testing the mantra, he eventually reached Bārāṇasī, where he sold mangoes and acquired great wealth.
Then one day, the park-keeper bought a mango from his hand and gave it to the king. After the king had eaten it, he asked, "Good man, where did you get such a mango?
"Your Majesty, a certain young brahmin brings out-of-season mangoes for sale;
I took it from him. "In that case, from now on, let him bring the mangoes right here," [the king commanded].
"Tell me," [the king said]. He did so. From then on, the young man brought mangoes to the royal palace.
Then, when the king said, "Attend upon me," he attended the king and, having received much wealth, gradually became a trusted confidant.
Then one day the king asked him, "Young man, from where do you obtain such mangoes, so perfect in color, fragrance, and flavor, at this unusual time?"
"Do you obtain these mangoes because a nāga, a supaṇṇa, or some deity gives them to you, or is it the power of a mantra?
"Great King, no one gives them to me; however, I possess a priceless mantra, and it is by its power.
"In that case, we too wish to see the power of your mantra for one day. "Very well, Your Majesty, I shall show it to you. The king—
On the following day, having gone to the park with him, he said, "Show me [the mango tree].
He replied, "Very well," approached the mango tree, and standing at a distance of seven paces, recited a mantra and struck the tree with water.
At that very moment, the mango tree, in the manner described below, took hold of fruit and rained down a shower of mangoes like a great cloud.
The great multitude gave shouts of approval and raised their garments in celebration.
Having eaten the mango fruits and given him much wealth, the king asked, "Young man, from whom did you receive such a marvelous spell? The young man thought, "If I say, 'From a caṇḍāla,'..."
Thinking, "I shall become an object of shame, and they will reproach me; moreover, my mantra is well-mastered and will not now be lost;

I shall claim a world-renowned teacher as my authority," he uttered a falsehood and renounced his own teacher, saying, "It was received by me in the presence of a world-renowned teacher at Takṣaśilā. At that very moment—
The charm vanished. The king, filled with joy, took it and entered the city.
On the following day, thinking, "I shall eat mangoes," he went to the park, sat upon the auspicious stone slab, and said to the young brahmin, "Young man, bring the mangoes.
The youth replied, "Very well," and as he approached the mango tree, he stood seven paces away, thinking, "I shall recite the charm. Then he began the incantations.
Realizing that [the mangoes] were no longer being presented because they had vanished, he stood there feeling ashamed.
The king thought, "In the past, this man would bring mangoes right into the midst of the assembly and give them to us, making it rain a shower of mangoes like a thick cloud;
now he stands as if stiff with pride. What could be the reason? Thinking thus, he asked him, speaking the first verse:
“Formerly, O Brahmacārī, you took my mango fruits, both small and large;
by those very same mantras, O Brahmā, the fruits of the tree no longer appear for you.
In this context, *ahāsi* means he took; *dumapphalā* means the fruits of the tree.
Having heard that, the young man thought, "If I say, 'Today I will not take the mango fruit,' the king will be angry with me; I shall deceive him with a lie. He then spoke the second verse:
"I await the conjunction of the constellations; I do not perceive the right moment or the hour in my spells.
Having obtained the conjunction of the constellations and the right moment, I shall surely take the abundant mango fruit."
In that context, "addhāharissambaphalaṃ" means "I shall certainly bring the mango fruit.
The King, wondering, "This man never spoke of the conjunction of the constellations before; what indeed is this? asked two verses:
"He never spoke of the conjunction of the constellations before, nor did he ever mention a moment or an instant before;..."
“Brahmā, you yourself brought these many mango fruits, endowed with color, fragrance, and flavor.
For in the past, by means of your incantations and chanting, the fruits of trees would appear for you;
yet today you cannot even recite your incantation. What kind of Dhamma is this of yours today?”
In that context, *na pāresi* means "you are not able. *Jappampi* means "even while crying out" or "even while struggling. *Ayaṃ so* means "this very one is your true nature;

who indeed has been born today? Having heard this, the young man thought: "It is not possible to deceive the king with a lie. Even if he should issue a command once my true nature has been told, let him do so; I shall speak only the truth. Having reflected thus, he recited two verses:
"The son of a Caṇḍāla gave me away; by right (dhamma) he taught me the mantras and my true nature (pakati)."
“May it not be that when questioned about my name and clan, I should conceal the truth and let the power of the spell be lost.
Thus, O lord of people, when questioned among the folk, overcome by malice, I spoke a falsehood:
‘These spells belong to the brahmin. That was false; having lost the spell, I am a wretched man and I weep.”
Therein, "by means of the Dhamma" means he gave them without concealment, by way of fair dealing.
"And he told them their nature" means he told them their inherent disposition, thinking: "Do not hide my name and clan when questioned; if you hide it, your spells will perish.
"Of the brahmin, [he said] 'false'" means: "These spells were received by me in the presence of the brahmin."
“I spoke falsely; because of that, those mantras of mine have been lost. Now, having lost my mantras, I am a pauper and weep.

Hearing this, the king became angry, thinking, “This man of evil character did not even look upon such a jewel-like mantra. For when such a supreme jewel-like mantra has been obtained, what will one’s birth avail? And reproaching him, he said:
“Whether they be *eraṇḍa* trees, *pucimanda* trees, or even *pālibhaddaka* trees;”
One who desires honey should find the honey; for he is the best of trees to him.
“The khattiyas, brahmins, vessas, suddas, caṇḍālas, and pukkusas—from whom one may learn the Dhamma, he is indeed the best of men to him.”
“Having inflicted upon him both punishment and death, seize this wretch by the throat and cast him out! He who,
through pride and arrogance, has destroyed the supreme goal he had attained with such great difficulty.”—
Thus he spoke these verses.
In this context, "one who seeks honey" refers to a man seeking honey in the forest who, while looking for it, identifies the tree from which he obtains honey;

that very tree is called his "supreme tree. In the same way, among the kṣatriyas and others, whichever person from whom one may understand the Dhamma, the reason, the appropriate meaning, and the benefit—that person alone is called one's "supreme man. "And the punishment for him... [and so forth].

"Having inflicted upon this one of evil nature the punishment of stripping off the skin from his back with bamboo splinters and other such tools, and having executed him, seize this wretch by the throat and thresh him;
having reduced him to a state of being threshed, cast him out and drive him away!
What is the use of this man living here?"
The king’s men, having done so, deprived him of his position, saying: “If you can go to your teacher, win him over, and obtain the mantras again, you may return here;
if not, do not even look toward this direction. Thus rendered destitute, he thought:
“Apart from my teacher, I have no other refuge; I must go to him alone.”
"Having gone there and propitiated him, I shall ask for the mantra once again," he said, and weeping, he went to that village.
Then, seeing him approaching, the Great Being addressed his wife: "My dear, look at that man of evil character coming back again, having lost his mantra.
He approached the Great Being, paid homage, and sat down to one side, saying: "For what reason..."
When asked, "Have you come? he replied, "Teacher, having told a lie and abandoned my teacher, I have met with great ruin.
Having thus confessed his transgression, he begged for the mantras once more:
"Just as one who thinks it level might fall into a pit, a cave, a chasm, or a place of rotting corpses;"
“As one might step on a rope thinking it is a black snake, or as a blind man might grasp at a flame;
even so, O wise one, you have burned me again and again for my transgression, though I have abandoned [all] counsel. Thus he spoke this verse.
Therein, “as one thinks... even”: just as a person, thinking “this is level ground,” might fall into a pit or a cave.
Or he might fall into hell, which is defined as the place where the earth has split open, or into the *pūtipāda* (the Rotting Foot).

"The Rotting Foot" is the name of a great chasm that exists in a certain region of the Himalayas; it occurs when great trees have withered and died, and their roots have rotted away, leaving a vast pit in that spot.
"He would step over the fire" means he would cross over a flame. "Even so" means even in this way, I too [possess] the eye of wisdom.
“Abhāva, being blind and not knowing your distinction, I have stumbled among you;
having recognized that stumbling of mine, O wise one endowed with knowledge who has abandoned [wrong] counsel, give it to me once again.

Then the teacher said to him, “Dear son, what are you saying? For a blind man avoids pits and such by means of the perception given to him. I told you this very thing at the outset; for what purpose have you come to me now?”
“I bestowed this spell upon you according to the Dhamma, and you too received it according to the Dhamma.
I spoke to you with a mind full of affection; since you stand firm in the Dhamma, the spell shall not forsake you.
This foolish spell, which was obtained with great difficulty and is rare to find today in the world of men—”
"Even though he obtained his livelihood, the one of little wisdom destroyed it by speaking falsehoods.
To the fool, the deluded, the ungrateful, the liar, and the unrestrained—such as you—we do not give our mantras.
Where are the mantras? Go away! You are not pleasing to me."
He spoke these verses.
Therein, "by means of the Dhamma" means: I too, without taking even a portion of teacher’s fee from you—whether gold or silver—bestowed the mantra solely by means of the Dhamma;
and you too, without giving anything, received it by means of the Dhamma alone, in accordance with what is right. "Established in the Dhamma."
He was established in the duty of honoring his teacher. Regarding the phrase "of such a kind," [the teacher said]: "We do not give such mantras as these, which cause one to take fruit out of season;
go, for you are not pleasing to me.
Thus dismissed by his teacher, he thought, "What is the use of my life? and having entered the forest, he died an orphaned death.
Having delivered this Dhamma teaching, the Teacher said, "Monks, it is not only now;
in the past as well, Devadatta met with great ruin after rejecting his teacher," and he then identified the Jātaka:
"At that time, the ungrateful youth was Devadatta, the king was Ānanda, and the Caṇḍāla’s son was none other than myself."
The First: The Amba-Jātaka Commentary [475].
2. The Phandana-Jātaka Commentary:
"A man with an axe in his hand"—this was spoken by the Teacher while dwelling on the bank of the Rohiṇī River, concerning a quarrel among kinsmen.
He related the story. The background of the matter, however, will be made clear in the Kuṇāla Jātaka. At that time, the Teacher addressed his kinsmen:
"Great King, in the past, when Brahmadatta was ruling in Bārāṇasī, there was a carpenter’s village outside the city.
There lived a brahmin carpenter who earned his living by bringing timber from the forest and making chariots."
At that time, there was a great *phandana* tree in a region of the Himālayas. A certain black lion, having sought his prey and returned, lay down at its foot.
Then one day, as the wind blew, a dry branch fell and struck him upon his shoulder.
With his shoulder slightly pained, he rose up in fear and trembling, sprang away, and then turned back again.
Looking back along the path he had come, seeing nothing at all, he thought: "There is no other lion or tiger following me;
however, I suspect the deity born in this tree cannot endure my lying down here. Very well, I shall find out.
Holding a grudge against the wrong object, he struck the tree and said: "I am not eating even a leaf of your tree, nor..."
"I am breaking off a branch; you tolerate other deer living here, yet you do not tolerate me.
What fault is there in me? Wait a few days; having uprooted that tree by its very roots, I shall have it cut into pieces.
Having thus threatened the tree deity, he wandered about seeking out a man. At that time, that brahmin carpenter [sought] two or three men...
Taking the chariot wood for his purpose, he went to that place by cart;
having parked the cart in one spot, he went toward the *phandana* tree with axe and hatchet in hand, searching for timber.
Seeing him, the black lion thought, "Today it is fitting for me to see the back of my enemy," and went to stand at the foot of the tree. The carpenter—
Looking here and there, he set out toward the vicinity of the Phandana tree.
Thinking, "I shall speak with him while he has not yet passed by," he spoke the first verse:
"A man with an axe in hand stands having entered the forest."
“Tell me, friend, when asked: what kind of wood do you wish to cut?
In this context, “man” means: “You stand here alone, axe in hand, having entered this forest.
Having heard his words, [the deer thought]: “It is truly wonderful! Never before has a deer spoken in human speech to me.”
Thinking, "I have seen him before; he will know the wood suitable for a chariot wheel, so I shall question him," he spoke the second verse:
"You roam through the forests, both level and uneven;
tell me truly, my friend, when asked, what wood is strong enough for a chariot rim?"
"In this matter, you too are a lone black lion who roams the forests; you will know the timber suitable for a chariot.
Hearing this, the black lion thought, "Now my heart's desire shall reach its fulfillment," and spoke the third verse:
"Neither *sāla*, nor *khadira*, nor *assakaṇṇa*, much less *dhava* [timber];"
“And there is a tree named Phandana; its wood is strong for a chariot-rim.

Having heard this, he was filled with joy and thought, “Indeed, today I have entered the forest on an auspicious day! Even a beast of burden points out to me wood suitable for a chariot. Oh, how excellent! Then, asking his question, he spoke the fourth verse:
“What are its leaves like, and what is its trunk like?”
“Good sir, being asked by me, explain how we may understand the *phandana* tree.
Then, explaining it to him, he spoke these two verses:
“The branches of which hang down and bend, yet do not break;”
“Thus there is a tree named Phandana, at the foot of which I stand.
‘For all your wheels, hubs, shafts, and linchpins, this Phandana shall be serviceable.’”
In that context, he said "without thorns" after thinking, "When will he ever stop taking this tree?
I shall speak of its virtues. Regarding the phrase "for the pole, the rim, and the rest of the chariot," it means:
"For all of these—the pole, the rim, and the remainder of the chariot—he will be serviceable and capable of performing his task."
Having spoken thus, he wandered off to one side with a joyful mind, while the carpenter began to cut down the tree.
The tree deity thought: "I have not dropped anything upon him;
yet he has harbored malice toward me in an improper place and is destroying my mansion, whereby I too shall perish. By some means, I shall destroy this enemy."
Becoming like a forest worker, he came into his presence and asked, "O man, you have found a pleasing tree;
what will you do after cutting this down? "I shall make a chariot-rim," he replied.
"Who told you that a chariot would be made from this tree? "By a black lion. "Excellent, very well!"
He declared, "With this tree, a beautiful chariot will be made;

having flayed the skin from the neck of a black lion and encircled the wheel-rims with it to a depth of four finger-breadths—like a band of iron—the wheels will become firm, and you shall obtain much wealth.
[The king asked,] "From where shall I obtain the skin of a black lion? [The man replied,] "You are a fool! This..."
Your tree stands in the forest and does not flee; go to the one who pointed out your tree, deceive him by asking, "Master, in which place shall I cut the tree you showed me?
and bring him here. Then, while he is unsuspecting and stretching out his snout to point, saying, "Cut it here and there," strike him with a sharp great axe.
"Having crushed him and brought him to the end of his life, take his hide, eat his choice meat, and then cut down the tree!
Thus he swore an oath. To illustrate this matter, the Teacher spoke these verses:
"Thus even the Phandana tree then addressed him:"
I too have a word, Bhāradvāja; listen to me.
"From the shaft of the yoke, having raised it four finger-breadths, he extended the pole;
thus it would become even stronger."
“Thus even the trembling tree, for that moment, harbored enmity;
it brought suffering to both the jealous ones who were born and those yet unborn.
Therein, *bhāradvāja* is an address by means of his clan name. *Upakkhandamhā* means from the trunk. *Ukkacca* means having cut out.

Having heard the words of the tree deity, the carpenter thought, "Oh, today is my auspicious day! and after killing the black lion and cutting down the tree, he departed. To illustrate this matter, the Teacher said:
"Thus indeed did the *phandana* tree and the lion, Through mutual contention, cause each other's destruction."
“In the same way, wherever disputes arise among human beings,
they dance the peacock’s dance, like those trembling with pride.
Therefore I say this to you for your welfare, all you who have gathered here:”
Rejoice together, do not dispute; do not harbor the agitation of rivalry.
"One should train only in harmony; this is praised by the Buddhas.
One who delights in harmony and stands firm in the Dhamma does not fall away from the security from bondage."
In this context, "they cause to kill" means they have them killed. "They dance the peacock dance":

for when there is a dispute among people, O Great King, just as peacocks dancing would reveal a secret matter that ought to be concealed, so too do people, exposing each other's faults, perform what is called the "peacock dance."
"Just as those who were trembling with envy danced, as it were, while exposing each other's faults—'voti' means for that reason I say to you. 'Bhaddaṃ voti' means may it be well for you.
'Yāvantettha' means as many as there are here, do not become like those who tremble with envy. 'Sāmaggimeva sikkhetha' means you should train yourselves in harmony alone."
"Train yourselves; this is praised by the wise who have grown in wisdom. "Established in the Dhamma" means established in the Dhamma of good conduct.
"He does not fall away from the security from bondage" means he does not decline from Nibbāna, which is secure from the bonds; thus [the Buddha] took up the pinnacle of the teaching with Nibbāna.
Having heard the discourse on the Dhamma, the Sakyan princes became reconciled.
Having delivered this Dhamma teaching, the Teacher identified the Jātaka, saying: "At that time, having understood that matter, I myself was the deity dwelling in that forest grove.
This is the second commentary on the Phandana Jātaka.
3. The Commentary on the Javana-haṃsa Jātaka.
"O swan, alight right here!"—this was spoken by the Teacher while residing at Jetavana, concerning the teaching of the *Daḷhadhamma-dhanuggaha-sutta*. For the Blessed One said:
"Bhikkhus, suppose there were four archers of firm strength, well-trained, skilled of hand, and practiced in their craft, standing in the four directions;
then a man might come and say: 'I shall [shoot] these four archers of firm strength...'"

‘Suppose there were archers, well-trained, practiced in hand, and experienced, who were to shoot arrows in the four directions and, before they had even touched the ground, catch them and bring them back.
‘What do you think, bhikkhus, would it be appropriate to say that such a man was “swift, endowed with supreme speed”? ‘Yes, venerable sir. ‘And as for him, bhikkhus—’

The speed of that man, and the speed of the moon and sun, and even the speed of those deities who run ahead of the moon and sun— the formative forces of life (*āyusaṅkhārā*) perish more swiftly than all of these. Therefore, monks, in this regard:
“Monks, you should train yourselves thus: ‘We shall dwell heedfully. For this, monks, is how you should train.
On the day after this sutta was spoken, the monks raised a discussion in the Hall of Truth:
“Friends, the Teacher, standing within the domain of his own Buddhahood, [declared that] the life-formations of these beings are short-lived and weak.”
Having explained this, he caused the ordinary monks to fall into great terror, exclaiming, "Oh, the power of the Buddha!
The Teacher approached and asked, "Monks, about what discussion are you gathered here now?
When they replied, "About this very matter," he said, "It is not surprising, monks, that I, having now attained omniscience, [should speak thus] regarding the formations of life."
"Having shown the brevity of existence and stirred the bhikkhus, I teach the Dhamma. For in the past, even when reborn as a causeless swan,
I showed the brevity of the life-formations and, beginning with the King of Bārāṇasī,
taught the Dhamma to stir the entire royal assembly," he said, and then related a story of the past.
In the past, when Brahmadatta was reigning in Bārāṇasī,
the Bodhisatta was reborn in the womb of a swift swan and lived on Mount Cittakūṭa, surrounded by ninety thousand swans. One day,
after eating wild rice at a certain lake in Jambudīpa together with his retinue, he rose into the air like a great golden palm-leaf fan being unfurled.
Surrounded by his retinue, he proceeded toward Cittakūṭa from the vicinity of the city of Bārāṇasī with a very slow and graceful gait.

Then, seeing him, the King of Bārāṇasī said to his ministers, "This one must also have been a king like myself," and having conceived affection for him, he took flowers, perfumes, and ointments; and looking upon the Great Being, [he prepared] all the musical instruments.

He had them taken up. Seeing that they were being honored in such a manner, the Great Being asked the swans, "What does the king expect in return for showing me such honor? "Friendship with you, O Lord," they replied.
"In that case, let there be friendship between the king and us," he said, and having established friendship with the king, he departed.
Then one day, while the king had gone to his pleasure garden, [the Great Being] went to Lake Anotatta, took water with one wing and sandalwood powder with the other, and returned.

Having bathed the king with that water and sprinkled him with the sandalwood powder, he went to Mount Cittakūṭa together with his retinue even as the great multitude looked on. From that time forth, the king [relied upon] the Great Being...
Desiring to see him, he remained watching the path for his arrival, thinking, "My friend will come today; my friend will come today.
At that time, the two younger swan chicks, the Mahāsatta’s younger brothers, consulted together, saying, "We shall race with the sun," and informed the Mahāsatta, "We wish to race with the sun.
[The Mahāsatta replied: "Dear ones, what is called 'the speed of the sun'..."
"You will not be able to race with the sun; you will perish along the way, so do not go!
Though they entreated him a second and a third time, the Bodhisatta likewise refused them up to three times.
Arrogant and unaware of their own strength, they disregarded the Great Being and thought, "We shall race with the sun."
Having set out while the sun had not yet risen, they sat upon the summit of Mount Yugandhara.
Not seeing them, the Great Being asked, "Where have they gone? Upon hearing what had occurred, he thought, "They will not be able to keep pace with the sun;
they will perish along the way. I shall grant them their lives. He too went and sat right there on the summit of Mount Yugandhara.
He sat down. Then, when the solar disc had risen, the young swans took flight and soared away together with the sun;
the Great Being also soared away with them. The younger brother flew until mid-morning and became exhausted;
it was as if fire were erupting from the joints of his wings. He gave a signal to the Bodhisatta: "Brother,..."
“I cannot,” he replied. Then the Great Being said to him, “Do not fear; I shall give you your life.
Encircling him with the web of his wings, he comforted him, led him to Mount Cittakūṭa, and placed him among the geese.
Then, flying up again, he reached the sun and set out together with the other. He too [remained] with the sun until nearly midday.
Having flown, he grew weary; it was as if a time of fire had broken out at the joints of his wings.
Then he gave a signal to the Bodhisatta, saying, "Brother, I am unable. The Great Being likewise comforted him and, taking him with the cage of his wings, went straight to Cittakūṭa.
At that moment, the sun reached the middle of the sky.
Then the Great Being, thinking, "Today I shall test the strength of my body," leaped with a single bound and sat upon the peak of Mount Yugandhara;
from there he sprang up again and reached the sun in a single bound, racing now before it and now behind it, and then reflected: "My racing alongside the sun is indeed useless."
“Born of improper attention, what use is this to me? Having gone to Bārāṇasī, I shall speak words appropriate to the purpose and appropriate to the Dhamma to my friend, the king.
Turning back, even before the sun had passed the meridian, he traveled all around the interior of the entire Cakkavāḷa, gradually diminishing his speed.
Having traveled throughout the entire land of Jambudīpa from one end to the other, he reached Bārāṇasī. The entire city, twelve yojanas in extent, appeared as if covered by swans;
no opening whatsoever could be discerned. Gradually, as his speed diminished, openings became visible in the sky.
The Great Being, slackening his pace, descended from the air and [landed] at the lion-window.

He stood in the place facing [the king]. The king, filled with joy at the thought, "My friend has arrived," prepared a golden seat for him to sit upon and, saying, "Friend, enter; sit here," he spoke the first verse:
"Alight right here, O swan; your sight is dear to me."
“You have arrived as the lord; declare what there is here.
In this context, “here” refers to the golden throne. “Nipata” means sit down.
“Issarosī” means you have come having become the lord and master of this place. “Yamidhatthi pavedaya” means that which exists in this dwelling—declare it.
“There is something; tell it to us without hesitation.

The Great Being sat down upon a golden throne. The king, having anointed the Great Being’s wings with oils refined a hundred and a thousand times, caused him to be served honeyed parched grain, sweet water, and sugar-water on a golden platter, and offered him a most pleasant welcome.
Having done so, he asked, "Friend, you have come alone; where did you go? He related the events in detail.
Then the king said to him, "Friend, show me too the speed of racing with the sun.
"Great King, it is not possible to show that speed," he replied. "In that case, show me at least something similar to it," the king said. "Very well," [he replied].
"Your Majesty, I shall show you a mere likeness; assemble archers who can hit a moving target. The king assembled them.

The Great Being took four archers, descended from his residence, had a stone pillar driven into the royal courtyard, had a bell tied to his own neck, and sitting atop the stone pillar, [he addressed] the four...
Having had the archers stand leaning against a pillar facing the four directions, he said:
"Great King, let these four men discharge four arrows simultaneously toward the four directions; before they reach the ground, I shall retrieve them and drop them at their feet.
You will know that I have gone to retrieve my arrows by the sound of the bell."
Having said, "You shall know me, but you will not see me," he brought back the arrows shot by them all at once,
dropped them at their feet, and while remaining seated right there on top of the stone pillar, he showed himself to them, saying, "Great King, you have seen my speed.
Then he added, "Great King, this speed of mine is neither supreme nor middling."
“Great King, our speed is limited and inferior; such is our swiftness,” he said.
Then the king asked him, “Friend, is there any other speed swifter than yours?
“Yes, Great King; compared to our supreme speed, theirs is a hundredfold, a thousandfold, and a hundred-thousandfold.”
"The life-formations of beings waste away and break up more swiftly;
they go to destruction"—thus he showed the cessation of material phenomena by way of momentary cessation, and thereafter that of mental phenomena.
Having heard the Great Being’s words, the king, terrified by the fear of death and unable to maintain his mindfulness, fell to the ground; the great multitude was struck with alarm.
The water reached [the king’s face]. Having sprinkled the king’s face with water, he caused him to regain consciousness. Then the Great Being exhorted him, saying: “Great King, do not fear;
cultivate mindfulness of death; practice the Dhamma; perform meritorious deeds such as giving; be heedful, O Deva. Then the king said:
“Master, we have been taught by a teacher endowed with wisdom-power such as yours...”
“We shall not be able to live without you. Please do not go to Cittakūṭa, but remain right here as my preceptor and teacher, teaching me the Dhamma.
Thus entreating him, he spoke two verses:
“By merely hearing of one, people become dear; but upon seeing another, desire is extinguished.
"Having seen and heard you, you have become dear to me; I hope you are indeed dear to me by the very sight of you.
"You are dear to me by hearing, and even more so by coming into my sight;
thus, being so dear to behold, dwell near me, O swan!"
The meaning of this is as follows: O King of Swans, through hearing, some people become dear to others;
having heard that "he possesses such virtues," one loves them because of what has been heard. However, for some, upon merely seeing others, their desire vanishes and their affection disappears;
they appear like *yakkhas* who have come to devour them. For yet others, it occurs in both ways—both by seeing and by hearing.
"You are dear; therefore I ask you this: 'Do you indeed delight in seeing me? means: "Do you perhaps love me?
But you were already dear to me by hearing of me; now that you have come to see me, you are even more dear.
Thus, being one whose sight is so dear to me, do not go to Cittakūṭa, but dwell here in my presence.
The Bodhisatta said:
"We shall dwell in your house, always honored and worshipped;
but once, when I am intoxicated, cook the king of swans for me."

"In this regard, O Great King, although we dwell in your house constantly honored, there may come a time when you, intoxicated by liquor, say for the sake of eating meat, 'Cook the king of swans for me.
Then your dependents might kill and cook me; what then shall I do?"
Then the king, thinking, "In that case, I shall not drink liquor at all," spoke this verse to give his promise:
"Fie on that drinking of liquor, which is dearer to me than you!
And I shall not drink liquor as long as you dwell in my house."
Thereafter, the Bodhisatta spoke these six verses:
“The cries of jackals and the calls of birds are easy to understand;
but the speech of humans, O King, is even more difficult to discern than that.”
“Even if a person thinks, ‘He is my kinsman,’ or ‘He is my friend,’ or ‘He is my companion’—
one who was previously well-disposed but later turns into an enemy.
He in whom the mind takes delight is not far away, even if he is close at hand.”
For he is far away even though near, in whom the mind does not enter.
He is near even though across the ocean, if his heart is serene;
he is far away even though across the ocean, if his heart is corrupt.
“Those who dwell together, O bull among chariot-warriors, end up living apart in different directions;
but the virtuous dwell far apart, yet remain close in mind, O increaser of the kingdom.
Through dwelling together for too long, even a loved one becomes disliked.”
"Indeed, we shall go to you, before we become unpleasant to you.
In this context, O Great King, "the cry" refers to animals whose hearts are straightforward; therefore, their cry is easy to understand.
But humans are harsh, and thus their speech is more difficult to understand—this is the meaning. "Who previously... refers to whoever...
A person, having first become delighted and thinking, "You are my kinsman, my friend, as dear to me as my own life, my companion," might even imagine this;
yet later, that very same person becomes a stranger or an enemy. Thus, indeed, the human heart is difficult to know.
It settles, O Great King: in whichever person the mind settles through affection, that person, though dwelling far away, is not distant.
"Even dwelling together is indeed called 'dwelling' [only in name]. But that person in whom the mind does not settle and departs—even though he dwells nearby, he is far away.
He is truly 'within,' O Great King, who is a friend with a clear heart; because he is joined by the mind, even though he dwells on the other side of the ocean, he is indeed within.
But he whose heart is corrupted—because he is not joined by the mind—even though he dwells within..."
"Across the ocean" means: those who are enemies and adversaries, even if they dwell together, are said to dwell far away;
but the virtuous and wise, though standing at a distance, dwell as if together when they attend upon them with a mind developed through loving-kindness (*mettā*).
"Before we become such" means: "As long as we are not yet your enemies, let us depart after addressing you."
Then the king said to him:
“If you do not acknowledge the salutation of those who thus entreat you,
and if you do not follow the words of us hundreds of attendants;”
"Thus we entreat you; please act accordingly.

In this context, "thus" means: O King of Swans, if you do not perceive this salutation of ours as we entreat you with palms joined, and if you do not heed the words of us who are your attendants, then we entreat you in this manner.
"Make it so that you come here again from time to time; turn back for the sake of returning here"—this is the meaning.
Then the Bodhisatta said:
"If we dwell in this manner, there shall be no obstacle."
"And may you too, O Great King, and I, O Increaser of the Realm, perhaps meet again at the passing of days and nights.
Therein, "If it should be so, O Great King," means: do not worry, if there should be no obstacle to our lives while we are dwelling thus.
"I shall not remain; perhaps we might yet see one another.

Furthermore, having placed the very counsel given by me in my stead, you should—being heedful in this transient worldly existence—perform meritorious deeds such as giving, and rule the kingdom righteously without violating the ten duties of a king. For it is by acting according to my counsel that..."
"He will surely see me. Having thus exhorted the king, the Great Being went back to Mount Cittakūṭa.

The Teacher, having delivered this Dhamma teaching, said: "Thus, monks, even when born in the animal realm in the past, I taught the Dhamma by demonstrating the frailty of the life-faculties," and he identified the Jātaka.
“Then King Ānanda was [the king], Moggallāna the youngest, Sāriputta the middle one,
the rest of the flock of swans were the Buddha’s retinue, and I myself was the swift swan.
This is the third commentary on the Javanahaṃsa Jātaka.
[477] 4. The Commentary on the Cūḷanāradajātakaya.
“Those logs were not split,” the Teacher said while residing at Jetavana, concerning the seduction of a young woman.
It is said that there was a daughter of a certain family living in Sāvatthī who was fifteen or sixteen years of age.
She attained great beauty, yet no one restrained her. Then her mother thought: "My daughter has reached maturity, yet no one restrains her.
Like a fish enticed by bait, I shall seduce a certain Śākyan bhikkhu with worldly goods, cause him to leave the order, and live depending upon him.
At that time, there was a son of good family living in Sāvatthī who, in the Dispensation...

Having given his heart [to the world] and gone forth, from the time of his full ordination (*upasampadā*), he abandoned the desire for training and lived indolently, devoted to the adornment of his body.
The Great Laywoman (Mahā-upāsikā), having prepared rice gruel, hard food, and soft food at home, stood at the door;
she was able to capture one particular monk as he walked along the street, binding him with the craving for flavors.
While searching, she saw no one worthy of being taken among those who were traveling with a great retinue as holders of the Tripitaka,

the Abhidhamma, and the Vinaya; nor did she see anyone among those walking behind them who were sweet speakers of the Dhamma and alms-collectors resembling fresh rain-clouds— until finally, she reached the very edge of the outskirts.
Having seen him approaching— his eyes anointed, his hair smoothed down, wearing a lower garment of fine dukūla cloth, clad in a robe polished and burnished,
carrying a bowl the color of a jewel, holding a beautiful parasol, with his senses relaxed and his body full of vigor—
the king thought, "It is possible to capture him. He went forward, paid homage, took the bowl, and said, "Come, venerable sir."
Having brought him home, made him sit down, and served him with rice gruel and other foods, she said to the bhikkhu who had finished his meal, "Venerable sir, from now on, please come here.
From that time forth, he went there regularly and later became a trusted friend.
Then one day, the Great Laywoman stood within his hearing and said, "In this house, the amount of enjoyments and requisites..."
"But there is no son or son-in-law of mine capable of managing the household," she said.
Upon hearing her words, he felt as if his heart were slightly pierced, wondering, "For what purpose does she speak thus?
She then said to her daughter, "Entice him and bring him under your control. From that time on, she adorned and beautified herself.
She tempted him with feminine gestures and charms. Regarding the term "stout maiden" (*thullakumārikā*): it should not be understood as referring to one who has a corpulent body;
whether she be stout or lean, she is called a "stout maiden" because of her stoutness of passion for the five strands of sensual pleasure.
That youth, falling under the sway of defilements, thought, "I will no longer be able to remain established in the Buddha’s teaching."
Having reflected thus, he said, "I will go to such-and-such a place;

when I have gone to the monastery and handed over my bowl and robes, please send me some clothes there. Having spoken, he went to the monastery, handed over his bowl and robes, and told his teacher and preceptor, "I am weary of the religious life.
They took him and led him into the presence of the Teacher, saying, "This monk is weary."

They reported this to the Teacher. The Teacher asked, “Is it true, monk, that you are weary of the religious life? When he replied, “It is true, Venerable Sir,” the Teacher said, “By whom have you been made weary?

When he replied, “By a young woman of great stature, Venerable Sir,” the Teacher said, “Monk, previously, while you were living in the forest, she created an obstacle to your holy life and brought you great harm; yet again, you—”
Having said, “Why are you dissatisfied, relying on this very [life]? he was requested by the monks to relate a past event.
In the past, while Brahmadatta was ruling in Bārāṇasī, the Bodhisatta was reborn into a wealthy brahmin family in the kingdom of Kāsi.
Having mastered the arts, he established a household; then his wife gave birth to a son.
He passed away. He thought, "Just as death has come for my beloved wife, so too will it come for me; what is the use of this household life?
I shall go forth. Having abandoned sensual pleasures and taking his son with him, he entered the Himalayas.

Together with him, he went forth into the ascetic life of a seer (*isipabbajjā*), developed the meditative absorptions (*jhāna*) and direct knowledges (*abhiññā*), and lived in the forest subsisting on roots and fruits.

He dwelt there. At that time, bandits living in the border regions entered the countryside, plundered a village, seized the tax-collectors, and having made them carry their bundles, they returned to the borderlands.
Among them was a beautiful young woman endowed with cunning intelligence, who thought: "They will take us and enjoy us as slave-possessions."
"It would be better to escape by some means. She said, "Husband, I wish to attend to my bodily needs;
please step back a little and wait," and having thus deceived the robbers, she fled. As she entered the forest, she left the Bodhisatta’s son in the hermitage;
then, when he had gone out for fruit, she reached that hermitage in the morning and [approached] him.
Having enticed the young ascetic with sensual pleasures and violated his virtue, she brought him under her control and said, "What is the use of your dwelling in the forest?
Come, let us go and live in the village; for there, the objects of desire such as forms and so forth are easily obtained.
He agreed, saying, "Very well," and added, "My father has gone from the forest to gather fruits."
"Having seen him, we both shall go together," he said.
She thought: "This young boy knows nothing; however, his father must have gone forth into homelessness when he was old.
When he comes, he will beat me, saying 'What are you doing here?', seize me by the feet, drag me away, and [leave me] in the forest."
“He will throw it; before he arrives, I shall flee. Then, saying to him, “I will go on ahead;
you should follow behind,” and having pointed out the way, he departed. From the moment she had gone, he was overcome with dejection;
without performing any of his former duties, he covered his head with his upper robe and remained inside the leaf-hut.
She lay down lost in thought. The Great Being, having brought various fruits and returned, saw the footprints of that woman;
thinking, "These are the footprints of a woman; my son’s virtue must have been broken," he entered the leaf-hut, set down the fruits, and asked his son, speaking the first verse:
“You have not split your wood, nor have you brought water;
you have not even tended your fire—why do you burn like one who is dull-witted?
In this context, “you have not even tended your fire” means you have not kindled your fire. “Like one who is dull-witted” means like one devoid of wisdom, like a blind fool.
Having heard his father’s words, he rose, paid homage to his father, and, out of reverence, spoke these two verses to express his lack of enthusiasm for dwelling in the forest:
“I am not able to dwell in the forest; I beg you, Kassapa, [to grant me leave].
Dwelling in the wilderness is painful; I wish to go to the kingdom.”
“‘Just as I, having gone from here to whatever country I dwell in, might train in proper conduct (*ācāra*), O Brahmā—teach me that Dhamma.
In this context, ‘I address you, Kassapa’ means I call out to you, Kassapa. ‘Gantave’ means to go. ‘Ācāraṃ’ [means proper conduct].”
"Wherever I dwell, while living there, may you instruct and advise me so that I may train in and understand the proper conduct and customs of that country," he said.
The Great Being replied, "Very well, dear son, I shall tell you the local customs," and spoke these two verses:
“If, having left the wilderness and its roots and fruits, you prefer to dwell in the kingdom, then listen to this Dhamma from me:
Do not consume poison; avoid the precipice.”
"Do not sink in the mud, and proceed with caution toward the venomous snake.
In this context, "the Dhamma" means: if you find pleasure in living in a kingdom, then you must observe the Dhamma that constitutes the conduct of the country.
"Proceed with caution toward the venomous snake" means: one should move about alert and prepared in the presence of a venomous snake, being able to deal with the venomous snake.
"You should avoid it"—this is the meaning.
Not understanding the meaning of what was spoken in brief, the young ascetic asked:
"What indeed is poison, or a precipice, or a swamp for those living the holy life?"
“Whom do you call a venomous snake? Tell me that when asked.
The other explained it to him:
“O dear one, in this world, ‘āsava’ is called by the name ‘surā’ (liquor).”
"Charming, fragrant, and lovely, sweet as a small dose of ghee—
yet the Noble Ones call it poison, O Nārada, in regard to the holy life.
'Women in this world, my dear, overwhelm one who is heedless.'"
They carry away the mind of the young man, as the wind carries away a loose tuft of cotton.
This, O Nārada, is declared to be a precipice for the holy life:
gain, fame, honor, and worship from the families of others.
And this, O Nārada, is declared to be the mire of the holy life:
"O dear one, kings with their armies dwell upon this earth;
they, O dear Nārada, are such great lords of men."
“One should not walk at the feet of lords or masters;
O Nārada, he is declared to be like a venomous serpent for one living the holy life (brahmacariya).
When one approaches a house at mealtime for the sake of food,”
Whatever wholesome there may be here, one should know that, and therein seek food for sustenance.
Having entered another’s family for the sake of drink or food,
one should eat in moderation and consume in moderation, and should not set the mind on forms.

“Gambling, liquor, and trade, the assembly hall, and frivolous diversions—avoid these from afar, as one would a dangerous path. In this context, *āsava* refers to fermented drinks such as *pupphāsava*.
Regarding the phrase “they call it poison,” the Noble Ones [regard] that liquor known as *āsava* as [the destruction of] the holy life (*brahmacariya*).
"Visa" means they speak [of it]. "Pamatta" means one who is muddled in mindfulness. "Like cotton blown away" means like cotton that has fallen after being scattered from a tree.
"Akkhāta" means proclaimed by the Buddha and others. "Silo" means fame and praise. "Sakkāra" means such things as the performance of reverential salutations.
"Pūjā" means worship with perfumes, garlands, and so forth. "Paṅka" is called "mud" in the sense of causing one to sink. "Mahanta" means great.
"Having attained greatness": "One should not walk at their feet" means one should not walk in their presence;
the sense is that one should not become a courtier of kings. For kings, like venomous snakes, may become angry in an instant and bring about ruin and disaster.
Furthermore, the meaning here should also be understood by way of the dangers previously mentioned regarding entering the royal harem.

"Bhattattho" means being one who has need of food. "Yadettha kusalaṃ" means that among those houses which are to be approached, whatever you know to be wholesome, blameless, and free from the five improper resorts—that is where you should go for alms;
this is the meaning. "Na ca rūpe manaṃ kare" means that even while eating food in another's family, having known the proper measure, you should not set your mind on the appearance [of the food].
"Do not set your mind on the form of a woman; do not open your eyes and seize upon the sign of a woman's form"—thus he says.
Regarding the phrase "goṭṭhaṃ majjaṃ kirāṭaṃ," this is the reading found in the manuscripts;
however, in the Aṭṭhakathā, having stated "goṭṭhaṃ majjaṃ kirāsañca," it explains: "Goṭṭha means a place where cattle stand. Majja means a tavern. Kirāsa..."

It is said, "wicked people and those who frequent brothels. "Assemblies and places for scattering gold and silver" refers to both social gatherings and locations where gold and silver coins are strewn about.
"From afar" means one should avoid all of these from a distance. "Just as if" is like one traveling by means of a vehicle carrying ghee or oil avoiding a rugged path.
While his father was still speaking, the young man regained his mindfulness and said, "Father, enough for me with the path of men.

Then his father explained to him the cultivation of loving-kindness and the other [immeasurables]. Abiding by that instruction, he soon produced the meditative absorptions (jhāna) and the higher knowledges (abhiññā).
Both father and son, without falling away from their meditative attainments, passed away and were reborn in the Brahma-world.

Having delivered this teaching on the Dhamma, the Teacher identified the Jātaka: “At that time, the young girl was this very girl; the ascetic youth was the discontented bhikkhu; and the father was none other than myself.
The Explanation of the Cūḷanāradajātakavaṇṇanā, the fourth.
[478] 5. The Explanation of the Dūtajātakavaṇṇanā.
“O Brahmin, we shall send a messenger to you. This was said by the Teacher while dwelling at Jetavana, concerning his own praise of wisdom.
In the Hall of Truth, the monks initiated a discussion: “See, friends, the skill in means of the One of Ten Powers!
Having shown the host of celestial nymphs to Nanda, the son of the Sakyans, he bestowed upon him the state of an Arahant; and to Cūḷapanthaka...”
“Having given a small cloth, he bestowed Arahatship along with the analytical knowledges; having shown a lotus to the smith’s son, he bestowed Arahatship.
Thus, by various means, he disciplines sentient beings. The Teacher approached and asked, “Monks, about what discussion are you gathered here now?
When they replied, “About this very one,” he said, “Monks, it is not only now that the Tathāgata...”
"Having said, 'He is skilled in means even now, thinking "by this, that comes about," he was indeed skilled in means in the past as well," he related a story of the past.
In the past, while Brahmadatta was ruling in Bārāṇasī, the countryside became destitute of gold.
For he oppressed the countryside and gathered only wealth. At that time, the Bodhisatta was reborn in a brahmin family in a village of Kāsī, and having reached maturity—
Having gone to Takkasilā and said, "Afterwards, I shall wander for alms in accordance with the Dhamma and bring back the teacher's fee," he began his craft.
Once he had completed his training and received his certificate of proficiency, he asked permission, saying, "Teacher, I shall bring you your fee.
Departing from there, he wandered through the countryside, seeking [wealth] righteously and justly, and having obtained seven coins, he returned.
Thinking, "I will give it to my teacher," he set out on his way and boarded a boat to cross the Ganges.
While the boat was tossing about there, that gold fell into the water. He thought, "Gold is difficult to obtain;
if I were to search for my teacher’s wealth again in the countryside, there would be much delay. What if I were to [dispose of it] right here on the bank of the Ganges?"
“I shall sit without food; gradually the king will learn of my sitting there, and then he will dispatch his ministers.
I will not consult with them, so the king himself will come.
By this means, I shall obtain the teacher’s fee from him. Thus, having wrapped his upper garment on the bank of the Ganges, [he took] the sacrificial thread...
Leaving the area outside, he sat upon the sand, which was the color of a silver plate, like a golden statue.
Seeing him sitting there without food, the great multitude asked, "Why are you sitting here? but he did not speak to anyone.
On the following day, the inhabitants of the neighboring village, having heard that he was sitting there, came and questioned him, yet he did not speak to them either.
Seeing his exhaustion, they departed while lamenting. On the third day, the city dwellers arrived;
on the fourth day, the prominent people from the city; on the fifth day, the king’s men.
On the sixth day, the king sent his ministers, yet he did not speak with them either. On the seventh day, the king, overcome by fear, approached him.
Having approached him and questioning him, he spoke the first verse:
“O Brahmā, I sent messengers to you while you were meditating on the bank of the Gaṅgā;
when questioned, you did not explain to them—was suffering a secret doctrine to you?”

In that context, "Is this suffering of yours considered secret? means: "O Brahmin, is this suffering that has arisen for you considered by you to be a secret, such that it should not be told to anyone else?
Having heard this, the Great Being said, "Great King, suffering should indeed be told only to one capable of removing it, and not to anyone else," and he spoke these seven verses:
"If suffering should arise for you, O increaser of the kingdom of Kāsi..."
"Do not tell it to one who will not release you from suffering. But to one who might,
by means of the Dhamma, release even a single part of that mass of suffering, you may certainly reveal it to him."
“O King, the cries of jackals and the calls of birds are easy to understand,
but the speech of humans is even more difficult to discern than that.
Even if a person thinks, ‘He is my relative,’ or ‘He is my friend,’ or ‘He is my companion’...”
“He who, having been well-disposed before, later becomes otherwise; that person who,
when questioned about his own suffering, proclaims it at an improper time—
his friends rejoice, for they wish him well, yet they themselves become sorrowful because of his suffering.”
“Having recognized the right time for such a person, and knowing the wise man to be single-minded,
the steadfast one should speak of the intense matters of another, releasing speech that is gentle and meaningful.
And if he should know it to be beyond his own capacity— that it would not lead to his own happiness— then he should remain silent.”
"Alone, the wise man should endure even intense pains, for he regards truth, shame, and moral dread.
In this context, "if it should arise for you" means if it should happen to you. "Do not speak" means do not say it.
"Harder to discern than that" means harder to discern even than the urinating of animals; therefore, for one who is unable to carry it away without knowing it as it truly is—
"One should certainly not speak of one's own suffering. Furthermore, the meaning of the verse beginning with "Api ca" has already been explained.
"Anāpuṭṭho" means asked again and again. "Pavedaye" means tells. "Akālarūpe" means at an improper time. "Kālaṃ" means the proper time for telling one's secret.
"Tathāvidhassa" means that having recognized a wise person as being of one mind with oneself, one should disclose it to such a person. "Tibbāni" means intense sufferings.
“Saceti” means: if one should know that one’s own suffering is unbearable, or that it cannot be remedied by human effort—either for oneself or for others.
“Te hi” means those very same worldly conventions; the meaning is “the eight worldly conditions. This is what is intended:
now, this worldly convention has not arisen solely for my own sake to bring about happiness, [for] I am not liberated from the eight worldly conditions.
Since there is no such thing [as a permanent self], when this is the case, it is not fitting for one who aspires only to happiness to inflict suffering upon another;
this is not something to be done by one endowed with moral shame (*hirī*) and dread of blame (*ottappa*).

Thinking, "I possess moral shame and dread of blame," and thus regarding the moral shame and dread of blame truly existing within oneself, a wise person should endure even intense sufferings alone, without telling anyone else.
Having thus taught the Dhamma to the king with seven verses, the Great Being spoke four verses, showing how he was seeking the teacher’s fee:
“Wandering through the kingdom, through market towns and royal capitals,
I beg for alms, O Great King, desiring wealth for my teacher.”
“Householders, royal officers, and great householders who were brahmins,
O lord of men— I received from them seven coins of gold,
O Great King; those have been lost to me, and therefore I grieve intensely.”
“Those men, O Great King, were merely conceived in my mind;
they were not capable of liberating one from suffering, and therefore I did not speak of them.
But you, O Great King, were indeed conceived in my mind.”
“It is sufficient to liberate one from suffering; therefore, I have declared this to you.
In that context, “wandering for alms” means begging from these householders and others. “Those seven coins of mine” refers to those seven coins which were lost while I was crossing the Ganges;
they fell into the Ganges. “Those men,” O Great King, are your messenger-men. “Considered” means...
“I knew, ‘These are not able to free me from suffering. Therefore—for that reason—I did not disclose my own suffering to them.
He related [this] by saying “pavedayiṃ” (I told).

Having heard his discourse on the Dhamma, the king said, “Do not worry, brahmin; I shall give you the teacher’s fee,” and he gave him double the wealth. To clarify this matter, the Teacher spoke the concluding verse:
“Out of faith in him, the prosperer of the kingdom of Kāsi gave fourteen deposits of gold in chests made of *jātarūpa*.
Regarding that, “in chests made of *jātarūpa*” means he gave those fourteen deposits of gold in chests made specifically of *jātarūpa*, not in chests of just any kind of gold.

The Great Being, having given counsel to the king and having given wealth to his teacher, performed meritorious deeds such as giving alms; the king also, abiding by that counsel, ruled the kingdom righteously, and both went according to their respective karma.
Having delivered this teaching on the Dhamma, the Teacher said, "Monks, it is not only now, but in the past as well, that the Tathāgata was skilled in means," and he identified the Jātaka:
"At that time, the king was Ānanda, the teacher was Sāriputta, and the brahmin youth was [the Buddha himself]."
"But I myself was he.
The fifth *Dūta-jātaka* commentary.
[479] 6. The commentary on the *Kāliṅga-bodhi-jātaka*.
"King Kāliṅga was a wheel-turning monarch"—this the Teacher related while dwelling at Jetavana, concerning the great worship of the Bodhi tree performed by the Elder Ānanda.

For when the Tathāgata had set out on a tour of the countryside for the sake of gathering those who were ready to be trained, the inhabitants of Sāvatthī, carrying perfumes, garlands, and other offerings, went to Jetavana;
finding no other place worthy of worship, they stood at the door of the Perfumed Chamber.

Having trampled it down, they depart, and thus they do not experience sublime joy. Knowing this reason, when the Tathāgata had arrived at Jetavana, Anāthapiṇḍika went to the presence of the Venerable Ānanda and said:
"Venerable sir, while the Tathāgata has gone on his alms-round, this monastery remains without support; it is not a place for people to honor with perfumes, garlands, and the like."
“It would be well, Bhante, if you would inform the Tathāgata of this matter and let us know whether it is possible for there to be a single place worthy of veneration,” he said.
Having agreed, saying “Very well,” he asked the Tathāgata, “Bhante, how many shrines (cetiyas) are there?
“Three, Ānanda,” [the Buddha replied]. “Which three, Bhante? “The bodily relic, the use-relic, and the commemorative relic.”
“An offering,” he said. “But, Bhante, would it be possible to build a shrine while you yourselves are still living?
“Ānanda, it is not possible to build one with bodily relics, for that occurs at the time of the Buddhas’ final nibbāna.
An offering is baseless and consists merely of a mental dedication; even while the Buddhas are still living, the Great Bodhi tree is already enjoyed by the Buddhas.”
“...the shrine itself. “Venerable sir, when you have departed, the Jetavana monastery will be without a refuge; the great multitude will not have a place of worship.
I shall bring a seed from the Great Bodhi tree and plant it at the gate of Jetavana, venerable sir.
“Very well, Ānanda, plant it; if this is done, my residence in Jetavana will be as if constant.”
The Elder informed King Pasenadi of Kosala, Anāthapiṇḍika, Visākhā, and the others;

then, having had a pit dug at the gate of Jetavana at the place where the Bodhi tree was to be planted, he said to the Elder Mahāmoggallāna: "Venerable sir, I shall plant the Bodhi tree at the gate of Jetavana;
please bring me a branch from the Great Bodhi tree. The Elder consented, saying, "Very well."
Having traveled through the air to the seat of enlightenment (bodhimaṇḍa), he caught with his robe the ripe fruit as it was falling from its stalk before it had even reached the ground;
taking it, he gave it to the Elder Ānanda. The Elder Ānanda, thinking, "Today we shall plant the Bodhi tree," announced this to the King of Kosala and others.
At the time of evening, the King, accompanied by a great retinue and all necessary requisites, [set out].
Having had it dug out, they returned; likewise did Anāthapiṇḍika, Visākhā, and other faithful people.

At the site for planting the Great Bodhi tree, the Elder placed a large golden basin, made a hole at the bottom, filled it with fragrant mud, and gave it to the King, saying, "Plant this Bodhi seed, O Great King. He thought, "Kingship does not last forever..."
"It remains in our hands; it is fitting that this be planted by me, Anāthapiṇḍika.
He placed that Bodhi-branch into the hands of the Great Merchant. Anāthapiṇḍika, having cleared away the fragrant mud, set it down there.
At the very moment it was released from his hand, while everyone was looking on, it grew to the size of a plow-handle.
The Bodhi trunk rose up fifty cubits in height, and five great branches—extending in the four directions as well as upward—each emerged fifty cubits long.
Thus, at that very moment, it stood having become the eldest of forest trees.
The king, having filled eighteen vessels of gold and silver with scented water and adorned them with blue lotuses, handfuls of jasmine, and other flowers, [presented them].
Having surrounded the Great Bodhi tree, he placed full jars in a row;
he had a railing made of the seven precious gems constructed, scattered sand mixed with gold, built a surrounding wall, and erected a gateway pavilion made of the seven precious gems;
the honor shown was great.

The Elder approached the Tathāgata and said, "Venerable Sir, please enter the meditative attainment you entered at the foot of the Great Bodhi tree while sitting at the foot of the Bodhi tree I have planted for the benefit of the great multitude. "Ānanda, what are you saying?
While I was seated having entered that meditative attainment at the foot of the Great Bodhi tree, another location—"

“I am unable to sustain it. “Venerable sir, for the benefit of the great multitude, please enjoy this site of the Bodhi tree through the bliss of meditative attainment (samāpatti) according to a fixed schedule.
The Teacher enjoyed it through the bliss of meditative attainment for one night.
The Elder, having explained this to the King of Kosala and others, established what is known as the Bodhi Festival. That Bodhi tree as well—
Because it was planted by the Elder Ānanda, it became known as the Ānanda Bodhi. At that time, the monks in the Dhamma Hall began a discussion:
"Friends, while the Tathāgata was still living, the Venerable Ānanda planted the Bodhi tree and performed a great festival of worship;
oh, how great are the virtues of this Elder! The Teacher approached and asked: "Monks, what is the subject of your discussion just now?"
Having asked, "Are you sitting together? and being told, "Indeed we are," he said, "Monks, it is not only now;

in the past as well, Ānanda, having taken people from the four great continents along with their retinues and brought many perfumes, garlands, and other offerings, caused a festival for the Bodhi tree to be held at the Great Seat of Enlightenment (Mahābodhimaṇḍa).
Having said this, he related a story of the past.
In the past, in the city of Dantapura in the kingdom of Kaliṅga, a king named Kāliṅga reigned.
He had two sons, Mahākāliṅga and Cūḷakāliṅga. The fortune-tellers declared, "The elder son shall rule the kingdom after his father’s passing;
however, the younger son shall go forth as an ascetic and wander for alms, while his son [the grandson] shall become a wheel-turning monarch."
"He will become one," they prophesied. Later, when the father passed away, the eldest son became king, while the younger was made viceroy.
Thinking, "My son shall indeed become a wheel-turning monarch (cakravartin)," the viceroy became arrogant on account of his son.
The king, unable to endure this, commanded an attendant: "Go and seize Cūḷakāliṅga. He went and said, "Prince,..."
The king, wishing to have him seized, said, "Save your own life! He showed his seal-ring, a fine woolen blanket,
and a sword— these three items— to the minister who served him, saying, "By this token,
you should grant the kingdom to my son," and having spoken thus, he entered the forest and established a hermitage on a delightful spot of ground.
Having undertaken the ascetic life of an *isi*, he went forth and made his dwelling on the bank of a river.
In the kingdom of Madda, at the city of Sāgala, the chief queen of King Madda gave birth to a daughter. The fortune-tellers prophesied concerning her:
"She will sustain herself by wandering for alms, but her son shall become a universal monarch (*cakkavattī*)."
When the kings throughout the entire land of Jambudīpa heard this news, they arrived all at once and besieged the city of Sāgala.
King Madda thought to himself, "If I give her to one, the other kings will be enraged; I must protect my daughter.
Taking his daughter and his wife, he fled in disguise, entered the forest, and...
Having established a hermitage on the upper slopes above the hermitage of Prince Cūḷakāliṅga, she went forth and dwelt there, sustaining herself by the practice of gleaning.
Her parents, thinking, "We must protect our daughter," left her at that hermitage and departed to gather various fruits.
While they were away, she gathered various flowers and fashioned a flower-cushion.
There was a single mango tree in full bloom that had grown like a flight of stairs built on the bank of the Ganges;
having climbed it and played there, he threw a flower cushion into the water. One day, it became caught on the head of Prince Cūḷakāliṅga as he was bathing in the Ganges.
Seeing it, he thought, "This was made by a certain woman, and not..."
Thinking, "This is the deed of an old woman; let me first test her," he went upstream along the Ganges out of defilement.
There, having sat upon an *amba* tree while she was singing with a sweet voice, he heard her sound.
Going to the foot of the tree and seeing her, he said, "Bhadde, what is your name? She replied, "I am a human woman, my lord."
“Then come down,” he said. “I cannot, sir; I am a kṣatriya. “My dear lady, I too am indeed a kṣatriya; come down.
“Sir, one does not become a kṣatriya by mere words. If you are a kṣatriya, speak the kṣatriya’s manner.
So they both spoke the kṣatriya’s manner to one another. Then the princess descended.

They committed misconduct with one another. When her parents arrived, she told them in detail about his being the son of King Kāliṅga and the reason for entering the forest. They accepted this, saying, "Very well," and gave her to him.
As they lived together in mutual affection, the princess conceived, and after the lapse of ten months—
She gave birth to a son endowed with the marks of grain and merit, and they named him Kāliṅga.
When he reached maturity, he attained perfection in all the arts under his father and grandfather.
Then, his father, having learned through the conjunction of the stars that his brother had passed away, said: "Dear son, do not dwell in the forest; your paternal uncle Mahākāliṅga has died."
"Go to the city of Dantapura and seize the entire kingdom belonging to your family," he said;

and having given him the seal-ring, the blanket, and the sword that he himself had brought, he added, "Dear son, in the city of Dantapura, on such-and-such a street, there is a minister who is our benefactor;
descend into the middle of his bedchamber and [leave] these three jewels with him."
"Show him and declare that he is my son; he will establish you in the kingdom," he instructed.
Having paid homage to his parents and his paternal grandparents, he traveled through the air by means of the great power of his merit.
Alighting right upon the back of the minister’s bed, when asked, "Who are you? he declared, "I am the son of Cūḷakāliṅga," and [presented] those jewels.
He showed it [to the king]. The minister announced it to the royal assembly. The ministers had the city decorated and raised a white parasol over him.
Then his family priest, named Kāliṅga-Bhāradvāja, explained to him the ten duties of a wheel-turning monarch (*cakravartin*).
He fulfilled those duties. Then, on the fifteenth day of the observance (*upoṣatha*), from the Cakkadaha lake, the Wheel-Treasure appeared; and from the Uposatha household...

The elephant-treasure arrived from the Valāhaka lineage, the horse-treasure from Mount Vepulla, and the jewel-treasure from Mount Vepulla; the woman-treasure, the householder-treasure, and the counselor-treasure appeared as well.

Having taken possession of the sovereignty over the entire interior of the Cakkavāḷa, one day, surrounded by a retinue thirty-six yojanas in extent, he mounted a pure white elephant resembling the peak of Mount Kelāsa and proceeded with great majesty and splendor.
He set out toward his parents. Then, above the Great Seat of Enlightenment—the Mahābodhimaṇḍa, which is the navel of the earth and the place of victory for all Buddhas—the Nāga was unable to proceed.
Although the king urged him again and again, he simply could not go.
To clarify this matter, the Teacher spoke the first verse:
“The Kalinga king, a wheel-turning monarch, ruling the earth with righteousness, approached the vicinity of the Bodhi tree by means of a majestic elephant.
Then the king’s domestic priest, traveling together with the king, thought: “There is no obstruction in the sky; what indeed—”

The king was unable to send forth his elephant; thinking, "I shall investigate," he descended from the sky and beheld a portion of ground that had become like the navel of the earth, serving as the victory throne for all Buddhas.
At that time, it is said, in a space measuring eighteen royal karīsas, there was not even a blade of grass the size of a hair, and sand with the color of silver plates was strewn about.
The grasses, creepers, and forest trees on all sides circumambulated the seat of enlightenment (bodhimaṇḍa) clockwise, revolved around it, and stood facing toward the seat of enlightenment.
The brahmin, looking at that spot of ground, thought, "This is indeed the place where all Buddhas have shattered all defilements;
even by Sakka and the other gods, it is not possible to go above this. Having reflected thus, he went into the presence of King Kāliṅga.
Having praised the seat of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*), he said to the king, "Descend. To clarify this matter, the Teacher spoke these verses:
"Kāliṅga and Bhāradvāja, having escorted King Kāliṅga—the low-born ascetic—as he set the Wheel of Dharma in motion, spoke thus with palms joined in reverence:"
“Descend, Great King, for this ground has been made level by the ascetic.
Here, the Buddhas, the unsurpassed ones, having attained full enlightenment, shine forth.
On this ground, the grasses and creepers turn to the right.”
“The essence [of the earth] is at the navel of the earth; thus we have heard in the mantras, O Great King:
‘Of this earth that supports all beings, bounded by the ocean, this is the very center;
having descended there, pay homage.’”
“Those who are called ‘nāgas’ and those who are high-born elephants—
by this much alone, these [ordinary] nāgas do not even reach their status.
A high-born nāga may, at will, send forth a tusker elephant.”
"To this extent, O Nāga, it is possible for you to approach this place.
