Having heard that, the Kāliṅga king, having reflected upon the words of the fortune-teller, dispatched the Nāga, thinking:
"We shall find out whether this statement of his is true or not."
“Having been struck by the king, the elephant, trumpeting like a crane, turned back and sat down, unable to bear the heavy burden, as if it were a weight.
In this context, *samaṇakolañña* means the son of the ascetics (*tāpasa*). *Cakkaṃ vattayanto* means while turning the wheel.
"Cakkavatti" means a wheel-turner. "Having encompassed" means having examined the portion of ground. "Exalted by recluses" means praised by all the Buddhas.
"Incomparable" means peerless and immeasurable. "Shining" means that, with all the darkness of the defilements dispelled, they shine while seated here like the young sun.
"Grass and creepers" means both grasses and climbing plants. "The circle" [refers to] the area measuring two hundred and forty thousand yojanas in thickness.

The essence and core of the earth is the Unconquered Place (*anabhibhūta-acalaṭṭhāna*); when the world-system is being formed, it is the first to be established, and when it is perishing, it is the last to perish.
"Thus we have heard"—in this way, we have heard it by means of the *lakkhaṇa-mantra*.
"Having descended" means having descended from the sky; [homage] to this place where the defilements of all Buddhas are destroyed.
"Perform it! Pay honor and respect! "Those who...
refers to those elephants reckoned as the elephant-treasure (*hatthiratana*) of a wheel-turning monarch (*cakkavatti-rāja*), born into a lineage of Uposatha elephants.
"To such an extent" means that even all of them do not reach this much space; even when being struck with a goad, they do not approach it at all. "Noble-born" (*abhijāta*)...
Having overcome and surpassed the eight breeds of elephants beginning with the *gocariya*, he was born into the *uposatha* breed.
"An elephant" means the most excellent. "Only this far" means this much ground can be approached by this tusker; beyond this, it is not possible.
"If you desire [him to go further], give a signal with the diamond-hook and drive him on. "Having considered the words of the fortune-teller," monks... [he said].
The meaning is that the king, having listened to the words of that fortune-teller and physiognomist, Kāliṅgabhāradvāja, and having reflected upon them,
sent forth the elephant while investigating, thinking, "We shall know whether this man's word is true or false.
"Having cried out like a heron," monks, means that the elephant, by him—
Like a crane sent forth and urged on by King Vajiraṅkusa, he cried out and turned back;
then, tossing up his trunk and stretching out his neck, he sat right there in the air as if unable to bear the heavy burden.
Being struck again and again by him, he was unable to endure the pain and passed away. But the king—
Not knowing the state of the elephant's mind, he remained sitting right there on the back. Kāliṅgabhāradvāja said, "Great King, your elephant has passed away;
mount another elephant. To clarify this matter, the Teacher spoke the tenth verse:
"Kāliṅgabhāradvāja, having realized that the elephant’s life-span was exhausted..."
Hurrying toward King Kāliṅga, he addressed him:
“O Great King, there is another bridge; this elephant’s life has reached its end.
In that context, “the elephant’s life has reached its end” means the elephant has met the destruction of his life; by doing anything [else], it cannot be helped.
[The king] was unable to proceed to the summit of the Bodhi-maṇḍa while seated on the back [of the elephant]. "He transfers to another elephant":
by the power of the king’s merit and spiritual majesty (*puññiddhibala*), another elephant came from the Uposatha family and offered its back.
The king sat upon its back. At that moment, the dead elephant fell to the ground. Explaining this matter, the Teacher spoke the following verse:
“Having heard that, the King of Kalinga hurriedly approached the elephant;
as soon as the king had stepped forward, the elephant fell right there upon the ground.
Just as the words of the physiognomist had spoken, so it came to pass for the elephant.”
Then the king, descending from the sky and gazing upon the seat of enlightenment, saw the miracle and spoke in praise of Bhāradvāja:
"The King of Kalinga said this to the brahmin of Kalinga:
'You alone are the Fully Enlightened One, the all-knowing, the all-seeing.'"
The brahmin, unable to endure that, placed himself in a low position and, exalting the Buddha alone, praised him. To clarify this matter, the Teacher spoke these verses:
“Unable to endure that, O Kāliṅga, the brahmin said this:
‘For we are diviners, O Great King, while the Buddhas are all-knowing.’”
“The All-Knowing and All-Seeing Buddhas do not know by means of physical marks;
for we Buddhas understand everything through the power of the traditional teachings.
In this context, O Great King, “interpreters of marks” refers to those who, having seen a mark, are capable of making a prediction based on what they have heard and understood.
However, the Buddhas are omniscient and all-knowing. For the Buddhas know and see everything, including its divisions such as the past and so forth;
they know all by means of their knowledge of omniscience (*sabbaññutaññāṇa*), not by means of a mere characteristic mark (*lakkhaṇa*).
We, on the other hand, know by the power of scripture and by the power of our own craft, and that only partially; but the Buddhas understand everything.
Having heard of the Buddha’s qualities, the king was filled with joy.

He had vast quantities of perfumes and garlands brought by all the inhabitants of the entire Cakkavāḷa, and after staying for seven days at the Great Seat of Enlightenment (Mahābodhimaṇḍa), he performed a great worship of the Bodhi tree.
To illustrate this matter, the Teacher spoke these two verses:
“Having honored him for full enlightenment while various musical instruments were being played,
and having presented garlands and ointments, the king then departed.
He caused sixty thousand cartloads of flowers to be gathered.”
“The Kalinga king worshipped the unsurpassed Bodhi-maṇḍa.
Therein, *manupāyāsī* means he went into the presence of his mother and father. On the Great Bodhi-maṇḍa, he erected a golden pillar eighteen cubits high.
He had a railing made for it consisting of the seven precious gems, and sand mixed with jewels.
Having had it sprinkled with water, he had it enclosed by a rampart; he had a gateway pavilion made of the seven precious gems constructed;
and he had sixty thousand wagon-loads of flowers gathered daily. In this manner he honored the Bodhimaṇḍa.
In the Pāḷi, however, only this much is recorded: "sixty thousand wagon-loads of flowers."

Having thus performed the worship of Great Enlightenment, he took his parents and his paternal and maternal grandparents, brought them to Dantapura itself, and having performed meritorious deeds such as giving alms, he was reborn in the Tāvatiṃsa heaven.
Having delivered this teaching on the Dhamma, the Teacher said, "Monks, it is not only now;
in the past as well, Ānanda performed the worship of Enlightenment," and he identified the Jātaka: "At that time, the young brahmin Kāliṅga was Ānanda, and Kāliṅga Bhāradvāja was [the Buddha]."
"But it was I myself who was he.
The sixth: The Commentary on the Kāliṅgabodhi Jātaka.
[480] 7. The Commentary on the Akitti Jātaka.
"Seeing Akitti, they are appeased. The Teacher spoke this while dwelling at Jetavana concerning a lay follower, a master of generosity, who resided in Sāvatthī.

It is said that after he had invited the Teacher and given a great almsgiving for seven days to the Saṅgha of monks headed by the Buddha, on the final day he offered all the requisites to the Noble Saṅgha.
He gave it. Then the Teacher, offering words of appreciation right in the midst of the assembly, said:
"Lay follower, great is your sacrifice! Oh, what a difficult deed you have performed! For this is indeed the lineage of giving, the lineage of the ancient sages.
Giving must certainly be practiced both by the householder and by the one gone forth. Yet the ancient sages, even while having gone forth and dwelling in the forest..."

"Even while eating *kāra* leaves sprinkled with only a little water as a saltless seasoning, they gave as much as was desired to those who approached them as supplicants and sustained themselves through the bliss of joy," he said.

When requested by him, saying, "Venerable sir, this gift of all requisites is indeed well known to the great multitude; but tell us that which you have spoken of as 'not well known'," he related a story of the past.
In the past, while Brahmadatta was reigning in Bārāṇasī, the Bodhisatta was born into the family of a wealthy brahmin of eighty crores of wealth;
they gave him the name Akitti. At the time he began walking on his own feet, his sister was also born, and they gave her the name Yasavatī.
When the Great Being reached the age of sixteen, he went to Takkasilā and mastered all the arts.
Having mastered them, he returned. Then his parents passed away. After performing their funeral rites, while he was conducting an inventory of the wealth, he heard it said:
"So-and-so, having accumulated this much wealth, has passed away; so-and-so, this much.
Hearing these words, his mind was filled with agitation, and he thought: "Only this wealth is visible here, but there are no gatherers of that wealth."
“All these have departed having abandoned this wealth, but I shall go taking it with me. Having summoned his sister, he said, “You take charge of this wealth.
She asked, “But what is your intention? He replied, “I wish to go forth into the religious life.
She said, “Brother, I will not receive upon my head the spittle discarded by you; I have no need for this.”
“I too shall go forth. Having taken leave of the king, he caused a drum to be beaten, proclaiming: “Let those who have need of wealth come to the house of the wise Akitti.
After he had distributed a great gift for seven days, and while his wealth was not yet exhausted, he reflected: “These conditioned phenomena are wasting away.”
"What is the use of my playing with wealth? Those who need it shall take it.
Having said this, he opened the gate of his residence and, saying "Let them take what has been given," he abandoned his home along with its silver and gold.
While his circle of kinsmen was lamenting, he took his sister and departed from Bārāṇasī. The gate through which he departed became known as the Akitti Gate.
The very ford by which he had descended into the river became known as Akittitittha.
Having traveled two or three leagues, he built a leaf-hut in a delightful place and went forth into homelessness together with his sister.
From the time of his renunciation, inhabitants of many villages, market towns, and royal capitals went forth as well. He came to have a great retinue and received great gain and honor.
His manifestation was like the time of a Buddha’s appearance; his career proceeded accordingly. Then the Great Being, thinking, "This gain and honor are great, and my retinue is large;

it is fitting that I dwell all alone," departed by himself at an unusual hour, without informing even his sister, and after traveling by stages, reached the kingdom of the Damilas near the city of Kāvīrapaṭṭana.
While dwelling in the park, he attained the meditative absorptions (*jhāna*) and the higher knowledges (*abhiññā*).
There, too, great gain and honor arose for him. Disgusted with that, he abandoned it and traveled through the air, landing at Kāradīpa near Nāgadīpa.
At that time, Kāradīpa was known as Ahidīpa. There, relying on a large *kāra* tree, he constructed a leaf-hut.
He made his dwelling there. No one knew of his presence there.

Then his sister, searching for her brother, eventually reached the Damila kingdom; not finding him, she stayed at the very place where he had lived, yet she was unable to attain meditative absorption (jhāna).
Due to his fewness of desires, the Great Being did not go anywhere; when that tree bore fruit, he ate the fruits, and when it had leaves, he ate the leaves sprinkled with water.
By the power of his virtue, the stone throne of Sakka, known as Paṇḍukambala, began to feel warm.
Sakka, reflecting, "Who indeed wishes to displace me from my position? perceived the wise Akitti.
Having seen him, he thought: "For what purpose does this ascetic observe these precepts? Does he aspire to the status of Sakka, or perhaps something else?
I shall test him. For he maintains his livelihood through hardship; he eats water-soaked *kāra* leaves.
If he aspires to the status of Sakka, he will give me his own soaked leaves; if not, he will not."

He went into his presence in the guise of a brahmin. The Bodhisatta, having soaked and drained some *kāra* leaves, sat at the door of his leaf-hut thinking, "I shall eat them once they have become cool. Then Sakka stood before him for alms.
Seeing him, the Great Being was filled with joy and thought, "It is indeed a gain for me that I see a supplicant; today my heart's desire—"
Thinking, "I shall give this gift after reaching the summit," he took it in the very same vessel used for cooking and went;

then, saying, "May this gift of mine be a condition for the attainment of omniscience," he placed it in that man's bowl without leaving anything for himself. The brahmin took it and, having gone a short distance, vanished.
The Great Being, having given it to him and paid his respects once more, spent the time in the bliss of joy.
On the following day, having cooked [the meal], he sat right there at the door of the leaf-hut.
Sakka came again in the guise of a brahmin. Having given it to him once more, the Great Being spent the time in the same manner.
On the third day as well, having given in the same way, he thought: "Oh, what a gain for me! By means of these leaves, I have produced great merit."

"Devoted" means that, filled with joy, although he was weak from having gone without food for three days, he emerged from his leaf-hut at midday and sat at the door of the hut reflecting upon the gift. Sakka also thought:
"This brahmin, though so weak from being without food for three days, gives this gift with a heart full of gladness."
“There is no change in his mind; I do not know that he gives this having made such a specific aspiration.
After questioning him and hearing his intention, I shall learn the reason for his gift.
Then, when midday had passed, he arrived before the Great Being, blazing with great splendor and glory like the young sun shining in the vault of heaven.

Standing before him, he asked, "O ascetic, why do you perform such penance in this forest, surrounded by salt water, while such hot winds are blowing? To explain the matter, the Teacher spoke the first verse:
"Seeing Akitti, the tranquil one, Sakka, the lord of beings, said:"
“Great Brahmā, desiring what do you meditate alone upon the heat?
Therein, “desiring what” means: is he desiring human prosperity, or perhaps one of the other prosperities such as that of Sakka?

Having heard this and knowing his state as Sakka, the Great Being spoke the second verse to declare: “I do not desire these prosperities; rather, desiring omniscience, I perform the practice of asceticism.”
“Rebirth, Sakka, is suffering, as is the breaking up of the body;
death in delusion is suffering; therefore, Vāsava, I pay homage.
In this context, “therefore” means because repeated birth, the breaking up of the aggregates, and death in delusion are suffering.
Therefore, by saying, "I am truly right here," while aspiring for that Nibbāna where these [defilements] do not exist, he demonstrates his own inclination toward Nibbāna.

Hearing this, Sakka, with a joyful mind, thinking, "It seems this man is weary of all states of existence and dwells in the forest for the sake of Nibbāna; I shall grant him a boon," spoke the third verse as an invitation to choose a boon:
"In this well-spoken, fitting, and beautifully uttered speech of yours..."
“I grant you a boon, Kassapa; whatever you desire in your mind.
Regarding this, “whatever you desire in your mind” means: “I give that which you wish for with your mind; choose a boon.
As the Great Being chose his boon, he spoke the fourth verse:
“If you would grant me a boon, O Sakka, Lord of all beings:
let that greed by which men, having obtained children, wives, wealth, grain, and dear things, are never satisfied, not dwell within me.”
In this context, "If you grant me a boon" means if you would give me a favor. "And dear things" refers to other objects of affection.
"They do not satisfy" means that sons and others are craved again and again; one never reaches satiety.
"May it not dwell in me" means may it not abide in me, may it not arise within me.
Then Sakka, being pleased, offered a further boon, and the Great Being, accepting the boon, spoke these verses:
“Since you have spoken so well, with words that are fitting and beautifully expressed,
I grant you a boon, Kassapa— whatever you desire in your heart.”
“If you would grant me a boon, O Sakka, Lord of all beings:
let no field, land, gold, cattle, horses, slaves, or servants—
by whose birth people are ruined— have power over me for any fault of mine.”
“Since you have spoken so well, with words that are fitting and beautifully expressed,
I grant you a boon, Kassapa— whatever you desire in your heart.
If you would grant me a boon, Sakka, Lord of all beings,”
One should not see a fool, nor hear one, nor dwell with a fool;
one should not engage in conversation or discourse with a fool, nor take pleasure in it.
“What has the fool done to you? Tell me the reason, Kassapa.”
“Why, Kassapa, do you not desire the sight of a fool?
‘The witless man leads himself to ruin; he yokes himself to what is burdensome.
A wrong course seems better to him; when spoken to rightly, he becomes agitated.’”
“He does not know the Vinaya; it is well for him that he is not seen.
“Since you have spoken so well and so appropriately, Kassapa, I grant you a boon—whatever you desire in your heart.”
“If you would grant me a boon, O Sakka, Lord of all beings:
may I see the wise, hear the wise, and dwell together with the wise;
may I engage in conversation and discourse with the wise, and find delight in that.”
“What have I done for you, O wise one? Tell me the reason, Kassapa.
For what reason, Kassapa, do you long to see the Wise One?
“The wise man follows the right method; he does not yoke himself to what is burdensome.”
A well-behaved person is more excellent; one who is rightly spoken to does not become angry.
Such a person understands discipline; it is good to have association with them.
Regarding this well-spoken and fitting speech of yours that has been beautifully articulated:
“I grant you a boon, Kassapa, whatever you desire in your mind.
“If you would grant me a boon, Sakka, Lord of all beings,
then at the end of this night, at the rising of the sun— ”
“May divine foods appear, and may those who are virtuous come as supplicants.
‘May my wealth not be exhausted while I give, and having given, may I have no regret;
may I gladden my heart by giving’—this, Sakka, is the boon I choose.”
“Since you have spoken so well, with words that are fitting and beautifully expressed,
I grant you a boon, Kassapa— whatever you desire in your heart.
If you would grant me a boon, Sakka, Lord of all beings,”
“You shall not come to me again—this, Sakka, is the boon I choose.
“Indeed, through many ascetic practices, both men and women long for a sight of you;
what fear could there be in seeing me?”
“Having seen such a celestial form, perfected in all its desires, I might neglect my asceticism; this is the danger in seeing you.
In that context, “by which [mind] was born” means by whichever mind was born, through which beings, being angry, commit acts such as the taking of life and thereby incur royal punishment.
Or, because these fields and so forth are being lost through his own death caused by eating poisonous food and the like, he asks [for them], thinking, "May that fault not fall upon me.
"He does not hear" means he would not hear [the news] for these reasons, such as: "He lives in such-and-such a place.
"What have they done to you? means: "Has your foolish mother been killed, or perhaps your father, or someone else?"
What kind of harm did that fool do?
He leads himself to ruin by taking what is not a cause to be a "cause"; he thinks of such harmful deeds as, "I shall make my living by committing the destruction of life and so forth.
He fails to apply himself to the burdens of faith, virtue, and wisdom.
He applies himself to what is improper. "Bad conduct is better for him" means that bad conduct itself becomes better for him;
he takes up the practice of the five types of unvirtuous actions and considers that very thing to be better, or he follows a course of conduct that is harmful and impossible to lead away from.
"When told correctly" means he becomes agitated when told by means of a reason or a cause. "They discipline" refers to such instructions as "one should approach in this manner," and so forth.
He does not know the discipline of proper conduct (*ācāravīnaya*) and does not accept admonition. "It is good for him"—for these reasons, it is better indeed that he not be seen.
"At the rising of the sun" means at the time of sunrise. "Supernatural food" (*dibbā bhakkhā*) means divine sustenance; "supplicants" are those who receive that divine food.
"By the practice of vows" (*vatacariyāhi*) means by means of the acts of giving, virtue, and the observance of the *uposatha*. "Sight" (*dassana*).
"Desiring" means they desire a vision of me. "Such as that" refers to one adorned with celestial ornaments.

"I might neglect" means I might fall into heedlessness. "I might long for the excellence of your glory"—if, while engaged in ascetic practices for the sake of Nibbāna, I were to long for the position of Sakka, I would indeed be called heedless; this is my fear regarding the sight of you.

Sakka said, “Very well, Bhante; from now on we shall not come into your presence,” and having paid homage and asked for forgiveness, he departed. The Great Being remained right there for the rest of his life, developed the divine abidings (brahmavihāra), and was reborn in the Brahma-world.
Having delivered this teaching on the Dhamma, the Teacher identified the Jātaka, saying: “At that time Sakka was Anuruddha, and the wise Akitti was none other than myself.
This is the seventh commentary on the Akitti Jātaka.
[481] 8. The Commentary on the Takkāriya Jātaka:
"I alone am the fool who spoke ill"—this the Teacher related while dwelling at Jetavana concerning Kokālika.
For during one rainy season, the two Chief Disciples, desiring to dwell in seclusion, left their company.
Having taken leave of the Teacher, they went to Kokālika’s dwelling place in the district of Kokālika and said to him:
"Friend Kokālika, by depending on you we shall have a comfortable stay, and by depending on us you shall have a comfortable stay;
let us dwell here for these three months. "But friends, how will you have a comfortable stay by depending on me?"
“Friend, if you were not to tell anyone that ‘the two chief disciples are staying here,’ we would dwell in comfort;
this, depending on you, is our ease. “And what ease for me would there be, depending on you?
“We shall teach you the Dhamma and deliver Dhamma discourses to you throughout these three months.”
“This comfortable dwelling is yours, having relied upon us. “Dwell, friends, according to your inclination,” he said.
He gave them a suitable lodging, and they dwelt happily in the bliss of the attainment of fruition (phalasamāpatti).
No one there knew that they were living there.
Having completed their rains retreat and performed the Pavāraṇā ceremony, they asked him, "Friend, we have lived happily depending on you; let us go to pay homage to the Teacher.
He consented, saying, "Very well," and taking them with him, he went for alms in the village ahead.
When the elders had finished their meal, they departed from the village. Kokālika dismissed them and turned back.

He informed the people, saying, "Lay followers, you are like animals; you did not know that the two chief disciples were dwelling in the Dhuravihāra for three months, yet now they have departed. The people said, "But why, venerable sir, did you not tell us?
and taking much medicinal oil, ghee, and so forth, as well as clothing and coverings, they approached the Elders.
Having paid homage, they said, "Venerable sir, please forgive us; we did not know that you were the Chief Disciples.
Today we have learned it through the words of the venerable Kokālika. Out of compassion for us, please accept these medicinal requisites, robes, and coverings.
Kokālika thought, "The elders are of few desires and contented; they will not take these robes themselves, but will give them to me."
Having reflected thus, he went into the presence of the elders together with the lay followers.
Because the food had been prepared by the monks, the elders took nothing for themselves from it, nor did they give anything to Kokālika.

The lay followers entreated them, saying, "Venerable sirs, if you do not take anything now, please come here again out of compassion for us. The elders, however, did not consent and [went] to the Teacher.
They went into his presence. Kokālika harbored a grudge, thinking, "These elders did not accept [the gift] themselves, so they did not have it given to me.

After the elders had stayed for a short while in the presence of the Teacher, they set out on a journey with five hundred monks from their own retinue and a thousand monks in total, and arrived at the district of Kokālika. Those lay followers—
They went out to meet him, took the elders with them, and led them back to that very monastery, where they performed great honors for them every day.

Abundant medicine, clothing, and requisites were provided; however, when the monks who had come with the elders were distributing the robes, they gave them only to the monks who had arrived together with them, and not to Kokālika.
The elders, too, did not allow anything to be given to him.

Kokālika, having failed to obtain a robe, reviled and abused the Elders, saying: “Sāriputta and Moggallāna are evil-intentioned; previously they would not accept alms when being offered, but now they take them. It is impossible to satisfy them; they do not even look at others.
The Elders thought, “This man, depending on us, is producing unwholesome karma,” and so they departed with their retinue, saying, “Venerable sir, [we shall seek] another.”
Even when requested by the people, "Please stay for a few days," they did not wish to return.
Then a certain young bhikkhu said, "Lay followers, how will the elders stay?
Your family-preceptor, the elder, will not tolerate their staying here. They went to him and said, "Venerable sir, it is said that you..."
They said, "You cannot endure the elders' dwelling here; go, ask their forgiveness, and return.
If you do not return, flee and dwell elsewhere. Out of fear of the lay devotees, he went and entreated the elders.
The elders said, "Go, friend; we shall not return," and they departed. Unable to make the elders turn back, he [returned] to the monastery itself.
He returned. Then the lay followers asked him, "Venerable sir, have the elders turned back?
"I was not able to turn them back, friends," he replied. Then, thinking, "As long as this man of evil character remains here, virtuous monks will not dwell here;
let us expel him," he said, "Venerable sir, do not live here. Because of us, you will receive nothing..."

“There is none,” they said. Having been driven out by them, he took his bowl and robe, went to Jetavana, approached the Teacher, and said, “Venerable sir, Sāriputta and Moggallāna have evil desires; they have fallen under the sway of evil desires.
Then the Teacher said to him, “Kokālika, do not speak thus; do not speak thus, Kokālika! Inspire confidence in them.”
“Kokālika, do not set your mind on Sāriputta and Moggallāna; those bhikkhus are virtuous,” the Teacher forbade him.
Although thus forbidden, Kokālika said, “Venerable sir, you and your chief disciples may believe as you wish, but I have seen it with my own eyes:
they are of evil desires, of concealed conduct, and immoral. Even though he was forbidden by the Teacher up to three times, he spoke exactly the same way.
Rising from his seat, he departed. As soon as he had gone, boils the size of mustard seeds broke out over his entire body;
these gradually grew until they were the size of *veluva* fruits, whereupon they burst and oozed pus and blood.
Groaning and overcome by pain, he lay down at the gateway of the Jeta Grove. [He thought: "By Kokālika, the two Chief Disciples..."
When the cry of "He has been reviled! reached as far as the Brahma-world, there was a single tumultuous uproar.

Then his preceptor, the Brahmā named Turu, knowing the reason for this, thought, "I shall ask the Elder for forgiveness," and coming there, he stood in the air and said, "Kokālika, you have committed a harsh deed; appease the Chief Disciples. "Who..."
"But you, friend? "I am indeed named Brahmā Turū. "Friend, have you not been declared by the Blessed One to be a non-returner?
And it has been said that a non-returner is one whose nature is not to return from this world; yet you say you will become a spirit in a rubbish heap!
Thus he reviled Mahābrahmā. Being unable to make him accept his words, [he said: "As for you..."
"By your own speech alone you shall be known," he said, and departed for the Suddhāvāsa heaven. Kokālika too, having passed away, was reborn in the Paduma hell.
Knowing that he had been reborn there, Sahampati Brahmā informed the Tathāgata, and the Teacher informed the bhikkhus. The bhikkhus, recounting his faults in the Dhamma Hall, said:
"How did they start this conversation? 'Friends, it is said that Kokālika, having reviled Sāriputta and Moggallāna, has been reborn in the Paduma Hell because of his own mouth.
The Teacher approached and asked, "Monks, for what discussion are you gathered here now?
When they replied, "For this very discussion," he said, "Monks, it is not only now that Kokālika..."
"Having been ruined by his own words, he experiences suffering because of his own mouth; indeed, in the past as well, he experienced suffering because of his own mouth.
Having said this, he related a story of the past:
"In the past, while Brahmadatta was reigning in Bārāṇasī, his family priest was Piṅgala, who had protruding teeth."
There was [a man] whose brahmin wife committed adultery with another brahmin, and he too was just like him.
Although the chaplain tried again and again to restrain his wife, being unable to do so, he thought:
"It is not possible for me to kill this enemy of mine with my own hand; I shall kill him by some stratagem. He approached the king and said: "Great King,..."
“Your city is the foremost city in all of Jambudīpa, and you are the foremost king; thus, for one such as you, O Foremost King, this southern gate is ill-suited and inauspicious.
“Teacher, what should be done now? “Having performed an auspicious rite, it should be joined [to the city].
“What is required to be obtained? “Having removed the old gate, [one should install] those things appropriate for an auspicious rite.”
“Having taken timber and offered a sacrifice (*bali*) to the spirits who guard the city, it is fitting to establish [the new gate] under an auspicious constellation.

“In that case, do so,” [the king replied]. At that time, the Bodhisatta, being a young brahmin named Takkāriya, was learning his craft in the presence of that chaplain. Having demolished the old gate and completed a new one, the chaplain informed the king.
He said: “It is finished, Your Majesty; the gate is ready. Tomorrow is an auspicious constellation;
it is fitting that before that time passes, an offering be made and the gate be re-established. “Teacher, what is required for the performance of the offering?
“Your Majesty, this gate is of great power and is protected by powerful deities; one tawny dog with protruding fangs [is required].”
“Having killed a brahmin who is pure on both sides, and having made an offering with his flesh and blood, you must cast his body beneath [the gate] and establish the door;
in this way, there will be prosperity for both you and the city.
“Very well, teacher; having killed such a brahmin, establish the door.”
With a delighted mind, thinking, "Tomorrow I shall see the back of my enemy," he became filled with zeal.
Having gone to his own home, unable to restrain his face, he hurriedly said to his wife: "O wicked, fierce woman! From now on, with whom will you take your pleasure?
Tomorrow, having killed your paramour, we shall perform an offering for you. [She replied: "He is innocent..."
“For what reason will you kill him? The king said, “Perform a sacrificial offering with the flesh and blood of the brahmin Kaḷārapiṅgala and restore the city gate.
She replied, “Kaḷārapiṅgala is your lover; having killed him, we shall perform the sacrificial offering.
She then sent a message to her lover: “It seems the king intends to [kill] the brahmin Kaḷārapiṅgala...”
“Having killed him, he intends to perform a sacrifice; if you wish to live, you should take other brahmins like yourself and flee at once.
He did accordingly. This became known throughout the city, and all those who were black-and-tawny fled from the entire city.
The chaplain, unaware that his enemy had fled, approached the king early in the morning and said, “Your Majesty,…”
“There is a brahmin named Kaḷārapiṅgala in such-and-such a place; have him seized,” he said. The king dispatched his ministers.
Not finding him, they returned and reported, “He has apparently fled. “Search elsewhere,” [the king said]. Though they searched the entire city, they did not see him.
Then, when told, “Search another place,” they replied, “Your Majesty, with the exception of the chaplain...”
“There is no one else like him,” they said. [Thinking] that the chaplain could not be killed, [the king asked: “Your Majesty, what are you saying?
Because of the chaplain, the city will be unprotected today since no guards have been stationed at the gates.
The teacher was saying: ‘Today the auspicious conjunction has passed; after the lapse of a year from now, one will obtain the conjunction again.’”
He said, "For a year there will be an opening for our enemies in this doorless city;
having slain this man and having had another capable brahmin perform the sacrificial offering (*balikamma*), we shall re-establish the gate.
[The king asked: "But is there another wise brahmin equal to the teacher? [The other replied: "There is, Your Majesty; he has a pupil, the young brahmin Takkāriya."
“Give him the position of chaplain and perform the auspicious rites for him.
The king summoned him, honored him, granted him the position of chaplain, and commanded that it be done accordingly.
He went to the city gate with a great retinue. They bound the chaplain by royal authority and brought him back.
The Great Being had a pit dug at the place where the gate was to be set up and had it surrounded with a curtain;
he then stood inside the curtain together with his teacher. The teacher, looking down into the pit and finding no firm footing for himself, thought:
"My purpose has indeed been accomplished; however, because of my foolishness, being unable to guard my mouth, I spoke with vehemence to Pāpithī."
Addressing the Great Being, he spoke the first verse while saying, "The destruction of oneself by oneself has been brought about":
"I alone, a fool, have spoken ill-spoken words, like a frog calling out 'snake' in the forest.
I am falling into this Takka-river pit; indeed, it is not good to speak beyond measure."
"In that regard, 'I spoke ill-spoken words' means: I spoke what was ill-spoken. 'Like a frog' means:
just as a frog in the forest, while croaking, is said to speak ill-spoken words when calling out to the snake that eats it, so too did I myself speak ill-spoken words.
'Takkāriyā' is her name; 'Takkāriyā' is a feminine noun, and he addressed her thus using that very name."
Having heard that, the Great Being spoke this second verse:
“The mortal who speaks excessively incurs imprisonment, execution, sorrow, and lamentation.
In this matter, you should blame only yourself, Ācariya, for they bury you in a pit.”
In this context, "one who speaks excessively" means that speaking beyond the proper time (*velā*) or beyond measure is not good;
the meaning is that a person who speaks excessively is not good. And "grief and lamentation":
O Teacher, in this very way, a person who speaks excessively encounters execution, imprisonment, grief, and loud lamentation. "One who is censured."
"Without blaming another, you should blame yourself alone. Regarding the phrase "in this matter":
"O teacher, that which is the rule (tan ti)" means, O teacher, for whatever reason they bury one in a pit, that very thing was done by you;
therefore, he says, "you should blame yourself alone."

Having spoken thus, he said, "Teacher, it is not only you who have fallen into suffering because you failed to guard your speech; others too have likewise fallen into suffering," and having said this, he brought up a story from the past to demonstrate the point.
It is said that in the past, in Bārāṇasī, there was a courtesan named Kāḷī, whose brother was named Tuṇḍila.
On a certain day, Kāḷī earned a thousand pieces of money. However, Tuṇḍila was a gambler with women, a drunkard, and a dicer. She [gave him some of her earnings].
He gave away his wealth, and whatever he acquired, he squandered. Although she tried to restrain him, she was unable to stop him.
One day, defeated at gambling, he gave away the clothes he was wearing, put on a tattered rag from a straw mat, and came to her house.
She had already commanded her maidservants: "When Tuṇḍila arrives, do not give him anything; instead, seize him by the neck..."
“...you must take him out. They did so. He stood weeping at the gate.
Then a son of a merchant, who was constantly having a thousand coins brought by Kāḷī, saw him and asked, “Why, Tuṇḍila, do you weep?
“Sir, I have come to my sister after being defeated at dice; these slave girls [are seizing] me by the neck...”
“...having taken it, they carried it out. [The brother replied: “In that case, stay here; sister, I shall speak with you.
Having gone there, he said, “Your brother is standing at the door wearing a piece of a straw mat;
why do you not give him clothes? She said, “I will certainly not give them; however, if you have affection for him, you may give them. But while she was with the courtesan—

This was the custom in that house: five hundred [pieces of cloth] were brought from a thousand [measures of wealth] for the courtesan, and five hundred were for the cost of garments, perfumes, and garlands.

When men arrived at that house, they would put on the garments provided there, stay the night, and when departing the following day, they would go away wearing those very same garments they had been given. Therefore, the merchant’s son took the garments given by her.
Having dressed himself in his own garment, he gave it to Tuṇḍila. Tuṇḍila put it on and, roaring and trumpeting, went and entered the tavern.
Kāḷī also commanded her maidservants, "Tomorrow, when he is about to leave, you must snatch away his clothes.
When he was departing, they ran hither and thither, plundering him; they seized his garments and said, "Now—"
"Go, young man! they said, and having stripped him naked, they sent him away. He departed naked. People mocked him.
Feeling ashamed, he lamented: "This was done by me; I alone was unable to protect my own face.
To show this, he spoke the third verse:
“Why indeed did I ask Tuṇḍila? He might have done so for his brother Kāḷika;
he was naked and worn out, yet he received a pair of garments—this matter, too, is similar to many others.

Herein, “similar to many others” means: the merchant’s son attained suffering through his own actions; therefore, you too [attained it], and thus this attainment of suffering by you is similar to that in many respects. It is similar to many causes.

Furthermore, in Benares, while two rams were fighting on the pasture ground due to the negligence of their herder, a certain *kuliṅga* bird thought, "Now these two will die with their heads split; I shall stop them.
Having tried to stop them, saying, "O uncles, do not fight," and having failed to gain their attention as they continued to fight, it sat upon both their backs and their heads.
Being unable to stop them after pleading with them, he entered between the heads of both, saying, "In that case, kill me and fight.
They fought one another right there, and he met his destruction by his own doing, like grain ground in a mortar.
To show this further reason, he spoke the fourth verse:
“The quail that, while they were fighting, did not fight, but flew up between the rams—there he was crushed by the heads of the rams;
this matter too is much like that. In this context, *meṇḍantaraṃ* means “between the rams.
*Accupatī* means “having flown up beyond,” the sense being that it stood in the air amidst their heads. *Piṃsito* means “crushed.”
Furthermore, some cowherds living in Bārāṇasī, seeing a palmyra tree bearing fruit, climbed the tree for the sake of a palm fruit.
While he was shaking down the fruits, a black snake emerged from an anthill and climbed the palmyra tree.
Those standing below, though striking with sticks, were unable to stop it. They cried out, "A snake is climbing the palmyra!"
They told him about the other one. Terrified, he let out a great cry.
Those standing below took a sturdy cloth by its four corners and said, "Fall onto this cloth! As he fell, he landed in the middle of the cloth, between all four of them.
However, unable to withstand the force of his fall, they struck one another with their heads.
Having struck one another, they met their end with their heads shattered. Demonstrating this reason as well, he spoke the fifth verse:
“Four men seized the book, while protecting a single person;
all of them lay down with their heads shattered. This matter, too, is of the same kind as the many others.”
In that context, "potthaka" means a hempen garment. "All four of them" refers to those four men who lay down with their heads split by what they themselves had done.

Furthermore, certain sheep-thieves living in Bārāṇasī, having stolen a goat at night, tied its mouth to prevent it from bleating so they could eat it in the forest during the day, and left it in a bamboo thicket. On the following day, in order to eat it...
As they were going along, they forgot their weapons and continued on their way. Thinking, "We shall kill a goat, cook its meat, and eat it;
bring back our weapons," they searched but did not see a weapon in the hand of even one among them. They said, "It is impossible to seize this meat even by killing him without weapons;
let him go, for he possesses merit," and so they released him. At that time, there was a certain reed-worker...
Taking his bamboo pole and thinking, "I will come back and take it again," the fletcher placed his knife among the bamboo thickets and departed.
The goat, satisfied with the thought, "I am free," was playing at the base of the bamboo when she struck with her hind legs and caused that knife to fall.
Hearing the sound of the knife, the thieves searched for it; finding it, they were delighted in heart and killed the goat.
They ate the flesh. Thus, in order to show that "that goat too died because of what she herself had done," he spoke the sixth verse:
"Just as the goat, while tied in the bamboo thicket, fell down and came upon the sword in its midst;
by that very thing her throat was cut—this matter, too, is much like the others."
In that context, "they throw down" means that while playing, they cast their hind legs down.
Having spoken thus, and having shown that "those who speak with moderation, protecting their own words, are released from the suffering of death," he related the story of the Kinnara.
It is said that a certain hunter living in Bārāṇasī went to the Himalayas and, by a certain stratagem, [captured] two Kinnaras together with their mate.
Having captured and brought them, he gave them to the king. When the king saw the kinnaras, whom he had never seen before, he was delighted and asked, "Hunter, what merit do these possess?
"Your Majesty, these sing with sweet voices and dance charmingly; humans do not know how to sing or dance in such a way.
The king, having given much wealth to the hunter, [dismissed] the kinnaras.
"Sing! Dance! he said. The kinnaras thought, "If we sing and are unable to make the syllables perfect, it will be a bad song;
then they will revile us and kill us. Furthermore, for those who speak much, there is also the danger of lying.
Out of fear of lying, even though the king told them again and again, they neither sang nor danced.
The king, having become angry, commanded, "Kill these, cook their meat, and bring it to me," and spoke the seventh verse:
"These are neither gods nor sons of Gandhabbas; they are deer who have come to my service.
Cook one for the evening meal, and cook another for the morning meal."
"In this regard, 'these deer' means that if these were gods or gandhabbas, they would dance and sing; but these are deer, belonging to the animal realm.
'They have come into my power for a purpose' means they have come into my hands for the sake of a purpose, because they were brought here by a hunter who expected some benefit.
'Let them cook one for the evening meal and one for the morning meal.'"
The Kinnarī thought, "The king is angry; he will undoubtedly kill me. Now is the time to speak," and she spoke the eighth verse:
"A hundred thousand ill-spoken words are not worth even a fraction of a well-spoken one.
Ill-spoken speech is a defilement that leads to ruin; therefore, O Kimpurisa, it is not fit for the wise to remain silent."

"In this context, 'transmigrating through defilement' means that sometimes while speaking, I might utter an ill-spoken word; thus, transmigrating through such ill-spokenness, one becomes defiled and exhausted. Therefore—for that reason—I did not sing before you out of childishness.
The king, being pleased with the kinnarī, spoke the following verse:
"Let her who spoke thus to me be released; let them lead her to the Himavat mountains."
“Give this to the kitchen, and let them cook it at dawn for the morning meal.
Therein, “yā me” means “this which is mine. “Dentu” means “let them give it for the sake of the kitchen.
Having heard the king’s words, the kinnara thought, “If I do not tell him now, he will surely kill me; it is right that I speak now,” and he recited the other verse:
“Cattle have the rain as their lord; this generation has the king as its lord.
You are the lord, O Great King; I am the lord of my wife.
Knowing which of us two is more worthy, he shall be released and go to the mountain.”
In this context, "the cattle have the cloud as their lord" means that the cattle which feed on grass are called "cloud-lords.
"This generation has the cattle as its lord" refers to this human generation; they subsist on the five products of the cow and thus have the cattle as their lord and support.
"You are my lord" means you are my support. "I am her lord" means I am the lord of my wife; I am her [support].
"A support. Having learned that one of us two is dead, the one who is freed may go to the mountain. [The other replied:
"Between us two, if one learns that the other is dead, he who is himself freed from death may go to the Himalayas;
but as long as we are both alive, we do not abandon one another. Therefore, even if you wish to send him to the Himalayas, kill me first and then send him."

Having spoken thus, and demonstrating: "Great King, it was not out of a desire not to follow your word that we remained silent; rather, seeing a fault in the discourse, we did not speak," he recited these two verses:
"Indeed, one should not avoid censure altogether, O Lord of Men, for people are diverse and must be associated with.
For by the very same means by which one person gains praise, by that same means another gains a censurer."
“The whole world is thought-conceived and over-conceived; the whole world possesses thought within this very thought.
All beings are diverse with their individual thoughts; who here can act according to the will of another’s thought?
In this regard, O Great King, it is said: “One should thoroughly avoid [blame]. For indeed, blame is not easily avoided. Various...
"People have diverse inclinations. By whatever virtue, such as moral conduct (*sīla*), one person receives praise, by that very same thing another receives blame.
For instance, among the *kinnaras* we are praised for our talk, yet among humans we are blamed for it;
thus, blame is indeed difficult to avoid. So how shall I receive praise from you?

"O Great King, 'the whole world is measured by mind' means that an ignoble person is defined by a mind such as the intention to take life, whereas a noble person is defined by a mind such as the intention to abstain from taking life;
thus, the meaning is that the whole world is measured by mind, by its mental states.
Furthermore, 'mindful of mind within mind' means that the whole world is called 'mindful of mind' by virtue of its own inferior or superior state of mind."
"Individual minds" means separate minds; all beings are distinguished by their manifold variety.
Among them, which one—whether yours, another's, or someone like me or a *kiṃnara*—could possibly act according to the mind of another?
Therefore, do not be angry with me, thinking, "This one does not act according to my will. For all beings proceed according to their own minds, O Deva.
The *kimpurisa* taught the Dhamma to the king.
The king, filled with joy at the thought, "This wise *kinnara* speaks only the truth," recited this final verse:
"The *kimpurisa* and his wife remained silent; it was only when he was terrified by fear that he spoke."
“Thus now released, happy and healthy, for among men it is speech alone that is meaningful and brings benefit.

In this context, “for among men it is speech alone that is meaningful and brings benefit” means that for these beings, speech—that is, their words—is itself what is meaningful and conducive to welfare.
The king, having had the kinnaras seated in a golden cage, summoned the hunter himself and said, “Go, my man!”

"Release him right where he was seized," he commanded. The Great Being then gave this illustration: "Teacher, thus it is that Kinnaras are liberated by speaking well-spoken words at the proper time after having guarded their speech; but you, by speaking poorly, have fallen into great suffering.
Having shown this example, he said, "Teacher, do not fear; I shall give you back your life."
He comforted him, saying, "Furthermore, you must protect me. When he said, "The conjunction of the constellations has not yet occurred," [the king] spent the day.

Then, immediately after the middle watch of the night, having had a dead sheep brought, and having dismissed him without anyone knowing by saying, "Brāhmaṇa, go wherever you wish and live," he performed a sacrifice with the sheep's flesh and closed the gate.
Having delivered this teaching on the Dhamma, the Teacher said, "Monks, it is not only now;

in the past as well, Kokālika was destroyed by his own speech," and he then identified the Jātaka: "At that time, Kaḷārapiṅgala was Kokālika, and the wise man of Takkasilā was none other than myself."
The eighth is the commentary on the Takkāriya Jātaka.
[482] 9. The commentary on the Rurumigarāja Jātaka:
"I shall give him that excellent village"—this the Teacher spoke while dwelling in the Veḷuvana monastery concerning Devadatta.
It is said that when the monks said to him, "Friend, Teacher Devadatta has been very helpful to you;

it was by relying on the Tathāgata that you received the going-forth, mastered the Three Piṭakas, and attained gain and honor," he replied, "Friends, the Teacher did not do me even as much benefit as a blade of grass;
I went forth by myself, and I mastered the Three Piṭakas by myself."
“I learned it and myself attained gain and honor,” he said. In the Hall of Truth, the monks began a discussion:
“Friends, Devadatta is ungrateful; he does not acknowledge what has been done for him.
The Teacher approached and asked, “Monks, what discussion are you having as you sit gathered here? When they replied, “This one,” he said, “Monks, Devadatta is not [ungrateful].”
"Even now he is ungrateful; even in the past he was ungrateful indeed. Even when I gave him his life in the past, he did not recognize even a fraction of my virtue.
Having said this, she related a story of the past.
In the past, while Brahmadatta was reigning in Bārāṇasī, a certain merchant of eighty crores of wealth, having obtained a son, [acted thus].
Having given him the name Mahādhanaka, his parents did not have him learn any craft at all, thinking, "My son will become weary while learning a craft.
He knew nothing other than singing, dancing, instrumental music, eating, and drinking.
When he reached maturity, his parents united him with a suitable wife and then passed away. Following their demise, he...
Surrounded by women, gamblers, drunkards, and others, he contracted debts through various avenues of misfortune.
Unable to repay them and being pressed by his creditors, he thought: "What is the use of my life?
Having become like another person in this single existence, death is better for me. He said to the creditors: "Come, take your debt-bonds and go."
“I have family wealth buried on the bank of the Ganges; I will give it to you. They went with him.
As if pointing out the location of the treasure, saying, “The wealth is here,” he fled and threw himself into the Ganges, intending to die.
Being carried away by the fierce current, he cried out in piteous lamentation.

At that time, the Great Being, having been reborn in the womb of a Ruru deer, abandoned his retinue and lived all alone at the bend of the Ganges in a delightful mango grove interspersed with *sāla* trees, where the blossoms were in full bloom, while observing the Uposatha.
The skin of his body was the color of well-polished gold plates; his hands and feet appeared as if treated with lac dye; and his tail...

His tail was like a yak’s tail, his horns were like silver tassels, his eyes were like well-polished jewel-beads, and his face, when he opened it, was like a red woolen ball placed upon a stand. Such was his appearance.
At the hour of midnight, hearing that sound of compassion, he thought, "The voice of a human being is heard; while I am still alive..."
Thinking, "Let him die; I shall give him my life," he rose from his bed of leaves, went to the riverbank, and comforted him, saying, "O man, do not fear; I shall give you your life.
Cutting through the current, he carried him on his back to the shore, brought him to his own dwelling, gave him various fruits, and after two or three days had passed...
“O man, I will lead you out from this forest and place you on the road to Bārāṇasī; you shall go there in safety.
However, do not tell either the king or the king’s chief minister that a golden deer dwells at such-and-such a place for the sake of wealth,” he said. He replied, “Very well, master.”
The Great Being, having obtained his promise, placed him upon his back, set him down on the road to Bārāṇasī, and turned back.
On the very day he entered Bārāṇasī, at dawn, the king’s chief queen, named Khemā, saw in a dream a golden-colored deer teaching her the Dhamma; she thought: “If such a one as this...”
“If that golden-hued deer does not exist, I shall not see it even in a dream; it must certainly exist. I will inform the king.
She approached the king and said, “Great King, I wish to see the golden-hued deer; I desire to hear the Dhamma from the golden-hued deer.
If I obtain this, I shall live; if not, there is no life for me. The king—
Having comforted him and said, "If such a thing exists in the human world, you shall obtain it," he summoned the brahmins and asked,
"Are there indeed deer of golden hue? When they replied, "Yes, Your Majesty,
there are," he placed a purse containing a thousand coins upon a golden staff on the back of a decorated elephant and declared that whoever should point out a golden-colored deer would receive it.
Desiring to give that elephant, along with a golden casket containing a thousand gold pieces and even more besides, he had a verse inscribed upon a golden plate, summoned a minister, and said:
“Come, my dear, speak this verse to the inhabitants of the city in my name.
Thus he spoke the first verse of this Jātaka:
“I shall grant him an excellent village and adorned women—whoever tells me of that deer, the supreme among deer.
The minister, taking a golden plate, had this proclamation made throughout the entire city. Then that merchant’s son [entered] Bārāṇasī...
As he was entering, having heard that story, he went to the minister and said, "I shall describe such a deer to the king;

show me to the king. The minister descended from the back of the elephant, led him into the presence of the king, and presented him, saying, "It is said, O King, that this man will describe that deer to you. The king said, "Is it true?"
“Ho there, men! he called out, and asked. He replied, “It is true, Great King; give this glory to me,” and speaking thus, he uttered the second verse:
“Give me a choice village and adorned women;
I shall show you the deer of Migamakkhi, the most excellent of deer.”
Having heard that, the king was pleased with the betrayer of friends and asked, “Ho! Where does that deer dwell?
When he replied, “At such-and-such a place, Your Majesty,” the king made that very man his guide and went to that place with a great retinue.
Then the betrayer said to him, “Your Majesty, have the army settle down,” and when they had settled down...
“Your Majesty, this golden deer lives in this forest,” he said, extending his hand to point it out, and spoke the third verse:
“In this grove of trees, mangoes and sal trees are in bloom;
Covered with indragopaka insects, there stands this deer.”
In that context, "covered with *indagopaka* insects" means that the ground of this forest grove is covered with a species of grass the color of *indagopaka* insects—
red and pleasant to the touch— and is as soft as the belly of a hare; by this,
he shows that "he stands here" in this delightful forest grove.

Having heard his words, the king commanded his ministers: “Without giving that deer any chance to escape, quickly surround the forest thicket with men bearing weapons in their hands. Having done so, they raised a great clamor.
The king stood to one side with a few attendants, while the other remained not far away. Hearing that noise, the Great Being—
He thought, "The sound of this great army is immense; surely these men must be afraid of me.
Rising up, he surveyed the entire assembly, and seeing the place where the king stood, he thought, "Safety will be found for me only at the very spot where the king stands;
it is fitting that I go right there. Having thus reflected, he set out toward the king.
Seeing him approaching, the king thought, "This deer comes with the strength of an elephant, moving as if leaping;
having strung my bow and frightened this deer, if he flees, I shall pierce him, weaken him, and capture him.
Having thus fixed his bow, he stood facing the Bodhisatta. To illustrate this matter, the Teacher spoke these two verses:
“Having made his bow free from trembling and having fixed an arrow, he drew near.
But the deer, seeing the king, addressed him from afar:
‘Wait, O Great King! Do not shoot me, O bull among charioteers!’”
"Who indeed told you this, that 'here this deer stands'?
Therein, "having made it non-dual" means having made it one and the same with both the bowstring and the arrow.
"Having aimed" means having fixed [the arrow]. "Wait" means: "Stop, Great King; do not shoot me; catch me alive."
He spoke with sweet human speech.
The king, captivated by his sweet words, lowered his bow and stood there out of respect.
The Great Being also approached the king, exchanged pleasant greetings, and stood to one side. The great multitude also [laid down] all their weapons.
Having abandoned him and returned, he surrounded the king. At that moment, as if shaking a golden bell, the Great Being asked the king in a sweet voice, "Who indeed told you, 'This deer stands here'?
At that moment, the wicked man stepped back a little and stood right within earshot. The king thought, "It was by this man that I was shown."
Speaking thus, he recited the sixth verse:
“This man of evil conduct stands far away, calling out ‘Friend!’.
He told me this: ‘The deer is standing right here.’”
In that context, "one of evil conduct" means one who has abandoned proper behavior.
Having heard this, the Great Being rebuked that betrayer of friends and, addressing the king, spoke the seventh verse:
"It seems they say truly here in this world, O man, that some people..."
"A log that has been washed ashore is better than a certain kind of man.
In this context, "washed ashore" means brought out [of the water]. "A certain kind of man" refers to a treacherous friend or a wicked person;
even if such a person were washed ashore while falling into the water, he would certainly not be better. For a log leads to benefit in many ways.
"But a wicked person who betrays friends leads to one's ruin; therefore, the ancient wise men said that even a piece of wood is better than such a person.
Yet, I have not acted upon their words.
Having heard this, the king spoke the other verse:
“Ruru, whom do you reproach among the deer, among the birds, or even among humans?
For a most unusual fear has seized me upon hearing that human voice speaking?
Therein, he asked: “Whom do you reproach—among the deer, or among the birds, or among humans?”
“*Bhayaṃ hi maṃ vindati* means that fear overcomes me; I am no longer master of myself, as if I were a slave to fear.
*Anapparūpaṃ* means great.
Then the Great Being, showing that “O Great King, I do not blame the deer, nor the bird, but I blame the human,” spoke the ninth verse:
“The raft that I was carrying, drifting upon the great waters of the Ganges with its swift current—because of that, fear came upon me.
Truly, O King, association with the wicked is suffering.
Therein, *vāhane* means in the flow of the Ganges, capable of carrying whatever falls into it. *Mahodake salile* means in the great water.
The meaning is "in the great water. By both [phrases], he demonstrates the vastness of the water carried by the Ganges.

"On that account," Great King, "that man who was pointed out to me by you—this very man, while being swept away by the Ganges, was rescued by me at the hour of midnight as he cried out with a piteous cry;
on that account, this fear has come upon me today because of those who are not true men."
“Meeting, O Great King, is indeed suffering.
Having heard this, the king became angry with him and thought, “He does not recognize the merit of one who has been so very helpful; I shall pierce him and bring about his death.
He then spoke the tenth verse: “I shall discharge at this four-footed bird, which cleaves the body, an arrow into its heart.”
“I blame that betrayer of friends who does what should not be done, he who did not recognize such a deed as it was being committed.

Therein, *catuppattaṃ* means possessed of four wing-feathers. *Vihaṅgamaṃ* means one who travels through the sky. *Tanucchidaṃ* means the cutting of the body. *Ossajāmi* means “I release [this arrow] into his heart.
Then the Great Being, thinking, “May this man not perish because of me,” spoke the eleventh verse:
“O Lord of Men, the virtuous never praise the execution of either the wise man or the fool.
Let that one of evil nature go home as he pleases, and give him back what was lost to him;
and I shall be at your service.”
In this context, "according to his wish" (*kāmaṃ*) means: let him go to his own home according to his desire.
"And give him what he has lost" means: give him that which you previously told him, "I will give this to you.
"Acting according to his wish" (*kāmakaro*) means acting according to his desire; do whatever you wish—whether eat my meat or turn me into a game animal for sport—in all respects.
The meaning is: "We shall act in accordance with them.
Having heard this, the king, with a joyful mind, spoke the following verse in praise of the Great Being:
"Truly, that Ruru is one among the virtuous who does not betray a human being when he has been betrayed."
"Let that man of evil character go home as he pleases; whatever has been lost by him, I give that to him, and I grant you freedom to act according to your will.
In this context, "you are one of the wise" means you are certainly among the hundreds of the learned. "Freedom to act according to your will" refers to my [granting] your discourse on the Dhamma.

Having gained confidence, he granted the Great Being a boon, saying: "I grant you freedom from fear and the power to act as you wish; from this day forth, dwell without fear, according to your pleasure.
Then the Great Being, reflecting that "O Great King, human beings indeed speak one thing with their mouths but do another with their bodies," spoke these two verses:
“The cries of jackals and the calls of birds are easy to understand,
O King, but the speech of humans is even more difficult to discern.
Even if a person thinks, ‘He is my relative,’ or ‘He is my friend,’ or ‘He is my companion’;”
“He who was formerly well-disposed, but afterwards becomes otherwise.
Having heard this, the king said, “O King of Beasts, do not think thus of me; for even if I were to abandon my kingdom, I would not relinquish the boon granted to you.
Have faith in me! And he gave him the boon. The Great Being, receiving the boon from him—
Beginning with himself, he chose the boon of granting fearlessness to all sentient beings.
The king, having granted that boon, led the Bodhisatta into the city; after having both the Great Being and the city adorned, he had the Great Being teach the Dhamma to the queen.
Beginning with the queen, the Great Being taught the Dhamma to the king and the royal assembly in sweet human speech.
Having instructed the king in the ten duties of a king and exhorted the great multitude, he entered the forest and made his dwelling surrounded by herds of deer.
The king caused a drum to be beaten throughout the city, proclaiming: "I grant safety to all living beings.
From that time forth, there was no one at all capable of even raising a hand against the deer and birds.
A herd of deer was devouring the crops of the people, and no one was able to stop them.
The great multitude went to the royal courtyard and protested. To explain this matter, the Teacher spoke this verse:
“The people of the countryside have gathered, and the townspeople have gathered;”
“The deer are eating the crops; may Your Majesty restrain them.
Therein, “may Your Majesty restrain them” means: may Your Majesty restrain that herd of deer.
Having heard this, the king spoke these two verses:
“Let the province perish, and let even the kingdom perish;
yet I would never deceive Ruru after having granted him the gift of safety.
Let my province not exist, and let even the kingdom perish.”
"But I would never speak a falsehood after having granted a boon to the king of deer.

In this context, "Let my kingdom be mine" means: "Granted that my realm might not belong to me; yet I would never, having given the gift of safety to the golden-hued king of the ruru deer, prove false to it.
When the great multitude heard the king's words, they were unable to say anything and withdrew. That story spread far and wide.

When he heard this, the Great Being gathered the herd of deer together and, after admonishing them, "From now on, do not eat the crops of humans," he had it proclaimed to the people: "Let them place leaf-signs in their own fields.
They did so, and because of that sign, the deer have not eaten the crops up to the present day.
Having delivered this Dhamma teaching, the Teacher said, "Monks, it is not only now; even in the past, Devadatta was ungrateful," and he concluded the Jātaka, identifying the births:
"At that time, Devadatta was the merchant's son, Ānanda was the king, and I myself was the king of the ruru deer."
The ninth: The Commentary on the Rurumiga-jātaka.
10. The Commentary on the Sarabha-miga-jātaka.
"Man indeed should hope..."—this was spoken by the Teacher while dwelling at Jetavana, concerning a question asked by himself in brief.
He spoke concerning the detailed exposition given by the General of the Dhamma. But when did the Teacher ask the Elder the question in brief?
At the Descent from the Heavens. Herein, this is the summary of the sequential account:
When the sandalwood bowl belonging to the Rājagaha merchant was taken by the Venerable Piṇḍola Bhāradvāja through his psychic power, the Teacher [addressed] the bhikkhus...

He prohibited the performance of miracles through psychic power (*iddhipāṭihāriya*). Then the heretics, thinking, “The ascetic Gotama has prohibited the performance of miracles through psychic power; now he himself will not perform them either,” became dejected.
When their own disciples asked them, “Venerable sirs, why do you not take up the bowl by means of psychic power? they replied, “This is not for us, friends.”
"It would have been difficult; moreover, who would have revealed their own qualities of smoothness and fineness for the sake of a wretched wooden bowl?
We did not take it, but the recluses, the sons of the Sakyans, took it by displaying psychic power out of greed.
Do not think, 'The performance of psychic power was a burden to us'; let alone the disciples of the recluse Gotama."
"But if we so desire, we shall display our psychic power alongside the ascetic Gotama;
for if the ascetic Gotama performs one miracle, we shall perform a double.
Having heard this, the monks reported it to the Blessed One, saying, "Venerable Sir, it seems the sectarians intend to perform a miracle."

The Teacher said, “Bhikkhus, let them do it; I too shall do it. Hearing this, Bimbisāra came and asked the Blessed One, “Venerable Sir, will you indeed perform a miracle? “Yes, Great King,” he replied.
“But, Venerable Sir, has not a training rule been laid down? “Great King, that was laid down by me for my disciples; for Buddhas—”

"But there is no training rule [prohibiting it]. For just as, Great King, in your own garden, flowers and fruits are forbidden to others but not to you—it should be understood that this case is exactly like that. "But where, venerable sir, will you perform the miracle?
"At the foot of the Kaṇḍama tree at the gate of the city of Sāvatthī. "What must we do there?"
“Nothing at all, Great King. On the following day, the Teacher, having finished his meal, set out on his alms-round.
People asked, “Venerable sir, where is the Teacher going?

The monks replied to them, “To perform the Twin Miracle that crushes the sectarians at the foot of the Kaṇḍama tree by the gate of the city of Sāvatthī. The great multitude exclaimed, “It is truly wonderful!”
Thinking, "A miracle will surely take place; we shall see it," he abandoned his house doors and went along with the Teacher.

The followers of other sects, thinking, "We too shall perform a miracle at the place where the ascetic Gotama performs his miracle," followed right after the Teacher along with their own attendants. The Teacher, traveling by stages, arrived at Sāvatthī.
When the king asked, "Venerable sir, will you perform a miracle? he replied, "I shall.
When the king asked, "On what day, venerable sir? he said, "On the seventh day from now, on the full moon of Āsāḷha.
"Shall I build a pavilion, venerable sir? "No need, Great King; at the place where I perform my miracle, Sakka, the King of the Devas, will create a jeweled pavilion twelve yojanas in extent."
“He will perform it,” [the king said]. “Shall I have this proclamation made throughout the city, venerable sir? “Have it proclaimed, Great King.
The king had Dhammaghosaka mounted on the back of a decorated state elephant and announced:
“The Blessed One, it is said, will perform a miracle that crushes the sectarians at the foot of the Kaṇḍama tree at the gate of the city of Sāvatthī on the seventh day from now. Up to this point...

On the sixth day, he made a proclamation every day. The heretics, thinking, "It will take place at the foot of the Kaṇḍama tree," paid their owners money and had the mango trees cut down in the vicinity of Sāvatthī.
On the full-moon day, Dhammaghosaka proclaimed early in the morning, "Today there will be a miracle of the Blessed One. Through the power of the deities, throughout the whole of Jambudīpa—
It was as if a proclamation had been made from the gate. Whosoever conceived the thought of going, each perceived themselves as having already arrived at Sāvatthī;
thus the assembly became twelve yojanas in extent.
At dawn, the Teacher set out to enter Sāvatthī for alms. A park-keeper named Kaṇḍa, who was about to go for his own meal—
Carrying a large mango fruit as big as a water-jar for the king, he saw the Teacher at the city gate and, thinking, "This is truly suitable for the Tathāgata," he gave it to him.
The Teacher accepted it, sat down right there to one side, and after eating it, said:
"Ānanda, plant this mango seed in this spot for the park-keeper."
"Give it," he said, "and this shall be known as Kaṇḍamba. The Elder did so.
The park-keeper cleared away the soil and planted it. At that very moment, the roots broke through the bone and descended;
a red sprout the size of a plow-handle rose up, and even as the great multitude looked on, it grew with a trunk fifty cubits long and branches fifty cubits wide, reaching a height of—
And a mango tree a hundred cubits high appeared; at that very moment, its flowers and fruits emerged.
Surrounded by bees and laden with golden-colored fruit, it stood filling the sky;
when struck by the wind, sweet ripe fruits fell. The monks who arrived later came having already partaken of them.
At the time of evening, Sakka, the king of the gods, while reflecting, realized, "The task of constructing the Jewel Pavilion for the Teacher is our responsibility.
Having understood this, he dispatched the divine son Vissakamma and had him construct a pavilion made of the seven precious gems, twelve yojanas in extent and covered with blue lotuses.
Thus, the devas of ten thousand world-systems assembled. The Teacher [proceeded to] the crushing of the heretics, which is not shared [with others].
Having performed the Twin Miracle with his disciples and perceiving the state of faith in the great multitude, he descended and sat upon the Buddha’s throne and taught the Dhamma.
Twenty koṭis of living beings drank the drink of the Deathless.
Then, reflecting on where previous Buddhas had gone after performing miracles, he knew it was to the Tāvatiṃsa heaven.
Rising from his Buddha-seat, placing his right foot upon the summit of Mount Yugandhara and treading with his left foot upon the peak of Sineru,
he entered the rains retreat upon the yellow sandalwood stone at the foot of the Pāricchattaka tree and taught the Abhidhamma Piṭaka to the devas for the duration of those three months.
The assembly, unaware of where the Teacher had gone, thought, "We shall go there as soon as we see him."
He dwelt right there for three months. When the invitation ceremony (*pavāraṇā*) was approaching, the Elder Mahāmoggallāna went and informed the Blessed One.
Then the Teacher asked him, "But where is Sāriputta now?
"Venerable Sir, having gained confidence through the miracle, he is dwelling at the gate of the city of Saṅkassa together with five hundred monks who have gone forth."
“Moggallāna, on the seventh day from now I shall descend at the gate of the city of Sāṅkāśya; let those who wish to see the Tathāgata assemble together in the city of Sāṅkāśya.

Having consented with “Very well,” the Elder returned and announced this to the assembly, and in a single moment he brought the entire company from Sāvatthī, a distance of thirty yojanas, to the city of Sāṅkāśya.
Having completed his rains retreat and performed the *pavāraṇā*, the Teacher announced to Sakka, "Great King, I shall go to the world of men.
Sakka summoned Vissakamma and said, "Construct three stairways for the Ten-Powered One’s journey to the world of men.
He then constructed the top of the stairs at the summit of Sineru, the main staircase at the gate of Saṅkassa city, and [the middle one] in between.
He had three staircases constructed: one made of jewels, one side made of silver, and one side made of gold, surrounded by railings made of the seven precious gems.
Having performed the miracle of revealing the world, the Teacher descended by the central staircase made of jewels.
Sakka took hold of his bowl and robe, while Suyāma held a yak-tail fan.
Sahampati Mahābrahmā held the parasol, while the deities of the ten thousand world-systems honored [the Buddha] with divine perfumes, garlands, and other offerings.
As the Teacher stepped onto the first step of the staircase, the Elder Sāriputta was the very first to pay him homage, followed by the rest of the assembly.
At that gathering, the Teacher thought: "Moggallāna is renowned as one 'possessed of psychic power,' and Upāli..."
“‘One who upholds the Vinaya’—but Sāriputta’s quality of great wisdom was not yet manifest [to the world]. Thinking, ‘There is no one else besides myself who is equal to him in wisdom;
I shall make his quality of wisdom known,’ he first asked a question within the domain of ordinary worldlings (puthujjana), and only the worldlings were able to answer it.
Then he asked a question within the domain of stream-enterers (sotāpanna).”
He asked him, and they too replied that he was indeed a stream-enterer; the worldlings did not know.

In this manner, he asked questions concerning once-returners, non-returners, those whose taints were destroyed, and the great disciples; in each case, those below did not know, while only those above could answer.
Even when questioned regarding the subject of the chief disciples, only the chief disciples [could answer].
They spoke, while others did not understand. Then he asked a question within the domain of the Elder Sāriputta;
the Elder alone explained it, while others did not understand.
The people, asking, "Who is this elder who converses with the Teacher? [learned that he was] the Dhammasenāpati.

Hearing that he was named the Elder Sāriputta, they exclaimed, "Oh, how great is his wisdom! From that time forth, the Elder’s quality of great wisdom became manifest among gods and men. Then the Teacher said to him:
"And those who have mastered the Dhamma, and those many here who are still in training;..."
“O Noble One, being asked, please explain to me their prudent conduct.
Having thus asked a question concerning the domain of the Buddha, he said: “Sāriputta, how should the meaning of this which has been spoken in brief be understood in detail?
The Elder, having reflected on the question, [thought]: “The Teacher [is asking me] regarding those in training and those beyond training...”
He asked, "What is the path by which the bhikkhus have come? Being free from doubt regarding the question, he was, however, uncertain as to the Teacher’s intention, thinking:
