"The 'path by which they have come' can be explained in many ways, such as by way of the aggregates; which way shall I explain it so that I may grasp the Teacher’s intention?
The Teacher [perceived]: "Sāriputta is free from doubt regarding the question, but he is uncertain as to the intention..."
"But it is doubtful to me; if I do not give him the method (*naya*), he will not be able to explain it.
I shall give him the method," [the Teacher] thought, and while giving the method, he said, "Sāriputta, consider this as having come to be. It occurred to him thus:

"Having grasped my intention, when Sāriputta explains, he will explain by way of the aggregates (*khandha*). Simultaneously with the giving of the method to the Elder, [the Elder attained realization].
That question presented itself through a hundred methods and a thousand methods. Standing upon the method given by the Teacher, he spoke on a question within the domain of the Buddha.
The Teacher taught the Dhamma to an assembly twelve yojanas in extent. Thirty koṭis of living beings drank the drink of the Deathless.
Having dismissed the assembly, the Teacher wandered on his journey and, proceeding by stages, arrived at Sāvatthī; on the following day, in Sāvatthī—
Having walked for alms and returned from his almsround, and after the monks had performed their duties, he entered the Fragrant Chamber.
In the evening, the monks sat in the Dhamma Hall discussing the virtues of the Elder:
"Friends, Sāriputta is of great wisdom, of vast wisdom, of swift wisdom, of sharp wisdom, of penetrative wisdom; by the One of Ten Powers, he was [instructed] with brevity..."
“He explained the question he had been asked in detail. The Teacher approached and asked, “Monks, about what conversation are you gathered here now?
When they replied, “About this very one,” he said, “Monks, it is not only now;
in the past as well, he explained in detail the meaning of what was spoken in brief. Having said this, he related a story of the past.
In the past, when Brahmadatta was reigning in Bārāṇasī, the Bodhisatta was reborn in the womb of a sarabha deer and lived in the forest.
The king was a skilled hunter, endowed with great strength, and he did not even count another human being as a "human.
One day, having gone out for the hunt, he said to his ministers: "Whichever side a deer flees toward, [that person shall receive the reward]."
"Therefore, that punishment must be given. They thought, "Sometimes they shoot at a deer standing in the middle, sometimes at one that has risen up, and sometimes even at one that is fleeing;
but today, by whatever means possible, we shall bring [the deer] right to the place where the king is standing.
Having thought this and made an agreement, they gave the king the main road. They [set up] a great...
Surrounding the monastery, they struck the ground with clubs and other weapons.
At the very beginning, the sarabha deer rose up, circled the monastery three times, and looked for a place to flee.
Seeing that in all other directions men stood packed shoulder-to-shoulder, bow to bow, without any gaps, he saw only one opening at the spot where the king was standing.
With his eyes opened wide, he went toward the king as if scattering sand before him.
Seeing that it had arrived so swiftly, the king raised his arrow and pierced it. Indeed, the śarabha deer are experts at evading arrows;
when an arrow comes toward them, they slow their pace and stand still, but when it comes from behind, they move with great speed.
Those coming from the front galloped on; those coming from above lowered their backs; those coming from the side moved slightly away;
those coming toward his belly turned around and fell; and when the arrow had passed through, they fled with the speed of a cloud torn by the wind.
When that [deer] turned around and fell, the king cried out, "I have struck the sarabha deer! The sarabha—

Rising up, he fled with the speed of the wind. The circle of warriors broke apart, and the ministers standing on both sides, seeing the deer fleeing, gathered together and asked, "On whose side did the deer leap? "On the King's side.
"The King says, 'I have been struck! Who struck him? We are free from blame, sirs!"
"O King, you have been pierced by the earth! they said, and they played various kinds of games with the king. The king thought, "These people are mocking me;

they do not know my measure. So, putting on his lower garment tightly, he took up his sword and went on foot, charging forward with speed, thinking, "I shall catch the sarabha. Then, seeing him, the sarabha pursued him for three leagues.
The sarabha entered the forest, and the king also entered it. There, on the path where the sarabha deer traveled, there was a great pit for rotten corpses measuring sixty cubits in size;
it was filled with water thirty cubits deep and concealed by grass.
The sarabha, having smelled the smell of the water, recognized the nature of the pit and retreated a short distance before proceeding. But the king—
As he was walking straight ahead, he fell into it.
Not hearing the sound of his footsteps, the sarabha turned back; not seeing him, and knowing that he must have fallen into a pit of hell, he came over and looked down.
Seeing him struggling in the deep water where there was no footing, he [considered] the offense committed by him.
Without taking it to heart, moved by compassion, he thought: "May the king not perish while I am still looking on;
I shall liberate him from this suffering. Standing at the edge of the pit, he said, "Do not fear, Great King;
I shall free you from this great misery," and as if exerting himself to rescue his own beloved son, for the sake of lifting him out, [he took] a stone...
Having prepared himself, thinking, "I shall pierce [the mountain]," he encountered the king who had come there.

He lifted the king up from the sixty-cubit deep pit, comforted him, placed him on his back, carried him out from the forest, set him down not far from the army, gave him instruction, and established him in the five precepts.
Unable to live without the Great Being, the king said: "Master, King of the Sarabha Deer!"
"Come with me to Bārāṇasī; I shall give you the sovereignty over the twelve-league city of Bārāṇasī, so rule it.
"Great King, we are animals; I have no need for sovereignty.

If you have any affection for me, then while guarding the precepts I have given you, cause the inhabitants of the kingdom to guard them as well. Having thus exhorted him, he entered the forest itself.
With eyes filled with tears as he recollected his virtues, he reached the army and, surrounded by his troops, entered the city.
There, he caused the drum of the Dhamma to be beaten, proclaiming: "From this day forth, let all the inhabitants of this city observe the five precepts.
As for the Great Being himself, however, he did not mention to anyone the service he had performed; instead, having eaten a meal of various choice flavors that evening, he—
Having lain upon his decorated couch, at the time of dawn, remembering the virtues of the Great Being, he rose and sat cross-legged on the back of the bed.
With a heart full of rapture, he uttered these six verses in exultation:
“A wise man should indeed aspire; he should not become despondent.”
“I see myself as I have become just as I desired.
A wise person should indeed aspire and not lose heart;
I see myself as one who has been pulled from the water onto dry land.”
“A person should indeed strive; a wise one should not despair.
I see myself as I have become exactly as I wished.
“A person should indeed strive; a wise one should not despair.”
I see myself as one who has been pulled from the water onto dry land.
“Even when brought to suffering, a wise person should not cut off hope for the arrival of happiness;
for many contacts, both harmful and beneficial, come upon one before death has arrived.”
“Even that which was unthought of comes to pass, and even that which was thought of perishes;
for riches, whether for a woman or a man, do not arise through mere thinking.
In this context, “a man should indeed hope” means that one should maintain hope in one’s own actions, without performing deeds that cut off such hope.
One should not be despondent. "Just as they wish": this indicates that I indeed wished for emergence from the sixty-fathom hell, and thus I was born exactly so;
I have emerged from there. "Both harmful and beneficial" refers to painful contacts and pleasant contacts;
it also means "contacts of death and contacts of life," for to sentient beings, the contact of death is harmful and the contact of life is beneficial.
This shows that even for those who have not thought of it and have not imagined it, the touch of death arrives.
"Even though it was not thought" means: "I did not think, 'I shall fall into a pit,' but I did think, 'I shall kill the sarabha';
now, however, my thought has perished, and what was unthought has come to pass. "Wealth" refers to the retinue of fame. These do not arise from thought.
Therefore, one who possesses wisdom should exert effort alone; for indeed, even the inconceivable comes to pass for one who is diligent.
Even as he was thus uttering this inspired utterance (*udāna*), the dawn broke.

And the royal chaplain, having come early in the morning to inquire after his well-being, stood at the palace gate; hearing the sound of that inspired song, he thought: "The king went hunting yesterday."
There, having missed the sarabha deer, and being mocked by his ministers,
thinking with the pride of a kshatriya, "I shall kill and bring it back," he will pursue it and fall into a sixty-cubit pit;
then, the compassionate king of the sarabhas, disregarding the king's offense, will lift the king out— for that reason, I think.

“He utters an inspired utterance. Having heard this inspired utterance of the brahmin, which was complete in its phrasing, the reason for what had been done by King Sarabha became as clear as the reflection of one’s own face when looking into a well-polished mirror.
He struck at the door with his fingernail. The king asked, “Who is this? “I am your majesty’s domestic priest,” he replied. Then, to him—
Having opened the door, he said, "Come this way, Teacher. He entered, offered his victory-greetings to the king, and standing to one side, said:
"Great King, I know the deed you committed in the forest. While you were pursuing a single sarabha deer, you fell into a pit;
then that sarabha, having fashioned a bridge of stone, rescued you from the pit. You—[that very person]..."
Having said, "Recalling his virtue, he uttered this inspired utterance," he spoke these two verses:
"O Sarabha, in the mountain fastness, whom you formerly followed;
you now live off the prowess of one whose mind is undaunted."
“He who rescued you from those difficult-to-cross hells, having fashioned a harness of stone for you;
he who liberated you, brought to suffering at the mouth of death—he was that deer of undaunted heart whom you speak of.
In this context, *anusarī* means he followed after [you]. *Vikkantaṃ* means having exerted effort for the purpose of pulling [you] out. *Anujīvasi* means...
"You live by means of it; the meaning is that through its power you have obtained your life.
"He rescued" means he pulled [it] out. "You speak of that deer": while sitting here on this magnificent couch, you described that golden *sarabha* deer.
Having heard this, the king thought, "This man did not go hunting with me, yet he knows the entire account. How indeed does he know? I shall question him," and he spoke the ninth verse:
“Were you yourself there at that time, or did someone tell it to you? Are you one whose veil is rent, seeing all things?
Or is your knowledge, O Brahmin, of such a terrifying nature? In this context, “of a terrifying nature” means:
is your knowledge of such a powerful kind that by means of it you know this?
The brahmin, demonstrating that "I am not an omniscient Buddha, yet the meaning of the verses spoken by you appears clearly to me without defiling the phrasing," spoke the tenth verse:
"I was not present there at that time, nor did anyone explain it to me;
yet, O Lord of Men, the wise bring forth the meaning of well-spoken verses even then."

In that context, "well-spoken" means spoken well without corrupting the phrasing (*byañjana*). "They bring forth the meaning" means they bring forth—that is, investigate—the meaning which belongs to them.
The king, being pleased with him, gave him much wealth. From then on, he became devoted to meritorious deeds such as giving;
and the people, likewise becoming devoted to merit, filled heaven itself after they died. Then one day, the king, thinking, "I shall hit the target," [set out].
Taking his domestic priest, he went to the park. At that time, Sakka, the king of the gods, seeing many young devas and celestial maidens, reflected, "What could be the reason for this?
As he investigated, he realized that the king had rescued the Sarabha deer from hell and established him in the precepts.
He understood, "By the power of the king, the great multitude is performing meritorious deeds; because of that, the world of the devas..."
"It is now fulfilled; however, the king has gone to the park to shoot the target.

Having tested him, made him roar the lion's roar, caused him to speak of the virtues of the sarabha deer, and made him recognize my own status as Sakka, I shall stand in the sky, teach the Dhamma, and after speaking of the virtues of loving-kindness and the five precepts, I will depart. Having thus reflected, he—
He went to the park. The king, thinking, "I shall hit the target," strung his bow and fixed an arrow.
At that moment, through his own power, Sakka caused a wild boar to appear between the king and the target.
When the king saw it, he did not release the arrow. Then Sakka, having taken possession of the body of the royal priest, spoke this verse:
“Having taken an arrow that destroys the prowess of enemies upon your bow, why do you hesitate?
Let the discharged arrow swiftly slay the deer; for this is something other than food for the king, O one of excellent wisdom.
Therein, *pattiṃ* means equipped with feathered wings (*vājapattehi*). *Paraviriyaghātiṃ* means that which destroys the strength of others.
"In the bow" means: "Having taken this arrow together with its feathers and having strung it upon the bow, why do you now hesitate?
Let this arrow, released by you with the intent 'Let him be slain,' quickly kill this śarabha.
For "this is food," O King of supreme wisdom, means that the śarabha is the king’s food, his prey.
Then the king spoke this verse:
“Truly, O Brahmin, I understand this as well: that a deer belongs to a Kshatriya.
Out of respect for what was done in the past, I therefore do not kill the Sarabha deer.”

"In this matter, O Brahmin, when you say 'because of what was done by him in the past,' I know this for certain: that the deer is food for the Kshatriya; however, I honor the service previously rendered to me by him, and therefore I do not kill him.
Then Sakka spoke these two verses:
"He is no deer, O Great King; he is Asura Disampati."
“Having slain him, O lord of men, become the sovereign of the immortals. “But if you, O King,
have doubts about slaying the deer Sarabha, your companion— O best of heroes among men,
together with your sons and wife— you shall go to Vetaraṇī, the realm of Yama.”
In that context, "asura" means "this one is an asura"; he speaks with the intention that Sakka is the chief of the asuras.
"Lord of the immortals" (Amarādhipo) means he says: "Having killed this Sakka, you yourself shall become Sakka, the king of the gods.
"Vetaraṇī of Yama" means: "If you do not kill him thinking, 'He is my friend,' then together with your sons and wife, you will [fall] into Yama’s Vetaraṇī hell."
“You will have gone!”—with these words he terrified him.
Then the king spoke two verses:
“Granted, I, all the people of the realm, my sons, my wives, and my circle of friends;”
"Let us go to that Vaitaraṇī of Yama; I would not kill him who has given me his life.
"This deer, in this terrible wilderness, was my sole helper when I was in distress.
Remembering such a prior service, O Great Brahmā, how could I knowingly kill him?"
In this regard, O Brahmin, he says: "He who is the giver of life to me—by whom my dear life was given—must not be killed by me even when I am entering hell;
he is not to be slain, he is blameless. And: "The one who is my slayer in the terrible wilderness"—meaning, while I have entered the dreadful forest alone and without a companion, he is my slayer.
"He is the one who gave me my life; how could I, remembering such a prior service performed by him and knowing his virtue, kill him?
Then Sakka, having moved away from the body of the chaplain and manifested his own form as Sakka, stood in the air and, proclaiming the king's virtue, spoke these two verses:
“O Mittābhirādhī, may you live long indeed! Rule this kingdom with the virtues of Dhamma.
Surrounded by throngs of women, may you rejoice in the realm like Vāsava in the Tāvatiṃsa heaven.
Being free from anger, with a mind always serene, and being one who welcomes all guests and is devoted to giving, [may you rule].”
"Having given and having eaten according to your means, blameless, go to the heavenly abode.
In this context, "pleasing friends" means pleasing and satisfying one's friends, not being treacherous toward them.
"All guests" means treating all righteous recluses and brahmins as guests and visitors, supporting them so that they become worthy of being solicited for alms.
"Blameless," he said, "having rejoiced by performing meritorious deeds such as giving, and being welcomed with joy by the world of the gods, you shall go to the heavenly realm.
Having spoken thus, Sakka advised him, saying, "Great King, I came to take charge of you; you did not allow yourself to be taken charge of. Be heedful! Then he departed for his own abode.
The Teacher, having brought forth this Dhamma teaching, said: "Monks, it is not only now; in the past as well, Sāriputta was [instructed] in brief..."
"Having spoken thus, he understands the meaning in detail. Having said this, he identified the Jātaka:
"At that time, the king was Ānanda, the chaplain was Sāriputta, and I myself was the Sarabha deer.
This concludes the commentary on the Sarabhamiga Jātaka, the tenth.
The Summary of the Jātakas:
Amba, Phandana, Javana, Nārada, Dūta, Kaliṅga;
Akitti, Takkāriya, Ruru, Sarabha—these are thirteen.
The commentary on the Thirteenth Chapter is finished.
14. The Miscellaneous Chapter [484] 1.
The Commentary on the Sālikedāra Jātaka.
“‘The rice-field is well-ripened’—this was spoken by the Teacher while dwelling at Jetavana concerning a monk who supported his mother.
The story of the present will be revealed in the Sāma Jātaka. However, the Teacher summoned that monk and asked, ‘Is it true, monk, that you support a householder?
When he replied, ‘It is true, Venerable Sir,’ the Teacher said, ‘Why...’”
Having said, "They were those," when [the monk] replied, "Venerable sir, they were my mother and father," the Buddha said, "Excellent, bhikkhu!

In the past, even though they were wise birds born from an excellent womb, when their parents grew old, they placed them in a nest and supported them by bringing back food with the tips of their beaks.
Having said this, he related a story of the past.
In the past, a king named Magadha reigned in Rājagaha. At that time, to the northeast of the city, there was a brahmin village called Sāliddiya.

To its northeast lay the fields of Magadha; there, a brahmin of the Kosiya clan residing in Sāliddiya took possession of a field measuring one thousand karīsa and had it sown with rice. When [the crop] had grown...
Furthermore, having had a strong fence built around the crop, he gave five hundred karīsa of land—some measuring fifty karīsa and some sixty karīsa—to his own men for their protection;
then, making the remaining five hundred karīsa of land a wage-earning estate, he gave it to one hired laborer. That man built a hut there.

Having done so, he dwelt there day and night. Now, in the northeastern direction of that field, on a certain mountain ridge, there was a vast forest of *simbali* trees where many hundreds of birds lived.

At that time, the Bodhisatta was reborn in that flock of birds as the son of the king of the birds. Upon reaching maturity, he was handsome, endowed with great strength, and possessed a body as large as the hub of a wagon wheel.
Thus it came to pass. Then, when his father reached old age, he entrusted the community to him, saying, "I am no longer able to travel far;
you must maintain this group. From that day forward, he did not allow his parents to go for alms;
instead, maintaining a flock of birds, he went to the Himalayas and, in a forest of wild *sāli* rice, ate as much as he required.
Having eaten the rice, he would bring back sufficient fodder for his parents when returning, and thus supported them.
Then one day, the dogs informed him: "Previously at this time, rice was ripening in the field of Magadha;
what has grown there now? He replied, "In that case, find out. So he sent two dogs. They went to the field of Magadha...
While descending, they entered the field of the watchman who was guarding it for hire;
having eaten the rice and taken a single ear of rice, they went to the *simbali* grove and, placing the ear of rice at the feet of the Great Being, said, "Such is the rice there.
On the following day, surrounded by his flock of parrots, he went there to that field belonging to the hired man.
Otari. Now, when that man saw the crows eating the rice the following day, he ran hither and thither trying to stop them, but he was unable to prevent them.
The other crows ate as much rice as they desired and went away with empty beaks;
but the crow-king gathered many heads of rice together, and surrounded by them, he brought the food and gave it to his parents.
From the following day onwards, the birds continued to eat the rice right there.
Then that man thought, "If these continue to eat like this for a few more days, nothing will be left; the brahmin will have the rice appraised and make me pay him a debt.
I shall go and inform him. With a handful of rice, he took a similar gift...
Having taken it and gone to Sāliddiyagāma, he saw the brahmin, paid homage to him, and presented the gift.
Standing to one side, when asked, "Sir, is the rice field successful?", he replied, "Yes, brahmin,
it is successful," and spoke these two verses:
“Kosiya, the crows are eating the ripe rice in the field;
I inform you of this, O Brahmā, for I am unable to stop them.
And there is one bird among them who is the most beautiful of all.”
“Having eaten the rice as much as it desires, it goes away taking some with its beak.
In this context, *sampanna* means complete and without deficiency. *Sālikedāra* means a field of rice.
*Sabbasundara* means beautiful in all its parts: red-beaked, with eyes resembling *jiñjuka* berries, red-footed, and marked with three red stripes.
"With his neck encircled, he is the size of a great peacock; having eaten as much rice as he desires, he goes along taking more with his beak.

When the brahmin heard this account, affection arose in him for the king of birds, and he asked the field-guard: "Good man, do you know how to set a snare? "Yes, I know," he replied. Then the brahmin addressed him with a verse:
"Let them set hair-snares, so that the bird may be caught."
“Having seized him alive, bring him into my presence.

In this context, *oḍḍentu* means “let them set out. *Vālapāsāni* refers to nooses made from cords such as horse-tails and the like. *Jīvañca naṃ* means “him while still alive. *Ānayehi* means “bring him.
Having heard that, the field-guardian, pleased because the debt had not been incurred after having the rice valued, went and [seized him] by the horse-tail...
Having calculated [the time], and having observed the landing place of the king of birds, thinking,
"Today he will descend at this spot," he constructed a cage the size of a bowl early the next morning, set a snare, and sat in his hut watching for the arrival of the birds.
Then the king of birds, surrounded by his flock of birds, arrived and— due to his habit of not being greedy for food— at the very spot where he had eaten yesterday...
He descended as if placing his foot into a set snare. Realizing he was bound, he thought:
"If I let out a cry of being caught right now, my relatives will be terrified by fear and flee even without gathering their food;
therefore, I shall endure this until they have finished eating. Once he knew they were well-fed, he was overcome by the fear of death.
Having offered the sacrifice, he let out a loud cry three times. Then all those crows fled.
King Suva lamented, "Among all these kinsmen of mine, not even one has turned back to look; what evil deed have I committed? and spoke this verse:
"These birds, having eaten and drunk, depart; ... [the rest of the verse follows]"
“I am caught by a snare; what evil deed have I committed?
Hearing the cry of the king of hounds being bound and the sound of the dogs leaping into the air, the field-guardian thought, “What can this be?
He descended from his hut, went to the place where the snare was set, and seeing the king of hounds, [thought], “To whom indeed was my snare laid?”
With a joyful heart, thinking, “He himself is bound,” the king released Suva from his bonds,
tied his two feet together, took hold of him firmly, went to the village of Sāliddiya, and gave Suva to the brahmin. Out of intense affection,
the brahmin grasped the Great Being firmly with both hands, seated him on his lap, and spoke these two verses while conversing with him:
“Surely the bellies of others are small, for yours, O bird, is not large at all;
having eaten rice as much as you desire, you go away taking it with your beak.
Have you filled a granary there, or do you bear enmity toward me?”
“Good sir, being asked by me, tell me: where will you store the rice?
In this context, “surely your belly” means: while the bellies of others are merely bellies, your belly is an *atiudara* (an exceedingly large belly).
“Therein” means in that *simbali* forest. “Filled it” means he filled it for the sake of the rainy season. “Store it” means as a hoard.
Having done so, he set it down; there is also a reading, “nidhīyasi.
Having heard that, King Suva spoke the seventh verse in a sweet human voice:
“I have no enmity with you, nor do I have any quarrel with you.”
“I release this debt, I pay this debt; having reached the *koṭasimbalī* tree, I shall bury my treasure there as well—know this, O Kosiya.

Therein, “I release this debt, I pay this debt” means he says, “Having taken your rice, I both release the debt and pay it. “I shall bury my treasure there as well” means that in that *simbalī* grove, I shall also bury a lifelong treasure.
Then the brahmin asked him:
“What kind is your taking of debt, and what kind is the release from debt?
Tell me of the treasure and its hoarding, and then you shall escape from the snare.”
In this context, "giving of debt" means the payment of a debt. "The depositing of a treasure" means the placing of a treasure in storage.
Thus, being questioned by the brahmin, King Suva answered him with these four verses:
"My young sons, O Kosiya, have not yet grown their wings."
“They will support me as their own; therefore, I shall give them a debt.
“My mother and father are aged, worn out, and past their youth;
by supporting them with my mouth, I shall be released from the debt incurred in former lives.”
“Furthermore, there were other birds there, with wings worn out and very weak;
desiring merit, I gave them away—what the wise call ‘a treasure.
Such was my gift of debt, and such was my release from debt.”
“I shall declare the treasure-store; know it thus, O Kosiya.

In this context, *hātūna* means having taken away. “That treasure” refers to that meritorious deed, which the wise call the “following treasure. “Treasure-store” (*nidhinidhāna*) means the store of treasure; there is also a reading “store-treasure” (*nidhānanidhi*), which has the same meaning.
Having heard the Great Being’s discourse on the Dhamma, the brahmin, with a mind full of faith, spoke two verses.
“Truly blessed is this bird, this twice-born one who is most righteous in his Dhamma!
Among certain humans, this Dhamma does not exist.
Enjoy the rice as you wish, together with all your kinsmen!”
"May we see you again, O bird; your sight is dear to me.

Therein, "Eat the rice," he said, offering even a thousand cartloads [of wealth] to him alone, meaning, "Eat from now on without fear. "May we see you" means, "May we see you on other days as well, when you have come of your own accord.
Having thus entreated the Great Being, the brahmin gazed upon him with a gentle heart, like a beloved son, and [removed] the bond from his foot.
Having had him washed and having anointed his feet with oil refined a hundred times, he had him seated on a splendid throne.
He had him eat honeyed parched grain from a golden platter and gave him sugar-water to drink. Then King Suvaṇṇa, saying, "Be heedful, O Brahmin," spoke these words of exhortation:
"Whatever you have eaten and drunk, O ascetic, and whatever pleasure we have found in your presence, Kosiya..."
"Give gifts to those who have laid down the rod; support your aged mother and father.
Therein, "in your own home" means in your dwelling. "Delight" means gladness.
Having heard that, the brahmin, with a joyful mind, uttered this inspired utterance in verse:
“Indeed, good fortune has arisen for me today, since I have seen the most excellent among birds;
having heard the well-spoken words of the Suva bird, I shall perform abundant meritorious deeds.
In this context, *lakkhī* means glory (*siri*), merit (*puñña*), and wisdom (*paññā*).
The Great Being, having refused the thousand measures of dung offered by the brahmin, accepted only eight.

The brahmin, having driven stakes into the ground and handed over his field to him, honored him with perfumes, garlands, and other offerings, and after asking for forgiveness, sent him away, saying, "Go, Master, and comfort your parents who are weeping with tearful faces. Thus he dismissed him.
With a joyful heart, he took the rice-ear, went before his mother and father, and set it down, saying, "Mother and father, arise!
Weeping with tearful faces, they arose; immediately a multitude of gods gathered and asked, "How were you released, O Lord?
He related everything to them in detail. Kosiya too—
Having heard the advice of King Suvaṇṇa, from that time forth he established a great almsgiving for righteous recluses and brahmins.
To clarify this matter, the Teacher spoke the concluding verse:
“Kosiya, joyful and elated, having prepared food and drink;”
“With food and drink, with a serene mind, he satisfied the recluses and brahmins.
Therein, “he satisfied” means he satisfied them by filling vessel after vessel.
Having brought forth this teaching on the Dhamma, the Teacher said: “In this way, bhikkhu, the support of one’s mother and father is indeed for the wise...”
Having said, "The bamboo," he proclaimed the Truths and identified the Jātaka.
At the conclusion of the Truths, that bhikkhu was established in the fruit of stream-entry. At that time, the flock of birds were the Buddha’s assembly; the mother and father were the royal family;
the field-guard was Channa; the brahmin was Ānanda; and I myself was King Suva.
The First Exposition of the Sālikedāra Jātaka.
[485] 2. The Exposition of the Candakinnarī Jātaka:
"Thinking, 'This is being brought to me,'" said this while the Teacher was dwelling at the Nigrodha Monastery in dependence upon the city of Kapilavatthu.
The Teacher spoke concerning Rāhula’s mother while at the royal palace. This Jātaka, however, should be told starting from its distant past (dūrenidāna).
That introductory narrative (nidānakathā) has been told up to the "Lion’s Roar" of Uruvelakassapa in the Laṭṭhivana in the Apaṇṇaka Jātaka;
from there onwards, up to the journey to Kapilavatthu, it will be made clear in the Vessantara Jātaka. The Teacher—
Having sat in his father’s residence and preached the Mahādhammapāla Jātaka during the interval between meals, the Blessed One finished his meal and thought,
"I shall sit in Rāhulamātā’s residence and, extolling her virtues, preach the Candakinnarī Jātaka.
Having had the King take his bowl, he set out for Rāhulamātā’s residence together with the two chief disciples.
At that time, forty thousand dancing girls lived in her presence; among them were more than ninety thousand daughters of the kṣatriya caste.
Having learned of the Tathāgata’s arrival, she had it announced to them, "Let all of you wear only saffron robes.
They did so. The Teacher arrived and sat upon the prepared seat. Then they all—
They cried out all at once, and there was a great sound of lamentation.
Rāhula’s mother, too, having lamented and dispelled her grief, paid homage to the Teacher and sat down with royal devotion and reverence.
The King began to speak of her virtues: "Venerable Sir, when my daughter-in-law heard that you were wearing saffron robes, she [donned] saffron robes herself."
"She lived [in seclusion]; hearing that she had renounced garlands and such, she renounced them; hearing that she slept on the ground, she became one who sleeps only on the ground;
at the time of your own renunciation, being a widow, she did not accept the gifts sent by other kings—thus, her mind is unshakable toward you. In these various ways, he spoke of her virtues.
The Teacher said, "It is no marvel, Great King, that she should now be full of affection for me in my final existence, with a mind unshakable and not to be led by others.
Even when reborn in the womb of an animal, her mind was unshakable toward me and she was not to be led by others.
Having said this, at his request, he related a story of the past.
In the past, while Brahmadatta was reigning in Benares, the Great Being was reborn in the region of the Himalayas in the womb of a Kinnara;
his wife’s name was Candā. Both of them lived on a silver mountain named Canda.
At that time, the King of Benares, having entrusted the kingdom to his ministers, donned two saffron robes and equipped himself with the five weapons.
He entered the Himālaya mountains all alone. While eating deer meat, he wandered along a small river and climbed upward.
During the rainy season, the kinnaras dwelling on Mount Canda do not descend but remain right on the mountain;
they descend only during the summer heat. At that time, the kinnara Candaka was together with his own wife.
Having descended, anointing himself with perfumes at various spots, chewing the pollen of flowers, wearing and wrapping himself in flower-cloths,
playing on swings made of creepers, and singing in a sweet voice, he reached that small river; descending at a certain turning-place,
scattering flowers upon the water, playing in the water, and then putting on his flower-cloths.
Having dressed himself and prepared a flower-seat with sand the color of silver plates, he took a bamboo staff and sat upon the couch.
Then the kinnara Canda played the bamboo flute and sang with a sweet voice.
The kinnarī Candi, stretching out her soft hands, stood not far from him, both dancing and singing. When the king heard their sounds, he—
Not hearing the sound of footsteps, he went slowly, stood in concealment, and upon seeing those two kinnaras, his heart became bound to the kinnarī.
Thinking, "I shall pierce that kinnara, bring him to the end of his life, and dwell together with this one," he remained there and pierced Candaka the kinnara. Overcome by pain, he began to lament.
He spoke these four verses:
“This day, I think, is being brought near, like the blood-red moon;
today I shall give up my life, for my vital breaths are ceasing within the moon.”
“Sinking down, suffering, my heart burns and I am fainting;
because of your grief, O Caṇḍī, I do not grieve from other sorrows.
Like grass or like a forest, I wither away; like a river that is not full, I am drying up.”
“As you grieve for Candi, no other sorrows can compare to this.
These tears of mine flow like rain upon reeds at your feet;
as you grieve for Candi, no other sorrows can compare to this.”
In this context, "it is being led away" means it is being led toward the cessation of the life-continuum.
"This" refers to life. "My breaths, O Bhaddā Candi, are ceasing. "It sinks for me" means my life is sinking. "I am fainting" means I am utterly exhausted.
"Because of you, O Candi"—this is my suffering; it is not due to other sorrows, but rather because of you, O Candi, who are grieving.
"Because you will grieve due to separation from me, therefore... is the meaning.
"I wither like grass, like a forest" means he says, "I wither like grass cast upon a hot stone, like a forest cut down at its roots.
"Upon the mountain slopes" means just as rain falling on a mountain slope flows away in an unbroken stream.
The Great Being, having lamented with these four verses, lay down upon the bed of flowers and, losing consciousness, rolled over.
The king remained standing. The other woman, intoxicated by her own pleasure, did not realize the Great Being’s state of being pierced;
however, seeing him unconscious and rolled over, she said, "What..."
Thinking, "Is it not my dear husband who suffers? she examined him;
seeing blood flowing from the site of the wound, and unable to restrain the intense grief arising for her dear husband, she lamented with a great cry.
The king, thinking, "The kinnara must be dead," came out and revealed himself. Seeing him, Candā said, "By this..."
“With my heart, my beloved husband will be pierced! Shaking with fear, she fled and stood upon the mountain peak, where, reviling the king, she spoke these five verses:
“You are a wicked man, O prince, you who have struck down my chosen husband, a wretched woman as I am.”
"You pierced him in the forest roots; thus, he lies pierced upon the ground.
O Prince, let your mother take upon herself this grief of my heart—the grief that I feel while looking toward the *kimpurisa*."
“O Prince, let your wife take upon herself this sorrow of my heart—
the sorrow of my heart as I gaze upon the Kimpurisa. O Prince,
let not your mother see either her son or her husband.”
“She who killed the kinnara, though he was innocent, did so because of her lust for me.
‘Neither your son nor your husband shall see you, O princess, for she who killed the kinnara,
though he was innocent, did so because of her lust for me.’”
In this context, *varākiyā* means "miserable woman. *Paṭimuñcatu* means "may she receive," "may she touch," or "may she obtain. *Mayhaṃ kāmā hi* means "by my desire.
Having rebuked her with these five verses, the King, while she was still standing on the mountain peak, spoke this verse to comfort her:
"Do not weep, O Canda, nor he either, you whose eyes are blinded by the darkness of the forest!"
"You shall be my wife, a woman honored by the women in the royal court.
In this context, he spoke thus because he had heard her name at the time of the Great Being’s lamentation. "With eyes like the *vanatimira* flower" means her eyes were like the *vanatimira* blossom.
"Honored by the women" means she would become the eldest of sixteen thousand women, the chief queen.
Having heard his words, Candā, letting out a lion’s roar as she cried, "What are you saying to me?", spoke the following verse:
"Surely I shall die; I will not be yours, O prince!
You who have slain a *kimpurisa* who was innocent of any offense toward me, for the sake of lust!"
In that regard, [the thought] "api nūna haṃ" means "I shall surely die by all means.
Having heard her words, he became free from desire and attachment, and spoke this other verse:
"O timid one, even though you desire to live, go, O Kimpurisa, to the Himavat."
"Other deer will delight in eating tālīsa and tagara; you, O timid one!"—here, "O timid one" means "O you who are of a timid nature.
"Eating tālīsa and tagara" means: "You are a doe whose food consists of tālīsa leaves and tagara leaves;
therefore, other deer will delight in you; you are not fit for the royal household. Go! Having said this to her, he spoke.
But he departed, remaining indifferent.
Having learned that he had gone, she descended, embraced the Great Being, led him to the mountain peak, and laid him down on the mountain slope.
Placing his head upon her own thighs, she lamented with powerful wailing and spoke twelve verses:
“Those mountains and those ravines, and those mountain caves remain exactly as they were;
seeing you not there, O Kimpurisa, how shall I live?
Those delightful beds of leaves, frequented by wild beasts—”
Not seeing him right there, O Kinnara, how shall I endure?
Those delightful places, strewn with flowers and frequented by wild beasts—
Not seeing him right there, O Kinnara, how shall I endure?
“Clear flow the rivers of the mountain forests, their currents strewn with blossoms;
yet not seeing you right there, O Kimpurisa, how shall I endure?
The blue peaks of the Himavat mountain are truly beautiful to behold.”
Not seeing you right there, O Kinnara, how shall I endure?
The peaks of the Himalaya mountain are beautiful to behold;
Not seeing you right there, O Kinnara, how shall I endure?
“The copper-colored peaks of the Himalaya mountain are beautiful to behold;
yet not seeing you there, O Kimpurisa, how shall I endure?
The lofty peaks of the Himalaya mountain are beautiful to behold.”
Not seeing you right there, O Kinnara, how shall I endure?
The white peaks of the Himavat mountain are beautiful to behold;
Not seeing you right there, O Kinnara, how shall I endure?
“The peaks of the Himavat mountain are variegated and beautiful to behold;
not seeing you there, O Kimpurisa, how shall I endure?
On Gandhamādana, frequented by hosts of yakkhas and covered with medicinal herbs...”
“Not seeing you right there, O Kimpurisa, how shall I survive?
On Gandhamādana, frequented by Kimpurisas and covered with medicinal herbs—
not seeing you right there, O Kimpurisa, how shall I survive?”
"There, those mountains—those very mountains among which we alone took delight, and those ravines and mountain caves, remain exactly as they were.
Not seeing him now, how shall I dwell there? What shall I do? Seeing no more that beauty of flowers, fruits, and foliage within them, how shall I be able to endure it?"
He laments. "Spread with leaves" means spread with fragrant leaves such as palm leaves and the like. "Clear" means having water that is perfectly transparent.
"Blue" means made of blue gems. "Yellow" means made of gold. "Copper-colored" means made of ruby (manosilā).
"Tall" means high and sharp-tipped. "White" means made of silver. "Variegated" means composed of a mixture of the seven precious gems. "Frequented by hosts of *yakkhas*."
frequented by terrestrial deities.
Having thus lamented with these twelve verses, she placed her hand upon the Great Being’s chest;
perceiving his state of intense anguish, she thought, "The moon still lives; by performing a rite of divine supplication, I shall grant him his life. Then she said, "What..."
"Are there no such beings as world-protectors, or have they gone away, or are they dead, that they do not protect my beloved husband? Thus she performed a rite of cursing the gods.
By the force of her grief, Sakka’s throne became hot. Sakka, reflecting on this, understood the cause;
he arrived with great speed in the guise of a brahmin, took water from his water-pot, and [sprinkled it] upon the Great Being.
He poured [the medicine]. At that very moment, the poison vanished, the wound healed, and even the place where it had been pierced could no longer be discerned.
The Great Being arose healthy and happy. Seeing her beloved husband free from illness, Candā was filled with joy;
bowing at the feet of Sakka, she spoke this subsequent verse:
“I revere you, noble Brahmin, who have sprinkled me, a wretched woman, with the one I desired as my husband;
I have been united with my most beloved.
In this context, she spoke thus because she perceived the water as “the Deathless” (*amata*). “Piyatamena” means “with the more beloved,” or this very reading is the correct one.
Sakka gave them this advice: “From now on, do not descend from Mount Canda to go toward the human realm;
dwell right here. Having spoken thus and instructed them, he returned to his own abode.
Canda also said, “Master, what need have we for this place of obstruction? Come, let us go back to Mount Canda itself,” and she spoke this concluding verse:
“Now let us wander through the mountains, forests, and rivers, whose currents are strewn with flowers, where various trees provide shelter, and where we may speak kindly to one another.
Having delivered this Dhamma teaching, the Teacher said: “It is not only now; in the past as well, she was of unshakable mind and not to be led by others toward me.”
Having said, "It was thus," he identified the Jātaka: "At that time, King Devadatta was the king; Anuruddha was Sakka;
Rāhulamātā was Canda; and I myself was the Kinnara Canda.
This is the second commentary on the Canda-Kinnarī Jātaka.
[486] 3. The Explanation of the Mahāukkusajātaka:
"The torches, the Cīla women, are binding. This was spoken by the Teacher while dwelling at Jetavana concerning the lay follower Mittabandhaka.
It is said that he was the son of a family in Sāvatthī that had fallen into decay; having sent a friend, he [went] to another...

Having caused the daughter of a noble family to be brought forth, when it was asked, "Does she have any friend or companion capable of helping her through this arisen crisis?", he replied, "There is none.
When it was further said, "In that case, let her at least bind herself to friends," he followed that advice and first established friendship with the four gatekeepers;
thereafter, he gradually did so with the city guards, the accountants, the high officials, and others.
Having established friendship with him, he also established friendship with the general and the viceroy. Together with them, acting as one, he established friendship with the king.
Then, together with the eighty great elders and also with the Elder Ānanda, acting as one, he established friendship with the Tathāgata. Then the Teacher [established him] in the refuges...
He established him in the precepts, and the king bestowed sovereignty upon him as well. Consequently, he became famous as "Mittabandhaka" (the Friend-Binder).
Then the king gave him a large house and performed his marriage ceremony. Beginning with the king, the great multitude sent him gifts.
His wife [took] the gift sent by the king [and gave it] to the viceroy, and by the viceroy...
Thinking, "The general has sent a gift," he used this stratagem to bind and seize all the inhabitants of the city.
On the seventh day, having performed great honors and invited the One of Ten Powers, he gave a grand alms-offering to the Saṅgha of bhikkhus headed by the Buddha, numbering five hundred.
At the conclusion of the meal, having heard the Teacher’s discourse of thanksgiving, he—
Both the husband and wife were established in the fruit of stream-entry (*sotāpatti-phala*).
The monks initiated a discussion in the Hall of Dharma, saying:
"Friends, the lay follower Mittabandhaka, relying on his own wife and acting upon her word, established friendship with everyone and received great honor from the king."
“...he obtained it; moreover, having established friendship with the Tathāgata, both husband and wife were established in the fruit of stream-entry.
The Teacher approached and asked, “Monks, about what conversation are you gathered here now?
When they replied, “About this very one,” he said, “Monks, it is not only now that he attained great fame by depending on this woman.”
"Even though he was previously reborn in the animal realm, by her word he formed friendships with many and was indeed released from the grief for his son," he said;
and being requested by them, he related a story of the past:
"In the past, while Brahmadatta was reigning in Benares, certain border-dwellers, wherever they were..."

They obtain much meat; having settled here and there in villages, they roam in the forest, kill deer and other animals, and bring back the meat to support their wives and children. Not far from their village, there is a great lake.
On its southern shore is a male hen-bird, on its western shore a female hen-bird, and on its northern shore is Sīha, the king of beasts.
On the eastern side lived the king of the *ukkusaka* birds. In the middle of the lake, on a raised spot, lived a tortoise.
At that time, the hawk said to his mate, "Be my wife. She replied to him, "But do you have any friend? "I have none, my lady," he said. [She asked:
"Is there anyone capable of removing the danger or suffering that may arise for us?"
"It is necessary to find either a friend or a companion; first, make friends," he said. "With whom shall I make friends, dear lady?

she asked. "Make friends with the king of the owls dwelling on the eastern side, with the lion on the northern side, and with the tortoise in the middle of the lake. Having accepted her words, he did exactly so.
Then, having made their home together, they lived in a nest they had built on a kadamba tree situated on an island in that very lake, which was surrounded on all sides by water.
After some time, two fledglings were born to them. One day, even before their wings had grown, [an event occurred].
Those country folk, having wandered in the forest during the day and obtained nothing, thought, "It is not possible to go home with empty hands;
we shall catch fish or turtles. Having descended into the lake and gone to that island, they lay down at the foot of that *kadamba* tree.
While being bitten by mosquitoes and other insects, they churned the fire-drill (*araṇi*) in order to drive them away.
Having produced fire, they made smoke. The smoke rose up and struck the birds; the young birds cried out.
Hearing that, the country folk said, "Friends, the sound of young birds is heard!
Arise and light fires! We cannot sleep from hunger; we shall eat the flesh of the birds and then sleep. Having spoken thus, they kindled a fire.
They set up torches. Hearing their sound, the female bird thought, "These men wish to eat our chicks;
we took these friends for the sake of warding off such danger. I shall send my husband to the presence of the king of the cranes.
Having thought this, she said, "Go, my lord, and report the danger that has arisen for our children to the king of the cranes."
He spoke the first verse:
“The Cīla-crow women bind torches on the island, longing to devour my offspring;
tell me, Senaka, friend and companion, explain the calamity that has befallen the birds.”
In this context, *cilāta* means "country folk. *Dīpeti* means "in the island. *Pajā mamam* means "my children," that is, my little sons.
*Senaka*—he addresses the bird Senaka by name. *Ñātibyasanaṃ* means "the misfortune of kinsmen," specifically the misfortune of his sons.
*Dijānaṃ*—"of our kinsmen who are birds"—he says, "Go to the presence of the king of the crows and report this misfortune."

So, with great speed, he went to his dwelling place, rained down, and made himself known as having arrived. Having been granted leave to enter, he approached, paid homage, and when asked, "For what reason have you come? he spoke the second verse, showing the reason for his arrival:
"O bird among birds, most excellent of winged creatures, O king of ospreys, we come to you for refuge.
My offspring desire to devour me; O hunter, O Cilāta, be my protection for my happiness."
In this context, "bird" means that you are both a bird and the most excellent among birds.
Having comforted him with the words, "Senaka, do not fear," King Ukkusa spoke the third verse:
"Wise men make friends and companions, seeking happiness at the right time and the wrong time."
“I shall do this for you, Senaka; for a noble one performs what is required for a noble one.

In this context, "at the right time" or "not at the right time" refers to both day and night. "Noble one" (*ariya*) here intends a noble one by way of conduct (*ācāra-ariya*). For one who is perfect in conduct surely performs what is required for another who is perfect in conduct; thus he says, "What is there to be done in this matter?
Then he asked him, "Friend, have the Cīlakas climbed the tree? "They have not yet climbed it; only the torches have."
“They are binding me. “In that case, go quickly, comfort my companion, and inform her of my arrival. He did so.
King Ukkusa also went and, while observing the Cīla hunters as they climbed up, sat upon the top of a tree not far from the Kadamba tree;
then, at the moment one of the Cīlas was climbing, [he watched] him at that nest.
When they had climbed not far away, he dived into the lake, brought water with his wings and his beak, and poured it over the torch;
the torch was extinguished. The *cilātas* thought, "We will eat both this bird and the young *senaka*," and having descended, they relit the torch and climbed back up.
Again, he extinguished the torch. By this means, each time one was caught...
Even as he was extinguishing the fires, midnight arrived. He became exceedingly exhausted; the fat in his lower abdomen grew thin, and his eyes turned bloodshot.
Seeing this, the female bird said to her husband: "Husband, King Ukkuṣa is extremely exhausted.
Go for a short while to let him rest and speak to the king of the turtles. He [went] to her...
Having heard these words, he approached the quail and addressed him with a verse:
“Whatever duty should be done by one who is compassionate, that noble deed has been performed for you by a noble one.
Protect yourself; do not perish, for we shall obtain sons while you are still alive.”
In that context, *tayīdaṃ* means "this [is] by you," or this very reading is the one used.
Having heard his words, roaring a lion’s roar, he spoke the fifth verse:
"Providing protection and defense for you alone, I am not afraid even at the dissolution of my body."
“Some perform a service for their friend, even giving up their own life; this is the way of the virtuous.
But on the sixth day, after having attained full enlightenment, the Teacher, praising his virtue, said:
“A bird that was born from an egg has performed a most difficult deed.”
“For the sake of his sons, the kurara bird, even when midnight had not yet come,” it is said.

Therein, “kurara” means the king of ospreys (*ukkusa*). Regarding “for his sons”: while protecting Senaka’s sons, for their sake, he exerted himself until midnight had passed—until one and a half watches of the night—and thus performed a difficult task.
Sena also said to the osprey, “Rest a little, my friend,” and having gone to the presence of the tortoise, he [spoke] to him...
Having raised him up, when asked, "What is it, friend, that you have come for?", he replied, "A danger such as this has arisen;
King Ukkaṇṭha, having exerted himself since the first watch of the night, grew weary, and therefore I have come to your presence. Having said this, he spoke the seventh verse:
"Even some who have fallen away and stumbled through their own deeds, find support through compassion from friends."
"My children are in distress; I have come to you for refuge. O you who move through the waters, act for my welfare.
The meaning of this is: "Sir, some indeed, even when fallen from their status or wealth, or even when they have stumbled due to their own karma, stand firm out of compassion for their friends.
And my children are distressed; therefore, I have come to you as my destination and my refuge."
“I have come here having made [this sacrifice], bestowing the gift of life upon my sons; O water-dweller, act for my welfare!
Hearing this, the tortoise spoke this other verse:
“With wealth, with grain, and even with their own selves, the wise make friends and companions.”
“Senaka, I shall perform this service for you, for a noble one performs what is required of him by a noble one.
Then his son, lying not far away, heard his father’s words and, thinking, “Let my father not be troubled; I will perform my father’s duty,” spoke the ninth stanza:
“Be at ease, dear father, and sit down; the son carries out the service that benefits his father.”
“I shall indeed act for this purpose of yours, protecting the sons of the army.
Then his father addressed him with a verse:
“Surely, dear son, this is the duty of the good: that a son should practice what is beneficial for his father.”
“Perhaps, seeing me with my body fully grown, the sons of Sena will not harm me.
Therein, “this is the nature of the wise” means this is the characteristic of the wise. “Sons” refers to the sons of Sena; “do not harm” means do not injure them.
Having spoken thus, Mahākacchapa said, “Friend, do not fear; you go on ahead, and I shall follow shortly.”
Having sent him away, he fell into the water, gathered up mud and algae, and taking them with him, went to the island, extinguished the fire, and lay down.
Cilāta thought, "What use have we for these young fishermen? We shall kill this black tortoise;
it will suffice for all of us. So he pulled up creepers, took his bowstring, and [unfastened] even the ragged cloth he was wearing.
Having released him and tied him up in various places, they were unable to turn the tortoise over.
Dragging it along, the tortoise went and fell into deep water. Out of greed for the tortoise, they too fell in with it;
exhausted by their bellies being filled with water, they emerged and said, "Sirs, by one of our cranes, until midnight..."
“The torches have been extinguished; now, having thrown this turtle into the water and given it water to drink, we shall fatten its belly.
Then, having lit a fire again, we will eat these young Senaka pigeons even when the sun has risen.
Having heard their conversation, the female bird said, “Master, at any time whatsoever, they might eat our little ones...”
“They will go; go to our friend Siha,” he said. At that very moment, he went to Siha’s presence.
When Siha asked, “Why have you come at an improper time? he reported the entire occurrence from the beginning and spoke this eleventh verse:
“Beasts and humans, O best of those who live by the hunt, when overcome by fear, go forth to seek the Best.
My sons, possessed of understanding, have come to me; you are our king, so be for my happiness.
Therein, “beasts” refers to all lower animals. This is what is meant: “O Master, best among those who possess vigor in the wild.”
"For in all the world, even all animals and humans, when overcome by fear, seek out the best;
yet my sons are distressed and afflicted. Therefore, having made you my refuge, I have come here. You are our king; may you bring us happiness.
Having heard this, the lion spoke this verse:
“Senaka, I shall do this for you: I am coming to that region to slay you.
For how could a wise man, capable and fully conscious, not strive for the protection of his own people?
In this context, “that region” (taṃ disaṃ) means that collection of regions; the meaning is: that host of your enemies. “Capable” (pahū) refers to [overcoming] enemies.
"Capable of slaying. "Being clearly comprehending" means knowing that fear has arisen in his friend.
"Of those people like himself" means of people who are equal to him in limb; the meaning is "of his friend.
Having spoken thus, and having dismissed him with the words, "Go, comfort your sons," [he saw] water the color of a gem.
Madamāna advanced. Seeing him approaching, Cilācā cried out, “First the hawk extinguished our torches;
likewise, the tortoise made even the rags we were wearing ownerless. But now we are lost;
the lion will surely bring about the end of our lives! Terrified by the fear of death, they fled in every direction.
Sīha returned to the foot of the tree and saw nothing there. Then the kurara, the tortoise, and the hawk approached him and paid homage.
He spoke to them on the benefits of friendship and, having exhorted them, saying, "From now on, do not violate the duty of friendship;
be heedful," he departed, and they too went to their respective places. The female hawk looked at her own children.
“Relying on a friend, we have obtained our children,” she said, and while sitting comfortably and conversing with Sena,
she spoke these six verses, manifesting the nature of true friendship:
“One should make a friend who is kind-hearted, and one should make a noble friend for the sake of attaining happiness.”
Like a woman dressed in fine cloth, having driven away her rivals, we rejoice, being united with our sons.
"Because of the deed of my own friend, that companion who did not flee,
the hairy creatures warble in response to his song, a sound that touches the heart."
“Having obtained a friend and a companion, the wise man enjoys his children, cattle, or wealth;
I, my children, and my husband have come together through the compassion of our friends.
These things—royal power and heroic valor—belong to one who has a perfect friend.”
Thus, one who possesses friends, who is renowned, and whose spirit is exalted, enjoys himself in this world, seeking his desires.
“One should cultivate friendships even when poor, O Senaka;
behold how, out of compassion for our friend, we kinsmen have become united.”
“The wise man who, being brave and strong, makes friends— thus he becomes happy, just as I and you, O Senakas. In this context,
“a friend” (mittañca) refers to anyone who is one’s own friend, a well-disposed person, a companion with a kind heart, or one designated as a master.
"And indeed, you should honor the noble one. Regarding the phrase "as one clad in armor strikes with arrows": here, *koca* means armor (*kavaca*).

Just as one who has donned armor strikes [and thus repels] arrows, so too he says, "May we also, having struck down our enemies by the power of our friends, rejoice together with our sons. "By the deed of his own friend" means by the prowess of his own friend.
“Of a companion who does not flee” means: of the lion-king, his companion who does not flee. “The hairy ones” refers to the birds;
our little sons, having let out that heart-stirring, sweet-sounding warbling, chirp along with him. “Being together” means: standing in one place.
“There is advantage for one who has a king like a lion and friends like hawks and tortoises.”
Because these exist, one who possesses a king and possesses heroes is able to achieve their purpose.

"For they become his" means that for one whose friends are excellent and who fulfills the qualities of friendship, these companions come to be. "Of exalted nature" means one whose character is elevated by glory and fortune.
"In this world" means he rejoices in this world known as *idhaloka*. "Desiring desires" is an address to the husband. He...

For one who desires sensual pleasures because of their longing for them is called a "seeker of sensual pleasure. "We are united" means we have been born together. "With kinsmen" means together with our children, who are our relatives.

Thus, with these six verses, she spoke on the virtues of the duty of friendship. All those companions, without breaking the bond of friendship, remained for as long as their lifespan lasted and then departed according to their karma.
Having brought forth this Dhamma teaching, the Teacher said: "Monks, it is not only now that he attained happiness by relying on his wife."
“Even in the past, he had already attained happiness,” he said, and then he identified the Jātaka: “At that time, the male and female vultures were the royal couple;
the young tortoise was Rāhula; the father was Mahāmoggallāna; the partridge was Sāriputta; and as for the lion, it was I myself.
This is the third commentary, the Mahāukkusajātaka.
[487] 4. The Commentary on the Uddālakajāta­ka.
“With coarse antelope skins, matted hair, and mud-stained teeth”—this the Teacher spoke while dwelling at Jetavana concerning a certain hypocritical bhikkhu.
For although he had gone forth in the Dispensation that leads to liberation, for the sake of the four requisites, he practiced three kinds of hypocrisy.
[He] fulfilled [his purpose]. Then, pointing out his fault, the monks initiated a discussion in the Dhamma Hall:
“Friends, a certain monk named so-and-so, having gone forth in such a liberating dispensation, maintains his livelihood by means of hypocrisy.
The Teacher, having arrived, asked: “Monks, with what conversation are you sitting gathered here now? [They replied: “With this one...”
When this was said, [the Buddha] remarked, "Monks, it is not only now; in the past, too, this man was a deceiver," and he related a story of the past.
In the past, while Brahmadatta was reigning in Benares, the Bodhisatta was his wise and capable court priest.
One day, having gone to a pleasure garden for recreation, he saw a beautiful courtesan and became infatuated with her.
He lived in cohabitation with her. On account of him, she conceived a child.
Knowing that the embryo was established, she said to him: "Husband, a child is conceived in me; when they give it a name at the time of birth, what name shall we give it?
He thought, "Since it has been born from the womb of a courtesan, it is not possible to give it a family name."
“Bhadde, this wind-destroying tree is called the *uddāla*; because it was obtained here, you should give her the name ‘Uddālakā.
Having said this, he gave her a finger-ring. He added, “If it is a daughter, you should raise her with this;
if it is a son, then when he has reached maturity, you must show him to me. Later, she gave birth to a son.
He gave him the name Uddālaka.
When he had reached maturity, he asked his mother, “Mother, who is my father? “The chaplain, dear,” she replied.
“If that is so, I shall learn the Vedas. Having taken a ring and a teacher’s fee from his mother’s hand, he went to Takkasilā.
Having gone into the presence of a world-renowned teacher to learn a craft, he saw a group of ascetics and thought, "There will be a superior craft in their presence; I shall learn it.
Driven by greed for that craft, he went forth among them, performed his duties and services, and said, "Teachers, teach me the craft of your knowledge. They [said] to themselves...
They taught him solely according to their own method of knowledge. Among those five hundred ascetics, not even one was wiser than he;
he alone was the foremost among them in wisdom. Then they gathered together and gave him the position of teacher. He then said to them:
"Sirs, you always subsist on forest roots and fruits and dwell only in the forest; [but] the path of men..."
"Why do you not go? "Venerable sir, people, having given a great gift, request a blessing, ask for a Dhamma talk, and pose questions; it is out of fear of that that we do not go there.
"Venerable sirs, even if it were the Wheel-turning Monarch himself, taking his mind [to task] and speaking to him would indeed be my burden."
Having said, “Do not be afraid,” he traveled on tour with them and, having reached Bārāṇasī in due course, stayed in the royal park.
On the following day, he went for alms with everyone to the gate-village; the people gave a great almsgiving.
On the next day, the ascetics entered the city; the people gave a great almsgiving. The Uddālaka ascetic—
He expressed appreciation for the gifts given, spoke auspicious words, and answered questions; the people, having gained confidence, offered many requisites.
The entire city was stirred by the news, "The wise teacher of the assembly, the righteous ascetic, has arrived," and they told the king as well.
The king asked, "Where does he dwell? and hearing, "In the royal park," he said, "Very well, I shall go to see them today."
He said: A certain man went and told Uddālaka, "It is said that the king will come to see you.
He too, addressing the company of seers, said, "Sirs, it is said the king will arrive; indeed, by pleasing a lord for even a single day, one has done enough for the rest of one's life.
"But what should be done, Teacher? he asked. He replied thus: "Among you, some..."
"Let some practice the vagguli-vow; let some devote themselves to the exertion of squatting;
let some use beds of thorns; let some perform the penance of the five fires; let some perform the practice of descending into water;
and let some recite mantras here and there. They did accordingly. But he himself [consulted] eight or ten proponents of wise counsel.
Taking up a beautiful manuscript and placing it upon a delightful stand, he sat down on a well-prepared seat provided with a cushion, surrounded by his disciples.
At that moment, the king, accompanied by his domestic priest and a large retinue, went to the park;
seeing them practicing false asceticism, he was inspired with confidence, thinking, "They are freed from the fear of the states of misery," and [he addressed] Uddālaka.
Having approached him and exchanged greetings, he sat down to one side and, with a joyful heart,
spoke the first verse while conversing with the chaplain:
“Those who wear rough deerskins, have matted hair, and teeth stained with dirt— those of ill-favored appearance who mutter mantras;”
"Surely you have escaped from the states of misery through human exertion; so says this wise one.

In this context, "wearing coarse antelope skins" means being equipped with skins of antelopes along with their hooves. "With soiled teeth" means having teeth stained with grime due to not chewing tooth-sticks.
"Of ill-favored appearance" means having unanointed eyes, an unadorned form, and wearing coarse patched robes.
“Human effort” means the energy that must be exerted by human beings. “Those who know this” means those who understand both the practice of asceticism and the recitation of mantras.
“From the states of misery”—he asks, “O Teacher, are these [beings] freed from the four states of misery?
Having heard this, the chaplain thought, “This king has placed his faith in the wrong place; it is not right for me to remain silent,” and he spoke the second verse:
“Commit evil deeds, O King, if one who is learned does not practice the Dhamma;
even one with knowledge of a thousand [verses] cannot, on that basis alone, be liberated from suffering without having practiced the conduct.
In this context, “if one is learned,” O Great King, means even if one is well-versed in the Vedas, thinking, “I am learned,” yet [does not practice] the Dhamma of the ten paths of wholesome action...
"He would not practice; he would only commit evils through the three doors.

Let alone the three Vedas—even if he were possessed of a thousand Vedas, by relying on that mere erudition, he would not reach the 'conduct' known as the eight meditative attainments, and thus he would not be released from the suffering of the states of woe.
Having heard his words, Uddālaka thought: "In one way or another, the king has gained confidence in this group of seers. This..."
"But that brahmin spoke as if striking a wandering ox with a staff, or as if throwing rubbish into a full meal;
therefore, I shall speak with him. Speaking with him, he recited the third verse:
"Even one who knows a thousand [Vedas] is not released from suffering by depending on that, unless he attains right conduct."
"I think the Vedas are fruitless; conduct alone, together with self-restraint, is the truth.

In this context, "fruitless" means that according to your doctrine, both the Vedas and other crafts would be rendered fruitless; why then do people study them? It follows that conduct alone, when accompanied by virtue and self-restraint, is the sole truth.
Thereupon, the chaplain spoke the fourth verse:
“The Vedas are not fruitless; rather, conduct accompanied by self-restraint is the truth.
For one attains fame by mastering the Vedas, but the tamed person purifies themselves through peace by means of conduct.
In this context, “na heva” means that I do not say, “the Vedas are fruitless”; rather, it is conduct accompanied by self-restraint [that is the truth].
"Truth alone is the supreme reality; for by means of it, one can be liberated from suffering.
He 'purifies peace' (santiṃ puṇāti) means that through conduct characterized by meditative attainment, the tamed one reaches Nibbāna, which brings one into the presence of fearlessness.
Having heard this, Uddālaka thought, "It is not possible to stand in opposition to him and say, 'I am your son.'"
Thinking, "There is no one who would not feel affection when this is said; I shall explain his status as my son," he spoke the fifth verse:
"Mother, father, and kinsmen are merely those by whom one is born;
he alone is truly oneself. I am Uddālaka, sir, born of a lineage of Sottiya brahmins."

In this context, "those to be supported" (*bhacca*) refers to those who must be maintained: the mother, the father, and the other relatives. However, he by whom one is born is indeed that very person.
For it is oneself alone that is born of oneself; and I was indeed begotten by you at the foot of the *uddālaka* tree, and the name was given by you alone: "I am Uddālaka, sir."
When he was told, "Are you, then, definitely Uddālaka? he replied, "Yes. When asked, "I gave a token to your mother;
where is it? he placed the signet ring in his hand, saying, "Here it is, Brahmin.
Recognizing the ring, the Brahmin said with certainty, "You understand the Dhamma of a Brahmin," and proceeded to question him on the Dhamma of a Brahmin.
He spoke the sixth verse:
“How, sir, does one become a brahmin? How does one become a perfected one (kevalī)?
And how is there final nibbāna? What is it that is called ‘one who stands firm in the Dhamma’?”
Uddālaka, explaining this to him, spoke the seventh verse:
“Having set aside the fire, the brahmin takes it up; sprinkling water, he raises the sacrificial post while sacrificing.
Acting thus, the brahmin becomes one who finds security; by that, they have made him abide in the Dhamma.”
In that context, "having made it continuous, taking the fire" means having taken the fire without interruption, he attends to it.

"Sprinkling water, he raises the sacrificial post while sacrificing" means that while performing the consecration rite—whether sacrificing the Sammāpāsa, the Vājapeyya, or the Niraggaḷa sacrifice—he causes a golden sacrificial post to be erected.
"Secure" means one who has attained security. "They caused [him] to dwell" means for that very reason.
They spoke of one established in the Dhamma.
Having heard that, the chaplain, censuring the brahminical doctrine spoken by him, recited the eighth verse:
“There is no purity through sprinkling, nor is one a true brahmin merely by birth.”
“Neither forbearance nor gentleness, nor is he one who has attained final Nibbāna.
In this context, by the phrase “by sprinkling,” having pointed out one among those brahminical duties mentioned by him, [the Buddha] rejects them all.
This is what is meant: “Purity is not attained through the tending of the sacrificial fire, or through the sprinkling of water, or through animal sacrifice.”
“...there is no such name; nor does one become a complete and perfect brahmin by this much alone;
nor is there forbearance through endurance, nor gentleness in virtue, nor is one said to be ‘fully extinguished’ (parinibbuto) by the total extinction of the defilements.
Then Uddālaka, asking him, “If that is so, how then does one become a brahmin? spoke the ninth verse:
“How does one become a brahmin? How does one become perfected?
And how does one attain final nibbāna? Established in the Dhamma, how is one called such?
Thus the chaplain spoke, and recited this other verse:
“Without fields as kinsmen, without ‘mine,’ without longing, free from greed and evil, with craving for existence exhausted—one who acts thus is a brahmin, a bringer of security.
Therefore, they honored him who stands firm in the Dhamma.

In this context, “without fields as kinsmen” means he has no fields, no relatives by marriage. This refers to the absence of attachment to the possession of fields, lands, villages, and towns, as well as the absence of attachment to kinship by blood, kinship by clan, kinship by friendship, kinship by companionship, and kinship by craft.

And he is free from "mine-ness," meaning he is devoid of craving and the conceit of "mine" regarding the formations of sentient beings. He is "free from longing," meaning he is devoid of hope for gain, wealth, sons, or life.
He is "free from evil greed," meaning he is devoid of sinful greed and depraved greed. He is "one whose greed for existence is exhausted," meaning his passion for becoming has been destroyed.
Then Uddālaka spoke this verse:
“Khattiyas, brahmins, vessas, suddas, caṇḍālas, and pukkusas—all of them are gentle and tamed; all of them have attained final nibbāna.
Among all those who have become cooled, there is neither superior nor inferior.”
Regarding that, as for the question "Is there one who is better or one who is worse?": all these people, such as the kṣatriyas and others, are endowed with gentleness and other virtues;

yet among those who have become thus, there exists a distinction of inferiority and superiority, such that one might say "this one is better" and "this one is worse. He asks whether such a thing exists or not.
Then, in order to show him that "from the moment of attaining arahantship onwards, there is no such thing as inferiority or superiority," the brahmin spoke this verse:
“Kṣatriyas, brahmins, vaiśyas, śūdras, caṇḍālas, and pukkasas—
all are gentle and tamed, all have attained final nibbāna.
Among all those who have become cooled, there is neither superior nor inferior.”
Then Uddālaka, censuring him, spoke these two verses:
“Khattiyas, brahmins, vessas, suddas, candālas, and pukkusas— all are gentle and self-controlled; all have attained final nibbāna.”
“For all who have become cooled, there is neither superior nor inferior;
yet you practice the life of a Brahmin, though born from a family of Sottiya.
The meaning of this is: if there is no distinction among those endowed with these qualities and they are of one single caste, then [so it is].

"While you exist, you destroy the state of being well-born on both sides; you wander as one who has lost his status as a Brahmin, you have become like a Caṇḍāla, and you have destroyed the lineage of the Sottiya family.
Then the chaplain, seeking to convince him by means of a simile, spoke these two verses:
“A celestial mansion becomes covered with garments of various colors;
yet no shadow is cast by those garments, for that passion has not arisen there.
In the very same way, when young men among humans are purified,”
“They release their own kind, having understood the Dhamma and being well-vowed.
In this context, “palace” (*vimāna*) means either a house or a pavilion. “Shade” (*chāyā*) refers to the shade of those cloths;
that various-colored dye does not enter it, and all the shades become of one color only. “In the same way” means that among humans, too, it is exactly like this for some.
Do not hold the view that "this is so" regarding those ignorant brahmins who proclaim purity within the four castes without any valid reason.
When young men are purified by the Noble Path, then, having realized the Dhamma of Nibbāna penetrated by them, wise men of good vows and virtuous conduct release them from their birth-status.
For from the moment one attains Nibbāna, so-called "birth" is indeed meaningless.
But Uddālaka, being unable to provide a reply, sat there speechless. Then the brahmin said to the king:
"Great King, all these men are deceivers who ruin the whole of Jambudīpa through their trickery.
