Disrobe Uddālaka and appoint him as your subordinate chaplain; disrobe the rest and, giving them wooden shields and weapons, make them your servants."
“Do so,” he said. “Very well, teacher,” the king replied, and acted accordingly. While attending upon the king, they passed away according to their respective kamma.
Having brought forth this Dhamma teaching, the Teacher said, “Monks, it is not only now; in the past as well, this man was a deceiver,” and he identified the Jātaka:
“At that time, Uddālaka was the deceitful monk, the king was Ānanda, and the chaplain was [the Buddha].”
"But it was I myself who was he.
The commentary on the Uddālakajātakā ends here.
[488] 5. Commentary on the Bhisajātakā.
“Horses, cattle, silver, and gold”—this was spoken by the Teacher while dwelling at Jetavana concerning a monk who was disenchanted with the religious life.
The background story will be made clear in the Kusajātaka. At that time, the Teacher asked, “Is it true, monk, that you are disenchanted?
When he replied, “It is true, Venerable Sir,” the Teacher asked, “On account of what?”

When he had spoken thus, and [the monk] replied, "It is defilement, Bhante," the Teacher said, "Monk, having gone forth in such a liberating dispensation, why do you become weary because of defilement?
In the past, when no Buddha had arisen, ancient wise men went forth in the external renunciations;
they dwelt having made a vow regarding the perception that arises concerning both sensual objects and the defilements of sensual passion. Having said this, he related a story of the past.
In the past, when Brahmadatta was reigning in Benares, the Bodhisatta was born as the son of a wealthy brahmin family possessing eighty koṭis of wealth;
they gave him the name Mahākañcanakumāra. Then, at the time he began to walk on foot, another son was born, and they gave him the name Upakañcanakumāra. In this manner, seven...
They had sons; however, there was one daughter who was the youngest of all, and they gave her the name Kañcanadevī.
When Prince Mahākañcana reached maturity, he returned after having mastered all the arts at Takkasilā.
Then his parents, wishing to bind him to the household life, said, "We shall bring you a maiden from a family of equal birth; establish a household."
They said, “Mother, I have no need for the household life. To me, the three realms of existence appear like a blazing fire, full of terror;
they appear like a prison, a hindrance; they appear loathsome, like a dungheap.
I have never even seen sexual intercourse in a dream. You have other sons; let them be invited to take up the household life.”
Although he was entreated again and again and even sent companions who pleaded with him, he did not consent.
Then his companions asked him, "Friend, what is it that you desire such that you do not wish to enjoy sensual pleasures?
He informed them of his inclination toward renunciation. Upon hearing this, his parents [spoke] to their remaining sons...
They invited him, but he did not accept their offer. Kāñcanadevī likewise refused. Later on, his parents passed away.

After the wise Mahākañcana had performed the funeral rites for his parents and bestowed a great almsgiving upon the poor and the destitute with eighty koṭis of wealth, he took his six brothers, his sister, one male slave, one female slave, and one companion, and departed.
Having gone forth on the Great Renunciation, he entered the Himalayas.
There, relying upon a certain lotus pond, they established a hermitage in a delightful region and, having gone forth, sustained themselves on forest roots and fruits.
When they went into the forest, they traveled together; wherever one of them saw a fruit or a leaf, they would call the others to that spot.
As they spoke of what they had seen and heard, they were picking [fruit], like a village laboring in its fields.

Then the teacher, the great ascetic Mahākañcana, thought: "For those of us who have gone forth after renouncing eighty million in wealth, such wandering for the sake of fruit and flowers out of a greedy disposition is indeed unbecoming.
From now on, I alone shall fetch the fruit and flowers."
Having reached the hermitage, he gathered them all together at the time of evening and, having announced the matter to them, said:
"You remain right here performing the duties of a recluse; I shall fetch fruits. Then Upakañcana and the others said to him:
"Teacher, we have gone forth in dependence upon you; you yourself remain right here performing the duties of a recluse..."
"Do this, sisters: let our sister also remain right here, and let her maidservant stay in her presence.
We eight people shall bring fruits and vegetables in turn, while you three remain exempt from the turn," they said, and thus they obtained their agreement.
From then on, among those eight people, each one brought fruits and vegetables in turn. The others [remained] as they were.
They remain right in the leaf-hut; they are not permitted to stay together without a specific reason. When it is his turn, he brings various fruits and enters a small hut where there is a stone slab.
Having divided it into eleven portions and made a signal with a wooden gong, he takes his own portion and goes to his dwelling place.
The others, having come out according to the signal of the gong, [do likewise].
Without being greedy, they proceeded with due respect; taking their own allotted portions, they went to their dwelling places, consumed them, and practiced the duties of a recluse.

Later on, bringing lotus roots and eating them, they dwelt performing the preliminary exercises for the *kasiṇas*, being intensely austere, fierce in asceticism, and possessing supreme mastery over their faculties. Then, of them—
By the power of his virtue, Sakka’s celestial abode trembled.
Sakka, reflecting upon it, understood the cause, yet he remained apprehensive, wondering, "Are these seers still intent on sensual pleasures?
Thinking, "I shall first examine these seers," he used his supernatural power to make the Great Being's body disappear for three days. On the first day...
Not seeing his portion, he thought, "He must have forgotten my portion.
On the second day, he thought, "It must be because of some fault of mine; I suspect he did not set aside my portion for the sake of dismissing me.
On the third day, he thought, "For what reason do they not set aside my portion? If there is a fault on my part, I shall ask for forgiveness."
At the time of evening, he gave the signal with the gong.
When they had all assembled, they asked, "By whom was the signal with the gong given? "By me, dear ones," [he replied]. "For what reason, teacher?
"Dear ones, on the third day, by whom were fruits brought? One among them stood up and said, "By me, teacher."

Having paid homage, he stood there. [The teacher said: "While dividing the portions, did you set aside a portion for me? "Yes, teacher; I set aside the largest portion for you. "Who brought it yesterday? "I did.
Another man arose, paid homage, and stood there. [The teacher thought: "While dividing the portions, he recollected me.
[The teacher said: "I have assigned the largest portion to you. "Who brought it today?"
“By me,” said another, rising and bowing, he stood there. “He was making a portion for me; he must have forgotten me while making the portions.
“I made you my eldest portion, dear one. “Father, today is the third day that I have received no portion.
On the first day, when I did not see a portion, I thought: ‘He will surely forget me while making the portions.’”

On the second day, I thought, "There will be some fault on my part," but today, thinking, "If there is a fault in me, I shall ask for forgiveness," I assembled you by the signal of the gong. You say, "We made these portions of lotus roots";
I do not receive them, yet it is necessary to know who among you has stolen and eaten them. [In matters of] sensual desires...
"Stealing even a mere lotus root from those who have gone forth after abandoning the world is indeed unbecoming.
When they heard his words, they all became agitated, exclaiming, "Oh, what a reckless deed!
Even the deity reborn in the preeminent tree of that hermitage descended and approached them.
He sat down nearby. A certain elephant, who had been subjected to the practice of making him motionless, being unable to endure the suffering, broke his tethering post and fled into the forest;
from time to time, he would pay homage to the group of seers, and having come there, he stood to one side. A certain monkey, a snake-handler, having escaped from the snake-charmer’s hand, fled away.
Having entered the forest, he dwelt right there in a hermitage. On that day, he too, having paid homage to the company of seers, sat down to one side.
Sakka, thinking, "I shall protect the company of seers," stood near them with his body invisible.
At that very moment, the Bodhisatta’s younger brother, the ascetic Upakañcana, rose from his seat, paid homage to the Bodhisatta, and—
Having shown respect to the others, he asked, "Teacher, may I be allowed to clear my own name without bringing others against me?
"Yes, you may," he replied. Standing in the midst of the company of seers, he uttered the first verse while making an oath: "If I have eaten your lotus roots, may I become such as this!"
“May he obtain here horses, cattle, silver, gold, and a pleasing wife;
may he be united with sons and wives—he, O Brahmin, who has taken away your lotus roots.

In this regard, it should be understood that by saying “horses, cattle,” he spoke while censuring sense-pleasures based on material things (*vatthukāma*), thinking: “To whatever extent there are dear objects, to that same extent sorrows and sufferings arise when one is separated from them.”
Hearing this, the company of seers covered their ears, saying, "Venerable sir, do not speak thus; your oath is too heavy.
The Bodhisatta also said to him, "Dear brother, your oath is too heavy; you have not eaten it, so sit down upon your own seat.
When he had finished his first oath and was seated, the second brother also rose up suddenly and [addressed] the Great Being.
Having paid homage and purifying himself with an oath, he spoke the second verse:
"May he wear garlands and Kāsī sandalwood, may his sons be many;
may he have intense longing for sensual pleasures—he, O Brahmin, who has taken away your lotus roots."
In this context, "intense" means that one should form a strong attachment toward sense-objects as bases and toward the defilements of sensual desire.
This was said by him precisely for the purpose of rejecting suffering, on the grounds that "he who has intense attachment toward these things encounters great suffering when separated from them.
When he had sat down, the others also each recited their respective verses in accordance with their own inclinations.
“Let him who took your lotus roots, O Brahmin, be a farmer with abundant grain, renowned, a householder with sons, and possessing all desires;
let him dwell at home without seeing his own decline.
Let him be a Kshatriya, a man of forceful action, a king among kings, powerful and illustrious.”
May he who took your lotus roots, O brahmin, rule over the great earth bounded by the four oceans.
May that brahmin remain one not yet free from passion, occupied for a moment with the paths of the stars;
may the illustrious lord of the realm honor him, O brahmin, who took your lotus roots.
“Let the whole world consider him a reciter, one who knows all the Vedas on every side, and an ascetic;
let the people of the countryside come together and honor him, O Brahmin, for he was the one who took away your lotus roots.
Let him enjoy a prosperous and excellent village, resounding with the four noises, which has been granted by Vāsava.”
Let him who took your lotus roots, O brahmin, meet death while still unliberated from passion.
Let him become a village headman among his companions, delighting in dance and song;
let him suffer no misfortune whatsoever from the king—he who took your lotus roots, O brahmin.

“May she who took away your lotus roots, O brahmin, become the most excellent among women— the foremost of thousands of women whom a single king, having conquered the earth, might appoint as his chief queen.
For she may eat the delicious food of all the seers assembled together, without wavering.”
Let him who stole your lotus roots, O brahmin, boast of his gain:
"Let him be a resident monk in the Great Monastery, let him be a supervisor of construction work at Gajaṅgalā;
let him provide light through the window every day—he who stole your lotus roots, O brahmin."
“Let him be bound with six hundred snares; let him depart from the lovely woods for the royal capital.
Let him be struck by all the hunters with their spears—he, O Brahmin, who has taken your lotus roots.
“Adorned with garlands of lac, his ears pierced with earrings, and struck by a staff, let him enter the mouth of a serpent.”
"May he who stole your lotus roots, O brahmin, wander with his neck bound by a rope.
In this regard, by the third verse mentioned, "kasimā" means one whose agricultural work is successful. "Putte gihī dhanimā sabbakāme" means:
may he obtain sons; may he be a householder; may he be wealthy through the seven kinds of precious wealth; and may he possess all sensual pleasures (sabbakāme) consisting of forms and so forth.

“Let him have it. [The Buddha thought: “Not seeing his own age, which is suitable for going forth in old age, let him continue to dwell in the very house that is abundant with the five strands of sensual pleasure.
He spoke this to show that one who is greedy for the five strands of sensual pleasure reaches great ruin through separation from those sensual pleasures.
In the verse spoken by the fourth [disciple], "king of kings" (*rājābhirāja*) means he is the supreme king among kings.
This was said by him while pointing out the fault in sovereignty, thinking: "When the power of those who possess authority has faded away, great suffering arises.

In the verse spoken by the fifth [disciple], "one not free from lust" (*avītarāga*) means one who still possesses craving for the position of royal chaplain (*purohita*). This was said by him regarding the chaplain...
He spoke in order to show that "great dejection arises when one has fallen from the position of family priest.
Regarding the verse spoken by the sixth [disciple], "tapassī" means "one endowed with the virtue of austerity"; let him think thus.
This was said by way of censuring gain and honor, showing that "great dejection arises through the departure of gain and honor."

Regarding the verse spoken by the ascetic Sahāya: "Abounding in four things" means it was crowded with people, abundant in grain, rich in timber, and endowed with water—thus it was overflowing with these four; the meaning is that it was possessed of these four excellences.
"By Vāsava" means as if given by Vāsava, it was immovable; [it was established] by the power of a boon obtained from Vāsava. One...
The meaning is that he had propitiated the king and was given [the village] by him. "One who is not free from lust" means being as if submerged in the mire of sensual desire, like a pig in mud.
Thus, while speaking of the danger of sensual desires, he spoke in this way.
In the verse spoken by the slave, "gāmaṇī" means the headman of the village. This one also spoke thus while likewise censuring sensual desires. [Regarding] Kāñcanadevī...
In the verse cited, "itthi" means "a woman. "Ekarājā" means "the supreme queen. The expression "of thousands of women" is stated for the sake of emphasis;
the meaning is: "let her be placed in the foremost position among sixteen thousand women. "Sīmantinīnaṃ" means "of women who bear the sīmanta (the parting of the hair).
Thus, although she remained in the state of a woman, she indeed reviled sensual pleasures as if they were a foul-smelling heap of excrement.

Thus she spoke. Regarding the verse spoken by the maidservant: "In the midst of all those assembled" means sitting in the middle of everyone gathered together, eating with a sweet flavor, being unshakable and not shrinking back—this is the meaning.
It is said that for maidservants, eating while sitting near their master is unpleasant; thus, because it was unpleasant to her, she spoke in this way. "Let him eat" (carātu) means let him consume.
"Boasting because of gain" means: performing acts of hypocrisy for the sake of gain, with the intention that she might wander about generating profit and honor.
By this, even while remaining in the state of a slave, she censures the sensual desires based on the defilements.
In the verse spoken by the deity, "the resident" refers to the one who maintains the monastery. "In Gajaṅgalā" refers to the city of that name.
It is said that building materials were easily obtained there. "Let him make a window in a single day"—that is, he should have a window made in just one day.
It is said that during the time of Buddha Kassapa, this son of the gods was a resident senior monk (saṅghatthera) at a ruined great monastery near the city of Gajaṅgala;
while performing repairs on the dilapidated monastery, he experienced great suffering.
Therefore, with reference to that very suffering, he spoke thus. In the verse uttered by the elephant, "with hundreds of snares" means with many snares.
"In six places" means in six locations: the four feet, the neck, and the region of the hips. "With thongs" means with long poles having two joints.
"With goads" means with ten types of goads or hooks. It is said that he spoke thus with reference solely to the suffering he himself had experienced.
In the verse spoken by the monkey, *alakkamālī* means "one who possesses a necklace of lac" (alakkamālā), which had been placed around his neck by a snake-charmer.
*Tipukaṇṇaviddho* means "one whose ears were pierced with a tipu-ornament. *Laṭṭhīhato* means "struck by a stick," having been struck with a stick while learning the art of playing with snakes.
This [monkey] also spoke thus, referring specifically to the suffering he himself had experienced at the hands of the snake-charmer.
When those thirteen people had thus made their oaths, the Great Being thought:
"Perhaps they might suspect me, thinking, 'He says that what is not lost is lost'; therefore, I too shall make an oath.
Then, making it, he spoke the fourteenth verse:
“He who says that what is not lost is lost, while others are obtaining and enjoying sensual pleasures, may meet death in the midst of his home;
or he who, sirs, suspects anything at all [of being lost]—[may meet death].
In this context, “sirs” (bhonto) is a form of address. This is what is meant: sirs, he who [regards] a portion that is not lost as “lost”...
“...so says he, or whoever suspects anyone among you: let him obtain and enjoy the five strands of sensual pleasure;
let him die right there in the midst of the household life, never having attained the delightful going-forth.
When the seers had thus made their oaths, Sakka, being afraid, thought: “It was I who made the lotus roots disappear, testing them.”
Thinking, "These people, reviling sensual pleasures as if they were lumps of spittle discarded from the mouth, are making a vow;
I shall ask them the reason for their revulsion toward sensual pleasures," the Bodhisatta, appearing in visible form, paid homage to him and, asking his question, spoke the following verse:
"What is it that these people, seeking after it, wander through the world for, which is so desired and beloved by many?"
“Dear and pleasing indeed is this world of living beings; why then do the seers not praise sensual pleasures?

In this context, “seeking after which” means that those beings who wander about in the world seeking after both objective sensual pleasure (*vatthukāma*) and defilement-based sensual pleasure (*kilesakāma*) by means of even and uneven occupations such as plowing and cattle-rearing—this is what is desired and beloved by many gods and humans.
"Dear and pleasing—why do the seers not praise sensual pleasures? is the meaning. By the word "kāme" (sensual pleasures), he shows that object in its specific form.
Then, answering his question, the Great Being spoke two verses:
"In sensual pleasures they are indeed slain and bound; in sensual pleasures suffering and fear are born."
“Negligent and intoxicated by sensual pleasures, out of delusion they perform evil deeds.
Having produced evil through their evil nature, at the breaking up of the body they go to hell.
Seeing the danger in the strands of sensual pleasure, for that reason the seers do not praise sensual pleasures.”
In this context, "in sensual pleasures" (*kāmesu*) means for the sake of sensual pleasures; the meaning is that they commit physical misconduct and so forth by depending on sensual pleasures.

"Are slain" (*haññare*) means they are struck with sticks and the like. "Are bound" (*bajjhare*) means they are tied with ropes and so forth. "Suffering" (*dukkha*) refers to unpleasantness, both bodily and mental.
"Fear" (*bhaya*) refers to all forms of fear, such as self-reproach and the like. "Lord of Beings" (*bhūtādhipati*) is an address to Sakka.
"Such a thing has these disadvantages and faults. This disadvantage, moreover, should be illustrated by such suttas as the *Dukkha-khandha*.
Having heard the Great Being’s words, Sakka, his mind filled with agitation, spoke the following verse:
"Deliberating thus, I took the seer’s lotus roots from the bank and placed them on dry land."
“Pure and free from evil, the seers dwell; these, O practitioner of the holy life, are your lotus stalks.
Regarding this, venerable sir, when I said “I am investigating,” I was investigating whether these seers were intent upon sensual pleasures or not.
“Of the seer” means belonging to you, the great seer. “Having taken them from the bank” means having taken those placed upon the bank.
"I placed one on the dry land to one side. "Pure," he said, "is now known by me through your act of oath:
'These seers dwell pure and sinless.
Having heard that, the Bodhisatta spoke this verse:
“They are not actors, nor are they fit for play; they are not kinsmen, nor are they your companions.
Upon what support do you rely, O thousand-eyed one, that you sport with seers, O King of Devas?
In this context, “They are not actors” means: O King of Devas, we are neither actors nor anything suitable for your amusement.
"Neither your kinsmen nor your companions are here; so, what support have you made for yourself, or upon what do you rely, that you sport with the seers?
This is the meaning.
Then Sakka, seeking to appease him, spoke the twentieth verse:
“You are my teacher and you are my father; O Brahmā, this is the support for one who has stumbled.
Forgive me for this one offense, O one of vast wisdom; for the wise do not have anger as their strength. In this context, “this is the support” means:

“May this shadow of your feet today be the support for me, who have stumbled and committed an offense. Regarding “having anger as their strength”: the wise are said to have patience as their strength, not anger as their strength.
Then the Great Being, having forgiven Sakka, king of the gods, spoke this further verse while himself asking forgiveness from the company of seers:
“O Vāsava, Lord of Beings, we have seen for a single night the seers who are well-perfumed.
May all these worthy ones be well-disposed, since the brahmin has offered us lotus stalks.”
In this context, "the single night’s dwelling of the seers was well-scented" means that even a single night’s stay by these venerable seers in this forest was indeed well-scented.
For what reason? Because we saw Vāsava, the lord of beings; for had we lived in the city, we would not have seen him.
"May you all," meaning may all of you venerable ones, be well-disposed and satisfied.
"May they forgive the King of the Devas. For what reason? Because the brahmin has offered these lotus roots, since your teacher has obtained these lotus roots.

Having paid homage to the company of seers, Sakka departed for the world of the devas. The company of seers, too, having realized the meditative absorptions and direct knowledges, became destined for the Brahma-world.
Having delivered this Dhamma teaching, the Teacher said, "Thus, monk, the ancient wise ones abandoned the defilements by making a solemn oath," and he proclaimed the Truths (*saccāni*).
At the conclusion of the Truths, the discontented monk was established in the fruit of stream-entry (*sotāpatti-phala*).
Then, identifying the Jātaka, the Teacher spoke three verses:
“I, Sāriputta, Moggallāna, and Kassapa;
Anuruddha, Puṇṇa, and Ānanda—these were the seven brothers at that time.
And Uppalavaṇṇā was the sister, and Khujjuttarā was the slave-girl then.”
"Citto the householder was Dāsa, and Sātāgira was the yakkha at that time.
Pālileyya was the elephant then, Madhudā the chief monkey, and Kāḷudāyī was Sakka. Thus you should remember this Jātaka."
The fifth: The Commentary on the Bhisajātaka.
[489] 6. The Commentary on the Surucijātaka.
"The chief queen was the wife of Suruci"—this [was said by] the Teacher while dwelling at the Migāramātupāsāda near Sāvatthī.
He spoke concerning the eight boons obtained by the great female lay disciple Visākhā.
On one occasion, having heard a discourse on the Dhamma in Jeta’s Grove, she invited the Blessed One together with the community of monks for the following day’s meal and then departed.
However, at the end of that night, a great rain cloud covering the four continents poured down. The Blessed One addressed the monks:
“Monks, just as it rains here in Jeta’s Grove, so does it rain over the four continents. Let yourselves be rained upon, monks; this is the final great cloud that covers the four continents.

Having said this, he vanished from Jeta’s Grove by means of his power of psychic potency while the monks were having their bodies rained upon, and appeared at Visākhā’s gate. The female lay devotee [said], “It is wonderful!”

"Truly wonderful, truly marvelous, friends! Such is the great psychic power and great majesty of the Tathāgata, that even while floods are flowing knee-deep and even waist-deep, not a single monk has his feet or his robes become wet!
Thus, joyful and elated, [they honored] the Saṅgha of monks headed by the Buddha.
When the meal was over and the Blessed One had finished his meal, she said to him: "Venerable sir, I wish to ask the Blessed One for eight boons.
"The Tathāgatas, Visākhā, do not grant boons," he replied. "Venerable sir, those that are allowable and blameless.
"Speak them, Visākhā. "Venerable sir, I desire [these] for the Saṅgha of bhikkhus..."
“For as long as life lasts, to give rain-cloaks; to give meals for newcomers; to give meals for those departing; to give meals for the sick;
to give meals for those attending the sick; to give medicine for the sick; to give regular rice-gruel;
and to give water-cloaks for the community of bhikkhunīs for as long as life lasts.”
The Teacher asked, “Visākhā, what purpose do you have in view that you ask the Tathāgata for eight boons?

When she had explained the benefits of those boons, he said, “Excellent, excellent, Visākhā! It is well indeed that you, Visākhā, seeing these benefits, ask the Tathāgata for eight boons. Having said this, he granted them to her.
"Visākhā, eight boons," he said, and having granted the eight boons and offered words of appreciation, he departed.
Then one day, while the Teacher was dwelling at Pubbārāma, the monks initiated a discussion in the Hall of Truth:
"Friends, the great female lay devotee Visākhā, even while remaining in a female body, obtained eight boons in the presence of the One of Ten Powers."
“Oh, how great are her virtues! The Teacher approached and asked, “Monks, about what conversation are you gathered here now?
When they replied, “About this very matter,” he said, “Monks, it is not only now that Visākhā receives boons from me;
she received them in the past as well. Having said this, he related a story of the past.
In the past, in Mithilā, there was a king named Suruci who, while ruling his kingdom, obtained a son and gave him the name Surucikumāra.
When he reached maturity, thinking, "I shall learn the arts at Takkasilā," he went there and sat in a hall at the city gate.
The son of the King of Bārāṇasī, named Prince Brahmadatta, likewise went there and [sat] beside Surucikumāra.
He sat down on the very same wooden bench. Having questioned one another and become confident in each other, they went together to the presence of the teacher;
having given him his teacher’s fee and begun their craft, before long they completed their training.
Taking leave of the teacher, they walked a short distance together along the road, and standing at a fork in the path, they embraced one another.
For the sake of preserving the bond of friendship, they made an agreement: “If a son is born to me, he shall be your daughter’s husband;
if a son is born to you, he shall be my daughter’s husband; thus we shall arrange their marriage.
While they were ruling the kingdom, a son was born to King Suruci, and they gave him the name Suruci Kumāra. A daughter was born to Brahmadatta, and they gave her the name Sumedhā.
When Prince Surucikumāra reached maturity, he went to Takṣaśilā, mastered the arts, and returned.
Then his father, desiring to consecrate him in the kingdom, thought, "It is said that the King of Bārāṇasī has a daughter who is my friend’s;
I shall make her his chief queen. With this in mind, he sent ministers with many gifts for her sake. Of them—
In the future, the King of Bārāṇasī asked his queen, "My lady, what indeed is the greatest suffering for a woman?

"The suffering of jealousy toward a co-wife, Your Majesty," she replied. "In that case, my lady, we shall give one of our daughters, Queen Sumedhā, to whoever can take her away alone, having freed her from that suffering," he said. He [the prince], by them—

When the ministers came and announced her name, he said, "Sirs, although I previously gave my word to my companion, I do not wish to cast this woman into the midst of a crowd of women; I wish to give her to whoever takes her alone.
They sent her to the presence of the king. But the king thought, "Our kingdom..."
“[The city of] Mithilā is great, seven yojanas in extent; the territory of the kingdom covers three hundred yojanas;
at the very least, one must obtain sixteen thousand women. Having said this, he did not find her pleasing.
But Prince Suruci, having heard of Sumedhā’s perfection of form, became bound by the contact of hearing [of her], and thought: “I [will take] her...”
"I shall take her alone; I have no need for a multitude of women. Let them bring her by herself," he sent word to his parents.
They did not disregard his wish, but sent much wealth and brought her with a great retinue.
Having made her the chief queen of the prince, they consecrated both of them together. He, having become known as King Suruci the Great, ruled according to the Dhamma.

While ruling the kingdom, he lived in loving union with her. Yet, although she resided in his household for ten thousand years, she obtained neither a son nor a daughter. Then the citizens assembled and raised a clamor in the royal courtyard.
When asked, "What is this?", they replied, "It is not the fault of the king; however, you have no son to perpetuate the lineage. To them...
“There is but one queen; moreover, in a royal household there ought to be at least sixteen thousand women.
Take a jar of women, Your Majesty; surely among them a woman of merit will obtain a son. Having said this, [the king replied]: “Dear ones, what are you saying?
I have given my promise that I would not take another, and she was brought here by me on that account; it is not possible for me to speak a falsehood.”
“I have no need for a collection of women,” the king replied, and they departed.
Having heard those words, Sumedhā thought, “The king has not brought other women because of his commitment to truthfulness;
however, I myself shall bring one for him. Thus, taking her place as the king’s mother and chief consort, she of her own accord [began to seek] among the daughters of the nobility...
He brought four thousand women: a thousand ministers’ daughters, a thousand householders’ daughters, and a thousand courtesans skilled in all arts.
These too lived in the royal palace for ten thousand years, yet they obtained neither a son nor a daughter. By this same means, he did so three more times, bringing four thousand each time.
He brought [another] thousand women. Yet they too obtained neither a son nor a daughter. By this time there were sixteen thousand women.
Forty thousand years had passed; including the ten thousand she had lived with previously, that makes fifty thousand years.
Then the citizens gathered together, and having summoned her once more, asked, "What is this?"
When this was said, they replied, “Your Majesty, please command your women to pray for a son. The king agreed, saying, “Very well,” and told them, “You yourselves must pray for a son.
From then on, longing for a son, they worshipped various deities and performed various vows, yet no son was born. Then the king [spoke to] Sumedha...

He said, "Bhadde, you too should pray for a son. She replied, "Very well," and on the fifteenth day of the uposatha, having undertaken the uposatha observance endowed with the eight factors, she sat upon a proper couch in the bedchamber, reflecting upon her moral precepts.
The others, having lived according to their respective clans and lineages, went to the park without obtaining a son.
By the power of Sumedhā’s virtue, Sakka’s celestial abode trembled. Then Sakka, reflecting, thought: “Sumedhā desires a son; I shall grant her a son.
However, it is not possible to give just anyone; I must seek out a son worthy of her.
As he searched, he beheld the deva-son Naḷakāra, for he was endowed with great merit.
In a previous existence, while living in Bārāṇasī, a certain being was going to the field at sowing time when he saw a Paccekabuddha.

He sent his slaves and laborers, saying, "Go and sow! Having turned back himself, he led the Paccekabuddha to his home, fed him, and then, bringing him back to the bank of the Ganges, he stood together with his son by a wall made of *udumbara* wood and reed.
Having built a leaf-hut, fitted it with a door, and constructed a walking-path, they had the Paccekabuddha dwell right there for three months.
When the rains retreat was over, the father and son presented him with the three robes and sent him forth.
In this same manner, they had seven or eight Paccekabuddhas dwell in that leaf-hut and gave them sets of three robes. [Thus spoke] the two father and son reed-workers.
It is even said that after making an offering on the banks of the Ganges while searching for bamboo, they saw a Paccekabuddha and spoke thus.

Having passed away, they were reborn in the Tāvatiṃsa heaven; there, moving through the six celestial realms of the sense-sphere in both forward and reverse order, they wandered about enjoying great divine sovereignty. Desiring to be reborn in the higher heavenly worlds after passing away from there, they...
They were there. Sakka, having learned of their departure, went to the door of one of their celestial mansions and said to him as he approached, paid homage, and stood before him:
"My dear sir, it is fitting for you to go to the human world. "Great King, the human world is indeed loathsome and repulsive;
those dwelling there perform meritorious deeds such as giving and aspire to the world of the devas."
“What will I do after going there? [Sakka replied: “Noble sir, you shall enjoy in the human world the prosperity that is to be enjoyed in the world of the devas;
you shall dwell in a jeweled palace twenty-five yojanas high, nine yojanas long, and eight yojanas wide.
Please consent. He consented. Having obtained his promise, Sakka, in the guise of an ascetic, went to the royal park.
Having gone there, he showed himself walking back and forth in the air above those women and said, “To which of you shall I give the boon of a son?

Which of you will take the boon of a son? Sixteen thousand women raised their hands, crying out, “Venerable sir, give it to me! Give it to me! Then Sakka said, “I give the son to those who possess virtue.”

“What is your virtue? What is your conduct? They clapped their hands and said, “If you wish to give [your daughter] to one who is virtuous, go to the presence of Sumedhā. He went through the air and stood at the lion-window of her dwelling place.
Then those women informed her: “Come, O Queen; Sakka, the King of the Gods, says, ‘I shall give you an excellent son.’”
“Having come through the air, he stood in the lion-window.

She, arriving with great ceremony, opened the lion-window and said, “Is it true, venerable sir, that you grant a noble son to one who possesses virtue? “Yes, Queen,” he replied. “In that case, grant him to me.
“But what is your virtue? Tell me; if it pleases me, I shall grant you a noble son.”
Having heard his words, she said, "In that case, listen," and spoke fifteen verses describing her own virtue of moral conduct:
"I was the chief queen, the wife of Suruci, whom he brought to himself first;
for ten thousand years, Suruci took me as his wife."
“O Brahmin, I do not recall ever having shown contempt for King Videha,
the ruler of Mithilā, either by body, speech, or mind, whether openly or in private.”
“By this utterance of truth, O Sage, let a son be born to me;
may my head split into seven pieces if I have spoken a falsehood.
My husband’s mother is my mother-in-law, and his father is my father-in-law.”
“O Brahmā, those who were my instructors remained [with me] as long as they lived.
I, delighting in non-violence, practicing the Dharma out of desire for it,
attended upon them with care, day and night, without weariness.”
“By this utterance of truth, O Sage, let a son be born to me;
may my head split into seven pieces if I have spoken a falsehood.
O Brahmin, [here are] sixteen thousand women, together with their wives.”
Among them, there was never at any time any envy or anger in me.
I rejoice in their welfare; no one is unloved by me.
Out of compassion for myself, I always regard all my co-wives as such.
“By this utterance of truth, O Sage, let a son be born to me;
may my head split into seven pieces if I have spoken falsely.
[Let there be] slaves, laborers, messengers, and whoever else are my dependents.”
I send [this blessing] according to the Dhamma, my faculties always joyful:
“By this utterance of truth, O Lord, may a son be born to you!
May my head split into seven pieces if I am speaking a falsehood!”
“To the ascetics and brahmins, and others as well who seek alms,
I always satisfy with food and drink, my hands ever pure.
By this utterance of truth, may a son be born to me, O Lord!”
If I am speaking falsely, may my head split into seven pieces.
On the fourteenth, the fifteenth, and the eighth day of the fortnight, as well as during the fortnight of miracles,
[may I observe the fast] perfectly endowed with its eight factors.
“I observe the Uposatha, always restrained in my virtues.
By this utterance of truth, may a son be born to you, O Lord;
if I have spoken falsely, may my head split into seven pieces.”
In this context, "chief queen" means the principal queen. "Of Suruci" means of King Suruci. "First" means the very first among the sixteen thousand women.
"When he brought me" means from the time that Suruci brought me, I lived alone in this house for ten thousand years.
"She despised me" means she despised me even for a moment, whether in my presence or in my absence.
"Beyond this, I know nothing and remember nothing; 'these' refers to those she addresses.
'Those two' means both my father-in-law and mother-in-law; they were my two instructors, by whom I was trained, and they gave me counsel as long as they lived.
'Delighting in non-violence' means being endowed with the delight known as non-violence. By me..."
Indeed, not even a flea or an ant had ever been harmed by her before. "Kāmasā" means exclusively for the sake of sensual pleasure.
"Dhammacārinī" means she fulfilled the ten courses of wholesome action. "Upaṭṭhāsinī" means she attended upon him, performing services such as massaging his feet.
"Sahabhariyāni" means those who had become wives of the same husband together with me. "Nāhu" refers to the nature of envy arising from the defilements.
"Nor has the nature of anger ever existed in me before. By 'for their welfare' is meant that I rejoice precisely in whatever is for their benefit;
seeing them, I am satisfied as if they were daughters dwelling upon my own breast. By 'not one' is meant that among them there is not even a single one who is unloved by me;
all are indeed beloved. By 'I have compassion' is meant that with a gentle heart, I have compassion for all those sixteen thousand as if they were myself."
"By means of the proper method" (sahadhammena) means by way of logic or reason; the sense is that "I employ whoever is capable of doing whatever task in that very work.
"With joyful faculties" (pamuditindriyā) means that when I send them out, I always do so with joyful faculties;
I have never, in any case, sent anyone out while angry, saying, "Hey, you wicked slave, do this! "With hands washed" (payatapāṇinī) means...

"With hands washed" means having hands stretched out [in readiness]. "And during the fortnight of miracles" refers to the four days consisting of the eighth, fourteenth, fifteenth, and the following day, by way of approaching and following [the Uposatha].
"Always" means at all times; she was restrained by the five precepts, meaning her person was shielded and protected by them.
Thus, there is no measure for the virtues of that verse even when they are being praised by hundreds or thousands;

while she was still praising her own virtues with those fifteen verses, Sakka, because of his many duties, did not interrupt her speech but, commending her, spoke these two verses: "Abundant indeed are your wonderful virtues."
“O illustrious princess, all those qualities of the Dhamma that you praise within yourself are truly found in you, O blessed lady.
You are a kshatriya, perfected by birth, noble-born, and renowned.”
“A son shall be born to you, a Dhamma-king of the Videhas.
In this context, “qualities of Dhamma” means qualities of intrinsic nature, qualities of reality. “They exist” means that all those which were mentioned by you are indeed found in you.
“Abhijāta” means well-born, pure-born. “Yasassin” means endowed with fame and endowed with a retinue.
“Endowed [with these qualities]. ‘One such as this son will be born to you;
do not worry’—having heard his words, she was filled with joy and, questioning him, spoke two verses:
“The one with matted hair, covered in dust and dirt, standing in the sky above the clouds;”
“You speak words that are pleasing, which are dear to my heart.
Are you a deity come from heaven, or are you a seer of great psychic power?
Who are you who have arrived here? Please reveal yourself to me.”
In this context, "Dummī" refers to Sakka, who had come unadorned and unanointed;
however, because he had arrived in the delightful guise of an ascetic, she spoke thus. "In a place free from obstacles" means in a location where there is no resistance.
"That which is mine": since you speak these pleasing words to me, you must be a deity who has come here from heaven, or perhaps a seer of great psychic power.
"Among the *yakkhas* and others, who are you that have arrived here? Reveal yourself to me; speak according to the truth," she said.
As Sakka spoke to her, he recited these six verses:
"He whom the hosts of gods worship, having assembled in the Sudhamma hall..."
Thus I, Sakka, the thousand-eyed one, have come into your presence.
"In this world of the living, that woman who conducts herself with equanimity—
who is wise, virtuous, devoted to her mother-in-law, and faithful to her husband."
“Devas and non-humans come to behold such a woman— wise, pure in her deeds, and human.
And you, Bhaddā, by virtue of what was well-performed and well-practiced in the past,”
“Born here in this royal family, you have all your desires fulfilled.
And for you, O princess, there is a double victory in both worlds:
rebirth in the realm of the gods and fame in this life.”
“O wise one, may you long be happy; protect the Dhamma within yourself.
I am now departing for the triple heaven; it was a pleasure to me to see you.
In this context, “sahassakkho” means “thousand-eyed” by virtue of seeing eight thousand [beings] at that moment. “Itthiyo” means...
"A woman. "One who conducts herself with equanimity" means she is endowed with right conduct through the three doors of action.
"To such a one" means to one of that kind. "Sumedhā" means one of excellent wisdom. "A victory in both respects" means this is your triumph in this present existence and in the future.
Among those two, [it refers to] rebirth in the world of the gods in the future, and fame while living here in this life—this is [the victory].
This is called "seizing the victory in both places. "Dhamma" means: protect for a long time within yourself that which possesses such an essential nature and virtue.
"Esāham" means: this is I. "Piyaṃ me" means: the sight of you is dear to me.
However, I have duties and tasks to perform in the world of the gods; therefore, I am going. "Be heedful," he said to her.
Having given this exhortation, he departed. But at dawn, the deva-son Naḷakāra passed away and took rebirth in her womb.
Knowing that she was pregnant, she informed the king, and the king provided for the care of her pregnancy.
At the end of ten months, she gave birth to a son, and they gave him the name Mahāpanāda.
The inhabitants of both kingdoms, saying, "This is the milk-money for our master’s son," each threw a kahāpaṇa coin into the royal courtyard;
it became a great heap of wealth. Although they were refused by the king, they departed without taking it, thinking, "It will serve as a dowry for our master’s son when he reaches maturity.
Meanwhile, the prince grew up with a great retinue and reached adulthood.
At the age of sixteen, he attained mastery in all the arts. Observing his son’s maturity, the king said to the queen:
“My lady, it is time for my son’s royal consecration; having had a delightful palace built for him, we shall perform the consecration.
She accepted, saying, “Very well, Your Majesty. The king then summoned a master of site-selection.
“Father, take a carpenter and build a palace for my son not far from our residence;
we shall consecrate him in the kingship,” he said. They replied, “Very well, Your Majesty,” and began to examine a site for the ground.
At that moment, the abode of Sakka manifested signs of heat. Knowing the reason for this, he [sent] Vissakamma...
Having addressed him, he sent him forth, saying: "Go, dear son, and build for Prince Mahāpanāda a jeweled palace nine yojanas in length, eight yojanas in width, and twenty-five yojanas in height.
He went to the carpenters in the guise of a carpenter and, having sent them away with the words, "Come after you have eaten your morning meal," he [proceeded] with his measuring-staff...
He struck the ground, and at that very moment, a seven-storied palace of the aforementioned kind rose up.
For Mahāpanāda, the three auspicious ceremonies—the consecration of the palace, the umbrella, and the marriage—took place all at once.
The inhabitants of both kingdoms gathered at the site of the auspicious rites and spent seven years in festive celebration; the king did not dismiss them.
All the clothing, ornaments, hard foods, soft foods, and so forth, belonged entirely to the royal household.

When seven years had passed, they were summoned by King Suruci and asked, "What is this? They replied, "Great King, seven years have gone by while we have been eating for our auspicious ceremony; when will there be an end to this auspicious feast? Then the king said, "Sirs,..."
He said, "I have not laughed for all this time because of my son; when he laughs, then you may go.
Then the great multitude, having had a drum beaten, assembled the actors. Six thousand actors assembled and, though they performed in seven divisions, they were unable to make the king laugh.
It is said that for a long time he had been accustomed to celestial dramas.
Because they were seen, their dancing became unpleasant.
Then two chief actors named Bhaṇḍukaṇḍa and Paṇḍukaṇḍa entered the royal courtyard, thinking, "We shall make the king laugh.
Of them, Bhaṇḍukaṇḍa first [pointed to] a large mango tree named Atula at the palace gate.
Having fashioned a ball of thread and cast it, he caused it to hang upon a branch of that tree; thus he ascended the *atula* tree.
It is said that the *atula* was Vessavaṇa’s mango tree. Then Vessavaṇa’s servants seized him as well, cut his limbs and members one by one, and threw them down.
The remaining dancers gathered those pieces together and sprinkled them with water. He [then put on] a flower-cloth...
Having dressed and put on his robes, he rose up as if dancing. When Mahāpanāda saw this, he did not laugh.
The actor Paṇḍukaṇḍa had a wooden pyre constructed in the royal courtyard and entered the fire together with his own retinue.
When that fire was extinguished, they sprinkled the pyre with water. He, along with his retinue, having dressed and put on flowered garments, rose up as if dancing.
He rose up. Seeing him too, the king did not laugh. Thus, being unable to make him laugh, the people became distressed.
Sakka, understanding the reason for this, sent a celestial dancer, saying, "Go, dear one, and having made Mahāpanāda laugh, return.
He came and, standing in the air over the royal courtyard, displayed what is called the "half-limb" dance: only one hand and only one...
One foot, one eye, and one tusk danced, moved, and quivered, while the rest remained motionless.

Seeing this, Mahāpanāda laughed slightly; however, the great multitude, laughing incessantly and unable to restrain their laughter or maintain mindfulness, relaxed their limbs and fell right there in the royal courtyard at that moment.
The auspicious conclusion is finished. The rest here should be described by means of the Mahāpanāda Jātaka, beginning with: "That king was named Panāda, whose sacrificial post was made of gold.
King Mahāpanāda, having performed meritorious deeds such as giving, went to the world of the devas at the end of his life.
Having brought forth this Dhamma teaching, the Teacher said: "Thus, monks, in the past Visākhā also [received blessings] from my presence..."
Having said, "May I obtain a boon," he identified the Jātaka: "At that time, Mahāpanāda was Bhaddaji;
Queen Sumedhā was Visākhā; Vissakamma was Ānanda; and as for Sakka, he was none other than myself.
This concludes the sixth narrative, the Surucijātaka.
[490] 7. The Commentary on the Pañcuposathajātakavaṇṇanā:
"Now you may be at ease, O pigeon. This was related by the Teacher while dwelling at Jetavana, concerning five hundred lay followers who had observed the Uposatha.
At that time, the Teacher was seated upon the adorned Buddha-throne in the midst of the fourfold assembly in the Dhamma Hall.
Having sat down and surveyed the assembly with a gentle mind, he discerned, "Today, what subject will arise for my teaching regarding these lay followers?
He then addressed the lay followers, asking, "Lay followers, have you observed the Uposatha? When they replied, "Yes, Venerable Sir," he said, "Well done by you!
This Uposatha is indeed the lineage of the ancient wise ones; for the ancient wise ones, in order to restrain the defilements such as lust..."
Having said, "They observed the Uposatha fast," he was requested by them to relate a story of the past.
In the past, there was a forest between three kingdoms, including the kingdom of Magadha.
The Bodhisatta, having been born into a prominent brahmin family in the kingdom of Magadha, reached maturity, renounced sensual pleasures, went forth, and entered that forest.
Having established a hermitage and gone forth into the ascetic life of an *isi*, he took up residence there.
Not far from that hermitage, a pigeon dwelt with his wife in a bamboo thicket; a snake lived in an anthill;
a jackal was in one forest glade; and a bear was in another forest glade. These four, from time to time—
They would approach the seer and listen to the Dhamma.
Then one day, the pigeon, having emerged from his nest together with his wife, set out for alms-food.
As he was departing, a hawk seized the female pigeon who was following behind him and flew away. Hearing her cry of distress, the male pigeon—
Turning back and looking, he saw him being carried away by that [hawk]. The hawk, having killed her while she was still screaming, devoured her.
Distressed by the separation from her and burning with the fever of passion, the pigeon thought: "This lust exhausts me excessively;
I shall not now depart for my feeding ground without first restraining it. Thus, he cut off his path to the feeding ground.
Having gone into the presence of the ascetic, she undertook the Uposatha vows for the sake of restraining passion and lay down to one side.
The snake, thinking, "I shall seek food," emerged from its dwelling place and went to a border village to search for food in a place where cows were roaming.
At that time, the village headman’s all-white auspicious bull had taken up his grazing ground in a certain spot.
Standing on the base of the anthill with his knees and taking up clay with his horns, he was playing.
Frightened by the sound of the cows' footsteps, a snake started to enter that anthill. Then the bull stepped on him with his foot.
Enraged, the snake bit him, and the bull met his death right there. Hearing that "the bull had died," the village dwellers...
All of them came together, wept and wailed, honored him with perfumes, garlands, and other offerings, buried him in a pit, and departed.
When they had gone, the snake emerged and thought: "Relying on anger, I deprived this man of life and instilled grief in the hearts of the multitude;
now, I shall not depart for my own feeding grounds without first subduing this anger."
Having reflected thus, he turned back, went to that hermitage, and having undertaken the Uposatha for the sake of subduing his anger, lay down on one side.
The jackal, while searching for food, saw a dead elephant and, thinking, "I have found a great feast," was delighted;
he went and bit it at the trunk, which felt as if he were biting a pillar. Finding no satisfaction there, he [bit] the tusks...
When he bit him on the head, it was as if he had been bitten by a stone. When he bit him in the belly, it was as if he had been bitten by a grain-sack.
When he bit him on the tail, it was as if he had been bitten by an iron rod. When he bit him in the anus, it was as if he had been bitten by a ghee-cake.
As he ate under the influence of greed, he entered inside the belly; there, at a time of hunger, [he ate] the flesh.
He ate; when thirsty, he drank blood; and at the time of lying down, he lay down having spread out his own intestines and lungs.
Thinking, "Food, drink, and a bed have been provided for me right here;
what shall I do elsewhere?", he took delight in that very place and, not going outside, dwelt within the belly itself. Later on, due to the wind and heat...
When the elephant’s carcass was drying up, the path of dung was covered over; the jackal, lying within the belly, being devoid of flesh and blood and having a pale body, did not see the way out.
Then one day, an unseasonable rain fell, and as the path of dung became moist and soft, it revealed an opening.
Seeing the gap, the jackal thought, "I have been exhausted for too long."
Thinking, "I will escape through this opening," he struck the path of dung with his head.
As he emerged with great force from his narrow passage, his body was so bruised that all his body hair became stuck in the dung path;
emerging with a hairless body like a palm stump, he thought: "It is because of greed that I have experienced this suffering."

Thinking, "I will not now go for my alms-round without having subdued this [craving]," he went to that hermitage, undertook the Uposatha vows for the purpose of subduing greed, and lay down on one side.
The bear also, having emerged from the forest, overcome by excessive desire, went to a border village in the kingdom of Mallā. The villagers—
Thinking, "Accha has surely arrived," they went out with bows, staffs, and other weapons in hand, and surrounded the thicket he had entered.
Realizing he was surrounded by the great multitude, he emerged and fled; as he was fleeing, they struck him with their bows, staffs, and other weapons.
With his head split open and blood flowing, he returned to his own dwelling place.
Having gone there, he thought, "This suffering has arisen for me due to excessive greed;
I will not now take my food without first restraining it. Thinking thus, he went to that hermitage, undertook the Uposatha for the sake of restraining excessive desire, and lay down to one side.
The ascetic, however, being arrogant on account of his own birth, was unable to produce meditative absorption (jhāna). Then one...
The Paccekabuddha, knowing that he was dependent on pride, thought: "This is no ordinary being; he is a sprout of a Buddha.
In this very auspicious aeon, he will attain omniscience. Having suppressed his pride, I shall demonstrate the manner of attaining meditative absorption.
While he was still sitting in the leaf-hut, the Paccekabuddha came from the northern Himalayas and [appeared] upon his stone slab.
He sat down. Having gone out and seeing him seated on his own seat, he became displeased due to his reliance on pride;
approaching him and snapping his fingers, he said, "Begone, outcaste! Wretched one! Shaveling! Wretched ascetic!
For what purpose have you sat upon my seat? Then the other said to him, "Noble sir, why are you so reliant on pride?"
“I have realized the knowledge of private enlightenment (paccekabodhi). In this very auspicious aeon (bhaddakappa), you will become an omniscient Buddha;
you are a sprout of a Buddha. Having come here to fulfill the perfections (pāramīs), after such a length of time has passed, you will become a Buddha.
Established in the state of Buddhahood, you will be named Siddhattha. Thus he spoke, declaring his name, clan, and lineage.
Having pointed out all [the Buddhas] beginning with the Chief Disciples, he gave him this instruction: "For what purpose did you become harsh while relying on pride?

This is not worthy of you. Although addressed in this way by him, he neither paid homage nor asked such questions as, "When shall I become a Buddha? Then the Paccekabuddha said to him, "By your birth..."

"Know the greatness of my virtues; if you are able, wander in the sky just as I do," he said, and having leapt into the air, he flew toward the Northern Himalayas, scattering the dust from his own feet into the ascetic's mass of matted hair.
When the ascetic saw him depart, he was overcome with spiritual urgency (*saṃvega*) and thought: "This recluse possesses such a heavy body, yet in the face of the wind..."
Leaping through the air like a tuft of cotton flung aloft, I thought:
"Because of my high birth, I neither bowed at the feet of such a Paccekabuddha nor asked him, 'When shall I become a Buddha? What indeed will mere birth accomplish?
In this world, the practice of virtue alone is great. Furthermore, this pride of mine, if it continues to increase, will lead me to hell."
Thinking, "I will not now go for the sake of fruits and fruitless pursuits without first subduing this conceit," the noble son Mahāñāṇa entered the leaf-hut,
undertook the Uposatha for the purpose of subduing conceit, and sat upon a mat of wood-chips. Having subdued his conceit, expanded the *kasiṇa*,
and attained the higher knowledges (*abhiññā*) and meditative absorptions (*samāpatti*), he emerged and went to the end of the walking-path.
He sat down upon a stone slab. Then the pigeons and others approached him, paid homage, and sat down to one side.
The Great Being asked the pigeon, "On other days you do not come at this time, but search for food;
why is it that today you have become one observing the Uposatha? "Yes, Venerable Sir," he replied. Then [the Great Being asked] him, "By whom..."
Asking for the reason, he spoke the first verse:
"Now you are free from anxiety, O pigeon; as a bird, you have no need for food.
Enduring hunger and thirst, why, sir, do you observe the *uposatha*?"
In this context, "one who has little concern" means one who is free from attachment. "There is no need for food for you" means: "Is there no need for food for you today?
Having heard that, the pigeon spoke two verses:
"In former times, overcome by passion, I was with my female pigeon; we both took delight in this very place."
Then the fowler seized the female dove; I was unwilling to be without her.
"Through separation from her in this various existence, I experience a mental anguish;
therefore, I shall observe the Uposatha, lest passion come upon me again."
"There we shall delight" means: "In this place on the earth, we shall delight in the pleasure of sensual desires. "The fowler" refers to the bird Sena.

When the pigeon had described his own practice of the Uposatha, the Great Being questioned each one among the snakes and others. They too answered him according to the truth: "O serpent, you move crookedly;
O snake, you have two tongues, you are armed with fangs, and you are possessed of terrible venom."
“Enduring even thirst for the sake of the Dhamma, why, O long-lived one, do you observe the Uposatha?
“There was once a powerful bull belonging to a village headman, possessing a trembling hump and endowed with beauty and strength.
He trampled me, and being enraged, he bit me; overwhelmed by pain, I met my death.”
“Then the people, having departed from the village, went away weeping and crying;
therefore, I observe the Uposatha, lest anger come upon me again.
There is much flesh of the dead in the charnel ground, yet that which is of pleasing appearance is for your food.”
“Enduring even thirst for the sake of the Dhamma, why, O jackal, do you observe the *uposatha* fast?
“I entered the belly of a great elephant; I delighted in carrion and was greedy for the flesh of elephants.
The hot wind and the sharp rays of the sun dried up the path of his dung.”
“I was thin and pale, O Blessed One, and there was no path for my departure.
A great cloud suddenly poured down rain, which soaked the path of loose soil.
Then, O Blessed One, I emerged like the moon released from the mouth of Rāhu.”
"Therefore, I too observe the Uposatha; let greed not come upon me again.
"Formerly you used to roam about, crushing the ants upon the anthill;
enduring hunger and thirst, why indeed do you sit here observing the Uposatha?"
“Out of excessive greed, I utterly despised my own home and went to the village of Mallagāma.
Then, people emerged from the village and beat me with clubs.
With my head split open and my body smeared with blood, I returned to my own home.”
"Therefore, I too observe the Uposatha; do not come back again out of excessive greed.
In this passage, he addresses him with the words "anujjugāmī" and so forth. "Calakkaku" means one whose hump is moving.
"Dukkhābhitunno" means that bull, being afflicted by suffering, became distressed. "Bahū" means many. "Pavisī" means I entered. "Rasmiyo" means...
“The rays of the sun shall emerge; they have emerged. “Ants” refers to termites. “Crushing” means devouring.
“With excessive contempt” means despising, censuring, and reviling. “With kodaṇḍakas” means with bow-staves and clubs.
Thus, after those four had praised their own observance of the Uposatha, they rose, paid homage to the Great Being, and said: “Venerable Sir,…”
"Other days you go at this time for the sake of gathering fruits;
why have you not come today, being observant of the Uposatha? Thus questioning him, they spoke this verse:
"What you asked us, O Blessed One, we have all answered according to our knowledge."
“We too ask you, venerable sir: why, O Brahmā, are you observing the Uposatha?
He also explained it to them:
“Unstained, a Paccekabuddha sat for a moment in my hermitage.”
Thus he knew my past and future courses, my name, my clan, and my entire conduct.
"In this way I did not bow at his feet, nor did I question him out of pride;
therefore, I shall observe the Uposatha, lest pride come upon me again."
In this context, "that which" refers to the matter you asked us about. "As we understood it" means we explained it according to our own way of understanding.
"Unstained" means untainted by all defilements (*kilesa*). "He knew me" means he now knows both the place where I am to go and the place where I have already gone:
"In the future, you will become a Buddha named such-and-such, belonging to such-and-such a clan."
"Such will be your conduct of virtue"—in this way he informed me of his name, his clan, and his conduct;

the meaning is that he made it known and spoke of them all. "Even though he spoke thus, I did not pay homage"—this means that even while he was speaking in this manner, I, relying on my own pride, did not bow at his feet.
Thus, having explained the reason for his own observance of the Uposatha, the Great Being exhorted them and sent them away;

they then entered the leaf-hut, while the others returned to their respective places. The Great Being, without falling away from his meditative absorption (*jhāna*), was destined for the Brahma-world, and the others, abiding by his instruction, were destined for the heavenly realms (*sagga*).
Having delivered this Dhamma teaching, the Teacher said, "Thus, lay followers, this so-called Uposatha is the lineage of the ancient wise ones;
it must be observed as a dwelling in the Uposatha. Having said this, he identified the Jātaka:
"At that time, Anuruddha was the pigeon, Kassapa was the hare, Moggallāna was the jackal, Sāriputta was the snake, and I myself was the ascetic."
The seventh is the commentary on the Pañcuposathajātakavaṇṇanā.
[491] 8. The commentary on the Mahāmorajātakavaṇṇanā:
"If indeed I were seized by you for the sake of wealth... This was spoken by the Teacher while residing at Jetavana concerning a certain monk who was dissatisfied with the religious life.
The Teacher spoke concerning that monk. For the Teacher asked that monk, "Is it true, as it is said, that you are disenchanted?
When he replied, "It is true, Bhante," the Teacher said, "Monk, how could this delight-and-lust (*nandīrāga*) not cause such a person to waver?
Indeed, the wind that uproots Mount Sineru does not feel shame for the withered leaves on its outskirts; formerly, for seven hundred years, the manifestation of internal defilements..."
"Having restrained themselves, these pure beings dwell [in peace]; this is like a fish in shallow water," he said, and then related a story of the past.
In the past, when Brahmadatta was reigning in Benares, the Bodhisatta took rebirth in the womb of a peahen in a border region.
When the fetus had matured, the mother laid her egg on the feeding ground.
He departed. Now, as for the egg, when the mother is free from illness and no other obstacle—such as a *dīghajātika* snake—is present, it does not perish.

Therefore, that egg, becoming golden-colored like a cluster of *kaṇikāra* flowers, split open by its own inherent nature at the time of maturity, and a golden-colored peacock chick emerged. Its two eyes were like *jiñjukā* fruits.
His beak was the color of coral, and three red stripes encircled his neck and ran down the middle of his back.
When he reached maturity, his body became as large as a merchant’s cart; he was handsome and beautiful.
All the peacocks gathered together, made him their king, and surrounded him.
Thus, one day while drinking water from a pool, seeing his own excellence of form, he thought:
"I am more beautiful in form than all other apes; if I live with these on the path frequented by humans, obstacles will arise for me.
I shall go to the Himālaya and live alone in a comfortable place. Then, during the night...
While the monks were in seclusion, he departed without letting anyone know, flew up, and entered the Himālaya mountains.
Having crossed three mountain ranges, in a certain forest on the fourth mountain range there was a lake covered with lotuses;
not far from it, standing against a mountain, was a great banyan tree, and upon its branch—
He lay down. Now, in the middle of that mountain there was a pleasant cave.
Desiring to dwell there, he lay down on the mountain slope facing its entrance. That place could not be ascended from below nor descended from above;
it was free from the dangers of wild cats, long-tailed snakes, and humans. He [thought], "This..."
Thinking, "It will be comfortable for me," he stayed right there that day.
On the following day, rising from his mountain cave and sitting on the mountain peak facing the east, he saw the rising solar disc.

To provide protection against the dangers of the day, he recited the protective charm (*paritta*): "This one with eyes, the sole king, is rising. Having done so, he descended to the feeding ground, took his food, and departed.
Returning in the evening and sitting on the mountain peak facing west, he would see the solar disc set;
then, for the sake of protection against the night, he would recite the protective charm, "Apehi yaṃ cakkhumā ekarājā," and dwell there by this means.
Then one day, a certain hunter, wandering in the forest, saw the peacock sitting on the mountain peak.
Having seen this, he returned to his own residence and, as the time of his death drew near, said to his son:
"My dear son, in the forest beyond the fourth mountain range there is a golden-colored peacock; if the king asks about it, you should point it out to him.
Then one day, at dawn, the chief queen of the King of Bārāṇasī, named Khemā, saw a dream. Such was the dream she had:
“A golden-colored peacock was teaching the Dhamma; she gave her applause and listened to the Dhamma, and after the peacock had finished teaching, it rose up and flew away.
Even as she said, “The king of peacocks is departing! Seize him! she woke up.
Having woken up, she realized it was a dream and thought, “If I say it was a dream, the king will not take it seriously.”
Thinking, "When I say, 'I have a pregnancy-longing,' he will fulfill it," she lay down as if she were indeed longing for such things.
Then the king approached her and asked, "My lady, what is making you unwell? "A pregnancy-longing has arisen within me. "What do you wish for, my lady?
"O King, I wish to hear the Dhamma from a golden-colored peacock. "My lady, where could such a thing come from?"
“Shall I obtain a peacock? [The queen replied: “Your Majesty, if I do not obtain one, I shall have no life. “Do not worry, my lady;
if there is one anywhere, you will obtain it,” the king said, comforting her. Having gone and sat upon his royal throne, he asked his ministers:
“Sirs, the queen desires to hear the Dhamma from a golden-colored peacock. Are there such things as golden-colored peacocks?”
"Will they be so? "The brahmins will know, Your Majesty.
The king summoned the brahmins and questioned them. The brahmins replied: "Great King, among those born in water, fish, turtles, and crabs;
and among those born on land, deer, swans, peacocks, and partridges—these animals and humans may all be of golden complexion."

“This is mentioned in our manuals of physiognomy,” they said. The king assembled the hunters throughout his realm and asked, “Has a golden-colored peacock ever been seen by you? The others replied, “Never before.
But he to whom it had been described by his father said, “It has never been seen by me either; however, my father told me that in such-and-such a place there was a golden-colored one...”
"I am here," he replied. Then the king, giving him much wealth, sent him off, saying, "My good man, you will have given life to both myself and my queen;
go, bind him, and bring him back. Having given the wealth to his wife and children, he went there, and seeing the Great Being, he set a snare and said, "Today he shall be bound; today..."
Thinking, "He will be bound," he died without being bound at all; the queen also died without obtaining her wish.
The king, becoming angry and overcome by wrath, thinking, "My beloved wife has died because of that peacock," said:
"In the Himalayas, on the fourth mountain range, there roams a golden-colored peacock; by eating its flesh, people become free from old age and immortal."
Having had it inscribed upon a golden plate and placed that plate inside a precious casket, he passed away.
Then there was another king. Seeing the letters upon the golden plate, he thought, "I shall become ageless and immortal," and dispatched a hunter to seize it.
He too died right there. In this manner, six successive reigns passed.
The six sons of the hunter had already died in the Himalayas.
But the seventh hunter, sent by the king, having been unable to catch him for seven years—thinking "today, today indeed"—reflected:
"What now could be the reason that the foot of this peacock-king does not step upon the snare? Then, while examining it morning and evening, he [discovered it].
Seeing him performing the *paritta*, he reasoned: "There is no other peacock in this place; it must be this practitioner of the holy life (*brahmacārin*).
It is by the power of his holy life and the power of the *paritta* that his foot is not caught in the snare.
Having thus identified him, he went to a border region, captured a peahen, and when she was struck with a whip—
It cries when rained upon and dances when struck with the hand; having thus trained it, he took it and went away.
Before even performing the protective rite for the Bodhisatta, he set a snare, snapped his fingers, and made the peahen cry out.
The peacock heard her sound, and at that very moment, his defilements—which had lain dormant for seven hundred years—reared up like a venomous snake that has been struck by a staff.
He rose up as if startled. Being afflicted by defilements and unable to perform a protective chant (*paritta*), he went toward her with great haste;
even as he was placing his foot into the snare, he descended from the sky. That snare, which had not been stepped upon for seven hundred years, immediately became functional and bound his foot.
Then the hunter’s son, seeing him hanging from the tip of the pole, thought:
"Six hunters’ sons could not capture this king of peacocks, nor could I for seven years;

yet today, having come here afflicted by defilements because he was unable to perform a protective chant (*paritta*) on account of this peahen, he has been caught in a snare and hangs there with his head downward."
“Such a virtuous being has been exhausted; it is unfit to bring one such as this as a gift for the king.
Of what use is the honor bestowed by the king? I shall release him. Then he thought again: “This man possesses the strength of an elephant and is endowed with great power.
When I approach him, terrified by the fear of death and thinking, ‘He is coming to kill me,’ he will struggle and [kick] my foot...”

“Or he might break my wing; instead, without approaching him, I will stand in concealment and cut his bowstring with a razor-sharp arrow, so that he will depart of his own accord, according to his pleasure.
Standing in concealment, the hunter strung his bow, fixed a razor-sharp arrow, and drew it back. The peacock thought, “This hunter is making me suffer from affliction...”
Realizing that he was bound, [the hunter] thought, "He will come here free from apprehension; where indeed could he be?
Looking here and there, he saw him standing with his bow strung.
Thinking, "He must intend to kill me and take me away," and being terrified by the fear of death, he begged for his life and spoke the first verse:
“If indeed I have been seized by you for the sake of wealth, do not kill me after having captured me alive;
lead me, my good man, into the presence of the king, and I think you will obtain no small amount of wealth.
In this context, *sace hi tyāham* means “if indeed I am yours”; *upantikaṃ nehi* means “lead into his presence”; *lacchasi anapparūpaṃ* means “you will obtain no small (or vast) amount.”
Hearing this, the hunter’s son thought: “The peacock king thinks, ‘He has fixed his arrow because he wishes to pierce me’; I shall reassure him. Reassuring him, he spoke the second verse:
“This arrow fixed upon the bowstring today is not for your slaughter;
I shall release your snare as well, so that the peacock king may go at his ease.”
There, they will strike him down and tear him apart.
Then the peacock king spoke these two verses:
“He who followed me for seven years, enduring hunger and thirst day and night;”
“Now why do you wish to release me from this bond, when I have been brought into the power of the snare?
Have you refrained from taking life, or has fearlessness been granted by you to all beings—
that you wish to release me from this bond, when I have been brought into the power of the snare?”
In this context, "tattha yaṃ" means: since you have followed me for so long, therefore I ask you;

the meaning is: "Why do you wish to release me from bondage when I have been brought under the power of the snare? "Virato nu sajja" means "Are you perhaps detached today? "Sabbabhūtesu" means "toward all beings."
Beyond this—
“Tell me, O King of Peacocks, of one who abstains from taking life and gives fearlessness to all beings:
I ask you about this matter, what happiness does he obtain when he passes away from here?”
“I declare that for one who abstains from taking life and who grants fearlessness to all beings, there is praise in this very life, and he goes to heaven upon the dissolution of the body.
Some say, ‘There are no gods; the soul meets its end right here.’”
"Likewise, they declare that there is fruit for good and evil deeds, and that giving is ordained as a duty;
having faith in the words of those Arhats, I therefore oppress these birds.
These verses, which explain the connection [of the narrative], are to be understood according to the method of the Pāḷi.
Regarding the phrase "therein some say": certain ascetics and brahmins speak thus.

"Not believing the word of those Arhats" means that his personal attendants were naked ascetics who held the doctrine of annihilationism (*ucchedavāda*). Although that being was endowed with the necessary support (*upanissaya*) for the knowledge of *paccekabodhi*, they caused him to adopt the doctrine of annihilationism.
Through association with them, he came to hold the view that "there is neither wholesome nor unwholesome."
He kills the bird. Thus, this so-called "association with unworthy persons" is a great transgression. Thinking they were indeed "Arahants," he spoke thus.
Having heard that, the Great Being, thinking, "I shall explain to him the existence of the next world," while hanging head-downwards from the crossbar of his bed, spoke this verse:
"The moon and the sun, both beautiful to behold, travel illuminating the sky;..."
"Regarding this world or the other world, how indeed do they speak of you in the world of men?
In this context, "imassa" means: "Do they speak of you as being in this world, or rather in the other world? Or, this genitive case may be used in the sense of the locative.
"Kathaṃ nu te" means: "In these celestial mansions, how indeed [do they speak] of you, O sons of the gods, Moon and Sun?"
