They speak; they speak of whether something exists or whether it does not exist, or whether they are gods or whether they are humans.
The son of the hunter recited this verse:
“The moon and the sun, both beautiful to behold, travel across the sky illuminating it.”
“They do not belong to another world, nor to this one; they are called ‘gods’ in the world of men,” he said.
Then the Great Being replied to him:
“Right here your base doctrines are cast out—those who, being causeless, do not speak of karma.”
"Likewise, the fruit of good and evil deeds, and those who say 'giving has been ordained'—right here they are defeated, these base proponents.

In this context, "right here they are defeated, these base proponents" means: if the moon and sun are situated in the world of the gods and not in the human world, and if they are gods and not humans, then right here, at this very explanation, your supporters—the base proponents—are defeated.
They are as follows. The "Ahetuka" (Causeless) are those who maintain the doctrine that there is no karma that serves as the cause for either purification or defilement.
The "Dattupaññatta" (Established by Givers) are those who say that giving was established by fools.
Having observed this while the Great Being was speaking, he recited two verses:
“Truly, this word of yours is the truth; for how could a gift ever be fruitless?
Likewise, how could there be fruit for well-done and ill-done deeds, and how could the giving of alms be established as a rule?
What must one do, what must one perform, what must one practice, what must one cultivate, and by what quality of asceticism?”
"O King of Peacocks, explain this matter to me, so that I may not fall into hell.
In this context, "dattupaññattaṃ" means: how could there be such a thing as a gift established by the giver? "Kathaṃkaro" means:
performing what kind of action? "Kiṃtikaro" means: for what reason or cause would I not go to hell?
The others are synonyms for that same thing.
Having heard this, the Great Being thought, "If I do not explain this question, the world of humans will become as if empty;
therefore, I shall speak of the existence of righteous ascetics and brahmins. Having reflected thus, he spoke two verses:
“Whatever recluses there are on this earth, clad in saffron robes and living the homeless life,
they wander for alms early in the morning at the proper time, for being virtuous, they abstain from wandering at the wrong time.
Having approached them there at the right time, ask whatever may be dear to your mind.”
“They will speak to you according to their own understanding for the welfare of this world and the next.
In this context, “those who are at peace” (*santa*) refers to the wise *paccekabuddhas* who have stilled all evil.

“According to their own understanding” (*yathāpajānaṃ*) means they will speak to you by way of their own realization, having cut through your doubt. “For the welfare of this world and the next” (*imassa lokassa parassa catthaṃ*)—by this...
"Ask those who will explain the purpose of this world and the next world, saying: 'By this kamma one is reborn in the human world; by this, in the heavenly world; and by this, in hell and so forth.
Having spoken thus, he threatened him with the fear of hell. But that Paccekabodhisatta, who had fulfilled the perfections, [endured] the touch of the sun's rays..."
Having looked [at him], he who possessed matured wisdom wandered about like a full-blown lotus. Listening to his discourse on the Dhamma, he remained standing exactly where he stood;
having comprehended the conditioned phenomena (*saṅkhāra*) and contemplated the three characteristics (*tilakkhaṇa*), he penetrated the knowledge of *paccekabodhi*.
His penetration and his liberation from the Great Being’s snare occurred at one and the same moment.
The Paccekabuddha, having shattered all defilements and standing at the very limit of existence, uttered this inspired exclamation (udāna) in verse:
“As a snake sheds its worn-out old skin, as a green tree casts off its pale leaves—so has this cruel nature been abandoned by me; I cast away this core of cruelty.”

The meaning of this is as follows: Just as a serpent casts off its old, worn-out skin, and just as a tree with green and ripening blue leaves sheds a withered, pale leaf wherever it may lie, even so have I today cast off my cruelty and ferocity and remain [here].
This cruelty of mine has now been abandoned; "It is well indeed that I have abandoned the state of a hunter today."
"Jahāmahanti pajahiṃ" means "I have abandoned what was great.
Having uttered this inspired utterance, he thought, "As for myself, I am now liberated from all the bonds of the defilements;
however, there are many birds kept in my dwelling who have been tied up. How shall I set them free? Having reflected thus, he questioned the Great Being.
“O King of Birds, there are many birds bound in my dwelling; how shall I release them?
The knowledge of encompassing skillful means (*upāyapariggahañāṇa*) belonging to the omniscient Bodhisattvas is indeed greater than even that of the Pratyekabuddhas. Therefore, he said to him:
“Perform an act of truth (*saccakiriya*) based on that knowledge of Pratyekabuddha-enlightenment which you have realized by shattering the defilements through the Path.”
“Do this, and there shall be no being in the entire land of Jambudīpa who remains in bondage.
Standing at the gate where the Bodhisatta had given him instructions, he uttered a verse while performing an act of truth:
“And as for those birds of mine that are bound—several hundred of them in my dwelling;”
"Today I give them my life, and they shall attain liberation and their own abode.
In this context, "and they shall attain liberation" means: "I myself have attained liberation, having realized the knowledge of Pacceka-bodhi;
out of compassion, I grant these beings the gift of life by means of this truth. "Their own abode" means all of them...
He said, "Let all beings go to their respective dwelling places.
Then, at the very moment of his declaration of truth (*saccakiriyā*), they were all released from their bonds and returned to their own abodes while uttering cries of joy.
At that instant, throughout the entire Jambudīpa, from cats on down, all those who had been held in captivity in their various homes...
There was no one named Satta. The Paccekabuddha raised his hand and touched his head;
at that very moment, the marks of a householder vanished and the marks of one who has gone forth appeared.
Possessing the proper deportment like a sixty-year-old elder and wearing the eight requisites, he extended his joined palms toward the peacock king and said, "You alone have been my support."
Having performed a circumambulation, he sprang into the air and went to the Nandamūlaka mountain cave.
The peacock king also, having flown up from the tip of the staff, took his food and returned to his own dwelling place.
Now, illustrating how even after wandering for seven years with a snare in hand, the hunter was liberated from suffering by means of the peacock king, the Teacher spoke this concluding verse:
“A hunter, carrying a snare in his hand, wandered in the forest to harass the illustrious lord of peacocks;
having bound the illustrious lord of peacocks, may he be released from suffering just as I am released.
In this context, *bādhetu* means “to kill,” or rather, this is the reading itself. *Bandhitvā* means “having bound [him] while he stood [there], [the hunter heard] a discourse on the Dhamma.”

"Having heard [this], he became filled with spiritual urgency (*saṃvega*); this is the meaning. "Just as I" means: "Just as I am liberated by self-enlightened knowledge (*sayambhuñāṇa*), so too is he liberated.

Having delivered this Dharma teaching and proclaimed the Truths (*sacca*), the Teacher identified the Jātaka. At the conclusion of the Truths, the monk who was despondent attained Arhatship. "At that time, I myself was the peacock king."
The Eighth: The Commentary on the Mahāmoraja Jātaka.
[492] 9. The Commentary on the Tacchasūkara Jātaka.
"While wandering about seeking..."—this was spoken by the Teacher while dwelling at Jetavana, concerning two elder monks who were great in years.
He related the story: it is said that when Mahākosala gave his daughter to King Bimbisāra, he gave the village of Kāsī as the dowry for the daughter’s bath-water.
When King Pasenadi, after Ajātasattu had killed his father, seized that village, the two kings fought over it;
initially, Ajātasattu was victorious, and the King of Kosala suffered defeat.
He asked his ministers, "By what means might we capture Ajātasattu? [The ministers replied,] "Your Majesty, monks are indeed skilled in counsel;
it would be well to dispatch spies to ascertain the conversation of the monks in the monastery.
The king consented, saying, "Very well," and said, "Come, you must go to the monastery and remain hidden there to observe the venerable ones."
"How do you apprehend it? he thus dispatched secret agents. In the Jeta Grove as well, many royal officials had gone forth into homelessness.
Among them were two elder monks living in leaf huts on the outskirts of the monastery:
one was the elder named Dhanuggahatissa, and the other was the elder named Mantidatta. Having slept throughout the entire night, they woke at the time of dawn.
Among them, the Elder Dhanuggahatissa kindled a fire and said, "Venerable sir, the Elder Mantidatta! "What is it, venerable sir?

"You are sleeping. "I am not sleeping; what should be done? "Venerable sir, this King of Kosala is truly a glutton, for he knows only how to eat as much as would fit in a small bowl. "Then what, venerable sir? [He replied: "In his own belly..."
“King Ajātasattu has defeated the king with merely a handful of poison. “But what, venerable sir, ought to be done?

“Venerable sir, regarding the chariot-formation, the wheel-formation, and the lotus-formation—these three kinds of battle formations taught by the Elder Mantidatta—it is fitting for one who wishes to capture his nephew Ajātasattu to capture him by forming the chariot-formation at such-and-such a place.”

"By stationing brave men on both sides of the mountain pass, displaying our force in front, and then, once we know he has entered within, shouting and roaring, we shall be able to seize him—like a fish that has entered a net—by closing him up within our fists.
When the dispatched men heard this account, they reported it to the king. The king went forth with a great army and acted accordingly.
Having seized Ajātasattu and bound him with iron shackles, he deprived him of his pride for several days;
then, consoling him with the words, "Do not act in such a way again," he released him, gave him his daughter named Vajirakumāri, and sent him away with a great retinue.
[This was] through the mediation of the Elder Dhanuggahatissa with the King of Kosala.
The talk among the bhikkhus arose thus: "Ajātasattu has been captured! They raised that very same discussion even in the Hall of Truth.
The Teacher, having arrived, asked, "Bhikkhus, with what conversation are you sitting gathered here now?
When they replied, "With this one indeed," he said, "Bhikkhus, it is not only now; formerly too, Dhanuggahatisso was [unsuccessful] in the preparation for battle."
Having said, "Cheko-yeva," he related a story from the past.
Long ago, a carpenter living in a village near the gate of the city of Bārāṇasī went into the forest for timber and saw a young pig that had fallen into a pit.
He brought it back, gave it the name "Taccha-sūkara" (the clever pig), and raised it. It—
He became a helper to him. Turning over trees with his snout, he gave them to him;
wrapping them with his tusks, he pulled out black ropes; biting with his mouth, he brought axes, chisels, and mallets.
When he had grown up, he became very strong and possessed a massive body. Then the carpenter, having established affection for him as a son, [thought]: "While he is living here..."
“May no one at all harm him,” he thought, and released him into the forest. He reflected, “I will not be able to live alone in this forest;
I shall seek out my kinsmen and dwell there surrounded by them.
Searching for boars in the thicket of the woods, he saw many boars and, being delighted, spoke three verses:
“Wandering about, we searched through mountains and forests;
seeking them, we roamed, and now these kinsmen have been found by me.
There is much of this root and fruit, and this food is no small amount.”
“Delightful indeed are these mountain peaks; there will be a comfortable dwelling.
Right here I shall dwell, together with all my kinsmen—free from anxiety, free from fear, sorrowless, and without dread from any quarter.”
In this context, *yadesamānā* means "while we were searching for that circle of kinsmen. *Anvesanti* means "for a long time indeed, while searching, we wandered.
*Temeti* refers to these [kinsmen]. *Bhakkho* is simply the food consisting of forest roots and fruits.
*Appossuko* means having become free from anxiety.
Having heard his words, the pigs spoke this fourth verse:
“Seek another shelter, for our enemy is here.
He kills the pigs one by one, coming here and choosing the best.”
In this context, *tacchā* means they address him by that name. *Varaṃ varaṃ* means that while killing pigs, he kills only the best, the very best, of the thick-fleshed ones.
From here on, the verses with clear connections should be understood according to the method of the Pāḷi:
“Who indeed is our enemy here? Who is a kinsman when we have come together?”
"One who destroys those who are difficult to destroy—tell me of him when asked.
"The king of beasts, whose stripes point upward, the powerful beast armed with tusks as weapons;
he comes here and slays boars one by one, the best among them."
“We have no fangs, nor is strength placed within our bodies;
yet, all of us acting together, we shall bring this solitary one under our control.
O carpenter, you speak words that are heart-pleasing and pleasant to the ear.”
"Even if someone should flee in battle, we shall slay him afterwards.
Regarding that, he said: "Who indeed is our enemy?"—upon seeing you, I thought, "These pigs have little flesh and blood;
they must be afraid," therefore tell me: who indeed is our enemy here? [He replied: "One with a ridge of hair running upward."
"He was endowed with prominent streaks on his body. This was said with reference to a tiger. "Whoever" means:
"If even one among us should flee, we shall kill him afterwards.
The boar, having made all the pigs single-minded, asked: "At what time will the tiger arrive?"
"Today at dawn he took one [sow] and went; tomorrow at dawn he will return.
Being skilled in battle, he understood the strategic terrain, knowing, "Standing in this place, it is possible to conquer.

Therefore, having observed a certain spot and having caused the pigs to take their fodder that very night, starting from the time of the powerful dawn, [he thought], "Battle, indeed, is by way of the *vyūha* of chariots and so forth..."
Having said, "It is threefold," he arranged the lotus-array. In the central place, he placed suckling piglets;
surrounding them were their mothers; surrounding them were barren sows;
next to them were the young piglets with tusks like buds; next to them were those with large tusks.
Immediately after them came the old pigs; then, having formed groups of ten, twenty, and thirty there, he stationed a troop of soldiers.
For his own benefit, he had one pit dug, and for the tiger’s downfall, he had a slope shaped like a snout excavated. Between the two pits, for his own dwelling place—
He had a platform constructed. Taking with him strong, skilled warriors, he went about from place to place, encouraging the boars. While he was doing this, the sun rose.
Then the tiger-king, having emerged from the hermitage of Kūṭajaṭila, stood upon the mountain slope. Seeing him, [he thought:]
The boars said, "Venerable sir, our enemy has arrived! He replied, "Do not fear; whatever he does, do all that by imitating him.
The tiger shook his body and, as if retreating, passed urine; the boars did exactly the same.
The tiger looked at the boars and roared a great roar; they too did exactly the same.
Seeing their activity, he thought: "These are not as they were before; today they stand in separate factions, having become my adversaries.
They even have a commander to coordinate them. It is not fitting for me to go near them today.
Urged by the fear of death, he turned back and went into the presence of the false ascetic. Then...
Seeing that his hands were empty, he spoke this ninth verse:
“Have you today refrained from taking life? Has fearlessness been granted to all beings by you?
Are there no fangs for you to kill deer? You who have received alms from the Saṅgha, why do you sit brooding like a pauper?”
In that context, "a pig in a herd" means: "You, who have become like a pig in a herd, sit brooding like a beggar because you have found no food.
Then the tiger spoke three verses:
"My tusks do not lack strength; power is established within my body."
Having seen my kinsmen gathered together in harmony, I therefore meditate alone in the forest.
"In the past, these people went here and there, scattered and seeking refuge because they were overcome by fear;
now they dwell together in one place, and wherever they stand, they are difficult for me to overcome."
“Endowed with leaders, united, speaking with one voice;
they might harm me while being in concord, therefore I do not long for them.
In this context, “united as one” means having become together, standing in unity. “Imassudanti” means these very [eyes] were indeed by me.
Having merely opened their eyes and looked about in every direction, they previously went their separate ways. "Puthu" means individually.
"Yatthaṭṭhitā" means standing on whichever portion of ground they were situated. "Pariṇāyakasampannā" means endowed with a commander-in-chief.
Therefore, for that reason, I do not desire them.
Having heard that, the rogue ascetic, seeking to inspire him with zeal, spoke this verse:
“Indra alone conquers the Asuras; Sena alone slays the birds by force;
the tiger alone, when it encounters a herd of deer, kills the choicest of the best—for such is its power.”

In this context, "having reached the herd of deer" means that, having joined the deer-herd, he kills the choicest deer one after another. For such indeed is his strength; for his strength is of such a kind.
Then the tiger spoke this verse:
“Neither Indra, nor Sena, nor even the tiger, the lord of beasts [is my equal].”
“United and harmonious kinsmen do not bring themselves under the power of a tiger.

In this context, “under the power of a tiger” means that even though they stand there acting like tigers—shaking their bodies and so forth—they do not come under his control; he is unable to make them subject to his own will.
Again, the matted-hair ascetic (jaṭila), encouraging him, spoke two verses:
“Kumbhīlaka birds, living in flocks and moving in groups,
fly up and soar together, rejoicing in one another’s company.
And as they are soaring, one among them sometimes withdraws.”
"And a hawk strikes it down; such is the fate of the tiger.
In this context, "kumbhīlakas" are small birds of that name. "Flying up" means they fly up while foraging.
"And soaring" means, having taken their prey, they travel through the air. "One among them retreats" means one of these [birds] withdraws.
Or it goes off to one side or separately. "It strikes" means it seizes [the prey] after striking it.

"That destination is indeed for the tiger" (*veyyagghi*): it belongs to tigers (*byagghānaṃ*), thus it is "for the tiger. Even when they are traveling together in a group, such a destination is called the very same destination as that of tigers.
For it is not possible for all to go together; therefore, he who is alone there in that situation—
He went and seized him.
Having spoken thus, he encouraged him, saying: "O King of Tigers, you do not know your own strength;
do not fear! Simply roar and spring forward; two who go together cannot possibly be defeated. He did so accordingly.
The Teacher, elucidating that matter, said:
“Encouraged by the matted-hair ascetic with his eye for worldly gain,
Dāṭhī fell among the fanged ones, thinking as he had done before.”

In this context, "the fanged one" (dāṭhī) refers to one who himself has fangs as weapons and leaps upon other fanged creatures. "As before" means he perceives it exactly as he perceived it previously;
perceiving it in that very way, it is said that he went and stood upon the mountain slope. The boars reported to Taccha, "Master, the thief has come back again.
He reassured them, saying, "Do not be afraid," and rising up, he sat upon a stool between two pits.
He stood there. The tiger, gathering momentum, sprang toward the wild boar. The wild boar turned around and fell backward into the front pit.
The tiger, unable to check his momentum, went on and fell into the pit near the Suppa rock, where he remained standing like a heap of flesh.
The wild boar rose up with speed and [struck] him between the shoulder blades.
Having thrust in his fangs, he slit open [the man] as far as the heart, ate the flesh, bit him with his mouth, and having thrown him outside the pit, he said, "Seize this slave!
Those who arrived first received only the single act of his thrusting in his snout;
those who arrived later, receiving nothing at all, said, "What indeed is tiger-meat like? Then the boar-tyger emerged from the pit.
The boar looked at him and said, "Why indeed are you not satisfied? "Master, one tiger has already been captured;
however, there is another who is worth ten tigers," he replied. "Who is this? "He is a fraudulent ascetic who eats the meat brought back by the tiger.
"In that case, come along; we shall capture him. With these words, he rushed forward with them in great haste.
The matted-hair ascetic, thinking, "The tiger is taking a long time," watched the path of his approach.
Seeing many wild boars coming along, he thought, "I suspect these are coming to kill me after having killed the tiger," and so he fled and climbed up a *udumbara* tree.
The boars said, "He has climbed that tree. [They asked: "What tree? [They replied: "An *udumbara* tree."
“Very well then, do not worry; we shall take it now,” he said. He summoned young pigs and had them clear away the soil from the base of the tree;
he had the female pigs bring water to fill their mouths, and he had the large-tusked boars cut the roots on all sides.
Only one root remained, which had grown straight down. Then he told the remaining pigs, “You may go.”
Having pushed him aside and braced himself on his knees, he struck at the root of the fang;
it broke off as if struck by an axe and fell away. The tree turned over and fell. As that fraudulent ascetic was falling, they caught him and devoured his flesh.
Seeing this marvel, the deity of the tree spoke this verse:
“Excellent, O many kinsmen, even though you were trees born in the forest;
for the tiger was slain on the narrow path by the swine acting in unison.
In this context, “slain on the narrow path” means slain precisely at the place where there is only one way to go.
Then, revealing the fate of both of them, the Teacher spoke the following verse:
“Having killed both the brahmin and the tiger,
the boars were joyful and delighted, and they let out a great roar.”
Again, the boar Taccha asked them, "Do you have any other enemies? The boars replied, "There are none, Master.
Saying, "Having consecrated him, we shall make him king," they searched for water;

finding a water-jar belonging to a matted-hair ascetic, they filled that right-spiraling conch-shell treasure with water and, having brought it forward, [anointed] the boar Taccha right there at the foot of the udumbara tree.
They consecrated him. When the consecration water had been poured out, they made Sūkarikā his chief queen.
From that time forth, having seated him upon a noble throne of Udumbara wood, the performance of the consecration with a right-spiraled conch began.
To clarify this matter as well, the Teacher spoke the concluding verse:
“Those boars, having gathered well at the foot of the udumbara tree, consecrated the carpenter, saying: ‘You are our king, you are our lord.
In this passage, *te* means “those”; *sū* is merely an expletive particle (*nipātamatta*). *Udumbaramūlasmiṃ* means “at the root of the udumbara tree.”
Having delivered this Dhamma teaching, the Teacher said, "Monks, it is not only now;
in the past as well, the Elder Dhanuggahatissa was skilled in the arrangement of battle," and he then identified the Jātaka:
"At that time, Kūṭajaṭila was Devadatta, Tacchasūkara was Dhanuggahatissa, and I myself was the tree deity."
The ninth: The Explanation of the *Tacchasūkara-jātaka*.
10. The Explanation of the *Mahāvāṇija-jātaka*:
"The merchants held a meeting"—this was spoken by the Teacher while dwelling at Jetavana concerning some merchants from Sāvatthī.

He related the story. It is said that while traveling for the sake of trade, they gave a great alms-offering to the Teacher, established themselves in the refuges and the precepts, and said, "Venerable Sir, if we return in safety, we shall once again pay homage at your feet.
Having set out with about five hundred wagons, they reached a wilderness and, failing to discern the path, became lost.
Wandering through a waterless forest where there was no food, they saw a banyan tree possessed by a nāga;
unyoking their carts, they sat down at the foot of the tree.
Seeing its dark, glossy leaves as if dripping with water and its branches as if filled with water, they thought: "Water seems to be circulating within this tree."

"It is visible; let us cut its eastern branch, and it will give us water. Then one of them climbed the tree and cut the branch, whereupon a stream of water as thick as the trunk of a palm tree flowed forth.
Having bathed and drunk there, they cut the southern branch, and from it came various kinds of exquisite food. Having eaten that, [they cut] the western branch...
They cut it down, and from it emerged adorned women. Having enjoyed themselves with them, they cut down the northern branch, and from it emerged the seven treasures.
Taking those and filling five hundred wagons, they returned to Sāvatthī.
Having safeguarded their wealth, they went to Jetavana with perfumes, garlands, and other offerings in their hands, and approached the Teacher.
Having paid homage and made offerings, they sat to one side and listened to a discourse on the Dhamma.
After inviting [the Teacher] for the following day, they gave a great almsgiving and said, "Venerable Sir, we give the merit of this gift to the tree deity who provided us with wealth.
Thus they gave the merit. When the Teacher had finished his meal, he asked, "To which tree deity do you give the merit?"
The merchants informed the Tathāgata of the manner in which they had acquired their wealth under the banyan tree.

The Teacher said, "It was because you were moderate and did not become slaves to craving that you obtained wealth; however, in the past, because you were immoderate and slaves to craving, you lost both your wealth and your lives.
Having said this, he related a story of the past when requested by them.

In the past, in the city of Bārāṇasī, it was that very same wilderness and that very same banyan tree. Having lost their way, some merchants saw that very banyan tree. When the Teacher had attained full enlightenment, he spoke these verses while explaining this matter:
“Merchants who had come from various countries, having formed a caravan, set out carrying wealth, having appointed one as their leader.”
Having reached that wilderness, which was without food or water,
they saw a great banyan tree, cool-shaded and delightful.
And having sat there in the shade of that tree, they—
The merchants reflected, being fools shrouded by delusion:
"This tree is alive; even water flows from it.
Come now, O merchants, let us cut off its eastern branch."
“That stream, though cut off, flowed on—clear and undisturbed water.
Having bathed there and drunk their fill, the merchants stayed as long as they wished.
Then those fools, shrouded by delusion, thought a second time:”
“Come now, merchants, let us cut the southern branch.
And once it was cut, much rice, meat, and boiled grain flowed out,
along with waterless-colored gruel, lentil soup, and split-pea curry.
Having eaten and consumed there as much as they desired, the merchants,
fools shrouded in delusion, thought a third time:
"Come now, O merchants, let us cut down this last branch."
"And she flowed away like a severed stream, while women were beautifully adorned—
wearing variegated garments and ornaments, with jewels and earrings fastened upon them.
Were there not even twenty-five women, O merchants?"
They surrounded him on all sides with the shade of that tree;
having entertained themselves with those [pleasures], the merchants remained there as long as they wished.
Then, shrouded by folly and delusion, those fools conceived a fourth thought.
"Come now, merchants, let us cut down the northern branch.
And as soon as it was cut, it flowed forth with much pearl and beryl,
silver and gold, fine fabrics, and garments.
“Kāśī cloths and woolen blankets from Uddiyāna—
having bound these as their cargo there, the merchants waited as long as they desired.
Then, shrouded by folly and delusion, those fools devised a fifth [plan].”
"Come now, let us cut down its root; we shall obtain even more.
Then the caravan leader, with palms joined in supplication, said:
"Nigrodha, what is he withholding? May it be well with you, O merchant!"
“The eastern branch provides water; the southern branch, food and drink;
the western branch does not provide water; and the northern branch provides all desires.
What has the banyan tree lost? O merchants, may it be well with you.”
“One whose shadow one might sit in or lie in—
the tree of that person one should not break a branch from, for a betrayer of friends is evil.
And many people, disregarding the word of that one individual— ”
"With sharpened axes, they set about it from the root.
Therein, "having made a meeting" means having assembled in Bārāṇasī; the meaning is that many became united as one.
"They set out" means they departed, taking merchandise produced in Bārāṇasī with five hundred carts. "The village headman" refers to one who was particularly wise.
"Having made him the caravan leader. "By the shadow" means by its shade. "Appearing moist" means it appears as if wet, like a vessel filled with water.
"As soon as it was cut, it flowed" shows that one person skilled in climbing trees climbed up and cut it, and as soon as it was severed, it flowed.
The same principle applies to the following cases as well.
*Appodakakummāse*: rice gruel with little water, resembling rice gruel with little water. *Siṅgi*: ginger and other such supplementary condiments (*uttaribhaṅga*).
*Vidalasūpiyo*: bean soups and the like. *Vāṇijā eke*: as many merchants as there were, for each one of them there was only one [woman];
however, near the caravan leader (*satthavāha*), there were twenty-five; this is the meaning. *Parivāriṃsu*: they surrounded [him].
Together with them, by the power of the *nāga*, cotton canopies, couches, and so forth, appeared and dripped [with moisture].
*Kuttiyo* refers to elephant-blankets and the like. *Paṭiyāni* refers to woolen coverlets; they also say they are "white woolens" (*setakambalāni*).
Regarding "Uddiyāni and woolens": there are indeed woolens called *uddiyāni*. Having bound those into bundles there—
"Taking as much as they desired, they filled five hundred wagons"—this is the meaning.
Addressing each merchant individually, he said, "May it be well with you," using the phrase *bhadram astu te*.

"And food and drink" means he gave both food and drink. "And all desires" means he gave all objects of desire. "For one who betrays friends" (*mittadubbho hi*) refers to those who are unfriendly toward friends.
For a man who speaks ill is indeed called wicked and base. "Without taking it to heart" means without accepting his words.
"They began to make an effort" means they began out of delusion to cut [the tree].
Then, seeing them approaching the tree for the purpose of cutting it, the Naga king thought: "I shall provide water for these people who are thirsty."
"I caused water to be given, then divine food, then beds and so forth as well as female attendants, and then five hundred carts full of jewels;
but now these men say, 'We shall cut the tree down from its roots.
These men are exceedingly greedy; it would be right to kill all except the caravan leader. He [said], "There are so many armored warriors..."
“Let them go forth! Let so many archers and so many shield-bearers go forth,” he ordered his army. To clarify this matter, the Teacher spoke this verse:
“Then the elephants went forth, twenty-five in number, equipped with armor;
three hundred archers and six thousand shield-bearers.”

There, "those who were girt" refers to those wearing armor and mail made of gold, silver, and so forth. "Three hundred archers" means three hundred archers with bows made from the horns of rams. "The six thousand clad in mail" refers to those holding shields and bucklers in their hands.
"Kill them! Bind them! Do not let them escape with their lives;
except for the caravan leader, reduce them all to ashes"—this is the verse spoken by the Naga King.
In that regard, "Do not let go of anyone's life" means: do not let the life of even a single person escape you.

Having done so, the nāgas loaded the rugs and other goods onto five hundred carts, took the caravan leader with them, and driving those carts themselves, went to Bārāṇasī; there they deposited all the wealth in his house.
Having taken leave of him, she returned to her own Nāga abode. Understanding the significance of this matter, the Teacher spoke these two verses by way of exhortation:
"Therefore, a wise person, clearly perceiving his own welfare, Should not come under the power of greed; he should destroy such a mind."
“Having thus understood this danger—that craving is the origin of suffering—a bhikkhu should wander mindfully, free from craving and without grasping.
In this context, “therefore” means: because those who were under the sway of greed met with great ruin, while the caravan leader attained supreme success; therefore.
"The mind that should be slain" means the mind belonging to the various enemies of greed that arise within;
the meaning is that one should slay the consciousness associated with greed. "Having thus understood the danger" means having known the danger in greed in this way.
"Craving is the origin of suffering" means craving is the source of the suffering of birth and so forth; from that, this suffering is produced.

"Thus, having understood that craving alone is the origin of suffering, a bhikkhu should wander forth—living and conducting himself free from craving, not grasping through the grasping of craving, and mindful with mindfulness attained by means of the Path. By this teaching, he took the peak of the discourse on Arahantship.
Having brought forward this Dhamma-teaching, [the Buddha said]: "In this way, lay followers, in the past these merchants, being under the sway of greed, met with great ruin..."
"Therefore, one must not be a slave to greed. Having said this, he proclaimed the Truths and identified the Jātaka.

At the conclusion of the Truths, those merchants were established in the fruit of stream-entry (sotāpatti). At that time, the Nāga king was Sāriputta, while the caravan leader was none other than myself.
The Tenth: The Commentary on the Mahāvāṇija Jātaka.
[494] 11. The Commentary on the Sādhina Jātaka.
"How wonderful indeed in this world!"—this was spoken by the Teacher while dwelling in Jetavana, concerning lay followers who were observing the Uposatha.

He related the story. For then the Teacher said, "Lay followers, in the past, ancient wise men, by virtue of their own observance of the Uposatha, went to the world of the devas in their very human bodies and dwelt there for a long time. When they requested him, he brought forth the past.
In the past, in Mithilā, a king named Sādhu ruled the kingdom with righteousness. At the four city gates...

Having constructed six alms-halls—one in the center of the city and one at each of the gates of his residence—he made the entire land of Jambudīpa free from debt and established a great distribution of gifts. Six hundred thousand [pieces of gold] were expended daily;
he observed the five precepts and kept the Uposatha fast. The inhabitants of the kingdom, too, abiding by his exhortation, practiced giving and the other perfections.
Having performed meritorious deeds, they passed away and were reborn right there in the city of the gods.
Seated and filling the Sudhammā assembly hall of the gods, the deities praised the King’s virtues, such as his moral conduct (*sīla*). Hearing this, the remaining gods also desired to see the King.
Sakka, the King of the Gods, perceiving their intention, said: "Friends, you wish to see King Sādhina. "Yes," they replied.
"O gods! he said. He commanded Mātali: "Go, harness the Vejayanta chariot and bring King Sādhina here.
Accepting the command with the words "Very well," he harnessed the chariot and went to the kingdom of Videha; at that time, it was the day of the full moon.
While the people were enjoying their evening meal and sitting at the doors of their houses engaged in pleasant conversation, Mātali arrived.

He sent the chariot together with the moon’s disk. People, saying, "Two moons have arisen," saw the chariot returning after leaving the moon’s disk behind and said, "This is not the moon; this is a chariot. A son of the gods is seen approaching.
Whose divine chariot, yoked with the mind-made steed, is he bringing here? It belongs to no one else but our king."
“Surely there will be a righteous king for us, a Dhamma-king! Having thus become filled with joy, they stood with palms joined in reverence and spoke this first verse:
“Truly wonderful is what has arisen in the world, causing the hair to stand on end!
“A divine chariot has appeared for the illustrious King of Videha.
The meaning of this is: “Truly wonderful is our king! A hair-raising marvel has arisen in the world, for whom a divine chariot has appeared—[the chariot] of the illustrious King of Videha.
Then Mātali, having brought that chariot, [passed it through] the city three times while people were worshipping it with perfumes, garlands, and so forth.
Having performed a circumambulation and gone to the gate of the king’s residence, he turned the chariot back, positioned it behind the lion-window threshold,
and stood there ready for mounting. On that day, the king, too, having inspected the halls of almsgiving and commanded,
"Give alms according to this fixed order," observed the Uposatha, passed the day, and was then surrounded by his assembly of ministers.
Seated upon the decorated great terrace, facing the eastern lion-window, he was sitting preaching a discourse on the Dhamma.
Then Mātali, having invited him to ascend the chariot, took him and departed. To illustrate this matter, the Teacher spoke these verses:
“The son of the gods, possessed of great psychic power, Mātali the divine charioteer;”
They invited King Videha, the ruler of Mithilā:
“Come, O best of kings, Disampati, mount this chariot!
The gods of the Tāvatiṃsa heaven, together with Indra, desire to see you.”
For the gods, being mindful, were disputing over Sudhammā.
Then King Sādhīna, the Videhan ruler of Mithilā,
mounted a chariot yoked with a thousand [horses] and went into the presence of the gods.
The gods rejoiced upon seeing the king arrive:
“Welcome to you, Great King! You have come from afar indeed;
Sit now, O Lord of Men, in the presence of the King of Gods.”
Sakka, the Lord of the Gods, welcomed the King of Videha, the ruler of Mithilā;
he invited him with sensual pleasures and offered him a seat.
"It is well that you have arrived at the abode of the Lord of Creatures."
“Dwell among the gods as their king, you who have all your desires fulfilled;
among the Tāvatiṃsa gods, enjoy pleasures that are superhuman.
Therein, *samacchara* means they envy. *Agā devāna santike* means he went into the presence of the gods. For in that...
Having ascended the chariot, while he stood there, the chariot leapt into the sky and vanished even as the great multitude looked on.
Mātali led the king to the world of the gods. Seeing him, the deities and Sakka, joyful and delighted, went out to meet him and performed a formal welcome.
To illustrate this matter, it is said: "The gods... and so forth. In that context, *paṭinandiṃsu* means...

They rejoiced again and again. "With a seat" means that having embraced the King, he invited him with the words "Sit here," offering his own *paṇḍukambala* stone throne as well as sensual pleasures; the meaning is that, having offered half of his kingdom, he had him sit upon the same seat.
In that regard, Sakka, the king of the gods, [offered] a divine city ten thousand *yojanas* in extent and two hundred and fifty million celestial nymphs (*accharā*).
Seven hundred years, measured by human reckoning, passed while he enjoyed the wealth bestowed upon him after splitting the Vejayanta Palace down the middle.
When the merit for dwelling in the deva-world through that particular existence was exhausted, world-weariness arose;
therefore, conversing with Sakka, he spoke this verse:
“Formerly, when I had gone to heaven, I delighted in dances, songs, and instrumental music;
but now today I do not delight in heaven. Is my life-span exhausted? Or is death near at hand?
Or have I become deluded, O best of lords of men?”

In this context, "Is my life-span exhausted? means: "Has my life-faculty (*jīvitindriya*) been exhausted by its own nature, or has death come near due to the power of kamma that cuts it off? He asks this. "O best among lords of men" (*janindaseṭṭha*) means:
O best among the lords of men, the gods. Then Sakka said to him:
"Your life is not exhausted, and death is far off; nor are you deluded, O best of heroes among men."
“Your merits are but meager, the fruit of which you are experiencing here.
‘Dwell by the power of the gods, O best of kings, Disampati;
among the Tāvatiṃsa devas, enjoy superhuman pleasures.’”
In this context, the phrase "trifling" (*parittakāni*) is said with reference to those merits that yield their result in the world of the devas through that particular existence;
however, his other merits are immeasurable, like the dust of the earth.
When he said, "Dwell by the power of the devas," he spoke thus to reassure him: "I will divide my own merits in half and give them to you; dwell by my power."
Then the Great Being, declining it, said:
"Just as a borrowed vehicle, just as borrowed wealth,
even so is this excellence that comes from the condition of giving by another."
“I do not desire that which comes from others by way of gifts;
the merits performed by myself—that is my unique wealth.
Having gone among humans, I shall perform much wholesome deed.”
"By means of giving, by even conduct, by self-restraint,
and by self-mastery— that which, having performed it, one becomes happy and does not later regret.
In this context, "because of being given by another" (dānapaccayā) means that whatever is obtained because it was given by another is exactly like something borrowed.
It exists. For they say that borrowed goods are given when one is satisfied, but when one is dissatisfied, they take them back by force.

"By even conduct" means by the non-performance of evil through body and so forth. "By restraint" means by the restraint of virtue (*sīla-saṃyama*). "By self-control" means by the control of the sense faculties. "Having done what" means:
"I shall perform only such a deed as, having performed it, one becomes happy and does not later regret it."
Having heard his words, Sakka commanded Mātali: “Go, dear one, take King Sādhina to Mithilā and set him down in the park.
He did so. As the king was walking in the park, the park-keeper saw him, questioned him, and went to report it to King Nārada.
Upon hearing that the king had arrived, he said, “You go ahead...”
"Having gone to the garden and prepared it, arrange two seats for him and for me," he commanded the park-keeper.
The keeper did exactly so. Then the king asked him, "Whose two seats have you arranged?
"One for you, O King, and one for us. Then the king thought, "What other being besides myself would sit upon a seat in my presence?"
Having spoken thus, he sat down on one side and placed his foot upon the other. King Nārada approached, paid homage at his feet, and sat down to one side;
it is said that he was his seventh [rebirth]. At that time, it was indeed an age when the lifespan was exactly one hundred years.
Yet, by the power of his own merit, the Great Being had passed through such a long period of time. He then took Nārada by the hand.
While wandering in the park, he recited these three verses:
“These are those fields; this is the coin with its fine earrings;
these are those lush meadows; these are the flowing rivers.”
“Delightful are these lotus ponds, resounding with the cries of ruddy geese;
covered with mandārava flowers and with pink and blue lotuses—
where have they gone, those for whom these were once their own?”
“Those very fields, that same stretch of land, those very groves and forest precincts—without seeing even that same people here, O Nārada, the quarters appear empty to me.
In this context, “fields” refers to the stretch of land. This is the outlet, and the drainage for water is exactly like that.
"Sukuṇḍala" means endowed with beautiful rings for inserting pestles.
"Haritānūpā" refers to marshy lands covered with green grass on both sides of the water drainage.
"Yassimāni mamāyiṃsu" means, dear Nārada, those who were my attendants and female musicians, wandering with me in great splendor in this pleasure grove.
"These places they cherished and loved; to which destination have they gone, where have they been sent?
'Those very fields here'—in this park, these are those very places for planting and growing.
'The precincts of the monastery and forest'—these are those very precincts of the monastery and forest; the meaning is 'the grounds of the vihāra.'"
Then Nārada said to him: “Your Majesty, seven hundred years have now passed since you went to the world of the gods;
I am your seventh [successor]. Your attendants and your harem have fallen into the jaws of death.
This is your own kingdom; enjoy it, Sire. The king replied: “Dear Nārada, I did not come here for the sake of the kingdom.”
“I have come; I have come for the sake of performing merit; I shall perform only merit,” he said, and spoke these verses:
“I have seen celestial mansions illuminating the four quarters, in the presence of the king of the gods and in the presence of the Thirty-three.”
“My divine mansion has been inhabited; superhuman pleasures have been enjoyed among the Tāvatiṃsa devas, where every desire is fulfilled.
Having abandoned such a state, I have come here for the sake of merit.”
“I shall practice the Dhamma alone; I have no need for kingship.
I will follow that path taught by the Perfectly Enlightened One, which is beyond the reach of punishment—the path upon which those of virtuous conduct travel.”
"In that place my divine palace Vejayanta was situated"—this he said with reference to it.

"Such as this, dear Nārada," he said, "I am one who, having abandoned such an excellence of the qualities of sensual pleasure—which cannot be fully encompassed even by a Buddha’s knowledge—has come here for the purpose of performing meritorious deeds.
It is 'not within the range of punishment,' meaning it is to be frequented by those who have laid down the rod, whose hands are free from the stick, and who prioritize right view."

"The Eightfold Path. "Those of good vows" means: "By whichever path the omniscient Buddhas go, I too, having sat at the foot of the Bodhi tree, shall set out upon that very same path to go to the direction never before traversed.
Thus the Bodhisatta spoke these verses, condensing them through his knowledge of omniscience. Nārada spoke again:
He said, "Sire, please rule the kingdom. "Dear son, I have no need for kingship; I wish to give away the wealth that has been accumulated over seven hundred years within just seven days.
Nārada, accepting his words with the reply "Very well," prepared a great distribution of alms.
Having given the alms for seven days, the king passed away on the seventh day and was reborn in the Tāvatiṃsa heaven itself.
Having delivered this Dhamma teaching, the Teacher showed that "this is indeed what is called the Uposatha observance, which is fit for such dwelling.
He then proclaimed the Truths and identified the Jātaka.

At the conclusion of the Truths, among the lay followers who had observed the Uposatha, some were established in the fruit of stream-entry, some in the fruit of once-returning, and some in the fruit of non-returning. At that time...
King Nārada was Sāriputta; Mātali was Ānanda; Sakka was Anuruddha; and King Sādhina was none other than myself.
This concludes the eleventh narrative, the Sādhina Jātaka. 12.
The Commentary on the Dasabrāhmaṇa Jātaka (The Birth Story of the Ten Brahmins)
The King said, "It was Vidhura. This story was told by the Teacher while dwelling at Jetavana concerning an incomparable gift.

It has already been explained in detail in the *Ādittajātaka* of the *Aṭṭhakanipāta*. It is said that when the King gave that gift, he made the Teacher the foremost, selected five hundred bhikkhus, and gave it only to those who were great ones with taints destroyed (*khīṇāsava*).

Then, while recounting his virtues, they raised a discussion in the Hall of Dharma, saying, “Friends, when the king gave this peerless gift, he gave it after carefully selecting a place where it would yield great fruit.
The Teacher came and asked, “Monks, what discussion are you sitting here having now? When they replied, “This one,” he said, “Monks, it is not surprising…”
"Since the King of Kosala, acting as an attendant to a Buddha such as I, gives a gift with discernment,
the ancient sages also gave gifts with discernment even when no Buddha had appeared," he said, and then related a story of the past.
In the past, in the kingdom of Kuru, in the city of Indapatta, a king named Koravya of the Yudhiṭṭhila clan reigned.
He had a minister named Vidhura who instructed him in both worldly profit and the Dhamma.
The king, having caused all of Jambudīpa to tremble, gave a great gift. Among those receiving and consuming it, there was not even one who observed the mere five precepts;
everyone was immoral. The gift did not please the king. The king, thinking, "A gift given with discrimination is of great fruit," [sought] those possessing virtue...
Desiring to give [the gift], he thought, "I shall consult with the wise Vidhura.
Having seated him who had come to his presence upon a throne, he asked him a question. To illustrate this matter, the Teacher spoke the half-verse:
"The King Yudhiṭṭhila, who loves the Dhamma, spoke to Vidhura."
Then there was an exchange of words between the King and Vidhura:
“Vidhura, seek out brahmins who are virtuous and learned,
who abstain from sexual intercourse, and who would eat the food offered by me.”
“We shall give a gift properly, wherein what is given bears great fruit.
‘O King, those brahmins who are virtuous and learned,
who abstain from sexual intercourse— such as these would partake of your food are difficult to find.’”
“Indeed, Great King, regarding those ten brahmin castes—
listen to me as I explain their classification and analysis in detail.
Having taken up bags that are full and covered with roots...”
“They compound medicines, bathe, and recite prayers.
O King, those who are like physicians are also called brahmins.
They have been described to you, Great King; we shall attend upon such as these.”
“Those who have abandoned the qualities of a brahmin, O King Koravya—
these are not called brahmins. Seek others,
Vidhura, those who are virtuous and learned.”
“Abstaining from sexual intercourse, those who would partake of my food—
To them we shall rightly give the offering where what is given bears great fruit.
Taking up small bells, they proclaim it even before you.”
“Even messengers go about, training in the maneuvers of chariots.
‘O King, even those who are like attendants are called brahmins.
Thus have they been described to you, O Great King; we bow down before such as them.”
“Those who have abandoned the status of a brahmin, O King Koraavya,
are not called brahmins. Seek others,
Vidhura, who are virtuous and learned.”
“Abstaining from sexual intercourse, those who would partake of my food—
such as these we shall rightly give the offering where what is given bears great fruit.
Having taken up their water-pots and crooked staffs, O brahmins...”
Kings will come to the villages and the market towns;
we shall not depart until what is given has been bestowed, whether in the village or in the forest.
O King, those who are like enforcers are also called brahmins.
“O Great King, those who have been described by you— such as these we revere.
But those from whom the qualities of a brahmin have departed (so said King Koriya)—
they are not called brahmins.”
“Seek out others who are upright, virtuous, and learned—
those who abstain from sexual intercourse and would eat my food.
We shall give our offering properly to those where what is given bears great fruit.”
“With their armpits, nails, and body hair grown long, with teeth stained by dirt and veins showing,
covered in dust and pollen, they wander about as beggars. O King,
even those who are like mere stumps or ruins are called ‘brāhmaṇas.’”
“O Great King, those who have been described by you—such as these we honor.
But they are devoid of true brahminhood; (thus spoke King Koravya) they are not called brahmins.”
"Seek out others who are upright, virtuous, and learned—
those who abstain from sexual intercourse— who might eat my food.
We shall give our gift properly to those where what is given bears great fruit."
“Harītaka, āmalaka, mango, rose-apple, and vibhītaka;
Labuja, tooth-sticks, beluva, and jujube fruits.
Rājāyatana, sugar-cane tube, smoking pipe, and honey-ointment.”
“They trade in high and low-priced goods, O lord of men.
‘O King, those who are like merchants are also called brahmins;
they have been described to you thus, O Great King, and we submit ourselves to such as these.’”
“Those who have abandoned the qualities of a brahmin, O King Kora-vya,
are not called brahmins. Seek others,
Vidhura, who are virtuous and well-versed in the scriptures.”
“Those who abstain from sexual intercourse and would eat the food offered by me—such people we shall rightly give our gift to, wherein what is given bears great fruit.
They practice farming and trade; they raise goats and sheep.”
“They give away their daughters in marriage and bring home brides for them.
They are equal to Ambaṭṭhas and Vessas, yet they too are called ‘brahmins.
These have been explained to you, O Great King; such as these we associate with.”
“Those who have abandoned the qualities of a Brahmin, O King Koraavya,
are not called Brahmins. Seek others,
Vidhura, who are virtuous and deeply learned.”
“Those who abstain from sexual intercourse and would eat the food offered by me—
such people we shall rightly give our sacrificial gift, where what is given bears great fruit.
Some priests in the villages eat alms that have been set aside.”
Many people question you: "There are those who castrate and brand cattle;
there, even animals are slaughtered—buffaloes, pigs, and goats.
O King, even those who are like cow-slaughterers are called brahmins."
“O Great King, they have been described by you; we fall at the feet of such as those.
But those who have departed from the state of a Brahmin—thus spoke King Koravya—they are not called ‘Brahmins.’”
“Seek out others who are steadfast, virtuous, and learned—
those who abstain from sexual intercourse and would partake of my food.
We shall give our offerings properly to those where what is given bears great fruit.”
“Taking up a hide and grasping a sword,
these brahmins stand at the crossroads, even brandishing weapons.
They are equal to cowherds and hunters, yet they too are called ‘brahmins.’”
“O Great King, you have explained them to us;
we shall fall at the feet of such as you. “But those who have departed from the state of a Brahmin,” said King Koravya, “are not called Brahmins.”
"Seek out others who are virtuous and learned, O Vidhura—
those who abstain from sexual intercourse— who might consume my food.
We shall properly give the offering where what is given bears great fruit."
“Building huts in the forest, they cause other huts to be made;
they harass wildcats and mongooses, as well as antelopes, fish, and turtles.
O King, those who are like hunters are also called ‘brahmins.’”
“O Great King, they have been described to you; we bow down to such as those.
But those who have departed from the state of a Brahmin—thus spoke King Koravya—they are not called ‘Brahmins.’”
“Seek out others who are upright, virtuous, and learned—
those who abstain from sexual intercourse and would consume my food.
We shall give our offerings properly to those where what is given yields great fruit.”
“Indeed, others desire wealth; they step beneath the couches, while kings bathe above when the Soma sacrifice has been prepared.
O King, even those who are like filth and marrow are called ‘brahmins.’”
“O Great King, those who have been described by you— such as these we honor.
But those who have departed from the Brahminhood (so said King Koravya)—
they are not called Brāhmaṇas.”
“Seek out others who are upright, virtuous, and learned—
those who abstain from sexual intercourse— who might eat my food.
We shall give our gift properly to those where what is given bears great fruit.”

In this context, "virtuous" refers to those whose virtue has been acquired through the Path. "Learned" refers to those who are learned through penetration (*paṭivedha*). "Sacrificial gift" means alms-giving.
"Those who" refers to those righteous recluses and brahmins who might consume your gift; they are difficult to find. "Brahmin lineages" refers to families of brahmins.
"They investigate their classification" means that by my wisdom, I investigate the classification of those brahmins.
Listen in detail to the various states [of women]. "Restrained" means having their mouths bound.
"They tie up medicinal herbs" means that people give them after composing verses such as, "This is the medicine for this disease; this is the medicine for that disease.
"They bathe" means they perform what is called a ritual bathing. "And they mutter" means they recite spells for exorcising spirits.

“Physicians” means those who are like doctors. They too are called [Brāhmaṇas] because, not knowing whether they are Brāhmaṇas or non-Brāhmaṇas, they earn their living by the work of physicians and are thus called “Brāhmaṇas” in common parlance.
“They have been declared” means: these are the ones I have declared as the physician-Brāhmaṇas. “Speak now regarding those who fall away”—what about such people?
"Let us fall among the brahmins; let us approach them for the sake of an invitation; does this matter exist for you? [He asks.
"Brahmanhood" means by way of the dharma of a brahmin. "They are not called such" means that they, because of having cast out evil, are not called "brahmins.
"Kiṅkiṇikā," O Great King, refers to other brahmins who, having abandoned their own brahmin-dharma, [live] for the sake of a livelihood...
Taking up bronze cymbals, they go along playing and singing in front of the kings, royal ministers, and great officials.

"Errands" means that they go on errands like slaves and laborers. "In the maneuvers of chariots" means they train in the art of chariotry. "Like attendants" means they are similar to slaves and laborers.
"A crooked staff" means a crooked wooden staff. "The kings will approach" refers to the kings, royal ministers, and great officials.
They frequent [those places] by depending on, resorting to, and having recourse to them. "In villages and market towns" means they sit at the doors of their dwellings.
"Equal to those who seize" means equal to the royal officers who act as enforcers and use force to capture;

just as those men, thinking "we will not leave without having seized him," use force and certainly take him, so too [they think], "Whether in the village or in the forest, even if we die without finding him..."
“They will not emerge,” they said, and so they observed the fast. “Those too” means those of evil nature who are like the fish-catchers.
“Covered with dust and dirt” means strewn with both dust and soil. “Beggars” means beggars for wealth.
“Resembling the clearing of charred stumps” refers to those men who, because their bodies are so filthy, resemble people digging the earth in a cremation field to extract charred stumps.
“Samānā” means they stood as if motionless with the thought, “We will not go without taking [the wealth]”;

thus, it also means they were like wooden stakes that have been driven in and left fixed. “Tepi” means those same immoral brahmins who, having employed the wealth they had thus obtained for the sake of interest, remained exactly as they were before.
*Ucchupuṭaṃ* means both sugarcane and a bag of molasses. *Madhuañjanaṃ* means both honey and collyrium.
*Uccāvacāni* means things of high and low value. *Paṇiyāni* means goods for sale. *Vipaṇenti* means they sell.
*Tepi* means those as well—these Brahmin merchants who make their living by selling such things. *Posayanti* means for the sake of making a living by selling dairy products.
They give away their daughters. "They bestow" means they take gold and bullion and give their daughters to others.
When they give them thus to others, it is called "marrying out" (vivāhanti); when they take them for the sake of their own sons, it is called "marrying in" (āvāhanti).
"By the Ambaṭṭha youths" refers to those equal to householders and family heads; they too, by way of conventional usage, are called "brahmins."
"Set-aside alms" refers to a regular portion of alms-food set aside for one's own benefit by someone acting as a village priest.
"Many are they" means that many people ask these village priests about auspicious days, moments, and lucky omens.

"Testicle-cutters and branded ones" refers to those who, having taken wages, cut the testicles of oxen and brand them with tridents and other marks; they are also called "interpreters of bodily marks."
The meaning is as follows. "Therein" means that in the houses of those village priests, these animals and others are also slaughtered for the purpose of selling meat.
"They too" refers to those Brāhmaṇas who, like cattle-slaughterers, are called by that name.
"Sword and shield" means both the sword-blade and the shield used for warding off arrows. "On the merchant-roads" means on the paths traveled by traders.
“They drive the caravans” means that having taken even a hundred or a thousand [coins] from the hands of caravan leaders, they escort the caravans past the robber-infested wilderness (*cora-aṭavī*).
“With cowherds and hunters” means together with cowherds and hunters who are robbers plundering villages.
“They too” means that such people as these are also called brahmins. “They cause huts to be built” means that they set up snares and the like.
"Sasabiḷāre" refers to both hares (*sasa*) and wild cats (*biḷāra*); by this, he indicates the animals that roam on land.

"Āgodhā macchakacchapaṃ" means that among those dwelling on land, from the *āgodhā* onwards, they oppress and kill both large and small creatures; and among those dwelling in water, the fish and turtles.
"Tepī" means that those [hunters] are called "brāhmaṇas," being equal to hunters.
"Others desire wealth," say other brahmins who long for riches.
"Crawling beneath the bed," they have had a jeweled bed constructed, thinking, "We shall perform the rites that bring about strife," and remain lying beneath it.
Then, when their *soma* sacrifice has arrived, the kings bathe over them; for it is said that after the *soma* sacrifice is finished, [the brahmins] come [to claim their reward].
They sit upon that couch. Then other brahmins wash them, saying, "We shall drive away the ill-fortune.
Both the jeweled couch and all the king's royal regalia remain for the one lying on the lower couch.
They too—meaning those brahmins who are said to be similar to bathers who merely scrub away dirt—are called "bathers."
Having thus shown these mere conventional brahmins, he now spoke two verses to show the brahmins in the ultimate sense:
“There are indeed, O King, brahmins who are virtuous and learned;
who abstain from sexual intercourse—let them eat your food.”
“They eat but one meal a day and do not drink intoxicants;
they have been described to you, O Great King—such as these we approach for the sake of an invitation.

In this context, “virtuous” means endowed with noble virtue (*ariyasīla*). “Learned” means endowed with great learning through penetration (*paṭivedha-bāhusacca*). “Such as these” means: “we approach such Paccekabuddhas and Brahmins, whose evil has been banished, for the purpose of an invitation.”
Having heard his words, the king asked, "Friend Vidhura, where do such supreme recipients of offerings as these brahmins dwell?
"In the northern Himalayas, in the Nandamūlaka cave, O Great King," he replied.
"In that case, wise man, by your own power seek out those brahmins for me," and with a joyful heart, he spoke this verse:
“These brahmins, Vidhura, are distinguished, well-born, and learned;
seek them out, Vidhura, and invite them quickly.
The Great Being, having accepted his words with the reply “Very well,” said, “In that case, Great King, have the city decorated.”
Having caused a drum to be beaten with the proclamation, "May all the city-dwellers give alms, observe the Uposatha,
and undertake the precepts," and having said, "You too, together with your retinues, should undertake the Uposatha," he himself ate in the early morning,
undertook the Uposatha, and in the evening had a golden casket filled with jasmine flowers brought to him.
Having prostrated with the five-limbed greeting together with the king, and having recollected the virtues of the Paccekabuddhas and paid homage,

he invited them, saying, "May the five hundred Paccekabuddhas dwelling in the Nandamūlaka cave in the Northern Himalayas accept our almsfood tomorrow," and he scattered eight handfuls of flowers into the air. At that time, there were five hundred [Paccekabuddhas] there.
The Paccekabuddhas were dwelling there, and flowers fell upon them as they passed by.
Reflecting on this, they understood the reason for it and thought, "Friends, we have been invited by the wise Vidhura. He is no ordinary being; he is a sprout of a Buddha.
In this very kappa he will become a Buddha; let us show him our support. Thus, they accepted the invitation.
The Mahāsatta, perceiving that the flowers had not arrived and understanding that [the king] had accepted [the invitation], said: "Great King, tomorrow the Paccekabuddhas will come;
provide them with honor and hospitality. On the following day, the king made great preparations and arranged magnificent seats upon the great terrace.
The Paccekabuddhas, having performed their bodily ablutions at Lake Anotatta, [arrived at] the appointed time.
Having observed [the signs], they came through the air and alighted in the royal courtyard.

With hearts full of faith, both the king and the Bodhisatta took the bowls from their hands, led them up into the palace, had them sit down, offered them water for the feet, and served them with excellent hard and soft foods.
At the conclusion of the meal, [they said] "for the sake of tomorrow's day."
Having thus invited them for seven days and given a great almsgiving, on the seventh day they presented all their requisites.
Having offered words of thanksgiving, they departed through the air right there, and the requisites went along with them.
The Teacher, having delivered this Dhamma teaching, said: "It is not surprising, monks, that the King of Kosala, my supporter..."
“Being mindful, one should give a gift after careful consideration; for even when no Buddha had yet appeared, the ancient wise men gave gifts.
Having said this, he identified the Jātaka: “At that time, King Ānanda was [the king], and I myself was the wise man Vidhura.
This concludes the twelfth narration, the Vidhura-paṇḍita-jātaka.
[496] 13. The Commentary on the Bhikkhāparamparā Jātaka.
"Seeing his delicate form"—this was spoken by the Teacher while residing at Jetavana concerning a certain householder.
It is said that he was faithful and confident, and he constantly offered great honor to both the Tathāgata and the Saṅgha.
He did so. Then one day he thought: "I constantly perform great acts of honor by giving excellent hard and soft foods as well as fine garments to the Jewel of the Buddha and the Jewel of the Saṅgha;
now I shall do the same for the Jewel of the Dhamma. How indeed should one act when performing honor for it?"
Thus, taking many perfumes, garlands, and other offerings, he went to Jetavana, paid homage to the Teacher, and asked:
"Venerable Sir, I desire to perform an act of honor for the Jewel of the Dhamma; how indeed should one who performs such an honor proceed?
Then the Teacher said to him: "If you desire to perform an act of honor for the Jewel of the Dhamma, [you should honor] the Custodian of the Dhamma..."
“Pay honor to Ānanda. Having consented with the words “Very well,” he invited the Elder;

on the following day, having led him to his own home with great honor, seated him upon a magnificent seat, worshipped him with perfumes, garlands, and other offerings, and served him various foods of exquisite flavor, he gave him two costly robes sufficient for the three garments (tricīvara). The Elder, too—

Thinking, "This honor has been paid to the Jewel of the Dhamma; it is not suitable for me, but it is suitable for the Chief Disciple, the General of the Dhamma," he took the almsfood and the robes to the monastery and gave them to the Elder Sāriputta.
He too thought, "This honor has been paid to the Jewel of the Dhamma; it belongs exclusively to the Fully Enlightened One, the Lord of the Dhamma."
Thinking, "This is suitable," he gave it to the One of Ten Powers. The Teacher, seeing no one superior to himself, partook of the alms-food and took the robe-cloth.
The monks raised a discussion in the Hall of Truth: "Friends, such-and-such a householder [gave this] to the Jewel of the Dhamma..."
Thinking, “I shall pay him honor,” he gave it to the Elder Ānanda, the Dharma-treasurer.
The Elder, thinking, “This is not suitable for me,” gave it to the General of the Dharma (Sāriputta). He too, thinking, “This is not suitable for me,” gave it to the Tathāgata.
Seeing no one superior to himself and recognizing his own sovereignty over the Dharma, the Tathāgata said, “This is indeed mine.”
"Suitable," he said, and he consumed that alms-food and took those robes as well;
thus, because it was suitable, that alms-food went to the very feet of the Master of Dhamma himself.
When the Teacher returned and asked, "Monks, for what discussion are you gathered here now? and they replied, "For this one," he said, "Monks, no..."

"Even now, the alms-food goes from one to another in succession as is appropriate; yet even in the past, before a Buddha had arisen, it went in that very same way," he said, and then related a story of the past.
In the past, in Bārāṇasī, King Brahmadatta, having abandoned wrong courses and not violating the ten duties of a king, ruled his kingdom according to Dhamma.
Even so, his court of justice was as if empty. The king was a seeker of his own faults.
Having made the offering, while surveying his inner apartments and other quarters, he saw no one speaking ill of him within the palace, the city, or the gateway villages; thinking,
"I shall search in the countryside," he handed over the kingdom to his ministers and,
accompanied by his chaplain, wandered through the kingdom of Kāsi in an unknown guise, and seeing no one speaking ill of him even there, he went to the border regions.

Having reached a certain town, he sat down in the outer hall. At that moment, a wealthy householder living in that town, possessing eighty crores of wealth, was going to the bathing place with a large retinue;
seeing the king of golden complexion and delicate body seated in the hall, affection arose in him, and he entered the hall and exchanged greetings.
Having said, "Stay right here," he went home, prepared various kinds of exquisite food, and set out with a large retinue, having had the food-vessels carried along.
At that moment, an ascetic dwelling in the Himalayas who possessed the five supernormal powers arrived and sat down right there.
A Paccekabuddha also arrived from the Nandamūlaka mountain cave and sat down right there.
The householder, having given water for the king to wash his hands, prepared a bowl of rice with various choice flavors of soups and condiments and presented it to the king.
The king took it and gave it to the brahmin household priest. The brahmin took it and gave it to the ascetic.
The ascetic went into the presence of the paccekabuddha and, with his left hand, [held] the bowl of rice.
Taking his water-pot with his right hand and pouring out the water of hospitality, he placed food into the bowl.
Without inviting anyone else and without asking for permission, he ate it. At the conclusion of his meal, the householder thought:
"I gave food to the king; the king [gave it] to the brahmin; the brahmin [gave it] to the ascetic; by the ascetic..."
“The Paccekabuddha has eaten without asking anyone’s permission. What indeed is the reason for these people giving so much, and what is the reason that he eats without asking anyone at all?
I shall ask them one by one. So, approaching each of them in turn, he paid homage and questioned them. They also told him:
“Seeing you of delicate form, who had come from the kingdom to the forest,
attended by a magnificent peaked-roofed house and a great couch—
out of love for you, I gave you rice with milk.”
“Having received that choice food of rice, pure and seasoned with meat, you gave it to the brahmin;
without even eating yourself, what is this doctrine? Hail to you!”
“The brahmin teacher is occupied with my duties and what must be done;
he is venerable and worthy of being addressed. I ought to offer him food.
Now I shall ask the brahmin Gotama, who is honored by kings.”
“The king gave you food, pure meat with sauce.
Having accepted that food, you gave it to the seer as his meal.
You were ignorant of the proper field for giving; what is this doctrine? Homage to you!”
“I support sons and wife, for I am attached to my homes;
I enjoy human pleasures and I rule over kings.
[Yet I have come] to the forest-dwelling seer, who has practiced austerities for a long night.”
“I am worthy to give food to one who is grown and developed in mind.
“And now I question this seer, so emaciated, his veins showing;
with the hair of his armpits, nails, and body grown long, with mud on his teeth and dust on his head.”
“You dwell alone in the forest, you do not crave for life;
by what means, O monk, are you superior to him to whom you gave food?
[He who eats] the stalks of the *āluka* and *kalamba*, and the tubers of the *bilāli* and *takkala*.”
I eat wild rice, millet, and wild grain, as well as gathered and gleaned food.
"Vegetables, lotus roots, honey, meat, and jujubes and myrobalans—having brought these, I eat them; this is my possession."
“While I cook for one who does not cook, for one who is free from possessiveness,
for one who is without grasping— while I, who am full of grasping, am cooking, I ought to give food to him.
Now I ask this bhikkhu, who sits in silence, observing his noble vows.”
“O Isi, you gave me this food, pure and seasoned with meat.
Having received that food, you eat it alone in silence;
you do not invite anyone else. What is this doctrine? Homage be to you!”
“I do not cook, nor do I cause to be cooked; I do not cut, nor do I cause to be cut.
Knowing me to be one who possesses nothing and who has abstained from all evils—carrying my alms-bowl in the left hand and my water-pot in the right.”
“Isi, you have given me food, pure and seasoned with meat.
For these indeed are worthy of receiving gifts—those who are impartial and possess dependents.
I consider it a contradiction for one to invite a giver.”
In this context, "having come to this wilderness" means having come to this frontier region which is like a waterless forest.
"Adorned with a magnificent gabled chamber" (*kūṭāgāravarūpeta*) means approached by a most excellent gabled chamber; the meaning is that she was a dweller in one such superior gabled chamber.
"Attended by a great couch" (*mahāsayanamupāsita*) means attended by a splendid bed well-prepared right there. "I felt love for her"—that is, seeing her in such a state, I felt affection for her.
"Out of affection for you. "Vaddhamodana" means excellent rice. "Vicitra" means made from polished grains of rice from which the broken pieces and black specks have been removed.
"Adāsayi" means he gave. "Attānaṃ" means by himself; this is indeed the reading. "Anasitvāna" means without having eaten.
"Koyaṃ dhammo" means, O Great King, what is this nature of yours? "Namatthu te" means homage be to you.
"You, who did not eat yourself but gave to another.
"Teacher" means: this householder is my teacher, the instructor of my conduct. "Engaged" means: intent. "One to be invited" means:
one worthy of being invited by me, suitable to receive the meal given. "I am worthy to give" means: "To one such as this..."
“I am worthy to give food to the teacher,” the king said, praising the brahmin’s virtue.
“You think yourself ‘one who knows not the field’—that is, you imagine, ‘I am not a field for giving; what is given to me does not bear great fruit.
“I shall instruct you”: setting aside my own interest, I shall instruct the king in his welfare and in the Dhamma.

Having thus spoken of his own lack of virtue, he spoke of the sage’s virtues: “Of the forest-dweller” means of the seer (*isi*). “Of the seer” means of one who seeks virtues such as moral discipline (*sīla*) and so forth.
“Of the ascetic” means of one who relies upon austerity (*tapas*). “Of the elder” means of the wise one, increased in virtue. “You do not desire it for yourself”:
having yourself become one whose food is difficult to obtain, you give such food to another; why do you not [desire] your own life?
"You doubt. [The Buddha asks: "By what quality, monk, is this monk superior to you?
"Digging up yams and *tāla*-bulbs," that is, digging up both yams (*ālū*) and *tāla*-rhizomes. "And *bilāli* and *takkala* roots," that is, both *bilāli* rhizomes and *takkala* rhizomes.
"Winnowing *sāmāka* and *nīvāra*," that is, having winnowed both *sāmāka* and *nīvāra*. "Spreading out the scattered [grain]," that is, spreading it out after it has been scattered.

He says: "I take these *sāmāka* and *nīvāra* grains, shake them, winnow them, dry them again, spread them out, blow on them with a bellows, pound them, take the rice, cook it, and eat. *Sāka* refers to any kind of leafy vegetable for soup.
