*Maṃsa* refers to the meat of lions, tigers, vultures, and so forth. "Having brought those" means having brought those vegetables and other items. "Of one who is without 'mine'" (*amamassa*).
"Of one who is free from intoxication by craving and views. "Possessing something" (*sakiñcana*) means having an impediment (*sapalibodha*).
"Of one who is without grasping" (*anādānassa*) means of one who is without seizing. "I am worthy to give" means that I am worthy to give the food obtained by myself to such a Paccekabuddha.
"Sitting in silence" means sitting without saying anything. "Without anything" (*akiñcana*) means free from the "something" of lust and so forth. "Withdrawn" (*ārata*)...
"Virataṃ" means one who stands having abandoned all evils. "Kamaṇḍaluṃ" means a water-pot (*kuṇḍikā*). "Ete hi" means these three people, beginning with the king;
saying this while pointing them out by extending his hand, he spoke thus. "Dātumarahanti" means they are worthy of giving to one such as me.
"Paccanīkaṃ" means a contrary course of conduct. For the invitation of a donor [involves] one or another of the twenty-one improper modes of seeking alms (*anesanā*).
The practice of wrong livelihood, consisting of seeking almsfood for the sake of maintaining one's life, is what is meant here.
Having heard his words, the householder was delighted and recited these two concluding verses:
"Truly, it is for my benefit that the Bull among Charioteers has come here today! ... [the rest of the verses follow]"
Today I understand where what is given bears great fruit:
“Kings are greedy for kingdoms; brahmins, for what should and should not be done;
seers, for roots and fruits; but the bhikkhus are utterly free.”

In this context, "the bull among chariot-riders" refers to the king. "In matters of duty and non-duty" means in the king's various tasks and obligations. "Monks," however, refers to the *paccekabuddhas*, who are liberated from all states of existence.
After the *paccekabuddha* had taught him the Dhamma, he returned to his own place; likewise did the ascetic. But the king, having stayed in his presence for a few days, returned to Bārāṇasī itself.
Having brought forth this teaching on the Dhamma, the Teacher said: "Monks, it is not only now that almsfood has been [received] as is appropriate."
"He goes, for he has already gone before," he said, and then identified the Jātaka: "At that time, the householder who paid honor to the Jewel of the Dhamma was the householder;
King Ānanda was the king; Sāriputta was the chaplain; and I myself was the forest ascetic from the Himālaya.
This concludes the thirteenth commentary on the Bhikkhāparamparā Jātaka.
The Summary of Birth Stories (Jātaka-uddāna): Kedāra, Candakinnarī, Ukkuṭa, Suddāla, and Abhisaka;
Suruci, Pañcuposatha, Mahāmora, and Tacchaka.
The Mahāvāṇija Sādhina, the Dasabrāhmaṇa Jātaka,
and the Bhikkhāparamparā— these thirteen are in the Miscellaneous Section.
The commentary on the Miscellaneous Section is finished.
15. The Section of Twenty [497] 1. The Commentary on the Mātaṅga Jātaka:
"From where do you come, you who dwell in rags? This was spoken by the Teacher while residing at Jetavana concerning Udena, the king of the bamboo-clans.
He spoke concerning this. At that time, the Venerable Piṇḍola-Bhāradvāja, traveling through the air from Jetavana, would mostly go to King Udena’s park in Kosambī for his midday rest.
It is said that in a previous existence, while ruling as a king, he had enjoyed prosperity with a great retinue in that very park for a long period of time. Because of that—
For the most part, following his former habit, he would sit right there for his midday rest and spend the time in the bliss of the attainment of fruition (*phalasamāpatti*).
One day, while he was sitting there at the foot of a beautifully blossoming *sāla* tree, Udena— having drunk a great draught of liquor for seven days and thinking,
"I shall enjoy a pleasure excursion in the park"— went to the garden with a large retinue and sat upon the auspicious stone slab.
A certain woman, lying on her lap, fell asleep due to intoxication from liquor and wine.
The women who had been sitting and singing cast aside their musical instruments and, entering the garden, were gathering flowers, fruits, and other things when they saw the Elder.
They approached, paid homage, and sat down. The Elder sat there preaching the Dhamma to them. The other woman [remained] on her lap.
Having shaken the king awake and been asked, "Where have those low-caste women gone? he replied, "They are sitting surrounding a certain ascetic.
Enraged, he went and reviled and abused the Elder, saying, "Come now, I shall make that ascetic eat copper-beetles!
And out of anger, he placed a pouch of copper-beetles upon the Elder’s body.
He had [the stupa] demolished. The Elder, standing in the air, gave him exhortation and descended right there at the door of the Perfumed Chamber in Jeta’s Grove.
When the Tathāgata asked him, “From where have you come? the Elder reported the matter to him.
The Teacher said, “Bhāradvāja, it is not only now that Udena harasses those who have gone forth; he harassed them even in the past. At his request, the Teacher related the past.
In the past, while Brahmadatta was ruling in Benares, the Great Being was reborn outside the city in the womb of a Caṇḍāla woman;
they gave him the name Mātaṅga. Later, when he reached maturity, he became renowned as the "Wise Mātaṅga.
At that time, the daughter of the Benares treasurer named Diṭṭhamaṅgalikā, at intervals of one, two, or three months...
Accompanied by a great retinue, she went to the park to play.
Then one day, while the Great Being was entering the city on some business, he saw Diṭṭhamaṅgalikā at the inner gate; stepping aside and drawing near, he stood there.
Peering through a gap in the curtain, Diṭṭhamaṅgalikā saw him and asked, "Who is this? He replied, "A caṇḍāla."
When she said, "Noble lady," he thought, "I see one who is indeed connected to what has never been seen before," and having washed his eyes with scented water, he turned back from there.
The people who had gone out with her, overcome by anger, cried out, "Hey, you wicked Caṇḍāla!
Today, because of you, our free supply of liquor and rice is ruined! and they struck the wise Mātaṅga with their hands and feet.
Having beaten him and rendered him unconscious, he departed. After a short while had passed and he had regained consciousness, he thought:
"Diṭṭhamaṅgalikā’s attendants have beaten me, though I am innocent and without cause. I shall rise only after obtaining Diṭṭhamaṅgalikā, not without obtaining her.
Having made this resolution, he went and lay down at the door of her father’s residence.
When asked, "For what reason are you lying down? he replied, "There is no other reason; I have need of Diṭṭhamaṅgalikā.
One day passed, and likewise a second, a third, a fourth, a fifth, and a sixth.
Since the resolve of the Bodhisattvas is always fulfilled, on the seventh day [he obtained] Diṭṭhamaṅgalikā.
Having carried him out, they gave him to her.
Then she said to him, "Rise up, my lord; let us go to your home.
He replied, "Bhadde, I am completely worn out by your attendants and am weak; lift me up, place me on your back, and carry me away. She did so.
While the city-dwellers were still looking on, he departed from the city and went to the village of the Caṇḍālas.
Then the Great Being, without violating the boundaries of caste distinctions, had him live in his house for several days and thought:
"I shall only be able to bring him to the pinnacle of gain and the pinnacle of fame by going forth into the religious life, and not otherwise. Then, addressing him, he said: "My dear lady..."
"If I do not bring back anything from the forest, our livelihood will not continue; until my return, do not be distressed—I shall go to the forest.
Having said this, he instructed his householders, "Do not neglect him," and having gone to the forest, he went forth into the ascetic life.
Being diligent, on the seventh day he attained the eight meditative attainments (*samāpatti*) and the five [supernormal powers].
Having developed the higher knowledges (*abhiññā*), thinking, "Now I shall be able to provide support for Diṭṭhamaṅgalikā," he went by means of psychic power (*iddhi*),
descended at the gate of the Caṇḍāla village, and approached the door of Diṭṭhamaṅgalikā’s house.
Hearing that he had arrived, she came out from the house and said, "Master, why have you gone forth, leaving me without a protector?"
She lamented. Then he said to her, “Bhadde, do not grieve; I shall now provide you with a glory even greater than that of your former husband.
However, will you be able to say in the midst of this assembly, ‘Mahābrahmā is my husband, not the wise Mātaṅga’? She replied, “Yes, sir, I shall be able. “Therefore...”
"For when you are asked, 'Where is your husband now?', you should say, 'He has gone to the Brahma-world.
And when asked, 'When will he return?', you should say, 'He will return on the seventh day from now, having pierced the moon on the full-moon night.
Having said this to her, the Great Being departed for the Himālaya itself.
Diṭṭhamaṅgalikā also spoke in that manner in various places among the great multitude in Bārāṇasī.
The great multitude believed, saying, "Aha! Even though he is the Great Brahmā himself, he does not go to Diṭṭhamaṅgalikā; this must surely be so.
On the full-moon day, when the moon was situated in the midst of the sky, the Bodhisatta also [assumed] the form of Brahmā.
Having made the entire kingdom of Kāsi and the city of Bārāṇasī, twelve yojanas in extent, one single mass of light, he descended after piercing the lunar disk.
He circled three times over Bārāṇasī while being honored with perfumes, garlands, and other offerings by the great multitude, and then headed toward the village of the Caṇḍālas.
The Brahmabhattas assembled and [went] to the village of the Caṇḍālas.
Having gone to the house of Diṭṭhamaṅgalikā, he covered the ground with clean cloths,
wiped it with four kinds of fragrant scents, scattered flowers, burned incense, spread out a canopy of cloth, prepared a great couch,
lit lamps with fragrant oil, and at the door, strewn sand the color of silver plates and scattered flowers.
They hoisted flags. When the house was thus adorned, the Great Being descended, entered within, and sat for a short while on the back of the couch.
At that time, Diṭṭhamaṅgalikā was in her fertile period. Then he touched her navel with his thumb, and a fetus took root in her womb.
Thereupon the Great Being addressed her: "Bhadde, a fetus has taken root in you; you..."
"You shall give birth to a son; both you and your son will attain the pinnacle of gain and the pinnacle of glory.
The water used for washing your feet will become the consecration water for all kings throughout the entire Jambudīpa.
Furthermore, your bathing water will become an elixir of immortality (*amatosadha*); those who pour it upon their heads will be freed from all diseases and will avoid misfortune."
"Those who place their heads at the soles of your feet and pay homage will give a thousand;
those who stand within the range of your hearing and pay homage will give a hundred; those who stand within the range of your sight and pay homage will give one kahāpaṇa and pay homage. Be heedful!
Having thus exhorted him, she departed from the house and, while the great multitude looked on, leapt up into the lunar disk.

She entered. The Brahmin householders gathered together and, having spent the night standing right there, they placed her at dawn upon a golden palanquin adorned with auspicious sights, lifted it onto their heads, and entered the city.

The great multitude approached her, thinking, "This is the wife of Mahābrahmā," and honored her with perfumes, garlands, and other offerings. They bowed down, placing their heads at the soles of her feet.
Those who obtained a thousand-fold purse gave them one; those who stood within earshot to pay homage gave them a hundred;
and those who stood within sight to pay homage gave them a single kahāpaṇa coin.
Thus, traveling about while taking that twelve-league city of Bārāṇasī with them, they acquired eighteen koṭis of wealth.
Then, having escorted him around the city and brought him back, they had a great pavilion constructed in the center of the city, surrounded it with a curtain, and prepared a magnificent couch;
there they had him dwell with great splendor and majesty.
Right next to the pavilion, they began constructing a seven-storied palace with seven gate-towers, and the building work was extensive.

Diṭṭhamaṅgalikā gave birth to her son right there in the pavilion. On the day of his naming ceremony, the brahmins assembled and, because he had been born in the pavilion, gave him the name Maṇḍabya Kumāra. Meanwhile, the palace was completed after ten months;
from then on, she lived with great splendor, and Maṇḍabya Kumāra likewise [lived] with a great retinue.
He prospered. When he was only seven or eight years old, the most eminent teachers from the plains of Jambudīpa gathered around him.
They had him master the three Vedas. From the age of sixteen, he began providing food for brahmins;
sixteen thousand brahmins ate there regularly. At the fourth gate-tower, he gave alms to the brahmins.
Then, on a great festival day, they prepared much milk-rice (*pāyāsa*) in the house.
Sixteen thousand brahmins sat at the fourth gate-tower and partook of the milk-rice, which was prepared with fresh ghee the color of liquid gold, along with honey, sugar-candy, and jaggery.
The prince also, adorned with all his ornaments and wearing golden sandals...
Having mounted [his elephant] and grasped a golden staff in his hand, he wandered about, directing others, saying, "Give ghee here! Give honey there!
At that moment, the wise Mātaṅga, sitting in his hermitage in the Himalayas, was reflecting, "What indeed is the news regarding Diṭṭhamaṅgalikā’s son?
Looking out, he saw that the youth had leaped over a place where there was no ford, and thought, "I shall go this very day to the young man..."
Thinking, "I shall tame him, and then, having caused a gift to be given where it will be of great fruit,
I will return," he went through the air to Lake Anotatta; having performed his mouth-washing and other rites, he stood upon a slab of ruby-colored stone,
put on his red inner garment, fastened his waist-band, donned his rag-robe (paṃsukūla-saṅghāṭi), and took up his clay bowl.
Having come through the air, he descended right at the fourth gate-tower where the almsgiving was taking place and stood to one side.

Prince Maṇḍabya, looking here and there, saw him and thought, "From where could this ascetic, so deformed and resembling a refuse-yakṣa, have come when arriving at this place? Addressing him, he spoke the first verse:
“From where have you come, you ill-clad one? You look like a wretched ghost made of dust, with a rag from a rubbish heap tied around your neck. Who are you, you who are unworthy of offerings?
In this context, *dummavāsī* means one whose patched outer robe (*saṅghāṭika-pilotikavasana*) is neither anointed nor adorned. *Otallaka* means miserable.
Or one who wears a ragged garment hanging down and trailing along. "Like a dust-demon" means like a demon in a place of refuse.
"A rag from a refuse heap" means a piece of cloth found in a place of refuse. "Having fastened it on" means having put it on. "You are unworthy of offerings" means:
"How have you come alone to this seat where these most worthy of offerings are seated? You are not worthy of offerings."
Having heard this, the Great Being, conversing with him with a gentle heart, spoke the second verse:
“O illustrious one, this food has been prepared for you; let it be eaten, consumed, and drunk.
You know me to be one who lives on what is given by others; I am one who receives the alms-food of those who stand up [to give).”
In this context, *pakataṃ* means prepared. *Yasassī* means endowed with a retinue.
*Taṃ khajjare* means they eat it, consume it, and drink it. For what reason do you get angry at me?
*Uttiṭṭhapiṇḍaṃ* means alms-food to be obtained by standing near, or alms-food to be obtained by standing below while those who have stood up give it. [They] receive it.
"Let even a *caṇḍāla* who is a *sapāka* receive [alms]. For those endowed with noble birth receive [them] wherever they may be;
but who gives to a *sapāka-caṇḍāla*? I am one for whom alms are difficult to obtain; therefore, O Prince, have food given to me for the sake of sustaining my life.
Then Maṇḍavya spoke this verse:
“This food has been prepared by me for the brahmins; it is for my own benefit, as I have faith in this.
Move away from here! Why do you stand here? People like you do not give to those such as me.
In that context, *attatthāya* means for the sake of one’s own prosperity. *Apehi etto* means depart from this place. *Na*... [the rest of the verse].
“People like me—those of noble birth such as the high-born brahmins—give gifts, not to you, a caṇḍāla! Go away, you wretch!
Then the Great Being spoke this verse:
“They sow seed both on dry land and in low-lying places, hoping for fruit in the fertile fields.”
"With this same faith, give a gift; perhaps you may thus please those worthy of offerings.
The meaning of this is: "O youth, those hoping for a harvest of grain sow seed in three kinds of fields.
Therein, in times of excessive rain, the crop on the high ground prospers, while that in the low ground becomes rotten; and in marshy fields, depending on both rivers and tanks—"
It is carried away by the flood. In times of scanty rain, it fails in the field on the high ground, succeeds slightly in the low-lying field, and succeeds fully in the marshy field.
In times of even rainfall, it succeeds slightly in the field on the high ground, but succeeds fully in the other two.
Therefore, just as those seeking fruit sow seeds in all three types of fields, so too should you [proceed] with this.
"Give alms to everyone who comes with faith for the sake of the fruit; perhaps, by giving thus, you will please those worthy of offerings and receive [merit] in return.
Then Maṇḍabya spoke this verse:
“The fields in this world are known to me, in which I plant my seeds;
those brahmins who are endowed with birth and sacred hymns—these here are the most excellent fields.
In this passage, “in which I” means “in whom I. “Endowed with birth and sacred hymns” means possessed of both noble lineage and the Vedic mantras.
Then the Great Being spoke these two verses:
“Arrogance regarding birth, excessive pride, greed, hatred, intoxication, and delusion—
those in whom all these defects reside are fields here that are not fertile.”
“Pride of birth and excessive conceit, greed, hatred, intoxication, and delusion—those in whom none of these defects exist are here the most excellent fields.
In this context, “pride of birth” is the conceit arisen thus: “I am well-born. “Excessive conceit” is... [another...]
"There is no one equal to me in terms of birth and so forth"—thus he speaks with overweening pride. Greed and the other [defilements] consist merely in being greedy, corrupt, deluded, and infatuated.
"Unpleasant" means that such persons have an unlovely character, like anthills filled with venomous snakes.
What is given to such as these does not bear great fruit; therefore, do not imagine that they possess the nature of a good field. For indeed—
“Those who possess birth [in noble families] are givers of heaven. But those Noble Ones (ariya) who are devoid of birth, pride, and the like—those fields are most excellent;
what is given to them yields great fruit, for they are givers of heaven.
Thus, as the Great Being spoke again and again, he became angry and recited this verse: “This man prattles on far too much! Where have these gatekeepers gone? They do not lead away this outcaste!”
“Where have Upajotiya, the preceptor, and Gaṇḍakucchi gone?
Having given him this staff and this beating, seize him by the throat and drag him away, you scoundrels!
In this context, “Where have they gone? means: where have these three gatekeepers—Upajotiya, the preceptor, and Gaṇḍakucchi—who were stationed at these three gates, gone?
Having heard his words, they came with speed, paid homage, and said, “What shall we do, Your Majesty?
“Have you seen this outcaste Jamma? “We have not seen him, Your Majesty; we do not know from where he has come.
“Who might this be—a magician or a master of occult sciences? Why do you stand here now? “What shall we do, Your Majesty?”
“Beat his face until it is broken, tear the skin from his back with bamboo splinters, inflict the death penalty, seize him by the throat, and cast this wretch into the dust! Drive him out from here!
Even before they had reached him, the Great Being sprang up, stood in the air, and spoke this verse:
“You dig at a mountain with your fingernails; you chew iron with your teeth;
you strive to swallow fire—O you who revile the seer.
In this context, “you strive to swallow fire” means you attempt to gulp down a flame.
Having spoken this verse, the Great Being leaped into the air even as the young Brahmin and the other Brahmins were looking on. To clarify this matter, the Teacher said:
“Having spoken this, the seer Mātanga, Who was resolute in truth, Leaped into the sky While the Brahmins looked on.”
In this context, "effort in truth" means effort regarding one's true nature.
Having gone facing toward the eastern direction and descended by way of a certain street, he made the resolution,
"Let my footprints appear," and while wandering for alms near the eastern gate, he collected mixed food and sat down in a certain hall.
He partook of a mixed meal. The city deities, unable to endure it, thinking, "This man speaks while harassing our noble lady," arrived.
Then the chief *yakkha* seized Maṇḍabya by the neck and twisted it;
the other deities seized the necks of the remaining brahmins and twisted them. Because of the Bodhisatta’s gentle nature of heart—
However, they did not kill him, saying, "He is his son," but merely tormented him. Maṇḍabya’s head turned and came to face his back;
his hands and feet remained straight and stiff, and his eyes rolled back as if he were already dead.
He lay there with his body rigid, while the other brahmins moved to and fro, vomiting phlegm from their mouths.
They were turning over. The young men reported to Diṭṭhamaṅgalikā, saying, "Madam, what has been born to your son?
She went in haste, and seeing her son, she asked, "What is this? and spoke this verse:
"The head is twisted back, and he stretches out his arm, which is useless for work."
“Her eyes are white like those of a dead man; who has done this to my son?
Therein, *āvellitaṃ* means turned over.
Then, a person standing at that spot spoke this verse to inform her:
“Here has come the ascetic Dummavāsī, a ragged wanderer like a dust-demon;
with a rag from a rubbish heap fastened around his neck, he has indeed fathered this son of yours.
Upon hearing this, she thought: “No one else possesses such power; without a doubt, it must be the wise Mātaṅga.”
“Moreover, this wise man who has perfected the cultivation of loving-kindness will not depart after causing such a multitude of people distress;
to which direction, then, could he have gone? Then, asking thus, she spoke this verse:
“To which direction did he of vast wisdom go? Young men, explain this matter to me.”
"Having gone, let us make amends for that transgression; perhaps we may regain our son's life.
Therein, "having gone" means having gone into his presence. "Let us make amends for that transgression" means we shall rectify that offense, confess it, and ask for forgiveness.
"Perhaps we may regain our son's life" means we might indeed obtain the life of our son.
Then the young men standing there, as they spoke, recited this verse:
“He of vast wisdom went through the air like the moon on the fifteenth day at the end of its journey;
indeed, that seer of noble form has gone toward the eastern quarter, true to his promise.”

Therein, "standing halfway along the journey" means he was situated midway along the path reckoned as the sky, like the moon on the fifteenth day. Furthermore, "he too had gone toward the eastern direction.

Having heard their words, she thought, "I shall search for my husband," and having had golden jars and golden water-vessels prepared, surrounded by a retinue of female slaves, she reached the place where his footprints were fixed and followed them.
As he was sitting on that bench eating, she went up to him, paid her respects, and stood there.
Seeing her, he set aside a little rice in his bowl. Diṭṭhamaṅgalikā gave him water from a golden pitcher.
He washed his hands right there and rinsed his mouth. Then she asked him, "By whom... [was my son...]
Asking, "What is this transformation that has been wrought? she spoke this verse:
"The head is twisted back, the arm is stretched out and useless;
the eyes are white like those of a dead man—who has done this to my son?"
Then follow their verses of speech and reply:
“There are indeed powerful yakkhas who have approached these sages of virtuous form;
having perceived that his mind was wicked and agitated, those yakkhas thus made him their son.”
“The yakkhas have thus made my son their own; O practitioner of the holy life, do not be angry with me.
It is to you alone that I have gone for refuge, having been overcome by grief for my son, O bhikkhu.
Indeed, both then and now, there is no malice whatsoever in my mind.”
“And your son, intoxicated by the pride of the Vedas, does not understand the meaning because he has merely recited the Vedas by rote.
‘Surely, O monk, in a mere moment a person’s perception becomes utterly deluded;
forgive this one transgression, O one of vast wisdom—for the wise do not act out of the power of anger.’”
In this context, "yakkhas" refers to the yakkhas who protect the city. "Anvāgatā" means having followed after;

the meaning is "knowing them to be seers of noble form, endowed with virtuous qualities. "Tet" (they) refers to those [yakkhas] who, having recognized the virtues of the seers and having perceived that your son possessed a wicked and agitated mind, said:
"Let him alone be mine. If the yakkhas, being angry, have done this, let them do so; for as for deities, they [require] no more than a single water-pot.
"It is possible to satisfy them; therefore, I do not fear them. Only you, however, must not be angry with my son.
'Anvāgatā' means I have come. 'Bhikkhu'—addressing the Great Being thus—she begs for the gift of her son's life.
'Tadeva hi'—at that time, when Maṅgalikā saw [the sight], and even when she was reviling your son, I had no malice in my mind."

And even now, although you are begging from me, there is no ill-will whatsoever in my mind toward you. "By intoxication with the Vedas" means by the pride [thinking], "The three Vedas have been mastered by me.
"Incessantly" means that even after mastering the Vedas, one does not know what is meaningful and what is meaningless.
"In a mere moment" means immediately after mastering anything at all.
When she had thus asked for his forgiveness, the Great Being said, "In that case, I shall give you the Amata medicine so that these yakkhas may flee," and he spoke this verse:
"And let Maṇḍabya, who is of little wisdom, eat this alms-food of mine which has been set out;
then the yakkhas will not harm him, and he shall become your son, free from disease."
In this context, *uttiṭṭhapiṇḍa* means a morsel of food left over; there is also a reading as *ucchiṭṭhapiṇḍa*.
Having heard the Great Being’s words, she said, "Sir, give me the medicine of immortality," and offered him a golden bowl.
The Great Being poured the leftover sour gruel into it and said, "First, let half of this go to your son."
"Pour it into his mouth, then mix the remainder with water in a bowl and pour it into the mouths of the other brahmins;
they all will become free from disease," she said, and having spoken, she flew up and went back to the Himalayas.
She too, taking that bowl upon her head and saying, "I have obtained the medicine of immortality," went to her home and first poured the sour gruel into her son's mouth.
She sprinkled [him with water], and the spirit fled. The other, rising while wiping away the dust, said, "Mother, what is this?
"You alone shall know what you have done. Come, dear son, and see the result of your misdeed toward those worthy of offerings.
Upon seeing them, he was filled with remorse. Then his mother said to him, "Dear Maṇḍabya, you are a fool regarding the fact that giving has great fruit..."
“You do not know that those worthy of offerings are not like this; they are just like the wise Maṇḍabya.
From now on, do not give alms to these immoral ones; give to those who are virtuous. Having said this, he spoke:
“Māṇḍavya, you are a fool of limited wisdom, you who are unskilled in recognizing fields of merit.”
You give gifts to those with great red robes, who are defiled in their actions and unrestrained.
"Look at this generation, so unsightly: matted hair and locks, clad in deerskins, yet with faces like overgrown cesspools.
Neither matted hair nor deerskin protects one who lacks wisdom."
“In those for whom lust, hatred, and ignorance have been faded away, who are Arahants with taints destroyed—in giving to them, the fruit is great.
Herein, *mahakkasāvesu* means among those with great stains (*kasāva*), that is, those possessed of the great stains of lust and so forth. *Jaṭā*...
"And as for 'hair,' dear Maṇḍabya, you have bound some of the hair of those worthy of offerings into matted locks.

'Clad in antelope skins' means they are clothed in antelope skins complete with the hooves. 'Like a well overgrown with weeds' means their faces are overgrown with long hair and beards, like an old well choked by thick grass.
'This progeny' refers to this very kind of appearance, with its coarse dress, neither anointed nor adorned."
"Behold the people! This matted hair and deerskin—this matted hair and deerskin cannot protect these people of little wisdom;
only virtue, wisdom, and the practice of austerity are the true refuge for these beings.

"Of whom"—because of whom these [defilements] consisting of lust, hatred, and delusion, as well as the eightfold ignorance whose nature is to lust, hate, and delude, have been abandoned and removed; and because they have been removed...
Furthermore, among these defilements, what is given to those Arhats whose taints are exhausted bears great fruit;

therefore, my dear son, from now on, instead of giving to such immoral people, give gifts to those in the world who have attained the eight meditative absorptions and the five supernormal powers—namely, righteous recluses and brahmins, as well as Pacceka Buddhas. Come, my dear son, [your...]

Saying, "We shall make them healthy by having them drink an antidote," he had the Cāṇḍāla give the sixteen thousand brahmins leftover sour gruel, which he had placed in a water-skin, and caused it to be poured into their mouths.
Each one stood up while still wiping away the dust. Then those brahmins said, "These men have drunk the leftovers of a Cāṇḍāla!"

They treated him as a non-Brahmin. Feeling ashamed, they departed from Bārāṇasī and went to the Middle Country, where they lived in the presence of the King of the Middle Country; Maṇḍabya, however, remained right there.

At that time, near the city of Vettavatī, on the bank of the Vettavatī River, a certain Brahmin named Jātimanta had gone forth into the religious life and, on account of his birth, maintained great pride. The Great Being—
Thinking, “I shall break his pride,” he went to that place and took up residence upstream from him.
One day, after chewing a tooth-stick, he made a resolution, saying, “May this tooth-stick stick in the matted locks of the one possessing the spell,” and threw it into the river.
It stuck in the matted locks of the other as he was rinsing his mouth with water. Upon seeing it, he [realized].
Having said, "Begone, outcaste! and thinking, "Where has this ill-omened one come from?
I shall investigate him," he went upstream; seeing the Great Being, he asked, "What is your caste? "I am a Caṇḍāla. "Did you drop a tooth-stick into the river?
"Yes, by me. "Begone, outcaste Caṇḍāla! Do not live here; go down the stream!"
Having said, "Go away, outcaste," as the tooth-stick thrown by him while living downstream came back upstream and became entangled in his matted locks, the Great Being said, "Begone, outcaste!
If you remain here, on the seventh day your head shall split into seven pieces.
The Great Being thought, "If I were to become angry with him, my virtue would be unprotected; therefore, I must deal with him through skillful means."
Thinking, "I shall shatter his pride," on the seventh day he obstructed the rising of the sun.
People, becoming distressed, approached the high-born ascetic and asked, "Venerable sir, you are not allowing the sun to rise.
He replied, "That is not my doing; however, a Caṇḍāla lives on the riverbank, and this must be his doing."
People approached the Great Being and asked, "Venerable sir, you do not allow the sun to rise?
"Yes, friends," he replied. "For what reason? "A forest-dwelling ascetic who was a family associate of yours cast a curse upon me though I was innocent;
I shall release the sun once he has come and fallen at my feet to ask for forgiveness. They went [and found him].
Dragging him away, they brought him and laid him at the feet of the Great Being; having asked for his forgiveness, they said, "Venerable sir, release the sun.
"It is not possible to release it; if I were to release it, this man's head would split into seven pieces. "Then, venerable sir, what shall we do? He replied, "Bring me a lump of clay."
Having had it brought, he had it placed upon the ascetic’s head and ordered, "Lower the ascetic and set him in the water.
Once he was set there, he released the sun. As soon as the sun’s rays struck him, the lump of clay shattered into seven pieces and the ascetic submerged in the water.
Having tamed him, the Great Being reflected, "Where now do those sixteen thousand brahmins dwell? and while searching for them, he—

Knowing he was in the presence of King Majjha, [the monk] thought, "I shall subdue them. Traveling by means of psychic power (*iddhi*), he descended on the outskirts of the city and, taking his bowl, went for alms within the city.
When the brahmins saw him, they thought, "Even though this man has stayed here for only one or two days, he will leave us without support.
They went in haste and said, "Great King, there is a certain sorcerer, a master of spells (*vijjādhara*) and a thief."
"He has arrived; seize him! they reported to the king. The king accepted, saying, "Very well.
The Great Being, having taken his mixed meal, sat upon a bench leaning against a certain wall and began to eat.
Then, while he was still consuming his food with distracted attention, the men sent by the king struck him on the neck with a sword.
They brought about his death. Having passed away, he was reborn in the Brahma-world. It is said that in this Jātaka, the Bodhisatta was Koṇḍadamaka.

Because of that very state of being bound to another's tether, he met his end. The deities, becoming enraged, caused a hot shower of glowing embers to rain down upon the entire Middle Kingdom, turning the land into a wasteland. Therefore it is said:
“Having struck down Mana, the illustrious Mātaṅga, he and his retinue were destroyed; at that time, the Middle Forest was cleared.
Having delivered this Dhamma teaching, the Teacher said: “It is not only now; in the past as well, Udena used to harass those who had gone forth.”
Having spoken thus, he identified the Jātaka: "At that time Maṇḍabya was Udena, but the wise Mātaṅga was none other than myself.
This concludes the first commentary on the Mātaṅga Jātaka.
[498] 2. Commentary on the Cittasambhūta Jātaka.
"Everything well-performed by men bears fruit"—this was said by the Teacher while dwelling at Jetavana concerning two monks who were co-residents under the Venerable Mahākassapa.
It is said that they were supremely trustworthy and shared their gains without distinction;
even when going for alms, they went together, and they returned together.
They were unable to exist apart from one another. In the Hall of Truth, the monks sat there praising their very mutual trust.
The Teacher, having arrived, asked, "Monks, with what discussion are you gathered here at present?
When they replied, "With this one indeed," he said, "Monks, it is not surprising that these two [lived] in a single body."
"Reliability—ancient sages did not abandon their state of friendship even as they passed through three or four successive existences.
Having said this, he related a story of the past.
In the past, in the kingdom of Avantī, a great king named Avantī Mahārāja reigned in Ujjenī. At that time, outside of Ujjenī...
There was a village of Caṇḍālas. The Mahāsatta was reborn there, and another being was also reborn as his maternal uncle’s son.
Of these two, one was named Citta and the other was named Sambhūta.
When they both reached maturity, they learned the craft known as the washing of bamboo poles for the Caṇḍālas. One day, at the gate of the city of Ujjenī, [they displayed] their craft...
“Let us display our skills,” they said. One displayed his craft at the northern gate, and one at the eastern gate. In that city there were two women who considered sights to be auspicious:
one was the daughter of a merchant, and the other was the daughter of the royal chaplain.

Having had much solid food, soft food, garlands, perfumes, and so forth prepared, they thought, “We shall go for a pleasure excursion to the park,” and one departed by the northern gate, while the other departed by the eastern gate.
Seeing those sons of the Caṇḍālas demonstrating their craft, he asked, "Who are these? Upon hearing, "They are the sons of the Caṇḍālas," he thought, "Alas, we have seen what ought not to be seen!
He washed his eyes with scented water and turned back. The great multitude said, "O wicked Caṇḍāla!
It is because of you that we did not receive our free meals of liquor, rice, and other provisions."
Having beaten both brothers, he brought them to ruin and disaster.
When they regained consciousness and rose up, they went toward one another;
meeting at a certain spot, they informed each other of the occurrence of that suffering, wept and lamented, and deliberated, saying, "What shall we do?"
“Suffering has arisen for us because of this birth; we will not be able to perform the work of a caṇḍāla.
Let us conceal our birth and, assuming the appearance of brahmin youths, go to Takkasilā and learn a craft.
Having thus resolved, they went there and became students of the Dhamma in the presence of a world-renowned teacher.
They established themselves in a craft. It was reported throughout the land of Jambudīpa that "two Caṇḍālas, having concealed their birth, are learning a craft.
Of these two, Cittapaṇḍita’s training was completed, but Sambhūta’s was not yet finished.
Then one day, a certain village dweller invited the teacher, saying, "I shall perform a recitation for the Brahmins. He [the teacher] went to him alone...
After it had rained during the night, the rain filled the paths, ravines, and other such places.
Early in the morning, the teacher summoned Cittapaṇḍita and said, "Dear son, I shall not be able to go. You must go with the young brahmins;
after pronouncing auspicious blessings, eat what you receive from them, and bring back for us what we have received. He replied, "Very well," and set out taking the young brahmins with him.
While the young brahmins were bathing and washing their faces, the people increased the quantity of milk-rice and set it aside, saying, "Let it cool.
The young brahmins returned and sat down even before the rice had cooled. The people gave them the water of dedication (*dakṣiṇodaka*) and placed the bowls before them.
Sambhūta, as if his elements were agitated by greed, perceiving it as "cool," [took it].
Having picked up a lump of milk-rice, he placed it in his mouth; it burned his mouth like a glowing iron ball.
Trembling and unable to maintain mindfulness, he looked at Cittapaṇḍita and spoke in the language of the Caṇḍālas: "Khaḷu khaḷū.
He too, likewise unable to maintain mindfulness, spoke in the language of the Caṇḍālas: "Niggala niggalā."
The young brahmins looked at one another and said, "What kind of language is this? Cittapaṇḍita recited a blessing.
The young brahmins went outside and, sitting here and there in groups, examined the language;
realizing it was the "language of the outcasts," they cried out, "Hey, you wicked outcasts! For all this time you have been deceiving us by saying, 'We are brahmins'!"
Both of them struck him. Then a certain good man, stopping them by saying, "Go away," sent them both off, saying, "This is the fault of your birth;
go and live as renunciants in some other land. The young brahmins reported their outcaste status to the teacher.
Having entered the forest wilderness and gone forth into the ascetic life of an *isi*, they passed away not long thereafter and were reborn on the banks of the Nerañjarā River in the womb of a doe.
From the moment they emerged from their mother’s womb, they wandered together and were unable to be apart. One day, having taken up food, they were at the foot of a tree.

Seeing them standing there chewing their cud after having joined snout to snout, horn to horn, and beak to beak, one hunter threw a spear and deprived them of life in a single stroke. Passing away from there, they were reborn in the womb of a crab on the banks of the Nammadā River.
There too, having grown up and gone out for food, [they joined] snout to snout and beak to...
Seeing them standing there with their beaks pressed together, a certain spear-trapper bound and killed them both at a single stroke.
Then, passing away from that state, Citta the Wise was reborn as the son of a court priest in Kosambī.
Sambhūta the Wise was reborn as the son of the King of Uttarapañcāla. From the day their names were given, they [remembered] their own birth...
They recollected [their past lives]. Among them, the wise Sambhūta was unable to recollect continuously and recollected only his fourth birth as a caṇḍāla;
the wise Citta, however, recollected all four births in succession.

Having gone forth at the age of sixteen, he entered the Himalayas, took up the ascetic life of an *isi*, and having developed the meditative absorptions (*jhāna*) and direct knowledges (*abhiññā*), lived in the bliss of those absorptions.
He lived there, passing his time. When his father passed away, the wise Sambhūta raised the royal parasol;
on that very day of the auspicious ceremony of raising the parasol, he composed an auspicious song in the midst of the great multitude and, as an inspired utterance (*udāna*), recited two verses.
Upon hearing this, thinking, "This is the auspicious song of our king," both the women of the harem and the musicians sang that very same song. In due course, [the fame of] the king—
"Dear song"—thus all the people living in the city sang that very thing.
While still dwelling in a region of the Himalayas, Cittapaṇḍita, reflecting, "Has my brother Sambhūta indeed obtained the royal parasol, or has he not?
and having learned that he had indeed obtained it, thought: "Now, for his new reign..."
Thinking, "Even if I go now, I will not be able to awaken him; rather, when he has grown old, I shall approach him, preach the Dhamma, and cause him to go forth," he did not go for fifty years.
When the king’s sons and daughters had grown up, he went by means of psychic power, descended into the park, and sat upon the auspicious stone slab like a golden image. In that...
At that moment, a certain boy was gathering firewood while singing that song. Cittapaṇḍita called out to him.
He came, paid homage, and stood before him. Then he said to him: "From early morning until now, you have been singing only this song;
do you not know any others? "Venerable sir, I know many other songs as well, but these two are the king’s favorite songs."
"Therefore, I shall sing only these. "But is there anyone who can sing a response to the king's song?
"There is none, venerable sir. "Then will you be able to sing a response? "If I know it, I shall be able.
"In that case, when the king has sung two songs, you should sing this as the third," and having given him the song, [he sent him].
“Go into the presence of the king and sing; the king, being pleased with you, will grant you great sovereignty,” he sent him off.
He went quickly to his mother, had himself adorned, and went to the palace gate.
Having announced to the king, “It is said that a certain boy will sing a counter-song for you,” and when the king said, “Let him come,” he entered.
Having gone and paid homage, he was asked, "Is it true, dear sir, that you will sing a response? He replied, "Yes, Your Majesty;
assemble the entire royal assembly. When the assembly had gathered, he said to the king, "Your Majesty, please sing your own song first, and then I shall sing the response. The king spoke two verses:
“Everything well-performed by men bears fruit; there is nothing whatsoever that is fruitless through karma.
I see one who has come to be possessed of great majesty, endowed with the fruit of merit through his own karma.
Everything well-performed by men bears fruit; there is nothing whatsoever that is fruitless through karma.”
"Could it be that even for the mind it is exactly thus, and his mental power is as great as mine?
In this context, "there is nothing whatsoever that is fruitless through karma" means that among well-done or ill-done deeds, not even a single action is called fruitless;
it does not remain without result, but perishes only after having given its ripening—this refers to karma to be experienced in subsequent lives (*aparāpariyavedanīya-kamma*).

He spoke with intentional meaning (*sandhāya*). "Sambhūta" means he speaks of himself; "I see the venerable Sambhūta reborn through his own kamma, reborn by the fruit of merit depending on his own kamma"—this is the meaning.
"Perhaps even of the mind?"—for we two, having been together, did not observe the precepts for long. I...
"By the fruit of that [merit], he has attained such great fame; I wonder if my brother’s mind is likewise so successful and fulfilled?
At the conclusion of his song, the boy sang this third verse:
“Every well-performed deed of men bears fruit; there is nothing whatsoever that is in vain through karma.
Know the mind to be exactly like that too, O Deva, for his mental power is just as yours is.
Having heard this, the king spoke the fourth verse:
“Sir, did you hear this from someone else, or did someone tell it to you?
These verses are well-sung; I have no doubt about them. I shall give you an excellent village and a hundred [pieces of gold].
In this context, *sutamaññato te* means: “From whom did you hear it?”—referring to Citta himself as he says, “I am Sambhūta’s brother, named Citta.”
The meaning is: "Has it been heard by you from his presence? Someone said: "Has Citta, the brother of King Sambhūta, been seen by you?
Someone told him this matter. "Well sung" means: "In every respect, this verse is well sung;
I have no doubt about this. "And a hundred choice villages" means: he says, "I give you a hundred choice villages."
Then the boy spoke the fifth verse:
“I have not heard this from anyone else, nor did the seers tell me this matter.
Having gone to the king, he recited the verse; perhaps, being well-pleased, he might grant you a boon.”
In this context, "this matter" means that while sitting in your park, a certain seer explained this matter to me.
Having heard this, the king said, "He must be my brother Citta; I shall go and see him right now," and as he was giving orders to his men, he spoke these two verses:
"Yoke indeed the royal chariots, well-fashioned and covered with fine cloth;..."
“Bind the girths of the elephants and fasten the neck-ornaments.
Let the kettledrums, tabors, and conchs be sounded, and let the swift vehicles be harnessed.
This very day I shall go to that hermitage where I shall see the Seer sitting.”
In this context, "let them strike" means let them beat [the drum]. "That hermitage" refers to that very hermitage.

Having spoken thus, he mounted his chariot and traveled swiftly; having halted the chariot at the gate of the park, he approached Cittapaṇḍita, paid homage, and sitting to one side with a joyful heart, he spoke the eighth verse:
"Truly, a great gain has been mine, for well-sung verses have been recited in the midst of the assembly."
“Having seen the seer endowed with virtuous conduct, I am thrilled and well-pleased.

The meaning of this is: “Truly, it was a great gain for me that on the auspicious day of the festival, in the midst of the assembly, my song was so well-sung; and today, having seen the seer perfected in virtuous conduct, I have become filled with joy and gladness.
From the moment he saw Cittapaṇḍita, being thus filled with gladness, he spoke the ninth stanza while giving orders such as, “Spread a couch for my brother! and so forth:
“May your honor accept our seat, water, and foot-washing water;
we ask your honor regarding the guest-offering (*aggha*); may your honor perform the guest-offering for us.
In this context, *aggheti* means: “We ask your honor regarding the guest-offering which is appropriate to be given to a guest. *Kurutu no* means: “May your honor accept this guest-offering of ours.”
Having thus exchanged such sweet greetings, and bestowing the kingdom by dividing it in the middle, he spoke the other verse:
“Let them build a delightful dwelling for you; enjoy yourself with throngs of women.
Grant us the opportunity to show favor; let both of us exercise this sovereignty.”
"In this regard, 'this sovereignty' means that we two shall divide the kingdom in the city of Uttarapañcāla in the realm of Kapila and exercise it together.
Having heard those words, Cittapaṇḍita spoke six verses while teaching the Dhamma:
"O King, having seen the fruit of misconduct, And the great result of well-practiced virtue;..."
Restraining oneself alone, one should not long for children, cattle, or wealth.
"The lifespan of mortals here is ten times ten years;
before reaching its full extent, one withers like a cut reed."
“In this matter, what joy is there, what play, what delight, or what seeking of wealth?
What use have I for sons and wives, O King? I am released from bondage.
Thus do I understand: Death does not spare me.”
“For one seized by the End-maker, what joy is there? What is the pursuit of wealth?
“O Lord of Men, the birth of men that is base is the womb of a Caṇḍāla, the lowest among bipeds.
Through our own most evil deeds, we formerly dwelt in the womb of a Caṇḍāla.”
“We were Caṇḍālas among the Avantis, deer by the Nerañjarā, and crows on the banks of the Nammadā;
today we are Brāhmaṇas and Khattiyas. Regarding that, [the Buddha said]:
“O Great King, you know the fruit of good conduct alone, but I [know] the fruit of bad conduct as well.”
"I see the fruit indeed. For we both, as a result of our misconduct, were reborn in the womb of a Caṇḍāla in this fourth existence.
There, after guarding my virtue for no long time, by the fruit of that you were reborn in a khattiya family and I in a brahmin family.
Thus, having seen the fruit of misconduct and the great ripening of what was well-performed,"
"I shall restrain myself alone by means of the restraint of virtue; I do not long for a son, nor cattle, nor wealth.

O Great King, these ten decades are: the decade of dullness, the decade of playfulness, the decade of beauty, the decade of strength, the decade of wisdom, the decade of decline, the decade of stooping, the decade of crookedness, the decade of delusion, and the decade of lying on the bed."
Indeed, by way of these ten decades, the lifespan of these mortals here in the human world consists of exactly ten decades of years.
Yet this [lifespan] does not necessarily reach all of these decades; rather, even before reaching that full extent, one withers like a reed cut down.
Even for those who live a full hundred years, it is during their final decade that they become feeble.
The material and immaterial phenomena that have arisen are severed and wither right there, disappearing like a reed cast into the sun;

they do not reach the "decade of play" (khiḍḍādasaka) beyond that physical mass (odhi), nor do the "decades of beauty" (vaṇṇadasaka) and so forth that had arisen within the "decades of play" and the rest.
In that state—while life is thus withering away—who would take delight by depending on the five strands of sensual pleasure? Who [would indulge] by means of bodily play and the like?
*Khiddā*: What is pleasure by way of mental joy? What is the seeking of wealth? [The meaning is: "What use have I for sons, what use for a wife?
I am released from that bond of children and wife. *Antakenādhipannassa*: Of one who is seized by Death, the ender of life.
*Dvipadākaniṭṭhā*: The lowest among bipeds. *Avasimhā*: We two both lived.
"O Great King, we were Caṇḍālas. Four births prior to this, in the city of Ujjeni in the kingdom of Avantī, we were Caṇḍālas.
Having passed away from there, both of us became deer on the bank of the river Nerañjarā.
There, while we two were standing at the foot of a single tree leaning against one another, a hunter deprived us both of our lives with a single stroke of his spear."
"I deprived him of his life; having passed away from there, we were born as ospreys on the banks of the Nammadā River.

There too, while we were perched together, a single hunter bound us all at once with a single throw and brought us to our death. Having passed away from there, we have now been born today as a brahmin and a kshatriya.
I was reborn in a brahmin family in Kosambī, and you have been born here as a king."
Having thus revealed his low birth in the past, and now demonstrating the brevity of the life-force even in this present birth, he spoke these four stanzas to inspire him toward meritorious deeds:
“Life is being led away, its span is short; for one led by old age, there is no refuge.
O Pañcāla, do my bidding; do not perform deeds that result in suffering.”
“Life is being led away, its span is short; for one led by old age, there is no refuge.
O Pañcāla, do as I say; do not perform deeds that bear bitter fruit.
Life is being led away, its span is short; for one led by old age, there is no refuge.”
“Do as I say, Pañcāla; do not perform deeds that lead to the dust of rebirth.
Life is being led away, its span is short; old age destroys the beauty of a man as he grows old.
Do as I say, Pañcāla; do not perform an act that leads to rebirth in hell.”
In this regard, O Great King, "it is led toward" means that this life approaches death.
For the life of these beings is limited, being short both in terms of its essential nature and its duration; it is like a drop of dew on the tip of a blade of grass at sunrise.
"There is no refuge" means that for one led toward death by old age, sons and others do not constitute a refuge.

"Are called. "This is my word" means this speech of mine. "Do not do" means: do not, on account of the qualities of sensual pleasure such as forms, fall into negligence and perform deeds that increase suffering in the hells and other realms. "Having suffering as their fruit" means having suffering as their result.
"With hair grey with dust" means with heads covered by the dust of the defilements (*kilesa*). "The complexion" refers to the bodily complexion of a man who is growing old.
Old age destroys. "For the sake of rebirth in hell" means for the purpose of arising in hell, which is devoid of satisfaction.
While the Great Being was speaking thus, the king, being pleased, recited three verses:
"Truly, this speech of yours is the truth, just as you, O seer, have spoken; it is indeed so."
“Sensual pleasures exist for me in manifold forms, which are difficult for a monk like me to abandon.
Just as an elephant sunk in the middle of a mire, though seeing dry land, is unable to reach it;
even so, I am sunk in the mire of sensual pleasures and cannot follow the path of a bhikkhu.”
“Just as both mother and father instruct their son, ‘How might he be happy?
even so, Bhante, do you instruct me, so that after passing away I may be happy for a long time.
In this context, *anapparūpā* means those who are not of limited birth, but many and immeasurable. “They are difficult to be born by one such as I,” O brother.
“You stand having abandoned the defilements, while I am submerged in the mire of sensual desire; therefore, for one such as me, those sensual desires are difficult to abandon.
With the words “Like an elephant,” he shows a simile for his own state of being submerged in the mire of sensual desire. In that context, *byasanna* means sunken or entered;
this is indeed the reading. “The path” refers to the path of your advice and instruction, which I do not follow.
“I am unable to go forth; rather, while I remain right here, please give me your instruction. Thus they instructed him.
Then the Great Being said to him:
“O Lord of Men, if you are not able to abandon these human sensual pleasures, [then listen].”
“O King, establish a righteous offering; let there be no unrighteous practice in your realm.
“Let messengers run forth to the four quarters, inviting recluses and brahmins.
Serve them with food and drink, and with clothing and the requisite of lodgings.”
“With a mind full of faith, satisfy the recluses and brahmins with food and drink;
having given and having eaten according to your means, blameless, go to the heavenly realm.
And if, O King, while you are being entertained by throngs of women, intoxication should overcome you;”
Keep this very verse in mind, and recite it in the midst of the assembly:
“A man who slept under the open sky, suckling milk as he went along,
and was surrounded by dogs— today he is called ‘king.’”
In this context, *ussahase* means "you strive. *Dhammaṃ baliṃ* means he collects a tax that is righteous, equitable, and not excessive;
such is the meaning. *Adhammakāro* refers to an unrighteous act carried out by violating the legal principles (*vinicchayadhamma*) established by ancient kings.
*Nimantakā* refers to those who invite and summon righteous recluses and brahmins. *Yathānubhāvaṃ* means according to their power or status.
"According to one's strength, according to one's capacity. He said this with reference to what is to be stated now: "This very verse. Herein, the intended meaning is as follows:

"Great King, if pride should overcome you—if, while surrounded by a host of women, pride should arise in you concerning forms and other objects of sensual pleasure, or concerning the bliss of sovereignty—then you should reflect thus: 'In the past, I was in the womb of a *caṇḍāla*...'"
Because I was born with not even a small grass hut to cover me, I lived in the open air.
At that time, my mother—a woman of the Caṇḍāla caste—would go into the forest for firewood, leaves, and other necessities;
she would lay me down in the open amidst a pack of dogs, give me her own milk to drink, and then depart. Thus, surrounded by dogs, I was [nourished] by those very same [dogs].
“Having drunk milk together with a female dog, he grew up; thus, though being of low birth, today he has become known as a king.
“Therefore, O Great King, admonishing yourself by this example:
that person who formerly lay in the open air in the forest, while a fierce woman was wandering here and there and a female dog was drinking milk...”
“You should recite this verse: ‘He who was suckled by dogs, surrounded by them, and raised by them, is today called a king.
Having thus given him this advice, the Great Being said, “I have given you my counsel;
now, whether you go forth or not, you yourself shall experience the ripening of your own karma. Having said this, he flew up into the sky and [disappeared] from his sight.
Dropping the dust of his feet upon the Great Being’s head, he departed for the Himālaya. The king, too, seeing this, was moved by a sense of spiritual urgency;
having given the kingdom to his eldest son and dismissed his army, he set out toward the Himālaya.

The Great Being, knowing of his approach, came forth surrounded by a company of seers, took him with him, and after leading him away, ordained him and instructed him in the preliminary practice of the *kasiṇas*.
Thus he attained the meditative absorptions and the superknowledges. In this way, both of them went to the Brahma-world.

Having delivered this teaching on the Dhamma, the Teacher said, "In this way, monks, even as they passed through three or four future existences, the ancient wise men remained firm in their trust," and he identified the Jātaka: "At that time..."
"Sambhūta-paṇḍita was Ānanda, while Cittapaṇḍita was none other than myself.
This concludes the second commentary, the Cittasambhūta Jātaka.
3. The Commentary on the Sivi Jātaka.
"Seeing not from afar, the elder," this was spoken by the Teacher while dwelling in Jeta’s Grove concerning a peerless gift.
That story has already been related in detail in the Sivi Jātaka of the Aṭṭhaka Nipāta. At that time, however, on the seventh day, the king provided all the requisites and requested a blessing;
the Teacher departed without having offered one. Having finished his morning meal, the king went to the monastery.

“Venerable sir, why did you not offer words of thanksgiving? he asked. The Teacher replied, “Great king, the assembly was not pure,” and he taught the Dhamma with the verse: “The miserly do not go to the world of the gods.
The king, having gained confidence, honored the Tathāgata with a Siṇḍhava blanket worth a hundred thousand pieces of gold, and then entered the city.
On the following day, they raised a discussion in the Dhamma Hall: "Friends, after giving such an incomparable gift, the King of Kosala was not satisfied even with that kind of almsgiving;
when the Ten-Powered One taught the Dhamma, he again gave a Sīveyyaka cloth worth a hundred thousand pieces.
Truly, friends, the king is insatiable regarding gifts. The Teacher approached and asked, "Bhikkhus, what is it that you are discussing?"
Having asked, "For what discussion are you sitting together now? and being told, "For this one," [the Buddha said], "Monks, external goods are indeed well-given.
Even when the ancient wise men made the whole of Jambudīpa free of plows and gave gifts every day by relinquishing six hundred thousand [pieces of gold], they were not satisfied with external giving.
Thinking, 'The giver of what is dear receives what is dear,' they [gave] to those supplicants who had arrived..."
"Having gouged out their eyes, they gave them to him," he said, and then related a story of the past.
In the past, while King Sivi was ruling in the city of Ariṭṭhapura in the kingdom of Sivi, the Great Being was born as his son;
they gave him the name Sivi Kumāra. When he reached maturity, he went to Takkaśilā.
Having mastered his craft and returned, he displayed his skill to his father and obtained the position of viceroy. Later, upon his father’s passing, he became king.
Abandoning the path of ruin and not violating the ten royal duties, he ruled the kingdom according to Dhamma.
He established six halls of almsgiving—at the four city gates, in the center of the city, and at the door of his own residence—and gave away six hundred thousand [pieces of gold] every day.
He established a great distribution of alms. On the eighth, fourteenth, and fifteenth days of the lunar fortnight, he would regularly go to the hall of almsgiving and look over the offerings.

Once, on the full moon day, sitting at dawn upon his royal throne beneath a raised white parasol, as he reflected upon the alms he had given, he saw no external object that he had not already bestowed. Thinking, "By me, as for external objects..."
"There is nothing that has not been given; external gifts do not satisfy me. I desire to give internal gifts.
Oh, would that some supplicant should come to my hall of giving today and, instead of asking for an external thing, should name something internal!
For if someone were to name the flesh of my heart, I would strike my chest with a golden spear."
Like one pulling up a lotus with its stalk from clear water, I shall extract my heart, dripping with drops of blood, and give it to you.
If the name "flesh of the body" were to be mentioned, I would cut away the flesh of my body and give it, like one scraping oil from a horn with a scraping tool.
If the name "blood" were to be mentioned, [I would give it] at the mouth of the machine...
Having leaped in and filled the vessel brought to me, I will give blood.

Or, if anyone should say, "Work does not proceed in my house; do the work of a slave for me," I will cast off the royal disguise, stand outside, announce myself, and perform the work of a slave. If anyone should take my name, "Akkhika,"...
He thought, "I will pluck out my eyes and give them to him, as if extracting the core of a palmyra fruit.
Thus he said:
"Whatever human gift there may be, nothing remains that I have not already given."
"Even if someone were to ask me for my eye, I would give it without hesitation.

Having thus reflected, he bathed with sixteen jars of scented water, adorned himself with all his ornaments, partook of various foods of exquisite flavor, and, mounted upon the back of a magnificent, decorated state elephant, proceeded to the hall of almsgiving. Sakka [perceived] his intention...

Having understood that King Sivi had thought, "Today I shall pluck out the eyes of those who have arrived as supplicants and give them," and wishing to test whether he would indeed be able to give or not, [the Bodhisatta] assumed the guise of an old, blind brahmin.
At the time when the king was proceeding to the place of giving, [the brahmin] extended his hand toward a certain elevated spot and addressed the king.
Having obtained victory, he stood there. The king, having sent an elephant toward him, asked, "Brāhmaṇa, what do you say?
Then Sakka said to him, "Great King, the entire world of living beings is filled without interval by the fame arising from your inclination toward generosity;
I am blind, while you possess two eyes. Having spoken thus, he spoke the first verse, requesting an eye:
“Living far away, this elder has come to beg for my eye;
we shall become one-eyed, so give me my eye as I have requested.
In this passage, *dūre* means living far from here. *Thero* refers to an elder worn out by old age. *Ekanettā* means: “Give me one eye, so that in this way we two shall each have one eye.”
Hearing this, the Great Being thought, "Just now, while sitting in my palace, I came here after reflecting; oh, what a gain for me!
Today my heart's desire will reach its fulfillment; I shall give a gift never given before. With a joyful mind, he spoke the second verse:
"By whom were you instructed, O mendicant, that you have come here to beg for the sight of my eyes?
"You ask for the head, which is most difficult to give up—that which is called by men 'the eye, so hard to surrender.

In this context, he addresses him as 'mendicant' (*vanibbaka*). 'The path of the eyes' (*cakkhupathāni*) is a name for the eyes. 'Which they call' (*yamāhu*) means that which the wise describe as 'difficult to give up.
From here on, the verses with clear connections should be understood according to the method of the Pāḷi text itself."
“He whom they call Sujampati among the gods, and Maghavan in the world of men—
I have come here instructed by him, a beggar to ask for the objects of his sight.
Grant me, who am a beggar, that unsurpassed gain which I have requested as the objects of my sight.”
Grant me your unsurpassed sight, which is said by men to be the hardest thing to give up.
May those intentions for which you have come and for which you have prayed be fulfilled; receive back your eyes, O Brahmin.
“I shall give you both [eyes] as you request them;
go forth with your sight while people look on, and whatever you desire, may that be accomplished for you.
In this context, *vanibbato* means “to one who is begging. *Vanī* means “a request. *Te te* means “those [desires] of yours,” referring to the intentions regarding that purpose.
"O you who possess eyes," he said, "having become one with eyes through my own eyes;
may whatever you desire from me be fulfilled for you.
Having spoken thus much, the king thought, "It is not fitting that I should pluck out my eyes and give them right here."
Taking the brahmin with him, he went to the inner palace, sat upon the royal throne, and having summoned the physician named Sivika, said, "Purify my eye.
A great clamor arose throughout the entire city: "It seems our king wishes to gouge out his own eyes and give them to a brahmin!
Then the commander-in-chief and other royal favorites, the citizens, and the women of the harem—
And they all assembled together and, dissuading the king, spoke these three verses:
“Do not give us your eye, O Lord; do not drive us all away.
Grant us wealth, Great King—many pearls and beryl gems.”
“Give me, O King, yoked chariots and well-adorned thoroughbred horses;
give me elephants, O Great King, clothed in golden trappings.
Just as all those wives were always provided with their attendants, chariots, and horses...”
“They would surround you on all sides; give [them], O bull among charioteers.
In this context, *parākarī* means “he abandoned. For they spoke thus with the underlying intention: “If your eyes are given away, you will not exercise sovereignty;
another will become king, and in this way we shall indeed be abandoned by you. *Parikireyyuṃ* means “they would surround.”
“They would surround him. “Give him such [a gift] as the Śivis would surround one whose eyes were unimpaired;
give him only external wealth, not his eyes. For if his eyes were given away, the Śivis would not surround him.
Then King Tissa spoke three verses:
“He who, having said ‘I will give,’ sets his mind on not giving,
fastens the snare that fell upon the ground around his own neck.
He who, having said ‘I will give,’ sets his mind on not giving...”
“Evil becomes even more evil for one who has reached the abode of Yama.
‘Whatever one asks for, that one should give; what one does not ask for, that one should not give.
Therefore, I shall give only that which this brahmin asks of me.’”
In this context, "he fastens on" means he causes [it] to enter. "Evil, even more evil" means that he becomes not only base, but even more base.
"Arrived at the abode of Yama's executioners" means that he has indeed reached the Ussada Niraya, the place where the commands of Yama are carried out.
For whatever a beggar might ask for, the donor should give that very thing, and not what was unasked; and this brahmin—
"He asks for my eye, not for wealth such as pearls and the like; I shall give him that very thing," he said.
Then the ministers, asking him, "For what do you desire that you give your eyes? spoke this verse:
"Is it life, or beauty, or happiness, or strength? For what purpose, O Lord of Men, do you give?"
“How indeed could a king, unsurpassed as he is, give away his eyes for the sake of the next world?
Therein, “for the sake of the next world,” O Great King, means: how indeed could a wise man such as yourself, abandoning visible sovereignty, give away his eyes for the sake of the next world?
Then, while speaking to them, the king uttered this verse:
“I do not give this for the sake of fame, nor do I desire sons, nor wealth, nor a kingdom;
rather, because the ancient Dhamma of the virtuous has been practiced, my mind delights in giving alone.
In this context, *na vāhaṃ* means “indeed, I do not. *Yasassā* means “for the sake of fame,” whether celestial or human. *Na*... [the rest of the sentence follows].
"I do not desire a son as the fruit of this gift of my eyes, nor wealth, nor a kingdom;
rather, it is the practice, the constant practice, and the ancient path of the wise and omniscient Bodhisattvas, namely, the fulfillment of the perfections (pāramīs).
For without fulfilling the perfections, it is impossible to attain omniscience at the seat of enlightenment."
"There is one who is capable, and I too desire to become a Buddha by fulfilling the perfections (pāramīs).
For this reason—'Thus my mind delights in giving'—he says that his mind is devoted solely to giving.

Even the Perfectly Enlightened One, when teaching the Cariyāpiṭaka to the Elder Sāriputta, the General of the Dhamma, said this in order to demonstrate: "Of my two eyes, omniscient knowledge (sabbaññutaññāṇa) alone is dearer to me."
“Neither of my two eyes is to be given away by me, nor is my own self to be given away;
omniscience is dear to me, therefore I gave you my eye.
Having heard these words of the Great Being, while his ministers stood silent, the Great Being addressed the physician Sīvika with a verse:
“Sīvika, you are my companion and friend; being well-trained, do my bidding well.
Having plucked out my eyes from me as I desire to conquer, place them in the hands of this mendicant.
The meaning of this is: “O dear Sīvika, you are my companion and friend, and you are well-trained in the science of medicine.”
“Do as I say. While I am examining and looking for one to conquer, pluck out my eyes like the core of a palmyra fruit and place them in the hands of this beggar.
Then the butcher said to him, “The gift of the eyes, sire, is a heavy burden; reflect upon it, O King. [The King replied: “Butcher, it has been reflected upon.”
"I say this so that you do not engage in further elaboration, and do not converse at length with me.
He thought, "It is improper for a well-trained physician such as myself to let a blade of grass fall upon the King's eyes.
Having ground various medicinal herbs and infused blue lotuses with the resulting powder, he applied it by blowing it into the right eye. The eye—
The eye turned back and painful feeling arose. "Observe this, Great King; restoring it to its original state is my burden.
"Enough, dear sir; do not make such a fuss," he replied. He massaged it again and sniffed at it once more;
the eye was released from the socket, but an even stronger pain arose. "Observe this, Great King; am I able to restore it?"
"Let me do it. "Do not make a fuss," [the king said]. On the third attempt, he ground it even more finely and offered it.
By the power of the medicinal herb, the eye rolled back, emerged from the socket, and remained suspended by a thread of sinew.
"Observe this, O Lord of Men; my power lies in restoring it to its natural state once more. Do not make a fuss," he said.
Intense pain arose; blood flowed, and his lower garment was soaked with blood.
The attendants and ministers fell at the king’s feet and wailed with great lamentation, crying, “Sire, do not give your eyes!
The king, enduring the pain, said, “Dear ones, do not make such a fuss. He replied, “Very well, sire,” and with his left hand—
Having held his eye and taken a lancet with his right hand, he cut the tendon of the eye, extracted the eye,
and placed it in the hands of the Great Being. Looking from his left eye at his right eye, and enduring the pain, he called out to the brahmin,
"Come, brahmin," and said, "A hundredfold, a thousandfold more than this eye of mine..."
"Even the eye of omniscient knowledge is dearer to me than a hundred thousand [other things];
let this be the means for me to attain it," he said, and gave his eye to the brahmin. The brahmin plucked it out and placed it in his own eye.
By the power of the Great Being, it settled there like a blooming blue lotus. Having seen that eye with his left eye, the Great Being...
"Ah! I have given my eye well," he thought, and being filled continuously with joy that had welled up within him, he gave his other eye as well.

Sakka placed that eye also in his own eye, departed from the royal palace, and while the great multitude was looking on, he left the city and went back to the world of the gods. To illustrate this matter:
The Teacher spoke one and a half verses:
“Urged by the King of Sivi, the obedient Sīvika plucked out the king’s eyes and presented them to the brahmin.”
“The Brahmin possessed sight; the blind king entered [the womb].

Not long after, the king’s eyes began to swell. As they swelled, before reaching the state of being hollowed out, they were filled with protruding lumps of flesh like balls of wool, so that his eyes became like those of a painted figure. There was intense pain.
...was cut off. Then the Great Being, having lived in the palace for a few days, thought: "What is the use of sovereignty for a blind man?
Having handed over the kingdom to the ministers, I shall go to the park, go forth, and practice the duty of a recluse.
Having summoned his ministers, he informed them of this matter and said: "I require only one person who will provide me with mouth-washing water and other such things, acting as my attendant."
“Let it be near me; even at the places where the bodily functions must be performed, bind a rope for me,” he said.
Then, addressing his charioteer, he said, “Yoke the chariot.

However, the ministers, not allowing him to go by chariot, carried him away in a golden palanquin, seated him on the bank of a lotus pond, and having established a guard, they departed. The king sat cross-legged...
Seated there, he reflected upon his own gift. At that moment, Sakka’s seat became warm.
Reflecting on this, and seeing the reason for it, he thought, “I shall grant a boon to the Great King and restore his sight.
Having so resolved, he went there and paced back and forth not far from the Great Being. Explaining this matter, the Teacher spoke these verses:
Then, after a few days had passed and his eyes had fully healed,
the King, the prosperer of the Śivi kingdom, addressed his charioteer:
“Charioteer, harness the vehicle, and report when it is ready.”
“Let us go to the park grounds and to the lotus ponds and groves.
Then, on the bank of that lotus pond, he sat down cross-legged;
and Sakka, the king of the gods and husband of Sujā, appeared before him.
Sakka, too, having heard the sound of the Great Being’s footsteps, asked, “Who is this? and spoke this verse:
“I am Sakka, the lord of the gods; I have come into your presence.
Choose a boon, O King of Kings, whatever you desire in your mind.”
When this was said, the king spoke this verse:
“Abundant is my wealth, Sakka, and my army and treasury are not small;
yet now that I am blind, death alone is pleasing to me.”
"In that regard, O King of Devas, death alone is what pleases me; now, because of my blindness, death alone is pleasing to me, so grant it to me.
Then Sakka said to him, "King Sivi, do you desire death because you wish to die, or rather because of your blindness?
"Because of my blindness, O Deva. "Great King, giving is not for the sake of the future life alone."

“Giving is bestowed; it serves as a condition even for welfare in this very life. Since you gave two eyes when asked for only one, perform an act of truth with that. Having thus prompted him, he said:
“O Prince, Lord of Bipeds, speak those truths which you possess.”
“If you speak the truth, your eye shall be restored.
Having heard this, the Great Being said, “Sakka, if you wish to give me back my eye, do not employ any other means;
let my eye arise through the very power of the merit of my gift. When Sakka replied, “Great King, I am Sakka, the king of the gods,” he continued:
