When it was said, "I am not able to give my own eyes to others; by the very fruit of the gift you have given, your eyes will arise," he replied, "In that case, my gift has been well-bestowed. Then, performing an act of truth (*saccakiriya*), he spoke this verse:
"To those who come to me to beg, mendicants of various clans..."
"Whoever among those who come to beg from me asks me there, he too is dear to my mind;
by this utterance of truth, may my eye be restored.
In that context, "those who [say] 'me'" refers to those petitioners who have come to beg from me; when those petitioners have arrived, whoever among them asks me...

"He too is dear to my mind. By this [he meant]: "If all supplicants are indeed dear to me, and this which I have spoken is the truth, then by this word of truth, let one eye arise for me—let it arise! he said.
Immediately after his words, his first eye appeared. Then, for the sake of the second one arising, he spoke two verses:
“When that brahmin came to me to beg, saying, ‘Give me your eyes,’ I gave my eyes to that brahmin who was a seeker.
Even more than before, rapture and no small measure of gladness took possession of me.”
“By this utterance of truth, may a second [eye] arise for me.
In this context, *yaṃ* means “whoever”; *maṃ* means “me”; *yācati* means “he requests. *So* refers to that blind brahmin who came to request, saying, “Give me an eye.
*Vanibbato* means “of one who is begging. *Bhiyyo maṃ āvisī* means that after giving my eyes to the brahmin, [a third eye] entered me.

From that time of darkness onwards, disregarding the suffering of such a nature during that dark period, as I reflected, "Oh, what a gift well-given by me!", an even greater and more abundant rapture (pīti) entered me;
it penetrated my heart, and an infinite and immeasurable gladness (somanassa) arose within me. By this—if at that time there was no small measure of rapture and gladness in me—
"This is indeed the truth that I have spoken; by this word of truth, let a second eye arise for me," he said.
At that very moment, a second eye arose. However, those eyes of his were neither ordinary nor divine.
For it was impossible to restore to its natural state the eye given to the brahmin Sakka, as his physical basis had been impaired.
And although what is called the divine eye did not arise [in him], those eyes were said to have been produced through the power of his perfection of truth (*saccapāramitā*).
At the very moment they appeared, by the power of Sakka, the entire assembly of kings gathered together.
Then Sakka, offering praise right in the midst of the great multitude, spoke these two verses:
“O Increaser of the Śivi Kingdom, these verses spoken in accordance with the Dhamma—
these divine eyes of yours are now clearly visible.
Transcending walls and mountains, they pass over even the highest peaks.”
“May they enjoy the sight of you for a hundred leagues all around.
Therein, “spoken according to the Dhamma” means, O Great King, these verses of yours were spoken according to the Dhamma, by their very nature.
“Divine” means endowed with divine power. “They appear” means they become visible. “Through walls,” O Great King, these [verses] of yours...

The meaning is: "May they, like the eyes of the deities, transcend and pass over any mountain whatsoever—be it another peak or another crag—and experience and accomplish the vision of forms for a hundred leagues in all ten directions.
Having thus spoken these verses in the midst of the great multitude while standing in the sky, he said to the Great Being, "Be heedful!"
Having given this exhortation, he departed for the world of the gods. The Great Being, surrounded by a great multitude and entering the city with great honor, ascended the Sucandaka palace.
The fact that he had regained his sight became known throughout the entire kingdom of Sivi. Then, in order to see him, the inhabitants of the whole kingdom arrived, bringing many gifts.
The Mahāsatta, thinking, "In this great assembly of people, I shall praise my own generosity," had a great pavilion constructed at the palace gate.
Seated upon a royal throne beneath raised white parasols, he caused a drum to be beaten throughout the city and summoned all the soldiers, saying:
"O inhabitants of the Sivira kingdom, having seen these divine eyes of mine, from this day forward [you must practice] giving."
"Do not eat without having given," he said, teaching the Dhamma as he spoke these four verses:
"Who here, when asked, would not give wealth—even that which is excellent and dearly beloved to himself?
Behold now, all you Śivis gathered together, my divine eyes today!"
“Penetrating through walls and through rocks, having crossed over mountains,
I enjoy a vision extending for a hundred leagues all around.
And there is nothing beyond my reach in this life of mortals.”
“Having given away human vision, I have obtained superhuman vision.
‘Seeing this too, O people of Sivi, give gifts and enjoy them;
having given and enjoyed according to your power, being blameless, go to the heavenly realm.’”
In this context, *konīdha* means "who indeed here? *Api visiṭṭhaṃ* means "even though it is supreme.

*Cāgamattā* means that there is nothing else more excellent than the measure of generosity. *Idha jīvite* means "in this world of living beings. There is also the reading *idha jīvataṃ*, which means "of those living in this world.
*Amānusaṃ* means "supernatural"; the divine eye has been obtained by me, for this reason...
"It should be understood that there is nothing higher than generosity. Having seen this—that is, having seen this divine eye obtained by me—he taught the Dhamma with these four verses.
From then on, having gathered the great multitude every half-month on the Uposatha days of the fifteenth, he constantly taught the Dhamma with these verses. Having heard it, the great multitude...
Having performed meritorious deeds such as giving, he departed as if filling the world of the devas.
Having delivered this Dhamma teaching, the Teacher said, "Thus, monks, the ancient wise ones were not satisfied with external gifts;
they even plucked out their own eyes and gave them to those who came as supplicants. Having spoken thus, he proclaimed the Truths.
He made the identification: “At that time, the physician Sīvikā was Ānanda; Sakka was Anuruddha;
the rest of the assembly was the Buddha’s assembly; and King Sivi was none other than myself.
This is the third commentary on the Sivi Jātaka.
[500] 4. The Exposition of the Sirīmantajātakavaṇṇanā (83–103).
The question of Sirīmant, "One endowed with wisdom but devoid of prosperity," will be revealed in the Mahāumaṅga.
This concludes the fourth exposition, the Sirīmantajātakavaṇṇanā.
[501] 5. The Commentary on the Rohaṇamiga Jātaka:
“These herds are retreating. This was spoken by the Teacher while dwelling in the Veḷuvana monastery concerning the Venerable Ānanda’s sacrifice of his life.
That sacrifice of his life, however, is related in the Cūḷahaṃsa Jātaka of the Asīti Nipāta, in the subduing of Dhanapāla.
"It will become manifest. When the Venerable Ānanda had thus sacrificed his life for the sake of the Teacher, they raised a discussion in the Dhamma Hall:
"Friends, the Venerable Ānanda, having attained the analytical knowledges of one still in training, has sacrificed his life for the sake of the One Possessed of the Ten Powers.
The Teacher arrived and asked, "Monks, for what discussion are you gathered here now?"
Having asked, "Is it indeed she? and being told that it was, he said, "Monks, it is not only now;
in the past as well, he sacrificed his life for my sake," and he related a story of the past.
In the past, when Brahmadatta was reigning in Benares, Khemā was his chief queen. At that time—
The Bodhisatta was reborn in the region of the Himalayas in the womb of a deer; he was golden-hued and possessed of supreme beauty.
His younger brother, named Cittamiga, was also golden-hued, and his younger sister, named Sutanā, was likewise golden-hued.
The Great Being, however, became a king of deer named Rohaṇa. In the Himalayas, these two...
Having crossed over the mountain ranges, he took up residence near a lake named Rohaṇa in the third interval, accompanied by a retinue of eighty thousand deer.

There he supported his blind and aged parents. Now, a certain son of a hunter living in a village near Bārāṇasī entered the Himālaya, and having seen the Great Being, he returned to his own village; some time later—
As he was about to die, he informed his son: "Dear son, in our land of kamma, at a certain place, there dwells a golden-colored deer;
if the king should ask, you must tell him this.
Then one day, at dawn, Queen Khemā saw a dream. Such was that dream: a golden-colored...
The deer came, sat upon a golden throne, and, as if striking a golden bell, preached the Dhamma to the queen with a sweet voice;
she, having given her approval, listened to the Dhamma. Before the discourse on the Dhamma was finished, the deer rose and departed;
she woke up while still crying out, "Catch the deer! Catch him! Her attendants...
Hearing her voice, they laughed, saying, "In this house, the doors and windows are closed so tightly that there is not even room for a breeze;
Noble Lady, at such an hour, you are having a deer caught! At that moment, realizing it was a dream, she thought:
"If I say it was a dream, the King will pay it no heed; but if I say a longing has arisen, he will seek it out with great care."
“I shall listen to the Dhamma discourse of the golden-colored deer. Having made this her pretext for illness, she lay down.
The king came and asked, “My dear, what is making you unwell? “Your Majesty, there is nothing else;
however, a longing has arisen within me. “What do you wish for, Queen? “I desire to hear the Dhamma from the golden-colored Dhamma-deer.”
“O gods! [she cried]. “My lady, that which does not exist is what you have conceived a longing for; there is no such thing as a golden-colored deer.
Thinking, “If I do not obtain it, my death shall be right here,” she lay down on the king’s back.
The king sat in the midst of his assembly and, in the manner described in the Mora Jātaka, addressed his ministers: “If it exists, you shall obtain it.”
Having questioned a brahmin and heard that there were indeed deer called "Golden-Colored," he gathered the hunters together and asked, "By whom has such a deer been seen?

By whom has it been heard of? When the hunter’s son recounted what he had heard from his father according to the facts, [the king said], "Friend, when that deer is brought here, I shall pay him great honor."
Having said, "Go, bring her," he gave him travel expenses and sent him off.
He too replied, "If I am unable to bring her back, O King, I will bring her hide; if I am unable to bring that, I will bring even her hair;
do not worry. Having spoken thus, he went to his own home, gave travel expenses to his wife and children, and there—
Having gone there and seen the king of deer, he reflected, "In what place might I set a snare so that I may capture this king of deer?
While thus investigating, he saw a suitable spot at a watering-place.
He wound a strong leather thong and set a stick-snare at the spot where the Great Being would drink water.
On the following day, the Great Being, having grazed with eighty thousand deer, went to that place thinking, "I shall drink water at my usual watering-place.

As he was stepping down, he was caught in a snare. He thought, "If I cry out now that I am bound, my kinsmen will be terrified and flee without even drinking the water. Having reflected thus, he remained silent.
Leaning against the post and bringing it under his own control, he was like one drinking water.
Then, after eighty thousand deer had drunk the water and stood on the bank having crossed over, he pulled [the post] three times, thinking, "I shall cut the snare.
On the first pull, the hide was torn; on the second pull, the flesh was torn; and on the third pull, having severed the sinew—
The snare remained fastened to his bone. Unable to break free, he let out a cry of distress;
the herds of deer, terrified, fled in three separate groups.
The Citta-deer, not seeing the Great Being among the three groups, thought, "This danger that has arisen must have befallen my brother," and went to him.
He saw [the deer] bound. Then the Great Being, seeing him, said, "Brother, do not stay here; this place is dangerous," and as he urged him away, he spoke the first verse:
"These herds are fleeing, O Cittaka, terrified of death."
"Go, you too; do not be anxious; they will live together with you.
In this context, "these" refers to those who have passed beyond the range of sight and gone far away.
"Patiyanti" means they go back; the sense is that they flee. "Cittaka" is an address to him. "Together with you" means that you shall stand in their place.
“Become king; these shall live together with you.
Then, for both of them, there are three alternate verses:
“I am not going to Rohaṇa, my heart is being torn away;”
“I will not abandon them; here I shall give up my life.
For they will surely die, blind and without a guide.
Go yourself, do not despair; they will live together with you.”
“I am not going to Rohaṇa, my heart is being torn away;
I will not abandon that which is bound [to me], for here I shall lay down my life.
In this passage, he addresses the Great Being by name, saying “Rohaṇa. “Is being torn away” means it is being dragged, or it is being dragged along by grief.
"Surely they," he thought, "our parents, will certainly become leaderless when both of us have died here;
being left uncared for, they will wither away and die. Therefore, brother Cittaka, you go;
they will live together with you. This is the meaning. "I shall remain here" means: "I shall give up my life in this very place."
Having spoken thus, he stood leaning against the right side of the Bodhisatta, supporting him and comforting him.

Sutanā, the young doe, having fled and not seeing her two brothers among the deer, thought, "This danger must have arisen for my brothers," and she turned back and came to their side. As she was approaching—
Seeing this, the Great Being spoke the fifth verse:
“Go, O timid one, flee away! I am bound by iron shackles.
Go, do not desire me; they shall live together with you.”
In this context, "timid" refers to women, for they are afraid even of the slightest thing; thus he addresses her in this way.
"A snare" means a concealed trap. "A net" means that it is set by pounding an iron bar inside the water and binding a pole made of hard wood to it;
therefore he speaks thus. "Together with you" means those eighty thousand deer will live together with you.
After that, there are three verses in the same manner as before:
“I am not going to Rohaṇa, my heart is being torn away;
I will not abandon you, for here I shall lay down my life.”
“They will surely die, blind and without a leader;
you too should go, do not hesitate—they will live along with you.
“Rohaṇa, I am not going; my heart is being torn asunder.”
"I will not abandon him while he is bound; I shall give up my life right here.
In this context, "for surely they" refers once again to his mother and father.
Having likewise refused them, she stood by the left side of the Great Being, comforting him.
The hunter, seeing the deer fleeing and hearing their cries, thought, "The king of deer must have been caught," and so he fastened his belt tightly,
took up his deer-killing spear, and rushed forward with great speed. Seeing him approaching,
the Great Being spoke the ninth verse:
“Here comes that hunter, of cruel appearance and armed with his weapons;
he will slay us today, whether with an arrow or even with a spear.
In this context, “of cruel appearance” means one of a fierce nature. “Even with a spear” means he will strike and kill us even with a spear; therefore, flee while he has not yet arrived.

Even upon seeing him, the deer of the mind did not flee. But Sutanā, unable to maintain her composure and terrified by the fear of death, fled a short distance, thinking, "Where shall I flee, abandoning my two brothers?
Then, giving up her own life, she returned with Death upon her forehead and stood at her brother’s left side. To illustrate this matter, the Teacher spoke the tenth verse:
“Having fled for a moment, terrified and trembling with fear, that timid woman performed what was most difficult to do:
she turned back toward death. In this context, “turned back toward death” means she approached for the sake of dying.
The hunter also arrived and, seeing those three people standing together, conceived a mind of loving-kindness.
Thinking of them as brothers born from the same womb, he reflected: "The king of beasts is bound by a snare, yet these two men are bound by the fetters of moral shame and dread of blame;
who indeed could they be to him? Then, questioning him, he spoke this verse:
“What indeed are these deer to you, that they approach the bound while being free?
They do not wish to abandon you, even for the sake of their own lives.
Herein, *kiṃ nu temeti* means “what indeed are these [to you]?”; *upāsare* means “they approach.”
Then the Bodhisatta explained to him:
"They are my brothers, hunter, born of the same womb and the same mother;
they do not wish to abandon me, even for the sake of their own lives."
Having heard his words, he became even more gentle in heart. Knowing his state of mind, Cittamigarāja said, "Friend hunter, do not think of this king of deer as being merely 'a common deer.
For he is the king of eighty thousand deer, endowed with virtue and conduct, gentle toward all beings, and possessed of great wisdom. To the blind...
"You support your aged parents. If you were to kill such a righteous deer as this, by killing it you would be killing us five people—your parents, yourself, and me, your sister.
Therefore, by giving life to my brother, you are the giver of life to all five of us. Having said this, she spoke this verse:
“They will surely die, blind and without a guide;
grant life to the five, O hunter, and release your brother.
Having heard his discourse on the Dhamma, with a mind full of confidence, he said, “Do not fear, my lord,” and immediately spoke this verse:
“Thus I shall deliver this deer who supports his mother and father;
let his mother and father rejoice upon seeing the great deer released.
In this passage, *vo* is merely a particle. *Muttam* means having seen [the deer] released from its bonds.
Having spoken thus, he thought: "What will this fame bestowed by the king do for me?
If I were to kill this king of deer, either the earth would split open and swallow me, or a thunderbolt would fall upon my head;
therefore, I shall release him. He approached the Great Being, dropped his staff, and cut the leather thong.
Having embraced the king of elephants and laid him down at the water’s edge, he gently untied the bonds with a gentle heart;
then, joining sinew to sinew, flesh to flesh, and hide to hide, he washed away the blood with water and rubbed him repeatedly with a mind of loving-kindness.
By the very power of his loving-kindness and by the power of the Great Being’s perfections, [the elephant was restored].

All the sinews, flesh, and skin were joined together; his foot became covered with skin and covered with hair, so that it was not even discernible where it had been bound. The Great Being stood there having attained a state of ease.
Seeing this, the deer Cittamiga, filled with joy, spoke this verse as an expression of appreciation to the hunter:
“Thus, hunter, may you rejoice together with all your kinsmen, just as I rejoice today upon seeing the great deer released.
Then the Great Being thought: “Did this hunter seize me out of his own desire, or rather [on behalf of someone else]?”
Thinking, "By command," he asked about the reason for his capture. The hunter's son said, "Master, I have no business with you;
however, the King’s chief queen named Khemā wishes to hear your discourse on the Dhamma.
For that purpose, by the King’s command, you were captured by me. "Friend, if that is so, it would be a most difficult task indeed for one who releases me."
“Do this: come, take me and show me to the king; I shall preach the Dhamma to the queen.
“Master, kings are indeed harsh. Who knows what might happen? I have no business with the king, as my livelihood has been provided by him.
Go as you please. Again the Great Being thought: “By releasing me, this man has performed a most difficult deed for the sake of acquiring glory.”
Thinking, "I shall devise a means for this," he said, "My good man, first rub my back with your hand.
He rubbed it, and his hand became covered with hair the color of gold. "Master, what shall I do with this hair?
"My good man, take these and show them to the king and the queen, saying: 'These belong to that golden-colored deer.'"
“Having said, ‘It is hairs,’ stand in my place and teach the Dhamma to the queen with these verses; upon hearing them, her craving will surely subside.

Having had him learn the ten verses on the practice of Dhamma, beginning with “Practice Dhamma, O Great King,” and having given him the five precepts and exhorted him to heedfulness, he sent him forth. The son of the hunter [approached] the Great Being...
Having established him in the position of teacher, he circumambulated him three times, paid homage at four places, took his hair in a lotus leaf, and departed.
Those three men also followed him a short distance, and taking food and water in their mouths, they went into the presence of his parents. His parents said, "Dear Rohaṇa, it seems you..."
Asking, "How were you released while bound by the snare? they spoke this verse:
"How did your liberation come about when your life was at stake?
How, my son, did you free yourself from the hunter's trap?"
In this context, "I have been brought near" means: when you were brought near to death while still alive, how was there any escape?
Having heard that, the Bodhisatta spoke three verses:
"Speaking words pleasant to the ear, touching the heart and dear to the heart;"
“With well-spoken words, Cittaka released me.
Speaking words pleasant to the ear, touching the heart and dear to the heart—
with well-spoken words, Sutanā released me.”
“Having heard words pleasant to the ear, heart-pleasing and heart-attracting;
having heard these well-spoken words, the hunter released me.

Therein, *bhaṇanti* means *bhaṇanto*. *Hadayaṅgamam* means heart-reaching (*hadayaṅgamaṃ*). In the second verse, *bhaṇanti* means *bhaṇamānā*. *Sutvā* means he, having heard the speech of both of them.
Then his parents, expressing their appreciation,
said: "May the hunter, together with his wife, be thus delighted,
just as we are joyful today, having seen Rohaṇa come."
The hunter, having departed from the forest and gone to the royal palace, paid homage to the king and stood to one side. Seeing him, the king spoke this verse:
“Did you not say, O hunter, ‘I have brought deer-skins’?
Then for what reason indeed have you not brought the deer-skins?”
In this context, "deer-skins" means either the deer itself or its skin. "I will bring" means "I shall bring. This is what is meant:
"O hunter, did you not say, 'If I am unable to bring the deer, I will bring the skin;
if I am unable to do that, I will bring the hair'? For what reason, then, have you brought neither the deer nor the deer-skin?"
Having heard that, the hunter spoke this verse:
“That deer came within reach of my hand and my snare;
he bit that king of deer, yet they released him and approached him.”
“Then a sense of urgency arose within me, extraordinary and hair-raising:
‘If I were to kill this deer, I would offer its life today.
In that regard, O Great King, that deer came into my reach, into the range of my hand, and into the snare of the trap I had set.
He arrived and was caught in that snare. When he was freed, he approached;
and while he was bound, two other deer who were free and unbound stood near him, relying on him and comforting him. "A wonder" (*abbhuta*) means something that had not happened before.
"And this thought occurred to me": then, being deeply moved, it occurred to me, "If I were to kill this deer, this very day, right here..."
"In this place I shall give up my life.
Having heard that, the king said:
"What kind of deer are yours, hunter? What kind of deer are righteous?"
“What is their appearance like? What is their conduct? Why do you praise them so highly?
Thus the king asked again and again out of wonder. Having heard this, the hunter spoke this verse:
“With white horns and pure tails, resembling skins of gold;”
“Their feet are red; their eyes are anointed and beautiful.
In this context, “with white horns” means having horns resembling strings of silver. “With pure hair” means endowed with pure hair like that of a yak-tail fly-whisk (*cāmara*).
“Red” means having red nails resembling coral. “Feet” refers to the parts ending in the hooves. “Anointed eyes” means—
They were endowed with eyes of pure fivefold clarity, as if anointed.
Thus, even as he spoke, the Great Being placed the golden-colored hairs upon the king’s hand and, describing the physical beauty of those deer, he uttered this verse:
“Such are these deer, O King; such are these righteous deer.”
"O King, he is one who supports his mother and father; he cannot be brought to you as a gift.
In this context, "one who supports his mother and father" means he nourishes his aged and blind parents; such is their righteous conduct.
"He cannot be brought to you as a gift" means that it is not possible for anyone to bring that king of deer to you as a present.
The meaning is: “*Abhihārayin*”—this is also a reading; its meaning is: “I did not bring that for the sake of a gift (*paṇṇākāra*), nor did I offer it.
Thus, having described the virtues of the Great Being, the deer-king, and the young doe, he said: “Great King, that king of deer commanded me:
‘Show your own fur, stand in my place, and [recite] the ten verses on the practice of the duties of a king (*rājadhamma*).’”
“Having been instructed and made to learn, ‘You should preach the Dhamma to the queen,’ he was thus commanded,” he said.
Upon hearing this, the king had him bathed, dressed him in new garments, and seated him upon a couch inlaid with the seven precious gems;
then, sitting on a low seat to one side together with the queen, he raised his joined palms and made a request. As he taught the Dhamma, he said:
“Practice the Dhamma, O Great King, toward your mother and father, O Kshatriya;
having practiced the Dhamma here in this world, O King, you shall go to heaven.
Practice the Dhamma, O Great King, toward your sons and wives, O Kshatriya.”
“Having practiced the Dhamma here, O King, you will go to heaven.
“Practice the Dhamma, Great King, toward friends and companions, O Khattiya;
having practiced the Dhamma here, O King, you will go to heaven.”
“Practice the Dhamma, O Great King, among your mounts and your forces;
having practiced the Dhamma here, O King, you will go to heaven.
Practice the Dhamma, O Great King, among the villages and the market towns.”
"Having practiced the Dhamma here, O King, you will go to heaven.
Practice the Dhamma, Great King, throughout the kingdoms and the provinces;
having practiced the Dhamma here, O King, you will go to heaven."
“Practice the Dhamma, O Great King, toward recluses and brahmins;
having practiced the Dhamma here, O King, you will go to heaven.
Practice the Dhamma, O Great King, toward beasts and birds, O Kshatriya.”
"Having practiced the Dhamma here, O King, you will go to heaven.
Practice the Dhamma, Great King; the Dhamma, when practiced, brings happiness.
Having practiced the Dhamma here, O King, you will go to heaven."
“Practice the Dhamma, O Great King; together with Indra and the gods, including Brahmā, they have reached heaven by means of well-practiced conduct. Do not be negligent in the Dhamma, O King.
Thus, the son of the hunter, as if causing the celestial Ganges to descend according to the method taught by the Great Being, acted with the grace of a Buddha.
He taught the Dhamma. The great multitude raised thousands of shouts of "Sādhu! Upon hearing the discourse on the Dhamma, the queen’s longing subsided.
The king, being delighted, gratified the hunter’s son with great honor and spoke these three verses:
“I give you a hundred gold coins, O hunter, and a large jeweled earring;”
“A four-sided couch with a headrest, resembling an *umā* flower;
two wives of equal beauty, and a hundred bulls—by these I shall rule the kingdom righteously. You have been of great service to me, hunter.”
“[Live by] farming, trade, lending at interest, and the profession of a hunter;
support your wife with these, and do not commit evil again.
In that context, *thūla* means something of great value, such as a jewel, an earring, or an ornament; I give them to you. *Catussada* means having four elevations.

The meaning is "having four golden tips. "Resembling the color of an umā flower" means it is endowed with a luster resembling an umā flower because of its blue covering, or else it is made of dark-colored heartwood.
"Of equal status" means they are similar to one another in both form and wealth. "A hundred cows and a bull" means a hundred cows with a bull as the leader.
"I give them to you. You shall cause the ten kingly duties to be practiced; I shall rule the kingdom solely by Dhamma, without violating those duties.
'You have been very helpful to me'—because you stood in the place of the golden-hued king of deer and taught the Dhamma, you have been of great service to me.
Just according to the method spoken by the king of deer, I have established you in the five precepts. 'Agriculture and trade... O friend..."
"Hunter, I too, having not seen the king of beasts but having merely heard his word, have established myself in the five precepts.

From now on, you too should be virtuous. By whatever means of livelihood—be it farming, trade, lending money, or gleaning—you should support your wife and children with that very right livelihood; do not commit evil again."
Having heard the king’s words, he said, "I have no need for the life of a householder; grant me permission to go forth, O King.
Having obtained this permission and given the wealth bestowed by the king to his wife and children, he entered the Himalayas.
There, having gone forth as an ascetic and attained the eight meditative absorptions (*samāpatti*), he became destined for the Brahma-world. The king, too, followed the Great Being’s instruction...
Having established himself, he filled the city of heaven, and his instruction prevailed for a thousand years.
Having delivered this Dhamma teaching, the Teacher said, "Thus, monks, even in the past Ānanda sacrificed his life for my sake," and he identified the Jātaka:
"At that time the hunter was Channa, and the king was Sāriputta."
"The goddess Khemā was the bhikkhunī; my mother and father were the royal families; Sutanā was Uppalavaṇṇā; Cittamiga was Ānanda;
the eighty thousand deer were the Śākya clan; and as for Rohaṇa, the king of deer, he was none other than myself.
This is the fifth, the Commentary on the Rohaṇa Deer Jātaka.
[502] 6. The Explanation of the Cūḷahaṃsa Jātaka:
"These swans are departing. This was related by the Teacher while dwelling in the Veḷuvana Grove, concerning the Venerable Ānanda’s sacrifice of his own life.
For at that time, too, as the monks were discussing the virtues of the Elder in the Dhamma Hall—
The Teacher arrived and asked, "Monks, about what topic are you gathered here now?
When they replied, "About this very one," he said, "Monks, it is not only now; in the past as well, Ānanda sacrificed his life for my sake. Having said this, he related a story of the past.
In the past, in Bārāṇasī, a king named Bahuputtaka reigned. His chief queen was named Khemā.
Then the Great Being, having been reborn in the womb of a golden swan, dwelt on Mount Cittakūṭa surrounded by ninety thousand swans.
At that time as well, the queen, having seen a dream in the same manner previously described, informed the king of her longing to hear the Dhamma teaching of a golden-colored swan.
The king, having questioned his ministers, learned that "golden-colored swans indeed dwell on Mount Cittakūṭa."

Having heard this, he had a lake named Khema constructed, had various kinds of grain for sowing planted there, and caused the proclamation of safety to be made daily at its four corners. He then appointed a hunter to capture the swans.
The manner of his appointment and how he scrutinized the birds there regarding the golden swans—
The report made to the king upon the bird's arrival, the manner in which the stone trap was set, the manner in which the Great Being was caught in the snare,
and how Sumukha, the commander of the swan-host, turned back after failing to see him among the three flocks of swans—
all this will be revealed in the Mahāhaṃsa Jātaka. Here too, the Great Being, having been caught in the rod-snare, while still hanging from the snare-rod...
Stretching out his neck and watching the path taken by the swans, he saw Sumukha approaching.
Thinking, "I shall test him when he arrives," he recited three verses as the other arrived:
"These Vakkaṅga swans are flying away, driven by fear; ... [the rest of the verses follow] ..."
“O Harīṭaka, golden-hued one, go forth at will, O Sumukha!
Having abandoned me—who am alone and fallen under the power of the snare—my kinsmen depart without looking back; why do you remain behind all alone?”
“Of those that fly, the falcon is the best; there is no companionship for one who is bound.
Do not let this [opportunity] slip away while you are free from distress; O Sumukha, depart as you desire.
Therein, *bhayameritā* means impelled by fear, terrified by fear, or shaken by fear. *Harittaca hemavaṇṇā* refers to both [the falcon and the parrot].
With these words he addresses her alone: "O golden-skinned one, O golden-hued one, O fair-faced one, you have certainly departed;
what is the use of your coming here? "Leaving me behind" means she has flown away after abandoning him.
"Without looking back" means those kinsmen of mine go on without even glancing at me. "Let her fall" means let her fly up. "May she not be distressed" means having gone from here...
"Do not let your energy fail in attaining the state free from suffering.
Then Sumukha, sitting upon the surface of the mud, spoke this verse:
"O Dhatarattha, do not abandon me because I am overcome by suffering."
“Whether life or death be mine, it shall be together with you.
Therein, O Great King, by the mere words “you are overcome by the suffering of death,” I do not abandon you.
When Sumukha had thus uttered his lion’s roar, Dhatarattha spoke this verse:
“This is noble and excellent, O Sumukha, that you speak thus;
and while reflecting upon it, I have cast off this [body] as it fell.
In this context, “this is noble” means that what you say—“I shall not abandon you”—is [the mark] of one perfected in conduct.

The noble and excellent word of the Arahant. When I said, "Let it fall," it was not because I wished to release it, but rather, testing him, I uttered those words; the meaning is that I told him, "Go.
Even as they were thus conversing, the son of the hunter arrived with speed, taking up his staff. [He addressed] Sumukha and Dhataraṭṭha.
Having comforted him and approached him face-to-face, he showed him honor and spoke of the virtues of the swan-king.
At that very moment, the hunter’s heart became gentle. Knowing that his heart had become gentle, he went back again and stood there comforting the swan-king himself.
Then the hunter, having approached the swan-king, spoke the sixth verse:
“The sky-roaming bird goes from footless place to footless place;
you did not perceive the snare from afar, O most excellent of swans.

In this regard, “from footless place to footless place,” Great King, means that a sky-roaming bird such as yourself travels through the footless sky by making footprints there. “You did not perceive” means: he asks why you, being such a one, did not perceive—that is, did not know—this snare even from a distance.
The Great Being said:
"When ruin comes upon a person at the end of his life, then,
even though encountering a net and a snare, he does not wake up."

In this context, "when ruin" means, O son of a hunter, when ruin—non-prosperity and destruction—is reached, then the person, when the end of life has arrived, does not know even though he has fallen into the net and the snare; such is the meaning.
The hunter, having welcomed the words of the king of the swans, spoke three verses while conversing with Sumukha:
"These Vakkaṅga swans are flying away, driven by fear."
“O green one, golden-hued, you alone are being left behind.
Having eaten and drunk here, these birds depart, Vakkaṅgas who have no regard for you;
you alone continue to wait upon them.”
“Why indeed do you, a brahmin, remain here, while being free, you wait upon one who is bound?
The birds are flying away, leaving him; why are you the only one left behind?
In this context, “you yourself” means “you alone are left behind,” thus he asks. “Upāsasi” means “you wait upon” (payirupāsasi).
Sumukha said:
"That brahmin is my friend, the king, and he is a companion as dear to me as my own life;
I shall not abandon him until the end of time."
"In this matter, O son of a hunter, as long as time lasts, until the very end of my life, I shall never abandon him.
Hearing this, the hunter’s heart became filled with faith, and he thought:
"If I should offend these who are so perfected in virtue, even the earth would open up to swallow me. What use have I for the wealth obtained from the king? I shall release him."
Thinking, "It shall not be so," he spoke this verse:
"Since you wish to sacrifice your life for the sake of your friend, I release that companion of yours; let him be your follower as king."
In that context: "And you" means "you who are named"; "he" means "I. "A follower of yours" means: "May this king of swans come under your control; may he dwell in one place together with you.

Having spoken thus, he caused Dhataraṭṭha to descend from the staff-snare, led him to the shore of the lake, released the snare, and with a gentle heart, washed away the blood and restored his tendons and other parts. Because of his gentle-heartedness toward the Great Being...
By the power of the perfections (*pāramitā*), his foot immediately became whole again, and not even a trace of where it had been bound remained visible.
Sumukha, looking at the Bodhisatta with a joyful heart, spoke this verse of appreciation:
“Thus, hunter, may you rejoice together with all your kinsmen!”
"Just as I rejoice today, O lord of birds, having seen you set free.
Having heard this, the hunter said, "Go, sir.
Then the Great Being asked him, "But why, my friend, did you bind me for your own sake, or was it by the command of another? When he [explained] that reason...
When this was announced, he reflected: "What would be better for me—to go from here to Cittakūṭa, or to the city?
While considering this, he thought: "If I go to the city, the hunter’s son will obtain wealth;
the queen’s longing will be appeased; Sumukha’s friendship will become manifest; likewise, my power of knowledge, safety, and the gift of fearlessness [will be demonstrated]."
Having made the resolution, "I shall obtain [my goal] by doing this;
therefore, it is better to go to the city itself," he said, "Hunter, take us on your carrying-pole and lead us to the presence of the king. If the king wishes to release us, he will release us.
"O Master, kings are indeed cruel; you two go! [The other replied,] "We consider even such a hunter as gentle."
"Let us do so; it is our duty to please the king. 'Very well,' they said. He did accordingly.

Upon seeing the swans, the king was filled with joy; he had both swans sit upon a golden throne, fed them honeyed parched grain, gave them sweet water to drink, and, raising his hands in reverent salutation, requested a discourse on the Dhamma. The king of the swans [spoke] to him...
Knowing his desire to hear, he first extended a greeting. In this regard, these are the verses of exchange between the swan and the king:
"Is it well with you, sir? Is it free from ailment with you?"
“I hope this kingdom is prosperous, and that you govern it according to the Dhamma.
“It is well with me, O swan, and likewise, O swan, I am free from illness;
moreover, this kingdom is prosperous as I govern it according to the Dhamma.”
“Is there no fault found among your ministers?
Are your enemies far away from you, like a shadow to the south?
“There is indeed no fault found among my ministers.”
“Moreover, my enemies are far away, like a shadow to the south.
I hope your wife is your equal— obedient, sweet-spoken,
endowed with children, beauty, and fame, and following your will and authority?”
“Moreover, my wife is like myself—obedient and sweet-spoken;
she is endowed with the beauty and fame of a son, and follows my will and authority.
O Increaser of the Kingdom, I hope you have many sons, well-born?”
Endowed with the swiftness of wisdom, they converse from here and there:
"Dhataraṭṭha, I have heard that I have one hundred and one sons;
tell them their duty, for they do not disregard your word."
In this context, "healthy" (*kusala*) means freedom from illness; the other term is a synonym for that very state. "Prosperous" (*phīta*):
he asks, "Is this kingdom of yours prosperous, well-supplied with food, and do you govern it according to the Dhamma? "Fault" (*dosa*) means an offense.
"Does your shadow not grow toward the south?": just as a shadow facing the southern direction does not lengthen, so he asks, "I hope your enemies do not increase."
She speaks. "Of similar [status]" means equal in terms of birth, lineage, family, and station; for such a woman is not an adulteress. "Obedient" means one who accepts his words.
"Endowed with sons, beauty, and fame" means possessed of children, physical form, and reputation.
"By the speed of wisdom" means by the impetus of wisdom; having quickened her wisdom, she is capable of discerning various duties—thus he asks.
"Wherever they are engaged, there they greet one another; they do not conflict," he asks.
"I have heard" means "I have become renowned. He says: "For the world calls me 'the King with Many Sons';
thus, by depending on me, they have become renowned and well-known, and so they are said to be 'heard of by me'. "Tell them their duty."
"Tell my sons what they must do, saying, 'Do this and that'; they do not disobey your word, so give them this instruction"—it was with this intention that he spoke thus.
Having heard that, the Great Being uttered five verses while giving him counsel:
“Even if one has been reborn with refinement in birth or conduct,
yet later fails to apply oneself to practice, one sinks into misfortune and distress.
For that person of diminished wisdom, a great gap arises.”
Just as one might perceive gross forms at night,
he does not find the intelligence that knows how to apply itself to the essential amidst the unessential;
like a deer in a mountain pass, he perishes right in the middle.
“Even if one is of low birth, if that person is industrious and resolute,
endowed with good conduct and virtue, he shines like a fire on the sacrificial altar.
Having made this my simile, teach your sons the sciences.”
"May the wise man grow [in virtue], like seed in a field by means of rain.
In this context, "by means of discipline" (vinayena) refers to conduct. As for the phrase "he exerts effort later":

if one does not apply effort or diligence toward the trainings that ought to be practiced during youth, but instead does so later in old age, such a person will later encounter a corresponding kind of suffering.
Or, when calamities arise, he sinks down; he is unable to extricate himself. Regarding the phrase "of one whose wisdom has been carried away" (*saṃhīrapaññassa*):
because he has not trained himself, his wisdom must be carried here and there; he is of a constantly wavering intellect. "He discloses" means he reveals the flaws in his wealth and so forth;
the meaning is "decline. "Blind by night" (*rattandho*) means blind at night. This is what is meant: "Just as one who is blind by night..."
“One who is night-blind sees only gross forms by means of the moonlight and such at night, but is unable to see subtle ones;
likewise, one who is untrained and of weak wisdom, when some fear arises, is unable to perceive subtle matters and perceives only coarse ones.
Therefore, it is right that you should have your sons trained while they are still young.”
He expounds upon the worldly doctrines and the Vedic traditions which lead to no transcendence. Thinking, "This doctrine is associated with mindfulness;
it knows the application of mindfulness," he does not find wisdom at all—even though he has studied much, he does not obtain discernment.
"In a mountain pass" means that just as a sarabha, when coming to its own dwelling place, [encounters] even an uneven path along the way...
Just as one who, thinking it level, comes with speed through a mountain pass and falls into a precipice of hell,
perishing midway and failing to reach his destination, so too does one who learns this essence-less Lokāyata doctrine with the perception that it is essential meet with great ruin.
Therefore, you should train your sons by engaging them in tasks that are grounded in purpose and bring about prosperity.
"O Great King, even one of low birth, if endowed with qualities such as diligence, shines like a mass of fire at night.

'This is mine'—having made this statement, and having used the simile of the night-blindness and the mass of fire, you should cause your sons to study the sciences and engage them in the trainings that ought to be learned. For when engaged in this way, just as in a fertile field..."
"Just as a seed sprouts when there is good rain, so too does the wise man flourish; he increases in both fame and wealth.
Thus the Great Being taught the Dhamma to the king throughout the entire night, and the queen's longing was pacified.
At the very moment of dawn, the Great Being established the king in the five precepts, exhorted him with diligence, and [departed] together with...
Emerging through the northern lion-window with Sumukha, he went back to Cittakūṭa itself.
Having delivered this Dhamma teaching, the Teacher said, "Thus, monks, even in the past this man sacrificed his life for my sake," and he identified the Jātaka:
"At that time, Channa was the hunter; the King was Sāriputta."
“The goddess was the bhikkhunī Khemā; the flock of swans was the Śākya clan; Sumukha was Ānanda; and as for the king of the swans, it was indeed I myself.
This concludes the sixth narrative, the Commentary on the Cūḷahaṃsa Jātaka.
[503] 7. The Commentary on the Sattigumba Jātaka.
"O Great King, the deer-catcher," this was spoken by the Teacher while dwelling in the Deer Park at Maddakucchi, concerning Devadatta.
For when a stone had been hurled by Devadatta, a splinter pierced the Blessed One's foot, and intense pain arose.
Many monks gathered to see the Tathāgata. Then the Blessed One addressed the assembly:
Seeing them gathered together, he said, "Monks, this lodging is too cramped; the assembly will be large.
Take me on a palanquin to Maddakucchi. The monks did so. Jīvaka made the Tathāgata’s foot comfortable.
While seated in the presence of the Teacher, the monks initiated a conversation: "Friend,..."
“Devadatta himself is wicked, and his retinue is also wicked; thus he dwells as one who is wicked with a wicked following.
When the Teacher asked, “Monks, what are you discussing? and they replied, “This very thing,” he said, “Monks, it is not only now;
in the past as well, Devadatta was wicked with a wicked following,” and he related a story of the past.
In the past, in the city of Uttarapañcāla, a king named Pañcāla reigned.
In a forest region on a certain mountain with plateaus, in a *simbalī* grove, the Great Being was reborn as the son of a golden king; there were two brothers.
On the windward side of that mountain, there was a village of thieves, the dwelling place of five hundred bandits.
In the lower wind region was a hermitage where five hundred seers resided.
At the time when those young birds were departing from their nest, a whirlwind arose. Struck by it, one young bird fell among the weapons of the robbers in the village of thieves;
because he had fallen there, they gave him the name "Sattigumba" (The Sword-Clump). Another [fell] on the sandy surface of the hermitage.
He fell into the midst of flowers; because he had fallen there, they gave him the name "Pupphaka" (Flower).
Sattigumba grew up among thieves, while Pupphaka grew up among seers.
Then one day, the king, adorned with all his ornaments, mounted his excellent chariot and set out with a great retinue.
Having gone from the city to a delightful grove of *upagumba* trees, which was in full bloom and fruit, not far away, he said, "Whosever side the deer flees to, his shall be the neck.
Then, dismounting from his chariot and having it covered over, he took up his bow and stood at the entrance provided for him.
While the men beat upon the forest thickets to drive the deer out, [the king remained there].
A certain deer arose and, looking toward the path of departure, saw that the place where the king stood was secluded;
he charged straight toward it and fled. The ministers asked, "In whose direction did the deer flee?
and having learned that it was in the direction of the king, they engaged in a jest with him. Due to his conceit (*asmimāna*), the king [laughed] at their jest.
Unable to endure this, thinking, "I shall capture that deer now," he mounted his chariot, commanded his charioteer, "Drive swiftly!
and set out along the path taken by the deer. As the chariot sped along, the retinue was unable to follow.
Having traveled with only his charioteer until midday and failing to see the deer, the king turned back toward that village of bandits.
Seeing a delightful cave nearby, he alighted from his chariot, bathed, drank, and climbed back out.
Then his charioteer, having taken down the chariot’s upper covering, prepared a bed in the shade of a tree, and the king lay down there.
The charioteer sat beside him, massaging his feet. From time to time, the king would fall asleep and wake again.
The bandits living in Coragāma also entered the forest for the purpose of guarding the king.
Only two remained behind in the village of Coragāma: Sattigumba and a man named Patikolambo, who was the cook.
At that moment, Sattigumba left the village, and seeing the king, thought, "I shall kill him while he is still asleep and take his ornaments."
Having reflected thus, he went into the presence of Paṭikolamba and reported the matter to him.
To clarify this point, the Teacher spoke these five verses:
“The great king, the deer-hunter, the bull among charioteers of the Pañcālas;”
Departed with his army, he came alone into the forest.
There in the wilderness, he saw a hut built by hunters;
coming out from that hut, a bird uttered harsh cries.
“A man with a well-equipped chariot, young, with earrings properly set, shines with his crimson turban;
he glows like the sun in the day.
At the high noon, the king slept together with his charioteer.”
"Let us take all his hand ornaments by force!
Even now at night, the king is sleeping in secret along with his charioteer;
let us take the cloth, the jewel, and the earrings, and having killed him, let us cover him over with branches!"
In this context, "deer-hunter" (*migaluddo*) is so called because he seeks deer like a hunter. "Solitary" (*ogaṇo*) means having been separated from or deprived of a group.
"He built a hut for the doers" means that the king saw a village there in the forest built for the dwelling of thieves.
"From him" means from that thieves' hut. "He speaks harshly" means together with a counter-reproach.
He speaks harsh words. "Possessed of mounts" means possessed of horse-mounts. "Red turbaned" means endowed with a red turban-band.
"At this very moment" (*sampati*) means now; the meaning is: at such a time as this, namely, at the time of midday.
"By force" (*sāhasā*) means he says, "I shall seize him by using force, by employing violence. "Even at night, in secret now" (*nisīthe pi rahodāni*).

"At night as well as now, it is in secret. He says this to mean that just as at "night"—that is, at the time of midnight—people lie down exhausted and it is called "secret," so too it is even now at the time of midday.
"Having killed" means having slain the king, taken his clothes and ornaments, and then, having seized him by the feet and dragged him away, concealed him in a secluded spot with branches.
Thus, with great speed, he would emerge once and go back to the presence of the pillar once. Having heard his words, [the man] emerged and, looking about, recognized the king’s identity;
terrified, he spoke this verse: “Why do you speak like one who is mad, O cluster of spears?
For kings are difficult to approach, like a blazing fire.”
Then the cock addressed him with a verse:
“Now you, O crow, caw loudly like one intoxicated;
why indeed do you feel such disgust for my mother while she is naked?”

In that context, *atha tvam* means "surely you. *Matta* means having become intoxicated by the leftover liquor obtained from the thieves, you previously roared those great roars. *Mātari* refers to the wife of the chief thief;
it is said that at that time she was wandering about dressed only in a garment made of broken tree branches. *Vijigucchase* means: "How can you feel disgust toward my mother while she is naked?"
“You now feel disgust for the work of a thief and do not wish to do it.
When the king woke up and heard the words of the one speaking with him in human speech, he thought, “This place is dangerous,” and as he was rousing his charioteer, he spoke this verse:
“Arise, my friend, quickly; harness the chariot, charioteer!”
“The bird does not please me; let us go to another hermitage.
He too, rising quickly and yoking the chariot, spoke this verse:
“The chariot is yoked, O Great King, and the powerful draft-animals are harnessed.”
"Wait, Great King; let us go to another hermitage.
In this context, "with powerful draft-animals" means having a great force of draught-animal transport; the sense is that he was endowed with horses of great strength. "Wait" means mount.
As soon as he had mounted, the steeds leaped forward with the speed of the wind. Seeing the chariot moving along, Sattigumba was moved by a sense of spiritual urgency and spoke two verses:
“Where indeed have they all gone, those who were my attendants?
Only this Pañcāla goes, released from their sight.
Take up your bows, your spears, and your javelins!”
"He goes away, the Pañcāla; do not let him escape alive. Therein, "Who indeed?
means "Where indeed are these? "In this" means in this hermitage. "Attendants" refers to the thieves.
"By way of non-seeing" means that he goes having been released by way of the non-seeing of these thieves; that is, having been released from their hands, he has gone out of their sight.
"Is going" is also the meaning. "Bows" means *kodaṇḍakas*. "While you are living, do not release [him]!
Run with weapons in hand and seize him!
Thus he cried out, and even as he was running back and forth, the king reached the hermitage of the seers. At that moment—
The seers had gone out for the sake of fruits and fruitless trees. A single bird, a *pupphaka-suva*, remained in the hermitage.
Seeing the king, it went out to meet him and offered him hospitality. To illustrate this matter, the Teacher spoke these four verses:
“Then another, a bird with a red beak, greeted him joyfully;”
"Welcome to you, Great King; indeed, you have come from afar.
You have arrived as a lord; declare whatever is here.
"Tinduka fruits, piyāla fruits, madhūka flowers, and kāsumāri berries;"
"O King, eat the finest of these various small fruits.
This cool drinking water too has been brought from the heart of the mountain;
drink from it, Great King, if you so desire."
“Those attendants of mine who have gone to the forest for alms—arise yourselves and take [the food];
I have no hands with which to give.
Therein, *paṭinandittha* means she was pleased the very moment she saw the king. *Lohitatuṇḍako* means one with a red beak, having attained the pinnacle of beauty.
"Madhuka" refers to madhuka fruits. "Kāsumāriya" refers to fruits of that name, or alternatively, *kāra* fruits.
"Drink from there" means: having taken water from that drinking shed, drink the water. "Those who are attendants here, O Great King," refers to those seers wandering in this hermitage;
they have gone into the forest for alms-gathering (*uñcha*). "Take [them]" refers to the various fruits.
"Take it. "Dātabbe" means "to give.
Having gained confidence through the king’s hospitable reception, he spoke these two verses:
"Truly auspicious is this bird, a twice-born one most righteous in his nature;..."
But that other bird, a crow, cried out harsh words:
"Kill him! Bind him! Do not let him go alive!
While he was thus lamenting, I reached safety at the hermitage.
In this context, "the other" refers to the thief who was sleeping in the robber’s hut. "Thus indeed" means: while he was thus lamenting, I reached this hermitage in safety.
Having heard the King's words, Pupphaka recited two verses:
"We are brothers, O Great King, born of the same womb from one mother; ... [text truncated] ..."
“Both of us were raised on a single tree, yet we have gone to different fields:
he is among the sword-wielding thieves here, while I am among the seers.
He belongs to the wicked, I to the virtuous; by that very principle, we are not alike.”
"In that regard, O Great King, 'we two brothers' means that both he and I were brothers.
'Of thieves' means that he was raised in the presence of thieves, whereas I was in the presence of seers.

'He among the wicked, I among the virtuous' means that he approached the company of the unrighteous and immoral, while I approached the company of the righteous and virtuous. By that principle, O Great King, we are distinguished."
"The thieves disciplined Sattigumba according to the thief's way, by means of the thief's practice; the seers disciplined me according to the seer's way, by means of the seer's virtue and conduct.
Therefore, he could not exist without that thief's way, and I too cannot exist without the seer's way.
Now, explaining that Dhamma in detail, he spoke these two verses:
“In that [other world], there is killing and binding, trickery and deceptions, morsels of food, and acts of violence; these he trains in there.
But here, there is truth and Dhamma, non-violence, self-restraint, and self-control.”
“I was reared on your lap, O Bearer of the Burden, by those who provided seats and water.
In this context, *nikati* means deception through pretense; *vañcanāni* refers specifically to straightforward deceptions. *Ālopā* refers to daytime raids upon villages;
*sāhasākārā* refers to acts of violence committed after entering a house and threatening with death.
*Sacca* means true nature (*sabhāva*). *Dhamma* means the dharma of good conduct. *Ahiṃsā* means the preliminary stage of loving-kindness (*mettā*). *Saṃyama* means restraint through virtue (*sīla*).
*Dama* means the taming of the sense faculties. *Āsanūdakadāyīnaṃ* refers to those whose habit is to give seats and water to visitors.
*Bhāradhā* is an address to the king.
Now, teaching the Dhamma to the king, he spoke these verses:
“Whatever person one associates with, O King— whether they be virtuous or not,
whether they possess moral conduct or lack it— one comes under their very influence.”
“Whatever kind of friend one makes, and whatever kind of person one serves, one becomes just like them; for such is the nature of living together.
By serving one who serves, by touching one who touches another, [one is affected].”
As one who has smeared himself with lac sticks to a bundle of grass, so does one who is defiled smear that which is undefiled.
Out of fear of such defilement, the wise person should never have evil friends.
Just as a man might carry a putrid fish on the tip of a blade of kusa grass...
Even kusa grass emits a foul odor; such is the consequence of associating with fools.
But when a man wraps tagara with palāsa leaves, even the leaves emit a sweet fragrance;
such is the consequence of associating with the wise.
“Therefore, just like one who knows the ripening of his own alms-bowl,
the wise person should not associate with the wicked, but should associate with the virtuous;
for the wicked lead one to hell, while the virtuous cause one to reach a happy destination.”
In this context, whether it be one who exists or does not exist, a true person (*sappurisa*) or an untrue person (*asappurisa*):
"one who serves while serving" means the teacher being served by the pupil;
"touched" means the teacher touched by the pupil, or the pupil touching another, namely the teacher; "untainted" refers to that pupil.
Just as a well-sharpened arrow, though untouched by the poison of a poisonous creature, taints the rest of the arrow-shaft, so too is it with "association with fools.
For one who associates with fools becomes like a blade of kusa grass used to apply a putrid fish;

even if they do not commit evil deeds themselves, they receive disrepute and lack of fame. As for "association with the wise," a person who associates with the wise is like a leaf that wraps around fragrant substances such as tagara.
It is as if one becomes so; even one unable to become wise gains a reputation for virtue by serving a good friend.
"Just as with a leaf-cup" means just as with a leaf used for wrapping fragrant or foul-smelling substances.

"Knowing its own ripening" means knowing one's own maturation and cultivation through association with a good friend—this is the meaning. "They lead to a happy destination" refers to those who are noble and possess right view.
He brought the teaching to its proper conclusion by stating that beings who rely on themselves reach heaven itself.
The king gained confidence through his discourse on the Dhamma, and the company of seers also arrived.
The king, having paid homage to the seers, said, "Venerable sirs, out of compassion for me, please dwell in my residence," and having obtained their consent, he went to the city.

He granted safety to the ascetics. The seers also went there. The king, providing dwellings for the company of seers in the park, attended upon them for as long as he lived and thereby filled the city of heaven.
Then his son, raising the royal parasol, likewise looked after the company of seers;
thus, throughout that succession of families, seven kings provided gifts for the company of seers. The Great Being [dwelt] in the forest.
"Like a spring breeze, he has gone according to his karma.
Having delivered this Dhamma teaching, the Teacher said, "Monks, even in the past, Devadatta was evil and surrounded by an evil retinue," and then he identified the Jātaka:
"At that time, Sattigumba was Devadatta, and the thieves were Devadatta’s retinue."
"King Ānanda was the community of seers, the Buddha’s retinue; but as for Pupphaka-suvo, it was I myself.
This concludes the seventh narrative, the Sattigumba Jātaka.
[504] 8. The Narrative of the Bhallāṭiya Jātaka.
"Bhallātiya was the name of a king"—this the Teacher spoke while dwelling at Jetavana, concerning Queen Mallikā.
It is said that one day she had a quarrel with the king regarding their bed. The king, becoming angry, did not look at her.
She thought, "Does the Tathāgata not know the king's state of anger toward me?"
The Teacher, having understood that reason, entered Sāvatthī for alms on the following day surrounded by the community of monks;
he went to the gate of the king’s palace. The king went out to meet him, took his bowl, and escorted the Teacher up to the palace.
Having seated the community of monks in order, he offered water for the ritual gift, served them with exquisite food, and—
At the conclusion of his meal, he sat down to one side. The Teacher asked, "Great King, why is Mallikā not to be seen?

When the king replied, "Because she is intoxicated with the pride of her own pleasure," the Teacher said, "Great King, did you not previously, having been reborn in the womb of a *kinnara*, spend seven hundred years wandering about in lamentation after being separated from your *kinnarī* for a single night?"
Having said this, being requested by him, he related a story of the past:
"In the past, in Bārāṇasī, a king named Bhallāṭiya, while ruling his kingdom, thought, 'I shall eat the meat of wild animals roasted on coals.
Having entrusted the kingdom to his ministers, he equipped himself with the five weapons and was surrounded by a pack of well-trained, noble hounds."
Having departed from the city and entered the Himālaya mountains, he traveled along the Ganges;

unable to ascend further upward, he saw a river that had descended into the Ganges and followed its course. Killing deer, pigs, and other animals, and eating their meat roasted on coals, he ascended to a high place.
There was a delightful stream there, which at the time of fullness had water reaching the size of a breast.
Having been offered as an oblation, it flows; at other times, its water is only knee-deep. Therein, various kinds of fish and turtles move about.
Along the banks of the water, there is sand the color of silver plates on both shores;

trees bent down, laden with various flowers and fruits, are surrounded by flocks of various birds and bees intoxicated by the essence of the flower and fruit juices, and the area is frequented by diverse herds of wild animals.
A cool shade. Thus, on the bank of that delightful Hemavat river, two kinnaras, embracing and kissing one another, wept while lamenting in various ways.
As the king was ascending Mount Gandhamādana along the bank of that river, he saw those kinnaras and thought, "What indeed is this?"
Thinking, "They are lamenting in this way; I shall question them," he looked at the dogs and snapped his fingers.
The well-trained noble dogs, understanding that signal, entered the thicket and lay down on their chests.
Knowing that they were in retreat, he leaned his bow and quiver, as well as his remaining weapons, against a tree and, making no sound of footsteps, approached slowly.
Having approached them, he asked the kinnaras, "For what reason are you weeping?
To clarify this matter, the Teacher spoke three verses:
"There was a king named Bhallātiya; having abandoned his kingdom, he went hunting. ... [the rest of the verses follow]"
He went to the excellent mountain Gandhamādana, which was in full bloom and frequented by kimpurisas.
Having restrained the host of Sāḷūras and laid aside his bow and quiver,
he approached the place where the kimpurisas were stationed, desiring to speak these words.
“When the winter has passed, why do you stand here on the bank of this Hemavatā river and constantly consult one another?
I ask you, you who possess the form of human bodies: how are you known in the world of men?
In this context, *sāḷūrasaṅgha* means a pack of dogs. *Himaccaye* means when the four months of winter have elapsed. *Hemavatāya* means on the bank of this Hemavatā river.
Having heard the king’s words, the kinnara remained silent, but the kinnarī conversed with the king:
“On Mount Malla, the white mountain with three peaks, we roam along the Sītodakā River;
deer and humans of similar appearance know us as *kimpurisas*, yet hunters do not.”
"In that regard, 'Malla-giri' means: 'Friend hunter, we roam about this Malla-giri, Paṇḍaraka, Tikūṭa, and these rivers.
There is also a reading, 'Mālā-giri. 'Nibhāsa-vaṇṇā' means having a shining appearance;
the meaning is that their bodies are visible."
Then King Tissa spoke these three verses:
“You lament in a truly miserable state, though you were embraced by one dear to you.
I ask you, who possess the form and color of human bodies: why do you weep here in the forest, so devoid of joy?”
“You lament in a most piteous manner, though you were embraced by your beloved.
I ask you, who possess the form of human bodies: why do you wail here in the forest, so full of despair?
You lament in a most piteous manner, though you were embraced by your beloved.”
“I ask you who possess human forms: why do you grieve here in the forest, so full of despair?
Therein, *sukiccharūpaṃ* means as if having truly fallen into suffering. *Āliṅgito cāsi piyo piyāyā* means your beloved was embraced by that beloved woman.
There is also a reading, *āliṅgiyo cāsi*, which has the same meaning. Why here?
"For what reason do you weep here in the forest, having embraced one another again and again, kissed one another, and spoken words of affection,
yet remaining unsatisfied? Then follow verses concerning the conversation and dialogue between the two:
“O hunter, we spent one night apart, unwillingly and remembering each other;
grieving over that single night, we sorrowed, thinking, ‘That night shall never come again.
That which you now regret for a single night is like wealth lost or a father who has passed away.”
“I ask you, O you who have the form of human bodies: how did you manage to dwell here without a shelter?
“This river that you see, with its swift current, its canopy of various trees, and its rocky banks—that was dear to me as I crossed it during the rainy season, thinking, ‘It will follow after me.’”
“I am gathering aṅkolaka flowers, and atimuttaka, sattali, and yothika;
‘May he become dear to me as one who wears garlands, and I too shall approach him as one wearing garlands.
I am also gathering this kuravaka, uddālaka, pāṭali, and sindhuvāraka.”
“He will be dear to me, wearing a garland; and I, wearing a garland, shall approach him.
“I myself, having gathered flowers from a well-flowered *sāla* tree, shall make a garland;
‘He will be dear to me, wearing a garland; and I, wearing a garland, shall approach him.’”
“I shall gather the flowers from this well-blossomed *sāla* tree and make a load of them;
these will serve as a bed for us, where we shall dwell for the night.
And I, being heedless, am grinding agallochum and sandalwood upon a stone.”
‘He will be dear to me with his limbs reddened, and I too, being reddened, shall approach him.
Then there came a torrent of water with a swift current, pushing aside the *sāla*, *salaḷa*, and *kaṇṇikāra* trees;
in that brief moment it filled [the river], so that in the evening the river was very difficult for me to cross.
“Standing then on both banks, we gazed upon one another;
now we would weep, now we would laugh, for that night passed for us with great difficulty.
At dawn, when the sun had risen, having crossed the river at the fourfold ford, O hunter—”
Embracing one another, we both sometimes weep and sometimes laugh.
"O hunter, seven hundred and three years ago, we lived here together;
this life is now but a single rain-season, O protector of the earth—who could dwell here apart from their beloved?"
“How long, my friend, is your lifespan? If you know it, please tell me your life-span.
Whether from tradition or from what you have learned from your elders, declare this to me without hesitation.
“Our lifespan, Ludda, is a thousand years; there is no evil disease that comes between us.”
"Little indeed is the suffering, while happiness is greater; we shall depart from this life still not free from passion.
In this context, "for one night by us" means for one night by us. "We dwelt apart" means we lived separated [from our loved ones].
"Regretting" means reflecting upon that single night, thinking: "The single night has passed while we were unwilling [to part]. "It will not come again" means...
"We grieve thinking, 'He will not be again; he will not come back.

Like lost wealth, like a father who has passed away—whether it be lost wealth, or a father, or a mother who has met their end—what indeed were you reflecting upon, and for what reason did you allow him to dwell apart from you for even a single night? Tell this to me. "Yamimaṃ... (That which this... [he asks].
"This [place] called Selakūla" refers to the stream flowing between two rocks. "At the time of rain" means at the time when a single cloud has arisen and is raining.
For while we were wandering for pleasure in this forest grove, a single cloud arose;
then my beloved husband, thinking that [the cloud] was coming from behind him, said, "He is crossing this river."
"And I," she says, "unaware that he had gone to the further shore, was plucking flowers such as the *aṅkolaka* in full bloom.
There, while gathering the *sattali*, the *yothika*, the *kundāla* flower, and the golden *yothika*, I did so with this motive:
'My beloved will be wearing a garland, and I, having become garlanded myself, will approach him.'"
"I gather. "The *uddālaka*, *pāṭali*, and *sindhuvāraka* flowers—these too have been gathered by me," he says.
"Having gathered" (*oceyya*) means having gathered. "Sandalwood and *agalu*" refers to black *agalu* and red sandalwood. "With limbs anointed" (*rositaṅgo*) means with his body smeared.

"Having anointed" (*rositā*) means having become smeared. "I shall approach the bed" (*ajjhupessanti*) means I will go near the couch. "Pushing aside the *sāla*, *salaḷa*, and *kaṇṇikāra* trees"—these...
"The flowers I had gathered and placed on the bank were being pushed away and carried off. Regarding "difficult to cross":

while she was still standing on the near bank, the river's water rose; at that very moment the sun set, lightning flashed, and since those called *kinnaras* are terrified of water, she did not dare to descend.
Therefore he said: "This river became difficult for me to cross."
"Beholding" means seeing at the time when flashes of lightning appear.
"We weep" means that we weep when not seeing during the darkness, but we laugh when seeing at the time when flashes of lightning appear. "Saṃvarī" means night. "The fourfold" means empty.
"Having crossed over" means having gone beyond. "Three less than seven hundred" means seven hundred years minus three. "Whatever here of mine... [is as follows:]...
"When we last dwelt here, he says, it was seven hundred years less three from now.
'What is a year? he asks; 'This is one year; for you, this life is but a single century.
'Who here? he asks; 'In such a short life, who indeed would remain here without their beloved? It is improper.'"
He indicates that he must exist without his beloved wife.
Having heard the kinnarī’s words, the king thought, “I shall ask what their lifespan is,” and asked, “How long is your life?
[The kinnarī replied: “Anussava means: if you have heard it from someone as they were speaking.”
"Or there is a tradition received from our mothers, fathers, elders, or those of old;
therefore, speak this to us without wavering, for it has come down to us through oral transmission from those elders.

'There is no obstacle' means that our lifespan is a thousand years, and in the meantime, there is no evil disease that causes an interruption to our lives. 'Not free from passion' refers to one another."
"Without their affection having departed.
Having heard this, the king thought: "Indeed, these beings, though they are animals, wander about weeping for seven hundred years due to the separation from one another for a single night;
yet I, having abandoned the great prosperity of a kingdom three hundred leagues in extent, am wandering in the forest."
“Alas! I have done what should not be done! Thinking thus, he turned back from that very spot and went to Bārāṇasī.
When asked by his ministers, “Great King, what wonderful thing did you see in the Himālaya? he related everything in full.
From then on, he gave gifts and enjoyed his wealth. To illustrate this matter, the Teacher said:
“Having heard this from the non-human beings, that the life of Bhallātiya was short, turn back and do not go hunting; give gifts and enjoy your wealth.
Having spoken this verse, he spoke two further verses as he continued his exhortation:
“Having heard this from the non-human beings, rejoice and do not engage in quarreling;
let there be no remorse for you because of the transgression of your own deeds, as was the case with those Kimpurisas for a single night.
Having heard this from the non-human beings, rejoice and do not engage in disputes.”
“May you not suffer for the fault of your own deeds, just as you did for one night with the *kimpuruṣa*.

Therein, “non-human beings” refers to the *kinnaras*. “Fault of one’s own deeds” means the defect of one’s own karma. “Just as you did for one night with the *kimpuruṣa*” means: just as the fault of your own karma was suffered by you for one night with that *kimpuruṣa*, so too may you not suffer; this is the meaning.

Having heard the Tathāgata’s teaching of the Dhamma, Queen Mallikā rose from her seat, extended her hands in reverential salutation, and while offering praise to the One of Ten Powers, she spoke this concluding verse:
“With a joyful mind, I hear your various words, which are full of meaning;
releasing your voice, you dispel my fear. O ascetic who brings happiness, may you live long for me!
In this context, “with a joyful mind, I hear your various [words]” means, venerable sir, that we have heard you having adorned [your speech] with various and manifold reasons.
I listen to the teaching of the Dhamma with a delighted mind and a serene heart.
"The path of words" refers to those various words spoken by you. Releasing your voice, you indeed dispel my fear;
emitting a sweet sound pleasant to the ear, you dispel and carry away the sorrow and distress in my heart. O ascetic, bringer of happiness, live!
“Long live you, O Blessed One, ascetic equal to a Buddha! Long live my lord, King of Dhamma, who brings about celestial and human, mundane and supramundane happiness!
May you live long! From that time forth, the King of Kosala lived in harmonious union with her.
Having delivered this teaching on the Dhamma, the Teacher identified the Jātaka: “At that time, the Kinnara was the King of Kosala; the Kinnarī was Queen Mallikā; and I myself was King Bhallāṭiya.”
The eighth: The Commentary on the Bhallāṭiya Jātaka.
[505] 9. The Commentary on the Somanassa Jātaka:
"Who indeed harms or injures you? This was spoken by the Teacher while dwelling at Jetavana, concerning Devadatta’s attempt to bring about his own death.
The Teacher spoke concerning this. For then the Teacher said, "Monks, it is not only now; in the past as well, he sought to kill me," and he related a story of the past.
In the past, in the kingdom of Kuru, in the city of Uttarapañcāla, a king named Reṇu ruled.
At that time, an ascetic named Mahārakkhita, having lived for a long time in the Himālayas with a retinue of five hundred ascetics, [set out] for the sake of seeking salt and sour food...
While wandering on his alms-round, having reached the city of Uttarapañcāla and stayed in the royal park, he arrived at the palace gate while walking for alms together with his retinue.
When the king saw the group of seers, he was inspired by their dignified deportment;
he had them seated upon a great, decorated terrace, served them excellent food, and said, "Venerable sirs, please stay in my park for this rainy season."
Having gone to the park with them, he had dwellings constructed, gave them the requisites for the life of a renunciant, paid homage to them, and departed.
From that time forth, they all ate at the royal residence. However, the king, being childless, longed for a son, yet no sons were born to him.
