At the end of the rainy season, Mahārakkhita thought, "Now the Himalayas are delightful;..."
“Let us go right there,” he said. Having taken leave of the king and received the honors and hospitality bestowed by him, he departed.
On the way, at midday, he left the road and sat down with his retinue beneath a tree providing dense shade, upon a bed of young grass.
The ascetics initiated a conversation: “In the royal palace, there is no son to preserve the lineage; it would indeed be well if...”

“If the king should obtain a son, the lineage would be continued. Having heard their words, Mahārakkhita reflected, “Will there indeed be a son for the king, or not? Perceiving that “there will be,” he said:
“Sirs, do not worry. This very day, at the time of dawn, a certain son of the gods, having passed away, [will enter] the chief queen of the king.”

“...will take rebirth in a womb. Having heard this, a certain Kuṭaja-jaṭila thought, “Now I shall become an attendant to the royal family,” and when the time came for the ascetics to depart, he lay down making a pretense of illness.
When told, “Come, let us go,” he replied, “I am not able. Mahārakkhita, knowing the reason for his lying down, said, “When you are able...”
Having said, "Then you should come," he took the company of seers and went back to the Himālayas.
The impostor, however, turned back and arrived with great speed, standing at the palace gate. He had the king informed, "The ascetic who was Mahārakkhita’s attendant has arrived.
Summoned by the king with haste, he ascended the palace and sat upon the prepared seat. The king [addressed] the impostor ascetic...
Having paid homage and sat down to one side, he inquired after the health of the seers and said, "Venerable sirs, you have returned very quickly;
for what purpose have you come in such haste? "Yes, Great King," they replied, "the company of seers was sitting comfortably when they raised this discussion:
'How wonderful it would be if a son were born to the king who would protect his lineage. Having heard this discussion, I—"

Thinking, "Will there indeed be a son for the king, or not? he surveyed with his divine eye and saw that a deity of great psychic power, having passed away, would be reborn in the womb of the chief queen Sudhammā. Seeing this, he thought, "They might destroy the embryo out of ignorance;
I shall inform them. It was for the purpose of telling you that I have come. I have spoken to you; now I shall depart.
“Great King! The king, delighted and joyful with a clear mind, said, “Venerable sir, you cannot go,” and having led the fraudulent ascetic to the park, he provided and gave him a place to stay.
From then on, he lived eating at the royal palace, and his name became simply “The One with Divine Vision.”
Then the Bodhisatta, passing away from the Tāvatiṃsa heaven, took rebirth there.
On the day of his naming ceremony, they gave him the name Somanassa Kumāra. He grew up with the care and privileges due to a prince.
Meanwhile, the fraudulent ascetic, on one side of the park, [planted] various kinds of vegetables for soup and climbing fruits.
Having planted them, he established wealth by selling them in the hands of merchants. When the Bodhisatta was seven years old, the king’s frontier region rose in revolt.
Entrusting the prince with the charge, "Do not neglect the ascetic with divine vision," the king departed, thinking, "I shall pacify the frontier.
Then one day, the prince went to the pleasure grove, thinking, "I shall see the matted-hair ascetic."
Seeing a certain fraudulent ascetic wearing one saffron robe as a lower garment and another as an upper cloak, carrying two water-jars in both hands and pouring water upon a vegetable garden,
[the Bodhisatta] realized, "This fraudulent ascetic, failing to perform his own duty as a recluse,
is instead engaged in the work of a vegetable-seller. He then put him to shame, saying, "What are you doing, you householder-vegetable-seller?"
Without even bowing, he departed. Kūṭajaṭila thought, "This man has now become such an enemy; who knows what he might do? It is right to destroy him this very moment.
Then, at the time of the king's arrival, he threw a stone slab to one side, broke the water jar, scattered the grass in the leaf-hut, and smeared his body with oil.
Having smeared himself with dust, he entered the leaf-hut, covered his head, and lay down on the couch as if overcome by great suffering.
The king arrived, circumambulated the city, and without even entering his own residence, thinking, "I shall see my master who possesses the divine eye," went to the door of the leaf-hut;
seeing that miserable state, he wondered, "What is this? and entered.
Having entered and seen him lying there, he massaged his feet and spoke this first verse:
“Who harms you or oppresses you? Why are you dejected and sorrowful, lacking joy?
For whom do mother and father weep today? Where on earth have you been struck down today?”
In this context, *hiṃsati* means he strikes; *heṭheti* means he reviles. *Kvajja setū* means who shall sleep today?
Having heard that, the fraudulent ascetic, groaning, rose up and spoke the second verse:
“I am delighted, O King, by the sight of you; after a long time, I behold you, O protector of the earth.”
“O non-violent one, having entered the dust, I have been struck down by your son, O Deva.
From here onwards, the verses concerning the clear connection should be understood according to the method of the Pāḷi:
“Let the gatekeepers with sword-belts come forward; let those wearing saffron robes enter the inner palace;”
“Having slain that Prince Somanassa, cut off his head and bring it here.
Sent by the king, the messengers spoke thus to the prince:
“You have been abandoned by the Lord; you have met your death, O Kshatriya.”
“Lamenting, that prince raised his ten-fingered hands in añjali and said:
‘I too wish to see you, O Lord of Men; having brought me back alive, please show me to him.
Having heard those words of his, they showed the king’s son.”
And the son, seeing his father, called out from afar:
"The gatekeepers with their swords fastened have come, O Lord of Men; let them kill me, for I am clad in saffron robes.
Being asked, tell me this matter: what offense have I committed here today?"
In this context, "non-violent" means that I am harmless toward anyone, endowed with virtue and good conduct. "I shall enter into the dust," O Great King, means:
"O Reṇu, I shall enter [your palace] together with your son and his great retinue, and having said, 'Hey, you fraudulent ascetic!
Why do you live here? I shall throw a stone slab, break the water-jar, and strike him with my hands and feet."
"I have been harmed"—thus he made that which was unreal appear as real and caused the king to believe it.

"Let them come" means "let them go. Having become angry, thinking, "From the time my master acted improperly toward me, he will no longer feel shame even before me," he spoke thus while ordering his execution.
"Kāsāviyas" refers to executioners. They too, with axes in hand, [went] themselves...
"Let them go according to the prescribed rite," he said. "They choose the boon; let them bring [the head], having cut off the head—the most excellent head.

"O King," monks, messengers sent by the king went swiftly, surrounded the prince—who had been adorned by his mother and seated on her lap—and spoke thus. "By the Lord" means by the king. "You have been granted [a boon]" means...
"You are abandoned. Monks, having heard those words, that prince—terrified by the fear of death—rose from his mother’s lap.
"He should show himself" means he should reveal himself.
Monks, when those messengers heard these words from the prince, being unable to kill him, they dragged him along with a rope like an ox.

Having led him away, they presented him to the king. But while the prince was being led away, Queen Sudhammā—surrounded by a host of female slaves and accompanied by the women of the harem—as well as the citizens, followed along with him, saying, "We will not allow them to kill the prince, who is innocent.
"They came" means they came into my presence at your command. "To kill me" means to put me to death.
“Who has buried me? What indeed is my offense here, that you have caused me to die? he asked.
The king, explaining his fault with the verse, said:
“At evening and at dawn she prepares the water; she always attends to the fire with diligent care.”
"Why do you address such a self-controlled celibate as 'householder'?

In this context, "he bathes in water" means he performs the ritual of descending into water. "Such a one" means "such a person," referring to my master, the ascetic endowed with the divine eye; she says, "Why do you address him with the title 'householder'?
Then the youth said, "Your Majesty, what fault is there in my addressing a householder simply as 'householder'? and spoke this verse:
“Palms, roots, and fruits, O King, and various kinds of possessions he has;
he guards and protects them with diligence. Therefore, I call him a householder.
In this context, “roots” refers to roots such as radishes and the like. “Fruits” refers to various kinds of vine-fruits. “He guards and protects them with diligence” means...
"This ascetic who supports your family is sitting and guarding while performing his work as a vendor;
he protects it by making a fence and watches over it with diligence. For that reason, this brahmin is called a 'householder' (gahapati).
Thus, I too addressed him as 'householder. If you do not believe me, have the vendors questioned at the four gates."
The king had it investigated. They replied, "Yes, we buy paper and various fruits from his hand.

Having had the paper inventory examined, he made it evident. Then the king's men entered the paper hall, brought out a bundle of coins and small change obtained from the sale of paper by the youth, and showed them to the king. The king—
Knowing the Great Being’s state of innocence, he spoke this verse:
“It is indeed true that you say, O Prince, ‘There are various possessions belonging to him;
he guards and protects them with diligence’—it is for that reason that one becomes a brahmin or a householder.”
Then the Great Being thought: "It is better to enter the Himalayas and go forth into homelessness than to live in the presence of such a foolish king.
Having exposed his fault in the midst of the assembly and taken my leave, I shall depart this very day and go forth.
Having paid homage to the assembly, he spoke this verse:
“Let all those gathered here in this assembly listen to me—both the townspeople and all the countryfolk!
Having heeded the words of a fool, this king, himself a fool, has had me executed for no reason at all.

In this passage, “a fool [having heeded] the words of a fool” means: this king himself is a fool; having heard the words of this foolish, fraudulent ascetic, he has had me executed for no reason whatsoever.
Having spoken thus and paid homage to his father, he spoke the following verse, requesting permission for his own renunciation:
“O Lord of Men, this bamboo has taken deep root, spread out, and grown large; it is difficult to uproot once its branches have flourished.
I bow at your feet; grant me leave, O King, for I shall go forth.”
Therein, *visaṭe* means when it has become wide and great. *Dunnikkayo* means difficult to draw out.
Following that are the verses of question and answer between the king and his son:
“Enjoy vast riches, O prince, and I give you all sovereignty;”
“Become the king of the Kurus this very day; do not go forth into homelessness, for the life of a wanderer is suffering.
“What wealth, O King, do you have here that I might enjoy before I delight in the world of the gods—with forms, sounds, and likewise tastes, scents, and delightful touches?”
“I have enjoyed pleasures in the world of the Thirty-three gods, surrounded by a host of nymphs;
yet, knowing you to be a fool led by others, I would not dwell in such a royal family.
If I am indeed a fool led by others, my son, forgive this one offense of mine.”
“Furthermore, if such a thing should happen, act with joy according to your own judgment.
Therein, “Suffering, dear one,” he entreated him: “Renunciation is indeed suffering because one’s livelihood is dependent on others; do not go forth, but be king!
“What, O Lord? [the prince replied]. “O Lord, among those enjoyments of yours, what indeed is there to be enjoyed?”
"It exists. "Surrounded" means attended upon; or this reading (*paricārito*) itself is correct.

It is said that the knowledge of recollecting past births (*jātissarañāṇa*) arose in him, and therefore he spoke thus. "To be led by others" means one who must be led by another like a blind man with a staff.
"In such a person": a wise man should not live in the presence of such a king; today I have obtained my life through the power of my own wisdom.
He spoke thus in order to make it known: "I will not dwell in your presence. He appeased his son, saying:
"Regarding 'according to my wish'—if such a fault should arise in me again, then you may act according to your own inclination.
Then the Great Being, instructing the king, spoke these eight verses:
“Action performed without reflection, thought out without stability,
has an evil result, like the failure of medicine.
But action performed with reflection, thought out with stability...”
Just as the excellence of medicine, its ripening is auspicious.
“A householder who is lazy while enjoying sensual pleasures is not good; one who has gone forth but is unrestrained is not good;
a king who acts without reflection is not good; and a wise man who is prone to anger is not good.”
“A ruler should act with deliberation, not without deliberation, O Lord of the Earth;
for the fame and renown of a king who acts with deliberation increase.
A lord should inflict punishment with deliberation; if inflicted impulsively, O Protector of the World, it brings remorse.”
Right aspiration brings benefit to a person, and it leads to no regret later.
For those who perform deeds that are free from regret— deeds that are analyzed according to the spheres of action in the world,
which are praised by the wise, which have happiness as their fruit, and which are approved by the Buddhas— they shall experience no remorse.
“Doorkeepers with girded swords, clad in saffron robes, came to kill me, O Lord of Men;
while I was sitting on my mother’s lap, O King, I was suddenly dragged away by them.
For I have fallen into a bitter confinement and a miserable plight, though I had obtained a life that is sweet, O King.”
“Today, through hardship, I am released from death; indeed, I am intent upon going forth.
In this context, “without reflection” means without looking back or without deliberating.
“Thought out without establishing” means thought out without settling, without weighing, or without reaching a conclusion. “The result is evil” means that, just as in the case of a medicine...
Dissolution is failure; in this very way, the result is evil. "Unrestrained" means one who is unrestrained in body and so forth, being immoral.
"That is not good" means that his anger is not good. "Not without reflection" means one should not perform any action without having reflected.
"One should establish" means one should set up or carry out. "With speed" means with haste or impulsively. And "right resolve."
The meaning is: actions performed with a mind established through wise reflection (yoniso) become free from regret later on for a person.
"Having analyzed" means having analyzed with wisdom thus: "These are appropriate to do; these are inappropriate. "Spheres of action" means deeds.
"Approved by the Buddhas" means they are approved by the wise and are blameless. "Bitter," O King, means bitter...
"I have fallen into a narrow strait, a painful plight, and the fear of death. "I have obtained it"—meaning he has obtained it through the power of his own knowledge.
"I am one whose mind is intent upon renunciation alone"—meaning his mind is directed solely toward going forth.
When the Great Being had thus taught the Dhamma, the king addressed the queen and spoke this verse:
“This young son of yours, compassionate and joyful in the excellent Dhamma, is a prince;
though I entreat him today, I do not obtain him. You too ought to entreat him.
In this context, *yācitave* means “to entreat.”
Encouraging him toward the going forth itself, she spoke this verse:
“Delight, my son, in the life of wandering for alms; having reflected upon the teachings, go forth as a wanderer.
Having laid aside the rod toward all living beings, blameless, you shall attain the state of Brahmā.”

In this context, "having reflected" means that when going forth, one should do so after careful reflection, abandoning the going forth of those with wrong view and instead undertaking the liberating going forth associated with right view.
Then the King spoke this verse:
"How wonderful indeed is the nature of this, O you who are well-versed in the Dhamma! You cause me, who am already suffering, to suffer even more."
“‘Beg for a son,’ thus being addressed, you only further incite the prince.
In this context, “of such a kind” means: “Indeed, what you say is truly wonderful! You cause me, who am already suffering by nature, to suffer even more.
Again, the Queen spoke this verse:
“Those who are fully liberated, enjoying blameless wealth, and have attained final Nibbāna, move about in this world;
I am unable to restrain that noble one as he proceeds upon the Noble Path, O Prince.
In this context, "fully liberated" means liberated from lust and the other defilements. "Attained final Nibbāna" means extinguished by the extinction of the defilements (*kilesa-parinibbāna*).
“I am not able, O King, to restrain my son as he enters upon that noble path which belongs to those Noble Ones, the Buddhas and others.
Having heard her words, the king spoke this final verse:
“Truly, those who are wise and learned, who reflect upon many matters, should indeed be served;
for having heard their well-spoken words, one becomes free from anxiety, devoid of sorrow, and established in the True Dhamma.

In this context, “those who reflect upon many matters” means those who contemplate many reasons. “Yesāyaṃ” means “of whom this [is]”; for it was precisely after hearing the well-spoken words of Prince Somanassa that [the people] became free from anxiety, and the King spoke thus with reference to that very fact.
The Mahāsatta, having paid homage to his parents and said, "If there is any fault on my part, forgive me," joined his palms to the great multitude.

As the people turned back, he departed toward the Himavat; and while they were returning, he was escorted by deities who had approached in human form, crossing seven mountain ranges until he reached the Himavat, where he stayed in a leaf-hut constructed by Vissakamma.
He went forth into the ascetic life of a seer (*isi*). There, until he reached the age of sixteen, deities alone attended upon him in the guise of members of the royal household.
The great multitude beat Kūṭajaṭila to death. Having attained the meditative absorptions (*jhāna*) and direct knowledges (*abhiññā*), the Great Being was reborn in the Brahma-world.
Having delivered this Dhamma teaching, the Teacher said, "Thus, monks, even in the past he strove for my death," and he identified the Jātaka:
"At that time the rogue was Devadatta; the mother was Mahāmāyā;
Mahārakkhita was Sāriputta; and Somanassa Kumāra was none other than myself."
The ninth: The Commentary on the Somanassa Jātaka.
[506] 10. The Commentary on the Campeyya Jātaka:
"Who is this that shines like lightning? This was spoken by the Teacher while dwelling at Jetavana, concerning the Uposatha ceremony.
Then the Teacher said, "Well done, lay followers, for you who dwell observing the Uposatha; even the ancient wise ones abandoned the prosperity of Nāgas and dwelt observing the Uposatha.
Having spoken thus, at their request, he related a story of the past:
"In the past, while kings were ruling over the kingdom of Aṅga in the province of Aṅga and the kingdom of Magadha in the province of Magadha, in those two provinces of Aṅga and Magadha..."
In between [the two kingdoms] was a river named Campā; there was a Nāga abode there. A Nāga king named Campeyya reigned there.
Sometimes the King of Magadha would seize the kingdom of Aṅga, and sometimes the King of Aṅga would seize the kingdom of Magadha.
Then one day, the King of Magadha, having fought with Aṅga and being defeated in battle, fled on horseback from the King of Aṅga.
Pursued by his soldiers, Puṇṇa reached the river Campā and, thinking, "Death in the river is better than falling into the hands of the enemy," he entered the river together with his horse.

At that time, the Nāga king of Campā, having fashioned a jeweled pavilion within the water, was drinking a great draught surrounded by a vast retinue. The horse, having submerged in the water along with the king, [reached] the Nāga king...

He descended before him. When the Nāga king saw the king adorned and prepared for state, he felt affection and, rising from his seat, said, "Do not fear, Great King," and having seated the king upon his own couch, he asked the reason for his submergence in the water.
The king told him the truth as it was. Then he said to him, "Do not fear, Great King; I shall [rescue] you from the two kingdoms..."
Having comforted him with the words, “I shall make you my husband,” she enjoyed great glory for seven days;
then, on the seventh day, she departed from the Nāga realm together with the King of Magadha.
By the power of the Nāga king, the King of Magadha captured the King of Aṅga, took his life, and ruled over two kingdoms. From that time forth, between the king and the Nāga king—
And his trust became firm. Every year, the king had a jeweled pavilion constructed on the bank of the Campā River and performed an offering ceremony for the Nāga King with great generosity.
He too, emerging from the Nāga realm with a vast retinue, accepted the offering.
The great multitude gazed upon the splendor of the Nāga King.
At that time, the Bodhisatta was born into a poor family. Having gone to the riverbank with the royal retinue and beheld the splendor of that Naga king, he conceived a desire for it;

longing for it, he gave gifts, observed the precepts, and passed away on the seventh day after the death of the Campeyya Naga king, to be reborn upon the royal couch in the bedchamber of the glory-chamber within the palace where that king had dwelt.
He was reborn. His body became large and the color of a jasmine garland. Seeing this, he became remorseful and thought:
"By the result of the merit I performed, sovereignty over the six celestial realms of sensual pleasure has become like grain stored in a granary.
Yet I have taken rebirth-linking in this animal womb; what is the use of my life?"
He resolved his mind upon death. Then, a young female nāga named Sumanā, seeing him, perceived that "a being of great power has been reborn here," and she gave notice to the other young female nāgas.
All of them, carrying various musical instruments in their hands, came and presented offerings to him. That nāga-abode of his became like the abode of Sakka; [his] thought of death—
He subsided; casting off his serpent-body, adorned with all ornaments, he sat upon the surface of the couch.
From that time forth, his fame became great.
While exercising sovereignty there as a king of the nagas, he later became remorseful and thought, "What use have I for this animal womb?"
Having observed the Uposatha fast, I shall depart from here, go to the human realm, penetrate the Truths, and bring an end to suffering.
Having thought thus, from that time forth he performed the Uposatha rites in that very palace.
Adorned Naga maidens would come into his presence, and for the most part his virtue would break. From then on, he departed from the palace.
He went to the park. They also went there, and the Uposatha ceremony was indeed broken.
He thought, "It is fitting for me to leave this Nāga-abode, go to the human world, and observe the Uposatha vows.
From then on, on Uposatha days, he would leave the Nāga-abode and [go] not far from a certain frontier village.
Near the Great Road, on the top of an anthill, he offered his body as a gift, saying, "Let those who need my skin and other parts take them;
let those who wish to make me a plaything for snakes do so," and having folded his limbs, he lay down and observed the Uposatha vow.
Those traveling along the Great Road, seeing him, would worship him with perfumes and other offerings before departing.

The inhabitants of the border village went there and, thinking, "This is a Nāga king of great majesty," constructed a pavilion over him, scattered sand all around, and worshipped him with perfumes and other offerings.
From that time on, people, having gained confidence in the Great Being and performed worship, prayed for a son; they prayed for a daughter.

The Mahāsatta, performing the Uposatha observance, would lie upon the top of an anthill on the fourteenth and fifteenth days, and on the first day of the lunar fortnight (pāṭipada), he would go to the Nāga realm. As he was thus observing the Uposatha, a long period of time passed.
One day, the chief queen Sumanā said: "Your Majesty, you go to the human world and observe the Uposatha there; the human world..."
“And it is full of lurking dangers and fears; if fear should arise in you, then tell us the sign by which we might know.
Then the Great Being led her to the bank of the Maṅgala lotus pond and said, “Bhadde, if anyone should strike me and tire me, the water of this pond will become turbid.”
"If a garuḷa seizes it, the water will boil; if a snake-charmer seizes it, the water will become the color of blood," she said.

Having thus explained these three signs to her, and having resolved upon the fourteenth-day Uposatha, she departed from the Nāga realm, went there, and lay down upon the summit of an anthill, [displaying] the beauty of her body.
Adorning the anthill, his body was as white as a silver garland, and his head was like a ball of red wool.
However, in this Jātaka, the Bodhisatta’s body was the size of a plough-pole; in the Bhūridatta Jātaka, it was the size of a thigh;
and in the Saṅkhapāla Jātaka, it was the size of a single-droṇa boat.
At that time, a young Brahmin living in Bārāṇasī went to Takkasilā and, having learned the Alampāyana charm from a world-renowned teacher,
was returning to his own home by that same route. Seeing the Great Being, he thought,
"By catching this snake and performing it as a spectacle in villages, market towns, and royal capitals, I shall acquire wealth."
Taking divine herbs and reciting a divine mantra, he went into his presence.
From the moment the divine mantra was heard, it was as if iron spikes were being driven into the Great Being’s ears, and it was as if his head were being crushed by a mountain peak.
Thinking, "Who could this be?", he raised his head from within his coils and looked out.
Seeing the snake-charmer, he thought: "My venom is great;
if I were to release a breath of my nostrils in anger, his body would be scattered like a handful of ashes, and thus my virtue (sīla) would be broken.
I will not look at him now. He closed his eyes and placed his head within the coils of the serpent.
The Brahmin snake-charmer, having consumed a medicinal herb and recited a mantra, spat upon the Great Being’s body.
Through the power of the herbs and the mantra, every spot touched by the spittle became like the moment when the scales of a snake begin to rise.
Then, seizing him by the tail and dragging him, he laid him out lengthwise and [proceeded] with the hoof of a goat...
Pressing with his staff and weakening him, he gripped the Great Being’s head firmly and squeezed;
he forced open the Great Being’s mouth. Then, having spat into his mouth and performed a medicinal incantation, he broke his teeth, and the mouth was filled with blood.
Out of fear of violating his own virtue, the Great Being endured such suffering and opened his eyes.
He did not even cast a glance at him. Thinking, "I shall weaken this Nāga king," he began from the tail and crushed his entire body as if grinding it to powder;

he bound him with what is called a cloth-wrap, rubbed him with what is called a cloth-scrub, and seizing the tail, he thrashed him with what is called a cloth-beating. [Thus] the entire body of the Great Being—
It became smeared with blood. He endured that great pain.
Then, perceiving his weakness, they constructed a chest from creepers, placed him inside it, and led him to a frontier village where they made him an object of sport in the midst of a great crowd.
[They did this] regarding colors such as blue and so forth, shapes such as round, square, and so forth, and dimensions such as minute and thick, and so forth.
Whatever measurement the brahmin desired, the Great Being would perform that very thing and dance;
he would even produce a hundred or a thousand hoods. The great multitude, being inspired with faith, gave much wealth.
In a single day alone, he received a thousand *kahāpaṇa* coins as well as requisites worth a thousand. From the very beginning, the brahmin had offered a thousand...

Having obtained it, he thought, "I shall distribute it. But having received that wealth, he thought, "I have already obtained this much wealth even in a mere border village; I shall obtain vast wealth in the presence of kings and royal ministers.
Taking a cart and a comfortable carriage, and placing his requisites in the cart, he sat in the comfortable carriage with great [splendor].

Accompanied by his retinue, the Great Being traveled through villages, market towns, and other settlements, playing for sport, with the intention: "I shall play before King Uggasena in Bārāṇasī and then release him.
He would kill frogs and give them to the king of the city. However, the Nāga king did not eat them, thinking, "He will kill me again and again because of these.
Then he gave him honeyed parched grain. The Great Being thought, "If I..."
“I will take food; otherwise, death will surely come within the basket,” he thought, and so he did not eat it either.
After about a month, the brahmin reached Bārāṇasī, where he won much wealth by making people gamble in the villages near the gates.
The king also summoned him and said, “Make us play. “Very well, Your Majesty; on the fifteenth day of tomorrow, for you—”
“I shall have him play. The king had a drum beaten, proclaiming: “Tomorrow the Naga King will dance in the royal courtyard; let the great multitude assemble and witness it.
On the following day, having had the royal courtyard decorated, he summoned the brahmin.
He brought the Great Being from the jewel casket, placed the casket upon a variegated rug, and sat down. The king also descended from the palace, surrounded by a great crowd.
He sat upon the royal throne. The brahmin brought the Great Being out and made him dance.
The great multitude, unable to maintain their composure, raised a thousand shouts of joy. A rain of the seven precious gems fell upon the Bodhisatta.
One month was completed after he had been taken [into captivity]. During all that time, he remained without food. Sumanā thought, "He has been gone for too long."
"My beloved husband—now that a full month has passed since he did not come here, what could be the reason?
Having thought this, she went and looked down into the lotus pond; seeing the water was blood-colored, she realized, "He must have been seized by a snake-charmer.
Then, emerging from the Nāga realm, she went to the vicinity of the anthill and [saw] the place where the Great Being had been captured.
Seeing the place where he had been exhausted, she wept and wailed; having gone to a border village and inquired, she heard the news of his fate.
She then went to Benares and stood in the royal courtyard in the midst of the assembly, weeping in the open air.
As the Great Being was dancing, he looked up into the sky, and seeing her, he was filled with shame; he entered the basket and lay down inside. At the moment he had entered the basket, the king—
Thinking, "What indeed could be the cause?", he looked here and there; seeing her standing in the air, he spoke the first verse:
"Who are you that shine like lightning, like a medicinal herb or a star?
Are you a goddess or a gandhabba? I do not think you are a human."
In that regard, "I do not consider her to be human" means: "I do not consider her to be a human woman; it must be that you are a single deity or a Gandhabba," he says.
Now follow the verses of their dialogue:
"I am neither a goddess, nor a Gandhabba, Nor a human woman, O Great King."
“I am a Naga maiden, venerable sir; it is for a certain purpose that I have come here.
Your mind is distracted and your senses are agitated; streams of water flow from your eyes.
What have you lost, or what do you desire, that you have come here, O woman? Pray, tell me this.”
“‘The one with the strength of a club, the serpent,’ so they say; ‘the Naga,’ so people call him, O Lord of Men.
A man seeking a livelihood seized him; release him from his bonds, for he is my husband.
How indeed did he, endowed with such power and vigor, fall into the hands of this mendicant?”
“Tell me that matter, O Naga maiden: how may we recognize one who has taken up the practice of a Naga?
‘A Naga could reduce even a city to ashes, for he is endowed with such power and energy;
yet a Naga who honors the Dhamma exerts himself and practices austerity.’”
In that context, "for this reason" means: "I have come here because of one particular cause. "With agitated faculties" means with exhausted faculties.
"A mass of water" means a multitude of teardrop-pots. "And they called him 'Uraga'" means that the great multitude of people spoke of him as "Uraga.
"The man seized him" means that this man seized that Naga-king for the sake of his livelihood. "Of the mendicant" means of this [man].
He asks: "How is it that this man, though possessing such great majesty, has come into the hands of a beggar?
And as for the phrase "honoring the Dhamma": he dwells honoring both the Dhamma of the five precepts and the Dhamma of the Uposatha observance;
therefore, even though he has been seized by this man, [he thinks]: "If I were to release a breath upon him, he would be scattered like a handful of ashes."
Thinking, “In this way my virtue will be broken,” he exerts himself out of fear for the breaking of his virtue; enduring that suffering, he practices austerity, he said, exerting only energy.
The king asked, “But where was he caught by him? Then, pointing it out to him, she spoke this verse:
“O King, on the fourteenth and the fifteenth day, the Naga king gathers at the crossroads.
A man seeking a livelihood seized him; release him from his bonds, for he is my husband.
Therein, “at the crossroads” means in a certain anthill near a place where four roads meet, [where the Naga] possessed of the four limbs [is present].
The meaning is: "Having made a formal resolve (*adhiṭṭhāna*), he lies down while observing the Uposatha fast. "Release him from his bonds" means:
having given wealth to this righteous and virtuous king of the *nāgas*, release him from the confinement of the chest.
Having spoken thus, she spoke two verses, further entreating him:
“Sixteen thousand women, adorned with jeweled earrings,
who dwell in water-houses— these women too have gone for refuge to him.
Release us by righteousness and not by violence, for a village, a coin, and a hundred cows.”
"Let the snake go forth with body cast off; seeking merit, let him release himself from bondage.
In this context, "sixteen thousand women" is said to show that you should not think, "Who is he? Is he some poor fellow?
For he has as many women as these, all adorned with every ornament, and his other prosperity is immeasurable. "Vārigehasaya" means...
Having constructed a water-shed and a water-chamber, she was accustomed to sleeping there. "Ossaṭṭhakāyo" means having abandoned her body [her usual residence].
"Carātu" means let her go.
Then King Tissa spoke these three verses to her:
“I release you by means of Dhamma, not by violence—with a village, a coin, and a hundred cows.
Let the snake go with its body cast off; let him who seeks merit be released from bondage.
I give you a hundred coins, hunter, and a large jeweled earring.”
“A four-sided couch and a palanquin, resembling the color of an umā flower;
two wives of equal beauty, and a hundred bulls— let the snake,
having cast off its body, wander seeking merit and be released from its bondage.”

In this context, "the hunter" refers to the king, who, having addressed the snake-charmer in order to release the serpent and intending to give him the gift that was to be bestowed upon him, spoke thus. The verses, however, have already had their meaning explained above.
Then the hunter said to him:
"O Lord of Men, even without a gift, at your word we shall release this serpent from its bonds."
"Let the serpent go forth with body cast off; seeking merit, let him be released from his bonds.
In this regard, "your word alone," O Great King, means that even without a gift, your word itself is weighty to us. "I shall release them"—he says this while declaring, "I will release these.
Having spoken thus, he took the Great Being out from the chest. The Naga king, having emerged, entered into the midst of flowers.
Having cast off that body, he emerged with his person adorned in the form of a young brahmin, standing as if splitting the earth open.
Sumanā descended from the sky and stood beside him.
The Naga king stood with palms joined in reverence, paying homage to the King. To illustrate this matter, the Teacher spoke two verses:
“Released, the Campeyyaka nāga spoke this to the king:
‘Homage to you, O King of Kāsi! Homage to you, O Increaser of Kāsi!
I extend my joined palms to you; may I see my own dwelling.’”
“Truly, they say this is hard to believe: that a human should place his trust in a non-human.
But if you ask me for this matter, O Nāga, let us see your dwellings.
Therein, “I might see my dwelling” means: my dwelling, the delightful abode of the Campeyya Nāgas, which is worthy to be seen.
"I wish to show it to you; come, O lord of men, and see it yourself with your entire army and retinue," he says.
"They will be difficult to trust" means they are hard to inspire with confidence. "If indeed" means: "If you entreat me, we might see your dwellings, yet nevertheless I do not believe you."
Then, in order to make him believe, the Great Being spoke two stanzas while taking an oath:
“Even if the wind were to carry away a mountain, and the moon and sun were to fall to the ground,
and all rivers were to flow upstream— nevertheless, O King, I would never speak a falsehood.”
“Even if the sky were to burst asunder, even if the ocean were to dry up, even if the earth that supports all beings were to crumble away,
and even if Mount Meru, the heap of rock, were to fly up with its very roots— nevertheless, O King,
I would never speak a falsehood. In this passage, “the earth that supports all beings” (bhūtadharā) and “the bearer of wealth” (vasundharā) refer to the same thing.

"The great earth would indeed crumble like a mat of reeds; even Mount Sineru, the Great Mountain, would be uprooted and, rising up with its very foundations, would leap into the sky like a withered leaf.
Even when the Great Being had spoken thus, he did not believe it.
“Truly, they say this is difficult to trust: that a human should place his confidence in one who is not human.
But if you ask me for this purpose, O Naga, we shall see your dwellings.

Having spoken that same verse again, he spoke the other verse, making known: “You are worthy to know the merit I have performed; as for whether it is appropriate or inappropriate to have faith, I shall know that.”
“You are indeed fierce-venomed, formidable, of great power, and quick to anger;
yet for my sake you were released from bondage. You ought to know what has been done for us.
In this context, *uḷārā* means those with formidable venom. *Jānituye* means to know.
Then, in order to make him believe, the Great Being spoke this verse while again taking an oath:
“May he who does not recognize such a deed as this be cooked in a terrible hell;
may he never obtain any bodily pleasure, and may he, bound in a cage, meet his death.”

In this context, "paccatu" means "let it be cooked. By saying "kammakataṃ," he says: "May one who does not know a person like you—who has performed such deeds and possesses such virtues—be of such a nature.
Then the king, having placed his trust in him, spoke this verse in praise:
"Let this be your word of truth: may you be free from anger and free from malice."
"And let all those families of nāgas and supaṇṇas avoid you, as one avoids a fire in the summer heat.
In this context, "let this be for you" means let this promise of yours be true.
"As one avoids a fire in the summer heat" means just as people, not desiring the torment during the summer season, avoid a blazing fire, so too let them avoid you.
"May they avoid [this place] from afar!
The Great Being, offering praise to the king, spoke the following verse:
"O Lord of Men, you have compassion for the race of Nāgas, just as a mother has for her own beloved only son."
"And I, together with the Naga clan, shall perform great service for you.
Having heard this, the king, desiring to go to the Naga realm, spoke this verse while ordering his army to prepare for the journey:
"Harness indeed the royal chariot, well-adorned; yoke the Kambojan mules, well-tamed!"
“And harness the steeds with golden trappings; let us behold the dwellings of the Naga.
Therein, “well-trained Kambojan colts” means: harness the colts born in the kingdom of Kamboja that have been well-disciplined.
The other verses are those spoken upon his full enlightenment.
“Kettledrums, tabors, drums, and conchs resounded for King Uggasena;
King Pāyāsi set forth, looking exceedingly magnificent, preceded by a host of women in their midst.

Therein, “looking exceedingly magnificent,” monks, means that the King of Bārāṇasī, preceded and surrounded by sixteen thousand women, set forth from Bārāṇasī toward the abode of the Nāgas, appearing most splendidly in the midst of that host of women.

At the very moment he departed from the city, the Great Being, by his own supernatural power, caused the Naga realm to appear as if made entirely of jewels, including its walls, gates, and watchtowers;
he then prepared the path leading to the Naga realm, making it beautifully adorned and ready.
The King, together with his retinue, entered the Naga realm by that path and beheld a delightful region.
And he saw the palace. Explaining this matter, the Teacher said:
“Kāsivaḍḍhana beheld the ground strewn with golden sand, and the palace made of gold, spread with slabs of beryl.”
That king entered the celestial mansion, the residence of Campeyya;
it was like the color of the sun, radiant with the luster of bronze and lightning.
It was covered with various trees and perfumed by diverse fragrances.
Thus the King of Kāsi entered the residence of Campeyya.
When the King of Kāsi had entered the residence of Campeyya,
divine musical instruments resounded and the daughters of the nāgas danced.
“The King of Kāsi, full of faith, ascended along with his retinue that path traversed by the Nāga maiden;
he sat upon a golden seat provided with a cushion and smeared with the essence of sandalwood.
Therein, “strewn with gold” means covered with golden sand. “The vault” refers to the decorated abode of the Nāgas.
"Of Campeyya": having entered the nāga-abode, he entered the residence of the nāga-king Campeyya.
"Shining with the luster of bronze and lightning" means it was radiant like golden lightning flashing within the mouth of a cloud.
"Perfumed with various scents" means it was permeated by diverse kinds of divine fragrances. "Frequented by a host" means that residence was frequented by a multitude of nāga-maidens.
He wandered about. "Smeared with the essence of sandalwood" means he was anointed with divine, choice sandalwood.
As soon as he sat down there, they brought him various kinds of exquisite divine food, as well as for the sixteen thousand women and the rest of the king's retinue.
Having enjoyed divine food, drink, and other luxuries for about seven days together with his followers, he—

Having delighted in divine objects of sensual pleasure and sitting upon a comfortable couch, he praised the glory of the Great Being and asked, "O King of Nagas, why have you abandoned such prosperity and dwell in the observance of the Uposatha, lying upon the top of an anthill in the human world?
He explained it to him as well. To clarify this matter, the Teacher said:
“Having thus eaten there and likewise enjoyed yourself, the King of Kāsi said to Campeyyaka:
‘These most excellent palaces of yours are radiant with the color of the sun;
nothing like this exists in the world of humans. For what purpose, O Nāga, do you perform these ascetic penances?’”

“Those women, wearing shell bracelets and armlets, well-dressed, with rounded fingers and copper-red palms, possessing extraordinary beauty, are holding [the ladles] and pouring [the water]; there is nothing like this in the world of humans.
What do you aspire for, O Naga, that you perform such asceticism?”
“Rivers with broad-scaled fish, echoing with the cries of āṭa-birds and pleasant bathing-places—there is nothing like these in the world of men.
For what purpose, O Nāga, do you perform this asceticism?
Kurawis, peacocks, celestial swans, and cuckoos with melodious voices fly about.”
"There is nothing like this in the world of men; longing for what, O Naga, do you perform these austerities?
"The mangoes, the *sāla* trees, the *tilaka*, the *jambu*, the *uddālaka*, and the flowering *pāṭali*—there is nothing like this in the world of men;
longing for what, O Naga, do you perform these austerities?"
“Around these lotus ponds of yours, divine fragrances waft constantly; there is nothing like this in the world of humans.
For what purpose, O Naga, do you perform these austerities?
‘Neither for the sake of sons, nor for the sake of wealth, nor even for the sake of long life, O Lord of Men, [do I practice them].’”
“Longing for human birth, therefore I strive and practice asceticism.
Therein, “those” refers to the sixteen thousand Naga maidens. “Wearing shell-bracelets and armlets” means wearing golden ornaments.
“With rounded fingers” means having rounded fingers resembling coral sprouts. “Possessing copper-colored palms” means having beautiful, reddish-pink palms of the hands and feet.
Endowed with these qualities. "They cause them to drink" means that having lifted up divine drinks, they cause them to drink.
"With broad-leaved fish" means endowed with various fish that have broad fins. "Resounding with the cries of *āṭā* birds" means resounding with birds known as *āṭās*.
"With beautiful bathing places" means possessing lovely landing-stairs. "And divine swans" refers to celestial swans. "Flying about" means crying out with charming sounds.
They fly from tree to tree. "Divine fragrances" means that in those lotus ponds, divine scents waft continuously.
"Longing for" means I wander about with longing. "Therefore" means for that reason, having exerted effort and applied energy, I practice austerity and observe the Uposatha.
When this was said, the king spoke:
“With blood-red eyes and a broad chest, adorned and with hair and beard trimmed,
well-anointed with red sandalwood, you illuminate the quarters like the King of the Gandhabbas.”
“You have attained divine power, O one of great majesty, endowed with all sensual pleasures.
I ask you, O King of Nagas, about this matter: which is better than this, the world of humans?
In that context, *surosita* means well-anointed.
Then the Naga king, explaining it to him, said:
"O Lord, purity or self-restraint is not found anywhere other than in the human world.
Having obtained a human birth, I shall bring an end to birth and death."
"In this regard, O Great King, apart from the human world, there is no purity—whether it be the purity known as the great Nibbāna of the Deathless or the restraint of virtue.
'The end' means: having obtained birth in the human womb, I shall perform asceticism so that I may make an end to birth and death.
Having heard this, the king said:
“Truly, those who are wise, learned, and contemplative of many things should indeed be attended upon.
Having seen these women and you, O Naga, I shall perform no small amount of merit.
In this context, “having seen these women” means she says, “Having seen both these daughters of the Nagas and you, I shall perform many meritorious deeds.”
Then the Naga king said to him:
"Truly, those who are wise and learned, who reflect upon many matters, should indeed be served.
And having seen both me and these women, O King, perform abundant meritorious deeds."
"In this matter, 'do' means you should do it, O Great King.

When this was said, Uggasena, desiring to depart, asked for leave, saying, "O King of Nagas, we have stayed long enough; we shall go now. Then the Great Being, wishing to give him wealth, said as he presented it:
"And here is my abundant gold, heaps of gold as tall as palm trees;"
"Having carried these golden houses away from here, have them build a wall of silver.
Having carried away five thousand loads of pearls mixed with beryl from here, let them spread them upon the ground of the inner palace; it shall become free of mud and free of dust."
“Dwell in such a place, O best of kings, in this most excellent and highly resplendent celestial mansion (vimāna).
Rule over the city of Bārāṇasī, which is prosperous and flourishing, O you of peerless wisdom.
In that context, “piles” refers to heaps the size of palm trees at various locations. “Golden houses” means golden dwellings.
"Nikkaddamā" means: thus the ground within your inner palace will become free from mud and free from dust. "Etādisaṃ" means:
such as this, with golden walls and silver ramparts, and floors strewn with pearls and beryl. "Phītaṃ" means: dwell in the prosperous city of Bārāṇasī. "Anomapaññā" means: one of unsurpassed wisdom.
Having heard his words, the king consented. Then the Great Being had a drum beaten throughout the Naga realm, proclaiming:
"Let the entire royal retinue take as much wealth as they desire, such as gold and bullion.
He also sent wealth to the king by means of many hundreds of wagons. The king, departing from the Naga realm with great splendor, returned to Bārāṇasī itself.
He departed. From that time on, it is said, the surface of Jambudīpa became possessed of gold.
Having delivered this Dhamma teaching, the Teacher said, "In this way, the ancient wise ones abandoned the prosperity of the nagas and observed the Uposatha vows," and then he identified the Jātaka:
"At that time, the snake-charmer was Devadatta, and Sumanā was the mother of Rāhula."
“Uggasena was Sāriputta, but I myself was the Nāga king Campeyya.
This concludes the commentary on the Campeyya Jātaka, the tenth.
[507] 11. Commentary on the Mahāpalobhana Jātaka.
“Having fallen from the Brahma-world,” the Teacher spoke this while dwelling in Jeta’s Grove concerning one who was pure yet defiled.
The story has already been related in detail below. On this occasion, however, the Teacher said, “This class of women, indeed, brings even a pure being to defilement,” and then related a past event.
Regarding the phrase "In the past, at Bārāṇasī," the story of the past should be expanded upon in the same manner as told in the *Cūḷapalobhana*.
At that time, however, the Great Being, having descended from the Brahma-world, was reborn as the son of the King of Kāsi;
he was named Anitthigandha Kumāra. He could not be held by women's hands; they fed him milk while he was dressed in male attire, and in the meditation chamber—
He lived there, yet he did not see women. To clarify this matter, the Teacher spoke these four verses:
“Having passed away from the Brahma world, a son of the gods possessed of great psychic power was reborn as the son of a king, amidst the fulfillment of all his desires.”
“Neither sensual pleasures nor the perception of sensual pleasure exist in the Brahma-world;
therefore, by means of that very perception, you should feel revulsion for sensual pleasures.
For him, a well-constructed meditation-hall had been prepared within the inner palace.”
Thus, secluded there, you should meditate alone in solitude:
“The king lamented, overcome by grief for his son:
‘This only son of mine does not enjoy sensual pleasures.’”
In that context, "in the fulfillment of all desires" means that one son of a god was reborn as the son of a king who stood in the possession of the fulfillment of all desires.
"He indeed" refers to that prince. "By that very [perception]" means by that very perception of jhāna produced in the Brahma-world.
"Well-constructed" means it was constructed by his father, having made it very pleasing. "Meditate in seclusion."
He lived there without seeing any woman. "He lamented" means he wailed.
This is the fifth verse of the king’s lamentation:
"What indeed might be the means here? Or who knows anything at all?"
“Whoever would entice my son, as one might desire sensual pleasures”—in this context, “what indeed is the means here?
(*ko nu khvettha upāyo*) means: what indeed is the means for him to enjoy these sensual pleasures? There is also a reading: “What indeed is the means here?
(*ko nu kho idhupāyo so*), but in the *Aṭṭhakathā* it says: “What indeed is that cause of seduction by which he fasts? (*ko nu kho etaṃ upavasitvā upalāpanakāraṇaṃ*).
It is said, "Who knows anything? The meaning is: who indeed knows the cause of this hindrance?
Following that, there are one and a half verses concerning the Fully Enlightened One:
"A maiden appeared right there, endowed with beauty and form;..."
“Skilled in dance and song, and adept in instrumental music.
“Having approached him there, she spoke thus to the king”:
in this context, monks, “there” means that among the junior dancers in the very same inner palace, there was a certain young maiden. “Adept” (padakkhiṇā) means well-trained.
“I would indeed entice him, if he were to become my husband.
This half-verse was spoken by the maiden.
In this context, “if he were to become my husband” means: “if he will be my spouse.”
To that princess who was speaking thus, the king said this:
“You yourself must entice him, saying, ‘He shall be your husband.
In this context, ‘your husband’ means he will become your lord; you alone shall be his chief queen. Go, entice him, and let him know the flavor of sensual pleasure.”
Having spoken thus, the king sent messengers to the prince’s attendants, saying, "Let them grant her an opportunity.

At dawn, she took her lute, went there, and standing not far outside the prince’s bedchamber, she played the lute with her fingertips and enticed him by singing in a sweet voice. To illustrate this matter, the Teacher said:
Having gone to the inner apartments, she spoke many verses connected with sensual pleasures—
charming, heart-stirring, lovely, and varied.
And having heard the sound of that woman as she sang, [he...]
Desire for sensual pleasures arose within him, and he questioned the people:
“Whose is this sound? Who is it that speaks so much, both high and low—a voice that touches the heart, is lovely, and is such a delight to my ears?”
“This, O King, is indeed delight; this is play that never ceases.
If you were to enjoy sensual pleasures, they would satisfy you more and more.
Come now, let us go a little further; she sings not far from here.”
"Let him sing in the vicinity of Assama, close to me.
Having sung beyond the wall, he entered the meditation chamber;
I bound him step by step, like a forest elephant.
“Having perceived the flavor of sensual pleasure, the quality of envy arose in him:
‘May I alone enjoy sensual pleasures; let no other man have them.
Then, seizing a sword, he set about killing men.”
“I alone shall eat; let there be no other man.
Thereupon all the people of the countryside gathered together and cried out:
“O Great King, this son of yours is harming the innocent folk!”
“The king married her and banished that kshatriya from the kingdom:
‘As far as my realm extends, you must not dwell therein.
Thereupon, taking his wife, he approached the ocean.”
Having built a leaf-hut, he entered the forest for gleaning.
Then a seer arrived there, traveling over the ocean;
at the time when the meal was ready, he entered his house.
“Yet his wife seduced him; see how truly dreadful it was!
Having fallen away from the holy life, he lost his supernormal powers.
And the prince, having gathered much forest root and fruit from gleaning,”
Taking his fire-sticks in the evening, he approached the hermitage.
But when the seer saw the kshatriya, he went toward the ocean;
thinking, "I shall go through the air," he sank down in the great sea.
And the khattiya, seeing the seer sinking in the great ocean,
out of compassion for him spoke these verses:
“Having come here in person by means of psychic power, while the waters were not yet overflowing, [he said:]”
Having approached a woman who has cultivated a female nature, you sink into the great ocean.
The Great Illusion is alluring and subverts the holy life;
knowing her, one should sink away from her and avoid her from afar.
“Flaming yet soft-spoken, difficult to satisfy like rivers;
knowing this, one should sink back [in fear] and avoid them from afar.
Whatever these women pursue, whether by desire or by wealth...”
Just as fire consumes its own place, they quickly burn him up.
Having heard the words of the Khattiya, the seer felt revulsion;
having regained the ancient path, he went through the air.
When the wise khattiya saw the seer traveling through the air,
he was moved by a sense of spiritual urgency and resolved to go forth.
Having then gone forth, he caused the passion for sensual pleasures to fade away.
“Having dispelled sensual lust, he went to the Brahma-world.
In this context, “the inner palace” refers to the prince’s dwelling place. “Much” means many various kinds.
“Performing songs connected with sensual pleasure” means singing songs dependent on sense-desires. “Of sensual desire” refers to the sensual desire of that Prince Anitthigandha.
[The sound] arose. They made their own female attendants, who were within their reach, understand [the situation].
"High and low" means both elevated and not elevated. "One might enjoy" means if one were to enjoy them. "They would please you" means these things called sensual pleasures would be to your liking.
Having heard the words "O wanton woman," he became silent. On the following day, the other [woman] sang again. Thus the prince became infatuated with her.
Desiring her arrival, he addressed his attendants and spoke the verse beginning with “Come now! (iṅgha).
“Tirokuṭṭamhī” means outside the wall of the bedchamber. “Mā añño” means let there not be another man who enjoys sensual pleasures [in this way].
“Hantuṃ upakkamī” means that having gone down into the street, he began to kill her. “Vikandiṃsu” means they cried out.
When the prince had struck several men, those men fled and entered their houses.
Not finding the men, he rested for a short while. At that moment, having assembled in the royal courtyard, they raised a clamor.
"He is one who harms people," they said; "he oppresses innocent folk—seize him! The king, by means of a stratagem...
Having had the prince taken away, he asked, "What should be done for him? When it was said, "Your Majesty, there is nothing else;
however, it is fitting to banish this prince from the kingdom along with that maiden," he did so. To clarify this matter, the Teacher spoke the verse beginning with "And him.
In that context, *vivāhesi* means "he banished. *Na te vatthabba tāvade* means "you must not stay here for long."
"You must not dwell in as much of my domain as there is. "Uñchā" means for the sake of gathering fruits and forest produce.
When he had entered the forest, the other woman cooked whatever was suitable to be cooked there and sat at the door of the leaf-hut, waiting for his arrival.
As time passed in this way, one day a resident of Antaradīpa...
A certain ascetic possessing supernormal powers, having departed from his hermitage, rose into the air as if treading upon water like a gem-slab;

while wandering for alms, he reached the upper part of a leaf-hut, and seeing smoke, thought, "I believe people dwell in this place," and descended at the door of the leaf-hut. She, seeing him, had him sit down.
Having become infatuated with him, she displayed feminine coquettish gestures and engaged in improper conduct with him.
To illustrate this matter, the Teacher said, "Then there," and so forth. In that passage, *isi māgacchī* means "the seer came.
*Samuddaṃ uparūparī* means "along the very surface of the ocean. *Passa yāva sudāruṇaṃ* means "Behold, monks, how truly dreadful!"
The meaning is that such an extremely cruel deed was committed by that young girl.
"In the evening" means at the time of sunset. "Having seen" means that, being unable to abandon him and having remained right there all day long, she saw the prince arrive in the evening;
thinking, "I shall go through the air," she made a gesture of leaping up in order to flee.
While doing so, he fell and sank into the great ocean. "Having seen the seer" means that, following after him, he went and saw him.
"Out of compassion": [he thought], "If this man had come by way of the earth, he would have fled and entered the forest;
since he has come through the air, even though he has fallen into the sea, he is still making the gesture of flying upward. Thus, having conceived compassion, and out of compassion for him alone—
He spoke. The meaning of those verses has already been explained in the *Tikanipāta*. "Disenchantment arose" means that disenchantment with sense pleasures was born.
"The ancient path" refers to the specific state of meditative absorption (*jhāna*) previously attained.

"Having gone forth" means that after leading that woman back to the human habitation and returning, he went forth as a seer (*isi*) in the forest and, having done so, caused the passion for sensual desires to fade away.
"Having shone forth, he went to the Brahma-world.

Having delivered this Dhamma teaching, the Teacher said, "Thus, monks, even pure beings become defiled on account of women," and after proclaiming the Truths, he identified the Jātaka. At the conclusion of the Truths, the monk who had been despondent—
He attained Arahatship. "At that time, I myself was the youth Anitthigandha," he said.
This concludes the eleventh commentary, the Mahāpalobhana Jātaka.
12. Commentary on the Pañcapaṇḍita Jātaka.
315–336. The Pañcapaṇḍitajātakam will appear in the Mahā-Ummagga.
The twelfth commentary, the Pañcapaṇḍitajātakavaṇṇanā, is concluded.
[509] 13. The commentary on the Hatthipālajātakam.
“After a long time, indeed, we see you!”—this was said by the Teacher while dwelling in Jeta’s Grove, concerning the Great Renunciation.
For then the Teacher, having said, “Monks, it is not only now that the Tathāgata has gone forth on the Great Renunciation;
in the past, too, he went forth,” he related a story of the past.
In the past, in Bārāṇasī, there was a king named Esukārī. His domestic priest had been his dear companion since childhood.
Both of them were childless. One day, while seated upon a comfortable couch, they deliberated:
"Our sovereignty is great, yet we have neither son nor daughter; what indeed should be done? Then the king—
He said to the chaplain, “Friend, if a son is born in your house, he shall be the master of my kingdom;
if a son is born to me, he shall be the master of the wealth in your house. Thus, they both made an exchange with one another.
Then, one day, the chaplain went to the village of Bhoga, and on his way back, as he was entering the city through the southern gate—
Outside the city, he saw a poor woman named Bahuputtikā. She had seven sons, all of whom were healthy:

one was carrying a cooking vessel and a mat, one was carrying a bed-frame, one was walking in front, one was behind, one was holding her finger, one was sitting on her lap, and one was on her shoulder. Then the chaplain questioned her.
“Good lady, where is the father of these children? “Master, these have no fixed father.

“How did you obtain seven sons such as these? Seeing no other way to explain, she pointed to the banyan tree standing at the city gate and said, “Master, it was from the presence of the deity dwelling in this banyan tree...”
"Having made a request, I obtained it; by means of this, my sons were given to me," he said. The chaplain replied, "In that case, you may go.
Having descended from his chariot and gone to the foot of the *nigrodha* tree, he grasped a branch and shook it, saying, "O deity, what indeed do you not receive from the presence of the king?
The king bestows a thousand [pieces of gold] upon you every year and performs an offering for you."
"You do not give him a son; what benefit has this woman of ill-repute done for you, that you gave her seven sons?
If you do not give our king a son, we shall have you uprooted from here on the seventh day from now and have you cut into pieces.
Having thus threatened the tree deity, he departed. He proceeded in this very manner...
On the following day as well, he spoke in this manner for six days in succession. On the sixth day, however, seizing hold of a branch, he said:
"O tree deity, only one night remains today; if you do not give me the king’s son, I shall finish you off tomorrow."
The tree deity, having reflected and understood the situation as it truly was, thought: "If this brahmin does not obtain a son, he will destroy my mansion;
by what means, then, would it be appropriate to give him a son?
She went to the presence of the Four Great Kings and reported the matter to them. They replied, "We shall not be able to give him a son."
They spoke. He went into the presence of the twenty-eight generals of the *yakṣas*, and they too spoke in the same manner.
Having gone into the presence of Sakka, the king of the gods, he told him [the news].
Sakka, too, while investigating whether or not the king would obtain suitable sons, saw four sons of the gods possessed of merit. It is said that in their previous existence, they were in Bārāṇasī...
Having become weavers, they divided whatever they earned from that craft into five portions;

they consumed four portions themselves, and taking the fifth, they gave it away together as an act of charity. When they passed away from there, they were reborn in the Tāvatiṃsa heaven, and from there in the Yāma heaven;
thus, experiencing prosperity in the six deva-worlds in both forward and reverse order, they wandered about.
At that time, however, it was their turn to pass away from the Tāvatiṃsa heaven and go to the Yāma heaven.
Sakka went to them, summoned them, and said, "Sirs, it is fitting for you to go to the human world;
be reborn in the womb of the chief queen of King Esukārī. Having heard his words, they said, "Very well, O Lord, we shall go."
"We have no need for the royal family; having been born in the house of the chaplain, we shall renounce sensual pleasures and go forth into homelessness at a very young age," they said.
Sakka, saying "Very well," took their promise and returned to report the matter to the tree deity.
With a joyful heart, she paid homage to Sakka and departed for her own celestial mansion.
On the following day, the chaplain also assembled strong men, had them take up axes, hatchets, and other tools, and went to the foot of the tree.
Grasping a branch of the tree, he said: "O deity, today is the seventh day of my begging of you;
now is the time for your departure. Thereupon, by means of great supernatural power, the tree deity [emerged] from the hollow of the trunk.
Having gone out, he addressed him with a sweet voice, saying, "Brāhmaṇa, let one son remain;
I will give you four sons. [The brāhmaṇa replied: "I have no need for your son; give me the son of our king. [The Bodhisatta said: "I give them to you alone. [The brāhmaṇa said:
"In that case, give two to me and two to the king. [The Bodhisatta said: "I do not give any to the king; all four are yours alone."
“I will give them; they shall merely be obtained through you, but instead of remaining at home, they will go forth into homelessness while still young.
“Give me your sons alone; the responsibility for ensuring they do not go forth is ours.
Having given him her boon of sons, she entered her own residence. From that time on, the honor shown to the deity became great.
The eldest son of the gods, having passed away, was reborn in the womb of the brahmin’s wife.
On the day of his naming ceremony, they gave him the name “Hatthipāla” and entrusted him to elephant keepers so that he would not go forth into the religious life.
He grew up in their care. At the time when he was walking on foot, the second [son of the gods] passed away and was reborn in the womb of a mare.
At the time of the third’s birth, they gave him the name “Horse-herd”; he grew up in the company of horse-herders.
At the time of the fourth’s birth, they gave him the name “Cow-herd”; he grew up together with cow-herders.
At the time of the fifth’s birth, they gave him the name “Goat-herd”; he grew up together with goat-herders. As they reached maturity, they attained great beauty and prosperity.
Then, out of fear that they might go forth [into homelessness], they removed from the king’s conquered territories all those who had gone forth;

not even a single person who had gone forth remained in the entire kingdom of Kāsi. Those princes became exceedingly cruel; in whatever direction they went, they plundered the offerings brought back from there.
When the king and the chaplain saw the physical perfection of Hatthipāla at the age of sixteen, they...
“The princes have grown up; it is time for the raising of their parasols. What indeed should be done? Having deliberated thus, [they thought]:
“From the time they are consecrated, these boys will become too arrogant. Then, renunciants will come from here and there;
seeing them, they will go forth [into homelessness]. When they have gone forth, the countryside will fall into turmoil. We shall test them.”
Thinking, “Let us wait until then; afterwards we shall consecrate him,” they both assumed the guise of ascetics and, wandering for alms, arrived at the gate of Prince Hatthipāla’s residence.
Upon seeing them, the prince was delighted and inspired with faith;
he approached, paid homage, and recited three verses:
“After a long time indeed we behold this brahmin with the appearance of a god,
with great matted locks, carrying a load, with mud-stained teeth and dust on his head.
After a long time indeed we behold this seer, who delights in the virtues of the Dhamma.”
“Clad in saffron robes, with a garment of bark as his covering—may your lordship accept from us a seat, water, and foot-washing water;
we ask your lordship’s favor; may your lordship show us the honor.”
In this context, "brahmin" refers to a brahmin who has banished evil. "Possessing the appearance of a god" means having the most excellent appearance;

the meaning is that he has entered the state of one who has gone forth, performing formidable austerities with supremely sharp faculties. "Carrying a khāri-load" means carrying a burden of a khāri measure.
"An ascetic" (isi) refers to one who stands having sought after the aggregate of virtue and so forth. "Delighting in the qualities of the Dhamma" means being devoted to the divisions of good conduct.
Regarding the word "seat" (*āsana*): having prepared a seat for them to sit upon, and having brought scented water and foot-unguent, he said this.
"Aggha" means: we ask whether these things—the seat and so forth—are acceptable (*aggha*). "Kurutu no" means:
may your reverence accept these things from us as acceptable.
Thus he spoke, warding off each one of them. Then the chaplain said to him, "Dear Hastipāla, you spoke thus because you thought, 'Who are these people?
"They are seers from the Himalayas," he replied. "We are not seers, dear one;
this is King Esukārī, and I am your father, the chaplain. "Then why did you assume the appearance of seers? "Because of you..."
“It is for the sake of testing you. “Why do you test me? “If, upon seeing us, you do not go forth, then we have come to anoint you in the kingship. “Dear father, I have no need for kingship;
I shall go forth. Then his father, saying, “Dear Hastipāla, this is not the time for going forth,” spoke the fourth verse while instructing him according to his own inclination:
“Seek wealth by means of learning; having established your sons and household, dear one, and having experienced all fragrances and flavors, the forest is good—the sage is praised therein.
Therein, “by means of learning” (*adhicca*) means by means of recitation. “Sons” means having raised the royal parasol and having provided for the actors in turn.
"Having increased with sons and daughters" means having established those sons in the household.
"All" refers to having experienced these—scent and flavor—as well as all other sensual pleasures (*vatthukāma*). "The forest is good; that sage is praised":
later, in old age, for one who has gone forth, the forest is found to be excellent. That sage who goes forth at such a time is [praised] by the Buddhas and others.
“He is praised by the noble ones,” he said.
Then Hatthipāla spoke this verse:
“The Vedas are not the truth, nor is the acquisition of wealth; one does not ward off old age by the acquisition of sons.”
"The virtuous say there is liberation from odors and tastes; through one's own karma, the arising of fruit occurs.
In this context, "not true" means that what they call heaven and the path, they do not accomplish; it is empty, unsubstantial, and fruitless.
And "not the acquisition of wealth" means that even the acquisition of riches, because it is shared by five [factors], does not possess a single uniform nature.
They grow old, dear one; indeed, no one is able to ward off either old age, or sickness, or death, even through the acquisition of a son.
These acquisitions (*upadhī*) are the very roots of suffering. Regarding "fragrances and tastes" (*gandhe rase*):

the wise, such as the Buddhas and others, speak of liberation (*mutti*) as the release from fragrances, tastes, and all other sense objects. "By one's own karma" (*sakammunā*) means by the very action performed by oneself.
"The rebirth and the accomplishment of results for beings occurs through their own karma, dear son, for beings are the owners of their actions.
Having heard the youth's words, the king spoke this verse:
"Truly, this speech of yours is the truth; rebirth as a result indeed comes about through one's own karma."
"And these aged parents of yours would see you for a hundred years in good health.
Therein, "for a hundred years in good health" means: "They would see you for a hundred years free from illness; and you too, living for a hundred years, should support your parents," he said.
Having heard that, the prince said, "Your Majesty, what is this you say? and spoke two verses:
“O King, best of heroes among men, for whom death is a witness and old age a friend,
even if one should know that he will never die, they would see him healthy for a hundred years.
Just as a man in the water who rows a boat brings it to the shore;”
"Even so, disease and constant old age lead the mortal into the power of the End.
In this context, "witness" refers to the nature of friendship. "By death" means: "Datta is dead," "Mitta is dead"—this refers to conventional death (*sammuti-maraṇa*).
"By old age" refers either to manifest old age, or to that with which one might have friendship—namely, this death and old age.
The meaning is: "One should not come with a friendly disposition.

If he drives them on, O Great King—just as a man, having placed a boat in the water at a river-ford and having embarked people bound for the further shore, might move it and push it along by exerting pressure with the rudder and pulling with the oar, and thus leads them to the further shore—in the same way, sickness and old age constantly [drive] one toward the End-maker.
"Only to bring them under the power of death.
Having thus shown the fragility of the life-process of these beings, he said: "Great King, you may stay;
while I am even speaking with you, sickness, old age, and death approach me. Be heedful!"

Having given his exhortation and paid homage to both the king and his father, he took his own attendants and departed from the city, renouncing the kingdom of Bārāṇasī with the thought, "I shall go forth.
Thinking, "This going-forth will indeed be glorious," the great multitude went out together with Prince Hatthipāla; the assembly was a league in extent. With that assembly...

Having reached the bank of the Ganges together with him, he looked at the water of the Ganges, performed the preliminary work for the *kasiṇa*, and having attained the meditative absorptions (*jhāna*), he thought:

"This gathering will be great; my three younger brothers, my mother and father, the king, and the queen—all of them with their retinues—will go forth into homelessness, and Benares will become empty until they..."
“I shall come back right here. He sat down right there, giving instruction to the great multitude.

On the following day, the king and the chaplain thought, “Prince Hatthipāla has already gone and sat on the bank of the Ganges, saying, ‘I will renounce the kingdom and go forth into homelessness taking the great multitude with me. Let us test Assapāla and then consecrate him.”
In just a few days, they arrived at the door of his house as well.
Seeing them, he approached with a serene mind and, saying things such as, "It has been a long time indeed since we have seen you," he conducted himself in that same manner.
They also addressed him in the same way and explained the reason for their coming. He said, "While my brother, Prince Hatthipāla, is still here, how could I [receive you] first?"
Having asked, "Will the white parasol come to me alone? and being told, "Dear brother, he has gone forth after saying, 'I have no need for kingship;

I shall go forth into homelessness,'" he asked, "But where is he now? When it was said, "He is sitting on the bank of the Ganges," he replied, "Dear brother, there is no business with the spittle spat out by my brother; for fools possess but limited wisdom."
“Beings are unable to abandon this defilement, but I shall abandon it. Speaking thus, as he taught the Dhamma to both the king and his father, he uttered these two verses:
“Sensual pleasures are a mire and sensual pleasures are a swamp; they are captivating, difficult to cross, and the realm of Death.
Sunk in this mire, mired in it, those of inferior form do not cross to the further shore. [The hunter thought:
"In the past he committed cruel deeds; now that he has been captured, he shall certainly not escape from me.
I will guard him with a barrier so that he does not commit cruel deeds again."
In this context, "mud" (*paṅka*) refers to any kind of mire. "Quagmire" (*palipa*) refers to fine sand mixed with soft mud.
Therein, sensual pleasures are called "mud" because they cause one to stick fast, and "quagmire" because they cause one to sink. "Hard to cross" means difficult to transcend.
