"The realm of Death" (*maccudheyya*) means the domain of Death. For beings who are both stuck in and submerged within these things are unable to cross over.
Being unable [to escape], they encounter both suffering and death, of the kind described in the Discourse on the Mass of Suffering (*Dukkhakkhandha-sutta*). Therefore he said:
"Sunk deep in this mire, those of inferior nature do not cross to the further shore. In that context, *byasannā* means sunk.
There is also the reading *visannā*, which has the same meaning. *Hīnattarūpā* means having an inferior mental disposition. They do not cross.
They are unable to go to the further shore, which is Nibbāna.

This, O Great King, is this sense of "mine" (*mamattabhāva*); having increased along with the horse-herders in the past, it committed much cruel and violent deeds against the multitude by means of plundering, harassing, and so forth. And that [sense of "mine"] was seized. Thus it is said.
"This is the ripening of that kamma which has been taken up by me.
For there is no escape for me"—this means that as long as the cycle of existence (*saṃsāra*) persists, there is indeed no liberation for me from this unwholesome fruit.
"I will guard him by restraining him"—now, closing off the doors of body, speech, and mind, I shall guard him by restraining him. For what reason? Lest he should commit such cruelty again.
"Kamma! For from this day forward, having ceased to do evil, I shall do only what is wholesome.
Having thus taught the Dhamma with these two verses, the horse-herd’s son gave this exhortation: "Stay back;
while I am conversing with you, sickness, old age, and death will come upon me. Then he [dismissed] the assembly that extended for a league.
Having taken him and departed, he went into the presence of Prince Hatthipāla.
Sitting in the air before him, he taught the Dhamma and said, "Brother, this assembly will be great; let us remain right here for now.
The other agreed, saying, "Very well. On the following day, the king and the chaplain approached Prince Gopāla by that same means.
Having gone to their residence, they were likewise welcomed by him, and they explained the reason for their coming.
He, too, like the young horse-herder, refused them, saying: "For a long time I have desired to go forth;
I have been wandering about searching for the going-forth as one searches for a lost ox in the forest. Therefore, [this matter] is like the track of a lost ox to my brothers."
"The path has been seen; therefore, I shall go by that very same path," he said, and recited this verse:
"Just as a man in the forest, O King, searching for a lost ox and not seeing it, so too is my purpose, the *esukārī* arrow, lost to me; how then should I, the King, not search for it?"
In this context, "O Esukārī" is how he addresses the king. "My welfare" means that my welfare, known as the life of renunciation, has perished like a bull in the forest.
"So haṃ" means: "Having seen today the path of those who have gone forth, how could I not seek renunciation?
O Lord of Men, I shall go by the very same path my brothers have traveled."
Then they said to him, "Dear Gopāla, wait for one day or two; after you have comforted us, you may go forth into homelessness.
He replied, "Great King, one should not say of a task to be done today, 'I will do it tomorrow.
A wholesome deed, indeed, must be performed this very day," and having said this, he spoke the following verse:
“Today indeed one wastes away, tomorrow one further declines;
knowing that the future does not exist, what wise man would reject a desire that has already arisen?
In this context, *hiyyati* means “wastes away”; *pareti* means “on the following day. This is what is meant: “O Great King, he who today...”
"Having said that a task to be done 'tomorrow' will be done 'the day after,' he does not do it;
he falls away from that [task] and is unable to perform that work. Thus did Gopāla preach the discourse known as the *Bhaddekaratta-sutta*.
This very meaning should be explained by means of the *Bhaddekaratta-sutta*: "The future does not exist"—that which is the future...
Knowing that "this does not exist," what wise man would reject or cast away the wholesome desire that has arisen?
Having thus taught the Dhamma with two verses, the cowherd’s son said, "Wait;
while I am conversing with you, sickness, old age, and death are approaching me. Taking a retinue of a league's distance, he departed.
He went into the presence of the two brothers. Hatthipāla taught the Dhamma to him as well.
On the following day, the king and the chaplain went to Ajapāla Kumāra’s residence by that same means;
being greeted by him in the same manner, they explained the purpose of their visit and said, "We shall raise the royal parasol for you. The prince replied:

“Where are my brothers? they asked. They replied, “We have no need for kingship,” and having abandoned the white parasol, they departed with a retinue three *yojanas* long and sat down on the bank of the Ganges.
“I will not wander about carrying on my head the spittle discarded by my brothers; I too shall go forth. “Dear son, you are still young and are our burden to support.”
“You shall go forth when you have reached the age of maturity. Then the prince said to them: “What are you saying?

Do these beings not die even in childhood and even in old age? There is no sign on anyone’s hand or foot indicating, ‘This one will die in childhood; this one will die in old age. I do not know the time of my own death; therefore—”
"I shall go forth this very day," he said, and spoke these two verses:
"I see a young maiden, like one intoxicated, with eyes like the *ketaka* flower;
Death seizes that girl and carries her away while she has not yet enjoyed wealth and is still in the prime of youth."
“Young, well-born, fair-faced, and handsome, with dark hair like scattered safflower—having abandoned sensual pleasures and left home beforehand, grant me your leave, O gods; I shall go forth.
In this context, *vo* is a mere particle; the meaning is simply “behold me. *Mattūpamaṃ* means intoxicated by laughter, smiles, and dalliance.
“Moving as if she were a celestial maiden. “With eyes like ketaka petals” means having wide, expansive eyes resembling the petals of a ketaka flower.

“Without having enjoyed life”: even while bearing such supreme beauty, a young woman in the prime of her youth, Death seizes her and departs, casting upon her parents a great sorrow before she has yet experienced the pleasures of life. “Well-born” means well-proportioned. “Fair-faced” means...
His face was like the full moon of Kanchanadāsa. "Sudassana" means one whose appearance is perfect due to possessing a supreme form.
"Sāma" means golden-hued. "Kusumbhaparikiṇṇamassu" means one whose facial hair is like the scattered filaments of a young saffron flower, both in its settled arrangement and its delicate texture.
By this it is shown that even a youth of such a kind falls under the power of death; for [death] is like one who shakes Mount Sineru as if it were a mere blade of grass.
It shows that Death proceeds taking [one] away without compassion: "Having first abandoned sensual pleasures and the home, grant me permission, O Lord;
I shall go forth. For when the bond of children and wife arises, that bond is difficult to sever; therefore he says:
"I shall abandon sensual pleasures and the home even earlier than before, and I shall go forth right now; grant me permission."
Having spoken thus, he said, "Stay here; while I am conversing with you, sickness, old age, and death will come upon me.
Having paid homage to both of them, he departed with a retinue of a league's length and went straight to the bank of the Ganges.
Hatthipāla also sat in the air, taught the Dhamma, and [said], "A great assembly will gather."
He sat down right there. On the following day, the chaplain, having sat down in the midst of his excellent palanquin, thought:
"My sons have gone forth; now I am left all alone, like a mere stump of a man. I too shall go forth.
While consulting with his brahmin wife, he spoke this verse:
“A tree receives its designation by means of its branches; but when its branches have been stripped away, they call it a stump.
O Vāseṭṭhī, for me who have now abandoned my sons, it is time for the life of a mendicant.

Therein, “receives its designation” means it acquires the conventional term “tree. “O Vāseṭṭhī” is an address to the brahmin woman. “For the life of a mendicant” means: “It is also time for my going forth; I shall go back to the presence of my sons.”
Having spoken thus, he summoned the brahmins; sixty thousand brahmins assembled.
Then he said to them, "What will you do? "But you, Master? "I shall go forth in the presence of my son.
"The hell is not hot for you alone; we too shall go forth. He [gave away] his eighty million in wealth.
Having entrusted [his wife] to the brahmin woman, he departed with a retinue of brahmins extending for a league and went straight to his sons.
Hatthipāla stood in the air together with that assembly and preached the Dhamma. On the following day, the brahmin woman thought:
"My four sons have gone, abandoning the white parasol, saying 'We shall go forth'; and now the brahmin too..."
“Having abandoned eighty crores of wealth along with the position of chaplain, he went into the very presence of his sons.
What shall I, all alone, do? I will go by the very path my sons have taken. Thus, citing a past example, she spoke this verse of exultation:
“As the cranes in the winter’s end, having burst through the nets that were set for them, fly away like swans from the abyss.”
"My sons and husband are departing; how then can I, knowing this, not follow after them?
In that context, "like cranes in the sky" means just as crane-birds travel through the air without being obstructed. "At the end of the cold season" means at the conclusion of the rains.
"The swans, having burst open the nets they had made"—it is said that in the past, ninety-six thousand golden swans [made a nest] sufficient for a year's supply.
Having deposited the rice in the Golden Cave, they do not go outside for fear of the rain, but dwell there for the four months of the rainy season.
Then a spider named Uṇṇanābhi weaves a web at the entrance of the cave.
The swans give two young swans a ball twice the size of their own; because of their great strength, the young ones break through that web and emerge in front.
They go; the rest follow by the path they have traveled. She, making this meaning clear, spoke thus.

This is what is meant: just as cranes move through the sky without being obstructed, so too, when the snow has melted and the rains have passed, two young swans break through the nets that were set and depart; then the other swans follow by the path they have taken.
"But now my sons have gone, having cut through the net of sensual desires like young swans breaking through a snare;
I too must go by the path they have taken. With this intention, she said: "My sons and my husband are departing;
how then can I, though discerning, not follow them?"
Thus she made a firm resolve, thinking, “How can I, knowing this, not go forth? I shall certainly go forth.
She summoned the brahmin women and asked, “What will you do? They replied, “But what about you, Noble Lady?
“I shall go forth,” she said. “We too shall go forth,” they replied. She then abandoned that wealth and [traveled] for a league—
Having taken their retinue, they went to the presence of their sons. Hatthipāla, seated in the air together with that entire assembly, preached the Dhamma.
On the following day, the king asked, "Where is the chaplain?
"Your Majesty, the chaplain and the brahmin lady have abandoned all their wealth and, taking a retinue two yojanas long, have gone to the presence of their sons."
The king, thinking, "Property without an owner falls to us," had wealth brought from his house.
Then the chief queen asked, "What is the king doing? When she was told, "He is having wealth brought from the chaplain's house," she asked, "Where is the chaplain?
Upon hearing that he had gone forth into homelessness together with his wife, she said, "This..."
“The king, deluded by ignorance, has had his own house filled with dung abandoned by a brahmin, a brahmin woman, and their four sons;

I shall awaken him by means of a simile. Having thus had meat brought from the slaughterhouse and piled in the royal courtyard, he cleared a straight path and had a net set around it. Seeing it from afar, vultures [flew] for its sake...
They descended. There, the wise birds, realizing the net had been spread, became too heavy to think, "We shall not be able to fly straight up";
so they discarded the flesh they had eaten, vomited it out, and without clinging to the net, flew straight up and departed.
But the blind fools, having eaten what they had discarded and vomited, became heavy and [could not fly straight].
Being unable to fly away, they came and became caught in the net. Then, having brought one vulture, they presented it to the queen.
Taking it with her, she went into the presence of the king and said, "Come now, Great King, let us witness a certain performance in the royal courtyard.
Opening the window-lattice, she said, "Look at these vultures, Great King," and spoke these two verses:
“Those birds that have eaten and then vomited depart;
but those who have eaten and did not vomit have come into my hands.
The brahmin has vomited his desires; you, however, will vomit them back.”
“O King, a man who eats what has been vomited is not worthy of praise.
In this context, “having eaten and having vomited” means having consumed meat and then having vomited it up. “You will re-vomit” means you will consume it again.

“One who eats what has been vomited” means one who eats what has been vomited by another. “Not worthy of praise” means that such a fool, being subject to craving, is not praised by the wise, such as the Buddhas and others.
He was not worthy of praise.

Upon hearing this, the king became filled with remorse, and the three realms of existence appeared to him as if ablaze. With a sense of spiritual urgency having arisen, thinking, "It is fitting for me to renounce the kingdom and go forth this very day," he spoke this verse in praise of the queen:
"Just as a strong man might lift up a weak man who has fallen and is sinking in the mud, so have you rescued me."
“Thus you have rescued me, O lady of Pañcālī, with well-spoken verses. In this context, *byasannaṃ* means submerged;

*visannaṃ* is also a reading for it. *Uddhareyya* means that one would lift [the person] up by seizing them by the hair or the hands and place them on dry land. *Udatārī* means he caused [me] to cross over from the mire of sensual desire (*kāmapaṅka*). *Udatāsī* is also a reading.
The reading is *pāṭho*; this is the very same meaning. There is also the reading *uddhaṭāsī*, which means "you have extracted [the essence]. *Pañcālī* means the daughter of the King of Pañcāla.
Having spoken thus, desiring to go forth at that very moment, he summoned his ministers and said, "What will you do?
"As for us, O Lord," they replied, "I shall go forth in the presence of Hatthipāla."

“We too shall go forth, O King,” they said. The king, having abandoned his sovereignty over the city of Bārāṇasī, which was twelve yojanas in extent, and saying, “Let those who wish raise up the white parasol,” went into the presence of the prince himself, accompanied by his ministers and taking along a retinue three yojanas wide.
Hatthipāla, seated in the air above that retinue as well, taught the Dhamma. The Teacher [then spoke] to the king.
Proclaiming his state as a renunciant, he spoke this verse: “Having said this, O Great King, Esukārī, the lord of Disā,
abandoned his kingdom and went forth, like an elephant breaking its bonds.”

On the following day, the people who had been left behind gathered in the city, went to the palace gate, and after announcing their purpose to the queen, they entered the residence. Having paid homage to the queen, they stood to one side and spoke this verse:
“The king, the most excellent hero among men, has renounced his kingdom and chosen the life of a wanderer.
You too must become as our king; protected by us, please rule the realm.”
In that context, "instruct us" means: "Having been protected by us, rule the kingdom according to the Dhamma.
Having heard the words of the great multitude, she spoke the remaining verses:
"The king, the most excellent hero among men, having abandoned his kingdom, has delighted in the life of renunciation."
“I too shall wander alone in the world, having abandoned delightful sensual pleasures.
“The king, the best of heroes among men, has renounced his kingdom and delighted in the going-forth;
I too shall wander alone in the world, having abandoned sensual pleasures as they were enjoyed.”
“Time passes and the nights flow by; the qualities of youth are gradually abandoned.
I too shall wander alone in the world, having renounced delightful sensual pleasures.
Time passes and the nights flow by; the qualities of youth are gradually abandoned.
“I too shall wander alone in the world, having abandoned sensual pleasures as they arise.
“Time passes, the nights hasten by; the qualities of youth are gradually cast off.
I too shall wander alone in the world, become cooled, having transcended all attachment.”
In this context, "alone" means that having been liberated from the confinement of children, wife, and defilements, I shall wander alone in this world.

"Sensual pleasures" refers to the strands of sensual desire, such as forms and so forth. "Whichever way they may be directed" means that I shall abandon them exactly as they are situated according to whatever direction they face;
the sense is that I shall not touch anything at all. "Times pass away" means that the periods of time, such as the morning and so forth, elapse.
"They carry across" means that, having become non-empty, they proceed by exhausting and consuming the life-formations (*āyu-saṅkhāra*).
"The qualities of age" refers to the three stages beginning with youth, or the ten sections beginning with the first decade.

"They abandon them successively" means that without reaching each successive section, they cease right there. "Become cool" means having abandoned the defilements (*kilesa*) which are hot by nature and which produce heat.
"Having become cool, and having transcended all attachments—such as attachment to sensual desire—I shall wander alone;
I will go into the presence of Prince Hatthipāla and go forth.
Thus, having taught the Dhamma to the great multitude with these verses, she summoned the wives of the ministers and said to them:
—“And what will you do, noble lady? she asked them. “I shall go forth into homelessness,” they replied. “We too shall go forth,” they said.
She said, “Very well,” and having had the gold treasuries and other stores opened in the royal palace, she had it written on golden plates:
“In such-and-such a place and such-and-such a place great treasures are buried; let those who need them take them, for they have already been given.”

Having spoken thus, he had a golden plate fastened to a pillar on the great floor, caused a drum to be beaten throughout the city, and having renounced his great prosperity, he departed from the city.

At that moment, the entire city was thrown into agitation: "The King and the Queen, it is said, are departing, having abandoned the kingdom with the thought, 'We shall go forth into homelessness. What shall we do here? and so they cried out from every side.
The people, abandoning their houses exactly as they had filled them, went out taking their children by the hands.
All the market stalls remained in the state they were laid out; there was no one who turned back to look. The entire city became empty.
The Queen also, taking a retinue three *yojanas* long, went right there. Hatthipāla [was with] her retinue as well.
Having sat in the air and taught the Dhamma, he set out toward the Himālaya mountains, taking with him a retinue twelve *yojanas* in extent.

The entire kingdom of Kāsi was thrown into agitation: "It is said that Prince Hatthipāla, having left the city of Bārāṇasī—twelve *yojanas* in size—empty, is going to the Himālaya mountains taking a great multitude of people with him, saying, 'I shall go forth. How much more so should we! Thus they cried.
Later on, his retinue became thirty *yojanas* in extent, and he entered the Himālaya mountains together with that assembly.
Sakka, perceiving this situation through his supernormal knowledge, thought: "Prince Hatthipāla has gone forth on the Great Renunciation;
a great gathering will take place, and it is necessary to find a dwelling place. He then commanded Vissakamma: "Go!"
“Having established a hermitage thirty-six yojanas in length and fifteen yojanas in width, prepare the requisites for one who has gone forth.
Having consented with “Very well,” he established a hermitage of the aforementioned dimensions on a delightful stretch of ground on the bank of the Ganges;
having arranged wooden mats, leaf-mats, seats, and so forth within the leaf-huts, he provided everything.

He had requisites for those who had gone forth constructed. At the door of each leaf-hut, he had a walkway built, demarcated by places for standing at night and by day, plastered with lime, and provided with a wall for support.
In various places there were flowering shrubs covered with fragrant blossoms of many colors. At the end of each walkway, he had a well filled with water, and near it—
Each was a fruit tree, and each one alone bore all kinds of fruits. All this came about through the power of the deities.

Vissakamma, having fashioned the hermitage grounds and placed the requisites for those who have gone forth within the leaf-huts, wrote inscriptions on the walls with vermilion, saying: "Whoever desires to go forth, let them take these requisites."
By his own supernatural power, he caused the terrifying sounds, the wild beasts, the birds, and the invisible non-human beings to retreat, and then returned to his own place.
Prince Hatthipāla entered Sakka’s hermitage by a narrow footpath;
seeing the letters, he thought, "Sakka must have learned of my great renunciation," and so he opened the door.
Having entered the leaf-hut, taken on the outward signs of the seers' renunciation, and emerged, he descended to the walking-path and paced back and forth several times.

Then, having ordained the rest of the multitude of people, as he was surveying the hermitage grounds, he assigned the leaf-hut to the women with young children in the middle section; after that, to the elderly women; and after that, to...
He gave the middle-aged women to the men after surrounding them on all sides.
Then, a certain king, having arrived thinking, "It is said there is no king in Bārāṇasī," looked upon the city adorned and prepared for him;
he ascended the royal residence and, seeing heaps of jewels here and there, [reflected]: "From the time I renounced such a city as this..."
“Indeed, this going forth will be sublime,” he said, and having asked the way from a drunkard, he set out toward the presence of Hatthipāla.
Hatthipāla, knowing that he had arrived at the edge of the forest, went out to meet him on the path;
sitting in the air, he taught the Dhamma to the assembly, led them to his hermitage, and ordained the entire company. By this same means, others as well—
Six kings went forth into homelessness; seven kings abandoned their wealth, and the hermitage became completely filled, extending for thirty-six *yojanas*.

To whoever contemplated any of the thoughts of sensual desire and so forth, the Great Man taught the Dhamma and explained to them the cultivation of the divine abodes (*brahmavihāra*) as well as the cultivation of the meditation objects (*kasiṇa*).
Having for the most part produced the meditative absorptions (*jhāna*) and direct knowledges (*abhiññā*), they...
Of the three portions, two portions were reborn in the Brahma-world.

Having divided the third portion into three parts, one part was reborn in the Brahma-world, one in the six celestial realms of sense-desire, and one, having performed service for the seers, was reborn in the human world among the three types of noble families.
Thus, Hatthipāla’s teaching became free from the states of hell, the animal womb, the realm of hungry ghosts, and the host of asuras.
In this island of Tambapaṇṇi, at the assembly of the Kuddāla, there were the Elder Dhammagutta, who caused the earth to tremble;
the Elder Phussadeva, a dweller of Kaṭakaṇḍhakāra; the Elder Mahāsaṅgharakkhita, a dweller of Uparimaṇḍala; the Elder Malayamahādeva; the Elder Mahādeva, a dweller of Abhayagiri;
the Elder Mahāsiva, a dweller of the Gāmantapabbhāra cave; and the Elder Mahānāga, a dweller of the Kāḷavallimaṇḍapa.

At the assembly of Mūgapakkha, at the assembly of Cūḷasutasoma, at the assembly of the wise Ayoghara, and at the assembly of Hatthipāla, they were the last men to depart. Therefore the Blessed One said:
"Hasten in what is good; restrain the mind from evil."
"For one who performs merit slowly, the mind delights in evil.
Therefore, the good must be done with the utmost haste.
Having delivered this teaching on the Dhamma, the Teacher said, "Thus, monks, even in the past, the Tathāgata made the Great Renunciation..."
Having said, "He has indeed gone forth," he identified the Jātaka: "At that time, King Esukārī was the Great King Suddhodana;
the Queen was Mahāmāyā; the family priest was Kassapa; the Brahmin woman was Bhaddakāpilānī;
the goat-herd was Anuruddha; the cowherd was Moggallāna; the horse-herd was Sāriputta; the rest of the assembly was the assembly of the Buddha; and the elephant-herd was none other than myself."
The Thirteenth: The Commentary on the Hatthipāla Jātaka.
[510] 14. The Commentary on the Ayoghara Jātaka.
"The night when they first set out..."—the Teacher spoke this while dwelling at Jetavana, concerning the Great Renunciation itself.
He related the story. Then, saying, "Monks, it is not only now that the Tathāgata has gone forth on the Great Renunciation;
in the past, too, he went forth," he brought up the past.
In the past, while Brahmadatta was reigning in Bārāṇasī, the chief queen of King Brahmadatta conceived a child.
Having conceived and protected her pregnancy until it was fully matured, she gave birth to a son just before dawn.
In a previous existence, a certain rival wife had made this aspiration: "May I be allowed to eat every child you give birth to.
It is said that she herself was barren and, out of anger toward the mother of her own children, made that aspiration.
She was reborn in the womb of a *yakkha*. The other woman, having become the king’s chief queen, gave birth to this son.
At that time, the *yakkhinī*, finding an opportunity, came while the queen was looking on, assumed a hideous form, seized the boy, and fled.
The queen cried out with a great voice, "A *yakkhinī* has seized my son and fled! The other woman also—
Chewing the boy like a root-tuber with a crunching sound, she departed after terrifying and threatening him by making gestures with her hands and other such movements.
When the king heard those words, he remained silent, thinking, "What can a female *yakkhinī* do?
Later, when it was time for the queen to give birth, he established a strict guard; the queen gave birth to a son once again.
The yakkhinī came, ate him as well, and departed. On the third occasion, the Great Being took rebirth in her womb.
The king, having assembled the great multitude, asked, "A certain yakkhinī eats every child born to the queen;
what indeed should be done? Then one person said, "Yakkhas, it is said, fear palm leaves; [let us give them to] the queen..."
"It is fitting to bind palm leaves to his hands and feet," he said. Then another said, "They fear an iron house; it is fitting to build an iron house.
The king, saying "Very well," assembled the smiths within his realm, commanded them, "Build an iron house," and assigned overseers to them.
They began constructing the house on a delightful spot of ground right inside the city.
Starting from the pillars, all the materials of the house were made of iron; in nine months, a great square hall made of iron was completed. It remained perpetually lit by lamps.
When the king knew that the queen’s pregnancy had reached maturity, he had the iron house adorned and, taking her with him, entered the iron house.
There she gave birth to a son endowed with the marks of grain and merit; they gave him the name Ayoghara Kumāra.

Having entrusted him to the nurses and provided great protection, the king took the queen, circumambulated the city, and ascended once more to the decorated upper story of the palace. The yakkhinī also went to the water gate [of Vessavaṇa].
Carrying water, she met her end. The Great Being, having grown up right there in the iron house, reached maturity and mastered all the arts in that very place.
The king, asking his ministers, "What is the age of my son?
and hearing from them, "He is sixteen years old, O King; he is brave and endowed with great strength, capable of resisting even a thousand *yakkhas*," [acted accordingly].
“I shall give him the kingdom; having decorated the entire city, bring him out from his iron house,” he said.

The ministers replied, “Very well, Your Majesty,” and after decorating Bārāṇasī for twelve leagues, they took a state elephant adorned with every ornament, went there, had the prince adorned, and seated him upon the back of the elephant.
“Your Majesty, having circumambulated the city adorned by your lineage, pay homage to your father, the King of Kāsi;
this very day you shall receive the white parasol,” they said.
As the Great Being circumambulated the city, he beheld the delightful parks, the delightful groves, the delightful lotus ponds, the delightful grounds, the delightful palaces, and so forth.
Having seen this, he thought, "My father has kept me in prison for all this time;
he did not allow me to see such a decorated city. What fault of mine could there be? He asked his ministers, "Sire, there is no fault of yours.
However, a certain *yakkhinī* devoured one of your two brothers; because of that, your father had you confined in an iron house. [He continued: "By means of the iron house..."
“Your life has been spared. Having heard their words, he thought:
“After dwelling for ten months in my mother’s womb as if in the Lohakumbhī hell or the Gūtha hell, from the moment I emerged from her womb, I have lived for sixteen years in this prison;
I was not even permitted to look outside, as if in the Ussada hell.”
"I was as if cast away; though released from the hands of the ogress, I am neither free from old age nor immortal.
What use have I for kingship? From the moment one stands in kingship, it becomes difficult to renounce.
This very day, having obtained my father's permission to go forth, I shall enter the Himālayas and become a monk. Having thus resolved, he circumambulated the city.
Having done so, he entered the royal palace, paid homage to the king, and stood before him.
The king, beholding the splendor of his body, looked toward his ministers with intense affection. They asked, "What shall we do, Your Majesty?
[The king replied: "Place my son upon a heap of jewels, consecrate him with the three conchs, and [clothe him] in a golden garland..."
“Raise the white parasol! The Great Being, having paid homage to his father, said:
“I have no need for the kingdom; I shall go forth into homelessness. Grant me permission to go forth. “Dear son, why do you reject the kingdom and go forth?
“Your Majesty, after dwelling in my mother’s womb for ten months as if in a hell of excrement, from my mother’s womb...”

Having escaped from the fear of the female spirit (yakkhinī), though I lived in prison for sixteen years and was not even permitted to look outside, feeling as if I were cast into a hell of intense suffering, and thinking, "I have been released from the hands of the female spirit," I am nonetheless neither ageless nor immortal.
This one called Death cannot be conquered by anyone; I am weary of existence (bhava) until—
"Before sickness, old age, and death come upon me, I shall go forth and practice the Dhamma; enough for me with kingship, O gods, grant me leave!
Having said this, he spoke the Dhamma to his father:
"The very first night that a young man dwells within the womb..."
He goes as if already risen; once gone, he does not turn back.
"Men do not grow old by fighting, nor are they overcome by force; they neither decay nor die.
All here are afflicted by birth and old age—this is my conviction, and thus I practice the Dhamma."
“The lords of the land, by force, conquer a fourfold army of beautiful appearance;
yet they are not able to conquer Death—this is my conviction, and so I practice the Dhamma.
Even those who are surrounded by elephants, horses, chariots, and infantry may be released from one danger;”
They do not strive to escape from Death; this is my conviction, and thus I practice the Dhamma.
With elephants, horses, chariots, and foot soldiers, heroes may shatter and destroy [their enemies], yet they do not strive to shatter Death;
this is my conviction, and thus I practice the Dhamma.
“Intoxicated elephants with temples split and bursting, trample cities and kill people;
yet they are not able to crush Death. This is my conviction: I practice the Dhamma.
Even archers who are skilled of hand, heroes who shoot from afar and hit the mark at the right moment—”
“Death does not strive to pierce him; this is my thought as I practice the Dhamma.
The oceans dry up along with their mountains and forests; all this, even over a long period, eventually dries up.
All this is broken down by the course of time; this is my thought as I practice the Dhamma.”
“Indeed, for all men and women alike, this life of living beings here is unstable and fleeting;
it is like a cloth to a gambler, or like a tree growing on a riverbank—this is my conviction as I practice the Dhamma.
Like the fruits of a tree, young and old alike, these mortals fall when their bodies break apart.”
Women, men, and those of middle stature—this is my thought as I practice the Dhamma.
This splendor, resembling the king of stars, has passed away; it is now gone forever.
For one who is aged, there is no delight, much less happiness; this is my thought as I practice the Dhamma.
“Yakṣas, piśācas, or even pretas—when enraged, they may breathe upon humans;
but they do not dare to breathe upon Death. This is my conviction as I practice the Dhamma.
Even toward yakṣas, piśācas, or pretas, when they are enraged, one performs appeasement.”
They do not bring about Death’s satisfaction; this is my conviction as I practice the Dhamma.
Kings, having recognized the fault, punish the offender, the corrupter, and the oppressor;
yet they cannot withstand Death’s punishment—this is my conviction as I practice the Dhamma.
“Those who are offenders, harmers, and oppressors may be brought to account by kings;
but they cannot bring death to account. This is my conviction: I practice the Dhamma.
One is not a kshatriya nor a brahmin merely by title; one is not wealthy, powerful, or even majestic [by such means].”
The King of Death has no regard [for such things]; this is my conviction, and thus I practice the Dhamma.
Lions, tigers, and even leopards, having overpowered them, devour those who are writhing;
yet they are not able to devour one seized by Death. This is my conviction, and thus I practice the Dhamma.
“Magicians, performing in the midst of a theater, may delude the eyes of people for a time;
yet they cannot delude Death. This is my conviction as I practice the Dhamma.
Even enraged, highly venomous serpents bite and even kill human beings;”
“Death does not dare to bite him; this is my conviction as I practice the Dhamma.
Just as physicians can neutralize the venom of angry, biting vipers, death cannot neutralize the venom of its own bite;
this is my conviction as I practice the Dhamma.”
“Dhammantari, Vettaraṇī, and Bhoja—having destroyed the poisons of serpents, they too are heard to have passed away when their time came; such is my thought as I practice the Dhamma.
Those who hold the spells, while studying the formidable incantations, attain invisibility through medicinal herbs.”
I do not seek an audience with the King of Death; this is my resolve: I practice the Dhamma.
"The Dhamma indeed protects the one who lives by the Dhamma; the Dhamma well-practiced brings happiness.
This is the benefit of the Dhamma well-practiced: the one who lives by the Dhamma does not go to a state of woe."
“Indeed, neither Dhamma nor non-Dhamma both have the same result;
non-Dhamma leads to hell, while Dhamma brings one to a happy destination.
In this context, “at which single night” refers to the fact that for the most part, beings take rebirth in the mother’s womb during the night itself.
They grasp [it], therefore he spoke thus. This, however, is the meaning here:

that which, having first taken rebirth-linking (paṭisandhi) for one night or by day, dwells in the womb known as the mother’s belly—that being, a "youth" (māṇava), is established in the state of the embryo (kalala).
"He goes forth as soon as he has arisen": that youth goes forth just as a cloud, known as "abha," has arisen.
Or, once produced, it returns back when struck by the force of the wind, just as it was:
"First there is the *kalala*; from the *kalala* comes the *abbuda*;
from the *abbuda* is born the *pesi*; from the *pesi* is produced the *ghana*."
Dense branches grow forth: hair of the head, body hair, and nails as well.
Whatever food, drink, and sustenance his mother eats, by that the person dwelling there within the mother’s womb is sustained.

This [embryo] constantly and continuously proceeds, undergoing the state of *kalala* and so forth within the mother’s womb, and, having emerged from the mother’s womb, attaining the state of the "weak ten-day" period (*mandadasaka*) and so forth. As it goes, it does not turn back;

for if, while proceeding thus, it were to return again from the *abbuda* stage to the state of *kalala*, or from the *pesi* stage to the state of *abbuda* and so forth, or from the "playful ten-day" stage (*khiḍḍādasaka*) to the state of the "weak ten-day" stage...
Or, it does not turn back from reaching the state of the "tenfold beauty" and so forth, or the "tenfold playfulness" and so forth.
Just as that cloud, being pulverized by the force of the wind, cannot think, "I arose in such-and-such a place;
now, turning back, I shall go there again and remain in my original state," but rather, having gone to whichever direction, it has simply gone there, and having vanished, it is gone.
That [previous state] has indeed vanished; likewise, as it proceeds through the stages of the *kalala* and so forth, it truly goes on.
In each respective part, the formations (*saṅkhāra*), acting as conditions for those preceding them, do not turn back from the prior state but break up right there where they are.
At the time of old age, the formations think: "Previously, we made this person young and endowed with strength."
It shows that when they think, "Let us turn back again and do it right there," they do not obtain [their goal], but rather vanish on the spot.
"Not fighting" means those who are fighting in a battle arrayed on both sides. "Not overcome by force" means not approached or possessed by physical strength or the strength of warriors.
"They do not age" refers back to the previous negative particle (*na*); even such as these...
The meaning should be understood as: "Men do not decay, nor indeed do they die.
For all this, O Great King—this entire circle of living beings—is constantly oppressed by birth and old age, like stalks of sugarcane being crushed by a great machine;
such is my conviction. It is for that reason that I have thought: "Having gone forth, I shall practice the Dhamma."
Intelligence arises; consciousness emerges.
"Fourfold" means endowed with the four components, beginning with elephants. "A terrifying army" means an army of a nature that is truly frightening.
"Victorious" means that sometimes certain kings are victorious by means of their own army. Not...
"Even those kings," meaning even they, are unable to conquer the army of Death (maccu), who possesses a great host;

they are not able to crush sickness, old age, and death. "Some are released": some enemies, though surrounded by these [forces] such as elephants and so forth, are released from the hands of their adversaries, yet they are not able to be released from the presence of Death. "They shatter" means by these...

With elephants and other [forces], they utterly destroy the cities of rival kings. "They crush" means that by crushing and grinding down the great masses of people, they bring them to the end of life.
"Not by Death" means that even when the time of death has arrived, they are unable to crush Death.
"With broken temples, overflowing" means having become overflowed in three places and dripping with rut-fluid; thus, their rut-fluid is flowing out.
"Meaning. "They cannot overcome Death": even they are not able to crush the Great Death (Māra). "Archers" (*issāsino*): archers are bowmen.
"Skilled" (*katahatthā*): well-trained. "Long-distance shooters" (*dūrepātī*): capable of shooting arrows to a great distance. "Unerring marksmen" (*akkhaṇavedhino*):
those who do not miss their mark, or those capable of piercing [a target] by the flash of lightning. "Lakes" (*sarāni*): the great lakes such as Anotatta and others.
They simply waste away. "Together with its mountains and forests" means that even the great earth, along with its mountain ranges and forest groves, wastes away.
For "all this," meaning all that which has come into the realm of conditioned phenomena (*saṅkhāra*), after remaining for a long duration, surely wastes away.
Upon encountering the fire at the end of an eon, even Mahāmeru itself melts away like a globule of honey in the mouth of a flame; not even an atom-sized conditioned phenomenon is able to endure.
"By way of time": having reached the period of time for destruction, everything breaks up; indeed, everything that has come into being (*saṅkhāragata*) must break up.
To illustrate this, the *Sattasūriya Sutta* (Discourse on the Seven Suns) should be cited.
"Fickle and unstable" means it is restless, incapable of remaining in its own state, and its very nature is inseparable from change and dissolution.
"The life of these living beings here in this world"—the life of these creatures existing here. "Like a cloth for a gambler, like a tree on a riverbank":
for a drunkard gambler, upon seeing liquor, drinks even after giving away the garment tied around his belly;
and just as a tree growing on a riverbank perishes when the bank collapses, so too are sentient beings, just as unstable as that cloth and that tree.

"Life, O King. "Like fruits from a tree": just as ripe fruits, struck by the wind, fall from the top of a tree to the ground, even so these youths—struck by the wind of old age—fall from life onto the earth of death.

"The young" refers even to those remaining in the stage of the *kalala* (embryonic mass). "Those of middle stature" refers to hermaphrodites (*ubhatobyañjanaka*) and eunuchs (*napuṃsaka*) who stand between women and men.
"Resembling the king of stars": just as the king of stars (the moon) wanes during the dark fortnight and waxes again during the bright fortnight, the decay of beings is not like that.
For whatever has passed away for beings, that is now simply gone; there is no returning to it again.
Whence can there be happiness? For one worn out by old age, there is no delight even in the strands of sensual pleasure (*kāmaguṇa*), much less the happiness arising in dependence upon them.
"From where? means from wherever. "Yakkhas" refers to yakkhas of great psychic power (*mahiddhika*). "Pisācas" refers to the *paṃsupisācakas* (dust-demons).
"Petas" refers to those belonging to the realm of the departed (*pettivisayika*). "They breathe upon" means they afflict with the wind of their breath, or the meaning is that they enter [the body].
"But not by Death" means that even they are unable to afflict or enter [the body] by means of their breath. "They perform a propitiatory rite" means by way of an offering (*balikamma*).

They ask for forgiveness and seek to appease them. "Offenders" (*aparādhaka*) refers to those who have committed offenses against the king. "Corrupters" (*dūsaka*) refers to those who corrupt the kingdom.

"Harassers" (*heṭhaka*) refers to those who harass the world through such acts as housebreaking. "Kings" (*rājāno*) means kings. "Having known the fault" (*viditvāna dosaṃ*) means having recognized the offense;
the meaning is that they punish with a penalty appropriate to the crime. "Not even Death" (*na maccuno*) means that even they are not able to punish Death itself.
*Nijjhapetuṃ* means to cause [the king] to be appeased by the witnesses making known their own innocence. *Na aḍḍhā balavā tejavāpi*: "These are wealthy;
this one is powerful through physical strength, wisdom, and so forth; this one is majestic"—even in this way, there is no regard for the vassal king;
there is no regard, affection, or endearment toward even a single being; rather, it is all...
"He crushes" is what is shown. "Having overcome by force" means having conquered through violence. "Not by death" means that even they are unable to devour Death.
"Practicing" means practicing illusion (*māyā*). "Deluding" means they delude by presenting what is unreal as real.
"Possessing fierce power" means being endowed with intense poisonous energy. "Physicians" means poison-doctors. "Dhammantari" [is the name of a specific type of physician].
Vettaraṇī and Bhojā—these are physicians with such names. "Reciting the Ghora" means they are studying a spell named Ghora.
Having recited either the Ghora or the Gandhārī spell, and having taken medicinal herbs, they go to the place where their adversaries cannot see them by means of those herbs.

"Dhamma" means the Dhamma of good conduct. "Protects" means that by which one is protected, it in turn protects him. "Happiness" means it brings about happiness in the six celestial realms of sensual pleasure. "Leads to" means it carries one there by way of rebirth-linking.
Thus, having taught the Dhamma to his father with twenty-four verses, the Great Being said:
"Great King, let your kingdom remain yours alone; I have no need for it. However, while I was merely conversing with you, sickness, old age, and death..."

Having said, "Stay, you all," he broke his iron chain like a rutting elephant, and like a lion cub breaking through a golden cage, he abandoned sensual pleasures, paid homage to his parents, and departed.
Then his father, thinking, "I have no need for the kingdom either," renounced the throne and went forth together with him; and when he had departed—
The queen, the ministers, the brahmins, the householders, and others—all the inhabitants of the city—abandoned their homes and went forth.
A great gathering occurred, and the assembly became twelve yojanas in extent. Taking her with him, the Great Being entered the Himavat mountains.
Knowing that he had departed, Sakka dispatched Vissakamma, who [constructed] a [palace] twelve yojanas in length...
He had a hermitage built with a width of seven yojanas and had all the requisites for those who have gone forth prepared.
From this point on, the Great Being’s renunciation, his giving of exhortation, his destination in the Brahma-world, and the fact that the assembly would not go to the states of misery—
all these are to be understood according to the method already explained below.

Having delivered this Dhamma teaching, the Teacher said, "Thus, monks, even in the past the Tathāgata went forth on the Great Renunciation," and he identified the Jātaka: "At that time, the parents were the royal family;
the rest of the assembly was the Buddha's own retinue; and the wise Ayoghara was none other than myself."
The fourteenth: The Commentary on the Ayogharajātaka.
The Summary of Birth Stories (Jātakuddāna):
Mātaṅga, Cittasambhūta, Sivi, Sirī, and Rohaṇa;
The Haṃsa, Sattigumba, and Bhallā; Somanassa and Campeyyaka;
Palobha and Pañcapaṇḍita, Hatthipāla and Ayoghara—these twenty Jātakas are recited in the fourteenth [section].
The commentary on the Vīsatinipāta is finished.
(The fourth part is finished.
Homage to that Blessed One, the Worthy One, the Perfectly Self-Awakened One.
The Jātaka Commentary (Jātaka-aṭṭhakathā) in the Khuddakanikāya (Fifth Volume)
16. The Book of the Thirties [511] 1. The Commentary on the *Kiṃchanda-jātaka*. "What is his desire?
What is his intention?"—this was related by the Teacher while dwelling at Jetavana, concerning the performance of the Uposatha ceremony.

One day, when many laymen and laywomen who had observed the Uposatha had come for the purpose of hearing the Dhamma and were seated in the Dhamma Hall, the Teacher asked, "Lay followers, have you observed the Uposatha?
When they replied, "Yes, Venerable Sir," he said, "It is well that you have performed the Uposatha;
by the result of performing even half the Uposatha rites of former times, you have attained greatness."
Having said, “They obtained fame,” when requested by them, he related a story of the past.
In the past, in Bārāṇasī, Brahmadatta was ruling his kingdom according to the Dhamma;

he was faithful and diligent in the practice of giving, virtue, and the observance of the Uposatha. He also encouraged his other ministers and officials in acts such as giving. However, his chaplain was a backbiter.
He was a taker of bribes and a fraudulent judge. On the Uposatha day, the king summoned his ministers and others and said, "Observe the Uposatha.

The chaplain did not undertake the Uposatha. Then, having taken a bribe during the day and having committed a fraudulent judgment, he arrived at the royal court; the king, asking the ministers, "Are you observing the Uposatha? [said to him], "And you too—"
"Teacher, are you observing the Uposatha? he asked. He replied, "Yes," and having uttered this falsehood, he descended from the palace.
Then a certain minister rebuked him, saying, "Are you not indeed observing the Uposatha? He said, "I ate only at the proper time;
however, having gone home, rinsed my mouth, and resolved upon the Uposatha, I shall not eat again tonight. At night—
“I will observe the precepts; in this way, my half-Uposatha observance will be fulfilled,” he said. “Very well, teacher,” [the other replied].

He went home and did exactly that. On another day, while he was sitting in that court of justice, a certain virtuous woman, unable to go home because she was involved in a lawsuit, thought, “I shall not let the Uposatha observance pass me by,” and as the time drew near—
At that time, she began to rinse her mouth. At that moment, a heap of well-ripened mangoes was brought to the brahmin.
Knowing that she was observing the Uposatha, he gave them to her, saying, "Eat these and observe the Uposatha.
She did so. This was the extent of the brahmin’s deed.

Then, at a later time, having passed away, he was reborn in a delightful region of the Himalayas on the bank of the Kosikī Gaṅgā, in a three-league-wide mango grove that had attained the highest splendor.

There, upon a golden celestial mansion (vimāna), on a decorated couch, he appeared like one just awakened from sleep—fully adorned and prepared, possessing supreme beauty, and surrounded by sixteen thousand celestial maidens. He...
He experienced that splendor and prosperity only during the night. For his rebirth as a *vemānika* peta was a result corresponding to his past actions;

therefore, at the rising of the dawn, he would enter a mango grove, and at the very moment of entering, his divine form would vanish and a body the height of eighty palm trees would manifest, its entire frame—
He meditates; he becomes like a *kiṃsuka* tree in full bloom. On each of his two hands there is but a single finger, and upon them are nails the size of large spades.
With those nails, tearing and ripping out the flesh of his own back, he eats it;
overcome by pain and uttering great cries, he experiences suffering. When the sun has set, that body vanishes.
A divine body is produced; adorned and prepared celestial nymphs surround him, taking up various musical instruments.
Experiencing great prosperity, he ascends a celestial palace in a delightful mango grove.
Thus, by the result of giving mango fruits to a woman observing the Uposatha, he obtains a mango grove three leagues in extent.
Furthermore, as a result of taking bribes and committing fraudulent gambling, he had the flesh torn from his back and ate it;
as a result of observing the half-Uposatha, he enjoyed prosperity during the night, surrounded by sixteen thousand dancing girls with whom he dallied.
At that time, the King of Bārāṇasī, having seen the fault in sensual pleasures, went forth into the ascetic life of an *isi* and dwelt on the delightful bank of the lower Gaṅgā.
Having had a leaf-hut built on a certain spot of ground, he lived there, sustaining himself by gleaning.
Then one day, a mango fruit as large as a great jar fell from that mango grove into the Ganges and was carried along by the current toward the bathing place where the ascetic used to bathe.
While washing his face, he saw it coming down the middle of the river.
Having seen it, he crossed the water, went there, took it, and brought it to his hermitage.
Placing it in the fire-hall, he sliced it with a knife and ate just enough to sustain himself.
He concealed the remainder with plantain leaves and ate it day after day until it was completely exhausted. When that was finished, he was unable to find or eat any other fruit.
Bound by craving for the taste, thinking, "I shall eat only that mango fruit," he went to the riverbank.
Looking at the river and making the firm resolve, "I will not rise until I have obtained a mango," he sat down.
There, without food, he withered away from the wind and heat for one day, two, three, four, five, and six days, [seeking] a mango.
He sat gazing [at the river]. Then, on the seventh day, the river deity, reflecting and perceiving the situation, thought:
"This ascetic, being subject to craving, has sat for seven days without food gazing at the Ganges. It is not right that I should not give him this mango fruit;
if he does not obtain it, he will die. I shall give it to him. Having thought thus, she came into the sky above the Ganges.
Standing there and conversing with him, she spoke this first verse:
“What is your desire? What is your purpose? Why do you meditate alone in the heat?
What do you hope for? What do you seek? For what reason, O Brahmin?”
In this context, *chanda* means intention (*ajjhāsaya*). *Adhippāya* means thought (*citta*). *Sammasi* means you are waiting. *Ghammāni* means in the summer heat. *Esaṃ* means seeking.
*Brāhmaṇa* is how he addresses the ascetic because of his renunciant status. This is what is meant:
"O Brahmin, with what intention, thinking what, longing for what, seeking what, and for what purpose are you here on this bank of the Gaṅgā?"
“Sitting there gazing at the Ganges,” he said.
Having heard that, the ascetic spoke these nine verses:
“As a great rain-cloud, as a well-rounded jar;”
“Just like that mango fruit, supreme in color, fragrance,
and taste— seeing it being carried away by the current in the middle of the pure river,
I seized it with my hands and brought it to the sacrificial fire-chamber.”
“Then, having placed it upon plantain leaves myself, I cut it up with a knife; thereby my hunger and thirst were dispelled.
Thus, with my distress gone and my suffering overcome, I became one who endures hardship.”
I find no gratification in any other fruits whatsoever.
Surely death will come to me after drying me up—
death that will bring me to that mango whose fruit is sweet, with a delicious core and enchanting to the mind.
“O Yamuddhari, you who were being carried away from the great ocean—
‘Everything has been told to you by me, because I am observing the fast;
I am seated here with my husband, covered all over with thick hair.’”
“You yourself must tell me, O lady who does not flee:
Who are you, O beautiful one? For what purpose have you come, O fair-waisted one?
You are like a woman adorned with a burnished gold band, like a tigress born upon a mountain ridge.”
"Whatever women there are among the gods who serve as the attendants of the gods,
and whatever women exist in the world of humans endowed with beauty—
there is none equal to you in beauty, whether among the gods, the gandhabbas, or in the world of humans."
“You have been questioned by me, O lady of beautiful limbs; tell me your name and your kin.
In this context, *vāridharo kumbho* means a water-jar. *Supariṇāhā* means well-proportioned.
*Vaṇṇagandharasuttamam* means supreme in color, fragrance, and flavor. *Disvāna* means having seen. *Amalamajjhe* means in the stainless center. *Devatam*.
Speaking thus, he said: "With hands" means with his own hands. "I brought the fire-sanctuary" means I brought [him] to my own hall for the fire-sacrifice (*aggihuta*).
"Having divided" means having cut apart; there is also a reading, "having carved. "He ate" is the remainder of the text.
"It took away from me" means that as soon as it was placed on the tip of my tongue, it pervaded the seven thousand channels that carry flavors, and [removed] my hunger and thirst.
*Hari*: "Free from distress" (*apetadaratha*) means one whose physical and mental distress has departed.
For it removes all distress from him, just as if he had eaten ambrosial food (*sudhābhojana*). "Became exhausted" (*byantībhūta*): its state of ripeness has come to an end;

the meaning is that the ripe mango has become completely consumed. "Enduring suffering" (*dukkhakkhama*): by means of suffering and unpleasantness, through both physical endurance and mental endurance.
"Endowed [with this]. However, he indicates that regarding other fruits such as plantains (*kadalī*) and jackfruit (*panasa*), he does not obtain even a slight taste;
rather, as soon as they are placed upon his tongue, they all turn out to be bitter for him.
"Having withered" means having withered and dried them up through lack of food. "That of mine" means that which belongs to me. "Of whom" means of whichever person.

The meaning is "it was. This is what is said: "I think that this mango, which was sweet to me and which I rescued from the great ocean—the vast mass of deep and wide water—in which I was being swept away, will bring about my death;
without obtaining it, my life will not continue. "I am fasting" means [due to] hunger and thirst.
"I have approached and am dwelling here. "Seated by the delightful [river]" means that I am seated by a beautiful river.
"Filled with many *puthuloma* [fish]" means this river is filled with many large fish (*puthuloma*), and thus it is vast and extensive;
the intention is: "Perhaps there might be safety for me from this. "Not fleeing" (*apalāyinī*)—he addresses that deity, meaning she stands before him without having fled.
“Apalāsinī” is also a reading; the meaning is: one whose body is free from blemish and faultless. “Kissa vā” means: for what reason have you come here?
He asks this. “Rūpapaṭṭapalimaṭṭhīvā” means:
like a gold plate that has been thoroughly polished. “Byagghīvā” means: by way of graceful charm.
Like a young tigress cub. "Of the gods" (devānaṃ) means of the sense-sphere gods (kāmāvacara-deva).

"And in the world of humans" (yā ca manussalokasmiṃ) means those who are in the world of humans. "Women endowed with beauty" (rūpenānvāgatitthiyo): she spoke thus out of self-conceit, thinking, "There are no women endowed with beauty [equal to me].
For her intention was: "There should be no one indeed who possesses a form like yours. "In the world of gandhabbas and humans" (gandhabba-manussaloke).
Among the gandhabbas who depend on the scent of roots and so forth, and in the world of humans.

"Cārupubbaṅgī" means one endowed with beautiful fore-limbs, characterized by shapely thighs. "Nāmañca bandhave ca" means "tell me my own name and lineage, and [the names of] my kinsmen"—thus she speaks.
Then the daughter of the gods spoke eight verses:
“O Brahmin, that delightful Kosika river upon which you sit— there I am,
rising from the depths of the earth, with a flood carrying a choice torrent of water.
The mountain caves are many and filled with various groves of trees.”
They flow with me as their head, surging like rain-clouds.
Moreover, many forest streams bearing dark waters,
and many rivers rich in treasures, overflow with water.
“Those mangoes, rose-apples, breadfruits, nīpas, palmyra palms,
and udumbara trees bring forth many kinds of fruit again and again.
Whatever fruit falls into the water from either bank— ”
“Without doubt, that is the fruit of the ear, following one's own mastery.
Having understood this, O wise one of broad insight, listen to me:
do not take pleasure in attachment, but restrain it, O lord of men.”
“I do not consider you to be growing old, O Raṭṭhābhivaḍḍhana, you who,
though being entreated, yearn for death, O royal sage.
Your fathers know of this, as do the gandhabbas and the gods together with Indra.”
"And those seers in the world who, being self-restrained, are ascetics—they too undoubtedly know [this], for they are established and renowned.
In that regard, "Kosikī" refers to you, O Brahmin, who are seated upon the lovely Kosikī River as it flows toward the Ganges. "Arising from a deep abode" means...
"Caṇḍasota-bhūsa-ālaya" means those who dwell in that celestial mansion (vimāna) whose abode is the Caṇḍasota;
the meaning is "the inhabitants of the Gaṅgaṭṭhaka mansion. "Varavārivahoghasā" means endowed with a flood that carries excellent water.
"Pamukhā" indicates: "These aforementioned mountain caves make me their leader; I am their chief. "Abhisandanti" means... [they flow].
They flow and move; the meaning is that they come from here and there and enter me, the Kosikī Gaṅgā.
"From the woods" means not only from the caves, but also many waters from many woods enter me.
"Bearing a flow of blue water" refers to the mass of water joined with blue water the color of jewels.
"Carrying [water]" means they bear it. "Possessing the wealth of nāgas" means endowed with water, which is either the source of sustenance for nāgas or is reckoned as their wealth.
"With water": he shows that many such rivers completely drench and fill me with water. "Those" refers to those rivers.
"Bringing forth" means they draw these mangoes and other fruits toward themselves; for all these [words] are used in the sense of the object (*upayoga*).
[The words] are in the nominative plural. Alternatively, *tā* is the accusative plural. "Bringing" (*āvahantī*) means these mangoes and other fruits come from those rivers;
the sense is that they approach. The intention is that once they have approached in this way, they enter my stream.
"Of the stream" (*sotassa*): whatever fruit falls from the trees growing on both banks into my water, all that is mine.
"It follows the very course of the stream. "There is no doubt about this"—thus he explained the reason for the mango fruit's arrival via the river current.
"O wise one, O one of broad wisdom"—both are merely forms of address. "Do not find pleasure"—thus, do not find pleasure in the attachment of craving (*taṇhābhisaṅga*).
"Restrain"—he advises the king, saying, "restrain it. "Increasing"—the state of increasing wisdom, that is, the state of being a sage (*paṇḍita*).
*Raṭṭhābhivaḍḍhana*: one who causes the kingdom to increase. *Āceyyamāno*: being filled with flesh and blood, growing;
the meaning is "being as if young again. *Rājisī*: he addresses him by that title. This is what is meant:
"That you, wasting away through lack of food, while still being young, desire death out of greed for mangoes—certainly I do not [approve] this of yours..."
"I consider myself wise. Regarding the word "his":

for that person who is subject to craving, the Brahmās—who have attained the designation "fathers"—together with the gods of the sense-sphere (kāmāvacara) and the Gandhabbas of the aforementioned kind, as well as the seers possessing the divine eye, [perceive] his state of being subject to craving.
And they know this without doubt. It is not surprising that those possessed of psychic power (*iddhimanta*) should know, "Such-and-such a person is indeed a slave to craving.
Furthermore, having heard the words of those who speak thus, even their renowned attendants who stand in their presence also come to know it.
For there is no such thing as secrecy for one who performs an evil deed; such is the case with the ascetic.
Arousing a sense of spiritual urgency, she spoke thus.
Then the ascetic recited four verses:
“Having understood in this way that all phenomena are subject to disintegration and the passing away of life, the wise one—”
No evil accrues to that man, provided he does not intend his death.
"O you who are known as one belonging to the assembly of seers, though thus recognized by the world, you are merely a counterfeit of the noble ones; you desire to pursue an evil deed."
“If I die, O broad-hipped one, on your bank,
there will undoubtedly come upon you ill repute once I have passed away.
Therefore, O woman of beautiful waist, guard yourself against this evil deed.”
“Let not all the people revile me after I have passed away.

In this context, “having thus understood” means having understood in the same way that I know both virtue and impermanence; it refers to one who stands [firm] as such. “The wise one” (vidū) means the one who knows.
“All phenomena” (sabbadhamma) means the entire dhamma of good conduct. For the threefold good conduct is what is meant here by “all phenomena.”
This is the intended meaning. "Destruction" means dissolution. "Falling away" means death. "Of life" means of the lifespan. This is what is meant:

for a wise person who stands thus having understood, who knows all the factors of good conduct and the impermanence of life—for such a person, evil does not accumulate or increase, even if they do not intend their own destruction.
"Of him": he does not intend or plan for the killing of that other person who has come into his range;
he does not intend the killing of another person, nor does he destroy the property of another.
"And I, having not intended the killing of anyone at all, but merely sitting looking at the Ganges with my attachment fixed on the ripe mango—what unwholesome deed do you see in me?"
*Isipūgasamaññāta*: well-known by the host of seers (*isigaṇa*), esteemed by the seers. *Evaṃ lokyā*:
known thus as "you" because you are beneficial to the world by removing evil. *Satī*: "O mindful one," "O beautiful one," "O supreme one"—this is an address.
*Anariyaparisambhāse*: possessed of ignoble, unseemly speech such as "His fathers know [him]," and so forth.

"Jigīsasi": although [the mango] does not exist within me, a sinner, you revile me in this way and, disregarding your own imminent death, you search for and produce [the desire for] your own evil deed.
"Tīre te": on your bank, namely, on the bank of the Ganges. "Puthusussoṇī":
endowed with broad and beautiful hips. "Petā": having gone to the other world without obtaining ripe mangoes.
The meaning is "I consider. *Pakuṭṭhāyi* means she reviled, censured, and reproached. There is also a reading, *pakvatthāsī*.
Having heard that, the daughter of a deity spoke these five verses:
"I have understood this; tell me what is impossible to do. I give myself and my mother to you."
“He who, having abandoned the strands of sensual pleasure, has resolved upon peace and the Dhamma.
‘He who, having left behind former bonds, stands amidst later fetters;
if he practices what is unrighteous, his evil increases.’”
“Come, I shall lead you there; be at ease as you wish.
I will bring you to a cool place; dwell there free from anxiety.
O subduer of enemies, with your limbs as delicate as the juice of flowers,” he said.
Cranes, peacocks, and divine birds, *kolaṭṭhi*, honey-sālikas,
and flocks of swans warbled there, while cuckoos raised their voices.
"The mango trees here, with their spreading branches, resemble heaps of straw."
“Kosamba, salaḷa, and nīpa trees, hanging with ripe tāla fruit.
In this context, “I do not know this” means: “When you say, ‘Censure will come upon you,’ you speak for the sake of the mango fruit”—this is the reason I do not know.
“One who speaks what is unbearable”: kings indeed endure what is difficult to bear; it is for that reason she addresses him thus.
He spoke thus: "Myself"—having embraced him and leading him to the mango grove—she said, "I give both myself and that mango.
"Sensual pleasures" refers to the objects of desire adorned with golden garlands and white parasols.

"Peace and the Dhamma" means both virtue, which is termed peace through the subsiding of misconduct, and the Dhamma of good conduct. "You are established" refers to you who have attained these qualities.
Or the meaning is: "established in these.
"Former fetter" (*pubbasaññoga*) means a prior bond. "Later fetter" (*pacchāsaṃyojana*) means a subsequent bond. This is what is meant:
"O ascetic, you who have abandoned the great glory and power of sovereignty for the sake of a craving for the mere taste of an *amba* fruit..."
Having been caught [in the net], he sits by the riverbank drying himself, disregarding the wind and the sun;

he is like a person who, after crossing the great ocean, sinks away at the shore. Such a person, being dominated by craving for flavors, practices what is unrighteous, and his evil deeds increase through that very craving for flavors.
Thus, censuring the ascetic, she spoke as follows.
"Be at ease as you wish" means: by all means, be without attachment to this mango grove. "In the cold" means in the cool mango grove.
As she was speaking thus, the deity embraced the ascetic, laid him down upon her breast, and flew up into the sky;

seeing the divine mango grove extending for three leagues and hearing the sound of birds, she spoke these words, "That," while pointing it out to the ascetic. "By those who have drunk the essence of flowers."
“By birds intoxicated by flower-juice. “By birds with curved limbs” means it resounds with the cries of birds that have curved necks.
Now, pointing out those birds, she says “Koñcā,” and so forth. Therein, “diviyā” means celestial (*dibbā*).
“Kolaṭṭhimadhusāḷikā” refers to the *kolaṭṭhi* birds and the golden *sāḷika* birds. She shows that these celestial birds dwell here.
"Resounding with flocks of swans" means it is warbled by and filled with the cries of swan-flocks.
"Cuckoos announce themselves here" means that in this mango grove, the cuckoos, while singing, announce and make themselves known. "Mangoes here" means there are mango trees here.
"With branches drooping low" means the tips of the branches are bent down by the weight of the fruit. "Resembling a granary of straw" [refers] to the accumulation of flowers.
"Resembling heaps of rice husks. "Hanging with ripe coconuts" means hanging with ripe coconut fruits.
He describes the mango grove as being where such trees exist.
Having described it, he then lowers the ascetic there [into the grove], saying: "Eating mangoes in this mango grove, for yourself..."
"Quench your thirst," he said, and then departed. Having eaten the mangoes, quenched his thirst, and rested, the ascetic wandered through the mango grove;
seeing that peta undergoing such suffering, he was unable to say anything.
But when the sun had set, seeing him surrounded by a retinue of celestial nymphs and enjoying divine splendor, he recited three verses:
“Wearing garlands, a crown, and armlets, adorned with bracelets and sandalwood paste,
you enjoyed yourself by night, but by day you experienced painful sensations.
Those sixteen thousand women who were your attendants— ”
“Thus you possess such great power, wonderful and hair-raising.
What evil deed did you commit in the past, bringing suffering upon yourself,
by doing which among humans you now eat the flesh from the backs?”
In this context, "garlanded" (*mālī*) means wearing celestial garlands. "Crowned" (*kiriṭī*) means wearing a celestial diadem. "Armleted" (*kāyūrī*) means adorned with celestial ornaments.
"Banded" (*aṅgadī*) means equipped with celestial armlets. "Anointed with sandalwood" (*candanussada*) means smeared with celestial sandalwood paste.

"He enjoyed" (*paricāresi*) means he caused his sense faculties to range over celestial objects. "By day" (*divā*), however, means that he experienced great suffering during the daytime. "Those which" (*yā temā*)... [text fragment]
"Those which are yours": "wonderful" (*abbhuta*) means it has never occurred before in the world of humans.

"Hair-raising" (*lomahaṃsana*) means the body hairs of those who see it stand on end. "In a former life" (*pubbe*) refers to a previous existence. "Bringing suffering to oneself" (*attadukkhāvaha*) means bringing suffering upon oneself.
"Among humans" (*manussesu*): he asks why, having done this in the world of humans, you now eat the flesh from your own back.
The peta recognized him and said, "You do not recognize me; I was once your chaplain.

This experience of happiness at night that I am enjoying is obtained as the result of the half-Uposatha fast I observed by relying on you, whereas this experience of suffering during the day is the result of the evil I myself committed. For I, while presiding over your legal disputes..."
“Having set aside [the truth], acting with fraud, taking bribes, and being a backbiter,
I am now experiencing this suffering as the result of that deed committed during the day,” he said, and recited these two verses:
“Having received fees for my recitations, I was addicted to sensual pleasures;”
“For a long time I have acted for the harm of others:
‘He who is a back-meat eater, who thus carves and eats—
just as I today eat my own back-flesh.’”
In this context, "Vedic recitations" refers to the Vedas. "Having received" means having accepted and studied them. "I practiced" means I engaged in them.
"For my own harm" means for my detriment and the destruction of my welfare. "One who eats the back-flesh" refers to that person who is a slanderer, one who consumes the back-flesh of others.
"Having cut off" means having sliced away.
Having said this, he asked the ascetic, "How did you come here? The ascetic related everything in detail.
[The other asked], "Now, venerable sir, will you stay right here or will you go? "I will not stay; I shall go back to my own hermitage.
The peta said, "Excellent, venerable sir! I will serve you constantly with mangoes."

Having spoken thus, he brought him down right there at the hermitage by means of his own supernatural power; and having obtained their promise with the words, "Dwell right here without longing for anything else," he departed.
From that time forward, he served them constantly with mangoes.

While consuming those, the ascetic performed the preliminary exercises for the *kasiṇas*, attained the meditative absorptions (*jhāna*) and direct knowledges (*abhiññā*), and became destined for the Brahma-world.
Having delivered this Dhamma teaching to the lay followers and proclaimed the Truths, the Teacher identified the Jātaka.
At the conclusion of the Truths, some became stream-enterers, some once-returners, and some non-returners.
At that time, the celestial maiden was Uppalavaṇṇā, and the ascetic was none other than myself.
The First Exposition of the Kiṃcanda Jātaka.
[512] 2. The Exposition of the Kumbha Jātaka.
"Who has appeared?"—this was spoken by the Teacher while residing at Jetavana concerning five hundred companions of Visākhā who had drunk liquor.

He spoke concerning women. It is said that when the wine festival had been proclaimed in Sāvatthī, those five hundred women prepared strong liquor for their husbands who were sporting at the festival, saying, "We shall enjoy the festival.
They all went to Visākhā and said, "Friend, we shall enjoy the festival. [Visākhā replied,] "This is a wine festival; it is not..."
When she said, "I shall drink liquor," they replied, "You give alms to the Perfectly Enlightened One;

we shall hold a festival. She consented, saying, "Very well," and having dismissed them, she invited the Teacher, prepared a great offering, and taking many perfumes and garlands, went at evening time with them to hear the discourse on the Dhamma.
Surrounded [by her attendants], she went to Jetavana. Those women, however, having gone with her while still drinking liquor, stood at the gatehouse;
after drinking more liquor, they went into the presence of the Teacher along with her.
Visākhā, having paid homage to the Teacher, sat down to one side. Among the others, some danced right in the presence of the Teacher, some sang, and some...
With fidgeting hands and feet, some of them began to quarrel.
To arouse a sense of spiritual urgency (*saṃvega*) in them, the Teacher emitted rays from the hair between his eyebrows, and it became pitch-black darkness.
They became terrified, struck by the fear of death; through that, their intoxication subsided. The Teacher sat upon his cross-legged seat.
Having vanished and stood upon the summit of Sineru, he emitted rays from his body-hair, like the simultaneous rising of a thousand moons and suns.
Standing there, the Teacher, for the purpose of inspiring a sense of spiritual urgency in them, said:
“What laughter, what joy, when there is constant burning? What pleasure can there be for one who dwells amidst the burning?”
“Enveloped in darkness, you do not seek a lamp.
Having spoken this verse, at its conclusion those five hundred women were established in the fruit of stream-entry.
Then the Teacher returned and sat upon the Buddha’s seat in the shadow of the Fragrant Chamber. Thereupon Visākhā, having paid homage to him, said: “Bhante, ...”
“When did this so-called drinking of fermented liquor, which destroys shame and dread of blame, first arise? he asked. As he explained it to her, he related a story from the past:

“In the past, while Brahmadatta was reigning in Bārāṇasī, a forest-dweller named Sura, a resident of the Kāsi kingdom, went to the Himālaya mountains in search of goods. There, a tree rose up to a height of one man’s stature.”
There was a period of three aeons (*kappa*). During those three aeons, there was a pit the size of a wine-jar. When it rained, it became filled with water;
surrounding it were *harītakī*, *āmalakī*, and pepper shrubs, whose ripe fruits fell into it after being broken off.
Not far from that, wild rice (*sāli*) grew of its own accord; from there, sparrows [took] the heads of rice.
Having brought it back, they sat upon that tree and ate it. As they were eating, grains of rice and husked rice fell there.
Thus, that water, being heated by the sun's rays, became red-colored in its essence.
During the hot season, flocks of birds, coming there parched with thirst, drank it; becoming intoxicated, they rolled about and fell at the foot of the tree. In that...
Having slept for a short while, they depart making grunting noises. The same principle applies to tree-dogs, monkeys, and so forth.
A forest-dweller, seeing this, thought: "If this were poison, these creatures would die; yet, having slept for a short while, they go about as they please. This is not poison.
Having drunk some himself, he became intoxicated and desired to eat the meat. Then—
Having made a fire at the foot of a tree, he killed partridges, chickens, and other birds;
