having roasted their flesh over the embers, he remained right there for one or two days, dancing with one hand while eating the meat with the other.
Now, not far from there, a certain ascetic named Varuṇa lived. On another occasion, a forest-dweller went into his presence.
He went. Then it occurred to him: "I shall drink this beverage together with the ascetic.

He filled a bamboo tube, brought it along with some cooked meat, and having gone to the leaf-hut, said, "Venerable sir, please drink this," and they both drank while eating the meat. Thus, because it had been seen by Sura and Varuṇa...

That drink received the names "Surā" and "Varuṇā. Both of them, thinking, "This is the means," filled bamboo tubes, took them on a carrying pole, and went to a border city; they announced to the king, "Producers of a beverage have arrived.
The king summoned them, and they presented the drink to him. After the king had drunk it two or three times,
The marrow lasted for only a day or two. Then he asked them, "Is there any more?
"There is, Your Majesty," they replied. "Where? "In the Himalayas, Your Majesty. "Then bring it back," he said.
They went and brought it back once or twice, but then, saying, "We will not be able to go there regularly," they prepared the necessary provisions and [cut] from that tree...
Starting with the bark, they added all the necessary ingredients and prepared liquor in the city.
After the citizens drank the liquor, they fell into negligence and became destitute; the city became as if empty.
Consequently, the liquor-makers fled from there and went to Bārāṇasī, where they informed the king, "The liquor-makers have arrived. The king summoned them and provided them with a livelihood.
He gave it to them. They brewed liquor there as well, and that city too was destroyed in the same manner.
Fleeing from there, they went to Sāketa, and from Sāketa they went to Sāvatthī.
At that time, there was a king in Sāvatthī named Sabbamitta. Having shown them favor, he asked, "What do you need?"
Having asked, when it was replied, "With the root-ingredients and rice flour, and with five hundred jars," he caused everything to be given.
They prepared the liquor in those five hundred jars; out of fear of mice, for the purpose of guarding the jars, they tied a cat near each individual jar.
When they had cooked it and were at the time of drawing it out, [they poured it] into the bellies of the jars.
Having drunk the flowing liquor, they fell asleep intoxicated. Mice came and, having gnawed off their ears, noses, teeth, and toes, departed.
The officials reported to the king, "The cats have died from drinking the liquor.
The king thought, "These must be poisoners," and had the heads of both men cut off. They [the mice]... the liquor...
"Your Majesty, it is sweet, Your Majesty! they cried out as they died. The king had them killed and ordered, "Break open the jars!
Even the cats, having risen from the fermented liquor, wandered about playing; seeing this, they informed the king.
The king thought, "If there were poison, these would have died; it must surely be sweet. I shall drink it. He entered the city...

Having had himself adorned with ornaments, a pavilion constructed in the royal courtyard, and having sat upon a royal couch under a white parasol raised in that decorated pavilion, surrounded by a host of ministers, he began to drink wine.
At that time, Sakka, the King of the Devas, wondered: "Who now, being heedful in the service of their mothers and other duties, are fulfilling the three types of good conduct?"
While surveying the world, he saw that king sitting down to drink liquor and thought, "If this man drinks the liquor, the entire Jambudīpa will perish.
I must act so that he does not drink it. Placing a jar full of liquor upon the palm of his hand, he approached in the guise of a brahmin and stood in the air directly in front of the king.

“Buy this jar! Buy this jar! he cried. King Sabbamitta, seeing him standing thus in the sky speaking those words, thought, “From where has this brahmin come? and as he conversed with him, he spoke three verses:
“Who has appeared in the sky from the triple heaven, illuminating it like the moon emerging from a cloud? Who is this being who stands in the air, shining like the sun at the end of the age?”
“Beams of light stream forth from your flanks, white like lightning in the sky.
‘You cut through the wind in the air, you go and stand in the open space;
has this psychic power been well-cultivated by you, surpassing even that of the deities who do not travel on foot?’”
“Having come from the sky, you stand here, saying, ‘Buy a jar! Who are you, and for what purpose is this jar?
Tell me this matter, O Brahmin. In that context, “Who appeared?
means from where have you become manifest, from where have you come? “From the triple heaven in the sky”—what [is meant]?
Having come from the realm of the Thirty-three, he asks: "Have you become manifest here in the sky, in the atmosphere?
"Saṃvari" means by night. "Sateratā" is her name. "So" means you. "Chinnavātaṃ": even a cloud is moved by the wind, but for him (the sun), even that wind does not exist;
therefore he says this. "Kamasī" means you move. "Aghamhi" means in the unobstructed [space].
"In the sky. "Made into a foundation" means made like a foundation, like a support.
"Even for deities who do not travel on foot": he asks whether even the psychic power (*iddhi*) of those deities who do not travel by walking—that is, who do not go on foot—is well-developed in you.
"Going and coming through the air" means depending upon, that is, based on, the lifting of feet as it occurs in the sky.
The phrase “tiṭṭhasi” (you stand) is connected with “ko vā tuvan” (who are you?); thus the meaning is: “Who are you who stands thus?
The phrase “yametaṃ atthaṃ” (this matter which) refers to what you say; it is connected with “kissa vā tāyaṃ” (for whose sake is this?), meaning:
“For whose sake do you say, ‘Buy this jar’? The sense is: “Whose jar is this for you?”
Then Sakka, saying, "In that case, listen," spoke while pointing out the faults of liquor:
"It is neither a jar of ghee nor a jar of oil, nor a jar of molasses nor a jar of honey;
there are no small faults in this jar—listen to the many defects inherent in what has entered the jar."
“Drink that which, having drunk, one falls headlong into a precipice, a pit, a cave, or a cesspool;
eat much that is unfit for food—buy this full jar of it!
Having drunk which, one wanders about with a restless mind like a bull seeking fodder.”
“Though she is not an ascetic, she approaches with song and dance; buy this full pitcher of hers!
‘Having drunk of which, one might wander naked and unclad through villages and between streets, with a deluded mind and sleeping past the proper time—buy this full pitcher of hers!’”
“Having drunk this, one rises up trembling, shaking the head and the arms;
he dances like a wooden puppet—buy this full jar of it!
Having drunk this indeed, people lie as if scorched by fire, even being devoured by jackals.”
“They bring about bondage, execution, and the loss of enjoyments—buy this full pitcher of hers!
‘Having drunk from it, one would speak what should not be spoken while sitting in an assembly, devoid of proper conduct;
smeared with filth, fallen into a pit, and ruined—buy this full pitcher of hers!’”
“Having drunk this, one becomes arrogant and clouded in appearance, thinking, ‘The entire earth belongs to me alone!
No king, even of the four quarters, is my equal!’—buy this full pitcher for that [pride]!
Pride, overweening pride, quarrels, and slander; it makes one ugly, naked, and a fugitive.”
“Buy this full pitcher of that woman who is the destination and the haunt of thieves and scoundrels!
‘May there be prosperous and flourishing families in the world with wealth amounting to many thousands,’ yet by her,
the inheritance has been cut off— buy this full pitcher of that woman!”
“Grain, wealth, silver, and gold, fields, and cattle—wherever these are squandered, they bring about the destruction of a family’s fortune. Buy this full jar!
Having drunk from it, a man, his appearance intoxicated, reviles both mother and father.”
“Buy this full pitcher for her, who would take even the mother-in-law and the daughter-in-law!
Buy this full pitcher for her, who, having drunk from it, becomes a woman of intoxicated appearance and reviles both her father-in-law and her husband;
she would take even a slave-girl as a servant—buy this full pitcher for her!”
“Having drunk of which a person might slay a recluse or a brahmin established in the Dhamma,
one would go to a state of misery because of that— buy this full jar of it!
Having drunk of which they practice misconduct by body, speech, and mind...”
“Those who have practiced evil conduct go to hell; buy this full pitcher of hers!
‘That which they did not obtain before even when begging and giving away much gold—having drunk that, he speaks falsehood; buy this full pitcher of hers!’”
“Indeed, having drunk this, even when being sent on an errand, when a matter requiring urgency has arisen, he does not understand the purpose even when told. Buy this full jar of it!
Even those possessed of shame drink to become shameless, intoxicated by its madness.”
"Though they are wise, they speak much: 'Buy this full pitcher!
Having drunk from it, people lie down with their hair matted, fasting, sleeping on the bare ground in hardship;
they undergo ugliness and the state of being a slave—buy this full pitcher!'"
“Having drunk this, men indeed lie down with their shoulders drooping, like cows struck by a club and not by Varuṇa’s bolt.
Its flow is like that of a well-pressed liquor; buy this full jar of it!
That which men avoid as they would a serpent of terrible venom—”
What man in this world would be fit to drink that which is like poison?
"Having drunk this, the sons of Andhakaveṇḍu, while sporting on the seashore, attacked one another with clubs; buy this full jar of it!"

“Having drunk that which caused the ancient gods to become heedless and fall from the three heavens, though they were associated with eternal bliss—how, O Great King, could one who knows such intoxicating liquor to be useless drink it?
There is neither curd nor honey in this jar; having understood this through direct knowledge, buy it not, O King.”
"Thus, O friend, all that has been told to you by me regarding this jar has been explained in its true form.
In this context, "vajjāni" means dangers or defects. "Gaḷeyya" means that while walking, one would stumble at every step.
"Yaṃ pitvā pateti" means that having drunk it, one would fall. "Sobbhaṃ" means a pit or a hole. "Candaniyoḷigallaṃ" means both a cesspool and a drain.
*Abhojaneyyaṃ* means unfit to be eaten. *Anesamāno* means one who has no mastery [over it]. *Goriva* means like a bull. *Bhakkhasādī* means a consumer of old straw;
the meaning is that he wanders about just as such a bull wanders about searching for fodder here and there.
*Anāthamāno* means like one who is helpless and without a protector. *Upagāyati* means [he approaches] another who is singing.
Having seen him, he approaches and sings. "Acelova" means like one who is naked. "Visikhantarāni" means the interior streets.
"Ativelasāyī" means he might fall asleep for too long a time. There is also the reading "ativelacārī," which means he would wander about excessively.
"Dārukaṭallako va" means like a wooden puppet. "Bhogajāniñcupenti" means they suffer the loss of their wealth.

The meaning is that having committed acts such as the destruction of life, they are oppressed by punishment, suffer the loss of wealth, and encounter other miseries such as execution and imprisonment.
*Vantagato* means one who has gone to what has been vomited out by himself. *Byasanno* means one who has fallen into calamity.
There is also a reading *visanno*; in that case, the meaning is "one who has settled down in that which was vomited. *Ukkaṭṭho* means: "I am a great warrior; who is there equal to me?"
Having thus reached the pinnacle. *Āvilakkho* means one with reddish eyes. *Sabbapathavī* means the entire earth; there is also a reading, *sabbaputhuvī*.
*Cāturanto* means a lord of the earth bounded by the four oceans. *Mānātimānā* means those who practice pride. The same method applies to the remaining terms as well.
*Gati* means rebirth. *Niketo* means a dwelling place. *Tassā puṇṇaṃ* refers to that which is of such a nature.
"Of her, it is full. "Prosperous" means well-flourishing. "Thriving" means blooming with clothes, ornaments, and articles of beauty.
"Made heirless" means they have been deprived of their inheritance and rendered destitute.
"Whereby they ruin" means that depending on whom and established where, they thus destroy even great wealth, grain, and property; they become wretched.
*Dittarūpo* means one who is intoxicated. *Gaṇheyya* means that, through the influence of defilements and the perception of her as a wife, he would take her by the hand.
*Dāsampi gaṇheti* means that, through the influence of defilements, he would even take her gift, thinking, "She is my wife. *Pivitvāna* means having drunk.
*Duccaritaṃ caritvā* means having thus committed the tenfold unwholesome action through the three doors. *Yaṃ yācamānā* means... [as requested].
A man who previously did not drink liquor, whom people—offering much gold and begging him—could not persuade to tell a lie, [now] "having drunk" means having stood after drinking.
When told, "He does not understand what was said," he does not know that meaning because of his misapprehension of the instruction when asked, "In what sense have you come?
"Even though possessed of shame" means even though his mind is endowed with a sense of moral shame (*hirī*).
"Ekathūpā" means being in one heap together even with those of low birth, like young piglets. "Anāsakā" means without food.
"Thaṇḍiladukkhaseyyaṃ" means they lie on the ground in painful sleep. "Āyasakyaṃ" means censure.
"Pattakhandhā" means with their shoulders fallen. "Kūṭahatāvā" means like oxen struck by a snare bound around their necks.
"Just as they lie without eating grass or drinking water"—this is the meaning of "lying in that manner. "Like a fierce poison" means like a terrible venom.
"Resembling poison" means similar to poison. "The sons of Andhakaveṇḍu" refers to ten royal brothers.
"They assailed" means they struck. "The ancient gods" refers to the asuras. "Tidiva" refers to the Tāvatiṃsa heaven. "Sassatiyā" means...

The meaning is: "the eternal worlds," that is, the divine realms (devaloka) which are considered permanent due to the state of long life. "Together with" (*samāyāti*) means along with the illusions of the asuras.
"One who knows thus": how could a wise person like you drink this, knowing "this is useless"?
"It has come into the jar by me" (*kumbhagatā mayā*); or rather, the reading is *kumbhagataṃ mayā*. "Of a nature already explained" (*akkhātarūpaṃ*): explained according to its true nature.
Having heard that and understood the danger of liquor, the king was delighted and, offering praise to Sakka, spoke these two verses:
“Neither my father nor even my mother is like you, who are so full of kindness and compassion, desiring my ultimate welfare. Therefore, I shall do your bidding this day.”

He said, "I shall give you five villages for every hundred thousand years of service.
Pointing out the ten golden, variegated chariots standing before him, he spoke thus.
Upon hearing this, Sakka manifested his divine form, and identifying himself, he stood in the air and uttered two verses:
“O King, let there be the very best of slave-girls for you; let the villages and the cattle be yours alone;
let the chariots yoked with thoroughbred horses be yours alone; I am Sakka, the lord of the thirty-three gods.
Eat rice with meat and milk-rice with ghee; eat honey-cakes and sesame cakes.”
"Thus, O lord of men, delighting in the Dhamma, blameless, go to the heavenly abode. Therein, "thus you, delighting in the Dhamma" means:

thus, while eating various kinds of choice food, abstaining from the drinking of intoxicants, and having abandoned the three types of misconduct, being one who delights in the Dhamma of the threefold good conduct, go to the heavenly abode without being blamed by anyone.
Having thus given him this exhortation, Sakka returned to his own place. He too, without drinking the liquor, [discarded] the vessels of liquor...
Having caused the [liquor] to be destroyed, he undertook the precepts, gave alms, and became destined for heaven.
In Jambudīpa as well, the drinking of liquor gradually reached a state of great proliferation.
Having delivered this Dhamma teaching, the Teacher identified the Jātaka: "At that time, King Ānanda was [the king], but Sakka was none other than myself."
The second explanation: the *Kumbhajātakavaṇṇanā*.
[513] 3. The Explanation of the *Jayaddisajātakavaṇṇanā*:
"Ah, after such a long time indeed for me... This was spoken by the Teacher while dwelling at Jetavana, concerning a certain monk who supported his mother.
He related the story. The present-day narrative is similar to the Sāmajātaka.
However, the Teacher, saying, "In the past, wise men abandoned Kanakamālā and the white parasol to support their parents," brought forth a story of the past.
In the past, in the city of Uttarapañcāla in the kingdom of Kapila, there was a king named Pañcāla. His chief queen—

Having conceived, she gave birth to a son. In a previous existence, a certain rival had become angry with her and made a resolution, saying, "May I be capable of devouring every child born to you. She had subsequently become a *yakkhinī*.
Having found an opportunity then, while the mother was looking on, she seized the boy, who was like a piece of raw meat.
Making a *murumura* sound, she ate it and departed. On the second occasion, she did exactly the same.
But on the third occasion, when she had entered the birth-chamber, they surrounded the house and established a strict guard.
On the day she gave birth, the *yakkhinī* came again and seized the infant once more. The queen raised a great cry, shouting, "A *yakkhinī*! [whereupon] those with weapons in hand...
Men arrived and, under the impression that she was the queen, pursued the yakkhinī.
Finding no opportunity to devour him, she fled from there and entered a water drain. The boy, thinking it was his mother, took her breast in his mouth.
She, conceiving maternal affection for him, fled from there again, went to the cemetery, and placed the boy in a stone cave.
She looked after him. Then, as he gradually grew up, she brought human flesh and gave it to him.
Both of them lived there, eating human flesh. The boy did not know his own human nature; he lived with the perception, "I am the son of a yakkhinī.
He was unable to cast off that physical form and disappear. Then, for the sake of making him disappear, she—
He gave one root. By the power of that root, he vanished and wandered about eating human flesh.
The yakkhinī, having gone to perform service for the Great King Vessavaṇa, passed away right there.
On the fourth occasion, the queen also gave birth to another son; because he was released from the yakkhinī, he was healthy. [His] enemy—
Because he was born after defeating a *yakkhinī*, they gave him the name Prince Jayaddisa.
When he reached maturity, having attained proficiency in all arts, he raised the royal parasol and governed the kingdom.
At that time, the Bodhisatta was conceived in the womb of his chief queen; they gave him the name Prince Alīnasattu.
They did so. When he reached maturity, having mastered all the arts, he became the viceroy.
Later, that son of a female *yakkha*, through negligence, lost the source [of his power]; unable to vanish, he remained visible in form and ate human flesh in the charnel ground.
Seeing him, people were terrified and went to inform the king: "Your Majesty, a certain *yakkha* is seen in visible form..."
"He eats human flesh in the charnel ground; he will gradually enter the city, kill people, and eat them.
It is necessary to have him captured. The king, having agreed by saying "Very well," commanded, "Seize him!
A body of troops went and stood surrounding the charnel ground. The son of the yakkhinī was naked, agitated in appearance, and terrified by the fear of death.
Full of courage, he leapt into the midst of people. Terrified by the fear of death, thinking "It is a *yakkha*," the people split apart in two.
He too fled from there and entered the forest, never again returning to the path of men.
Dwelling near a great *vattaniya* forest, he seized one person at a time from among those traveling on the road and [led them] into the forest.
Having entered, killed, and devoured [his prey], he made his dwelling at the foot of a banyan tree.
Then a certain brahmin caravan leader, having paid a thousand pieces of gold to the forest guards, set out upon that road with five hundred carts.
The human-yakkha rushed forward, shrieking; terrified, the people fell prostrate on their chests. He...
While fleeing after seizing the brahmin, he was pierced in the foot by a stump.
As the forest guards pursued him, he abandoned the brahmin and lay down at the foot of a tree where he used to dwell.
On the seventh day while he was lying there, King Jayaddisa, having ordered a hunt for deer, departed from the city. Just as he had left the city—
A Brahmin named Nanda, a resident of Takkasilā who supported his mother, arrived carrying four hundred stanzas worth a hundred pieces of gold and saw the king.
The king, thinking, "I shall listen after returning," had a residence provided for him;
then, having gone out on a hunt, he declared, "Whose side the deer escapes by, that person's is the responsibility. Then, a certain *pasada* deer rose up against the king.

Having gone forward, he fled. The ministers laughed at him. The king took up his sword, pursued him, and having reached a distance of three leagues, struck him with the sword, cutting him into two pieces.
Carrying them on a carrying-pole, as he was returning, he arrived at the place where the human-yakṣa lay;
sitting down upon some *dabbha* grass and resting for a short while, he set out to go further.
He began. Then, rising up, he seized him by the hand, saying, “Stop! Where are you going? You are my food!
and spoke this first verse:
“Ah, after a long time, today at the hour of the seventh meal, a great prey has indeed appeared before me!”
“From where have you come? Who are you? Please tell me; declare your birth as you are known.
In this context, *mahābhakkho* means “one who eats much. *Sattamibhattakāle* means at the time of the meal on the seventh day, having been without food since the first day.

“*Kutosi*” means “from where have you come? When the king saw the yakkha, he was terrified; his thighs became rigid, and he was unable to flee. However, having established mindfulness, he spoke the second verse:
“The King of Pañcāla has entered the hunt—he who is known to you as Jayaddisa.
I am wandering through the marshes and forests; eat this spotted deer, release me today!
Therein, “entered the hunt” means he has gone out from the kingdom for the purpose of killing deer. “Marshes” refers to mountain slopes. “Spotted deer” refers to a *pasada* deer.
Having heard that, the yakkha spoke this third verse:
“Like a general you cry out while boasting, ‘This herd of cattle which you speak of is my food!
Having devoured that famished herd of cattle first, I shall eat you afterwards; it is no time for lamentation.”
In this context, "by me alone" means by what belongs to me. "Paṇasī" means you bargain; you sell yourself. "Sassamāno" means being harmed.
"Taṃ khādiyāna" means having first eaten that. "Jighaññaṃ" means desiring to eat. "Khādissaṃ" means I shall eat this later.
"Na vilāpakālo" means do not lament; he says, "This is not the time for lamentation."
Having heard that, the King remembered the brahmin Nanda and spoke this fourth verse:
“There is no release for me by means of a price for going back after having departed;
having given that promise to the brahmin, I shall return again, guarding my truth.”
In this context, "there is no" means that there is no release for me through a ransom.
"Having gone" means: such being the case, having eaten this deer meat today and having gone to my city. "Promise" means:
take a promise for the purpose of returning on the very next day, at the time of breakfast. "That agreement" refers to my [promise] that "I will give you wealth."
"A promise was made to the brahmin; having given that to him, I shall return again while guarding this truth spoken by me"—this is the meaning.
Having heard that, the yakkha spoke the fifth verse:
“O King, what kind of deed do you regret now that death has come so near?
Tell me that, so that we may grant permission for your return.
In this context, *kammajātaṃ* means simply *kamma*. *Anutappate* means he regrets that. *Pattaṃ* means arrived at or approached. *Api*... [and so forth].
"‘I am able,’ means: ‘Perhaps, having heard that cause of your grief, I might be able to grant you leave to come back early in the morning.
The King, explaining the reason, spoke the sixth verse:
‘I made a promise to the brahmin for wealth; I have bound myself by that agreement and have not been released.’"
“Having given that pledge to the brahmin, I shall return again, guarding my truth.

Therein, having heard the four verses beginning with “It was fastened, not released,” [the brahmin said]: “I promised, ‘I will give you wealth,’ and having thus fastened it upon myself, I have set it aside; yet it has not been released, because the wealth has not been given.
Having heard this, the yakkha spoke the seventh verse:
“The hope for wealth you formed for the brahmin—that promise you have undertaken has not been released.
Having fulfilled that promise to the brahmin, return once more as one who guards the truth.
In this context, “return once more” (punarāvajassu) means “come back again.”
Having spoken thus, he dismissed the king. Thus dismissed, the king said, "Do not worry;
I shall return early tomorrow morning," and while observing the landmarks along the road, he approached his own army.
Surrounded by his forces, he entered the city, summoned the brahmin Nanda, had him seated upon a magnificent throne, and [recited] those verses.

Having heard this, he gave four thousand [pieces of gold], had him placed upon a vehicle, and dispatched the brahmin with the instruction, "Take him back to Takkasilā itself," providing him with attendants.
On the second day, desiring to return, he addressed his son and instructed him.
To illustrate this matter, the Teacher spoke these two verses:
“Having escaped from the hands of the man-eater and gone to his own palace, enjoying all his desires, he gave that promise to the brahmin and addressed his son, Alīnasattu:
‘This very day, have yourself consecrated to the kingship; practice the Dhamma toward both your own people and others.’”
“Let there be no injustice in your kingdom; I shall go to inform the man-eater.
In this context, *alīnasattu* refers to the prince of that name (though it is written as *ariṇasattu* in the Pāli text).
“This very day, O son, I give you the kingdom; this very day you should have yourself consecrated upon the head with the royal inauguration.”
“*Ñatti* means repetition; *santike* means in the presence [of].
Having heard that, the prince spoke the tenth verse:
‘O Lord, what deed have you done that you have not pleased me? I wish to hear about that.’”
“Whatever deed today you have caused me to exult in my sovereignty, even that sovereignty I would renounce without you.

Therein, *krubbanti* means “doing. “Whatever [deed] today”: tell me that unpleasing act by which you have today caused me to exult, to be uplifted, and established in my kingdom; for I do not desire even the kingdom without you—this is the meaning.
Having heard this, the king spoke the following verse:
“Not by deed nor by word alone, dear father, do I remember having committed an offense against you;
yet, having made a pact with that man-eater, I shall go back again, guarding my truth.
Therein, *aparādhitō* means “I have committed an offense (*aparādha*) against you. *Tuviyaṃ* means “belonging to you. This is what is meant: “Dear father...”
"I do not recall any offense or anything unpleasant toward you from either your actions or your words. "And as for the connection," he said:
"But once, while I had gone out hunting, a certain yakkha seized me, intending to devour me.
Then, having heard a discourse on the Dhamma from a brahmin and having paid him honor, I said: 'I shall come tomorrow at the time of your breakfast.'"
That man-eater, having made a pact of truth, has come; therefore, protecting that truth, I shall go there again, while you exercise the kingship—thus he spoke.
Having heard this, the prince uttered this verse:
“I shall go; remain right here. There is no escape for you from him while you live.
But if you must go, O King, I too shall go; we two shall not both be.

In this context, “right here” means “you remain right here. “From him” means there is no liberation for one who lives in his presence. “We two” means that such being the case, neither of us shall exist.
Having heard this, the king spoke this verse:
“Truly, dear son, this is the way of the virtuous;
yet that would be more painful to me than death itself—that Kammāsapāda, having cooked you, should force you upon a wooden stake and eat you.”
The meaning of this is as follows: "Certainly, my dear, this is the law and the very nature of the wise;

you speak rightly. Nevertheless, even more painful than death itself for me would it be if that Kammāsapāda were to split me open with a wooden stake—piercing me through with a sharp wooden stake, cooking me, and then forcibly devouring me by main force."
Having heard that, the prince spoke this verse:
“I will exchange my life for yours; do not go into the presence of the man-eater.
And so I will exchange my life for yours; therefore, I praise death over life.”
In this context, "I will exchange" means: "Right here, I shall exchange my life for your life.
Therefore, because I shall exchange this life of mine for your life, "for the sake of your life I praise my own death"—that is, I choose death itself;
the meaning is that I desire it.

Having heard this, the king, knowing his son’s strength, consented, saying, “Very well, dear one, go. He paid homage to his mother and father and departed from the city. To clarify this matter, the Teacher spoke this half-verse:
“Then indeed, the steadfast prince, having paid homage at the feet of his mother and father...
In this context, “at the feet” means that he departed after paying homage at their feet.
Then his mother, father, sister, and wife, together with the ministers and attendants,
also set out. Having departed from the city, he asked his father for directions, and once he had clearly ascertained the way, he paid homage to his parents,
gave advice to the others, and— undaunted like a maned lion— set out upon the path toward the abode of the yakkha.
Seeing him departing, his mother, unable to maintain her composure, fell to the ground.
His father, raising his arms, wept with a great cry. To explain this matter, the Teacher said:
“The mother of that suffering one fell upon the earth; his father, raising his arms, wailed.”
Having spoken half a verse, he uttered four further verses, proclaiming the blessing pronounced by his father, and the oaths of truth (saccakiriyā) made by his mother, sisters, and wife:
“Knowing that you were departing, your father, with hands joined in reverence, paid homage to you from behind your back.
And King Soma, King Varuṇa, Pajāpati, Candimā, and Suriya;”
“Protected by these from man-eaters, O dear one, go back in safety with my permission.
Just as your mother provided for your safety and well-guarded you when you went to King Daṇḍaki’s realm, so do I provide for your safety;
by this truth may the gods take heed of you!”
“Permitted, go back safely, my son.
“Whether openly or in secret, I have never known ill-will toward any being, even in my mind.
By this truth may the gods protect you; permitted, go back safely, brother.”
“Since you have no lack of confidence in me, O Master, and since you are not even disliked by me in my mind;
by this truth may the gods take heed! Permitted, go in safety, Master.
Therein, “with his back turned” means: “This son of mine goes with his back turned after having paid homage to his mother and father”; thus it is said.

"Having seen him going away with his back turned, and having understood [the situation], he paid homage with palms joined (*pañjalīko*); at that time, placing his joined palms to his head, he bowed and venerated the deity.
'From the man-eater' means from the presence of the man-eater; permitted by him, return safely.
'He did it for Rāma' means he acted for the sake of Rāma. It is said that there was a certain resident of Bārāṇasī named Rāma, a supporter of his mother, who [served] his parents..."
While tending [to his parents], he went for the sake of trade to the city of Kumbhavatī within the realm of King Daṇḍaki.
There, as the entire kingdom was being devastated by nine kinds of rain, he recollected the virtues of his mother and father.
Then, by the fruit of his service to his mother, deities brought him back safely and gave him to his mother. Having related this matter based on what he had heard, he spoke thus.
"Sotthānaṃ" means safety. Although that [safety] was indeed brought about by the deities, it is said that "the mother did it" because it arose in dependence upon her nursing.
"Taṃ te ahaṃ" means "I too shall bring you that very same safety";
the meaning is: "In dependence upon me, may your state of safety be likewise. Alternatively, "karomi" means "I desire [it]. By this—
“By truth”: if it is true that he was brought back safely by the deities, then by this truth may the gods remember my son as well;
the meaning is: “Just like Rāma, may they bring him back and show him to me.
“Permitted”: permitted by Porisāda with the words “Go”; [the father] says, “Return safely, my son,” through the power of the deities.
"Never indeed toward one who is not base-minded"—that is, "O my brother Alīnasattu, never at all, whether in your presence or in your absence, do I recall any ill-will in my mind;
no such ill-will was ever previously committed by me toward you"—in this way his younger brother made a truthful declaration.
And because you have not held me in contempt, O Lord—meaning, "O Lord Alīnasattu, since you have not held me in contempt."
"Having overcome and surpassed me, you did not desire another with your mind.
Nor were you unloved by my mind"—meaning, "You are not unloved by my mind either; we two are indeed those who dwell in mutual affection.
In this way, the chief queen made her vow true.
The prince also set out upon the path to the protection-grove according to the instructions given by his father. The yakkha, thinking, "Kshatriyas are indeed full of guile;
who knows what will happen?", climbed a tree and sat there watching for the king's arrival.
Seeing the prince approaching, he thought, "He must have turned back his father and come here as his son."
"I have no fear," he said, and having dismounted, he sat down showing him his back. The other came and stood before him.
Then the yakkha spoke this verse:
"Lofty, upright, and handsome-faced one, from where have you come? You do not recognize me, who dwell in the forest."
"Knowing me to be a hunter, [who would think], 'You are a man-eater; who, knowing himself to be safe, would rush here?

" In this context, "Who, knowing himself to be safe, would rush here? means: O Prince, what man indeed, knowing his own state of safety and desiring it, would come here? You have come, I suppose, without such knowledge.
Having heard that, the prince spoke this verse:
“I know you, hunter, as a man-eater; I do not not know you dwelling in the forest. And I am the son of Jayaddisa;
eat me today for the sake of my father’s release.
In this context, “for the sake of release” means: “I have come here having given my life for the sake of my father’s release; therefore, release him and eat me”—this is the meaning.
Then the yakkha spoke this verse:
“I know you are the son of Jayaddisa, for such is the complexion of both your faces.
This deed you have done is indeed very difficult to perform—for one who would desire the release of his father.”

In that context, *tathā hi vo* means "such as you are. The meaning is that the facial expression of both is exactly the same. Regarding the phrase *kataṃ tavedaṃ*, this refers to your deed which was so very difficult to perform.
Then the prince spoke this verse:
"I do not consider anything here to be difficult for one who desires to liberate his father."
"And for the sake of his mother, having gone to the next world, he is endowed with happiness and heaven.
In this context, "I do not conceive anything here" means:

O Yakkha, whatever person, having gone to the next world for the sake of liberating his father or for the sake of his mother, [is endowed] with happiness—that is, the happiness of being reborn in heaven.
“Since one who wishes to live must also wish to die, I do not consider the sacrifice of my life here for the sake of my parents to be difficult in the least.
Hearing this, the yakkha asked, “Young man, there is no being that does not fear death; why are you not afraid? As he spoke to him, the prince recited two verses:
“I have never concealed my own evil deeds, whether in public or in private;
I am one who has fully understood birth and death, just as it is here, so it shall be in the world beyond.
O you of great power, eat me now; do with this body what must be done.”
"Or I shall fall from the top of that tree; you have given me the meat, covering it [with your body].
In this context, "I do not remember at all" means that I do not remember it with absolute certainty.

"I am one who has fully understood birth and death" means that through my knowledge I have thoroughly discerned birth and death; I know that there is no being born who is not subject to death. Just as for me...

"Here" means: just as it is for me here, so it is in the world beyond; and just as it is in the world beyond, so too here there is no such thing as liberation from death—this too has been well-determined by my knowledge. "Perform your duties" means:
perform those duties that must be done with this body; this body of yours has been relinquished by me. While protecting it, you gave it to me.
"The tree-tops will think of me; when I am dead, you, covering and relishing it, shall point out whatever meat you desire from my body, saying, 'Eat this'—this is the meaning.
Having heard his words, the yakkha became terrified and thought, 'It is not possible to eat his flesh; I shall cause him to flee by means of a stratagem. Having reflected thus, he spoke this verse:"
“If this is pleasing to you, O prince, you would even sacrifice your own life for the sake of your father’s release;
therefore, acting with haste, gather wood and kindle a fire.

In this context, “kindle a fire” means: having entered the forest, bring back heartwood, kindle a fire, and when it is smokeless, make it into glowing embers; there, I shall cook my flesh and eat it—this is what he indicates.
Having done so, he went into his presence. Explaining the circumstances, the Teacher spoke the following verse:
“Then indeed, the resolute prince, having gathered wood and kindled a great fire, announced:
‘Now this great sacrificial fire has been lit.’”
The yakkha, having prepared a fire, looked at the prince who had arrived and thought, "This is a lion among men; even the fear of death does not exist for him.
In all this time, I have never before seen anyone so fearless. With his hair standing on end, he sat there looking at the prince again and again.
Seeing the yakkha's behavior, the prince spoke this verse:
“Eat me now, O impetuous one! Why do you look at me again and again with bristling hair?
I shall act toward you in such and such a way, just as you have approached me while covering yourself.
In this context, *muhuṃ* means repeatedly. *Tathā tathā tuyhamahaṃ* means: “I [shall speak] to you in such and such a manner.”
"I am doing it; now what shall I do? Since you have pointed me out while covering and pleasing me, thinking 'you will eat me,' therefore, eat me today!
Having heard his words, the yakkha spoke this verse:
“Who would deserve to eat such a one—him who stands firm in the Dhamma, a speaker of truth, and generous?
Even his head would split into seven pieces if anyone were to refuse what such a speaker of truth has offered.
Having heard this, the prince said, “If you do not wish to eat me, then why did you have the wood split and the fire prepared?”
Having said, "I had it made," when [the other] asked, "Is he perhaps going to flee? Is this for the sake of keeping you under guard?
he replied, "How will you guard me now, I who was born in the womb of an animal and did not even allow myself to be guarded by Sakka, king of the gods? and then he spoke:
“For this very reason, O Yakṣas, that wise hare, thinking ‘this is a brahmin,’ offered himself upon his own body today.
Therefore, that son of the gods Candima, praised as a hare, is now a wish-fulfilling [being].
The meaning of this is: for this very reason, that wise hare, perceiving him as a brahmin—thinking “this is a brahmin”—[offered himself] today.
"Having eaten my body, dwell right here"—thus he caused his own body to dwell within his own body;
the meaning is that he made it stay. He gave his body for the purpose of being consumed. Sakka pressed the essence of the mountains, took it, and fashioned the mark of the hare upon the lunar disc.
From that time forth, because of that very mark of the hare, that moon-deity is called "Sasī" (the Hare-marked).
"Thus praised by the world as 'the moon,' fulfilling desires and increasing affection, the Yakṣa shines today. For this miracle is one that endures for an eon.
Hearing this, the Yakṣa, releasing the prince, spoke this verse:
"Just as the moon, released from the mouth of Rāhu, or as the sun shines on the fifteenth day,"
"Thus released from the man-eater, shine forth, O one of great power, in Kappila!
Bring joy to your father and mother, and let all your circle of kinsmen rejoice.
In this context, "Bhānumā" means the sun. This is what is meant: just as the moon on the fifteenth day, released from the mouth of Rāhu...
“Just as the moon or the sun shines, so too, having been released by me, may you shine with great power in the kingdom of Kapila. “May he rejoice” means “may he be satisfied.

“Go, O Great Hero,” he said, thus dismissing the Great Being. He, for his part, having rendered him harmless and bestowed upon him the five precepts, began to investigate whether or not he was a *yakkha*, thinking:
“The eyes of *yakkhas* are red and unblinking.”
And no shadow was perceived; they were not afraid. "This is not a *yakkha*; this is a human being.
It is said that three brothers of my father were seized by a *yakkhinī*. Of them, two must have been eaten by her, and one must have been cared for out of affection for a son;
this must be him. Having led him away and informed my father..."
Thinking, "I shall establish him in the kingdom," he said, "Come here, my friend! You are not a *yakkha*; you are my father’s eldest brother.
Come with me and raise the royal parasol over the kingdom inherited by our family.
When the other replied, "I am no human being," he asked, "Do you not believe me? But is there anyone else whom you do believe?"
When it was said, “There is a divine-eyed ascetic in such-and-such a place,” he took him and went there.
Upon seeing them, the ascetic asked, “What are you doing, father and son, wandering in the forest? and he explained their relationship to him.
Porisāda, believing his words, said, “Dear one, you go; I am like one who has been born in two bodies within a single existence.”
“I have no need for kingship; I shall go forth,” he said, and in the presence of the ascetic, he took the renunciant’s life of an *isi*.
Then the prince, having paid homage to him, returned to the city. To illustrate this matter, the Teacher said:
“Then indeed the steadfast prince, with palms joined in reverence, addressed Porisāda according to the traditional method;”
“Permitted, safe, happy, and healthy, he has returned from Kapila, where his heart was weary.
Having spoken this verse, he spoke the concluding verse, showing the honors performed for him by the townspeople and others as he entered the city:
“The entire populace, both from the towns and the countryside—elephant riders, chariot-warriors, and foot-soldiers alike;”
“Paying homage with palms joined, they approached him, saying: ‘Homage to you, O performer of difficult deeds!
Hearing that the prince had arrived, the king went out to meet him. The prince, surrounded by a great multitude, went and paid obeisance to the king.
Then the king asked him: ‘Dear son, how were you released from such man-eaters? ‘Father,’ he replied.”
"This is not a *yakkha*; he is your elder brother. He is my father," he said, and after relating the entire account, he added, "It is fitting for you to see my father.
At that very moment, the king had the drum beaten and went into the presence of the ascetics with a great retinue. The great ascetic, having brought him [to his father],...
Without having eaten, he related in detail everything: the reason for his fasting, the reason for his lack of a yakṣa-form, and their kinship.
The king said, "Come, brother, rule the kingdom. "Enough, Great King," he replied. "In that case, come;
you shall dwell in the pleasure grove, and I will attend to you with the four requisites. "I will not come, Great King," he said.

The king, having built a mountain retreat not far from their hermitage, constructed a large reservoir, prepared rice fields, brought a thousand wealthy families, and established a great village, instituted alms-giving for the ascetics.
That village became known as Cūḷakammāsadamma-nigama. By means of the Great Being Sutasoma, [he saved] the man-eater...
Furthermore, that location should be understood as the town of Mahākammāsadamma.
Having delivered this teaching on the Dhamma and proclaimed the Truths, the Teacher identified the Jātaka.
At the conclusion of the Truths, the Elder Mātuposaka was established in the fruit of stream-entry. At that time, his mother and father were members of a great royal family.
Sāriputta was the ascetic; Porisāda was Aṅgulimāla; Uppalavaṇṇā was the youngest [sister]; Rāhulamātā was the chief queen;
and as for Prince Alīnasattu, it was I myself who was he.
This concludes the third commentary, the Jayaddisa Jātaka.
[514] 4. The Commentary on the Chaddanta Jātaka.
"Why do you grieve?"—this was spoken by the Teacher while residing at Jetavana concerning a certain young bhikkhunī.
It is said that she was a daughter of a noble family in Sāvatthī who, having seen the peril in the household life, went forth into the Dispensation. One day...
Having gone with the bhikkhunīs to hear the Dhamma and sat upon the decorated Dhamma-throne,
she beheld the physical form of the One Possessed of Ten Powers— a body endowed with supreme beauty produced by the power of immeasurable merit—
and thought: "Have I perhaps served as a handmaid at the feet of this Great Being while wandering through previous existences?"
She reflected. Then, at that very moment, the knowledge of recollecting past births arose within her:
"In the time of the elephant Chaddanta, I was formerly this Great Being’s female attendant. As she remembered this, a great surge of rapture and joy arose.
With the force of that rapture, she broke into a loud laugh and thought again: "A female attendant, indeed, [belongs] to her husbands..."
"Those with a disposition toward welfare were few; those with a disposition toward harm were far more numerous.
Did I, indeed, have a disposition toward the welfare of this Great Being, or a disposition toward his harm? As she reflected, she recalled:

"Having harbored a slight resentment in my heart, I sent the hunter named Sonuttara to the supreme Chaddanta Great Elephant King, who was a hundred and twenty ratanas in height, using a poisoned arrow."
Having extinguished [the lamp], he brought her to the end of life. Seeing this, grief arose within her;
her heart grew hot, and unable to sustain her sorrow, she sighed and gasped, weeping with a loud cry.
Seeing her, the Teacher broke into a smile. “Venerable Sir, what is the cause, what is the reason for manifesting a smile? he asked.
When questioned by the community of monks, he said, "Monks, this young nun is weeping because she remembers an offense committed against me in the past," and then related a story from the past.
In the past, in a region of the Himalayas, eight thousand noble elephants possessing supernormal powers dwelt near Lake Chaddanta.
...the Vehaṃsaṅgama. At that time, the Bodhisatta was reborn as the son of the chief elephant; he was entirely white, with a red face and feet.
Later, when he had reached maturity, he stood eighty-eight cubits high and measured one hundred and twenty ratanas in length.
He was endowed with a trunk resembling a silver wreath, fifty-eight cubits long. As for his tusks, in circumference—
They were fifteen cubits in length and thirty cubits in height, endowed with six-colored rays.
He was the chief of eight thousand nāgas and honored five hundred paccekabuddhas. He had two chief queens, Cūḷasubhaddā and Mahāsubhaddā.
The nāga king, surrounded by a retinue of eight thousand nāgas, [dwelt] in the Golden Cave.
It dwells there. Furthermore, that Chaddanta Lake is fifty yojanas in length and breadth.
In its center, at a place measuring twelve yojanas, there is neither moss nor algae;
only water with the color of a mass of jewels remains still. Immediately beyond that is a pure grove of white lotuses (*kalahāra*) one yojana wide, which surrounds that water.
Immediately following that, there stands a pure grove of blue lotuses (*nīluppalavana*) exactly one *yojana* in width, encircling it;

beyond that, there stand groves of red lotuses, white lotuses, red water-lilies, white water-lilies, and night-lilies, each exactly one *yojana* in width, standing in succession, each encircling the one preceding it.
Following these seven groves, for all of them as well—
By way of those groves of *kallahāra* and other lotuses, there is a mixed forest (*omissakavana*) one *yojana* in width, which stands surrounding them.
Immediately after that, in water reaching the depth of a nāga’s waist, there is a grove of red rice (*rattasāli*) one *yojana* in width;
immediately after that, along the edge of the water, there is a grove one *yojana* in width, strewn with blue, yellow, red, white, fragrant, and delicate flowers.
The Khuddakagaccha forest—thus these ten forests are each one yojana in extent. Following that is the Khuddakarājamāsa, Mahārājamāsa, and Mugga forest;
immediately after that, the Tipu, Sela, Āluka, Lābu, Kumbhaṇḍa, and Valli forests; then the sugarcane forest, as large as a betel-nut tree;
then the plantain forest, with fruits the size of elephant tusks; then the Sāla forest; and immediately after that, [the forest] with fruits the size of bowls.

First was a grove of *panasa* trees, then a grove of sweet-fruit *ciñcā* trees, then a mango grove, then a *kapiṭṭha* grove, then a great mixed forest thicket, and then the Bamboo Grove (*Veḷuvana*). This was its prosperity at that time;
however, in the *Saṃyutta-aṭṭhakathā*, only the prosperity existing at present is described.
Surrounding the Veḷuvana grove, however, stand seven mountains. Starting from their outer edge, the first is named Cūḷakāḷapabbata;
the second is named Mahākāḷapabbata; after that is Udakapabbata; after that is Candimapassapabbata;
after that is Sūriyapassapabbata; after that is Maṇipassapabbata; and the seventh is Suvaṇṇapassapabbata.
It is named [Nāga]. In height it measures seven *yojanas* and stands encircling the Chaddanta Lake like the rim of a bowl.
Its inner surface is golden-colored; by the radiance issuing from it, the Chaddanta Lake appears as if the young sun has just risen.
Among the outer mountains, one is six *yojanas* in height, and another...
Five [yojanas], one four, one three, one two, and one a single yojana;
thus, on the northeastern corner of that lake, which is encircled by seven mountain ranges, there is a great banyan tree in a place where the wind from the water strikes.
Its trunk is five yojanas in circumference and seven yojanas in height, and in the four directions—

Its four branches extend for six *yojanas*, and its branches rising upward are likewise six *yojanas* high; thus, from its base to its summit it is thirteen *yojanas* tall. From one end of its branches to the other, it spans twelve *yojanas*.
Adorned with eight thousand shoots, it stands shining with splendor like Mount Muṇḍamaṇi. [This is] of the Chaddanta Lake.
Furthermore, in the western direction on the Golden Slope Mountain, there stands a golden cave twelve yojanas in extent.
A royal nāga named Chaddanta dwells in that golden cave during the rainy season and the winter, surrounded by eight thousand nāgas.
During the summer season, seeking shelter from the wind and water, he stays at the foot of a great banyan tree, amidst its offshoots.

Then one day, when the young elephants came and announced, "The great *sāla* forest is in bloom," he went to the *sāla* grove with his retinue, thinking, "I shall play at the *sāla*-game. Having gone there, he struck a beautifully blossomed *sāla* tree with his water-pot.
At that time, Cūḷasubhaddā was standing on the side downwind; [therefore] upon her body... [mixed with dry twigs].
Old leaves and *tambakipillika* insects fell down. Mahāsubhaddā stood on the side downwind, and the pollen, filaments, and petals of the flowers fell upon her body.
Cūḷasubhaddā thought, "This Nāga king has caused the pollen, filaments, and petals to fall upon his own beloved wife; they have fallen upon my body mixed with dry stalks."
He threw down withered leaves and *tambakipillika* insects [upon the Bodhisatta], thinking, "Let it be; I shall know what must be done," and thus the Great Being conceived a grudge against him.
On another day, the Naga King, together with his retinue, descended into Lake Chaddanta for the purpose of bathing.
Then two young Nagas, holding bundles of *usira* grass in their trunks, bathed him as if they were washing Mount Kelāsa. When he had finished bathing and emerged from the water—
Two female elephants bathed him; having emerged from the water, they stood beside the Great Being.

Then, descending into the lake of eight thousand elephants, they sported in the water, brought various flowers from the lake, and—like adorning a silver stupa—adorned the Great Being first, and afterwards adorned the two female elephants. Then, one elephant, wandering about in the lake...
Having obtained a great red lotus called *sattuddaya*, he brought it and gave it to the Great Being.
He took it with his trunk, sprinkled pollen over his forehead, and gave it to his eldest wife, Mahāsubhaddā.
Seeing this, the other wife again harbored enmity toward him, thinking, "He gave this *sattuddaya* great red lotus only to his own beloved wife, not to me."
Then one day, while the Bodhisatta was feeding five hundred Paccekabuddhas with sweet fruits mixed with lotus roots and honey from lotuses,
Cūḷasubhaddā gave the fruits she had obtained herself to the Paccekabuddhas and said,
"Venerable sirs, after passing away from here, may I be reborn in the Madda royal family as a princess named Subhaddā."
Having reached maturity and become the chief queen of the King of Bārāṇasī, she became beloved and pleasing to him;
being capable of making him act according to her own will, she informed him, sent a hunter,
and had him strike this elephant with a poisoned arrow, bringing it to the end of its life as it emitted six-colored rays from its twin tusks.
She made this aspiration: "May I be capable of causing [food] to be brought.
From that time forth, she did not take any more fodder and, having withered away, she passed away before long and was reborn in the womb of the chief queen of the king of the Madda kingdom;
they gave her the name Subhaddā-Tissā. Then, when she had reached maturity, they gave her to the King of Bārāṇasī. She [became] his...
She was beloved and pleasing; having become the senior among sixteen thousand women, she acquired the knowledge of recollecting past births.
She thought: "My aspiration has been fulfilled; now I shall have those twin tusks of the elephant brought.
Then, having smeared her body with oil, put on soiled garments, and assumed the appearance of being ill, she went to the bedchamber.
Having entered, she lay down on a couch. The king, asking, "Where is Subhaddā?
and hearing that she was ill, entered the bedchamber, sat upon the couch, and while massaging her back, spoke the first verse:
"Why do you grieve, O lady of lofty limbs? Why are you pale, O woman of excellent complexion?"
“You with the large eyes, you fade away like a garland that has been crushed.
Regarding this, “anuccaṅgī” refers to one whose body resembles gold. “Like a garland that has been crushed” means like a lotus garland crushed by hands.
Having heard that, she spoke another verse:
“O Great King, a longing has arisen within me through a dream;
such a longing as mine is not easily obtained.

Therein, “it is not” means that the longing which arose for her through a dream—the longing seen by her while dreaming—is not as if it were easy to obtain; it is difficult to find. She said this implying, “If I do not obtain it, there is no life for me.”
Having heard that, the king spoke this verse:
“Whatever human pleasures there are here in this world, even in the Nandana grove—all those are abundant for me;
I shall grant them to you as a longing-fulfillment.”
In that context, "plentiful" means many and easily obtained.
Having heard this, the queen said, "Great King, my pregnancy longing is difficult to fulfill; I will not speak of it now.
However, summon all the hunters within your realm and I shall speak in their midst," she declared, and uttered the following verse:
“O King, let all the hunters who are within your realm assemble;
I shall tell them the nature of my pregnancy-longing.
The king, saying “Very well,” emerged from the inner chamber and summoned all the hunters throughout the Kāsī country, extending for three hundred leagues.
“Have the drum beaten to assemble them,” he commanded his ministers. They did so accordingly.
Before long, the hunters dwelling in the kingdom of Kāsi arrived, each bringing tribute according to his means; they reported their arrival to the king.
All of them numbered about sixty thousand. When the king learned that they had arrived, he stood at the window.
Stretching out his hand and informing the queen that they had arrived, he said:
"These are those hunters, O Queen; they are skillful and confident, familiar with the forest and knowledgeable of the deer, who have risked their own lives for my sake."
"In this context, 'these are those' refers to those whom you have assembled. 'Skilled in hand' means they are dexterous, well-trained, and proficient in piercing and cutting.
'Confident' means fearless. 'Familiar with the woods and familiar with the wild animals' means they know both the forests and the beasts.
'All these, for my sake, have abandoned their lives' means that they will do whatever I desire."
Having heard that, the queen addressed them and spoke this other verse:
“Listen, sons of hunters, as many as are gathered here:
In a dream, I saw a white elephant with six tusks.”
"I have need for its tusks; if they are not obtained, there is no life for me.
"Listen to that! means: listen. "Six-tusked" means: possessing six-colored tusks.
Having heard this, the hunters' sons said:
“Neither by our fathers nor by our grandfathers has a six-tusked elephant ever been seen or heard of;
yet the princess saw one in a dream—O King, tell us what kind of noble elephant it was.
In this passage, *pitūnaṃ* is a genitive case used in the sense of the instrumental. This is what is meant: “O Queen, neither by our fathers... [and so forth].

"Neither our grandfathers nor we ourselves have ever seen such an elephant before; therefore, describe it to us according to the characteristics you yourself have observed—what kind of great elephant was seen by you?
The subsequent verses were also spoken by them:
“The four cardinal directions, the four intermediate directions, above and below—these are the ten directions.
In which direction does the Naga king stand, whom he saw as the six tusks in his dream?
In this context, *disā* means “in the directions. *Katamaṃ* means “which among these directions? that is, “in which direction?”
When this was said, Subhaddā looked at all the hunters and, among them, [saw] Sonuttara— the Great Being’s former enemy—
who stood with feet spread apart, whose shanks resembled a bowl of rice, who had large knees and great calves, whose teeth were thick and prominent,
whose eyes were yellowish and protruding, who was misshapen and hideous, and who appeared towering over the heads of everyone else.
Having seen the hunter Nesaḍa and thinking, "He will be able to carry out my word," she obtained the king's permission,
took him with her, ascended to the uppermost floor of the seven-storied palace, opened the northern lion-window,
and stretching out her hand toward the northern Himalayas, recited these four verses:
“Straight ahead in this northern direction, having passed beyond those seven mountains, O Brahmā,
there is a magnificent mountain named Suvaṇṇapassa, in full bloom and frequented by kimpurisas.
Having ascended that rocky abode of the kinnaras, look down upon the foot of the mountain.”
Then you will see the king of banyan trees, cloud-like in color, with eight thousand roots.
There dwells an elephant with six tusks, all-white and invincible by others;
eight thousand elephants protect him—each with tusks as long as plow-poles, swift as the wind in their stride.
“They remain there watching the tumult, and they become agitated even by the wind’s stirring;
but upon seeing a human being there, they would reduce him to ashes—not even his dust would remain on her.
In this context, *ito* means from this place. *Uttariyaṃ* means by the northern [direction]. *Uḷāro* means great compared to the other six mountains.
"Higher. "Look down" means you should look about. "He dwells there" means he stands at the foot of that banyan tree during the summer season, receiving the cool breeze from the water.
"Hard to overcome" means that since there is no one else capable of approaching him and acting with force, he is difficult for others to overcome.
"With tusks like chariot-poles" means his tusks are equal to the poles of a chariot. "Carrying the speed of the wind."
Moving with the speed of the wind, these eight thousand nāgas—whose nature it is to strike at enemies—protect the Nāga King.
They stand emitting a breath accompanied by a tumultuous, terrifying, and great sound.
Even when there is the "erita"—that is, the sound-accompanied agitation, shaking, or trembling caused by the wind-swept [trees]—they become provoked; such is the ferocity of those nāgas.
"‘Nāssa’ means that even the dust of that [body], having been reduced to ashes by being blown away with the breath of his nostrils, would not remain.
Having heard this, Soṇuttara, terrified by the fear of death, said:
"O Queen, there are many ornaments of gold belonging to me in the royal palace."
“Pearls, gems, and those made of beryl—what will you do with this ivory ornament?
Do you wish to kill the six-tusked elephant, or rather, do you intend to have the hunters killed under the pretext of obtaining ornaments?

In this context, *piḷandhanā* means ornaments. *Veḷuriyamayā* means made of beryl. *Ghātessasi* means: “Do you intend to have the hunters killed under the pretext of obtaining ornaments?”—thus he asks.
Then the queen spoke this verse:
“O hunter, I am oppressed and suffering; I am withering away as I remember him.
O hunter, do this thing for me, and I will give you five excellent villages.”
In that context, *sā* means "I. *Anussarantī* means "recalling the enmity formerly committed against me by that elephant.
*Dassāmi te* means "When this purpose of yours has been accomplished, I shall give you five excellent villages, yielding a hundred thousand [pieces of gold] per year.
Having spoken thus, she said: "Friend, son of a hunter, having caused this Chaddanta elephant to be killed and [taken its] twin tusks..."
“I was able to cause [the food] to be brought,” she said, and having comforted him, she sent him off, saying, “In the past, after giving alms to Paccekabuddhas, I made an aspiration;
there is nothing that I have not seen even in dreams. That aspiration I made will surely be fulfilled;
do not fear as you go. He replied, “Very well, noble lady,” and accepted her words.
Having accepted [the request], he asked, "In that case, make it clear to me and tell me where his dwelling place is," and spoke this verse:
"Where does he dwell, and where does he go? What is the path for him when he has gone to bathe?
How indeed does that king of elephants bathe? How may we know the destination of the elephant?"
In that context, "where does he dwell? means where he resides. "Where does he go? means where he approaches;
the meaning is, where does he stand? "What is his path? means what kind of path belongs to him when he has gone to bathe;
by which road does he go? "How shall we know his destination? means: if it is not told by you, how shall we know the destination of that Naga king?
"Therefore, tell me where it is," was the meaning.
Then, pointing out the place she had seen directly through her knowledge of recollecting past births (*jātissarañāṇa*), she spoke two verses:
"Right there, not far away, is that lotus pond—delightful, with excellent bathing places and vast waters."
“Blossoming and frequented by swarms of bees, here indeed bathes that king of nāgas. With his head washed,
wearing a garland of lotuses, all-white, with skin as beautiful as a white lotus,
he goes joyfully to his own abode, placing the Great Sage, the All-Auspicious One, before him.”
"In each and every place" means right there, in his own dwelling place. "Lotus pond" refers to the Chaddanta Lake.
"In full bloom" means blooming all around with two kinds of water lilies (*kumuda*), three kinds of blue lotuses (*uppala*), and five-colored red lotuses (*paduma*).
For it is here that he—the Nāga king—bathes in this Chaddanta Lake. "Bearing a garland of lotuses."
Carrying a garland of water-born and land-born flowers such as the *uppala* and others;

"possessing a body white like a white lotus" (*puṇḍarīkattacaṅgī*) means endowed with limbs that are as white as the skin of a white lotus; "rejoicing" (*āmodamāno*) means gladdened and delighted; "his own dwelling place" (*sanniketaṃ*) means his own residence;
"having placed in front" (*purakkhatvā*) means having positioned the great seer named Sabbabhadda before him, surrounded by eight thousand *nāgas*.
“He is going to his own dwelling place.
Having heard this, Sonuttara replied, “Very well, noble lady; I shall kill that elephant and bring its tusks back to you,” and he accepted her proposal.
Then she, being pleased, gave him a thousand pieces of money and said, “Go home for now; after seven days have passed from here—”

Having dismissed him with the words, "You shall go there," he summoned the smiths and commanded them: "Sirs, we have need of axes, hatchets, spades, picks, hammers, knives for cutting bamboo thickets, sickles, grass-cutters, iron staffs, saws, whetstones, and iron tridents;
having made all these quickly, bring them here. Then, having summoned the leather-workers, he said:
"Sirs, it is necessary for us to have a leather bag capable of holding a load of jars; we also require leather thongs, dyed elephant-hide sandals, and leather umbrellas."
"There is no need; prepare everything quickly and bring it here," he commanded. Both of them prepared all those things quickly, brought them, and gave them to him.

She prepared his provisions for the journey, placing the fire-drills first and all the other equipment, including the bound arrows and so forth, as well as the provisions, into a leather bag; she packed all of that as well.
It amounted to only a single jar-load.
Sonuttara, having made his own preparations, arrived on the seventh day, paid homage to the queen, and stood before her.
Then she said to him, "My good man, all your equipment is complete; take this bag for now."
But that man of great strength possessed the power of five elephants;
therefore, lifting him up like a betel-box and placing him between his thighs, he stood there as if his hands were empty.
Subhaddā, having given the hunter a provision for himself and his family and having informed the king, sent Sonuttara away. He too, having paid homage to the king and the queen, departed.
Having descended from the royal palace and mounted his chariot, he departed from the city with a great retinue.

Traveling through a succession of villages, market towns, and districts, he reached the frontier; there he dismissed the provincial inhabitants and entered the forest together with the border-dwellers.
Having passed beyond the path of men and dismissed even those border-dwellers, he proceeded alone until he had traveled thirty yojanas, whereupon he first—

The six thickets are: the thicket of *dabba* grass, the thicket of *kāsa* grass, the thicket of ordinary grass, the thicket of *tulasi*, the thicket of *sara* reeds, and the thicket of *tirivaccha* trees.

Furthermore, there are the thicket of thorny bamboo groves, the thicket of cane, the mixed thicket, the thicket of reeds—which is similar to the thicket of *sara* reeds and difficult even for a snake to penetrate—and the dense forest thicket, the thicket of trees, the thicket of bamboo, and another thicket of bamboo groves.
Having reached the eighteen thickets in succession—the thicket of mud, the thicket of water, and the thicket of mountains—he cleared away the thickets of *dabba* grass and others with a sickle;
he cut through the thickets of *tulasi* and others with a knife for cutting bamboo clumps; he hewed down trees with an axe;
and having pierced very large trees with a gimlet, he made a path while constructing a ladder in the bamboo grove.
Having made a bamboo thicket, he climbed it, cut a bamboo, and threw it over another bamboo thicket;
having passed through the top of that bamboo thicket, he spread a dry tree-bark mat across a swampy thicket and went by it;
having spread another, he lifted the first and spread it further ahead, thus passing beyond it; and in a watery thicket, he constructed a raft.

Having crossed the water-thicket by that means, she stood at the foot of the mountain; having tied an iron tripod with a rope and flung it upward so that it caught on the mountain, she climbed up by the rope and pierced the mountain with an iron staff tipped with diamond;
having pounded a stump there, she stood upon it, pulled the tripod toward her, and once again made it catch on the mountain above. There—
Standing there, he hung down a leather thong, took hold of it, descended, and tied it to the lower post.
Grasping the thong with his left hand and taking a mallet in his right, he struck the thong, pulled out the post, and climbed back up again.
By this same method, having climbed to the summit of the mountain, he descended on the other side in the very same manner as before.
First, having pounded a wooden stake at the top of a mountain, he ties a cord to a leather bag, winds it around the stake, and sits inside the bag himself.
Then, as if releasing spider-silk from monkeys, he descends while unwinding the cord. Some even say that he descends like a bird, catching the wind with his leather umbrella.

Thus, having taken Subhaddā’s word and departed from the city, the Teacher spoke, revealing how he had passed through seventeen thickets, reached a mountain thicket, and there, after crossing six mountains, ascended to the summit of the Suvaṇṇapassa mountain:

[The Teacher said: "Subhaddā, when I was departing from the city, I passed through seven thickets; having passed through them, I reached a mountain thicket. There too, having crossed six mountains, I ascended to the peak of the Suvaṇṇapassa mountain."
Having learned those words right there, the hunter took his quiver and bow and traversed seven vast mountains until he reached the magnificent mountain named Suvaṇṇapassa.
Having ascended that rock, the abode of the kinnaras, he gazed down at the foot of the mountain.
There he saw the king of banyan trees, with the color of a cloud and eight thousand roots.
There he saw an elephant with six tusks, entirely white and difficult for others to overcome;
eight thousand elephants—each with tusks like plow-poles and possessing the speed of the wind—were guarding it.
“There he saw nearby a lotus pond, delightful, with excellent bathing places and abundant water;
it was in full bloom and frequented by swarms of bees—the very place where that Nāga king used to bathe.
Having seen the path and the dwelling place of the Nāga as he went to bathe along the road,”
“An ignoble form has come near, dispatched by her who follows the sway of her own mind.

In this passage, monks, that hunter, having heard the words of Subhaddā while she stood on that seven-storied palace, and having taken his quiver and great bow, reached the mountain thicket and thought: “Which one indeed...”
"Is this indeed the mountain named Suvaṇṇapassa? Thus he weighed and examined the seven great mountains.
While thus examining them, seeing the magnificent mountain named Suvaṇṇapassa, he thought, "This must be it. He looked upon it;
having ascended that mountain which was the abode of the *kinnaras*, by virtue of the signal given by Subhaddā—
He looked down. "There" means that at the foot of the mountain, not far away, he saw that banyan tree (*nigrodha*).
"There" means standing at the foot of that banyan tree. "There" means right there within the mountain, not far from that banyan tree, he saw the lotus pond where he used to bathe.
"Having seen" means having descended from the Golden-Sided Mountain (*Suvaṇṇapassapabbata*) along with the elephants.
In the past, having mounted an elephant-footed sandal, while searching for the place where that city king had gone—the place where he habitually stayed—he saw everything:
"He goes by this path; he bathes here; having bathed and emerged, he stands here.
Driven by that state of mind which follows the power of his heart, being devoid of shame and ignoble in character, he [prepared] a pit.
"He came and set about it; he dug a pit—this is the meaning.

Herein, this is the gradual account: "It is said that after reaching the Great Being’s dwelling place in seven years and seven months plus seven days, he observed his dwelling place in the manner already described."
“Having dug a pit here and standing within it, I shall pierce the lordly elephant with a poison-tipped arrow and bring him to the end of his life,” he resolved.
Having entered the forest, he cut down trees for the sake of posts and other materials,
prepared the necessary supplies, and when the elephants had gone to bathe, he used a large hoe at the place where that elephant lived.
It is like digging a square pit, clearing away the loose earth, sowing seeds, sprinkling water,
setting up posts upon the mortar-stones, installing the beam and the lever, laying down the planks,
making a hole the size of a bamboo joint, filling it above with earth and rubbish, and then creating for oneself an entrance on one side.

When the pit had been thus prepared, at the very time of dawn, the hunter fastened a head-covering, donned the saffron robes, took up his bow together with an arrow smeared with poison, descended into the pit, and stood there. To illustrate this matter, the Teacher said:
“Having dug a pit and covered it over with planks, the hunter concealed himself and took up his bow.”
The doer of evil deeds struck the noble elephant with a common arrow as it was coming toward him.
Pierced by the shaft, the elephant let out a terrible cry like a heron;
and all the other elephants fled in a fearsome manner, trumpeting loudly, running toward the eight directions in every way, trampling grass and wood in their flight.
“While he was searching for someone to kill, he saw the saffron robe, the banner of the seers.
As he was touched by suffering, this perception arose: ‘The banner of the Arahants is beyond reproach by the virtuous.
In that context, *odhāya* means having lowered or inserted. *Passāgataṃ* means having come to the edge of his own pit. He...
It is said that on the second day, having arrived, bathed, and emerged from the water, he stood in a place called the Mahāvisāla Māla.
Then, water flowed from his body down to the region of his navel and fell upon the hunter’s body through that opening.
By this sign, the hunter realized that the Great Being had come and was standing there; thus, he struck him with a broad arrow as he approached.
He struck and pierced him. "One who commits a misdeed" means one who performs a wrongful act by causing physical and mental suffering to that Great Being.
"Letting out a cry" means he uttered a cry of distress. It is said that his arrow entered through the navel and reached the liver and other organs.
Having crushed it and severed the edges, as if splitting the back portion with an axe, it surged up and leapt into the air.
Like dye from a broken silver jar, blood flowed from the wound;
intense pain arose. Unable to endure the sensation, overcome by that pain, he let out a single great cry that resounded throughout the entire mountain.
Making a great cry like a crane (*koñca*), he trumpeted three times.
And all of them—all those eight thousand elephants—having heard that sound, terrified by the fear of death, let out a terrible, echoing roar.
"Making a clamor" means that, having gone by that sound and seeing the elephant Chaddanta in agony, they thought, "We shall seize our enemy."

"Monks, while they were running about on all sides crushing grass, wood, and dust into powder, thinking, 'We shall kill him!', that Chaddanta elephant—after the other elephants had departed in all directions—stood by the side of the female elephant Subhaddā.
Standing there, she supported him and comforted him; and he, enduring the pain of the wound..."

Observing the place from which it had come, he reflected: "If this had come from the eastern direction or other such quarters, it would have entered through the mouth or other openings and emerged from the lower parts of the body;

but since it entered through the navel and leapt into the air, it must have been discharged while standing upon the earth. Having thus determined this, he desired to examine the spot where it had stood.
Thinking, "Who knows what will happen? It is right to remove Subhaddā," he said, "Bhadde, eight thousand elephants have scattered in all directions searching for my enemy; what are you doing here?
To which she replied three times, circumambulating him clockwise: "Your Majesty, I remained here supporting and comforting you; please forgive me."
Having performed obeisance at four places and having leaped into the air by means of that [power], the Nāga King struck the ground with his hoof-nail;
