a fissure opened and she departed. Peering through the opening, he saw Sonuttarā;
thinking, "I shall kill her," he aroused the intent to do so, thrust in his trunk—which was the color of a silver garland—and began to feel her about, [when he remembered] the Buddhas and the Sages.
He saw the saffron-colored banner. The hunter placed the saffron robe in the Great Being’s hand; lifting it up, he set it before him.

Then, even while he was afflicted by such suffering, this perception arose in him: "The banner of the Arahant is something that cannot be reviled by the virtuous and wise; rather, it is indeed to be honored and revered."
Thus, conversing with him, he spoke these two verses:
“He who, being impure, shall wear the saffron robe,
Lacking self-control and truthfulness, does not deserve the saffron robe.”
“But he who has vomited out impurities, who is well-composed in his virtues, and who is endowed with self-control and truth—he indeed is worthy of the saffron robe.
The meaning of this is: O son of a hunter, that man who is not free from the impurities of passion and so forth, yet possesses the restraint of the sense faculties...

One who is devoid of truth in both deed and speech, and has not attained those virtues, yet wears the saffron-colored robe dyed with the juice of *kasāya*—he does not deserve that saffron; he is not worthy of that garment.

But he who, because he has vomited up those *kasāyas*, is one whose *kasāya* is vomited out, who is well-composed in his moralities, firmly established, and perfect in conduct and virtue—he indeed [deserves it].
“It is indeed worthy of the name ‘saṅghāṭī robe’.

Having said this, the Great Being calmed his mind and asked, “Good man, for what purpose have you struck me? Is it for your own sake, or have you been instigated by another? To clarify this matter, the Teacher said:
“The elephant, though pierced by a broad arrow, spoke to the hunter with a mind free from malice:”
“For what purpose, for what reason, or by whose instigation have you killed me?
In this context, “for what purpose” means desiring what for the future. “For what reason” means for what cause or motive;
the intention is: “What enmity do you have with me? “By whose [instigation]” means by whom else was this act prompted?
"By whom was I incited to kill you? is the meaning.
Then, explaining it to him, the hunter spoke this verse:
"O Venerable One, she was the chief queen of the King of Kāsi; that Subhaddā was highly honored in the royal court."
“She saw him and spoke to me; she told me, ‘There is a tusk [treasure]’.
In this context, “honored” means she was honored by being established in the position of chief queen. “She saw” means, it is said, that she saw him in a dream.
“She spoke” means that after she had caused honor to be paid to me, she said, “In a region of the Himalayas, there is such a nāga in such-and-such a place...”
“He told me that he lives in such-and-such a place. Regarding the word “with tusks”: that elephant’s tusks were radiant with six-colored rays;
she said to me, “I have need of them, for I wish to have them fashioned into ornaments; bring them to me.

Having heard this and realizing, “This is the work of Cūḷasubhaddā,” the Great Being endured the pain and spoke two verses, demonstrating: “She has no need of my tusks; rather, she sent me because she wishes to kill me.”
“Many were these noble pairs of tusks that belonged to my fathers and grandfathers;
that angry princess knows this, and being foolish and seeking death, she has created this enmity.
‘Arise, you hunter! Take your axe and cut off these tusks before I die.’”
"You should speak thus to that wrathful princess: 'Behold, the elephant is slain; here are its tusks!
In this context, "these" refers to the tusks of his father's grandfather, which, it is said, had been collected in a cave so that they would not perish;
it was with reference to them that he spoke thus. "He knows" means he knows the tusks of many elephants gathered here. "Desirous of killing" means...
But she, desiring only to kill me, harbored a slight offense in her heart and thus created enmity for herself;
by such a cruel deed, she brought matters to their ultimate conclusion. *Kharā* means a saw. *Purā marāmi* means "as long as I do not die.
*Vajjasi* means "you would say. *Handa imassa dantā* means "Behold, this elephant has been slain by me; your desire is fulfilled."
"Having reached my head, take these teeth of mine.
Having heard his words, he rose from his sitting place, took a saw, and approached him with the thought, "I shall cut off the teeth.
But he stood there like a mountain of silver, eighty-eight cubits in height.
Thus, it did not reach his mouth. Then the Great Being, lowering his body, lay down with his head downward.
At that time, the hunter, crushing the Great Being’s trunk which resembled a silver garland, climbed up and stood upon his frontal globe as if atop Mount Kailāsa;
then, striking the flesh at the tip of his mouth with a bow, he thrust it inside and [pulled it] from the frontal globe.
Having risen, he inserted a saw into the Great Being’s mouth and pulled it back and forth forcefully with both hands.
Intense pain arose in the Great Being, and his mouth was filled with blood. Although the hunter moved it here and there, he was unable to cut through with the saw.
Then the Great Being, spitting out the blood from his mouth and enduring the pain, [remained still].
“What is it, my friend, that you cannot cut? he asked. “Yes, master,” he replied.
The Great Being, establishing mindfulness, said, “In that case, my friend, lift up my trunk and let me grasp the edge of the saw; I do not have the strength to lift my own trunk.
The hunter did exactly as he was told.
The Great Being took the saw with his trunk and moved it back and forth; his tusks were cut away like lotus stalks.

Then, having had them brought to him and taken hold of them, he said: "Good hunter, when I give these tusks to you, I do not give them because they are dear to me, nor because I am aspiring for the state of Sakka, Māra, or Brahmā; rather, by these..."
“Compared to my own teeth, the teeth of omniscient wisdom are dearer to me by a hundredfold, a thousandfold, and a hundred-thousandfold;
may this merit be a condition for my penetration of omniscient wisdom. Having thus given his teeth, he asked, “Friend, how long has it been since you arrived at this place?
and [the other replied], “Seven months and seven days more than seven years ago...”
When he said, “In years,” [the Teacher] replied, “Go; by the power of these tusks, you will reach Bārāṇasī within seven days itself.
Having spoken thus, he performed a protective charm for him and sent him forth.
But after sending him away, even before those Nāgas had returned and before Subhaddā had arrived, he passed away. To clarify this matter, the Teacher said:
“Rising up, that hunter took his axe, cut out the tusks of that supreme elephant—those lovely, beautiful, and peerless ones on this earth—and quickly departed from there, taking them with him.
In this context, *vaggū* means charming; *subhe* means beautiful; and *appaṭime* means peerless, being unlike any other tusks on this earth.
When he had departed, those nāgas, not seeing their enemy, returned. To clarify this matter, the Teacher said:
“Afflicted by fear, tormented by the slaughter of their kinsmen, those nāgas fled in the eight directions;
but not seeing the man who was the elephant’s adversary, they returned to where that king of nāgas was.”
In this context, "distressed by fear" means afflicted by the fear of death. "Distressed" (aṭṭā) means suffering.

"The elephant's enemy" means the adversary of the elephant. "Where he was" means that they returned to that place where the royal nāga, having died in the wide enclosure, fell like Mount Kelāsa. This is the meaning.
Mahāsubhaddā had also come along with them.

All those eight thousand elephants, having wept and wailed there, went into the presence of the Paccekabuddhas who were the Mahāsatta’s spiritual relatives and said, "Venerable sirs, the one who provided for your needs has been struck by a poison-smeared arrow and has passed away; please come to see his charnel ground."
They spoke thus. Five hundred paccekabuddhas also arrived through the air and descended at Visālamālaka.
At that moment, two young nāgas lifted the body of the nāga-king with their tusks, caused the paccekabuddhas to pay homage to it, placed it upon the funeral pyre, and cremated it.
Throughout the entire night, the paccekabuddhas recited the Dhamma at the cremation site. Eight thousand nāgas...
Having extinguished the funeral pyre, paid their respects, and bathed, they placed Mahāsubhaddā at their head and returned to their own dwelling place.
To clarify this matter, the Teacher said:
“Those nāgas, having wept and wailed there, scattered dust upon their own heads;”
“They all returned to their own abodes, placing the Great Seer, the All-Auspicious One, at their head.
In this context, “rubbish” refers to the dust from a cremation ground.
Sona-uttara also, having taken his teeth, reached Bārāṇasī even before the seventh day had passed. Explaining this matter, the Teacher said:
“Having taken the tusks of the supreme elephant—lovely, pure, and peerless on earth, with their golden streaks shining all around—that hunter went to the city of Kāsī.
He presented the tusks to the king’s daughter, saying: ‘The elephant has been slain; here, take its tusks.’”

In that context, "with golden streaks" means with the rays of golden streaks. "Shining all around" means shining forth on every side, making the entire forest grove appear as if it were golden-colored.

"He brought [the message]" means that he sent a message to the queen, saying: "I am coming, having taken up the twin tusks for the emission of the six-colored rays of the Chaddanta elephant; please have the city decorated. It was by her [that this was done].
Having informed the king and had the city decorated like the city of the gods, Sona-uttara entered the city, ascended the palace, and applied the tusks.
Having applied them, he said: "Madam, that elephant for whose slight fault you held a grudge in your heart has been killed by me; he is dead. Please inform him of my death."
“You know his state as one who has passed away; take them,” she said, and gave him the tusks.

She took the Great Being’s tusks—which were variegated with six-colored rays—with a jeweled fan, placed them upon her thighs, and looking at the tusks of her own husband from a previous birth, [she thought]: “Such a tusker, having attained such supreme beauty...”
"Having brought about the end of my life with this poisoned dart, he has returned after cutting off these tusks," she said, and as she recollected the Great Being, grief arose within her;
unable to endure it, her heart burst right there, and she passed away that very day. To clarify this matter, the Teacher said:
“Having seen the tusks of that supreme elephant, dear to his master, in his previous birth, she struck her own heart right there;
by that very act, the foolish woman met her death.
“Having attained full enlightenment, that one of great majesty let out a smile in the midst of the assembly.”
The monks whose minds were well-liberated asked: "Buddhas do not manifest [themselves] without a reason.
'That young maiden whom you saw wearing saffron robes, wandering the homeless life—she was indeed a princess at that time, and I was the king of the nāgas then.'"
“The hunter who, taking the beautiful, pure, and peerless tusks of the supreme elephant,
went to the city of Kāsī, was at that time Devadatta. This ancient conduct,
varied and long-practiced through many nights, was not without its consequences.”
“Free from fear, free from sorrow, and without taints, the Buddha spoke after realizing it for himself:
‘At that time, O monks, I was there;
I was then a king of the nāgas—thus you should remember this Jātaka.’”
These verses were composed by the Elders of the Dhamma Council while praising the virtues of the One Possessing the Ten Powers.

Regarding the phrase "he smiled": on one occasion, that Teacher who had attained full enlightenment, being of great majesty, was seated in the midst of the assembly upon the decorated Dhamma throne within the decorated Dhamma Hall, and he smiled. As for the words "not without cause": "Venerable Sir... [the text continues].
"Buddhas do not smile without cause, yet you have smiled; for what reason, then, was this smile made?

Thus the bhikkhus, who were great ones with taints destroyed, asked. Being asked, "What did you see?", friends, the Teacher, explaining the reason for his smile, pointed out a certain young bhikkhunī and said: "Bhikkhus..."
Behold that one young maiden, who had reached the prime of youth, clad in saffron robes and having gone forth into homelessness, practicing within this teaching.
She was once a princess sent by Sona Uttara with the command: "Pierce and slay the Naga king with an arrow dipped in poison. By him, she was sent and met her end.
The meaning is: "At that time, I was that Nāga king. Regarding "Devadatta": monks, the one who is now Devadatta was at that time that hunter.
"Anāvasūram" means not when the sun has set; the meaning is, while the sun has not yet gone down. "Cirarattasaṃsitam" means for a long time from here on.
It has been practiced, wandered through, and pursued throughout the course of many tens of millions of years. This is what is meant:

"Friend, even though this was done while wandering through the cycle of existence for many tens of millions of years from now on, it is—by virtue of his own conduct, as well as the conduct of that princess and of Sonuttara—like one who remembers in the evening what was done in the forenoon of that very same day."

This ancient conduct of going from low to high and from high to low has been spoken by the Buddha himself after he had realized it for himself—being "free from fear" (*vītaddara*) through the removal of the fears of passion and so forth, "free from sorrow" (*vītasoka*) through the absence of grief for kinsmen, wealth, and the like, and "without a dart" (*visalla*) through the departure of the darts of passion and other defilements.
In the phrase "I, indeed" (*ahaṃ vo*), *vo* is merely a particle; O monks, at that time and in that place, on the Chaddanta Lake, I [spoke].
The meaning is "I was. Furthermore, the meaning of "being a Nāga king" is that at that time I was not anyone else, but rather I was a Nāga king.
"And thus you should preserve it" means: "You should maintain, learn, and master this Jātaka in this way.
Moreover, upon hearing this teaching of the Dhamma, many became stream-enterers and so forth. And that bhikkhunī, having later practiced insight meditation, attained Arahatship.
The fourth is the Commentary on the Chaddanta Jātaka.
[515] 5. The Commentary on the Sambhava Jātaka:

"And having entered upon kingship..."—this was spoken by the Teacher while dwelling in Jetavana, concerning the perfection of wisdom (paññāpāramī). The story of the present will be made clear in the Mahā-Umaṅga Jātaka.
In the past, in the kingdom of Kuru, in the city of Indapatta, a king named Dhanañjaya Koravya reigned.
He had a brahmin chaplain named Sucirata who instructed him in matters of worldly prosperity and the Dhamma. The king, performing meritorious deeds such as giving, governed the kingdom righteously.
One day, having formulated a question known as the "Dhamma-sacrifice," he...
Having had the brahmin chaplain Sucīrata seated on a throne and having paid him honor, he asked a question,
speaking these four verses:
“We have entered upon kingship and hold sovereign power, O Sucīrata;”
“I wish to attain greatness and to conquer this earth.
By righteousness, not by unrighteousness; for unrighteousness is not pleasing to me.
Indeed, it is the duty of a king to practice righteousness, which is characterized by pure conduct.”
“By that through which we are not censured here, and by which we are not censured after passing away,
and by which we attain glory among gods and humans, O brahmin— by that very path I,
who desire to act for the sake of welfare and Dhamma, O brahmin, [proceed].”
“Being asked, O Brahmin, tell us that which is both the goal and the Dhamma.

“In this matter, Teacher, we have attained sovereignty over this city of Indapatta, seven yojanas in extent, and lordship—meaning the status of a ruler—over the Kuru kingdom, three hundred yojanas in extent. We have attained it,” he said.
"Let us become great. "Now, I desire to attain greatness"—that is, I wish to conquer and to overcome this earth through righteousness (*dhamma*).
"It is a duty"—the conduct practiced by kings among the rest of the people is a duty, something more to be performed.
For the world follows the king; when he is righteous, everyone becomes righteous as well.
Therefore, this duty called "Dhamma" is indeed the king's task.
"And blameless here" means that by this we shall be blameless in both this world and the next.
"By which we may attain" means that by this we shall not be reborn in the hells and other such realms, but shall attain fame, sovereignty, and good fortune among gods and humans.

"Tell us that reason. "O Brahmin, 'I' refers to me who desires to undertake, practice, and bring forth both the goal—which is reckoned as the ripening of the fruit—and the Dhamma which is the cause of that goal.
'You' refers to you, who, having easily ascended the path leading to Nibbāna, [shall attain] the state of being without rebirth."

To him who was thus aspiring for that goal, he asked the Brahmin the question regarding the sacrifice of Dhamma: "When you are questioned, explain both that goal and the Dhamma; speak, making it clear.
However, this question is profound and within the domain of a Buddha; it is fitting to ask it of an omniscient Buddha alone. Regarding that—
"He is a Bodhisatta seeking omniscience. However, because he had long since ceased to be a Bodhisatta, he was unable to answer the question;
being unable to do so, and instead of maintaining his pride as a scholar, he spoke this verse while declaring his own incapacity:
“O King, no one other than Vidhura is worthy to explain this, that which you, O Kshatriya, desire to do for the sake of both profit and Dhamma. The meaning of this is:
“This question, Great King, is beyond the scope of those like me. For I know neither its beginning nor its end.”
"I see nothing; I am as if entered into darkness. However, there is a brahmin named Vidhura who is the royal chaplain to the King of Bārāṇasī;
he would explain this to you. Apart from him, no one else is worthy to declare that purpose and Dhamma which you wish to perform."
Having heard his words, the king, wishing to send him with a gift, said this verse:
“Go now, sent by me, to the presence of Vidhura;
take this gold coin of pure gold and go, O man of noble conduct.”
“One should give this offering for the sake of instruction in the meaning and the Dhamma.
Therein, *upantikaṃ* means “in the presence of. *Nikkha* refers to one piece of fivefold gold (*pañcasuvaṇṇa*).
However, having given a thousand nikkhas of red gold, he spoke thus: “One should give this. This was said by him when this question on the sacrifice of Dhamma (*dhammayāga*) had been posed.
"Performing an offering of hospitality by instructing you in the meaning of the Dhamma, you should give me this thousand *nikkhas*.
Having spoken thus, he gave him a gold plate worth a hundred thousand [pieces] for the purpose of writing the answers to the questions,
a vehicle for the journey, an army for his retinue, and those ceremonial gifts, and at that very moment—
He sent him forth. Having departed from the city of Indapatta, instead of going straight to Bārāṇasī, he visited every place where wise men resided;
yet, finding no one in all of Jambudīpa capable of answering his question, he eventually reached Bārāṇasī, took up residence in a certain spot, and stayed there.
At the time for the morning meal, having gone with several people to Vidhura’s residence and announced his arrival,
he was summoned by him and saw him eating in his own home. Explaining this matter,
the Teacher spoke the seventh verse:
“Bhāradvāja, having reached his destination, went into the presence of Vidhura;
there the Great Brahmā saw him, not sitting at his own table.

In this passage, *svādhippāgā* means that he, belonging to the Bhāradvāja clan, had long since reached (*adhippāgā*)—that is, gone—to his destination. *Mahābrahmā* means the Great Brāhmaṇa. *Asamānaṃ* means [seeing him] while he was eating.
Now, his foolish companion, having learned a craft in the same teacher’s household, ate together with him;
and at the conclusion of the meal, while sitting comfortably, he was asked, "Friend, for what purpose have you come?
and explaining the reason for his arrival, he spoke the eighth verse:
“I have been sent as a messenger by the illustrious King Koravya;
Yudhiṭṭhila spoke thus: ‘Ask about what is beneficial and about the Dhamma.
Therefore, Vidhura, being questioned, explain that benefit and the Dhamma.”
In this context, "of the king" means: "I am the messenger of the illustrious King Koravya.
"Sent" means: dispatched by him, I have come here. "He asked" means: that King Dhanañjaya of the Yudhiṭṭhila clan asked me the question known as the *Dhammayāga* (Sacrifice of Dhamma).
Not being able to explain it myself, and knowing that you would be capable of doing so, I informed him; and he, having given a gift, [sent me].

"When he sent me to you for the purpose of asking questions, he said: 'Go to Vidhura and ask him the meaning and the textual doctrine of this question. Now that I have asked it of you, please explain it.

At that time, however, that brahmin, thinking "I shall win over the minds of the great multitude," deliberated upon the legal judgment as if he were damming the Ganges. There was no opportunity for him to answer the question. Explaining the matter, he spoke the ninth verse:
“They will block the Gaṅgā for me, O brahmin, yet I am not able to block that great ocean. How then could he be such?
When asked about the meaning and the Dhamma, I am not able to explain it to you.”
The meaning of this is as follows: O Brahmin, the intention arose in me, "I shall close off the Ganges, which consists of the various mental dispositions of the great multitude";

however, I am unable to close off that great ocean. Therefore, how could there be such an opportunity for me to answer your question? Thus, failing to obtain both one-pointedness of mind and an opportunity, [he remained silent].
“I am not able to explain the meaning and the Dhamma to you when asked.
Having spoken thus, he said, “My son is wise and possesses even greater knowledge than I; he will answer you. Go into his presence,” and spoke the tenth verse:
“My son Bhadrakāra is my own legitimate offspring;”
“Go, O brahmin, and having approached him, ask him about that matter and the Dhamma.
Therein, “legitimate son” (*orasa*) means one raised upon the breast; “own child” (*atraja*) means one born from oneself.

Having heard this, Sucira departed from Vidhura’s house and went to his own residence at the time when Bhadrakāra had finished his breakfast and was seated in the midst of his own assembly. To clarify this matter, the Teacher spoke the eleventh verse:
“Bhāradvāja, having attained his own purpose, went to the presence of Bhadrakāra;
Mahābrahmā saw him sitting in that very house.
In this context, *vesmani* means “in the house.”
Having gone there, he accepted the hospitality offered by the young Māṇava Bhadraka in the form of a seat, and having sat down, when asked the reason for his coming, he spoke the twelfth verse:
“I have been sent as a messenger by the illustrious King Koravya;
‘Ask about the goal and the Dhamma,’ thus said Yudhiṭṭhila.”
“Therefore, O Bhadrakāra, speak to me of that matter and the Dhamma.
Then Bhadrakāra said to him, “Dear father, during these days I have been intent upon the act of adultery;
my mind is distracted, and because of that, I shall not be able to answer you. However, my younger brother Sañcayakumāra—”
"Indeed, he is far more knowledgeable than I; ask him, and he will answer your question.
Speaking thus as he sent him into his presence, he uttered these two verses:
"Leaving behind the deer of flesh, I am pursuing the iguana; ... [the rest of the verse follows]"
“I am unable to explain the meaning and the Dhamma when questioned.
I have a younger brother named Sañjaya, who is pure in conduct;
go to him, O brahmin, and ask him about the meaning and the Dhamma.”
In this context, "carrying a load of meat" is said to illustrate how a man, while walking along carrying a load of meat from a large deer on a carrying pole,
might see a young jackal in the middle of the road, discard the meat-load, and pursue it; in the same way,
he spoke thus to show that he was discarding his own wife, who lived under his authority in his home, and was pursuing another woman who was protected and guarded by someone else.
At that moment, having gone to Sañjaya’s residence and being honored by him, he was asked the reason for his visit and explained it. To clarify this matter, the Teacher spoke these two verses:
“Bhāradvāja came from his own home to the presence of Sañjaya;
the Great Brahmā saw him seated in the nearby dwelling.”
“I have been sent as a messenger by the illustrious King Koravya;
Yudhiṭṭhila spoke thus: ‘Ask about what is beneficial and what is righteous.
Being questioned, you must explain that benefit and righteousness to him.”
But at that time, Prince Sañjaya was indeed consorting with another man’s wife. He said to him, "Father, I am consorting with another man’s wife;
while doing so, I go to the far bank after descending into the Ganges.
Yet, as I cross the river morning and evening, Death swallows me up, and because of this my mind is distracted; I am not able to tell you [of this]."
"But I have a younger brother named Prince Sambhava, who is seven years of age;
he possesses knowledge exceeding mine a hundredfold, a thousandfold, and even a hundred-thousandfold. He will explain it to you; go and ask him," he said.
To clarify this matter, the Teacher spoke two verses:
“Death swallows me always, both evening and morning, O Sucīrata;
I am unable to explain the meaning and the Dhamma when questioned by you.
My younger brother, Sucīrata, is named Sambhava.”
“Go, O Brahmin, and having approached him, ask about that matter and the Dhamma.
Having heard this, Sucirata thought, “This question will surely be extraordinary in this world; I believe there is no one capable of answering this question,” and he spoke these two verses:
“Truly extraordinary is this Dhamma! It does not please us.”
These three people—father and sons—are not wise in wisdom.
"When asked about the meaning and the Dhamma, you are unable to explain them;
how indeed could a youth know the meaning and the Dhamma when asked?"
In that regard, this "nāyanti" (they lead) is a marvelous phenomenon; indeed, one ought not to be capable of explaining this.
Therefore, as for what you say, "the prince will explain," this does not please us. In the word *te sū*, the syllable *su* is merely a particle (*nipātamatta*).
"Father" refers to the wise Vidhura; "sons" refers to Bhadrakāra and Sañcaya—these too [do not please us].
The meaning is: "These three—father and sons—do not know this Dhamma through wisdom; they do not understand it. Who else will know it? Regarding the phrase "not you":
you three people, when questioned, are unable to explain this. How indeed could a young boy of seven years, when questioned, know it?
By what means would he be able to know it? This is the meaning.
Having heard this, Prince Sañjaya spoke twelve verses, illustrating the prince’s excellence with parables that revealed the truth:
“Do not despise Sambhava as a youth without having questioned him; and so forth.
“Having asked, one should know the origin, O Brahmin, as well as the meaning and the Dhamma.
Just as the stainless moon, moving through the expanse of space,
outshines all the hosts of stars in the world with its radiance.”
“Even so, though he appears young, his origin is through the application of wisdom.
Do not despise him as ‘young’ without having inquired into his origin.
Having inquired into his origin, one should know his purpose and his Dhamma, O Brahmin.”
“Just as the month of Rammaka, O Brahmin, is among the summer months,
and shines with the blossoms of trees more than any other months; even so,
though still young in appearance, one’s excellence arises through the application of wisdom.”
"Do not despise him as being young, O Brahmin, without having inquired into his origin.
Having inquired into his origin, one would know his purpose and his Dhamma.
Just as Mount Gandhamādana, O Brahmā, is like the Himavat mountain..."
Covered with various trees, it is the abode of great hosts of beings;
with divine medicinal herbs, it shines and wafts its fragrance in all directions.
"In this way too, though appearing young, there is an arising through the application of wisdom."
"Do not despise him as 'young,' O Brahmin, without having inquired about his origin.
Having inquired about his origin, one may know his purpose and his Dhamma.
Just as fire, O Brahmā, is garlanded with flames and full of glory..."
Burning in the forest, he goes as a fire along the dark path.
With smoke for his banner and a vessel for his seat, the supreme consumer of the forest delights in burning;
at midnight upon the mountain peak, he shines with abundant fuel.
“Even so, though he appears young, his existence arises through the application of wisdom.
Do not despise him as ‘young’ without having inquired into his origin.
Having inquired into his origin, one should know his purpose and his Dhamma, O Brahmin.”
“They know a noble steed by its speed, and a draft-ox by its carrying;
they know a cow by her milk, and a wise man by his speech.
Even so, though appearing as a mere youth, one’s true nature is revealed through the application of wisdom.”
"Do not despise him as being young, without having inquired about his origin;
by inquiring about his origin, O brahmins, you shall know his purpose and his Dhamma. In this context, "you shall know" (*jaññā*) means you will come to understand.
"The moon" (*cando*) refers to the full moon. "Stainless" (*vimalo*) means free from stains such as clouds and the like. Thus it is said.

"Daharūpeto" means that although Prince Saṃbhava was endowed with youth, he outshone all other wise men throughout the entire surface of Jambudīpa by virtue of his application of wisdom (*paññā-yoga*).
"Rammako" refers to the month of Cittā. "Atevaññehi" means far more than the other eleven months.
"Evaṃ" means that in this way, Saṃbhava also shines through his application of wisdom. "Himavā" refers to the time when snow falls.

*Himavant* means "possessing snow"; it is called *Himavant* because it vomits forth snow during the summer season. *Gandhamādana* means it intoxicates (*madayati*) people who have arrived there with its fragrance.
*Mahābhūtagaṇālaya* means the dwelling place of the hosts of deities. *Disā bhāti* means it makes all directions appear as if they were a single radiance.

*Pavāti* means it blows through all directions with its fragrance. *Evaṃ* means that in this very way, even such a manifestation [of the mountain] is known through the application of wisdom (*paññāyogena*).
It shines and blows forth in all directions.
"Glorious" means glorious by virtue of the perfection of its splendor (*tejas*). "Garlanded with flames" means endowed with flames.
"He goes blazing through the forest" means he wanders, burning, in the great forest known as Gaccha. "The fire" means insatiable. Because of the blackness of the path it has traversed—
He has a black track (kaṇhavattanī). He eats the ghee offered as an oblation in sacrifice by way of the offering, thus he is "ghee-eater" (ghatāsana).

Smoke accomplishes his function as a banner, thus he is "smoke-bannered" (dhūmaketu). He burns the supreme forest; "forest" (ahevana) is said to mean a grove, so the meaning is that he burns the supreme grove.
At "midnight" (nisītha), that is, during the portion of the night. "On the mountain peak" (pabbatagga) means on the summit of a mountain.
"Pahūte" means having abundant fuel. "Virocati" means it shines forth in all directions. "Evaṃ" means:

even though my younger brother, Prince Sambhava, is young, he shines through his application of wisdom. "Bhadraṃ" refers to a noble thoroughbred horse; they recognize him as such because of his excellence in speed, not because of his physical form.
"Vāhiye" means: when there is a burden to be carried, by virtue of carrying that burden, [the horse thinks], "I am the best."
They know the ox tied for sacrifice. By "milking," they know the cow as "one that yields easily" through the excellence of her milk.
Regarding "speaking," one should cite here the sutta: "They do not know the wise man by his silence when he is among fools.
While he was thus describing the possibility of such a thing after a long time, [the king thought], "I shall find out by asking a question": "But where..."

"Which one is my younger brother? he asked. Then, opening the lion-window and extending his hand, he said, "That golden-colored youth who is playing with the other boys in the street at the palace gate—that is my younger brother.
Go up to him and ask him; he will answer your question with the grace of a Buddha. After a long time...
Having heard his words, he descended from the palace and went into the presence of the prince. At what time?
At the time when the prince had removed his lower garment, thrown it over his shoulder, and stood holding dust in both hands.
Explaining this matter, the Teacher spoke this verse:
“Bhāradvāja, having set out from his own home, went to the presence of Sambhava;
there Mahābrahmā saw him playing in the outer city.
In this context, “in the outer city” means in the outer dwelling.
The Great Being, seeing the brahmin who had arrived and was standing before him, asked, "Dear father, for what purpose have you come?

When the brahmin replied, "Dear son, Prince, while wandering throughout the land of Jambudīpa, I have come to your presence because I could find no one capable of answering the question I asked," [the Prince thought], "It seems there is a question that has not been resolved anywhere in all of Jambudīpa."
“‘He has come into my presence, and I am advanced in wisdom,’ thinking thus, he regained a sense of shame and moral dread;

casting away the dust held in his hand, taking a cloth from his shoulder, and putting it on, he offered the invitation of the Omniscient One, saying: ‘Ask, brahmin, and I shall answer you with the grace of a Buddha. Then the brahmin—”
“I have been sent as a messenger by King Yudhiṭṭhila, the illustrious Koravya, who said:
‘Ask about what is beneficial and what is righteous.
Being thus questioned, you must explain to him both that which is beneficial and that which is righteous.”
He asked a question in verse.
Its meaning became as clear to Sambhava Paṇḍita as the full moon in the midst of the sky.
Then, saying to him, "In that case, listen," he spoke this verse while answering the Dhammayāga question:
“Truly, I shall declare it to you, just as one who is skilled would;
but the king himself must know whether you will do it or not.
As he stood in the middle of the street teaching the Dhamma with a sweet voice, his sound reached twelve yojanas.
It overspread the entire city of Vārāṇasī. Then the king, the viceroy, and all the others assembled.
In the midst of the great multitude, the Great Being began his teaching of the Dhamma.
In this context, *taggha* is an emphatic expression. *Yathāpi kusalo* means "just as the All-Knowing Buddha, who is exceedingly skillful, explains."
In that way, they will certainly declare it to me; this is the point.
As for the King, I shall explain that question to him in such a way that your king is able to understand it.
Beyond that, the King himself alone knows whether he will act or not act, and whether it will belong to him if he acts or does not act.
He indicates, however, that he himself has no fault.
Having thus pledged himself to answer the question with this verse, he now spoke while explaining the "Gift of Dhamma" question:
"One should say, 'Today or tomorrow,' O King of pure conduct, when asked by a king."
“Let not King Yudhiṭṭhila, when a matter has arisen, be despondent after having acted.
When questioned by the king, O one of pure conduct, he should reflect only within himself;
he should not settle upon a wrong path like one who is deluded and mindless.”
“One should not overstep oneself, nor should one practice what is unrighteous;
one should not cross where there is no ford, nor should one be intent on what is harmful.
And that kshatriya who knows how to perform these deeds—”
That king always prospers, like the moon in the bright fortnight.
He is beloved by his kinsmen and shines among his friends;
at the breaking up of the body, that wise man is reborn in heaven.
In this context, *saṃseyya* means he would speak. This is what is meant:
"Dear Sucirata, if you were asked by your king, 'Today we shall give alms, we shall guard our virtue, and we shall perform the Uposatha observance,' you would say:
'Great King, let us first kill living beings today, enjoy sensual pleasures, and drink liquor; we shall perform wholesome deeds tomorrow.'"

If one were to speak thus to the king, and if, having acted upon the words of even that very high-ranking minister, your king of the Yudhiṭṭhila clan were to spend that day in negligence when such a critical occasion had arisen—do not let it be so!
Without disregarding his words, and without letting the wholesome state of mind that has arisen decline, he should indeed perform actions connected with the wholesome; this is for his sake.
"You should speak," [said the king]. Thus, by means of this verse—"Today itself the task for diligence must be done;
who knows if death will come tomorrow?"—the Great Being [taught] both the *Bhaddekaratta Sutta* and...
“Diligence is the path to the Deathless; negligence is the path of death.
Thus he spoke the discourse on diligence.
“Only within oneself,” dear Sucirata, did the wise Sambhava respond when you asked the question regarding the sacrifice of Dhamma.
When asked by the king, "Tell me," you should speak only of what is internal to the king himself;
you should say that the five aggregates, which constitute one's own internal nature, are impermanent because they are subject to non-existence. At this point, the Great Being [would have said]:
"When one sees with wisdom that all conditioned phenomena are impermanent."
“Impermanent indeed are conditioned phenomena, subject to arising and passing away”—
thus he spoke of impermanence as it has been clearly discerned.
“The wrong path,” O Brahmin, refers to that which is characterized by the sixty-two types of views, [taken] by the deluded, insentient, blind, foolish worldling.
"He follows a wrong path; thus, may your king not follow that wrong path, but may he follow only the path of the ten courses of wholesome action which leads to liberation.
You should speak to him in this way. Regarding "himself":
he would not let this personal existence established in a happy destination pass away, by means of which karma the three types of wholesome success [are attained].
The meaning is that one should not perform that karma by which, having transcended the heaven of all desires, one is reborn in the states of woe (*apāya*).
One should not practice "unrighteousness" (*adhamma*), which is defined as the threefold misconduct.

One should not cross over or descend into the "fordless place" (*atittha*), which consists of the sixty-two views. There is also a reading, "na tāreyya"; [this refers to] one who follows after one's own views.
One should not lead people astray. "Anatthe" means without cause. "Na yuto" means one should not be engaged in worldly involvement.

O Brahmin, if the king wishes to engage with you regarding the question of the sacrifice of Dhamma, you should tell him, "Let him conduct himself according to this instruction"—this is the intended meaning here.
“Always” means constantly. This is what is meant: “The khattiya who knows how to perform these duties, that king always increases like the moon in the bright fortnight.
“He shines” means he is resplendent, shining with his own virtues such as virtue, conduct, and wisdom in the midst of his friends and ministers.
Thus the Great Being, with the grace of a Buddha, answered the brahmin’s question as if raising the moon in the vault of the sky.
The great multitude roared, shouted, and clapped their hands, offering thousands of shouts of "Well done!
They waved their garments, snapped their fingers, and threw away their hand-ornaments and other belongings. The wealth thus thrown away amounted to a full ten million.

The king was pleased with him and bestowed great honor upon him. Sucirata, too, having performed worship with a thousand *nikkhas*, wrote the answer to the question on a golden plate using vermilion, and went to the city of Indapatta to explain the Dhammayāga problem to the king.
The king, practicing that Dhamma, filled the city of heaven.
Having delivered this Dhamma teaching, the Teacher said, "Monks, it is not only now; even in the past, the Tathāgata was possessed of great wisdom," and he identified the Jātaka thus:
"At that time, King Dhanañjaya was Ānanda; Sucirata was Anuruddha; Vidhura was Kassapa;
Bhadrakāra was Moggallāna; the young brahmin Sañcaya was Sāriputta; and the wise Sambhava was myself."
"But I myself was that one.
This concludes the commentary on the Sambhava Jātaka, the fifth.
[516] 6. The Commentary on the Mahākapi Jātaka.
“There was a king in Bārāṇasī”—this the Teacher spoke while dwelling in the Veḷuvana grove concerning Devadatta’s hurling of a stone.

Later, when the archers had been employed and a stone had been hurled, and the monks were speaking in dispraise of Devadatta, the Teacher said: “Monks, it is not only now; in the past as well, Devadatta [acted] toward me...”
"Having pierced through virtue," he said, and then related a story of the past.

In the past, while Brahmadatta was reigning in Bārāṇasī, a certain brahmin farmer in a village of Kāsī, having plowed his field and released his oxen, began to perform the work of digging with a spade. The oxen [went] to a bush for leaves...
While eating, they gradually entered the forest and fled. He, having observed the time and set aside his spade, looked for the oxen;
not seeing them, he became despondent. Searching for them, he entered deep into the forest and, wandering about, reached the Himalayas.
There, having lost his sense of direction, he wandered for seven days without food until he came upon a *tinduka* tree.
Having seen it, he climbed up and, while eating the fruits, slipped from a *tinduka* tree and fell sixty cubits into a hellish abyss.
Ten days passed there for him. At that time, the Bodhisatta, having been reborn in the womb of a monkey and eating various fruits, saw that man;
he fashioned a bridge with a rock, rescued the man, and [placed him] upon the rock.
Having seated him, he said: "O Brahmin, I am weary; I shall sleep for a moment, so guard me.
While he was sleeping, [the Brahmin] struck the top of his head with a stone. The Great Being, perceiving that deed of his, sprang up, sat upon a branch, and said:
"O man, you go on the ground; I shall [protect you] from above with the tip of this branch."
Thinking, “I will go along showing the way,” he led that man out from the forest, placed him on the path, and entered the foothills of the mountain himself.
Having offended the Great Being, that man became a leper and became a "ghost among humans" (*manussapeta*) in this very life.
Wandering for seven years, oppressed by suffering, he entered a park named Migājina in Bārāṇasī.
Having spread out a plantain leaf within the enclosure of his hut, he lay down, overcome by pain.
At that time, the King of Bārāṇasī, having gone to the park and wandering about there, saw him and asked, "Who are you, and what have you done to come to this suffering?
He explained everything to him in detail. To illustrate this matter, the Teacher said:
“In Bārāṇasī there was a king, the prosperer of the kingdom of the Kāsīs;
surrounded by his friends and ministers, he went to Migājina.
There he saw a brahmin, white, variegated, and afflicted with leprosy.”
“Like a withered *koviḷāra* tree, emaciated and covered with visible veins—
seeing this man who had reached such a state of extreme misery,
the king was struck with awe and asked: ‘Which of the *yakkhas* are you?’”
“Your hands and feet are white, and your head is whiter still;
your body is the color of rust, and you are full of leprosy.
Your back, resembling a row of rounded beads, is unevenly concave and convex.”
“Black indeed are your limbs; I see nothing else like them.
With feet bruised, parched, emaciated, and with veins standing out, you are famished and distressed in appearance. From where do you come, and where are you going?”
“You are difficult to look upon, you are ill-favored, and your appearance is terrifying;
even your own mother, your progenitor, would not wish to see you.
What deed did you do in the past? Whom, who was innocent, did you cause to be slain?”
“Having committed this evil deed (kibbisa), he has come to this suffering.
In that context, “Bārāṇasī” means in Bārāṇasī. “Surrounded by friends and ministers” means surrounded by friends who have firm devotion and by ministers.
“Migājina” is the name of a pleasure grove. “White” means white due to leprosy (setakuṭṭha).
He saw one afflicted with *kabarakuṭṭha*, variegated and broken by the itching leprosy (*kaṇḍūyana-kilāsa-kuṭṭha*), suffering from the pain of leprosy and lying upon a plantain leaf;
he was like a withered *koviḷāra* tree, resembling a blossoming *koviḷāra* because of the flesh oozing from the openings of his wounds;
and he was emaciated, his body in certain places being nothing more than skin and bone.
"Covered with a network of veins. "Byamhito" means one who is afraid or struck with wonder. "Of the yakkhas" means: among the yakkhas, what is your name?
"Resembling a string of beads" means they are like a string of round beads placed upon the vertebrae of the spine.
"Limbs" means your limbs are like black creepers. "None other" means I do not see any other man such as this.

"Ugghaṭṭapāda" means one whose feet are covered with dust. "Ātattarūpa" means one with a withered body. "Duddasī" means one who is difficult to look upon. "Appakārosi" means you are devoid of bodily form; the meaning is that you are ill-proportioned.
"Kiṃ kammaṃ akara" means what deed did you do previously? The meaning is "what have you done? "Kibbisaṃ" means a cruel deed.
After that, the brahmin said:
"Truly, I shall tell you according to my skill;
for in this world, the wise praise those who speak the truth."
“Wandering alone in search of my cattle, I became lost in the forest—
in a wilderness, desolate and treeless, frequented by various elephants.
Haunted by fierce beasts, I was utterly lost in the jungle.”
There I practiced for seven days, overcome by hunger and thirst.
There, being famished, I saw a *tinduka* tree growing on uneven ground,
hanging over a precipice, yet bearing a full abundance of fruit.
“Wind-blown fruits I ate, and they pleased me greatly;
unsatisfied, I climbed a tree, thinking, ‘I shall rest there.
One fruit was eaten by me, and for the second, I longed.”
Then she broke that branch, like one cut by an axe. "There I was,
along with the branches, with my feet up and my head down,
falling into a mountain precipice— without a foothold and without a support."
“Because the water was deep, I did not reach the bottom;
there I lay without joy for no fewer than ten nights.
Then a monkey came here, a cave-dweller named Gonaṅgula.”
Wandering from branch to branch, eating the fruit of the tree,
he saw me— emaciated and pale— and felt compassion for me, saying: "O,
who indeed is this person here, so distressed by such suffering?"
“Whether you be a human or a non-human, reveal yourself to me.
Having extended my hands in reverent salutation, I spoke these words:
“I am a human who has arrived here; I have no other destination than this.”
"I tell you this: may it be well with you; do you become my refuge.
"Having taken up a heavy rock, the monkey roamed about on the mountain;
having fashioned a seat from the stone, Nisabha spoke thus."
“Come, climb upon my back and grasp my neck with your arms;
I shall swiftly lift you up from this mountain crag.
Having heard those words of the glorious lord of monkeys, [the monkey king said:]
Mounting the back of the steadfast one, I grasped his neck with both my arms.
Then that powerful and radiant monkey rose up from there;
though he was distressed by the difficulty, he moved swiftly through the mountain pass.
“Having rescued me, the virtuous Nisabha said this:
‘Come now, my good friend, protect me for a moment while I tend to my cattle.
For lions and tigers, leopards, bears, hyenas, and jackals—’”
“They might harm me while I am heedless; seeing them, you must ward them off.
Having thus protected me for a moment, that guardian of cattle, I then adopted an evil view through improper reflection.
“Food is this for human beings, just like other deer in the forest;
what if I were to kill this one, and being hungry, eat the monkey?
And I shall go back, taking the meat as my provisions.”
“I shall cross the wilderness; it will serve as my provisions for the journey.
Then, having taken a stone, I struck my own head with it;
though my limbs were exhausted, the blow was weak.
“Thus, having reached me with great speed, the monkey, smeared with blood, looks up at me weeping with eyes full of tears.
‘Do not treat me thus, O Blessed One; you too should not act in such a way.’”
"And you indeed are named Dīghāvu; you ought to restrain others.
'O man, alas! You have performed such difficult deeds;
such uneven and treacherous precipices have been pulled up by me.'"
“‘I have been brought back from the world beyond;
you thought me one who could be deceived. Because of that evil deed, evil was conceived by that evil one.
May you, O upholder of unrighteousness, never touch such bitter feeling!’”
"Do not commit that evil deed; it will surely destroy you like a bamboo.
I have no confidence in you, O one of evil nature and unrestrained!
Come, follow behind me, remaining visible and close at hand."
“You have escaped from the hands of the wild beasts; you have reached human station.
This is the path established by the Dhamma; go by it as you please.
Having said this, the mountain-dweller washed his head in a lake.
Having wiped away my tears, I then ascended the mountain:
"Afflicted by that enemy and tormented by a burning fever,
with my limbs ablaze, I came here to drink water."
“Like a lake heated by fire, smeared with blood,
resembling pus and gore— everything became thus for me.
As many drops of water as fell upon my body,”
That many boils arose, resembling the hides of addhabela and uvasa animals.
They burst and oozed out for me— corpses, pus, and blood—
whichever way I went, whether among villages or market towns.
“Men and women, with sticks in their hands, ward me off;
I am besmeared with a foul stench—do not come near me!
Such is this suffering for me now for seven years.”
"I experience my own karma, the evil deed I committed in the past.
Therefore I say to you, O venerable ones—however many of you are gathered here:
do not betray your friends, for the betrayal of friends is an evil thing."
“He becomes a leper, afflicted with white leprosy, who betrays his friends here;
at the breaking up of the body, that betrayer of friends is reborn in hell.
In this context, “skilled” means I shall speak to you just as one who is clever and skilled speaks. “Seeking the cattle” refers to [cattle] that have been lost.
While searching for my ox, I crossed over the path of men and entered the Himalayas.

"In the forest" (*arañña*) means in a kingless, empty place. "In the wilderness" (*irīṇa*) means in a parched desert. "In a secluded place" (*vivana*) means in a remote spot. "Lost" (*vippanaṭṭha*) means having lost one's way.
"Hungry" (*bubhukkhitō*) means having become hungry, with a stomach tormented by hunger. "Hanging over a precipice" (*papātam abhilambantaṃ*) means facing toward a precipice.
"Hanging down. "Bearing abundant fruit" means bearing sweet fruit. "Blown by the wind":
first, I ate those that had already fallen due to the wind. "I shall be there": thinking "I shall be well-fed in that tree," I climbed it.
Then, "that branch breaks"—when my hand was extended for the sake of that which I desired, the branch upon which I had climbed broke.
She broke [him] as if a branch were being cut by an axe. "Without support" means devoid of any place to grasp.
"In a mountain defile" means in a rugged mountainous region.
"I lay down" means: "I am lying. "A monkey came" means: a monkey arrived. "Goṇaṅgula" means one whose tail is like the tail of an ox; alternatively, it is also called "Goṇaṅguṭṭha."
The reading is *gonaṅgulī*; some also read *goṇaṅgulī*. *Akarā mayi* means "there were no [injuries] in me.
*Ambho*, O Great King, that king of monkeys, having heard the sound of my being dashed against the water in that abyss of hell, addressed me as "Ambho!
and asked, "Who is this? *Byasampatto* means "one who has met with calamity," or its meaning is "one who has fallen under the power of the precipice."

“Bhadde” means “blessing”; therefore, I say to you: “May it be well with you. As for “the heavy rock,” Great King, when I had spoken thus, that king of monkeys comforted me, saying, “Do not fear,” and first taking hold of a heavy rock, he roamed the mountain preparing his equipment.
“Nisabha” refers to the bull among men, the supreme lord of monkeys, at the mountain precipice.
Standing there, he said this to me:
"With both arms—hold my neck firmly! With speed—swiftly! Of the glorious—one possessed of merit!
'Aggahi' means that as I descended by the force of the wind into the sixty-cubit deep abyss of the hell and stood upon the surface of the water, I..."
Climbing onto his back with speed, I seized his neck with both arms. "Vihaññamāno" means being exhausted.
"Kicchenā" means with difficulty or pain. "Santo" means wise; or alternatively, it means weary or fatigued. "Rakkhassu" means:
"I am weary from lifting you up, so let me rest for a moment while I tend to my cattle; therefore, protect me. Just as...
"Other forest animals" refers to lions and other wild beasts that are in this forest; however, in the Pāḷi it is written as "bears, hyenas, and jackals.
"Let him protect me" means, O Great King, that the monkey king thus made himself my protection and slept for a moment.
"Improperly" means by way of improper attention (*ayoniso-manasikāra*). "Food" means fit to be eaten. "Unbound, refreshed, and well-fed."
*Sambalanti* means provisions for a journey (*pātheyya*). *Matthakaṃ sannitāḷayiṃ* means I struck the head of that lord of monkeys.
There is also a reading: *sannitālaya*. *Dubbalo ahū* means he was not strong; he did not proceed according to his intention.
*Vegenā* means by the force of the stone thrown by me. *Udappatto* means arisen. *Māyyo*—by that man who was a betrayer of friends.
When the stone was hurled, it tore through the great hide and hung down, and blood flowed out. Overcome by pain, the Great Being thought:
"There is no one else in this place; this danger has arisen because of this man.
Terrified by the fear of death, he seized the hanging leather strap with his hand, leaped up, and climbed onto a branch.
While conversing with that wicked man, he said, "Do not, O Noble One," and so forth.
In this context, "Do not, O Noble One, do this to me, Venerable Sir" is a prohibition against him. "And you, indeed, by name... means:
"Having been pulled out from the abyss by me in such a way, you nevertheless perform such a harsh deed toward me; oh, what an improper thing you have done!"
"Aho vatā" (Alas!)—saying this, he spoke thus in reproach: "O you who have performed such difficult deeds! means: by offending against me, you have performed an exceedingly difficult act.
"As if brought from the other world" means as if brought from the next world. "One should betray" means one should be treacherous toward or should strike.
"Painful sensation"—even though it is so, you, who stand upon unrighteousness, [experience] such a sensation as the kind that I myself am experiencing. Such a sensation...
"May the bitter fruit of that evil deed not touch you; may it not strike you like a bamboo. Thus, Great King, he showed compassion for me as if I were his own dear son.
Then I said to him: "Noble sir, do not take the fault committed by me to heart; do not regard me as a base person."
“Destroy me in such a wilderness! I am disoriented and do not know the way; do not destroy the karma you yourself have made.
Grant me the gift of life; lead me out from the wilderness and place me on a path frequented by humans.
When this was said, he spoke to me in conversation, saying, “I have no confidence in you,” and so forth. In that context, *tayi* means “in you” from this point forward.

"I have no trust in you. Come now, good man; I will not travel along the path with you, but you come behind me, keeping close enough that your body remains visible, while I shall go by way of the tops of the trees. "I am free," [he said].
Then, O Great King, having led me out from the forest, he said, "Good man, from the wild beasts..."
“You have escaped from my hand; you have reached the human path,” he said, meaning that you have arrived at the human domain and this is your way; go by this path.
“A forest-dweller” means a monkey that roams the mountains. “Having washed” means having rinsed [the wound]. “I am pursued by him”:
O Great King, thinking, “I have been pursued by that monkey, for my evil karma has ripened, and thus I am pursued by him,” he spoke thus.
"Afflicted" means tormented. "I approached" means I went to a certain lake.
"It arose" means it was born; having become such, it appeared. "As many as" means however many. "Boils were produced" means boils arose.
It is said that, being unable to endure his thirst, he lifted up a handful of water, drank a little, and sprinkled the remainder over his body. Then, for him—
At that very moment, boils the size of half a *beluva* fruit arose through the counting of water drops; therefore, he spoke thus.
"Burst open" means that on that very day those boils burst, becoming putrid corpses with a foul stench, and pus and blood flowed out.
"By whichever way" means by whichever path. "Besmeared" means covered and surrounded by the foul stench.
"Surrounded. "Do not come within a month," meaning: "O wicked being, do not come within a month;
do not come into our presence"—thus they spoke, and the sense is that they were warding me off. "Now seven years for me," means:
O Great King, from that time until now, for seven years, I have experienced my own karma for this length of time.

Having thus related in detail his own act of treachery toward friends, he said, "Great King, no one should perform such an act after considering me alone," and then spoke the words beginning with "Therefore, for you. Therein, "taṃ" means "therefore.
The meaning is: because such an act has such a painful result, therefore [one should not do it].
“He becomes a leper, one afflicted with white leprosy, who betrays his friends here;
at the breaking up of the body, that betrayer of friends is reborn in hell.
This is the verse of the Perfectly Enlightened One. Monks, the meaning is: he who here in this world betrays and harms his friends becomes such as this.

Even as that man was still conversing with the king, the earth opened up for him. At that very moment, passing away, he was reborn in the Avīci hell. When the man had entered the earth, the king emerged from the park and entered the city.
Having delivered this Dhamma teaching, the Teacher said, "Monks, it is not only now;
in the past as well, Devadatta struck me with a stone," and having spoken thus, he identified the Jātaka: "The man who betrayed his friend at that time was Devadatta."
"The king of monkeys was none other than myself.
This concludes the sixth commentary, the Mahākapi-jātaka.
[517] 7. The Commentary on the Dakarakkhasa-jātaka.
224–257. “If you are being carried away... refers to the *Dakarakkhasa-jātaka*. All of that will be made clear in the *Mahāumaṅga-jātaka*.
This concludes the seventh commentary, the *Dakarakkhasa-jātaka-vaṇṇanā*.
8. Commentary on the *Paṇḍara-nāgarāja-jātaka* (The Birth Story of the White Naga King).
“‘Scattered speech’—this was spoken by the Teacher while dwelling in Jeta’s Grove concerning Devadatta’s sinking into the earth after he had uttered a falsehood.
For at that time, when the monks were speaking of his disrepute, the Teacher said, “Monks, it is not only now;
in the past as well, Devadatta sank into the earth after uttering a falsehood,” and he related a story of the past.
In the past, while Brahmadatta was reigning in Benares, five hundred merchants set out upon the ocean by ship.
On the seventh day, their vessel, unable to see the shore, was wrecked upon the surface of the sea;
with the exception of one, the rest became food for fish and turtles, but one man was carried by the force of the wind to a port named Karambiya.
Having thus emerged from the ocean, naked as he was, he wandered for alms right there on that very cloth.
People, honoring him with the thought, "This ascetic is of few desires and contented," paid him great respect.
Thinking, "I have found a means of livelihood," he did not wish for them even when they offered him a lower garment and an upper robe. They remarked, "There is no ascetic more modest than this one."
Becoming increasingly more confident, they established a hermitage for him and settled him there.
He became known as "Karambiya the Naked One. While he was dwelling there, great gain and honor arose for him;
a dragon king (*nāgarāja*) and a garuḍa king came to attend upon him. Among them, the dragon king was named Paṇḍara.
Thus it was said. Then one day, the King of Supaṇṇas went to him, paid homage, and sitting to one side, spoke thus:
"Venerable sir, our kinsmen who capture the nāgas cause many of them to perish;
we do not know the method for capturing these nāgas, for it is said they have a secret means. Would you be able to help us, out of affection for them?"
“I shall ask him about that cause. Having agreed, saying “Very well,” he paid homage to the king of the supaṇṇas and departed.
When the time came for the king of the nāgas to arrive, he paid homage to him as he sat down and asked:
“O king of the nāgas, it is said that many supaṇṇas perish when they seize you; how is it that they are unable to seize you? “Venerable sir, ...”
“This is our secret and mystery; by my telling this, death has been brought upon the circle of kinsmen.
“But, friend, do you have the notion that ‘this man will tell it to another’? I shall not tell it to anyone else;
rather, I ask out of a desire to know for myself. Having faith in me, speak without fear.”
The Nāga king, saying, “I will not speak, venerable sir,” paid homage and departed. On the following day he questioned him again, yet he still did not speak to him.
Then, when the Nāga king had come and sat down on the third day, [the monk] said to him: “Nāga king, today is the third day; for what reason do you not speak when I question you?
“Because I fear, venerable sir, that you might tell it to someone else. “To whom? [he asked.]
“I will not tell; speak without fear. “In that case, venerable sir, do not tell anyone else,” he said, and having obtained this promise, [the nāga continued]:

“Venerable sir, we would swallow large, massive rocks until we were heavy, and then lying down, we would open our mouths and bare our teeth at the time when the supaṇṇas were approaching, waiting for the supaṇṇas to bite us. When they arrived...”
"They seize us by the head; while we lie there as a heavy burden for them as they strive to lift us up, the water overflows.
Sinking down, they die right there in the water. For this reason, many *supaṇṇas* perish.
What is the use of seizing them by the head? Fools, having seized us by the tail with our heads downward..."
“Having taken hold of his range with her mouth, she made him discard it, lightened his burden, and was able to go,” he said,
telling that wicked man the secret of his own practice.
Then, when he had departed, the king of the supaṇṇas arrived, paid homage to Karambiya-Acela, and asked, “What was asked, venerable sir?”
"This is the secret reason of the Naga king," he said. "Yes, friend," he replied, and related everything exactly according to the account given by the other.
Upon hearing this, the Supaṇṇa thought, "The Naga king has acted improperly; one must not tell another the certain destruction of one's own kinsmen.
Well then, today itself I shall create a Supaṇṇa-wind and seize him first."
Thinking, "This will do," the Supaṇṇa created a whirlwind, seized the white Nāga king by the tail, turned him upside down, made him discard his caught prey,
and then leaping up, soared into the sky. As the white Nāga hung in the air with his head downward, lamenting,
"I myself have brought this suffering upon myself," he said:

“Fear follows one who speaks incoherently, who does not conceal his counsel, who is unrestrained, and who does not look ahead— just as the *supaṇṇa* bird preys upon a white elephant that lacks awareness.
But the man who, out of delusion, discloses a secret counsel that ought to be guarded while laughing…”
Swiftly does fear follow that broken counsel, just as the Supaṇṇa bird pursues the white elephant.
One who is not a close friend is not fit to know a grave and secret matter;
nor should one who is a close friend disclose it to one who is unenlightened, or speak of what is beneficial to one who is already enlightened.
“I placed my trust in the naked ascetic, who was esteemed as a monk of developed self;
I disclosed to him a secret matter, yet now that the matter is past, I weep miserably.
O Brahmā, I was unable to restrain my speech regarding that supreme secret of his.”
“Because of that very person, fear has come upon me; I weep like a miserable man for a past matter.
For that fool who, thinking the other a good friend, reveals a secret matter to one of low birth—whether out of malice, fear, or lust—has undoubtedly betrayed his trust.”
“He who has entered among the wicked with averted speech, uttering words in social gatherings—that man they call a foul-faced viper;
one should stay far, very far away from such a person in self-restraint.
Food and drink, Kāsi cloth and sandalwood, beloved women, garlands, and ointments—”
“Leaving behind all sensual pleasures, we are going; O Supaṇṇa, we have truly come to the state of living beings.
In this context, *vikiṇṇavācaṃ* means one whose speech is scattered. *Aniguyhamantaṃ* means one whose secret counsel is not concealed.
*Asaññataṃ* means one who is unable to guard the doors of the body and so forth. *Aparicakkhitāraṃ* means [one who is unable to guard] the secret counsel spoken by me.
"Will he be able? Will he not be able?"—thus unable to look upon or examine the person.

"Fear follows him" means that fear, which is self-made, follows that person who possesses these four factors—the ignorant one of poor wisdom—just as the *supaṇṇa* bird followed me, the Pāṇḍaraka Nāga. "He utters cries while laughing" means [to protect]...
He speaks out of amusement to a wicked man who is incapable [of keeping a secret].
He laments that one who is a friend merely by way of conformity, but not from the heart, is not fit to know a secret matter.
"Asambuddha" means not understanding, not knowing; the meaning is "one lacking wisdom. "Sambuddha" means understanding, knowing; the meaning is "one possessing wisdom. This...

It is said: “Whether he be a well-wishing friend or an enemy, whether he be lacking in wisdom or possessed of wisdom, if he is one who seeks what is harmful and acts for what is harmful, he too is not fit to know a secret.
Thinking, “This one approaches as an ascetic,” and perceiving him as “this is an ascetic,” as “one esteemed by the world,” and as “one whose self is cultivated,” I [confide] in him.
I gained his confidence; I spoke candidly. "Atītam-attha" means a past matter;
having become a thing of the past, he now laments, "I weep miserably. "Tassa" refers to that naked ascetic (acelaka). "Brahme" is an address to Supaṇṇa.
"Saṃyantuṃ" means I was unable to guard this secret speech, this hidden matter. "Tappakkhato hi" means...
"Now this fear has come upon me from that naked ascetic (acelaka), from his faction, from his side"—thus is the meaning of the past tense in "I weep piteously.
Thinking, "This one is my well-wisher" (*suhada*), he addresses him as such. "Of low birth" (*dukkulīna*) means one born of a base family.
"Because of faults" (*dosā*): whoever reveals such a secret for these reasons, beginning with hatred (*dosa*), is undoubtedly a fool who has been cast down.
"Having been turned over and set down," means it is as if already struck.
"Tirokkhavāco" means one whose speech is hidden because of the indirect manner in which one intends to speak what one wishes to say.
"Asataṃ paviṭṭho" means entered among the unvirtuous, included among the unwholesome persons (*asappurisa*). "In assemblies... [saṅgatīsu]...

One who utters such words—having heard the secret of others, proclaims in the midst of assemblies, "So-and-so has done this" or "So-and-so has said that"—of such a person they say, "He is a venomous snake with a foul face and a putrid mouth.
One should restrain oneself far, far away from such a man; the meaning is that one should keep aloof from him and avoid him from afar.
“Garlands and ointments” means garlands, divine fourfold scents, and ointments. “Having abandoned” means:
“O Supaṇṇa, having today abandoned and cast away all these divine objects of desire, such as food and so forth, we shall go.
O Supaṇṇa, we have indeed come to you for our lives; be our refuge.”
Thus Paṇḍaraka, hanging in the air with his head downward, lamented with eight verses.
Having heard the sound of his lamentation, the Supaṇṇa rebuked him, saying, "O King of Nagas, having now told your secret to this naked ascetic, for what purpose do you lament? and spoke this verse:
“Who among us three here incurs reproach, O King of Nagas, you who are a living being in this world—the ascetic, the Supanna, or indeed yourself? For what reason has Paṇḍaraka been seized?
In this context, *ko nīdha* means “who among us three here. In the phrase *asmiṃdha*, the word *idha* is merely a particle.
"In this world" is the meaning. "A living being" means one who has become a living being. Alternatively, "you yourself" means "only you.
In that regard, do not revile the ascetic first; for he questioned you about that secret by means of a stratagem. Do not revile the Supaṇṇa either; for I am indeed your adversary.
As for "seized by Paṇḍaraka," [he said], "Friend Paṇḍaraka, for what reason was I seized by the Supaṇṇa?"
Thinking, "He has been caught," he then reproached himself; for the intended meaning here is that by revealing the secret, you yourself have brought about your own ruin.
Having heard this, Paṇḍaraka spoke the following verse:
“The ascetic was esteemed by me as one whose self is perfected; he was dear to my mind and highly regarded.
I opened my eyes to his secret meaning, yet now that the matter is past, I weep piteously.
In this context, “esteemed” means that the ascetic was held by me in the estimation of being a “true person” (sappurisa). “Highly regarded” means that he was also honored by me.
Then the Supaṇṇa spoke these four verses:
“There is no being on earth that is immortal; there is no craft of wisdom that should not be censured.
A man here who speaks of what cannot be obtained—by means of truth, Dhamma, fortitude, and self-control—is beyond reproach.”
“Mother and father are the supreme among kinsmen; there is no third who is compassionate toward him.
One should not disclose even their greatest secret, fearing the betrayal of counsel.
Mother, father, sisters, brothers, or those who are one’s companions and partisans—”
One should not disclose even their supreme secret, fearing the betrayal of counsel.
Even if a wife— a young bride, sweet-spoken, endowed with sons, beauty, and fame, and honored by her circle of kinsmen— should speak of her husband’s fault;
"Even to him one should not disclose the supreme secret, fearing the betrayal of counsel.
In this context, "amaro" means that there is no such thing as a being whose nature is immortal. "Paññāvidhā natthi" contains the particle *na* used for metrical conjunction;

the meaning is "there is a distribution of wisdom" (*paññāvidhā atthi*). This is what is intended: O King of Nagas, in the world there is no one who is immortal, nor is there anyone who lacks the distribution of wisdom.
There exists that kind of wisdom, reckoned as a portion of wisdom belonging to others, which for the sake of one's own life should not be censured.
Alternatively, "a portion of wisdom" means there is no other class of phenomena (dhammajāti) comparable to wisdom that should not be censured;
why then do you censure it? For those, however, who read the text as "even a portion of wisdom should not be censured," the meaning is straightforward.

By truthfulness and so forth—in this world, by means of truthful speech, by conduct in accordance with the Dharma, by fortitude consisting of wisdom, and by the restraint of the faculties—a person attains, brings about, and accomplishes even that distinction known as the eight meditative attainments, the paths and fruits, and Nibbāna, which is otherwise unobtainable and rare.
Therefore, you ought not to revile the naked ascetic; rather, you should blame yourself alone.
The meaning is: having deceived him by means of his own wisdom and skill in means, he asks for a secret, hidden counsel.
"Supreme" (paramā) means these two are called the supreme kinsmen among all relatives. "He has no third" (nāssa tatiyo) refers to this person.
There is no third being other than one's mother and father who is so compassionate;
therefore, a wise person, fearing the disclosure of a secret counsel, would not reveal even the most profound secret to those parents.

But you, on the other hand, have told the naked ascetic that which should not have been told even to your parents—this is the meaning. "Or companions" means close-hearted friends. "Or kinsmen" refers to paternal uncles, maternal uncles, paternal aunts, and so forth.
"Relatives are those on one's own side. "Of these too" means that one should not speak even to these relatives and friends;
rather, you speak to the naked ascetic (acelaka)—thus he shows that you should be angry with yourself.

"And a wife" means even a wife who was a maiden, who speaks sweetly, and who is endowed with sons, beauty, and fame—even such a wife as this, if she were to say, "Tell me your secret," [one should not speak].
One should not disclose even that to others.
Beyond that:
“One should not reveal a secret matter; one should guard it like a treasure.”
For a wise person, a secret matter is better kept hidden than revealed.
A wise man should not disclose a secret to a woman, nor to an enemy,
nor to one who is led astray by material gain, nor to one who has his heart’s core in his grasp.
“The man who makes known a secret matter that has not yet been understood causes fear through the disclosure of counsel;
therefore, even one who is his slave endures him out of fear of such betrayal.
As many as there are counselors who know the secret purpose of a man—”
“Just as many [words] he has overheard, so many are his anxieties; therefore, one should not disclose secrets.
One should speak apart during the day; at night, one should not release speech beyond measure.
For eavesdroppers hear the counsel, and thus the secret quickly leads to a breach.”
The five verses will be made manifest in the *Pañcapaṇḍita-pañha* of the *Ummagga-jātaka*.
Following those:
"Just as if there were a great city, doorless, made of iron, and adorned with beautiful walls;”
“Endowed with moats and trenches all around— even such are these secret counsels of mine here.
Those men who keep their secret counsels, whose speech is not scattered, who are firm in their own aims and difficult to deceive—
by them enemies are kept far away, like a host of foes or venomous serpents.”
In the two verses, "Bhaddasāla" refers to a city endowed with marketplaces (*sālā*) and the like.
"Equipped with moats dug all around" means it is surrounded by three moats dug on every side. "Even so do they appear to me" means that those men appear thus to me.
Which ones? Those who hold secret counsel here. This is what is meant: just as in the case of an iron city without a gate...
The enjoyments and usages of human beings are internal; those within do not go outside, nor do those outside enter within;

the movement from one to another is cut off; secret-counseling men are of such a nature that they digest their own secrets within themselves and do not tell them to anyone else. "Firm in their own aims" means their own...
"Steadfast in their aims. "Double-tongued" refers to the Paṇḍaraka Nāga. "Moving away" means they retreat.
Regarding the phrase "like a venomous snake, a host of enemies," here *vā* is merely a particle; the meaning is "like a venomous snake, a host of enemies.
Just as people who desire life retreat far from a venomous snake, so too [should one act] toward those who possess secret spells.
"By means of men, enemies keep at a distance; they do not find an opportunity to approach," this is what is meant.
When the Supaṇṇa had thus spoken on the Dhamma, Paṇḍaraka said:
"Having abandoned the home, he has gone forth as a naked ascetic; shaven-headed and bare, he wanders for the sake of food."
"In that regard, I have indeed revealed the hidden meaning; both the purposes and the teachings have been fully proclaimed.
‘O King of Supaṇṇas, what must one do, what is his character, and by what conduct is he disciplined?
How does a renunciant, having abandoned all things cherished, act so as to reach the heavenly state?’"
In this context, "for the sake of food" means that he wanders about seeking solid and soft foods for the purpose of filling his belly, being devoid of dignity.

"We have fallen away" means we have departed from or declined. "How do you act?"—this the Naga king spoke, having recognized the naked man's state as a recluse and wishing to inquire about the practice of a recluse.
In this regard, "of what character" means endowed with what kind of conduct.

"By what wind? means by the undertaking of which vow he proceeds. "The ascetic wanders" means wandering in the life of renunciation, having abandoned craving and deceit; how does one become an ascetic whose evil is stilled?
And "how making heaven"—how does that ascetic reach the most excellent city of the gods? Thus it is said.
The Supaṇṇa said:
"Endowed with shame, patience, and self-control, free from anger and having abandoned slander;
practicing as a recluse and abandoning all things cherished—acting thus, one goes to the heavenly state."
