In this context, O Nāga King, one who is endowed with shame and dread of blame arising both internally and externally, who possesses the patience of endurance known as *adhivāsana-khanti*, and who has tamed his faculties;

who is by nature free from anger, who has abandoned malicious speech, and who, having cast off craving and the conceit of "mine," wanders as a renunciant—such a one is called a *samaṇa*. It is precisely by acting in this way that these wholesome qualities, beginning with shame, are fulfilled.
"By doing so, one goes to a heavenly state.
Having heard this Dhamma discourse from the Supaṇṇa king, Paṇḍaraka, entreating for his life, spoke this verse:
"Just as a mother, through her touch, causes her tender, young son to feel pleasure throughout his entire body;..."
"Thus have you appeared before me, O Lord of Birds, out of compassion for me as a mother for her son.

The meaning of this is: just as a mother, seeing her own newborn infant—her body-born child—in need of touch, lays him upon her breast and, while suckling him, causes her entire body to be touched by the contact of her son.
"Neither does a mother fear her son, nor does a son fear his mother; even so have you appeared before me, O Lord of Birds, King of Birds.
Therefore, look upon me with a gentle heart, as a mother looks upon her son out of compassion, and grant me my life.
Then the Supaṇṇa, granting him his life, spoke this other verse:
“Enough! Release him today, O double-tongued one, for he is my son; there is indeed no other.
The pupil, the given son, and the son born of my own body—any one of these was a son to me. In this passage, *muñca* means release;
or rather, *mucca* is the reading itself. *Dujivhā* is an address to her. *Añño* means another, namely a fourth.
A "son" (putta) does not exist [in the literal sense]. An "antevāsī" (resident pupil) is one who dwells in the presence [of a teacher] while learning a craft or listening to questions.
A "dinnaka" (given son) is one given by others with the words, "Let this one be your son. "Enjoy the kingdom" (rajjassu) means "take delight in it.
"One of them" (aññatara) indicates that among the three sons, you have become my resident-pupil son.
Having spoken thus, he descended from the sky and set him down upon the ground. To clarify this matter, the Teacher spoke these two verses:
"Thus did the bird, the double-tongued Supaṇṇa, respond with these words; having established him on the earth, the twice-born one said:
'Today you are released, having transcended all fears; whether on land or in water, remain protected by me.'"
“As a skilled physician for those who are afflicted, as a cool lake for those who are thirsty, as a dwelling for those tormented by the cold of frost—so too do I become a refuge for you.
Therein, “thus indeed is the statement”: having spoken these words, he released that Nāga king. [He said: “On the earth... So...
The bird, having established himself upon the ground, comforted that double-tongued serpent, saying: "Today you are released from this;
from now on, you shall have transcended all fears. On land and in water alike, you shall be protected and guarded by me.
*Ātaṅkinaṃ* means those who are ill. *Evampi te* means: "In this way, I shall be your refuge."
"Go," he said, and dismissed him. That nāga king entered the nāga abode.
The other [the garuḍa] also went to the garuḍa abode and thought, "I have released the white nāga after making him swear an oath and gaining his trust;
what indeed is the state of his heart toward me? I shall test him. Having gone to the nāga abode, he raised a windstorm of the garuḍas. That—
Seeing this, the Naga, thinking, "The King of Supaṇṇas must have come to seize me," manifested a body measuring a thousand fathoms;
having swallowed rocks and sand to become heavy,
he lay down with his tail tucked underneath and his coils coiled over his head like a hood, appearing as if he were eager to bite the King of Supaṇṇas.
Seeing him, the Supaṇṇa spoke this other verse:
“Having made an alliance with an enemy, O egg-born one, you who are born from a womb, You lie there with your fangs exposed;
from where has this fear come upon you?”
Having heard that, the Naga king spoke three verses:
"One should indeed be wary of an enemy, and one should not trust even a friend.
When danger arises from what was once safe, it cuts away even the very roots."
“How indeed can one trust him by whom a quarrel has been made?
One should stand firm with resolute conviction; he does not delight in all quarters.
One should inspire confidence in him, yet not place confidence in him; one should be suspicious where there is no cause for suspicion.”
"In such and such a way should a wise person strive, so that another may not know his true nature.
In this context, "from one who is fearless" means from a friend who has become a source of fearlessness; the fear that arises cuts away even the very roots known as life.
"From him" means in that person. "With whom" means with whom a quarrel was made. "By one who is resolute."
"By being constantly prepared. "He does not become intimate with his enemies" means that one who stands firm through constant preparedness does not become intimate with his own foes by way of trust;
consequently, he does not become subject to their doing as they please.
"He makes others trust him" means he should make another person trust him, yet he himself should not trust them. He is not suspected by the other.
"He himself would be suspicious. This means that however much a wise person exerts effort, others do not perceive his true state;
therefore, it is shown that a wise person must certainly apply energy.
Thus, having conversed with one another, the two of them, in harmony and with mutual joy, went together to the hermitage of the naked ascetic (Acelaka). To clarify this matter, the Teacher said:

“Those two, with the appearance of gods, possessing delicate forms, equal and well-controlled, being masses of merit, approached the naked ascetic Karambiya; they were like two well-trained elephants mingling together.
Therein, *samā* means having an identical form, being similar in shape. *Sujayā* means well-aged, or perfectly pure; this very [term]...
Or rather, this is the reading: "Masses of merit" (*puññakkhandhā*) means they were like masses of merit due to the wholesome deeds performed.
"Became mingled" (*missībhūtā*) means they came into physical contact with one another, as if grasping hand in hand. "Like two well-trained horses" (*assavāhāva nāgā*):
just as two well-bred draft horses yoked to the pole of a chariot, those two "elephants among men" (*purisa-nāgā*) went to his hermitage.
Having arrived, the king of the supaṇṇas thought: "This nāga king will not give up his life for the sake of this naked ascetic;
I will not pay homage to this one of immoral conduct. Standing outside, he sent the nāga king himself into his presence.
With reference to him, the Teacher spoke the following verse.
“Then Paṇḍaraka, having approached the naked ascetic himself, said this:
‘O you who have cast off all fear and transcended all dangers, surely we were not dear to your mind!
In that context, “piyamhā” means he reviled him, saying: “O you of immoral conduct, old and decrepit, speaker of falsehoods, surely we were not dear to your mind!”
Then the naked ascetic spoke this other verse:
“The king of the Supaṇṇas was indeed dear to me; without doubt, Paṇḍaraka, this is the truth.
Being stained by passion, I did this evil deed while fully conscious, not out of delusion.”

In that regard, "by Paṇḍaraka" means: "That Paṇḍaraka was dearer to me than you; this is the truth. "He" refers to myself: having become infatuated with passion for that Supaṇṇa, I committed this evil deed while fully aware of it, not out of delusion or ignorance.
Having heard this, the Nāga king spoke two verses:
"For one who clearly perceives both this world and the next, there is nothing either dear or undear to me."
“With the appearance of those who are well-restrained, you roam this world unrestrained.
You are a noble in the guise of a noble, or an ignoble one in the guise of a noble;
you are of dark birth and ignoble form, for you have practiced much evil misconduct.”

In this context, "It is not mine" means: O immoral one, chief of liars, for one who has gone forth and clearly perceives both this world and the next, there is no thought of "this is dear to me" or "that is not dear to me.
Yet you, while possessing the outward marks and the emblem of one who has gone forth, remain unrestrained among those who are well-restrained and virtuous;
you wander about deceiving this world. "You are a counterfeit noble one" means you are a mere imitation of a noble one.
"Unrestrained" means unrestrained in body and so forth. "Of dark birth" means of a dark nature. "Of ignoble form" means of a shameless nature. "He acted" means he did it.
Having thus censured him, now, while pronouncing a curse, he spoke this verse:
"You have betrayed one who was not hostile to you; you are both treacherous and malicious."
"By this utterance of truth, may your head split into seven pieces!
The meaning of this is: "O betrayer, you have betrayed a friend who was not wicked toward you, and you are a slanderer; by this utterance of truth, may your head split into seven pieces!
Thus, even as the Naga king spoke, the naked ascetic's head split into seven pieces right where he was sitting.
He gave a chasm in the earth. Having entered the earth, he was reborn in Avīci.
The Nāga king and the Supaṇṇa king also returned to their own abodes. The Teacher, proclaiming his state of having entered the earth, spoke this concluding verse:
"Therefore, one should not betray friends; there is no other evil greater than betraying a friend."
“The being was drenched and slain upon the earth, for by the word of Indra, Saṃvara was killed.
In this context, *tasmā* means because the ripening of the act of betraying a friend is harsh; therefore. *Āsittasatto* means a being drenched with poison.
*Indassa* means by the word of the Lord of Nagas (*nāginda*). *Saṃvaro* refers to the one who, by his own declaration, said, “I am established in self-restraint (*saṃvara*).”
"Thus was the Ājīvaka known as 'the slain'.
Having delivered this Dhamma teaching, the Teacher said, "Monks, it is not only now;
in the past as well, Devadatta entered the earth after having uttered a falsehood," and he then identified the Jātaka: "At that time, the naked ascetic was Devadatta."
“Sāriputta was the Nāga king, while I myself was the Supaṇṇa king.
This concludes the eighth commentary, the Paṇḍara-nāgarāja-jātaka.
[519] 9. The Commentary on the Sambula-jātaka.
"Kā vedhamānā..."—this was spoken by the Teacher while dwelling at Jetavana concerning Queen Mallikā.

The background story has already been explained in detail in the *Kummāsapiṇḍi Jātaka*. However, through the power of her gift of three lumps of rice-gruel to the Tathāgata, she attained the status of chief queen to the king on that very day; and by means of the five qualities, such as rising early and so forth...
She was endowed with virtuous qualities, possessed of wisdom, an attendant of the Buddha, and a devoted wife.
Her status as a devoted wife became renowned throughout the entire city. Then one day, a discussion arose in the Hall of Truth:
"Friends, it is said that Queen Mallikā is perfect in conduct, perfect in wisdom, and a devoted wife. The Teacher arrived and—
"Monks, for what discussion are you sitting together here now? he asked. When they replied, "For this very one," he said, "Monks, it is not only now;
in the past as well, she was endowed with virtuous conduct and devoted solely to her husband. Having said this, he related a story of the past.
In the past, in Bārāṇasī, King Brahmadatta had a son named Sotthisena. When the king saw that he had reached maturity—
He installed him in the position of viceroy. A woman named Sambulā, possessing supreme beauty and endowed with bodily radiance, became his chief queen;
she appeared like a flame of a lamp burning in a windless place. Later, leprosy arose on the body of Sotthisena, and physicians were unable to cure it.
As the leprosy broke out, he became loathsome and fell into remorse.
“What use have I for kingship? I shall die an unprotected death in the forest,” he said, and having had this announced to the king, he departed, abandoning his harem.
Although Sambulā was entreated by many means to turn back, she did not return;
instead, saying, “I will care for my husband in the forest,” she departed along with him. Having entered the forest, he—
In a place where roots, fruits, and flowers were easily obtained and which was well-supplied with shade and water, he built a leaf-hut and made his dwelling. The princess attended upon him.
How so? For, having risen early in the morning, she would sweep the hermitage grounds, set out drinking water and water for rinsing, and offer tooth-sticks and mouth-washing water;
then, once his mouth was washed, she would grind various medicinal herbs.
Having smeared his wound with medicinal ointment, fed him very sweet fruits, rinsed his mouth, and washed his hands,
he said, "Be heedful, O Deva," and after paying homage, took his basket, axe, and hook; then,
having entered the forest for the sake of fruit, he gathered fruits, set them aside in one place, and [filled] a water-jar.
Having brought water and bathed Soṭṭhisena with various powders and clay, she again presented him with sweet fruits.
At the conclusion of his meal, she offered scented water; having herself eaten the fruits, she prepared a grass mat.
When he had lain down upon it, she washed his feet and performed the services for his head, back, and feet.
Having prepared a bed, she would approach it and lie down; by this means, she attended to her husband.
One day, while gathering fruits and roots in the forest, she saw a mountain cleft.
She took down a basket from her head, set it at the edge of the cleft, and descended, thinking, "I shall bathe. There, she rubbed her body with turmeric.
Having bathed until her body was thoroughly cleansed, she stepped out of the water, put on her bark garment, and stood on the bank of the mountain cave.
At that moment, the forest became a single expanse of light due to the radiance of her body. At that very instant, a certain *dānava* who had been wandering about in search of grazing saw her;
his heart became bound with passion for her, and he spoke these two verses:
“Trembling in this mountain cave, you stand alone with your thighs joined;
you are placed between my arms that are as long as a palm tree’s trunk. Tell me your name and your kinsmen.
“Illuminating the lovely forest frequented by lions and tigers,” she replied.
"Who are you, O beautiful one? To whom do you belong, O lady of slender waist?
I salute you, O blessed one; may there be homage to you, O giver of gifts.
In this passage, "trembling" (*vedhamānā*) means shaking due to the coldness resulting from her recent bath. "With joined thighs" (*saṃhitūrū*) means with thighs pressed together.
"O you with the mark of excellent thighs! 'Pāṇipameyyamajjhe' means [you] whose waist is to be measured by the hand.
'Kā vā tvan' means who indeed are you? 'Abhivādemī' means I pay homage. 'Dānavāhan'—I alone am a donor;
let this salutation be yours, I offer my joined palms to you," he said.
Having heard his words, she spoke these three verses:
“He who is known by the wise as Sotthisena, the son of the King of Kāsi—I am Sambulā, his wife; know this, O Dānava.”
I salute you, venerable sir; I am Sambulā, may there be homage to you.
"The son of Vedehī, O Blessed One, dwells in the forest afflicted;
I, alone, attended upon him alone when he was overcome by illness."
“When I gather forest roots, honey, meat, and the burrows of wild animals, and bring them back as my food, surely he does not consume them today.
In this context, *Vedehaputta* means the son of the daughter of the King of Videha. *Rogasammattaṃ* means afflicted by disease. *Upaṭṭhahanti*...
I serve and attend upon him. There is also a reading: “upaṭṭhitā. Regarding “vanamuñchāya”: having gathered from the forest, having practiced the way of gleaning.
“Madhumansaṃ” means honey free of flies and the meat from the openings of wild animals—the remnants left over after lions, tigers, and deer have eaten.
“Taṃ bhakkho” means: he for whom that which I bring is food—he, my husband, is indeed my sustenance.
"Surely today, because he has not obtained food, his body— withers, suffers,
and fades like a lotus placed in the sun.
Thereafter follow the verses of the dialogue between the donor and her.
“What will you do with the prince in the forest, when he is afflicted?
Sambulā, by serving him, I shall become your husband.
What beauty remains for me, who am overcome by grief and ill-favored?”
“Seek another, O Blessed One, one more beautiful than I.
“Come, climb this mountain; I have four hundred wives.
You shall be the most excellent among them, possessing all desired things.”
“O you with the radiance of a star, whatever you desire in your mind, all that is abundant for me; enjoy yourself today together with me.
If you will not, O Sambulā, grant me the status of chief queen, [then I shall depart].”
"Enough for your breakfast! You shall become food for my questions.
Then the fierce man-eater, Sattajaṭa, Kaḷāra, seized Sambulā by the arm in the forest while she was not seeing her protector.
“Overpowered by a fierce piśāca with eyes greedy for flesh,
she has fallen under the control of her enemy, yet she grieves only for her husband.
This is not such a source of suffering for me as it would be if a rākṣasa were to devour me.”
"And as for my noble son, his mind will surely change.
Surely there are no gods who travel abroad; surely there are no guardians of the world here;
surely there are no ones to restrain those who act impulsively and without restraint."
In this context, "by one who has been served" means: what will you do with that sick person who has been served?

"To one afflicted by grief" means to one distressed by sorrow. There is also a reading, "sokaṭṭhāyā," which means "standing in grief. "To one poorly clad" means to a physical form that has fallen into a state of wretchedness and poverty.
"Come here"—do not think, "I am poorly clad"; this celestial mansion of mine is upon the mountain.
"Come, climb this mountain. In that celestial mansion of mine, there are another four hundred wives.
Whatever you desire—whether articles of enjoyment, necessities, clothing, or ornaments—all of that is indeed abundant, plentiful, and easily obtained for me;
therefore, do not think yourself miserable. Come, enjoy yourself with me," she says.
“Great Queen,” he said, “Bhaddā Sambulā, if you do not allow me to exercise my power as a great lord, you have already served your purpose for my breakfast;
therefore, I shall take you by force to my celestial mansion.
There, failing to win me over, you will become my prey at dawn tomorrow. Having spoken thus, that hunter, who was endowed with seven matted locks, [seized her].
The fierce one, whose tusks were protruding, seized Saṃbula by the arm as she wandered through that forest, unable to see any protector for herself.
*Adhipannā* means overwhelmed. *Āmisacakkhunā* means with an eye greedy for sensual objects due to defilements.
*Patimeva* means she grieved only for her husband, without thinking of herself. *Mano hessati* means that having perceived her delaying, his mind would become otherwise.
"There will be none. "There are no gods"—this she said while clutching her husband’s arm with her hand, seeking to provoke the deities.
"World-protectors"—she laments thus: "Surely there are no world-protectors here in this world who protect such virtuous women who regard their husbands as deities."
Then, by the power of her virtue, Sakka’s palace shook and his Pāṇḍukambala stone throne appeared hot to the touch.
Sakka, reflecting and understanding the cause, took his thunderbolt and went with speed;
standing over the head of the Dānava, he spoke this other verse:
“Among women, she is the most excellent and renowned, peaceful and even-tempered like a fire with rising flames.
If you devour this maiden, your head shall surely split into seven pieces;
do not burn her, release her who is devoted to her husband.”
In this context, *santā* means "calmed," or alternatively, "wise ones endowed with knowledge. *Samā* means "free from physical irregularities and the like.
*Adesi* means "you eat. *Phaleyya* means "may your head split open after being struck by this thunderbolt of Indra.
*Mā tvaṃ dahī* means "do not burn this chaff."

Having heard this, the Dānava released Saṃbulā. Sakka, thinking, "He might do such a thing again," bound the Dānava with a divine chain and released him into a third mountain cleft so that he would not return, after which he advised the princess with diligence and returned to his own abode. When the sun had set, the princess also—
She reached the hermitage by the light of the moon. To clarify this matter, the Teacher spoke these eight verses:
“She came to the hermitage, released from the man-eater, like a bird to its nest, or like one who has gone to its hornless lair.”
There the illustrious princess Sambulā, her voice choked with emotion,
lamented in the forest, not seeing her protector:
“I pay homage to the ascetics and brahmins, to those sages perfected in conduct.”
Not seeing the prince, I have come to you for refuge.
I pay homage to the lions and the tigers, and to whatever other wild beasts there are in the forest;
not seeing the prince, I have come to you for refuge.
“Grasses, creepers, shrubs, mountains, and forests— seeing no prince, we have come to you for refuge.
I pay homage to you, who are as dark as a blue lotus, garlanded with the stars at night.”
Not seeing the prince, I have come to you for refuge.
I pay homage to Bhāgīrathī Gaṅgā, the recipient of all flowing rivers;
not seeing the prince, I have come to you for refuge.
“I pay homage to Himavat, the best of mountain kings, the mass of rocks;
not seeing the prince, I have come to you for refuge.
In that context, regarding the phrase “like a bird to its nest”: just as a female bird, having taken food with her beak, [is protected] by someone...

The meaning is that she came to the empty hermitage, just as a female bird might come to a nest smeared with droppings because its young have been carried off by some calamity, or as a cow, greedy for her calf, might come to an empty calf-pen and a dwelling where the horns have vanished and the calves have departed.
For at that time, Sotthisena, thinking that Sambulā had been long away, [said]: "Women..."
Thinking, "She is fickle; she might even come back taking my enemy with her," he, full of suspicion, emerged from the leaf-hut and sat down, entering the space between the trees.
This is what is meant by that. "With eyes dimmed by the heat" means with eyes dulled by the heat produced by the force of her grief.
"Not seeing" means not seeing her lord, her husband, in that forest, [looking] here and there.
And running about, she lamented.
Therein, "to the recluses and brahmins" means to those recluses and brahmins who have stilled evil and cast out evil.
"To those perfected in conduct" means to these men who are perfected in conduct through both virtue and the eight meditative attainments. Having spoken thus, [she addressed] the prince.
"Seeing no other refuge, I have come to you for protection. If you know the place where my husband sits, please tell me," she lamented;
this is the meaning. The same method applies to the remaining verses as well. Regarding the verse, "The grasses, creepers, and herbs": "grasses" refers to those with internal pith and external bark;
"creepers" refers to climbing plants; and "herbs" refers to those with internal pith. This verse was spoken by a deity reborn among the grasses and so forth.
"Indīvarīsāmanti" means having a color like that of the *indīvarī* flower. "Nakkhattamālinin" means endowed with the sequence of the constellations.
"Tumhaṃmhī" (we are yours) was said referring to the night; he also said "tampi amhī" (we are also yours).
"Bhāgīrathiṃ Gaṅgan" refers to the Ganges river, which has such alternative names. "Savantīnan" means the recipient of many other rivers. [He addressed] the deity born from the Ganges.
He spoke thus with this underlying intention. The same principle applies even in the Himālayas.
Seeing her lamenting in this way, Sotthisena thought: "She is lamenting excessively; yet I do not know her true disposition.
If she acts thus out of affection for me, her very heart might break. I shall take hold of her."
Saying, "I will not go that far," he went and sat down at the door of the leaf-hut.
She too, while still lamenting, went to the door of the leaf-hut, prostrated at his feet, and asked, "Where have you gone, my lord?
Then, questioning her, he spoke this verse: "Bhadde, on other days you do not come at this hour; today you have arrived very late."
“O illustrious princess, you have indeed gone too far!
With whom have you now met? Who is dearer to you than I?
Then she said to him, “Noble son, as I was coming along carrying various fruits, I saw a certain *dānava*.”
“Having his mind fixed on me, he took me by the hand and said, ‘If you do not do as I say, I shall eat you.
At that moment, grieving for him alone, I lamented thus,” and she spoke this verse: “At that time, having been seized by that enemy, I said this:”
"This suffering of mine is not as great as the pain that would come if a *rakkhasa* were to devour me;
rather, it is the thought that my noble husband’s mind might turn away from me.
Then, reporting the rest of the events to him, she said: "But then, O King, I was seized by that *dānava* and had to surrender myself."
“Being unable to do so, I committed the act of inciting the gods to anger. Then Sakka, with the thunderbolt in hand, arrived and stood in the sky;
having intimidated the Dānava and caused him to release me, he bound him with a divine chain, cast him into the third mountain range, and departed.
Thus, by relying on Sakka, I obtained my life,” she said. Having heard this, Sotthisena—
“Lady, enough! Truth is indeed rare among women. For in the Himalayas there are many forest-dwelling ascetics, masters of spells, and others;
who would believe you? Having said this, he spoke this verse:
“Among thieves of many wiles, in whom truth is very hard to find;”
“The state of sloth is difficult to perceive, like a fish gone into the water.

Having heard his words, she said, “Noble son, I shall heal you who do not believe me by the very power of my truth,” and having filled a water-jar and performed an act of truth, she spoke this verse while pouring the water over his head:
“May that Truth protect me, if it shall indeed protect me!”
“As surely as I do not know anyone dearer to me than you, by this utterance of truth may your illness be pacified.
In this context, the word *tathā* (as) should be construed with the phrase “*ce mama*” (if for me). This is what is meant: as surely as I...
"I say this: if my word is true, then may it protect me now and it shall protect me in the future;
listen now to my words: 'As I do not know [otherwise]'. However, in the manuscripts it is written as "tathā maṃ saccaṃ pāletī" (thus truth protects me), but that is not found in the Aṭṭhakathā.
Thus, as soon as she had performed this act of truth and merely sprinkled water [upon him], Sotthisena’s leprosy vanished instantly, like copper-dross washed away by acid.
Having stayed there for a few days, they departed from the forest and, upon reaching Bārāṇasī, entered the royal garden.
When the king learned of their arrival, he went to the garden and right there—
Having raised the royal parasol over Sotthisena and had Sambulā consecrated in the position of chief queen, he escorted them into the city;
he himself, however, went forth into the ascetic life of an *isi* and took up residence in a park, eating his meals regularly at the king’s palace.
Sotthisena, for his part, granted Sambulā nothing more than the mere status of chief queen, but gave her no further [privileges].
There was some hospitality, yet he did not even notice her presence; he took his pleasure with other women.
Due to the malice of her rival, Sambulā became emaciated, turning pale and wan, with her limbs covered in a network of veins.
One day, she went to her husband, the ascetic, who had come to eat in order to dispel his sorrow, once he had finished his meal.
Having paid homage, she sat down to one side. Seeing her with her faculties withered, he spoke this verse:
“Those seven hundred noble elephants, equipped with weapons, protect [the city] day and night;
and sixteen hundred archers—how is it, Bhaddā, that you see such beings?”

The meaning of this is: "Bhadde, Sambule, our seven hundred elephants, with warriors mounted upon their backs and weapons ready for action, along with another sixteen hundred archers, protect Bārāṇasī day and night.
In such a well-guarded city, how could you see any enemies? Bhadde, for whom..."
“Even when you returned from the forest full of suspicion and fear, your body was endowed with radiance;
but now it is withered, the color of a faded leaf, and your faculties are exceedingly exhausted. Of whom are you afraid? she asked.
Hearing his words, she said, “Your son, O King, is not like he was before,” and spoke these five verses:
“Adorned with lotus-fiber garments, they move with the grace of swans;
hearing their measured songs and instrumental music, O Father, I am no longer as I was before.
Clad in golden robes, well-proportioned, adorned, and possessing the beauty of celestial nymphs.”
“O Father, blameless-limbed women of the warrior caste seek to win over Senāpi.
‘If I, Father, were to support my husband again in the forest as I did before by gathering wild fruits,
and if he would honor me and not treat me with contempt, then, Father, this would be better for me than even that.’”
“When abundant food and drink have been set out, and a woman is adorned with polished ornaments and well-decorated,
yet is unloved by her husband— death for her is better than that.
Even if she is poor, wretched, and destitute, with but a mat for her companion, yet is beloved by her husband;”
"Even for one endowed with every excellence, if she is unloved, this very state is better—even if she is poor—than one who is beloved.
In that context, "with skin like the interior of a lotus" means having skin as beautiful as the inside of a lotus; it indicates that a golden radiance issues forth from the entire body.
"Virāgitā" means with a slender body; the sense is "one with a thin waist. "Haṃsagaggarā" means...
He sees women with voices as sweet as such swans. Your son is terrified by those women;
having heard their measured songs, instrumental music, and so forth, he says, "Now, father, it does not proceed for me as it did before.
"Wearing golden *saṃkacca* ornaments" means wearing ornaments made of gold in the form of *saṃkacca*. "Adorned" means decorated with various kinds of ornaments.
"Like human nymphs" means like women who resemble celestial nymphs (*accharā*). "Dear to Sena" means dear to Soṇṇasena.
"They entice" means they lead away; they entice this son of yours.
"If it were so, dear father," means if it were as it was before—that if I were again to go to that husband of mine in the forest with leprosy just as previously.
"Having entered that forest for alms, I would carry [the food] back; he would again honor me and not despise me.
Therefore, even compared to this kingdom of Bārāṇasī, that very forest would be better for me, as it withers from the fault of enemies"—this is what he indicates.
"Whatever food and drink" means whatever food and drink. "Set aside" means placed and prepared. By this, he shows a house abundant in food and drink.

This, it is said, is her intention: "That woman who, though living alone in a house with abundant food and drink, being without a rival wife, adorned with polished ornaments and various decorations, and endowed with all virtuous qualities, is nonetheless unloved by her husband—for her, rather than being bound by a noose, a neck-cord, or a rope, death from that household life is better. [The word] *anāḷhīya* means...
"Without desire. "With a mat as her companion" means having a mat for lying down as her second. "A wife" means that even though she is poor, she is dear to her husband; she alone is supreme.
When she had thus told the ascetic the reason for her own withering away, the ascetic summoned the king.
“Dear Sotthisena, when you were overcome by leprosy and entered the forest, she entered with you and attended upon you;
by the power of her own truth, she quelled your disease and acted as the cause for your restoration to the kingdom.
Yet you do not even know her standing place or her sitting place—this which you have done is unseemly, an act of treachery against a friend.”
Having said, "This is indeed evil," he spoke this verse while exhorting his son:
"Very difficult for a man to find is a wife who is beneficial; even more difficult for a wife to find is a husband who is beneficial.
Since your wife is both beneficial and virtuous, O Lord of Men, practice the Dhamma for the sake of Sambulā."

The meaning of this is: "Dear son, a woman who is beneficial to a man, gentle-minded, and compassionate, and a husband who is beneficial to a woman and recognizes her performed service—both of these are very difficult to find.
This Sambulā is both beneficial to you and endowed with virtue;
therefore, practice the Dhamma toward her. Recognizing her performed service, be gentle-minded and gladden her heart."
Having thus given this exhortation to his son, he rose from his seat and departed.
When the father had gone, the king summoned Sambulā and said, "Bhadde, forgive me for the offense I have committed during all this time; from now on, I give you full sovereignty.
Having spoken thus, he recited the concluding verse:
“But if you, O Bhaddā, having obtained vast wealth, should meet death while overcome by envy, then I and these princesses of yours—all of us shall be obedient to your word.
The meaning of this is: Bhaddā, Sambulā, if you, having been established upon a heap of jewels and consecrated as the chief queen in that position...
Even after obtaining vast wealth, she fell into the grip of envy and met her death. [The king said: "I and these princesses shall all carry out your word;
you may govern this kingdom according to your own intention. Thus he granted her full sovereignty.

From then on, the two of them lived in harmony, performed meritorious deeds such as giving alms, and departed according to their respective karma. The ascetic, having developed the meditative absorptions (*jhāna*) and direct knowledges (*abhiññā*), was reborn in the Brahma-world.
Having delivered this Dhamma teaching, the Teacher said, "Monks, it is not only now; in the past as well, Mallikā was devoted solely to her husband," and he identified the Jātaka:
"At that time, Sambulā was Mallikā, Sotthisena was the King of Kosala, and the ascetic father was none other than myself."
The ninth is the commentary on the Sambulā Jātaka.
[520] 10. The commentary on the Gandhatinduka Jātaka:
"Heedfulness"—this was spoken by the Teacher while dwelling in Jetavana, concerning the exhortation to kings (*rājovāda*). The exhortation to kings has been explained below.

This has been explained in detail. In the past, however, in the city of Uttarapañcāla in the kingdom of Kapila, there was a king named Pañcāla who, established in wrong courses, ruled his kingdom unrighteously and negligently. Consequently, all his ministers and others likewise became unrighteous.
Oppressed by taxes, the inhabitants of the realm took their wives and children and wandered in the forest like deer; in the place of a village, there was no village.
There was no peace. Because of the fear of the king’s men, people were unable to stay in their houses during the day;

they would surround their homes with thorny branches, stay inside at night, and enter the forest just as the dawn was breaking. During the day the king’s men plundered them, and at night the thieves did so.
At that time, the Bodhisatta had become a deity dwelling in a *gandhatinduka* tree outside the city.
He was reborn and received an annual offering worth a thousand pieces from the king. He thought:
"This king governs with negligence; the entire kingdom will perish.
Apart from me, there is no one else capable of establishing the king in the proper way, and he is also my benefactor, providing me annually with an offering worth a thousand pieces."
"I shall worship him; I shall instruct him.
Then, during the night, he entered the King's bedchamber, stood at the head of the bed, emitted a radiance, and remained suspended in the air.
Seeing him blazing like the morning sun, the King asked, "Who are you, and for what reason [have you come]?"
“Have you come here? he asked. Hearing his words, he replied, “Great King, I am the deity of the Gandhatinduka tree;
I have come to give you counsel. When [the king] asked, “What kind of counsel will you give?
the Great Being said, “Great King, you have ruled the kingdom while being heedless; because of that, your entire realm has been plundered and destroyed.”

It is as if it has been destroyed; for kings who rule their kingdom through negligence do not remain masters of the entire realm, but having met with ruin in this very life, they are reborn again in the Great Hell in the future world.
When they fall into negligence, both their householders and outsiders likewise become negligent; therefore, the king must be especially heedful.
Having said, "It must be so," he began the teaching of the Dhamma by reciting these eleven verses:
"Heedfulness is the path to the Deathless; heedlessness is the path of death.
Those who are heedful do not die; those who are heedless are as if already dead."
“From intoxication comes negligence; from negligence comes ruin;
from ruin come corruptions. O bull among the Bharatas, do not be intoxicated!
For many Kshatriyas have perished, having ruined their wealth and their kingdom through negligence.”
Furthermore, those who go from village to village— whether householders or homeless ones—
all their possessions perish when a kshatriya is negligent in his kingdom; that, it is said, is the calamity for the king.
“This is not the way, O Great King, that you are excessively negligent;
thieves will destroy this prosperous and flourishing realm.
You shall have no sons, nor gold, nor grain.”
While the kingdom is being plundered, you live on all its enjoyments.
When all enjoyments have wasted away for a king or a kṣatriya,
his kinsmen, friends, and well-wishers no longer regard him as one who possesses honor.
“Elephant-riders, chariot-warriors, cavalrymen, and foot-soldiers—
though they live off him in this way, they do not consider him to be arrogant.
Yet the fool, whose actions are unprepared, who is ill-advised and lacks counsel,”
Fortune abandons the foolish man, just as a snake sheds its worn-out skin.
All riches increase for one who is well-ordered in his work, who rises early,
and is untiring— just as cattle thrive when led by a strong bull.
“Wander, O Great King, through the kingdom and the countryside as a listener;
having seen and heard there, you may then act accordingly.
In this context, “heedfulness” (appamāda) means not being separated from mindfulness. “The state of the Deathless” (amatapada) means the state of the Deathless—Nirvana—the cause for its attainment.

"Death's domain" means the cause of death. For those who are negligent—failing to develop insight and thus unable to reach the state of being without rebirth—are born and die again and again in *saṃsāra*; therefore, negligence is called "death's domain.
"They do not die" means that having developed insight and reached the state of being without rebirth, they no longer [enter] *saṃsāra*.
Because they are not reborn, they are said to "not die. O Great King, those persons who are heedless should be regarded as being exactly like the dead.

Why? Because of their failure to accomplish what ought to be done. For even in the case of one who is dead, there is no longer any mental application such as, "I shall give alms, I shall guard my virtue, I shall perform the Uposatha rites, or I shall fulfill wholesome deeds."
Because consciousness has departed, there is neither aspiration nor obsession; and for one who is heedless, there is an absence of diligence.
Therefore, these two are exactly the same.
Great King, three kinds of intoxication—namely, those consisting of health, youth, and life—are what is called heedlessness.
Thus, intoxicated with pride and fallen into negligence, he commits evil deeds such as the taking of life. Then kings have him executed or put to death, or they seize all his wealth;
in this way, through negligence, the destruction of his kin, wealth, and life occurs.
Furthermore, having reached the loss of wealth or the loss of fame, and being unable to survive, for the sake of maintaining his livelihood—
One performs misconduct of body and so forth; thus, through that, the stains of passion arise within him. Therefore, I say to you: "O Bharata Bull, do not be intoxicated! The meaning is:

"O Bharata Bull, the foremost bearer of the burden of the kingdom, do not fall into negligence. "The kingdom's welfare" (*raṭṭhaṃ atthaṃ*) refers both to the prosperity of the inhabitants of the realm and to the entire kingdom itself.

Many who are negligent have brought ruin upon these two. For the purpose of making this manifest, there are the *Khantivādi-jātaka*, *Mātaṅga-jātaka*, *Bharu-jātaka*, *Sarabhaṅga-jātaka*, and *Cetiya-jātaka*.
They should be spoken of thus: "Those who go" refers to both the village headmen and the villages themselves; many have been worn away, lost, and ruined through the fault of negligence.
"The homeless and those with homes" refers to both those who have gone forth and their practice as renunciants, and householders and their domestic life, including wealth, grain, and so forth;
he says that many of these have been worn away and lost. "That, O Great King, is called 'misfortune' (agha)," namely, the loss of fame and prosperity.
This is called the suffering of a king. For through the absence of wealth, the fame of one who is destitute declines;
and with diminished fame, he encounters great physical and mental suffering.
"This is not the Dhamma," O Great King—this is not the Dhamma of the ancient kings. "Prosperous and flourishing" means [abounding] in food, drink, and so forth.
"Prosperous" means flourishing and blooming with gold, bullion, and other riches. "They will not be your sons," O Great King, means that they will not be sons who protect the lineage.
For the inhabitants of the realm will say, "This is the son of an unrighteous king; what growth will he bring us?
We shall not grant him the royal parasol. Thus, in this way, they are not sons who protect the lineage.
“They are indeed no more. *Parijiṇṇa* means decayed or fallen away. “Even though he is a king”: even if he is a king, they do not honor him as such, despite his being a king;
that is, they do not treat him with the respect due to one who should be honored with a heavy heart, thinking, “This is a king.

“Even those who depend on him for their livelihood”: although these people live in reliance upon him, they do not honor him with a heavy heart, even to the extent that they might be expected to do so.
For what reason? Because of his unrighteousness.
"Fortune" (*sirī*) means glory and wealth. "Sheds" (*tacati*): just as a snake, loathing its worn-out skin, casts it off and does not look back at it again, even so does fortune abandon such a king.
"Well-ordered undertakings" refers to evil deeds through the doors of the body and so forth.
"Not doing. "Increasing" means they increase as they move forward. "Like a herd of bulls" means like a herd of bulls with a bull-leader (*sausabha*);
for the wealth of one who is heedful increases like a herd of cattle with a bull-leader as its chief. "Eavesdropping":

wander on tour throughout your own entire kingdom and countryside in order to hear about the conduct of the people. "Therein": while wandering in that kingdom, what is to be seen [should be observed].
"Having seen this, and having heard what ought to be heard, you shall make your own virtues and faults manifest before your eyes, and from that, you will practice for your own welfare.
Thus the Great Being, having exhorted the king with these eleven verses, said, "Go, do not delay;
take charge of the kingdom and do not let it perish," and he departed for his own abode. The king, too, having heard his words, was moved by a sense of spiritual urgency (*saṃvega*).
On the following day, having entrusted the kingdom to his ministers, he departed from the city through the eastern gate at an early hour together with his domestic priest.
Having traveled for the distance of a *yojana*, there was an elderly village dweller who, having brought a thorny branch from the forest, encircled and closed the door of his house;
then, taking his wife and children, he entered the wilderness. At evening...
When the king’s men had departed, as he was returning to his own home, he was pierced in the foot by a thorn at the door of his house.
Sitting down on his haunches and extracting the thorn, he said:
“May Pañcāla feel thus, when he is immersed in the arrow of battle!”
With this verse—"As I feel today, pierced by a thorn"—he reviled the king. However, that reviling occurred through the power of the Bodhisattva;
it should be understood that he reviled him only because he was possessed by the Bodhisattva. At that time, both the king and the chaplain were in disguise.
They stood right there in his presence. Then, having heard his words, the chaplain spoke this other verse:
“You are old and your sight is weak; you do not see forms clearly.
What is there for Brahmadatta that a thorn would seek out on the road?”
In this context, *maggeyya* means "one would pierce. This is what is meant:

"If you were pierced by a thorn due to your own lack of skill, what fault is there on the part of the king? Since you reviled the king, why should the thorn have been pointed out to you by the king only after he had looked at it?
Having heard this, the elder recited three verses:
“There is much here concerning Brahmadatta, O brahmin; I am on the road.
The people of the countryside are unprotected, struck down by the power of unrighteousness.
For at night the thieves devour them, and by day the tax-collectors devour them.”
“In this kingdom, under a treacherous king, the people are largely unrighteous.
When such a danger has arisen, dear son,
young men who are afraid of fear make shelters for themselves by gathering thorns in the forest.”
"In this regard, Brahmin, 'there is much here' means: I am sitting here fallen upon a path full of thorns.
There is much fault here on the part of Brahmadatta; for all this time you have not known that I was wandering on a path full of thorns because of the king's fault.
For his subjects are unprotected... [as before] ...a thorn. In this context, "they eat" means they plunder.
*Tuṇḍiya* refers to those who, having oppressed people through execution, imprisonment, and so forth, achieve their ends by unrighteous means. *Kūṭarājassa* means of an evil king.
*Adhammiko* means one whose actions are concealed. *Tāta* is how he addresses the chaplain. *Māṇavā* refers to men. *Nillenakāni* means places for hiding.
Having brought thorns from the forest—having brought thorns and closed the doors—he [entered] the house.
"Having abandoned their wives and children, they took up residence in the forest and made for themselves places of concealment within that wood;
or else, having brought thorns from the forest, they surrounded their dwellings with them.
Thus, I have been pierced by this very thorn because of the king’s fault; do not become a supporter of such a king."
Having heard this, the king addressed his chaplain, saying, “Teacher, the old man speaks rightly;
the fault is ours alone. Come, let us turn back; we shall rule the kingdom according to the Dhamma.
The Bodhisatta, having fixed his mind upon the chaplain’s body, went on ahead and said, “Let us first take possession [of the territory], Great King. From that village...
While traveling toward another village, they heard the voice of an old woman along the way.
It seems she was a poor woman who, out of concern for her two grown daughters, would not allow them to go into the forest.
She herself would fetch firewood and vegetables from the forest to look after her daughters. On that day, having climbed a thicket, she [was gathering] vegetables...
Seizing him as he was fleeing, she fell to the ground and, reviling the king with the prospect of death,
spoke this verse: “When indeed will this King Brahmadatta die,
In whose kingdom young maidens are violated without resistance?”
In that context, "without husbands" means she had no owners. For if she had had husbands, they would have supported her. But since this is the kingdom of a wicked king, I am experiencing suffering;
when indeed will he die? Thus she reviled him solely through the power of the Bodhisatta. Then the chaplain, seeking to restrain her, spoke this verse:
"O base woman, you have spoken ill, you who are skilled in words of harm!"
“Where is the king seeking a husband for his daughters?
Having heard this, the elder woman spoke two verses:
“O Brahmā, I have not spoken ill; I am skilled in the meaning of words.”
The people of the countryside are unprotected, struck down by the power of unrighteousness.
For at night the thieves devour them, and by day the tax-collectors devour them;
in the kingdom of a fraudulent king, the people are largely unrighteous.
"In a kingdom difficult to live in, with wives difficult to maintain, where could there be food for young daughters?
Regarding that, "skilled in the meaning of words" means: I am skilled and expert in the meaning of words—that is, in the words concerning the reasons—so do not praise this wicked king.
"Difficult to live in" means in a kingdom difficult to live in; "with wives difficult to maintain" refers to when people among whom [the king] has arisen are terrified and trembling in the forest.
"In the spring months, from where will the young women obtain husbands? From where will the young women find a husband?"—this was the meaning [of her words].
Having heard her speech, they thought, "She speaks rightly," and as they proceeded further, they heard the sound of a certain farmer.
It is said that while he was plowing, his ox named Sāliya lay down after being struck by the plowshare.
Thus, reviling the king, he spoke this verse:
“May Pañcāla lie thus, struck by a spear in battle,
just as this wretched man lies here, struck down by a ploughshare while harvesting rice.”
In that context, "yathā" means: "just as this ox, having reached the state of feeling [the consequences], lies down, so let him lie"—this is the meaning.
Then the chaplain, seeking to dissuade him, spoke this verse:
"But you, O wretch, are acting unrighteously by being angry with Brahmadatta."
“You who swear falsely against the king, having committed no offense yourself.
Having heard that, he spoke three verses: “In this matter, ‘unrighteously’ means without cause, without truth. Having heard that, he spoke three verses:
“O Brahmin, it is because of his righteousness that I am angry with Brahmadatta;
the people of the countryside are unprotected and destroyed by his unrighteous taxes.
For at night the thieves devour them, and by day the tax-collectors devour them.”
“In this kingdom of the treacherous king, the people are largely unrighteous.
Surely she has been cooked again, for she brought food at the wrong time;
while he looked toward her who was bringing the meal, the rice was destroyed by the plow.”
In this context, "by means of the Dhamma" means by reason alone; do not entertain the notion that one reviles without cause.

"Surely she has become ripe again, for she brought food at the wrong time"—O Brahmin, that woman who brings my meal must have been obstructed in the early morning while cooking my food by the slaves of Brahmadatta, who perform sacrifices contrary to the Dhamma.
"After they have finished eating, my meal will be cooked again; for that reason, he brought the meal at an improper time.
Thinking, "Today he has brought the meal at an improper time," I, with a mind consumed by hunger, watched for the one who was carrying the meal and struck the ox with a goad in the wrong place.
Because of that, he raised his foot and struck him with a plowshare, and thus he was killed by the plowshare.
“Rice! Therefore, do not form the perception that ‘this one has been killed by me’; this is merely a wicked wild beast that has been killed.

Do not speak in praise of it. They went on ahead and stayed in a certain village. On the following day at dawn, a rogue cow struck a milkman with her hoof and overturned him along with his milk. He, reviling Brahmadatta, spoke this verse:
“May Pañcāla be slain in such a way—slain by a sword in battle!”
"Just as I have been struck today, my milk has flowed forth.
Hearing this, the chaplain spoke this verse in protest:
"The milk that a beast ejects causes harm to its keeper."
"What is it about Brahmadatta that you, sir, reproach us for?
When the brahmin had spoken this verse, he (the king) spoke three further verses:
"Brahmā, Pañcāla is to be reproached by King Brahmadatta."
The people of the countryside are unprotected and struck down by the power of unrighteousness.
For at night the thieves devour them, and by day the tax-collectors devour them;
in the kingdom of a fraudulent king, the people are largely unrighteous.
“The fierce, wandering cow, whom we did not milk before—now today we shall milk her, being distressed by our desire for milk.
In this context, *caṇḍā* means harsh; *aṭanakā* means having the habit of wandering away; and *khīrakāmehi* refers to the men of the unrighteous king.
“Afflicted by those who force us to provide much milk, we are milking [the cows]. For if he were to rule the kingdom according to the Dhamma, such fear would not come upon us.
Thinking, “He speaks rightly,” they departed from that village, ascended the main road, and set out toward the city.
In a certain village, some sorcerers killed a young brindled calf for the purpose of performing a sacrifice and took its hide.
The mother cow, out of grief for her son, would neither eat grass nor drink water;
she wandered about lamenting. Seeing this, the village boys reviled the king and spoke this verse:
“Let Pañcāla cry out thus, let him wail and lament,
just as this wretched cow, deprived of her calf,
runs about. In this context, “runs about” means he runs while wailing.
Then the chaplain spoke this other verse:
“If cattle were to bolt or bellow against the herdsman,
what fault is there here for King Brahmadatta?”
"In that regard, 'it might run away or cry out' means it might either run off or bellow. This is what is meant:
'Dear ones, a beast, while being guarded by its herdsman, runs away and bellows; it does not even eat grass nor drink water.
What fault, then, is there here on the part of the king?'"
Then the village boys recited two verses:
“Great Brahmā, this was the transgression of King Brahmadatta:
The country folk were left unprotected and were struck down by unrighteous taxes.”
“By night the thieves devour, by day the tax-collectors devour;
in the realm of a king who acts with deceit, the people are largely unrighteous.
How is it that this milk-drinking folk, though we have neither sword nor staff, is being slaughtered?”
In this context, "Mahābrahmā" means the Great Brāhmaṇa. "Rājinā" means by the king. "Kathañ nu" means how indeed, or for what reason.
"Khīrapā haññate pajā" means that a suckling calf is being killed by the servants of the wicked king;
now that cow laments out of grief for her son, they reviled the king, saying, "May this king lament just like this cow."
Having said, "Speak your reasons well," they departed. Then, on the way, at a certain dried-up lotus pond, crows were pecking at frogs with their beaks and eating them.
When those [crows] arrived at that place, the Bodhisatta, by his own supernatural power, [caused] a frog—
“Let Pañcāla be devoured thus, slain in battle along with his son,
just as I am being devoured today by these villagers, though I was born in the forest!”—
thus he caused the king to be reviled.
In this context, "by the villagers" means by those living in the village.
Having heard that, the chaplain, conversing with the frog, spoke this verse:
"O frog, in the world of men, kings do not provide protection for all beings."
"To this extent a king is not unrighteous: that vultures should eat such a living being. Here, "jīvaṃ" means a living being.
"Adeyyuṃ" means they would eat. "Dhaṅkā" means crows. To this extent a king is not called unrighteous; for what can be done by a king who enters the forest and lives protecting it?
Having heard this, the frog spoke two verses:
“Indeed, this practitioner of the holy life has an unrighteous form; you speak what is pleasing to the kshatriya.
While the multitude of people is being destroyed, you honor the king who is utterly heedless.
If, O Brahmā, this kingdom were truly well-governed—prosperous, joyful, and serene—”
"Having received an offering and the first portion of alms, the crows would not give life to one such as me, even if they were vultures.
In this context, he spoke thus while censuring the chaplain. "Of a khattiya" means of such an evil king. "While being plundered" means while being looted;
or rather, "viluppamānāya" is the very reading used here. "While the multitude of people is being destroyed" means while the vast population is perishing.

"Pūjesi" means he praised. "Surajjakaṃ": if this were a well-governed kingdom—protected by a king who is heedful and who does not deviate from the ten royal duties due to lust and other such passions—it would be so. "Phītaṃ": when the gods pour down rain in due season, it is rich in crops.
"Na mādisaṃ": this being the case, even while I am still alive, the crows would not devour one such as me.
Thus, in all six instances, the abuse occurred solely through the power of the Bodhisattva.
Hearing this, the king and the chaplain said, "Starting from a forest-dwelling animal, a frog, everyone is abusing us alone.
Having spoken thus, they returned to the city and, ruling the kingdom with righteousness, followed the advice of the Mahāsatta.
Remaining steadfast, they performed meritorious deeds such as giving.
Having delivered this Dhamma teaching to the King of Kosala, the Teacher said, "Great King,
a king must abandon the path of evil and rule his kingdom according to the Dhamma," and then he identified the Jātaka, saying, "At that time, I myself was the Gandhatinduka deity."
The Tenth: The Commentary on the Gandhatinduka Jātaka. The Summary of the Jātakas (Jātakuddāna):
Kiṃchanda, Kumbha, Jayaddisa, Chaddanta, Then Paṇḍitasambhava, and Sirikapi.
Dakarakkhasa, Paṇḍaranāgavara, and then Sambula, Tinduka, and Devasuta.
The commentary on the Tiṃsanipāta is finished.
